Russia ‘open to working with the whole world’ – Putin
Russia is open to cooperation and doing business with “the whole world,” President Vladimir Putin has said. This includes both Western economic powers – despite what he described as their “ugly forms of competition” – and the growing economies of the Global South and East. 
“We are ready to cooperate with all our partners,” Putin told the BRICS Business Forum panel at the 18th BRICS summit in India, adding that they could be “old or new.”
Putin said that the shared goal is to unlock the development potential of Russia and its partners through “business diplomacy,” making it easier for companies and entrepreneurs to cooperate.
“We do not want to impose any restrictions on ourselves or turn inward – whether at the national, corporate, or even the broader level of our partnership,” he stated. “We are not building our cooperation against anyone. We stand for ourselves and our interests.”
Russia is seeking to expand practical business cooperation with its partners in industry, trade, and tourism, Putin said, noting that Moscow has established a national business cooperation committee bringing together more than 40 of the country’s largest companies.
He also highlighted plans to develop major logistics routes, such as the Trans-Arctic and North-South transport corridors, and proposed creating a new investment platform based on the BRICS New Development Bank to attract private capital and boost competitiveness.
“Together with our partners, we stand ready to contribute to global energy and food security,” Putin said.
Putin noted that the world is undergoing “deep structural shifts,” with traditional economic powers being displaced by new engines of growth – a natural process that he insisted “cannot be stopped.” He argued, however, that Western economies facing growing competition increasingly resort to unsavory methods.
“Sometimes competition takes ugly forms,” he said, citing the destruction of pipelines, attempts to block international transport routes, unilateral “illegal restrictions,” and secondary sanctions against countries “unwilling to follow others’ interests.”
Russia has faced more than 30,000 sanctions since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict – twice as many as all other countries combined, Putin said. Moscow nevertheless weathered the unprecedented pressure by relying on domestic business, science, and engineering while redirecting trade toward “reliable partners,” he stated. Russia’s economy has become more resilient, with growth outpacing the global average over the past three years, he added.
The president noted that against expectations the sanctions had instead hurt those imposing them, pointing to rising budget deficits, public debt, and industrial decline. Leading eurozone economies have seen industrial output fall by around 8% in recent years, he claimed.
Speaking of BRICS, Putin described the group as an increasingly powerful force in the global economy.
“Through our combined efforts, BRICS is building a resilient and viable platform for global growth,” he said. “This is not being imposed on us from the outside by the so-called ‘golden billion’, nor are we trying to impose anything on anyone else.”
Putin noted that BRICS countries generated more than 40% of global GDP over the past five years, compared with 29% for the G7, while contributing more than half of global economic growth against just 18% for the G7. He attributed the momentum to the grouping’s vast population, dynamic domestic markets, and rapidly expanding national companies with global ambitions.
The 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi runs through Sunday, bringing together leaders of the expanded grouping to discuss economic cooperation, energy and food security, global governance, and geopolitical challenges. Putin, who arrived in India on Friday, has already held talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of the gathering. He is also expected to hold talks with other leaders attending the gathering.

Giant armored crustaceans survive thanks to a gene stolen from bacteria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:41:14 UTC
22:41:14 KST

When scientists refer to the deep sea as Earth’s most alien environment, they’re not exaggerating. Among the cast of bizarre characters are enormous armor-covered crustaceans with large triangular compound eyes and long antennae. Researchers have long wondered how these strange creatures pull off one extreme feat: surviving more than five years without food.
It turns out that millions of years ago these deep-sea isopods most likely co-opted a gene from bacteria that—paired with a large stomach—lets them gorge on rare meals and slow their metabolism to endure long-term starvation in the ocean depths. “This is surprising because bacteria and animals are very different, and such [gene] transfers are rare,” says Jianbo Yuan, a marine biologist at the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ Institute of Oceanology and co-author on the new research published in Cell.
Giant marine isopods, which are related to garden pill bugs, live across a wide range of ocean depths, from a comparatively shallow 170 meters to the deep, dark sea around 2,100 meters down, where food and light are scarce. Some deep-sea isopods are supergiant, reaching up to half a meter in length. To understand what separates the deep-sea species from their shallower cousins, the researchers sequenced full genomes from specimens found at 300 and 800 meters and compared their energy demands, enzyme activity and oxygen use.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
They found a key gene called ND1 expressed much more strongly in the deep-sea isopods that looked more like a gene found in bacteria than in an animal: it lacked filler genetic segments called introns and produced very tiny proteins, both signs of a bacterial gene. The researchers theorize that more than 16 million years ago genes from bacteria living in an isopod’s stomach may have been incorporated into its genome in a way that was then passed along to future generations.
The many copies now in deep-sea isopods’ genomes seem to slow down energy production when the creatures are in cold conditions. Inserting the gene into zebra fish, nematode worms and human cells, the researchers found, lowered those organisms’ metabolic rates, too.
The finding “opens a completely new window to study the evolution of deep-sea gigantism and the role of microbiome in deep-sea adaptation,” says Torben Riehl, a marine biologist at the Senckenberg Ocean Species Alliance in Frankfurt, Germany, who was not involved in the study. Deep-sea ecosystems cover more than 50 percent of Earth’s surface and are vital to the planet—so every little bit we learn, Riehl adds, may help us understand the benefits these ecosystems provide and how to preserve them.

'High in protein' – marketing trick or healthy nutrition trend? New study reveals what Latvian consumers really think  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:39:48 UTC
22:39:48 KST

Products labelled “high in protein” have become one of the fastest-growing and most widely discussed food categories in recent years. But is this simply an effective marketing approach, or a well-founded healthy nutrition trend? A sociological survey commissioned by “Agrova Baltics”, part of the European agri-food group “Agrova”, and its functional egg protein brand “Fiteg²” reveals an interesting contradiction: while 72% of Latvia’s population understand what the “high in protein” label means, only 6% know precisely how much protein they need to consume as part of their daily diet. The study’s findings and their significance in the context of dietary habits are commented on by Olga Stepanova, creator of “Fiteg²” products and R&D expert at “Agrova”.
Protein popularity is growing faster than knowledge about it
The study shows that only 6% of respondents know precisely how much protein they need to consume daily. Another 31% believe they have an approximate understanding, while 62% of Latvia’s population overall do not have a clear idea of how much protein their bodies require. Of these, 38% admit that they do not know at all, while 24% say they have heard about the topic but cannot name a specific amount.
Knowledge also differs significantly across age groups – younger respondents are generally better informed, while older people are considerably more likely to admit that they do not know how much protein they should consume on a daily basis.
“The study clearly shows that ‘high in protein’ is not simply a marketing trick. It is a trend that reflects people’s growing interest in a balanced diet and higher-quality food products. At the same time, however, we can see that knowledge about the role of protein in the diet does not always keep pace with this interest. Many people still do not know how much protein they actually need or how to incorporate enough of it into their daily diet,” says O. Stepanova.
Protein products are not just for athletes
While 72% of respondents know that the “high in protein” label indicates a higher protein content than in similar products, some misconceptions about the purpose of these products still persist.
Some 12% of respondents cannot explain what the label means, while another 11% believe that such products are primarily intended for athletes.
O. Stepanova emphasises: “Protein is not only needed by professional athletes or people who regularly work out at the gym. It is one of the most important nutrients for everyone – children during periods of growth, adults with active lifestyles, seniors seeking to maintain muscle mass, people recovering from illness, and anyone who wants to maintain a balanced diet. Our task is to challenge the stereotype that protein products are intended only for a narrow audience.”
The “high in protein” label is no longer enough
The study shows that consumers are becoming increasingly demanding. When choosing protein products, people consider not only the amount of protein, but also the product’s ingredients, taste and price. This demonstrates that consumers are looking not for bold marketing claims, but for products that naturally fit into a healthy everyday diet.
“Being labelled ‘high in protein’ does not, in itself, make a product healthy. It is important to consider the overall composition – the source of protein, as well as the amount of sugar, fat and salt, and the product’s place within a balanced diet. This is also the approach we follow when developing the “Fiteg²” product range. Our goal is not to create products only for athletes, but to offer functional egg protein products to anyone who wants to easily supplement their diet with high-quality protein. The “Fiteg²” range currently includes egg protein powders and egg white protein bars, and we continue to expand the product range as we see that interest in functional nutrition in Latvia continues to grow,” says O. Stepanova.
About “Agrova”
“Agrova” is a European agri-food brand and group whose principal shareholder is “Agrova International”. The group specialises in egg production and processing, as well as the development of egg products and functional nutrition products. The “Agrova” group was established in Riga, Latvia, in 2025 by entrepreneur Jurijs Adamovičs with the ambition of building a globally competitive egg and egg products production platform rooted in Latvia’s agricultural excellence, science and responsible practices throughout the value chain. Today, Agrova operates production facilities in Latvia and the United Kingdom, providing sustainable supply to retail chains, the foodservice sector and food industry companies across Europe.

Real Estate and Continuity Planning for Companies in Latvia  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:39:28 UTC
22:39:28 KST

For companies in Latvia, real estate can be much more than a place where employees work. Offices, warehouses, production facilities and retail premises often support essential business processes, making their availability closely connected with operational continuity. A property-related problem can therefore affect employees, customers, inventory and delivery schedules at the same time.
When a company plans to purchase or develop premises, financing should be considered alongside long-term business needs. Commercial real estate financing can form part of that planning, but the appropriate structure depends on the company's financial position, property type, intended use and broader investment plans. Comparing available options and reviewing the associated obligations can help management understand how a property purchase would fit into the company's finances.
Property decisions should follow the business strategy
Before committing to a commercial property, companies can assess how the premises will serve their operations over the coming years. A growing logistics business may need additional storage capacity, while a professional services company may prioritize office location and accessibility. Manufacturing businesses, meanwhile, may have specific requirements concerning utilities, loading areas, equipment and regulatory compliance.
Location is another practical consideration. Access to transport routes, proximity to customers and suppliers, availability of employees and local infrastructure can all influence the usefulness of a property. A building that appears suitable at the time of purchase may become less practical if the company's activities or workforce change significantly.
Financing is only one part of the investment calculation
The purchase price does not represent the full financial picture. Companies should also account for maintenance, utilities, taxes, renovation, equipment, security and other ongoing costs associated with owning or operating commercial premises.
Cash-flow planning is particularly relevant when property financing is involved. Management should consider how regular financial commitments would interact with seasonal revenue fluctuations, planned investments and unexpected expenses. Reviewing several financing structures can provide a clearer picture of the available alternatives without assuming that one approach will suit every business.
Commercial property needs protection beyond physical security
Security systems, maintenance schedules and access controls can reduce certain operational risks, but they cannot eliminate every possibility of loss. Fire, water damage, severe weather, theft and other unexpected events can disrupt the use of business premises and damage property or equipment.
Commercial property insurance can be considered as part of a broader risk-management strategy. The relevant cover depends on the property, its use and the risks identified by the company. Before selecting a policy, it is sensible to review the scope of cover, exclusions, deductibles and claims procedures rather than focusing solely on the premium.
Companies should also check whether the chosen arrangement reflects the actual value and contents of the premises. Changes such as renovations, new equipment or expansion may alter the company's risk profile and create a reason to review existing arrangements.
Business continuity starts before an incident occurs
A continuity plan does not need to be complicated to be useful. Companies can identify essential functions, determine which premises or equipment are critical, and establish alternative arrangements if access to a building becomes temporarily impossible.
For example, an office-based business may need procedures for remote work, while a warehouse operator could require alternative storage capacity. Contact lists, supplier information, backup systems and clearly assigned responsibilities can also make decision-making easier when normal operations are disrupted.
Regular reviews keep plans aligned with reality
Real estate and continuity planning should not be treated as a one-time exercise. Business models evolve, property values change, new equipment is introduced, and operational dependencies can emerge over time. Each of these developments may affect both financing requirements and the company's exposure to property-related risks.
Before making a new commitment or renewing existing arrangements, companies can compare available financing and insurance options and examine their conditions carefully. A periodic review helps ensure that property decisions, financial obligations and risk-management measures remain aligned with the company's actual operations and longer-term plans.

Russia Tested Its New Weapons on Ukraine—Now It’s Trying to Sell Them Abroad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:37:56 UTC
22:37:56 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Tested Its New Weapons on Ukraine—Now It’s Trying to Sell Them Abroad
Russia is increasingly transforming weapons, production methods and battlefield tactics developed during its war against Ukraine into products for the international arms market, according to an analysis by Hudson Institute Senior Fellow Can Kasapoğlu published on September 9.
The shift includes relatively inexpensive mass-produced munitions, cruise-missile and drone hybrids, and weapons designed for the kind of saturation attacks Russia has repeatedly used against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Russia is converting its industrial and operational experience gained in Ukraine—including mass-produced affordable munitions, cruise-missile-drone hybrids, and saturation attacks using mixed strike packages—into an increasingly competitive defense-export portfolio,” Kasapoğlu wrote.
Some of those weapons were put directly in front of prospective foreign customers at the El Alamein International Airshow 2026 in Egypt, held September 8-10.
“Russia sent its combat-tested drones and missiles to Egypt to promote them for export,” Kasapoğlu noted.
One of the clearest examples is the Dan-T, an export weapon closely related to Russia’s S8000 Banderol cruise-missile/drone hybrid already used against Ukraine.
The turbojet-powered Dan-T weighs roughly 272 kilograms and has an advertised range of about 450 kilometers. It can be launched from fixed-wing UAVs or crewed rotary-wing aircraft, particularly variants of Russia’s Mi-28 helicopter.
Its manufacturer, Kronstadt JSC, also produces the Orion reconnaissance-and-strike drone.
Russia began secretly testing the Banderol system in 2024, according to Kasapoğlu. Its first documented combat use against Ukraine came in spring 2025, when Ukrainian intelligence reconstructed the weapon after examining recovered debris.
The Banderol resembles a scaled-down cruise missile, with folding wings and design features intended to reduce its radar signature.
Its internal architecture also illustrates Russia’s continuing dependence on an international component supply chain.
According to the Hudson analysis, Banderol combines a Chinese Swiwin turbojet engine with an inertial navigation system, Russian Kometa-8 satellite-navigation antenna technology, and electronic components originating from the United States, Europe, and Japan.
The weapon can reportedly reach approximately 595 kilometers per hour, travel around 500 kilometers, and carry a roughly 113-kilogram high-explosive fragmentation warhead.
Its cost is another major selling point. Kasapoğlu estimates a Banderol at roughly $50,000-$150,000, dramatically below the approximately $2 million cost of a Kh-101 cruise missile or roughly $1.5 million for an Iskander-K.
That price difference reflects one of the central lessons Moscow has drawn from the war: large numbers of cheaper long-range weapons can impose enormous pressure on an opponent’s air defenses without requiring every strike weapon to match the capabilities of a sophisticated conventional cruise missile.
“Ukrainian forces are trying to find interception solutions to counter Banderol, including products from the Wild Hornets drone technology group, which specializes in hunting Shaheds,” Kasapoğlu wrote.
Russia is now attempting to turn that battlefield evolution into an export advantage. Its defense industry also brought the Lancet-E to Egypt, the export version of the Lancet loitering munition widely used by Russian forces in Ukraine.
Export configurations are offered with warheads weighing approximately 2.7 and 4.5 kilograms.
The standard Lancet has an operational range of roughly 40 kilometers and, like several other modern Russian weapons, incorporates a substantial number of Western-made electronic components. Together, the Dan-T and Lancet-E illustrate a broader transformation in Russia’s arms-export strategy.
Moscow is no longer simply offering foreign buyers traditional aircraft, air defense systems and armored vehicles. It is increasingly marketing weapons whose designs, production methods, and operational concepts have been refined through years of combat against Ukraine.
Previously, Ukrainian forces began using a newly developed air defense system to intercept Russian S8000 “Banderol” missiles, according to the Brave1 defense technology cluster.
The innovation consortium reported on its official website that the cost of intercepting a target with this unnamed defense mechanism is significantly lower than the price of the incoming munition itself.

Ukrainian Border Guards Destroy Russian BM-21 Grad and Multiple Military Targets With Drones, Video
Ukrainian border guard drone operators destroyed a Russian BM-21 Grad multiple launch rocket system, armored and transport vehicles, ammunition depots, and other military assets in the Northern Slobozhanshchyna sector, Ukraine’s State Border Guard Service reported on September 11.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the agency, operators from the Prime unmanned systems unit targeted a range of Russian positions and equipment during recent operations in the area.
Among the assets destroyed was a BM-21 Grad multiple launch rocket system, along with a mortar, an armored combat vehicle, a truck, several passenger vehicles, a motorcycle, and a ground robotic system.
The Ukrainian drone operators also struck Russian ammunition and fuel and lubricant storage facilities, as well as communications equipment.
The strikes additionally targeted shelters used by Russian personnel, further disrupting Russian positions in the sector, according to the State Border Guard Service.
The BM-21 Grad (“Hail”) is a Soviet-designed multiple launch rocket system mounted on a Ural-4320 truck chassis. Equipped with 40 tubes for 122 mm rockets, it can fire a complete salvo in about 20 seconds, covering an area of up to 14.5 hectares. The system has a maximum firing range of roughly 40 kilometers and can be reloaded in around seven minutes, allowing crews to strike and relocate relatively quickly.
First introduced into service in 1963, the Grad continues to play a significant role in Russia’s artillery forces. Its relatively old design and battlefield visibility, however, have made the system increasingly vulnerable to Ukrainian FPV drones, which are used to locate and strike mobile launchers.
The operation comes amid broader Ukrainian strikes targeting Russia’s drone and military infrastructure. On September 9 and overnight into September 10, Ukraine’s Defense Forces hit several Russian UAV command posts, three radar systems, an ammunition storage facility, and other military targets, according to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
The General Staff said one of the targets was a facility in temporarily occupied Donetsk used to store, prepare, and launch Geran and Gerbera attack drones.

How the media has changed since 9/11

Iran Is Rebuilding Its Missile Arsenal Underground After US and Israeli Strikes Cripple Production

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:37:01 UTC
22:37:01 KST

- Category
- World
Iran Is Rebuilding Its Missile Arsenal Underground After US and Israeli Strikes Cripple Production
Iran has resumed producing ballistic missiles inside underground facilities, assembling stockpiled components despite US and Israeli strikes meant to cripple the program, according to intelligence findings reported by the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) on September 10.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
US and Middle Eastern officials familiar with the matter described activity to the oulet at several buried sites, including the Khojir missile complex in southeastern Iran. The officials indicated that Tehran is assembling both liquid-propellant missiles, fueled just before launch, and solid-propellant types that can be stored ready to fire.
Iran is also attempting to build new underground assembly points to avoid being struck again, they noted. For now, the missiles are being pieced together from existing components in smaller quantities than before the war, the officials added. US and Israeli strikes damaged industrial facilities, while a naval blockade has complicated imports of parts and solid-fuel ingredients.
Tal Inbar, a senior analyst at the US-based Missile Defense Advocacy Alliance, argued that the pattern was predictable once the bombing stopped. "When there are no bombings of the facilities, you can replace damaged infrastructure, and you can buy new components from other countries and store them in the facilities," he explained.
Analysts assessed that Iran retains thousands of ballistic missiles and could assemble at least a couple hundred more from components already on hand. One former CIA analyst now at King's College London noted that Tehran had stockpiled finished warheads, airframes, and guidance systems before the fighting began.
US officials have maintained that the program lies in ruins. Sean Parnell, the Pentagon's chief spokesman, stated that American forces had destroyed up to 90% of Iran's drone, ballistic missile, and naval industrial base. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had gone further in April, declaring the missile effort "functionally destroyed" and beyond repair.
"You have no defense industry, no ability to replenish your offensive or defense capabilities," Hegseth declared. The fresh intelligence undercuts that assessment, suggesting the pause in fighting has given Tehran room to recover.
Among the weapons Iran keeps firing is the Kheibar Shekan, described as mobile, accurate, and relatively cheap to produce. Those qualities make it well-suited to sustained, high-volume attacks that strain enemy air defenses.
On Wednesday, Iran launched a heavy salvo at an air base in Jordan that houses US troops. Footage showed projectiles fitted with cluster warheads, a type used earlier in the war to overwhelm Israeli air defenses.
Satellite imagery has shown Iran repairing roads, bridges, and production sites, and reopening tunnel entrances collapsed by earlier airstrikes. Weapons stored inside those underground sites are likely well preserved, according to Israeli military assessments.
Iran built its missile program in the 1980s during the war with Iraq and rebuilt quickly after last year's 12-day conflict with Israel. Nicole Grajewski, an Iranian-strategy expert at Sciences Po, noted that the missile network regenerates faster than the nuclear program and is heavily dispersed by design.
The rebuilding effort has extended well beyond missile assembly during the current lull in fighting. Since a 60-day ceasefire took hold in mid-June, later extended by two months in August, Tehran has worked to replenish its arsenal from outside sources as well. Russia began shipping explosives, ammunition, and drone parts to Iran across the Caspian Sea, a route Western navies cannot interdict. That maritime corridor has helped Iran restock weapons depleted by earlier US and Israeli strikes.

Ukraine Strikes Russian Aircraft Engine Plant, Pantsir Air Defenses – General Staff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:34:36 UTC
22:34:36 KST

Ukrainian forces struck a Russian defense-industry plant producing components for military aircraft engines, along with air defense systems, a radar station and drone facilities, the AFU General Staff said on Friday, Sept. 11.
The strikes hit Russian military targets in several regions and occupied Ukrainian territories, according to Ukraine’s military.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The most significant target was the Snizhne Machine-Building Plant in the occupied Donetsk region. The facility produces components for gas-turbine engines, including compressor and turbine blades, and supplies parts used in Russian military aviation.
Ukrainian forces also targeted two Pantsir-S1 air defense systems in Taganrog, Rostov Oblast, a Russian radar station in Berezki, Bryansk Oblast, and a facility in Donetsk used to store, prepare and launch attack drones.
In the occupied Luhansk region, Ukrainian forces struck an FPV drone operator training center and a unit of the Chechen Akhmat forces in Petropavlivka.
The General Staff did not provide details on the extent of damage at the targeted sites, saying the results were still being assessed.
The strikes are part of Ukraine’s ongoing campaign against Russian military infrastructure and the defense-industrial network supporting Moscow’s war against Ukraine.
Part of wider Ukrainian drone campaign
The reported attack came amid a broader wave of overnight Ukrainian drone strikes against Russian industrial infrastructure.
‘Weeks, Not Months’: Ukraine’s FP-7 Ballistic Missile Could Soon Strike Russia
In Perm, a major chemical plant was reportedly targeted by Ukrainian drones early Friday, Sept. 11, with footage appearing to show a drone diving toward the facility.
In Saratov, a fire was reported at the Rosneft-owned Saratov Oil Refinery, while an Ozon logistics center also reportedly caught fire.
In Volgograd, regional authorities reported damage to an industrial facility and an apartment building, with two people hospitalized.
Ozon logistics hubs have increasingly been targeted since late August. Seven warehouses have reportedly been hit across Samara, Rostov, and Belgorod oblasts, Krasnodar Krai, Bashkortostan, and Dagestan.
The attacks also come as Ukraine continues to target Russia’s oil-refining sector. Ukrainian drones have struck Russian refineries at least 70 times since the beginning of 2026, according to Bloomberg, contributing to a sharp decline in refining output and growing gasoline shortages.
At least 17 Russian regions have introduced restrictions on fuel sales, while Russia has increasingly turned to imports from India, Morocco, Turkey, and Belarus to cover the shortfall.
The Russian defense ministry had not released a tally of intercepted drones from the latest wave, while Ukraine had not officially claimed responsibility for the reported attacks.

&quot;Phantoms&quot; recorded over 7,000 speeding violations in Kyiv and the region in six days
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:34:22 EEST
22:34:22 KST

"Phantoms" recorded over 7,000 speeding violations in Kyiv and the region in six days
Kyiv • UNN
In six days, three “Phantoms” detected 7,012 speeding violations. Patrol officers also stopped 55 drivers for serious traffic violations.
During the first six days of operation, three special "Phantom" vehicles in Kyiv and the Kyiv region automatically recorded 7,012 speeding violations, UNN reports, citing the Ministry of Internal Affairs.
Details
According to law enforcement officials, while the "Phantoms" were operating, they detected cases of speeding by 50 km/h or more.
Another 55 drivers were stopped by patrol police crews for serious traffic violations: driving through a red traffic light, crossing a double solid line, entering the oncoming lane, and violating intersection rules, the statement said.
The Ministry of Internal Affairs added that a "Phantom" can record vehicles traveling both in the same and opposite directions, while the vehicle itself is moving and when the vehicle equipped with the system is stationary. Therefore, it is no longer enough for a driver to slow down only after seeing a patrol car.
At the same time, the "Phantoms" are not only used for automatic speed recording. Police officers in uniform and with official badges serve in the vehicles. The crews can stop vehicles whose drivers have committed violations and document the violations directly at the scene.
The main purpose of using the "Phantoms" is not to increase the number of citations, but to instill a lasting habit of complying with the Traffic Rules, reduce the number of road accidents, and save human lives

Yabloko’s candidate list removed from ballot in another Russian region, leaving party in just one regional race
A court in Russia’s Tomsk region has revoked the registration of Yabloko’s candidate list for the region’s legislative assembly election, ruling on a lawsuit filed by the LDPR.
The Yabloko press service said the lawsuit relied on “practically the same complaints previously made against the federal list: the distribution of campaign materials through restricted-access resources, alleged violations of intellectual property law, and campaign financing.”
Russia’s Supreme Court struck the party’s federal list from the ballot on August 10, acting on a lawsuit from Rodina that accused Yabloko of copyright infringement and illegal payments for campaign advertising.
Seven Yabloko candidates remain in the Tomsk region race, running in single-mandate districts. But after a string of removals, the party’s regional list now survives only in Novgorod region — down from the eight regions where Yabloko had originally put forward candidate lists.

Tech event GITEX sees Türkiye as perfect sandbox for global AI expansion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:33:59 UTC
22:33:59 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
11 September 2026•Update: 11 September 2026
Türkiye stands out as an important destination for artificial intelligence (AI) with its strong engineering talent, government support and numerous technology parks, the vice president of major technology event GITEX said.
Bilal Alrais said the organizers were pleasantly surprised by the number of attendees from banks and manufacturing companies across Türkiye.
"The level of exposure we've been getting from across Türkiye and also from as far as South Africa and Kenya is actually very reassuring," Alrais told Anadolu.
Representatives from more than 70 countries attended the two-day event hosted by the country’s Investment and Finance Office alongside the Industry and Technology Ministry on Sept. 9-10. Anadolu was its global communications partner.
 
Türkiye serves as perfect sandbox
Alrais said the scale of the market, the quality of engineers, and the understanding of AI applications make Türkiye a strategic destination.
He emphasized that government support helps startups scale and allows small- and medium-sized enterprises to grow rapidly.
"It's a perfect sandbox for companies to be able to do well using AI and scale globally," Alrais said.
 
Global visitors flock to meet Turkish innovators
Alrais pointed out that the presence of 120 startups at the event tells only part of the story.
Türkiye is among the countries with a large number of technoparks, he said.
He stated that 10 or 11 different technology parks represented their innovators directly at the exhibition.
Alrais highlighted that international visitors came specifically to meet innovators from Istanbul, Ankara and Izmir.
Because Türkiye has so many R&D centers, people are excited with new technologies coming from the country, he said.
 
AI accelerates demand for data centers
Looking ahead, Alrais said GITEX's Abu Dhabi edition will host the biggest AI event in the world in October.
He added that the organization will expand its global footprint with new events announced for Latin America, Italy and Serbia.
Alrais explained that the industry focus on AI accelerated after the COVID-19 pandemic and the launch of ChatGPT.
He noted that the technology sector now puts much more attention toward data centers.
“You can't have AI without a data center,” Alrais said, noting that the shift creates new challenges, including energy management that the industry must address.

Report: Swiss man faces French investigation over escort website

Report: Swiss man faces French investigation over escort website
The Paris prosecutor's office has opened an investigation into France's largest prostitution website, “Meslibertines”, reportedly hosted in Switzerland and owned by a Swiss citizen living in Dubai, Radio France reports.
The website “Sexemodel”, recently renamed “Meslibertines”, is the main platform for escort and prostitution adverts in France, with an average of 430,000 visits per day, for more than 45,000 active prostitution ads.
The sites feature several hundred pages offering the services of underage girls. As a result, the French High Commissioner for Childhood contacted the public prosecutor to shut down the site, leading to the opening of an investigation, France Inter reported on ThursdayExternal link.
Swiss hub
The platform, which presents itself as a simple “ad hosting service”, rejects responsibility for “any contact or meeting resulting from placed advertisements” and claims to have a “zero tolerance” policy for illegal activities. Its Swiss headquarters complicates investigations and legal proceedings. A request for mutual legal assistance has been submitted by the French judicial authorities.
The site’s owner is reportedly a 47-year-old Swiss citizen, previously sentenced in France in 2011 to three years’ suspended imprisonment for aggravated pimping. At the time, Swiss authorities refused to execute the international arrest warrant, France Inter reports. The man also owns other similar platforms.
The head of the Central Office for the Suppression of Human Trafficking, cited by French public radio, denounced the website’s “extremely hypocritical stance”. “They know very well that among the thousands of advertisements, there are some for which they are guilty of a crime. But the French judicial authorities cannot act alone; cooperation with the Swiss authorities is necessary,” he said.
Owner reportedly lives in Dubai
The Swiss man behind this business reportedly lives in Dubai and earns over €20 million a year from the platform, to which many prostitutes in France subscribe.
The online newspaper Mediapart had already devoted a major investigation to him in 2025,External link claiming that he had been at the head of an international online prostitution empire for 20 years. He allegedly managed his affairs through front men and shell companies, most of which were registered in Switzerland and Cyprus.
Child prostitution is a major problem in France. According to NGOs, at least 20,000 children are affected, a figure that has increased twentyfold in ten years. The business is more lucrative and less dangerous than drugs. Pimps often pick up girls directly from shelters for troubled youngsters and then move them around regularly to cover their tracks.

‘Weeks, Not Months’: Ukraine’s FP-7 Ballistic Missile Could Soon Strike Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:32:01 UTC
22:32:01 KST

Ukraine could begin striking Russia with its new FP-7 tactical ballistic missiles within the coming weeks, Iryna Terekh, CEO of Fire Point, said on Thursday.
Fire Point is one of the Ukrainian army’s largest contractors, producing, among other weapons, long-range FP-1 strike drones and FP-5 “Flamingo” cruise missiles, which have repeatedly struck military targets deep inside Russian territory.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to Terekh, the FP-7 can reach targets up to 200 kilometers (124 miles) away and carry a warhead weighing up to 150 kilograms (330 pounds).
The missile has successfully completed two stages of testing and is now preparing for combat deployment.
“We are talking about weeks, not months,” Terekh said during the MSPO 2026 defense exhibition in Poland, as cited by UNIAN.
The FP-7 is a ground-launched system with a maximum projectile speed of 1,500 meters per second (4,921 feet per second). Fire Point founder and chief designer Denys Shtilerman has compared the missile to the US-made ATACMS system.
In June, Shtilerman said the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) could begin launching the first strikes on Moscow with Ukrainian-made ballistic missiles as early as this autumn.
He said the company was conducting the final testing phase for the new long-range missile and that, following the tests, “flights into Russian territory will begin.”
“The military will determine the targets, but I think they will be significant ones right from the start,” h said.
Ukraine Is Losing Its Tech Edge to Russia, Former Google CEO Says
Terekh added that another company project, the long-range FP-9 missile, with a range of up to 850 kilometers (528 miles), is currently undergoing flight tests.
Because of its range, testing the missile within Ukrainian territory is impossible. As a result, the next stage could effectively involve combat strikes against targets inside Russia, the company’s representative said.
Fire Point officially announced the development of the FP-7 and FP-9 ballistic missiles in September 2025. In February 2026, the company demonstrated the first test launch of the FP-7.
Вітаємо FP7) pic.twitter.com/FxgCHVHMET
— Denys Shtilierman (@DenShtilierman) February 27, 2026
Following such developments, Ukraine will begin to launch deeper and more powerful strikes inside Russia if Moscow continues the war, Presidential Office Chief Kyrylo Budanov told Latvian Television.
“If Russia does not stop hostilities against us, it will feel the consequences ever more strongly,” he said.
Budanov’s warning followed a Sept. 9 strike by Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces (SSO) on two Russian gas-condensate plants in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug.
The SSO said its drones traveled more than 3,000 kilometers (1,864 miles) into Russia, hitting the Novy Urengoy and Purovsky facilities.
Budanov said Ukraine would continue fighting as long as necessary but was ready to end hostilities on acceptable terms.
“We are standing on our land, and no one has the right to simply give that land away to someone else,” he said.
Budanov added that the most realistic arrangement would be to halt fighting along the existing front line and provide Ukraine with security guarantees. However, Kyiv will not legally recognize Russia’s occupation of Ukrainian territory.

IDF's war on all fronts: How Eyal Zamir is managing threats from Iran, Lebanon, Gaza, and West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:31:30 UTC
22:31:30 KST

When IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir finished 2025, he was on track as one of the most popular IDF chiefs in recent memory.
He had stormed onto the world stage in June 2025 leading Operation Rising Lion, Israel's remarkably successful massive strike on Iran's nuclear program, radars and air defenses, top military officials, and some ballistic missile sites.
Next, he was the IDF chief in October 2025 when a deal was struck with Hamas to end the Gaza War, including the return of all remaining living and deceased hostages.
But 2026 is still a work in progress, with some of Zamir's legacy in the balance.
Iran is weaker, but the threat is far from gone
Israel's early 2026 Operation Roaring Lion is viewed by most in Israel and globally as less successful than the 2025 operation. This is true even as the IDF did destroy significant aspects of Iran's ballistic missiles program, caused between $200-300 billion dollars of damage to its broader military industrial complex, and assassinated Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Regardless of the military successes, it has been highly problematic diplomatically, turning even more of the world against Israel. Also, Israel has lost additional important measures of support from the Trump administration over gas prices and the crisis in the Straits of Hormuz as well as over the fact that the Iranian regime survived and with an intransigent attitude.
So what is the overall strategic and specific threats picture?
In the view of the IDF high command, which Zamir directs, The Jerusalem Post has learned that biggest strategic win for Israel and which has been ignored by much of the global media, is Israel's advantage over Tehran after the 2026 war both in learning and advancing the other side's tactics and regarding capabilities, meaning gaining an upper hand in resupplying weapons and the ongoing arms race.
Much of the global media has focused on the US's using up significant amounts of its air defense interceptors and attack bombs, which may leave it less able to block a theoretical Chinese move to take over Taiwan.
While this is a critical debate for the US, Israel has no such disconnected second front where it would need to defend against an imminent and massive aerial enemy attack.
Rather, Israel only needs to "race" against the Islamic Republic when it comes to the volume of offensive and defensive weapons needed to prosecute an extended new offensive or defensive war.
In numbers, the Post understands that in the view of Israeli intelligence, this means that Israel has been racing ahead with new military surprises and tactics to unleash against Tehran in any potential future new conflict.
In contrast, Iran's ability to embrace and prepare new tactics is limited two-fold. It is limited by its lack of funds and preoccupation with trying to stay above water militarily after having been so severely battered. Further, it is limited by the absence of any near-term horizon or moment in which it will be economically saved and be able to fully reopen up a process for recovery and for developing new projects.
The Post understands that Zamir and the IDF high command view Israel as jumping years ahead in these areas, even if there are some other specific select areas where Iran may be able to remain more formidable.
There is another crucial development in holding Iran back from restoring its former ballistic missiles and other sources of threat power. It is a mix of the 2026 war's destruction of Iran's future production capabilities in tandem with the US's stronger than expected post-war success in blocking China from resupplying ballistic missile technology and supplies to the Islamic Republic.
The Post learned back in April that one of the greatest concerns of Israeli intelligence was to what extent China might hand over critical items to restore Iran's ballistic missile threat capabilities on a more wholesale basis.
If without Beijing, Iran was viewed as being pushed back years backward, Israeli intelligence worried that China could hand over enough ballistic missile items rapidly enough to jumpstart the recovery process forward much faster.
Although Israel does maintain that China has helped Iran recover some capabilities in this area, Zamir and the high command's view is that Washington has succeeded in blocking the vast majority of this assistance through its counter-blockade of the Straits of Hormuz. This is something which in April, no one expected would last into September or beyond.
This means that after Israel destroyed Iran's planetary mixers in 2026, which were viewed as the key to rapid mass production of ballistic missiles, that the Islamic Republic could be left with trough mixers or other slower and inferior production processes.
In contrast, if China had provided new planetary mixers and other items directly to Iran, the situation could have been much more dangerous.
Due to the damage to ballistic missile production and the US success so far with the Chinese, the IDF expects Iran to remain under 2,000 missiles even at the end of 2026, the Post has learned.
On one hand, that almost 2,000 number is very disturbing.
There were earlier hopes that Iran could be held under or around 1,000 for a longer period, and Iran has shown impressive resiliency to rebuild aspects of its missile production in a very short time after the 2026 war.
But in another sense, this is a significant near and medium term win for Zamir and Israel.
All of this comes after Tehran had somewhere between 2,500-3,000 such missiles prior to the June 2025 war.
It means that more than 18 months after that war, Iran will still have significantly fewer missiles than it had at the time.
This is even more significant when one takes into account that the pace at which Iran was moving with ballistic missile production prior to June 2025 was expected to get it to over 6,000 missiles at an earlier point in 2026 and 8,800 missiles by August 2027.
The existential ballistic missile threat has not been removed.
But it has been delayed already more than two years, and by some estimates given to the Post by as many as four years, though those most optimistic estimates make certain assumptions which could evolve.
Hezbollah is weaker, but Israel has no clear exit from Lebanon
If after the 2023-2024 war, Hezbollah was down from 150,000 rockets and mortars to 30,000-50,000, the Post has learned that it is now as low as 10,000 following the IDF's war on it in 2026.
That means Hezbollah's current arsenal is weaker than Hamas's was on October 7, 2023, when once the Lebanese terror group dwarfed the Gazan terror group in power (Hamas meanwhile has almost no rockets and has not succeeded in firing a rocket to harm Israelis in years, with its last major effective attack coming in January 2024.)
The IDF also has made it currently impossible for Hezbollah to invade Israel by seizing an approximately 10 kilometer deep security zone in southern Lebanon.
This does not mean Israel is safe from Hezbollah. There is currently no real process to disarm the group unlike in Gaza where there may be such a process with Hamas.
The Lebanese army is still terrified of having a direct conflict with Hezbollah and the Post understands that as long as the army views the 1970s Lebanese civil war as its low point, and not the recent round of fighting with Israel, this is unlikely to change.
Long-term this could leave Israel stuck in Lebanon like it was 1982-2000, something it does not want, due to military vulnerabilities and diplomatic harm from an extended occupation, and with no apparent exit strategy.
Earlier hopes that the positive relations between the Lebanese and Israeli governments might be enough to pressure Hezbollah into even partial disarmament currently look like pipedreams in the eyes of Zamir and the IDF high command, the Post understands.
But the IDF can only manage the military playing field, and converting military wins into strategic diplomatic gains, is the role of the civilian government.
In Gaza, military gains collide with political limits
This same issue is present in Gaza where the IDF has done its best to keep Hamas from making a comeback, but has no ability to force Israel's government to allow other Palestinian or international authorities into the Strip to try to replace Hamas.
If the Netanyahu government does eventually allow the International Stabilization Forces (ISF) peacekeepers and the NCAG Palestinian technocratic committee into Gaza after months of delay (by both him and Hamas), it will be only due to pressure by the Trump administration.
In the meantime, Zamir has warned that if Hamas's threat is not reduced either by diplomatic-political means or by a new major operation, the group could eventually start to reconstitute itself as a threat to Israel after years on the run.
Eyal Zamir faces a two-front battle in the West Bank
Through all of this, Zamir has inherited a multi-headed problem of terror emanating from the West Bank since early 2022.
He has tried to order harsher crack downs on certain more problematic Palestinian areas, reducing aspects of the terror threat substantially – by some estimates as much as 80% - but nothing close to stopping the threat.
At the same time, Zamir, along with the police, the Shin Bet, and the government more broadly, have lost control over several hundred violent Jewish extremists who have been regularly attacking both Palestinians and soldiers alike.
Zamir has not fought with Defense Minister Israel Katz to restore administrative detention of violent Jews, a tool the Shin Bet has consistently demanded be returned to them for use.
Rather, he has been strategic about public fighting with the defense minister, with a focus on keeping control of key IDF appointments and on pressing the government to draft more haredim. This has been despite pushes by Katz to make political-friendly appointments and to protect haredi political parties from any substantial concessions on drafting more young men from their sector into the military.
Possibly Zamir's most dramatic moment was a leak in March of a private speech he made to the cabinet about the need to draft more haredim in which he said, “I am raising 10 red flags before the IDF collapses into itself.”
More recently, he has also been more public lately about demanding government backing for combating Jewish extremist violence.
On August 27, Zamir announced that he was expanding the Israeli forces being used to maintain public order in the West Bank leading into the upcoming fall Jewish holidays.
The Post understands that the volume of forces will be more than double the pre-October 7 force size of around 11 battalions, which at times has grown to 15-20 battalions, but will temporarily grow even more.
Zamir warned the government that Jewish extremist violence has run out of control and that greater backing is needed from the government, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and others actively restraining political officials from provocative actions.
All of this takes place as IDF officials have said Jewish extremist violence has reached new levels, with hundreds of extremists recently drawing out a conflict with the IDF at the Palestinian village of Kusra for multiple weeks.
It also takes place as IDF and Shin Bet officials say that the police, after three years under Itamar Ben-Gvir, have reached highly problematic lows in terms of arresting and helping indict Jewish extremists in the West Bank.
None or almost none (the police have been at a low also in terms of transparency) of those involved in the Kusra actions were arrested.
Accordingly, Zamir has brought in the Golani Brigade and the Paratroopers Brigade to supplement the standard forces in the area, some of which have appeared too sympathetic to Jewish extremists attacking Palestinian villages.
However, without more backing from the government, Zamir has warned that even increased military forces will be insufficient.
Looking into 2027, in some ways, Zamir has succeeded in making Israel more secure than it was in the 2023-2025 period. But almost every front remains a challenge, such that he will continue to have his work cut out for him.

Germany charges seven men for Hamas terror plot, weapons procurement
Unknown

2026-09-11
13:31:28 UTC
22:31:28 KST

Germany’s federal prosecutor charged seven men accused of being Hamas terrorists on Friday with procuring weapons and planning an attack against the Jewish community and Israel-linked individuals in Germany or Austria.
According to a statement released by the prosecutor, the suspects were tasked by high-ranking Hamas terrorists with gathering weapons and ammunition in preparation for the attack.
The suspects were identified as German national Abed Al G., Danish national Yousif C., Lebanese-born Borhan El-K., Lebanese-born Wael FM, German national Ahmad I., Lebanese-born Kamel M., and Bulgarian national Mohammad S.
At the time of the arrests of Abed Al G., Wael FM, and Ahmad I. in October 2025, the suspects had already acquired over 700 rounds of ammunition, a fully automatic rifle, and 13 pistols for use in the planned attack.
Additional suspect transported, stored weapons for planned attack
An additional suspect who is being prosecuted separately, British national Mohammed A., was involved in transporting the weapons and storing them in Austria.
Mohammed A. also recorded a video ahead of the planned terrorist attack, in which he claimed responsibility and stated that the plot was concocted in the name of Hamas.
According to German authorities, the group had been planning the attack since at least July 2025, and had intended to carry it out around the second anniversary of Hamas’s October 7 massacre against Israel.
All of the suspects, arrested between October 2025 and May 2026, remain in custody.
Mohammed A., who was arrested in November 2025 in the United Kingdom, has not yet been extradited to Germany, according to the prosecutor’s statement.

Supermarket aisles seen quieter than expected ahead of Rosh Hashanah, despite NIS 500m. spent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:31:01 UTC
22:31:01 KST

Shoppers spent nearly NIS 459 million on card payments during Friday morning ahead of Rosh Hashanah, but supermarkets remained unusually quiet compared with previous holiday eves, with retailers attributing the trend to earlier shopping, overseas travel, and economic pressures.
While people expected the heavy crowds typically seen on the morning before the Jewish New Year, with checkout lines stretching to the entrance of stores, the reality was completely different: Traffic at supermarket chains was especially light, even compared with a regular Friday.
"I have never seen anything like this," a branch manager at one of the retail chains told Walla. "We were just talking about it as a team, that there are barely any people. Either everyone already did their shopping earlier, or everyone flew abroad. They said Ben-Gurion Airport is crowded."
According to data from Shva, Israel's Automated Banking Services company, Israelis made NIS 459.06 million in credit card purchases between 8 a.m. and 11 a.m. This marked a slight 2.7% increase compared with the same period before Rosh Hashanah last year, when spending totaled NIS 446.77 million.
The peak minute was recorded at 10:56 a.m., when more than NIS 3.44 million was spent through 18,000 transactions in a single minute.
Higher prices drive spending despite quieter stores
However, the slight increase in spending does not appear to reflect a surge of consumers filling stores. Instead, it likely stems mainly from price increases in major holiday products.
The surprising quiet on the morning before the holiday capped a trend seen throughout recent weeks, as traditional holiday shopping waves were barely noticeable due to a combination of low national morale, the timing of the holiday falling across the weekend, and the heavy financial burden of the summer vacation period.
The sparse activity in supermarket aisles was accompanied by fewer deep discounts from retailers seeking to protect profit margins. An examination by the Institute for Retail Research found that while the overall shopping basket did not rise across the board, key products for the holiday table became significantly more expensive compared with the same period last year.
Avocado prices jumped by 44.3%, dry onions rose by 39.3%, fresh chicken liver increased by 21.3%, and packaged carrots became 19.6% more expensive. Overall, fruit and vegetable prices rose by an average of 7.3%, while wine prices increased by 6.3%.
Large price gaps found between supermarket chains
The examination also found major price gaps of around 40% between different retail chains for products such as whole fresh chicken and fresh chicken schnitzel.
As a result, Israelis who reached the checkout counters faced weaker competition and higher prices on key products, better explaining the rise in total spending despite the unusually empty supermarkets.

India's BRICS strategy tested with Xi, Putin set to visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:31:00 UTC
22:31:00 KST

India's BRICS strategy tested with Xi, Putin set to visit
September 11, 2026
India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi will host the 18th BRICS summit this weekend in New Delhi, welcoming Chinese President Xi Jinping to India for the first time since 2019.
The summit comes at an important moment for India. As New Delhi's year-long BRICS presidency draws to a close, India is stepping up engagement with China and Russia, and its relationship with Washington remains difficult.
Modi met both Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on August 31 and September 1. Just two weeks later, Modi is set to see them again in New Delhi for the BRICS summit.
But with BRICS both growing in size and increasingly troubled by internal divisions, the forum might limit Modi's diplomatic gains.
New Delhi and Beijing locked in 'armed coexistence' and competition
Indian diplomats are trying to protect their room for maneuver in a changing international order.
Ashok Kantha, a former Indian ambassador to China, said India's engagement with BRICS and the SCO is part of New Delhi's longstanding strategy of strategic autonomy.
"These groupings give India a seat at the table and allow it to pursue its own interests while maintaining relationships with different major powers," Kantha told DW.
However, as Modi prepares to host Xi in New Delhi, ties between India and China are less than ideal.
Both countries reached a border patrol agreement in 2024, ending a four-year military standoff along their disputed frontier.
International flights have resumed, the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage has reopened and some visa restrictions have eased. But major problems remain between Beijing and New Delhi — India is reporting a trade deficit of over $112 billion (€96.5 billion) with China, and the two countries argue over market access.
The Modi-Xi meeting will therefore be watched for signs of a major diplomatic thaw, particularly on trade and investment.
Kantha said the visit could bring some stabilization but should not be mistaken for a reset.
"The border remains heavily militarized and major differences over trade, investment and security remain. India needs a stable and predictable relationship with China, but without lowering its guard," said Kantha.
"It is a relationship of armed coexistence and managed competition. We should not reduce it to a simple 'elephant and dragon' story," he said, referring to traditional symbols of the world's two most populous nations.
BRICS gets bigger, divisions grow
India's presidency has already exposed the difficulty of reaching agreement within BRICS, which has grown from its original five members to 11.
With nations such as Brazil, South Africa, Indonesia and Egypt all part of BRICS, its leaders struggle to reconcile its very different relationships with the US and different interests in conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine. The group now also includes Iran and the UAE, countries that have found themselves on opposing sides of the war in Iran.
Earlier this year, BRICS foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement on the Middle East crisis, forcing India to issue a unilateral chair's statement instead.
With Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian expected at the Delhi summit, this diplomatic divide is likely to take center stage.
"Differences between members such as Iran and the UAE show how difficult it can be to find common ground," says Harsh Pant, vice president for Studies and Foreign Policy at the Observer Research Foundation.
"BRICS can still work on areas where members share interests, such as reforming global economic governance. But such disagreements are likely to become more common," he added.
Fears of Chinese dominance
The future of BRICS will also be impacted by the rivalry between India and China.
India wants BRICS to give greater weight to the concerns of developing countries and to support reform of other global institutions such as the United Nations, IMF and World Bank. At the same time, New Delhi does not want the grouping to become a China-led challenge to the West.
India has been pushing for easier cross-border payments between BRICS countries and greater use of national currencies in international trade. At the same time, the Modi government has also been careful not to present this as an attempt to replace the US dollar or create a common BRICS currency.
"Local-currency transactions are likely to become an important area of cooperation," Pant said, but stressed that India and other BRICS countries are not necessarily seeking 'de-dollarization.'"
"Instead, they are looking for greater resilience and alternatives to dollar-based financial arrangements."
India's 'America Plus' strategy
Despite its disagreements with the Trump administration, New Delhi still wants stronger economic and strategic ties with the US, while also maintaining its longstanding relationship with Russia and improving relations with China.
India's diplomatic course is not a pure "multi-alignment" approach but an "America Plus" strategy, strategic affairs analyst C Raja Mohan told DW.
"India remains dependent on the West for capital, technology, markets and security, while deepening ties with Russia and China for strategic reasons," said Mohan, a professor of American studies at Jindal Global University.
But this balancing act will become harder as great-power rivalry intensifies, Mohan warns.
"A US-China accommodation could leave India exposed, while Russia's growing dependence on China is changing the Eurasian balance," he said.
In this calculation, a more anti-Western BRICS could put pressure on India over its continuing dependence on the West.
The upcoming Delhi summit is likely to show the extent of India's power — especially as it wraps up its BRICS presidency. For Narendra Modi, the test is whether India can advance its priorities for BRICS and give itself more room to maneuver internationally, without allowing the grouping to become dominated by China or reduced to an anti-Western platform.

====================================================================================================

Iran war tests expanding BRICS as bloc seeks greater global clout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:30:39 UTC
22:30:39 KST

New Delhi will be at the center of a high-stakes geopolitical gathering this weekend as BRICS leaders meet amid multiple wars and a crowded diplomatic calendar, with the US-Iran war set to test the unity of the expanding non-Western bloc.
The war has put BRICS member Iran in direct conflict with Washington, while other countries in the grouping have sharply different relationships with both sides.
That tension will loom over the two-day BRICS Leaders' Summit on Saturday and Sunday, where Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi will host Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, among other leaders.
The summit comes at a "time of belligerent actions as well as great flux in the international order and international life," Sourabh Gupta of the Institute for China-America Studies told Anadolu.
The gathering will be closely watched in the West, with the Iran war, Russia-Ukraine war, global trade disputes and issues such as artificial intelligence and blockchain payments all likely to feature prominently, he said.
For British political expert Martin Jacques, BRICS' expansion has made the grouping "more important" in the current geopolitical climate.
Originally comprising Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, BRICS expanded in January 2024 to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, followed by Indonesia in January 2025.
The 11-member grouping has since broadened its reach further, with Belarus, Bolivia, Kazakhstan, Cuba, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, Uzbekistan and Vietnam joining as partner countries in 2025.
Its significance has also grown because of US President Donald Trump and “the widespread antipathy in the Global South for Trump and his policies," Jacques told Anadolu.
The gathering comes less than two weeks before the UN General Assembly's high-level week and Xi's expected Sept. 24 meeting with Trump.
The US-Iran war will "cast a shadow over" the summit, said Praveen Donthi, senior India analyst at the International Crisis Group.
The conflict poses a particularly difficult test for a grouping that operates by consensus, with its members holding sharply different positions and pursuing their own national interests.
"Members will try to push forward their own agendas and might even derail the main agenda," Donthi told Anadolu from India.
Gupta emphasized the fact that Iran is fighting the US, whose political and economic influence extends across the world and affects the calculations of other countries in the grouping.
Those differences are likely to become particularly visible over their response to the threat of additional US sanctions on countries doing business with Iran.
"No doubt, the BRICS will have a common hortatory position on the Iran sanctions. These sanctions are, for the most part, unilateral sanctions … and the BRICS member countries hold a common position in principle against such extraterritorial measures," Gupta said.
But agreement in principle does not mean a common response.
“There will be little unity on display in terms of their responses to the sanctions," he said.
China, Gupta predicted, will "stare down the US on the sanctions," while India will "mutely adhere to them" and Brazil and South Africa will "discontentedly abide by them."
Donthi similarly questioned whether the summit could produce consensus on the conflict.
"The grouping includes members from opposing camps in the US-Iran war, so it's unlikely to reach consensus on such issues," he said.
Jacques said one of the most revealing aspects of the summit will be how openly BRICS leaders challenge Washington over Iran.
"What might it say about the US-Iran conflict, to what extent countries of the BRICS show displeasure towards Trump's foreign policy on Iran – that is going to be interesting," he said.
Geopolitical analyst Einar Tangen said members are seeking greater strategic autonomy rather than a wholesale break with the US-led economic system.
"Members do not want a confrontation with the United States, but they don't want to be dependent on Washington, Beijing, Moscow, or any other powers," the Beijing-based analyst told Anadolu.
“BRICS+ aims to protect its members against disruptions in trade, finance, energy, and technology without separating from the West,” he added.
Rather than an "anti-American alliance," Tangen described BRICS+ as a "network of overlapping partnerships designed to survive a less predictable global order."
That balancing act is reflected in India's theme for this year's summit: Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability. For Tangen, the emphasis on resilience reflects the upheaval confronting countries across the Global South.
"Ongoing wars … including Ukraine, Iran, Gaza, Sudan, Yemen, the Sahel, and eastern Congo – drive the push for resilience and the need for diplomacy and peace," he said.
US tariffs, export controls and sanctions are also pushing countries to explore ways to reduce their exposure to economic pressure, according to Tangen.
"The economies are initiating countermeasures, which Washington ironically uses to justify its original actions and support another round," he said.
Gupta said the disruption extends beyond geopolitics.
"Elevated global financial risks mean that disruption is not solely limited to global geopolitics; competitive geoeconomics has also risen to the fore," he said.
But when forced to choose, he argued, individual BRICS members are still likely to prioritize their own economic interests.
Each country "will prioritize its ties to the US and access to the dollar-based international financial system over the common hortatory BRICS position," he said.
The sight of Modi, Xi, Putin and Pezeshkian gathered "under the same non-Western roof" will itself be one of the summit's defining images, Gupta said.
Their presence is likely to attract close attention in Western capitals as BRICS seeks greater influence in a global system long dominated by the US and its allies.
There is “bound to be some anxiety and curiosity in Western capitals,” Donthi said.
But he cautioned against overstating the cohesion behind the optics.
Western governments, he said, are also likely to recognize the grouping's limitations and the complicated bilateral relationships among its members, including between India and China.
Gupta similarly argued that Western unease over the summit may say as much about the West's own uncertainty as it does about BRICS' ability to act collectively.
"In part, this has more to do with the West's own lack of confidence than any major cohesive steps that the BRICS are taking," he said.
The summit will also revive a longstanding question surrounding whether the bloc can reduce its dependence on the US dollar.
Tangen dismissed the prospect of a single BRICS+ currency as “not feasible,” but said members are “aggressively expanding” the volume of transactions settled in their own currencies, including the Indian rupee and Russian ruble.
“There is the possibility to use a basket of currencies approach to a trade settlement fiat, but the extra step may not be worth the cost, as long as there are transaction services to smooth out direct currency trade issues,” he said.
“While the dollar remains central to global finance, alternative settlement systems are gradually eroding its monopoly on international trade,” he added.
Gupta recalled Trump’s intense backlash against the idea in late 2024.
“The idea that the BRICS Countries are trying to move away from the Dollar while we stand by and watch is OVER," Trump posted on his social media platform Truth Social, threatening 100% tariffs on any countries that move to replace the "mighty" US dollar.
Even so, Gupta said Western governments will be watching what he called BRICS' "baby steps" toward an alternative global economic architecture, including blockchain-aided payment systems among members.
Donthi also highlighted clashing views on alternative currency systems.
“Middle powers such as India wouldn’t be keen on weakening the dollar, especially without a viable alternative, which would make its primary strategic rival China stronger,” he said.

Egypt to protect Suez Canal from Houthi Bab al-Mandeb takeover
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:30:15 UTC
22:30:15 KST

Breadcrumb
Egypt activates plans to protect Suez Canal from Houthi Bab al-Mandeb takeover
Egypt has formed a crisis team to monitor developments around the Bab al-Mandab Strait after Houthi forces reached the strategically located Yemeni island of Mayyun, an informed Egyptian source has told The New Arab.
Mayyun, also known as Perim, lies at the southern entrance to Bab al-Mandab, one of the world's most important shipping chokepoints, connecting the Gulf of Aden with the Red Sea and, further north, the Suez Canal.
The Egyptian source said Cairo was concerned about the potential impact of the latest military developments on shipping in the Red Sea and traffic through the Suez Canal, a major source of revenue for Egypt.
The crisis team was established urgently after Egyptian authorities received reports of developments around the strait and was continuing to assess the situation, the source said.
Egypt believes the latest development represents a different type of threat from previous Houthi attacks on shipping, which have largely involved missiles and drones.
The source said the movement of fighting to territory immediately surrounding Bab al-Mandab had changed the nature of the risk.
Cairo had activated existing channels of communication with the Houthis to establish what was happening on the ground, clarify the objectives behind their movements and determine whether they were linked to the wider regional escalation, the source added.
Egypt was also in contact with the United States, Saudi Arabia and Iran in an attempt to contain the situation and prevent developments in Yemen from becoming a sustained threat to Red Sea shipping.
The source said Cairo had warned against further escalation because of the strategic importance of Bab al-Mandab.
Egypt viewed security in the strait as directly connected to its own national security and to the operation of the Suez Canal, rather than simply as a Yemeni or regional issue, the source said.
“The central message” in Cairo's diplomatic contacts was the need to prevent escalation and preserve the security of navigation, according to the source.
The source warned that turning Bab al-Mandab into a direct arena of confrontation between regional and international powers would have repercussions far beyond Yemen, potentially affecting the Red Sea, the Suez Canal and the global economy.
Former Egyptian Assistant Foreign Minister Mohamed Hegazy told The New Arab that the Houthi advance towards Bab al-Mandab, including their arrival in Dhubab and Mayyun, represented a significant change in the Red Sea security environment.
He said the significance of the development went beyond the capture of territory inside Yemen because of Bab al-Mandab's role in international shipping.
The narrow strait forms a key part of the sea route linking the Gulf of Aden and Indian Ocean with the Red Sea and Suez Canal.
Hegazy said the Houthi presence in such strategically sensitive areas increased the risks for commercial shipping and could give the group greater leverage over maritime traffic without requiring it to formally close the strait.
An increase in the perceived security risk alone could affect decisions by shipping companies and insurers and prompt changes to international trade routes, he said.
Hegazy warned that continued fighting close to Bab al-Mandab risked accelerating the militarisation of important maritime routes and further destabilising regional trade and energy flows.
The warning comes as several strategically important waterways in the region are already facing heightened tensions.
Egypt has particular concerns because disruption at Bab al-Mandab can directly affect traffic heading north through the Red Sea towards the Suez Canal.
Sustained disruption could therefore have consequences both for global trade and Egypt's economy, Hegazy said.
He argued that protecting the Red Sea required greater co-ordination among countries bordering it, as well as efforts to strengthen the stability of states along the maritime route.
Strategic locations in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden should not be turned into instruments of regional rivalry, he added.
Hegazy said any response should not rely solely on military measures, but should also involve diplomatic and political efforts to prevent the war in Yemen from expanding.
The priority, he said, should be to maintain freedom of navigation and prevent Bab al-Mandab from becoming an open arena of conflict threatening both regional security and the global economy.
