Breadcrumb
New York City marks 25th anniversary of 9/11 attacks
New York commemorated the 25th anniversary of the 11 September 2001 attacks Friday with a ceremony marked by controversy over President Donald Trump's absence and right-wing xenophobic outrage over the attendance of the city's first Muslim mayor, Zohran Mamdani.
In an unusual move, Trump was paying his respects at the Pentagon, rather than joining the event in New York, where hijacked planes destroyed the World Trade Center and killed almost 3,000 people.
Vice President JD Vance and Trump's four living predecessors—Republican George W. Bush, who was in office during the attacks, and Democrats Joe Biden, Barack Obama and Bill Clinton—were gathering at the Ground Zero site in lower Manhattan.
The ceremony, which began just after 8:40 a.m (1240 GMT), was designed to be apolitical, with no speeches.
Bereaved family members were reading out the names of all of those killed, with a bell tolling to mark major moments of the attack, which sparked years of US wars in the Middle East wars, killing and injuring millions and highlighting Washington's dire human rights record.
"Memorials like this and discussions about those events are an important part of keeping it alive and understanding how we prevent tragedies like this from ever happening again," said Robert Kafka, a Chicagoan in his 60s visiting the 9/11 Memorial.
Alongside the former presidents was Democratic Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the Big Apple's first Muslim mayor.
He faced a well organized campaign urging him to stay away spearheaded by the right-wing New York Post and former mayor and Trump-ally Rudy Giuliani.
A petition, which has gathered more than 100,000 signatures, accuses Mamdani of associating with unspecified individuals who are "dismissive of American institutions or insufficiently critical of extremist ideologies."
"It's concerning to me that the mayor is being treated differently simply because he is Muslim," city council member Shahana Hanif told CNN.
Mamdani won plaudits for recently revealing thousands of documents showing what city officials knew about toxicity levels of the air in Lower Manhattan following the attacks.
After the initial dust cloud that followed the collapse of the World Trade Center, months of pollution and lingering dust ensued, causing cancers from which thousands of New Yorkers still suffer today.
'Toxic air'
Nineteen Al-Qaeda operatives hijacked four airliners on the nearly cloudless autumn day in 2001. Two of the jets slammed into the World Trade Center's Twin Towers, causing the iconic 110-storey buildings to collapse.
A third plane struck the Pentagon, while a fourth—believed to have been aiming for Congress or the White House—crashed into a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers fought back.
Beyond those killed on 11 September, more than 9,400 other people have died from 9/11-related illnesses, according to the federal program established to provide medical care to those affected.
Logan Miller, 32, lost his uncle during the attacks, and his grandfather to 9/11-related illness in the aftermath.
"I think the next generation just can't fathom what actually transpired and how someone could be impacted by that, and so I actually find them asking more questions," he told AFP.
Huge crowds were expected to gather in Lower Manhattan for the memorial service.
The Secret Service, which protects presidents, erected a security ring around the site of the 9/11 Memorial and Museum.
City police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said an anti-drone team would be deployed as a precaution, but stressed there was no intelligence of a specific threat.
Al-Qaeda meanwhile has marked the anniversary by releasing a video showing images of late leader Osama bin Laden and his son Hamza, who Trump said in 2019 had also been killed during a "war on terror" that has impacted millions of lives.
Ahead of the memorial, a drone show with 2,977 lights rose above New York Harbor, one for each person killed in the attacks.

MAPUTO, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese-built higher polytechnic institute has been inaugurated in Quissico, southern Mozambique, with President Daniel Chapo attending the ceremony and inaugurating the institution.
Speaking at the ceremony on Thursday, Chapo said Mozambique borders the Indian Ocean and is endowed with abundant rivers, lakes, freshwater and marine resources, adding that the Quissico Higher Polytechnic Institute will help strengthen local fish production and processing capacity, enhance young people's employment and entrepreneurial skills, and create more development opportunities for local communities.
Located in Quissico, Zavala District of Inhambane Province, the institute offers programs including aquaculture engineering, fish processing and quality control engineering, as well as logistics and transport.
Sergio Mulema, director-general of the institute, said Zavala is home to many artisanal fishing communities, while insufficient fish preservation and processing capacity has long constrained the development of the local fisheries sector.
With the institute now operational, training and related services in aquaculture and fish processing will help reduce post-catch losses and increase the added value of fishery products, Mulema said.
He added that the modern and practical infrastructure built by the Chinese company can meet the needs of polytechnic education and laboratory practice, while creating better conditions for local young people to pursue higher education and acquire skills in fish production and processing.
According to Wei Wei, general manager of the Mozambique branch of China Jiangsu International Economic and Technical Cooperation Group Ltd., the institute has eight classrooms, five laboratories, two computer rooms and a library. Its student dormitories can accommodate 216 people, while the campus is also equipped with aquaculture ponds, fish processing facilities and supporting service facilities.
"Young people are an important force for Mozambique's future development. We hope the institute will train more professionals in marine and fisheries technologies, provide talent support for local industrial development, and contribute to the friendship between the peoples of China and Mozambique," Wei said. ■

NAIROBI, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- Kenya is committed to the regional integration agenda and rejects xenophobia and discriminatory treatment targeting small-scale traders from neighboring countries amid reports of harassment and attacks against them, senior officials said Thursday.
Musalia Mudavadi, prime cabinet secretary and cabinet secretary for foreign and diaspora affairs, said that Nairobi welcomes commercial activities by foreign nationals provided they comply with local regulations.
The clarification came as dozens of Burundian traders gathered at their embassy in Nairobi to regularize their immigration status or prepare to leave the country following President William Ruto's Sept. 2 order restricting foreign participation in small-scale businesses.
The presidential directive triggered widespread anxiety among foreign nationals, particularly Burundian migrants and residents from Central and East Africa, who work as street-vended merchandise sellers, small retailers, hoteliers, construction workers, and agricultural laborers.
The government clarified that it does not intend to expel foreign small-scale traders, and asked non-citizens to formalize their immigration status, register their businesses, and comply with national tax regulations.
Reiterating Kenya's commitment to mutual respect, shared values, and human dignity, Mudavadi said that the presidential directive aims to protect vulnerable economic sectors, promote fair market competition, and safeguard local livelihoods rather than drive out traders from neighboring countries.
"Kenya is not implementing a blanket ban on foreign nationals engaging in small-scale businesses but is seeking to ensure that their participation is consistent with the East African Community Common Market Protocol and applicable national law," Mudavadi told foreign diplomats in Nairobi.
He outlined Kenya's stance on key issues including its commitment to regional integration, multilateralism, preparations for the 2027 general elections, economic performance, and responses to emerging challenges such as health threats and seasonal El Nino rainfall.
"We continue to advance regional integration and continental unity by facilitating the free movement of people, capital, goods and services in accordance with applicable legal frameworks," said Mudavadi.
Kenya has for decades served as a haven for refugees and asylum seekers fleeing conflict, economic distress, and climate shocks across the region, noted Abraham Korir Sing'Oei, principal secretary at the State Department for Foreign Affairs.
Sing'Oei reaffirmed the government's unwavering commitment to protecting the lives, property, and livelihoods of all citizens from East African Community member states residing in Kenya. ■

China unveils AI-powered mineral exploration, geological mapping systems

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
21:11:22 CST
22:11:22 KST

TIANJIN, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- China on Friday unveiled two mineral exploration and geological mapping systems powered by AI. The launch marks their global debut and aims to make geological workflows more efficient and intelligent.
The two systems, AI-OreSeeking and AI-GeoMapping, were released by the Ministry of Natural Resources at the ongoing 28th China Mining Conference and Exhibition held in north China's Tianjin Municipality.
Traditionally, mineral prospecting has relied heavily on experts to analyze data from multiple sources. The AI-OreSeeking system integrates data, knowledge, algorithms, models and tools used in mineral exploration to automate the prospecting workflow. This shifts the process from experience-driven to intelligence-enabled.
The new system can gather and integrate multi-source geoscience data, interpret and extract key mineralization information, delineate favorable prospecting areas, estimate mineral reserves, generate professional maps in batches, and produce evaluation reports.
Test data from AI-OreSeeking show that mineral prediction and evaluation that once took half a year can now be completed in just one week.
So far, it has been trialled in more than 100 projects across over 10 provincial-level regions in China, including Xizang, Xinjiang, Fujian, Shandong and Inner Mongolia.
As for geological mapping, it is like drawing a navigation map for the subsurface mineral world, said Ren Shoumai, an official with the China Geological Survey.
The AI-GeoMapping system is designed to cover the full process from preliminary research, data collection, to map generation and map compilation. It can identify geological bodies with an overall accuracy exceeding 90 percent and improves the efficiency of data processing, integrated analysis, and geological map compilation by more than 50 percent compared to traditional methods.
The system has been trialled in nearly 100 map sheets at a scale of 1:50,000 across Qinghai, Xizang, Xinjiang, Fujian and other provincial-level regions in China. The system has also been promoted and applied in countries such as Morocco, Saudi Arabia, and Laos.
The two systems, independently developed by the China Geological Survey, are expected to provide a technical reference for the intelligent transformation of global mineral exploration and inject new momentum into global geological survey technological innovation, said Ren at the conference.
Themed "Win-Win Cooperation, Green and Intelligent," the event has attracted more than 650 domestic and overseas enterprises. Running from Thursday to Saturday, it features forums, exhibitions and mining rights trading activities, focusing on topics that include high-quality development of the mining sector and mine ecological restoration. ■

Germany’s far-right party, Alternative for Germany (AfD), has announced that it has filed a defamation complaint against Friedrich Merz, Politico reports.
In a speech, Merz stated that the “remigration” plan proposed by the AfD was akin to ethnic cleansing.
Stephan Brandner, an AfD representative in the Bundestag, emphasized in a statement that Merz’s insinuation—suggesting the AfD parliamentary group (which is firmly grounded in the German Constitution) was committed to ethnic cleansing, specifically deportation and murder—was so explicit that the justice system ought to intervene in the matter.
Merz commented on the AfD proposal during a Bundestag debate on the 9th of September. He stated that “remigration” is nothing more than a synonym for ethnic cleansing based on skin color and ethnicity.
Merz also added that the AfD’s plan to reduce migration would ruin the German economy.
Under Article 46 of the German Basic Law, members of the Bundestag are protected from legal proceedings regarding statements made in parliament. However, this protection does not extend to defamatory insults. In Brandner’s view, Merz’s remarks crossed the line, thereby paving the way for legal action. Merz has not commented on the AfD’s proposal, and his press representatives also did not respond to a request for comment.
“Remigration” is a far-right concept used by the AfD to refer to the deportation or return to their countries of origin of migrants whom the party deems ineligible to remain in Germany. It can encompass a wide range of scenarios, from the deportation of individuals without legal status to the mass expulsion of migrants and their descendants. The AfD dedicated an entire chapter to immigration and remigration issues in its election manifesto for the federal state of Saxony-Anhalt.

Arab Americans rise from 9/11 shadows to US political power

2026-09-11

Breadcrumb
From 9/11 surveillance to the ballot box: How Arab and Muslim Americans are building a new political power in the US
For 25 years, Arab Americans and Muslim Americans have lived in the shadow of the September 11 attacks, watchlisted at airports, treated as security threats, and monitored by federal agents who viewed their mosques with suspicion.
In the summer of 2026, two Egyptian American candidates won Democratic primaries, putting a long-surveilled community on the November ballot, backed by a new financial infrastructure built specifically to challenge the pro-Israel lobby's dominance in Democratic politics.
In New Jersey, Adam Hamawy won a crowded Democratic primary for the open 12th Congressional District on June 2, defeating 11 other candidates with roughly 28% of the vote to succeed retiring Representative Bonnie Watson Coleman.
Weeks later, on August 4, Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeated Representative Haley Stevens, 48.7% to 47.3%, to win Michigan's Democratic Senate nomination for the seat Senator Gary Peters is vacating.
Both men were born in Egypt. Both ran on platforms sharply critical of US support for Israel's war in Gaza. Both face Republican opponents on November 3: Hamawy against Gregg Mele in a safely Democratic district, and El-Sayed against Mike Rogers in a race expected to help decide control of the Senate.
Both candidates were backed by American Priorities, a pro-Palestinian super PAC formed on February 12, 2026, led by Hannah Fertig, a Jewish political strategist who previously worked on Bernie Sanders' 2020 presidential campaign.
The group has pledged to spend more than $10 million during the midterms, drawing largely from a small pool of wealthy donors, many of them Muslim American technology and business figures, aiming to shield Israel-critical candidates from the kind of spending AIPAC has historically deployed against them.
By July, it had spent more in New Jersey's 12th District than in any other race, over $1.5 million backing Hamawy.
Hamawy, a retired US Army combat surgeon, served in Iraq, where he is credited with saving the life of then-Lieutenant Colonel Tammy Duckworth, now a US Senator, who endorsed his campaign.
In 2024, he volunteered to treat civilian patients in Gaza, an experience that shaped his central promise to end US military aid and weapons sales to Israel.
He raised $1.4 million by primary day and secured endorsements from the entire Congressional Progressive Caucus, including Sanders, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and Rashida Tlaib.
"We were told that an outsider couldn't win. That we couldn't compete. Well, I think we competed," Hamawy told supporters on primary night.
His campaign was not without controversy. Opponents resurfaced his history as a defence witness in the 1995 terrorism trial of Omar Abdel-Rahman, the Egyptian-born "blind sheikh" convicted in a plot connected to the 1993 World Trade Centre bombing.
Rival candidate Adrian Mapp, mayor of Plainfield, called Hamawy a "radical extremist" over the association.
Hamawy's campaign responded that he "condemns that man's violent rhetoric and actions, and all violence, hatred, and terrorism," calling the attacks "bad-faith, guilt-by-association" tactics against Muslim and Arab candidates. The episode did not stop his win. If elected, Hamawy would become New Jersey's first Muslim member of Congress.
'Maybe they see us now'
For voters like Mariam Fouad, 58, a retired schoolteacher and mosque volunteer in Lawrence Township, the win carried a weight no ad campaign could capture.
"For years, my son Mina would get pulled aside at Newark airport before every trip. The first time he flew after 9/11, he was 14. He came home and asked me, 'Mama, do they think I'm a terrorist?' I didn't have an answer," she tells The New Arab.
"This summer, when Hamawy won, Mina called me from work. He said, 'Mama, maybe they see us now.' I stood in my kitchen and cried. I have voted in every election since I became a citizen, but I never put a yard sign in front of my house. This year I put one up. That is what this win means to me. Not that everything is fixed. But my kids can look at a ballot and see someone who has our name, our face, our story."
That shift showed up door by door, too.
Yousef Hamed, 26, a pharmacy student at Rutgers, served as a canvass captain for Hamawy's campaign, knocking doors in Trenton most nights after class.
"What people don't see is the same conversation happening over and over," he tells The New Arab.
He recalled one door in particular, an older Egyptian man in his seventies who initially waved him off. "He told me, 'We don't do politics. We keep our heads down.' I almost left. Then I said, 'Hamawy is a combat surgeon. He went to Gaza.' He went quiet. He came back with a photo of his brother's family in Khan Younis and asked me, 'Is this man really going to say our names out loud?' I said, 'He already has.'"
The man gave Hamed his phone number on the spot. "By the last three weeks, I was sleeping in my car between shifts. We knocked on over 15,000 doors," Hamed said. "It wasn't one big speech. It was one locked door at a time, one family story at a time."
'A tool for building political power'
In Michigan, El-Sayed's race became the most expensive Democratic primary in the state's history, with outside groups spending more than $60 million on Stevens's behalf.
AIPAC and affiliated groups alone poured in more than $30 million, the largest single investment AIPAC has made in any US election contest to date.
Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer endorsed Stevens late in the race in what was widely seen as an attempt to stop El-Sayed's momentum. He won anyway, by roughly one percentage point.
El-Sayed, a physician, Rhodes Scholar, and former director of Detroit's Health Department and later Wayne County's Department of Health, Human and Veterans Services, called Israel's military campaign in Gaza a genocide and demanded an end to US military aid to Israel.
It was his second bid for statewide office, after losing the 2018 Democratic gubernatorial primary to Whitmer. If elected in November, he would become the first self-identified Muslim senator in American history.
Jim Zogby, founder of the Arab American Institute, called the win "a watershed moment in US politics," telling Arab News: "He defeated dark money. He showed that Israel and their lobby could be publicly debated and defeated."
Maya Berry, the Institute's executive director, said Michigan voters "did not buy" an advertising campaign that ignored policy and instead attacked "an Arab American Muslim man named Abdul."
"I am thrilled for the rest of the country to learn that Michigan is not going to take it," she told Al Jazeera.
That sentiment echoed on the ground in Dearborn, home to one of the country's largest Arab American communities, where roughly 100,000 Michiganders had withheld their vote from President Biden in 2024's "uncommitted" protest over Gaza.
"Our basic needs continue to go unmet, and this definitely impacted the election results," Ahmad Abubakar, a Dearborn resident and journalist, tells The New Arab.
"Arab Americans in Michigan see primary ballots as a tool for building political power, not just a protest," adds Safiya Umar, a Michigan voter and resident.
Neither Hamawy nor El-Sayed has been elected to Congress yet.
Both face voters again in seven weeks, in races being watched closely as a test of whether a financial counterweight to the pro-Israel lobby can hold up in a general election, and whether a community defined for a generation by post-9/11 surveillance can now help decide who represents it in Washington.
Umar Ibrahim Agaie is an independent journalist and researcher covering environmental justice, tech-surveillance, and human rights

NAIROBI, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- The China-Africa Costume Culture and Art Exhibition was held Thursday in Nairobi, the Kenyan capital, featuring traditional Chinese costumes and a fashion show blending Chinese and African elements.
During the opening ceremony, Hanna Wendot Cheptumo, cabinet secretary for Kenya's Ministry of Gender, Culture and Children Services, said in a speech read on his behalf by Kiprop Lagat, director of culture at the ministry, that costumes are more than clothing, as they express identity, history, beliefs, social values and creativity.
Cheptumo noted China's rich traditions of clothing, textiles, embroidery, and weaving reflect its long history and craftsmanship, with the Mamianqun, or "horse-face skirt," being one example.
"Culture provides an important foundation" for engagement between nations and peoples, he said, noting that Kenya-China cooperation has expanded beyond economic and development partnerships to areas including education, tourism, science, technology, and people-to-people and cultural exchanges.
Zhang Zhizhong, charge d'affaires of the Chinese Embassy in Kenya, said the event is not only about appreciating beauty and creativity, but also about sharing expertise, building capacity and creating opportunities.
He quoted a Chinese proverb, "Virtue is not left to stand alone, and he who practices it will have neighbors," alongside an African proverb, "If you want to go fast, go alone; if you want to go far, go together."
These two sayings, though originating from different civilizations, convey a remarkably similar wisdom: lasting progress is achieved through partnership, solidarity and mutual support, he noted.
Zhang said China is willing to work with Kenya and other African countries to further deepen exchanges and cooperation in the fields of culture, tourism, women and creative economy, and across the board, so as to lay a solid foundation for building an all-weather China-Africa community with a shared future for the new era.
Noah Otiende Ochieng, secretary for Creative Economy at the State Department for Youth Affairs and Creative Economy, said Kenya's young population is increasingly active in fashion, music, film, visual arts, design and digital content, noting that partnerships can help turn creativity into opportunities, enterprises and sustainable livelihoods.
Ochieng encouraged Kenyan and Chinese designers, artists, cultural practitioners, students and creative entrepreneurs to work together, adding that events such as the exhibition can help build networks, exchange knowledge, develop partnerships and open new markets. ■

Slovakia's tourist accommodation numbers hit record in July
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
21:11:07 CST
22:11:07 KST

BRATISLAVA, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- The number of tourists staying in accommodation facilities in Slovakia rose 17 percent year-on-year to almost 780,000 in July, the highest level ever recorded for the month, the Slovak Statistics Office reported Friday.
The figure surpassed the record set in July 2019. Domestic visitors numbered 450,000, accounting for 58 percent of all visitors and up nearly 13 percent from a year before. Foreign arrivals jumped 23 percent year-on-year to nearly 330,000, also reaching an all-time high and exceeding the previous July peak in 2019 by 11 percent.
Visitors from the Czech Republic formed the largest group of foreign tourists, with about 102,000 arrivals, or 31 percent of the total. Polish tourists ranked second, with nearly 56,000 arrivals, accounting for 17 percent.
In total, visitors spent nearly 2.3 million nights at hotels, guest houses and other accommodation facilities across Slovakia in July. Domestic guests accounted for 1.4 million overnight stays, up by 8 percent year-on-year, while overnight stays by foreign tourists surged 25 percent to 855,000, 2 percent above the previous July record set in 2019.
Bratislava was the most popular destination among foreign visitors, with nearly 113,000 foreign guests. It was also the only Slovak region where foreign visitors outnumbered domestic tourists. ■

40,000 grounded icebergs around Antarctica mapped in high resolution
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
21:11:03 CST
22:11:03 KST

MELBOURNE, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- Nearly 40,000 stationary icebergs around Antarctica have been mapped for the first time, providing a new baseline for modelling coastal ice stability and understanding broader environmental changes.
Researchers have mapped crucially important features of the Antarctic coastal zone in high resolution by training an artificial intelligence tool to accurately recognize grounded icebergs from satellite radar images, according to a statement released Friday by the Australian Antarctic Program Partnership (AAPP).
Grounded icebergs are large icebergs that run aground on the Antarctic seafloor, where they can anchor sea ice, help hold back land ice from slipping into the ocean, and provide habitat and nutrients for marine ecosystems, according to the study published in Earth System Science Data.
The project aimed to replace manual satellite-image analysis with accurate, continent-wide automated mapping of grounded iceberg distribution and size, said Jiao Kaihong, a PhD student with the AAPP at Australia's University of Tasmania, who led the project.
Researchers used satellite radar imagery to map 39,619 stationary icebergs in 2025, covering a combined area of 13,430 square km and extending along 57 percent of the Antarctic coastline.
They found that tiny icebergs less than 1 square km accounted for 93 percent of all grounded icebergs and 54 percent of the total grounded area.
The researchers said tiny icebergs are more susceptible to melting than larger ones and becoming ungrounded as oceans warm, potentially causing abrupt changes in the stability of landfast ice. ■

22:10:33 KST

ADEN, Yemen, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group seized the strategic Mayun Island in the Bab al-Mandab Strait on Friday after government troops withdrew, a local government official told Xinhua.
The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Houthi forces had arrived on the island early Friday aboard several boats and took control without military resistance. The Houthis also deployed armored vehicles and other military equipment along the nearby coast, he said.
Houthi forces have also advanced into Dhubab district near the strait after government troops withdrew southward following the Houthis' capture of the Red Sea port city of Mocha on Thursday, the official said.
Mayun, also known as Perim, lies inside the Bab al-Mandab and divides the narrow waterway into two shipping channels. Its capture, following the Houthis' recent advances along Yemen's western coast, gives the group control of key positions overlooking the vital maritime trade route linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.
The Houthis captured Mocha after fierce fighting and took control of its strategic port, airport and key government facilities. They have made rapid territorial gains along Yemen's western coast since launching a major offensive last week.
The Bab al-Mandab, between Yemen and the Horn of Africa, is a critical corridor for international trade and energy shipments, linking the Red Sea and Suez Canal with the Gulf of Aden and the Arabian Sea.
The latest developments come amid an escalation in Yemen's conflict. The country has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, forcing the internationally recognized government out of the capital. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in the conflict in 2015 in support of the Yemeni government. ■

Putin arrived in India’s capital and is scheduled to hold a number of meetings on the sidelines of the summit.
India-Russia relation
Moscow is one of New Delhi's most important strategic partners and military suppliers, and the two leaders were shown by Indian broadcasters grinning and patting each other on the back at the New Delhi conference centre where Saturday's summit will be held.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the US-Iran war in part by turning to Russia, despite Moscow's war in Ukraine and pressure from Washington and other Western capitals.
Putin last visited India in December 2025, but the two leaders met earlier this month at a Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan.
Modi, speaking in Bishkek, had urged Putin to move from an "endless war towards the end of war".
With more than 320,000 seafarers, India makes up a major part of the global merchant shipping workforce, and several have been killed or wounded in attacks on vessels in the Gulf as well as the Black Sea region.
Indian refiners nearly doubled crude imports from Russia in March, the weeks after the Middle East war erupted, helped by temporary US waivers.
Shipments then rose sharply to 2.71 million barrels per day in June and a record 2.81 million in July, according to trade intelligence firm Kpler.
Imports fell to 2.07 million barrels per day in August but remained significant, Kpler data showed.
Bilateral goods trade reached $59.9 billion in 2025-26, with India exporting $4.49 billion and importing $55.37 billion, according to Indian government data.

ChatGPT invented fake police testimony in murder appeal, New Mexico high court says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:05:00 UTC
22:05:00 KST

ChatGPT invented fake police testimony in murder appeal, New Mexico high court says
- A New Mexico lawyer used ChatGPT to create a court brief with fabricated police testimony and witnesses in a murder appeal, leading to a contempt ruling by the state's Supreme Court.
- The court fined attorney Stephen Aarons US$5,000 for submitting false information and will refer him to a disciplinary board, citing his lack of remorse and concern for his client.
- Aarons admitted he did not understand AI's tendency to "hallucinate" facts and called it an honest mistake, highlighting growing legal risks of unverified AI-generated documents.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – A defence lawyer appealing his client’s murder conviction submitted a brief containing made-up police testimony and witnesses fabricated by OpenAI’s ChatGPT, New Mexico’s highest court said.
The New Mexico Supreme Court on Sept 9 fined the attorney, Stephen Aarons, and held him in contempt for failing to verify the accuracy of the court filing, which Aarons said he prepared with help from the AI programme.
The filing “contained false testimony from wholly fabricated witnesses”, the court said.
The panel also said Aarons had “demonstrated a lack of remorse and a lack of concern for his client”.
The justices fined Aarons US$5,000 (S$6,340) and said they will refer him to an attorney disciplinary board for investigation.
Aarons, in a statement to Reuters, said he had used ChatGPT to summarise the trial proceedings when he agreed to take up the defendant’s appeal in 2025, and did not understand the degree to which AI could “hallucinate” facts.
“I am remorseful but hopeful that the disciplinary board takes into account it was an honest mistake,” he said. “It is a lesson learnt for all professionals who rely upon this powerful but sometimes unstable technology.”
OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The court’s sanction is the latest in a growing number of cases in which state and federal judges have disciplined lawyers for submitting court documents generated by AI tools without adequately vetting them.
Dozens of lawyers have been sanctioned for filing briefs where AI made up case citations or misquoted the law. Aarons’ filing appears to have gone further, containing fabricated witness testimony in a criminal appeal.
Aarons, a private attorney based in Sante Fe, was handling the appeal of Oscar Renee Sandoval, who pleaded not guilty to the murder of the mother of his children before he was convicted and sentenced in 2025 to life in prison.
The appeal is still pending and was assigned on Sept 2 to Kim Chavez Cook, a New Mexico public defender. Cook declined to comment.
The district attorney’s office for Dona Ana County also declined to comment.
The state supreme court in August ordered Aarons to explain how the fabricated material, which it said appeared to include “fictional statements that the shooter was wearing dark pants and a white shirt”, was included in his primary brief in the appeal.
Aarons told the court at an Aug 21 hearing that he fed a computer-generated transcript and other case materials to ChatGPT, presuming it would generate “a bulletproof summary”.
The justices sounded incredulous that Aarons was not fully aware of how AI can make mistakes.
“Counsel, do you watch the news? Do you listen to the radio? Do you read anything about what’s going on in the world?“ Justice C. Shannon Bacon said at the hearing.
“Because the problem with lawyers relying on AI hallucinations is an above-the-fold story every single day.” REUTERS

US lawmakers urge secretive British court to open up about Apple case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:03:33 UTC
22:03:33 KST

A bipartisan pair of American politicians is telling Britain’s most secretive court to stop hiding its handling of Apple’s legal fight against a government demand to break into its customers’ encrypted data, warning that Whitehall’s taste for secrecy is “needlessly” straining relations between the two allies.
The letter, shared with the Guardian ahead of being sent to the investigatory powers tribunal (IPT) on Friday, is signed by the Democratic senator Ron Wyden of Oregon and the Republican congressman Warren Davidson of Ohio.
The row dates back to January 2025, when the Home Office served Apple with a technical capability notice under the Investigatory Powers Act, which requires companies to assist law enforcement in providing evidence. The UK government demanded that Apple provide a mechanism to access encrypted iCloud backups worldwide, a call the company met by withdrawing its Advanced Data Protection encryption feature from UK users the following month. Apple’s challenge to that order at the IPT was later thrown out after the Home Office withdrew the original notice and issued a narrower one targeting only British users’ data.
“It is wholly inappropriate for a foreign executive body to attempt to dictate the distribution of powers within the US government, nor should it be permitted to use secrecy directives under the Investigatory Powers Act to frustrate Article I powers under the US Constitution,” the pair wrote.
In August this year, Apple lodged a fresh complaint at the tribunal challenging the government’s power to issue such notices at all, with a case-management hearing on how that claim will proceed now listed for this month – the very hearing the new letter is aimed at.
Wyden and Davidson also signed an earlier letter to the tribunal in March 2025, alongside other lawmakers, pressing for the case to be heard in public. That intervention appears to have had an effect: weeks later the IPT rejected the government’s attempt to keep the case entirely secret, ruling that the “bare details” of Apple’s claim, including the identities of the parties, could be made public after receiving representations that, the tribunal noted, “strongly argued in favour of open justice and against the proceedings taking place in secret”.
In the new letter, Wyden and Davidson write that Congress “is not only a co-equal branch of government, it is the First Branch”, and argue that no government can be allowed to place “its demands beyond the reach of legislative inquiry”. They accuse the Home Office of trying to use a foreign secrecy order to override the constitutional powers of the US legislature, after Apple told Congress it had been permitted to brief only the attorney general, the vice-president and their staff – but not lawmakers – about the dispute.
They argue that Britain’s own constitutional traditions hold that no government can place its actions beyond the reach of legislative scrutiny – the same principle, they say, the Home Office is now violating.
“The UK government,” they write, “cannot champion legislative oversight at home while using administrative gag orders to kneecap the constitutional authority of the US Congress.”

World leaders gathered in Bishkek for the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation’s 25th anniversary summit, as Kyrgyzstan concluded its year as chair.

From bottle stoppers to rockets: How Portugal is reinventing cork
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:00:56 UTC
22:00:56 KST

Portugal produces around half of the world’s cork. Here, the world’s largest cork company, Corticeira Amorim, continues to open new markets by transforming this ancient natural resource into high-tech materials. In this report, we explore its methods, from harvesting to production.
Work begins at dawn in Corticeira Amorim’s cork oak forests. Cork harvesting takes place between late May and August, and much of it is still done by hand.
“On average a tree can produce for 170 years, 200 years more or less, giving us 15 to 17 extractions.” explains Carlos Abreu, from the Communication Department at Amorim Florestal.
A cork oak takes at least nine years to regenerate its bark, and around 25 before it can be harvested for the first time. These long timeframes are difficult to reconcile with the needs of small and medium-sized producers who account for 90% of Amorim’s suppliers.
“With our initiatives in our forests, we are trying to show to other landowners that is possible to manage the forest differently and to have a good income.” Says Nuno Oliveira, Forestry Director at Amorim Florestal.
The Rio Frio estate showcases Amorim’s latest innovations. One of the world’s largest human-planted cork oak forests, it serves as an open-air laboratory. Here, researchers are testing ways to speed up the first harvest, select the best plants and increase productivity without disrupting the ecosystem. Healthy trees also produce better quality cork.
Harvesting is only the first step. An even more complex challenge is turning this raw material into an ever-expanding range of products. I travel to northern Portugal, to Amorim’s historic factories, where cork enters one of the world’s most advanced industries.
Founded as a family business in 1870, Amorim is now a multinational company with around 4,000 employees, operating in more than 100 countries and generating over €1 billion in annual revenue.
Today, cork is used in over 30 industries, from construction and insulation to flooring and sealing systems. Aerospace is among the fastest-growing sectors and also one of the most protected by industrial secrecy. But in the showroom, you can get your hands on these high-tech materials. Eduardo Soares, Innovation & Business Development Director, shows me one of their flagship products.
“P50, one of our best-known materials, which is essentially a cork composite, a thermal protection shield that is used in multiple stages of a launcher device, so whenever there is a need for protection from the heat.”
Amorim says it has invested over €90 million in research and development over the past 10 years. That high-tech approach has also transformed its core business: cork stoppers. The company declared long ago that it defeated TCA, the compound behind cork taint, which can spoil wine.
For Portugal, cork is more than a business. It is part of the country’s natural and cultural heritage. Finding new ways to use it also means keeping that heritage alive.

George W Bush’s impunity led to Trump’s lawlessness | Kenneth Roth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:00:05 UTC
22:00:05 KST

If George W Bush’s abusive response to the September 11 attacks had been prosecuted rather than swept under the rug, Donald Trump would be less able to pursue his lawless policies. We can’t rewind history, but we can learn from our historic failure.
Twenty-five years ago, on a clear and crisp morning, I was sitting in the Human Rights Watch office in the Empire State Building with an unobstructed view of the World Trade Center towers as al-Qaida operatives flew two commercial jets into them. The horror of the attack required a response, but Bush and his vice-president, Dick Cheney, chose to react by throwing out the rulebook. They deployed torture and endless detention without trial in Guantánamo.
At first, Americans were so fearful of another al-Qaida attack that many accepted the Bush administration’s argument that extraordinary measures were required. But as the utter brutality of the response became apparent, dissenting voices grew more pronounced. Yet the reluctance of later administrations to repudiate these measures laid the foundation for Trump’s misconduct.
A May 2009 meeting I had with Barack Obama epitomized the problem. He had recently assumed office and invited me and several colleagues to the White House to discuss his counter-terrorism program. The meeting was disappointing.
Our top priority was securing prosecution of the senior Bush administration officials who had ordered the systematic torture of terrorist suspects. Obama declined, wanting to look forward, not back. His priority was working with Congress to secure healthcare reform (ultimately the Affordable Care Act, or Obamacare) as well as on issues such as education and climate change. He felt that prosecuting senior Bush officials would be too contentious.
Other steps had already been taken to end the torture. Public outrage, hastened by the leaked Abu Ghraib photographs of US servicemembers mistreating detainees in Iraq, led even the Bush administration to stop. The Detainee Treatment Act of 2005, sponsored by the senator John McCain, himself a torture victim, closed some of the legal loopholes used by the Bush administration to justify the unjustifiable. But no senior official was ever prosecuted for the torture.
That left a legacy of impunity that haunts us. Later presidents have not revived the torture, although the administrations of Joe Biden as well as Trump have continued the flow of military aid to Israel despite its systematic torture of Palestinian detainees.
Yet the deliberate use of excessive force by Trump’s deportation agents suggests confidence in a similar impunity for today’s declared crisis du jour: immigration. The Trump justice department has closed its eyes even when immigration officials gratuitously shoot, and sometimes kill, people.
Bush’s lengthy detention of suspects without trial at Guantánamo has had even greater lethal consequences. Ordinarily, a criminal suspect must be charged and tried within a reasonable time or released. But the Bush administration often had no evidence to justify charges beyond confessions secured by torture. The military commissions designed to allow prosecution despite the torture proved to be travesties that to this day have not even begun the trial of the principal 9/11 suspects.
The legal device that the Bush administration used to justify endless detention without trial was to call the suspects “enemy combatants”. In war, it is possible to hold opposing combatants without trial until the end of the armed conflict, but there was no armed conflict with al-Qaida, only a series of horrible terrorist attacks.
Bush concocted the “war on terror”, but it wasn’t a real war because there was no organized military force on the other side to justify invoking the rules of war. Rather, the rhetoric was a contrivance to sidestep the requirements of criminal prosecution.
At the time, I argued that allowing this legal subterfuge could have dangerous consequences. If a declared but fake enemy combatant could be held indefinitely without charge, why could he not also be shot? After all, in war, there is no duty to capture combatants from the other side. So long as they are not in custody, they can be killed.
I made the argument in the meeting with Obama as a reason to close Guantánamo – to charge or release all its detainees. I couldn’t imagine that the US government would really start to shoot suspects whom it could detain. But that is what Trump is now doing, not with alleged al-Qaida terrorists but with drug suspects, using a similar theory.
Like Bush, Trump has concocted a war, this time with drug traffickers, even though there is no organized military force on the other side fighting the United States. He then declared suspected traffickers in boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific to be “narcoterrorists”. His aim is to justify summarily killing them by drone rather than capturing and prosecuting them. Trump has taken the Bush theory, modified it for the new enemy, and intensified the consequences.
Precursors to these murders can be found in the actions of the Obama and Biden administrations. They summarily killed people in Yemen and north-western Pakistan but at least maintained the pretense, though untenable, that these terrorist suspects posed an imminent threat to the United States because arrest was impossible in the relatively lawless terrain of these distant lands. That is, they invoked an exception in policing rules that allows lethal force rather than the fiction that these people were enemy combatants.
But that misuse of policing rules isn’t available for the drug suspects whom Trump is targeting because the US Coast Guard has a long tradition of successfully interdicting them at sea. Trump thus relies on his fake war to order them murdered instead.
The lesson I take is that when past abuses are glossed over rather than prosecuted, they set precedents that can come back to haunt us. It is never easy to establish the rule of law when the perpetrators are powerful officials. An administration rarely prosecutes itself, and later administrations have their own priorities. Addressing the past is often believed to require too much political capital.
But the rule of law is important. It is a value worth upholding even at a price. It is too late to address the Bush-era atrocities, but it is not too late to address Trump’s. He won’t do it, but we should insist that the next administration does. Meanwhile, state and international prosecutors should start now.
- 
  Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author of Righting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive Governments

====================================================================================================

How the Bold and Bloody True Story Behind The Uprising Reverberates Through History
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:00:04 UTC
22:00:04 KST

The wind reaches the fens of eastern England before the light does, moving over the marshes in long gray sweeps. Andrew Garfield, muddied and short of breath, labors through it: a farmer with his ox, cutting furrows into the land. His character, Ploughman, is a man who refers to himself simply by what he does. Grief has pared him down to labor and memory. The plague took his wife and children, and all that remains is a hut, the animal that shares it through the winter for warmth, and the daily toll of survival. It’s slow and thankless work, the kind a kingdom takes for granted as readily as the earth beneath its feet.
That lone farmer anchors Paul Greengrass’ new film The Uprising, in theaters Sept. 11. Written and directed by Greengrass, the filmmaker’s deepest reach into the past yet dramatizes the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, when tens of thousands of English commoners, taxed past endurance in the long shadow of the Black Death, marched on London to demand a fairer world. Around Garfield, Greengrass assembled a cast that includes Jamie Bell as the rebel priest John Ball, Cosmo Jarvis as the revolt’s military leader Wat Tyler, Thomasin McKenzie as Alyce, a fictional follower of Ball, Woody Norman as the boy king Richard II, and Katherine Waterston as the Countess, Richard II’s mother.
The film follows its hero from fens to road and road to London, then London toward the forest—as private grief grows into collective fury and fury reaches the gates of power. Beneath the armor and beyond the crowds, Greengrass’ epic hinges on the moment when people long treated as expendable begin to act on their claim to dignity and agency.
Greengrass invented Ploughman for the film, but the forces pressing in on him are no invention. The director opted not to build The Uprising around one of the revolt’s historical figures, such as Tyler or Ball. “I didn’t want my central character to be a soldier or a priest,” he tells TIME. “I wanted him to be emblematic of all the tens of thousands of people who rose up. They were all ordinary farmers, ordinary people who lived in villages and small towns, who’d had enough.”
That decision turns a vast uprising into the story of one man whose loss forces him to confront the larger indignities of the world that remains. Garfield recognized that feeling across centuries. “I think that everyone watching will feel that connection,” he says. “A kind of sense of: What do you do in the face of such grave injustice? How do we heal? How do we fight for our right to live a life of freedom and of dignity, and of connection?”
A glimpse of what life could be
The Black Death reached England in the summer of 1348, most likely aboard ships that came into the Dorset port of Melcombe. Moving through the country at an estimated one to five miles a day, it reached London by November and, within two years, killed as much as half of England’s population. In its wake, whole villages were left empty. The horror was intimate and unrelenting: households vanished, kin buried kin, and parishes lost the priests who once baptized and married their people. Fields went to weed, and livestock wandered untended; the familiar rhythms of rural life gave way to an eerie void.
The plague also changed the terms on which the survivors lived. Labor became scarcer, and scarce labor has a price. “What life could be is probably at the heart of this whole story,” says Dan Jones, the historian whose 2009 book Summer of Blood remains a defining account of the revolt. “Basic economics tell us that if you lose half the people, wages should go up. Rent should come down. Life for survivors ought, in theory, to get better.” Those left standing had reason to believe that life might improve.
That possibility ran up against what Jones calls the “vested interests of power structures.” In England, he says, the government “immediately passes laws to suppress wages”: It imposed a maximum wage and sent judges into the countryside to enforce it. Mass death had made the old hierarchy newly fragile, and Parliament moved to restore it, with the laborer kept in his place and the landowner’s command protected.
Then came the demands of war. England’s long conflict with France, a struggle over disputed territory as well as English claims to the French crown, continued, ruinous as ever, even as the plague cut the tax base and diminished the country’s productive power. The crown’s answer was a series of poll taxes, imposed on a population already strained by loss, labor restrictions, and military levies. There is, Jones says, “a class analysis to this rebellion”: elites were “taking aim squarely at the ordinary people,” first preventing them from improving their lot and then taxing them in ways they had not faced before.
By the spring of 1381, deprivation gave way to imagination. People who ached for a better life were being ordered back into the old one, by statute and tax collector alike. The revolt drew force from a realization that threatened every hierarchy above it: the social order was made by people, and people could change it.
When the country catches light
It began at the end of May, when villagers in Essex turned on the commissioners sent to collect the tax from them yet again. Within days, the uprising spread to Kent. On June 7, Tyler, likely a veteran of the French wars, emerged at the head of the Kentish rebels, who freed Ball, who had been jailed for seditious preaching, from the Archbishop’s prison at Maidstone; by June 10, they entered Canterbury.
The couplet most famously associated with Ball put the rebellion’s challenge in a single question: “When Adam delved and Eve span, who then was the gentleman?” In a kingdom that understood rank as God’s design, the question was revolutionary. Adam worked the soil and Eve spun thread; no aristocrat stood beside them. So who, the couplet asks, gave one class the right to rule another?
Jones describes Tyler and Ball as the revolt’s two hands, one holding the sword and the other the scriptures. Tyler brought military organization; Ball gave the movement its moral argument. “Between them, they create a very potent movement, because it’s not only organized but it’s radicalized,” Jones says.
The name history settled on undersells the people who rose up. “It’s a very broad coalition,” Jones says, and the term “Peasants’ Revolt,” a historian’s term, can “obscure just what a wide range of people were involved.” This was not a rising merely of the utterly destitute. Whole villages moved with their structures intact: local leaders, parish priests trusted with their neighbors’ souls, craftsmen, and laborers, were joined in the capital by Londoners keeping their own accounts of unfairness. By Jones’ estimate, the coalition’s grievances ran through some 85% of the country, aimed at a thin sliver at the top—not at the king, whom they claimed as their own, but at the advisers, bishops, aristocrats, and officials they believed corrupted the realm.
Women were certainly among the rebels. The surviving records place them at critical moments, including the storming of the Tower of London. Jones calls the revolt a “truly popular movement,” one that did not require its participants to possess the formal power otherwise held by men in a patriarchal society.
What happened inside the city is the part no telling can sanitize. The rebels threw open the prisons and set fire to the New Temple, a Thames-side compound where lawyers-in-training lived and kept the books and records that helped sustain the kingdom’s legal order. They breached the Tower itself, where the king sheltered, dragged out the two men they blamed for the tax, Archbishop Simon Sudbury and Treasurer Robert Hales, and beheaded them.
Jones contends the revolt demands two judgments at once. The grievances were real, and the people were being exploited. But the rising also became brutal, with violence extending beyond royal officials to others who were perceived as enemies of the revolt but had no hand in the tax. “You have to say that this was a good cause, and the rebellion got hideously out of control,” he says.
By midsummer, the revolt reached its breaking point. Richard II was 14, a boy raised from infancy to believe he was fated to save the realm. On June 14, he rode out to meet the rebels and granted their demands, the abolition of serfdom among them. At Smithfield the following day, Tyler was killed during a parley with the king’s entourage. Richard calmed the crowds by declaring they would have no leader but him, then turned against the rising. Within weeks, he canceled the freedom charters granted in London. His government hunted down the movement’s leaders and executed them, and the king is said to have told the petitioners that serfs they were and serfs they would remain, on terms harsher than before.
There is a catch in knowing this version of events. Many chroniclers were churchmen, and the church was among the rebels’ targets. The legal records are rich, Jones says, but were created from the “perspective of the suppression of the rebellion.” Historians, he says, “have to read against the sources.” The archive preserves the rebellion mostly as seen by those who feared or punished it.
A hero the record never named
The Uprising grew from an ambition Greengrass held for years. The filmmaker behind United 93, Captain Phillips, The Lost Bus, and three of the Bourne films had long wanted to make a historical epic in the tradition of Gladiator and Braveheart. The material found him during the COVID-19 pandemic. He began writing on the second day of lockdown, when there were no vaccines and no way of knowing how far the crisis would spread. The last pandemic on that scale led him back to the 14th century. By the time Jones first met with Greengrass, a map of London during the rebellion was already hanging in the director’s office. Soon, the filmmaker says, the period felt “eerily contemporary.”
The script’s first title shows how early the film had ties to the Robin Hood legend. “When I wrote it in lockdown, it was called The Hood because of the ending,” he says. Ploughman begins as a farmer, but his journey ends beyond the reach of the king’s law, in the forest. That turn places him beside an outlaw tradition already circulating in the late 14th century. William Langland’s Piers Plowman, the poem that helped inspire Greengrass’ protagonist, contains the earliest known written reference to Robin Hood, evidence that tales of the outlaw were already familiar before the surviving ballads were committed to writing.
Jones sees the Peasants’ Revolt and medieval outlaw tales, including stories of Robin Hood, as products of the same political world: one in which ordinary people saw legal authority serving the powerful rather than protecting them. The early Robin Hood was no polished folk hero, Jones says, but a violent, devout yeoman pushed to society’s edge by corrupt officials. Its central tension was the “fundamental difference between law and justice.” As Greengrass puts it, at a time when people “felt powerless and betrayed,” they told stories “about outlaws who stood up to power when they couldn’t.”
That rich idea shaped Greengrass’ choice of hero. Tyler and Ball could have supplied the film with a soldier and a priest, two historical figures already established in the record. Instead, the filmmaker begins with a farmer at the first spark in Essex, then follows him as the uprising gathers people, reaches London, and begins to turn against itself. The character is invented, but he comes from the revolt’s own language. Jones notes that actual letters found on Ball after his arrest, written to sustain the rebellion’s spirit, appeal to archetypal figures of the working land, including ploughmen like the one Garfield plays.
Giving Ploughman a life
Garfield felt the pull of his role at once. “It’s not often that I will read something and fight to play that part, and I did that with Paul,” he says. His note arrived after years of halting development, from an actor Greengrass knew only casually. “It’s the email you dream of getting from a brilliant actor who says, ‘I’ve read your movie. I really want to be in it,’” Greengrass says.
To prepare, Garfield began with the rhythms Ploughman would know. “It’s a man that lives in a very, very different time and in a very, very different rhythm to me,” he says. “Connection to the earth and connection to nature, that felt very, very important.” He researched the seasons, harvests, clothing, daily labor, and the habits of the ox. Before filming, he spent time in Ploughman’s hut with the animal, learning the terms of a household in which the ox slept indoors through winter to provide warmth. “Connection to his ox, that was the primary relationship in the story,” Garfield says. The animal is at once Ploughman’s companion, source of heat, and fellow laborer.
His wife and children are dead before the film begins, but Garfield imagined the life Ploughman lost so he could carry that grief across the film. He developed their history and their absence until they became, as he puts it, the “kind of invisible visible spirit characters that are there throughout the story.” Their absence helps explain why the character continues to seek justice, even after the uprising begins to lose its way. “They are the characters that are drawing him forward throughout the action of the film,” Garfield says.
That loss follows Ploughman beyond the hut and into his encounter with Richard II. He was taught that the king speaks with God’s authority. When the crown proves capable of betrayal, Garfield sees the break as spiritual as much as political. “It’s like waking up from a cult,” he says. “It’s like waking up from being manipulated and misled and brought down a path that was being governed by evil, power-hoarding, oppression, being disguised as a kind of spirituality.”
Greengrass places Ploughman’s awakening beside Richard’s. “Here’s this powerless farmer who is struggling to find agency in the world,” he says, and opposite him is “this 14-year-old boy king” trying to find agency of his own. Their paths cross, then diverge. “One goes from being the farmer to the outlaw, and the other goes from being the powerless king to the tyrant.”
Outside Ploughman’s hut, Greengrass worked to establish the larger world that makes that private life so vulnerable. “Deep period movies have quite a close relationship with science fiction,” he says. “They’re both really cinematic world creations.” Greengrass uses costumes to mark the division between court and country. The period’s sumptuary laws regulated dress by rank, especially the cost and luxury materials people could wear. In the film, Ploughman and the people around him move through a restricted color palette; Richard II’s court does not.
With little of medieval London still standing, Bavaria offered spaces that could be more readily adapted for the film’s 14th-century settings. At Penzing Studios, the open-air museum at Bad Windsheim, the fortress at Lichtenau, and sites in Nuremberg, the production found medieval stonework, corridors, chapels, crypts, and staircases suited to the royal court. St. Sebaldus Church, built in the 13th century, became several locations within the film. Constructed sets and visual effects widened those spaces.
The London uprising scenes required the opposite approach: not courtly rooms and corridors, but night shoots packed with bodies, smoke, fire, and a city coming apart. Garfield does not think of the German supporting artists who stayed through the shoot as simply “extras.” “These supporting actors were the vital ingredient of this project,” he says. “It was a really profound experience to share that march and those fights with the same group of people every day.” Greengrass moved that company through a handful of locations, recomposing them for each setup until a modest crowd read on screen as a revolt spilling across the capital, and shot the scenes in firelight, with takes that could last 15 or 20 minutes. Within those long takes, Garfield had to keep track of his character, what he saw, and how he responded as the crowd shifted around him. The firelit crowds give the film its largest scenes. But more critical than the technical logistics of these shoots was posing the questions that arose from their aftermath. What remained, the film asks, after Richard II effectively took London back and the revolt ended?.
What the revolt left behind
By summer’s end of 1381, the rising was broken: Tyler dead, Ball captured and executed, and the freedom charters canceled. Measured against its concrete demands, the revolt failed almost completely.
But the decades that followed tell a more complicated story. Serfdom, the institution the rebels once asked their king to abolish, withered; by 1450, Jones says, when England’s next great rising came under Jack Cade, it was effectively finished, and the people who marched that time were more politically fluent than their grandparents. Greengrass sees in 1381 a distant beginning for the individual rights that developed over centuries. Jones brings the historian’s longer view to that reading. “Straight lines can only be drawn through history with retrospect and with the blinkers on,” he says. “But this is a moment when the ordinary people step onto the political stage in the English-speaking world, and they are never thereafter off it.”
Greengrass’ ambivalence about such moments in history stems from his early work as a documentarian, when he filmed upheaval in Northern Ireland, apartheid South Africa, and other places where political orders were breaking apart. “Revolutions always eat themselves,” he says. “They start off with people’s intense hopes and dreams, but once you pull authority down, the result is chaos, and it’s only later, when it’s all over, that you can draw a ledger.” How to weigh that ledger, Greengrass leaves to the audience: gripped, he trusts, by Ploughman's journey, recognizing something of their own restless present in its medieval setting, and free to draw their own conclusions.
The man who ends the film in the forest is, for Garfield, the man he always was: an invisible person, the kind who passes unseen through an ordinary day as “someone who simply wants to live a life of truth and dignity.” “I think that we can all identify with that in a deep way, in a kind of core way," the actor says. He hopes audiences, once they see the film, will notice the invisible people around them, and the invisible parts of themselves that ask only for small liberties: wind on the face, a dance every once in a while, a walk amid what he calls the "hard work of being alive.”
That invisibility is rooted in centuries of historical silence. The archive remembers the crown, the church, and the officials who repressed the uprising more fully than it preserves the villagers who made it possible. Nearly everything that survives of the rebels comes down through their enemies’ pens; Greengrass’ film reaches toward lives that history left largely unseen. And while the revolt was put down in a distant summer, the claim beneath it—to dignity and agency—was not. It outlived the gallows, the revoked charters, and the chroniclers who reduced the people to a mob, and it endures in a handful of letters attributed to Ball urging the ploughmen of England to hold fast, written as if their author knew that in some inky field, one of them would look up. With The Uprising, Greengrass made a film about the man who does.

The Sept. 11 disasters still shape people’s health 25 years later
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

The Sept. 11 disasters still shape people’s health 25 years later
The health needs of those harmed in the terrorist attacks have evolved since 2001
Denise Harrison was working at Bellevue Hospital in New York City on September 11, 2001. The hospital had cleared the emergency room, anticipating a massive influx of patients after the terrorist attack at the World Trade Center, she says. “But it never really happened.”
“We had more doctors there than patients,” Harrison says. “We knew why. That was saddening.” Thousands died on September 11, when fires burned and buildings fell.
But for hundreds of thousands more who responded to the disasters, worked in the recovery or cleanup, or lived near ground zero, that day and its toxic aftermath continue to reverberate.
In New York City, when the twin towers collapsed, spewing dust and debris and polluting the air, the massive destruction and toxic exposures fueled respiratory diseases, cancers and mental health disorders.
It’s now 25 years later, and new health challenges are arising. Responders to the disasters are aging, developing health issues that can complicate their Sept. 11–related conditions. Retirement can deepen mental health struggles. Anniversaries can be triggering. The news reports and images dominating the airwaves and social media for this latest milestone “will definitely reactivate the emotions, the memories. And it doesn’t all go away on September 12,” says Jodi Streich, the mental health director at the World Trade Center Health Program at Rutgers University in Piscataway, N.J. “It stays.”
The paths of people harmed by the terrorist attacks have or may eventually intersect with the WTC Health Program, created to screen, monitor, treat and research the related health conditions. The program cares for people who worked in rescue, response, recovery and cleanup at the disaster sites in New York City, the Pentagon in Arlington, Va. and the plane crash site near Shanksville, Pa. It also covers people in New York City who lived, worked or attended school near the World Trade Center. As of summer 2026, more than 154,000 people are enrolled in the program, which is funded through 2090.
“Most disasters don’t end when the event ends,” says Harrison, medical director of the WTC Health Program at New York University. The WTC Health Program is “like a safety net” for her patients, Harrison says, where medical providers know their stories and their struggles. “They come where they are understood.”
Ongoing conditions, ongoing care
The WTC Health Program includes clinical centers in New York and New Jersey and a national network of participating doctors. People who qualify have an initial evaluation and yearly check-ups along with necessary specialized care at no cost to them. The program officially began in 2011, after Congress dedicated long-term funding to Sept. 11 health care.
The dust from the collapse of buildings at ground zero — the 110-story twin towers and a neighboring 47-story office building — clung to the air for nearly two weeks until it finally rained. Although crews continued to douse the debris pile with water, the work to recover bodies and clean the area stirred up the toxic dust again and again. Samples taken in the days after the disaster revealed metals, asbestos, carcinogens, lead, pesticides and many more toxic components in the dust.
On September 8, New York City released around 170,000 documents that discuss air quality and health risks just after the terrorist attack and suggest leaders at the time may not have fully revealed what they knew.
Iris Udasin, director of the Rutgers WTC Health Program, has been caring for people who responded to the Sept. 11 disasters since the beginning. “Initially everybody was coughing, a lot of them had asthma, a lot of them had sinus problems,” she says. Considering the toxic dust and fumes people were breathing, these health issues were expected.
Later, gastroesophageal reflux disease, or GERD, afflicted many people who responded to the disasters. In a cohort of more than 27,000 World Trade Center rescue and recovery workers, the incidence of GERD rose from close to 6 percent before the disaster to 39 percent nine years after the disaster.
Rescue and recovery workers from the New York City Fire Department suffered from a number of respiratory diseases, including obstructive airway disease, researchers reported just after the 20th anniversary of the attacks.
Notably, many people who responded to the World Trade Center disaster developed sleep apnea, despite lacking usual risk factors such as age and obesity. Through WTC Health Program research, “we discovered that sinus problems, especially related to environmental exposures, are a major risk factor for sleep apnea,” Udasin says.
Dozens of cancers are tied to Sept. 11 exposures, including prostate, skin and thyroid cancers. Mental health disorders including post-traumatic stress disorder, depression and anxiety are also elevated among people who responded to the disasters.
Many firefighters, police officers and other disaster site workers in the WTC Health Program are now in their 50s and 60s. With age, some are getting sicker, Udasin says, developing cardiovascular disease or diabetes, for example, which makes it more difficult to treat Sept. 11–related conditions.
And retirement “has brought on a whole different host of mental health setbacks,” Streich says. For some of her patients, work was a kind of therapy — a way to suppress what happened to them. Losing that structure can set people adrift.
Research has found that people who responded to the World Trade Center disaster report stigma associated with seeking mental health care. Streich says that some don’t come in for care until they’re at their lowest point. People who survived the disasters can also feel a tremendous amount of guilt that they made it through while friends and colleagues didn’t.
Streich also sees some of her patients struggling with memory and attention. Recent research has found a growing risk of cognitive dysfunction resembling dementia in people who responded to the disaster at ground zero or were survivors. The evidence suggests that the risk is associated with exposure to air pollutants and chronic post-traumatic stress disorder.
Responding to a new milestone
Even though it’s been 25 years, there are still people coming in to be screened for the first time, says Keisha Bennett, a nurse practitioner at NYU’s WTC Health Program. The initial visit includes a detailed questionnaire focused on the patient’s experiences related to September 11. “There are a lot of emotions that are involved,” Bennett says. She reminds her patients, “you’re not doing this alone.”
This is a big anniversary. But grief “is not a one size fits all,” Streich says. And trauma can surface on its own timeline: It “could be a year, it could be five and sometimes 25.” Some responders are grappling with the years lost “due to the mourning, due to the PTSD.”
During Streich’s tenure, the Rutgers program has started numerous mental health groups that have video meetings. One group has been together since the 20th anniversary of the disasters. Other groups focus on firefighters, police officers, retirees, cancer support or chronic pain issues. These spaces provide a sense of community, Streich says, and another source of support along with program check-ins and counseling appointments.
In her day-to-day providing care, Udasin sees the personal milestones her patients reach. She recounts one man, a disaster responder, who was left with a bad wound after having a severe mouth cancer removed. He realized he needed to see a psychiatrist because he was taking his unhappiness and anger out on his family. Since then, he told her he’s living a much better life.
“When I can get these big, tough policemen and firemen to go and get their mental health taken care of, that’s a really big deal to me,” she says. “We feel like we’ve been able to get these great people better care then they would have obtained if they had not come through program.”
