AI ’80s nostalgia craze sweeps Arab world — but not everyone is amused
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:28:38 UTC
20:28:38 KST

The artificial intelligence-fueled 1980s nostalgia trend has spread far beyond Israel, sweeping across the Arab world as celebrities, restaurants, banks and other companies embrace AI-generated images that transport them back to the decade of neon colors, vintage fashion and grainy photography.
In recent days, celebrities from several Arab countries have posted AI-generated images depicting themselves as if they had lived through the “colorful decade.” Businesses have seized on the craze for advertising, while television networks and newspapers have devoted reports and analysis to the phenomenon — including warnings about privacy, artificial nostalgia and the risks of handing personal photographs to AI platforms.
The trend received an especially skeptical examination from Qatar-based Al Jazeera, which asked why so many people who never experienced the 1980s are eager to portray themselves as if they had.
“Images with an ’80s aesthetic are popping up everywhere,” the network said in a report. “Yellow flash, warm tones and vintage fashion.”
But what appears to be a simple social media fad, the report argued, may reflect something deeper: Many of those participating have no actual memories of the decade they appear to miss.
“Why do we feel such powerful nostalgia for an era we never knew?” Al Jazeera asked. It attributed the phenomenon to what it described as “indirect nostalgia” — a longing for a time people did not personally experience but whose imagery they absorbed through movies and other media until it became part of their imagination.
The Al Jazeera presenter, who appeared less than enthusiastic about the trend, went further, questioning what happens when nostalgia becomes something that can be packaged and sold.
“What happens when an entire society escapes into this imagined past?” she asked. “Here, nostalgia turns from a personal feeling into an entire market that exploits our longing for the past and sells it back to us as a product or an AI filter.”
She also warned that such nostalgia could be used to influence people by appealing to romanticized notions of “the good old days.”
“The truth is that we don’t really love the ’80s or the ’90s,” she concluded. “We simply love any era in which we are promised that tomorrow will not surprise us with new fears.”
She left viewers with a question particularly suited to the age of generative AI: “Is the picture you posted a real memory, or a longing for a memory that never happened?”
From nostalgia to privacy concerns
Other Arab media outlets focused less on psychology and more on cybersecurity and privacy.
One television channel warned viewers that the photograph they upload to create an ’80s-style portrait may contain far more valuable information than they realize.
“Your ’80s-style picture looks great, but do you know where your picture goes afterward?” the report asked, warning that faces contain biometric information that can potentially be used in facial recognition technology.
The report also cautioned that links circulating online that claim to offer access to the trend could be fraudulent and potentially expose information stored on users’ phones.
Before uploading an image, it advised users to examine the application, its privacy policy and the link they are using.
“Going back to the ’80s may take only a few seconds,” it warned, “but your picture could remain online for years.”
Despite the criticism, plenty of businesses across the Arab world have enthusiastically joined the craze — and found ways to turn nostalgia into advertising.
A Saudi hamburger restaurant used AI to create its own retro images, writing: “Maybe we didn’t live through the ’80s, but we managed to imagine them in our own way.”
International banking group ADCB, which operates in Egypt, played on the contrast between old-fashioned technology and modern banking.
“If you thought life was easy in the ’80s, you’re wrong,” its advertisement said, adding that ADCB has made banking transactions even easier today.
A Saudi telecommunications company similarly posted an ’80s-inspired image featuring an old computer, accompanied by the line: “Days worth remembering, but never experiencing again.”
In Lebanon, the ’80s carry a darker meaning
Perhaps more surprisingly, the trend also caught the attention of Lebanon’s Al-Akhbar newspaper, which is affiliated with Hezbollah.
“A wave of nostalgia has swept social media, taking users back to the 1980s,” the newspaper wrote Friday.
But Al-Akhbar cautioned that what users see online is not necessarily an authentic representation of the decade.
Social media trends tend to select the most attractive elements of the past, it said — “colors, clothes, music, images and a general atmosphere of life that, from the distance of time, appears simpler.”
“The more substantial details of that period are often absent from the picture,” the newspaper added.
In Lebanon, that selective nostalgia carries particular historical baggage.
“In Lebanon, the matter is more sensitive,” Al-Akhbar wrote. “The return to the ’80s cannot be completely separated from the country’s history.”
Behind the family photographs, clothing and retro colors, the newspaper said, lie memories of “years of war, division, displacement and deprivation.”
The craze has meanwhile continued to draw attention across major Arab media outlets.
Saudi-based Asharq reported Tuesday on numerous Egyptian artists who had shared images of themselves as part of the trend.
Saudi-owned Al Arabiya took a more cautionary approach the same day, publishing a report under the headline, “Warning over Egypt’s ’80s trend: A trap for collecting photos and data.”
The network said the danger stems from the sheer volume of photographs and personal information users may be sharing through the various applications used to generate the retro images.
For now, however, those warnings do not appear to have stopped the flood of artificially aged photographs. Across Arab social media, a decade many of the trend’s participants never experienced has become one of the internet’s newest shared memories — created not by cameras or photo albums, but by AI.

Beijing lodges diplomatic protests over Taiwan official’s visit to Italy
European Parliament official says conference attendance by Hsiao Bi-khim was kept confidential to safeguard her participation
Beijing has strongly condemned a visit to Italy by senior Taiwanese officials and lodged formal diplomatic protests with both Rome and Brussels.

Materials on the criminal organization, which specializes in cryptocurrency fraud, have already been handed over to law enforcement.
The head of the State Financial Monitoring Service stressed that transactions involving virtual assets remain the hardest to trace due to the lack of regulation and transparent oversight mechanisms in Ukraine, but said such schemes are nonetheless successfully uncovered through analysis of financial flows, links between companies, and owners' digital footprints.

9/11 conspiracy theories that continue to circulate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:26:00 UTC
20:26:00 KST

9/11 conspiracy theories that continue to circulate
September 11, 2026
The terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001, also known as 9/11, were the worst such attacks in history. Twenty-five years on, they have been thoroughly investigated and analyzed — yet many people still believe the conspiracy theories that swirl around the suicide attacks in the United States.
First, a reminder of the event itself. On September 11, 2001, the Islamist terrorist network al-Qaeda hijacked four passenger planes. Two were flown into the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York City. A third crashed into the Pentagon, just outside Washington, D.C., the headquarters of the US Department of Defense. The fourth airliner is believed to have been heading for the Capitol in Washington, the seat of the US Congress, but it crashed in rural Pennsylvania after passengers staged an intervention to prevent the hijackers from reaching their target. The suicide attackers killed almost 3,000 people that day, and injured thousands more. Live footage of the attacks was broadcast all around the world.
September 11 was an event that changed the world — not only in terms of terrorism, but also conspiracy theories.
"September 11 was a trigger point that led to so many things: debates in society as a whole that hadn't happened before, security problems no one had had to deal with before," historian Claus Oberhauser explained in an interview with fact checkers from BR-Faktenfuchs.
Daniel Jolley is a professor of social psychology at the University of Nottingham who researches the societal repercussions of conspiracy theories. He told DW that conspiracy theories often spring up around events like this. Even today, many people still wonder how it was possible for the most powerful country in the world to be so utterly blindsided — and some believe conspiracy narratives provide the answer.
20% of Americans believe the government was involved
According to a 2023 YouGov survey, one in five Americans believe the US government was behind the 9/11 terrorist attacks. It's a claim that has been circulating for decades. Jolley said it shows that many people mistrust institutions and "those in power."
A conspiracy narrative that bolsters this myth is the claim that the twin towers and other World Trade Center buildings were brought down not by two passenger jets — or not by these alone — but with controlled explosions.
Not only does this allegation continue to spread on social media, it is also based on the assertions of a small number of scientists. For example, one of their arguments is that the horizontal clouds of smoke seen when the towers collapsed supposedly indicate controlled explosions in lower floors.
However, there is no evidence whatsoever that explosives or bombs were found at the site. Investigations like the one carried out by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) explain how the two passenger planes crashing into the twin towers caused them to catch fire and collapse. According to the NIST, videos of the attack support the scientific evidence.
Other analyses, like those done by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) or the consultancy firm Weidlinger Associates, reached the same conclusion.
Why do people believe conspiracy theories?
Events like 9/11 can leave certain psychological needs unfulfilled, Jolley explained: "The needs being: to want to feel in control, to want to feel certain, to want to not feel anxious."
Initially, especially with sudden, expected events like this, there are many unanswered questions and gaps in our knowledge. How did the attack happen? Who was behind it?
"These gaps in our knowledge are precisely what encourage conspiracy theories to spring up," said Oberhauser. And then some people start to entertain the possibility that an even bigger conspiracy is behind it all.
Karen Douglas, a professor of social psychology at the University of Kent, confirmed this. "Anyone can fall into conspiracy theories if the circumstances are right," she told DW.
However, Jolley added that it's not the case that a person wakes up one day and suddenly distrusts the world. "Rather, this may have been a journey based on their life experience; for example, the adversities in their life," he said. The way a person generally deals with crises is also relevant. An anxious person is more likely to succumb to conspiracy theories, he added.
Social networks in particular contribute to the rapid spread of myths. Social media already existed before September 11, 2001, but its big breakthrough came with Facebook in 2004. Apps like Instagram, WhatsApp, Telegram and YouTube are now used by billions of people. They're used to share false information and conspiracy narratives, and the platforms don't always act swiftly to take them down.
"They become part of our everyday content, whether it's on our phones, on TikTok, on other social media platforms, where we can kind of come down that rabbit hole very, very quickly," said Jolley. "Going down a rabbit hole" means taking a very intense interest in a subject, clicking from one link to another, and "falling" ever deeper — like Alice in Wonderland.
Why are conspiracy theories problematic?
There are three main reasons why conspiracy theories are so dangerous.
- Conspiracy narratives hold out the promise of making people feel less anxious and more secure. But as Jolley explained, the opposite is more likely to be the case. This can result in even greater mistrust of the government, and of other people, resulting in social isolation.
- A conspiracy theory mixes reality and misinformation; and, unlike disinformation, it cannot easily be exposed as false as it is not based on clear statements that can be verified or disproved. The very essence of a conspiracy theory is the idea that a group of conspirators are acting in secret and the general public are not supposed to know anything about it.
- Conspiracy theories have consequences, and can influence how people act, said Douglas. "Conspiracy theories historically have been linked with prejudice, genocide, risky health behavior, climate denial, and more recently some disturbing behavior related to QAnon and COVID-19 conspiracy theories."
One group has been a particular focus of conspiracy theories around 9/11: Jews. The myth that Jewish people were behind the attacks has been widely shared on social media. This claim can be traced to the antisemitic trope that "the Jews" are a collective supposedly seeking world domination or to control the world. There is no evidence whatsoever to support this conspiracy theory, either.
According to Jolley, certain groups — including Jews, Muslims and LGBTQ+ people — are often blamed for crimes they did not commit. Throughout history, Jews in particular have often been the focus of conspiracy myths, and this continues to this day. An example from Germany is that of the right-wing extremist who tried to storm a synagogue, then killed two people at a nearby kebab shop in Halle in 2019. He had been sharing antisemitic conspiracy theories online.
How can societies respond to conspiracy narratives?
In Germany, nongovernmental organizations like the Amadeu Antonio Foundation or the Federal Agency for Civic Education (bpb) give advice on how to deal with friends or family who believe conspiracy theories. For example: Communicate with each other on equal terms, and conduct research together to find reliable information, and call out antisemitism, racism and other extreme positions, and make it clear that you oppose them. The historian Oberhauser stressed that people need to learn to go back to trusting facts and science.
This article, translated from German, was written as part of a collaboration with the ARD public broadcaster's fact-checking network.

Rosh Hashanah 2026: The sound of the shofar as a vessel for victory, struggle, and self-sacrifice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:23:54 UTC
20:23:54 KST

Fun fact: Nowhere in the Torah do we find the term “rosh hashanah.”
Leviticus 23:24 refers to the festival of the first day of the seventh month as zichron teruah (memorial of sounding the horns), while Numbers 29:1 calls it yom teruah (day of blowing [the horn]).
“Rosh hashanah” does appear once in Tanach, in the Book of Ezekiel (40:1), but it has a different meaning: either a general reference to the beginning of the year, a possible reference to Yom Kippur, or even referring to the month of Nisan (when the Hebrew calendar begins).
In our prayer books – the siddur or mahzor – Rosh Hashanah is also called Yom Hazikaron, the day of remembrance (not to be confused with the modern Israeli Remembrance Day for fallen soldiers and terror victims).
Rosh Hashanah is one of the four Jewish New Years, this one being the new year for calculating ordinary calendar years, sabbatical years, jubilee years, and dates inscribed on legal deeds and contracts. It also commemorates the creation of humankind, which allowed God to form a relationship with all creations and be crowned as King over them.
High Holy Days encompass events of whole year instead of one event
All of the Jewish holidays – with the exception of the High Holy Days – focus on a specific event. Passover relates to the Exodus; Sukkot connects to our journey through the desert; Shavuot recalls the giving of the Torah; Hanukkah, the battle against the Syrian-Greeks; Purim, the threat of Haman to commit genocide against us.
But Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur employ a wide, 360-degree lens that encompasses all we do, all year long. Their universal, timeless message of sin and forgiveness is conveyed by sound – by Rosh Hashanah’s shofar and Yom Kippur’s extensive prayer. And sound is pervasive. It fills the entire room, and it fills the senses, inspiring us and bringing the Almighty into our souls.
There is another message regarding the “rosh” of Rosh Hashanah. If our prayers are going to be answered; if we truly want God to bless us in the months ahead, we need to use our rosh, our head. We need to think very seriously about where we have been, where we are going, who we are, and how we can best influence others and sanctify this life which has been granted to us.
I WANT to share a story from my past as a synagogue pulpit rabbi, a story that emphasizes just how crucial it is to see the bigger picture and utilize our head, our sechel (common sense), to make the right choices.
The story is true, though the names have been changed to protect the innocent. I will leave it to you to judge just who is innocent and who is not.
The story starts with Marlene. She was the president of my shul’s ladies’ auxiliary. Though not fully Orthodox, she was a very committed Jew, and she gave generously of herself in wonderful service to the synagogue. She was a major asset to our congregation and quite popular, with many friends.
Marlene had a younger brother, Max, a brilliant young man who graduated at the top of his high-school class. He was on his way to China – to study Chinese in its natural habitat before beginning his university classes – when he decided to stop en route in Israel.
Max never made it to China. When he came to visit the Kotel, he was befriended by a young rabbi (one of the energetic “Wall-nuts” who reach out to the unaffiliated) who invited him to spend a Shabbat in Jerusalem before moving on to Beijing. Max loved that Shabbat so much that he canceled his flight, enrolled in a yeshiva, and went on to study for quite some time. He would be ordained and start a successful rabbinic career. The Land of the Rising Sun had lost out to the Land of the Rising Soul.
Lessons learned from Marlene's story
Fast-forward several years. Marlene’s daughter is approaching bat mitzvah, and the family is planning the accompanying celebration. I visited Marlene and asked her whether she was planning to make this party kosher.
She put her head down and nervously said, “Rabbi, you know we are not fully observant, and just how expensive kosher catering is, compared to non. Yes, we would like to make it kosher, but it’s just not in our budget.”
“Marlene,” I said, “if finances are the problem, I will provide a generous amount from my discretionary fund to help you with the added cost.
“You are a community leader; your decision will undoubtedly influence many others to make their own parties kosher.
“And think of something else – you have a deeply religious brother; I’m sure he will refuse to join in if the event is nonkosher. Don’t you want him to be included? Won’t it be wonderful if he is also able to attend?”
Marlene promised to think about what I had said, and I felt confident she would do the right thing. But when the invitations came out a few weeks later, I was saddened to read that the party was indeed to be held at a nonkosher venue.
I immediately called Marlene.
“What happened?” I asked her. “I really had hoped you would reconsider and opt for the kosher catering!”
Marlene sighed, and then said: “Rabbi, I really was impressed by your words, and I was ready to make the function kosher – especially to accommodate my brother so that he and his family would attend.
But then he told me that it didn’t matter if the food was kosher; if there wouldn’t be separate seating at the meal, then he and his family would not attend. So I thought, Why should I go to all that expense if Max won’t come anyway?!”
I was stunned; shocked really, both at my own failure to convince Marlene, and at her brother’s total lack of vision and failure to seize a golden opportunity.
I could not just let this moment pass without doing something, so I picked up the phone and called Max. But try as I did, I could not convince him to change his position.
Finally, I left him with this message. “Max,” I said, “you will no doubt accomplish amazing things in your career and achieve a high position.
“Yet no matter what good things you will do, how many people you will reach, you can never atone for this decision you have just made, for you will never know how many waves of positive acts you could have generated had you seen the bigger picture, had you put aside your personal desires for the spiritual good of the community.”
THE SHOFAR is a deeply personal, elemental experience. Some of us hear the sound of victory; others hear the sound of struggle.
But at its core, the shofar is the sound of self-sacrifice. It echoes Abraham’s willingness to sublimate his own wishes to those of God, prompting all of us to submit to a greater good, one that is beyond our own personal wants and desires.
So do not ask for whom the shofar blows. It blows for us.■
The writer is director of the Jewish Outreach Center of Ra’anana. rabbistewart@gmail.com

Vladimir Putin may be fighting his brutal and costly war against Ukraine with a distorted picture of what his forces are achieving.
A Western official says there is evidence in the public domain of Putin beign given a distorted view. If battlefield setbacks are being softened or concealed, the Russian president’s calculations about how long he can sustain the invasion may rest on what are, quite simply, false assumptions.
But the assessment also raises a difficult question for Western governments, how do you influence a leader whose closest advisers may be shielding him from the reality on the ground?

That leaves an enormous gap between what the regime in Moscow wants and a settlement that preserves the sovereignty of Ukraine.
There is a more reassuring assessment on the risk of the war widening, however. Despite increasingly intense attacks and Russian rhetoric about European targets, the official says he sees no indication yet of the armed conflict spreading beyond Russia and Ukraine. Russia’s forces remain tied down, limiting their ability to take the war to NATO.

Taxis in Finland will be identifiable by green number plates from next year, under new regulations approved by the government.
The plates will have a green background with black registration numbers. The change will apply to all taxis, including vehicles booked through ride-hailing platforms.
The new system is due to take effect on 1 January 2027, with a six-month transition period. Green plates will become mandatory for taxis from 1 July 2027.
Taxis will also be required to display a taxi sign on the roof.
In addition to the new plates, taximeters will become mandatory from next February in all vehicles used in taxi transport.
More regulation
Some rules related to the taxi sector tightened at the start of this month.
Taxi drivers must now provide passengers with clear information about the fare before a journey begins. Changes that came into effect on 1 September include closer scrutiny of drivers' criminal backgrounds, which is aimed at improving passenger safety.
Finland liberalised its taxi market in 2018, but since then there have been numerous reports of concerns over pricing, passenger safety and the quality of taxi services.

Europe spends record €7.3bn on Russian Arctic gas in just eight months, surpassing 2025 total
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:21:43 UTC
20:21:43 KST

Two European companies dominate the Arctic shipping network: Scotland's Seapeak and the Greek-linked shipping firm Dynagas. Together, vessels tied to these two European companies managed 72% of all Yamal LNG exports.
Despite public declarations that economic ties with Russia will be severed, Europe has paid an estimated €7.28 billion for liquefied natural gas (LNG) from Moscow's Arctic Yamal project in just over eight months this year, already surpassing the €7.3 billion spent in all of 2025.
The figures were revealed by an investigation by Urgewald, an NGO that exposes the financial institutions and companies backing climate-damaging projects.
During the first eight months of 2026, European ports received 156 Yamal LNG cargoes carrying 11.39 million tonnes, compared with 142 cargoes and 10.34 million tonnes between January and August 2025 – an increase of 10.1% year on year, according to the German NGO Urgewald.
Real-time data from the market intelligence firm Kpler reveals that between 1 January and 5 September this year, European ports swallowed 88.9% of Yamal's total global exports, up from 78.2% in 2025.
"This is a sign that EU buyers are maximising imports ahead of the January 2027 ban. Most of these volumes are from existing long-term contracts, as LNG from short-term contracts was banned in April this year," Charles Costerrouse, Kpler's energy analyst, told Euronews.
Energy analysts said the EU has outspent its previous full-year total in only eight months and five days driven by a perfect storm of higher European gas prices and increased cargo volumes as the war in the Middle East disrupted a key energy trade route through the Strait of Hormuz.
Two European companies dominate this shipping network: the Glasgow-based Seapeak and the Greek-linked shipping firm Dynagas. Together, vessels tied to these two European companies managed 72% of all Yamal LNG exports.
Six Arc7 tankers linked to Seapeak’s Glasgow-based operations carried 65 cargoes and 4.73 million tonnes from Yamal between January and August. Greek-linked Dynagas vessels carried another 62 cargoes and approximately 4.5 million tonnes.
“Europe says it is moving away from Russian energy. These figures show the opposite,” said Alexander Kirk, senior campaign manager at the environmental NGO Urgewald. “The EU took 10% more Yamal LNG and almost 9 out of every 10 tonnes the project exported during the first eight months of the year.”
Costerrouse added that among the top importers of Yamal LNG to Europe are France (4.4 million tonnes), Belgium (3 million tonnes), Spain (2.7 million tonnes) and the Netherlands (1.1 million tonnes).
EU leaders meet in the Arctic
Meanwhile, this trade boom comes at a highly sensitive time, as European leaders arrive in Finland on 13 September for the European Arctic Summit and diplomats in Brussels draft the EU's 22nd sanctions package – with Greece having secured an exemption from a full ban on Russian LNG.
According to the investigation, Europe is not only Russia's primary customer but also the logistical backbone of Arctic trade, which exposes a major vulnerability for Moscow.
Because the Arctic waters freeze over for most of the year, Russia relies on 15 specialised Arc7 ice-class tankers to cut through the ice. Short journeys to European ports let these vessels quickly drop off fuel and return to Siberia. If Russia had to send these same ships all the way to Asia during the winter, the trip would take weeks longer and Russia's total gas exports would collapse.
In August 2026, Yamal split its exports almost exactly equally. Seven cargoes carrying 497,945 tonnes were delivered to European ports, while seven cargoes carrying 493,855 tonnes arrived at Asian destinations.
However, while the summer opening of the Northern Sea Route allowed Russia to temporarily split its exports evenly between Europe and Asia in August, that window is closing. By December, the frozen eastern route to Asia becomes impassable for direct shipments, forcing Russia back toward European waters.
Looming ban on Russian LNG imports
But the ultimate trial will arrive on 1 January 2027, when the EU's official ban on Russian LNG imports and maritime services is scheduled to take full effect. Experts warn that without access to EU ports, Russia's ability to sustain its Arctic operations will face unprecedented pressure.
As European leaders gather in Rovaniemi, Finland, to coordinate Arctic security against Russian expansion, campaigners argue that the Kremlin's war chest is being directly funded by European utilities.
“They cannot ignore that EU money, ports, and maritime services are helping one of Putin’s flagship Arctic energy projects enjoy a bumper year,” warned Sebastian Rötters, sanctions campaigner at Urgewald.
With the 22nd sanctions package currently under negotiation in Brussels, activists are demanding that European governments close existing loopholes. They are calling for an immediate ban on servicing the Arc7 fleet and a strict embargo on selling specialised LNG tankers to Russian entities.
Whether EU countries, still wary of winter energy price shocks, have the political will to sever this multibillion-euro cord remains to be seen.

9/11 – spies, strategy, missed opportunities and lessons learned
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:20:52 UTC
20:20:52 KST

For decades, countless leaders have stated that a government’s primary duty is to protect its citizens, yet the 11th of September, 2001, demonstrated that this can fail: intelligence was available, but no one pieced the connections together, reports the BBC.
The attack on the Twin Towers shaped security, intelligence, and foreign policy for decades to come. On the 11th of September, 2001, as Al-Qaeda suicide pilots crashed into the World Trade Center skyscrapers, BBC journalist Frank Gardner had just finished a stint at the broadcaster’s Middle East bureau. While driving the journalist to Tel Aviv airport, a Palestinian taxi driver suddenly turned up the radio volume and said that something massive had happened in the US. The driver was not exaggerating—2,977 people lost their lives that day.
The attacks did not come out of the blue. The US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) had known for years about Al-Qaeda and the activities of its leader, Osama bin Laden. The CIA had even established a task force to capture bin Laden. Nine days after the attacks, then-US President George Bush declared a war on terror. The subsequent 25 years brought both significant successes and major failures in the field of intelligence on both sides of the Atlantic. Successes included the thwarting of terrorist plots and the arrest of criminals. What was the broader picture? How have intelligence, counter-terrorism operations, and strategic planning evolved over these 25 years?
No one disputes that the 9/11 attacks represented a serious intelligence failure.
At the time, both the CIA and the Federal Bureau of Investigation possessed information that—had it been properly shared between the agencies—could have prevented the terrorist attack. The subsequent report attributed the failure to shortcomings in imagination, policy, capabilities, and management within the US government. It concluded that the CIA and FBI failed to adequately assess and share intelligence, and to take the necessary steps to thwart the attack.
The major lessons have been learned—albeit not entirely—and information sharing among Western intelligence agencies has become far more comprehensive than it was in 2001. Since the 9/11 attacks, a comprehensive reorganization of US intelligence agencies has taken place, and the National Counterterrorism Center and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence have been established near Washington to facilitate the flow of necessary information among the 18 American intelligence agencies. The relationship between the CIA and Britain’s MI6 is arguably the closest of its kind in the world. This is complemented by the Five Eyes alliance, which coordinates the exchange of intelligence information among the US, Canada, the UK, Australia, and New Zealand.
However, catastrophic failures have occurred even after the Twin Towers terrorist attack. Prior to the US-led invasion of Iraq, MI6 allowed the intelligence in its possession to become politicized; this dealt the greatest blow to the British service’s reputation since the exposure of Soviet double agents in the 1950s and 1960s.
Facing immense political pressure to find evidence that Iraq—under Saddam Hussein—still possessed weapons of mass destruction,
MI6 passed flawed intelligence to the government of then-Prime Minister Tony Blair.
Iraq had previously possessed weapons of mass destruction, but these had been eliminated following the 1991 Persian Gulf War. After the 2003 invasion of Iraq, MI6 completely overhauled its procedures for evaluating intelligence obtained from field agents. There is now a clear separation between the work of active field agents (who gather information in places like North Korea or Iran, or from within terrorist groups) and the intelligence assessment team. The assessment team verifies the data and often requests additional information before drawing conclusions. General Richard Shirreff, who commanded a division in Iraq, stated that the 2003 invasion was based on flawed intelligence. He asked whether lessons had been learned from this, answered “no” himself, and remarked that “learning is not our strong suit.”
The invasion of Iraq prompted further inquiries, which eventually resulted in the Butler Report. It concluded that British intelligence regarding Iraq’s alleged weapons of mass destruction was deeply flawed and relied on unverified sources.
MI5, too, has made mistakes amidst its numerous successes.
Lord Jonathan Evans, who led the service from 2007 to 2013, noted that following the 9/11 terrorist attacks, the assessment was that Al-Qaeda—along with associated individuals and groups—posed the greatest security threat to Britain. However, with a database of 20,000 subjects of interest and numerous simultaneous investigations, MI5 did not always set its priorities correctly. In 2005, the service failed to prevent the terrorist attack carried out by suicide bombers in London, which claimed 52 lives. MI5 was aware of Mohammad Sidique Khan, the group’s leader, but did not know what he was planning to do. A similar error led to the Manchester Arena bombings in 2017.
Lord Evans noted that while the terrorist threat has not disappeared, the landscape has changed. Threats to national security—in various forms—emanate from Russia, Iran and its allied groups, and China.
One could argue that US President Donald Trump’s decision to launch attacks on Iran alongside Israel was also an intelligence failure. All US allies in the Persian Gulf region were aware of the possibility that Iran might close the Strait of Hormuz. The warning signs were clearly visible, yet Trump lacked a contingency plan when Tehran did exactly what had been predicted.
The immediate aftermath of the 9/11 terrorist attacks was marked by the fear that a similar event might occur again.
Al-Qaeda had even threatened a swarm of planes carrying out attacks on buildings. In their haste to prevent a recurrence of such attacks, the US and its allies committed numerous human rights violations. Suspects were captured in Afghanistan and Pakistan, often based on flimsy evidence. Hundreds of individuals were transported to the Guantanamo base, where they were imprisoned without trial and subjected to torture. Human rights groups have described this as a moral stain on the US conscience. Scandals also emerged regarding the cruel treatment of detainees in Iraq and Afghanistan. Although some of the individuals involved were held accountable, critics have pointed out that high-ranking figures escaped punishment. The US continues to practice detention without trial at the Guantanamo base. Human rights violations also occurred in Great Britain following the 9/11 terrorist attacks. MI6 was involved in the 2004 abduction of Libyan Islamist Abdelhakim Belhaj and his wife in Thailand, and their subsequent rendition to Libya. There, they spent years in prison, where they were subjected to torture. The case later came to light, and in 2018, Great Britain issued a public apology.
Sir Alex Younger, who headed MI6 from 2014 to 2020, stated shortly after leaving office that by focusing on counter-terrorism operations, the British had overlooked China’s emergence as a military power and a strategic challenge.
In 2016, General Shirreff published the political thriller War With Russia, in which he predicted a full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine. In the wake of the 9/11 attacks,
Western nations were preoccupied with the War on Terror
—fighting the Taliban and ISIS, and attempting to stabilize the situation in Iraq—while failing to notice Russia and China developing massive armament programs featuring innovations in hypersonic missile technology. The military successes of both superpowers have significantly eroded the military superiority NATO once enjoyed. Like Iran, Russia, and North Korea, China is considered a challenging target for intelligence gathering. While the use of biometric data was still in its infancy in 2001, technological advancements have since made it much harder for agents to infiltrate China.
Alongside Russia, China is one of MI6’s primary targets. Sam Olsen, a senior analyst at the security intelligence firm Sibylline, noted that while Western intelligence agencies possess a great deal of information about China, the threat lies in the fact that they often see only isolated fragments without fully grasping how they fit together. China’s strength no longer resides solely in missiles, ships, and troops; it increasingly lies in semiconductors, critical minerals, batteries, ports, communication systems, and industrial capacity. Olsen emphasized that the challenge often lies not in gathering intelligence, but in interpreting it strategically.
Twenty-five years ago, US intelligence personnel held the pieces of the puzzle but failed to assemble them and clearly see what lay ahead. Ultimately, intelligence gathering is pointless if the information cannot be utilized for strategic purposes.

NATO member risking nuclear standoff – Kremlin

NATO member risking nuclear standoff – Kremlin
Russia will respond to any deployment in Lithuania of nuclear weapons aimed at the country by adjusting its own posture accordingly, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has warned.
The Baltic NATO state is currently moving to abolish a constitutional ban on hosting weapons of mass destruction, which President Gitanas Nauseda described as outdated in July. Speaking to Russian TV on Friday, Peskov said Vilnius would cause another rise in tensions with the proposed move.
“If you host nuclear weapons, they are aimed at somebody. Those won’t be aimed to the west. They will be aimed to the east, i.e. at us,” Peskov said. Consequently, “our nuclear weapons will be aimed at” the hosting nation.
Lithuanian media has described the proposed constitutional reform, which could be approved as soon as this winter, as creating a legal framework for a proposed EU nuclear-sharing scheme. France, the only nuclear power in the economic bloc, is considering moving some of its weapons to other member states.
NATO already has a nuclear-sharing arrangement under which US nuclear bombs are stored in non-nuclear countries, including Belgium, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Türkiye, and the UK.
Earlier this week, a Lithuanian parliamentary committee on legal affairs approved a proposal to amend the constitution, with two MPs voting against. The opposition argued that the change should be put to a referendum, while Nauseda’s government said approval by parliament is sufficient. Constitutional amendments in Lithuania require two separate votes in parliament at least three months apart.
The provision outlawing weapons of mass destruction also bans foreign military bases and was included in the basic law to safeguard the post-Soviet republic’s neutrality. Lithuania joined NATO in 2004 along with Latvia and Estonia. Germany is currently working to deploy a heavy tank brigade in the country.
Russia has described NATO’s expansion in Europe as a key cause of current tensions with the US-led military bloc. Moscow views the forward deployment of nuclear-capable weapons near Russia’s borders as a major risk because it significantly reduces the time available to determine whether a detected attack is a false alarm or an actual strike warranting nuclear retaliation.

Waves of plague compounded by wars and drought in Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:19:00 UTC
20:19:00 KST

Waves of plague compounded by wars and drought in Estonia
A new study involving Estonian researchers sheds light on the complex history of the Black Death and subsequent plague outbreaks. The plague reached Estonia on multiple occasions and gained renewed momentum during wars.
The plague epidemic known as the Black Death devastated Europe from 1347 to 1353, killing millions of people. It is often viewed as a single historical event that came and went. In reality, the plague did not disappear after its first devastating outbreak. Over the next five centuries, the disease returned to Europe again and again, having a major impact on communities and reshaping cities and trade routes.
A new study led by the University of Tartu's Institute of Genomics provides a highly nuanced picture of the plague's long and complex history. Researchers analyzed genetic material from plague bacteria found in the remains of people who lived between the 14th and 18th centuries. Using this material, they mapped how the plague spread, evolved and persisted across Europe, including Estonia, during the period that began with the Black Death and continued afterward, known as the second plague pandemic.
The plague was also a frequent uninvited visitor to Estonia
The study reconstructed 26 genomes of the plague bacterium Yersinia pestis. The samples came from individuals who lived hundreds of years ago and were recovered from 11 archaeological sites in Estonia, Russia, England, the Netherlands and Switzerland.
The results show that the plague did not reach Estonia just once. The disease was repeatedly introduced into the country throughout nearly the entire second plague pandemic. Researchers also discovered previously unknown lineages of the plague bacterium and found genetically almost identical strains in different locations. This suggests that plague outbreaks spread very rapidly across Europe through contacts between different regions.
One of the most notable findings was evidence that the plague bacterium underwent genetic diversification between approximately 1450 and 1500. During this period, the bacterium split into three major branches that established new reservoirs of infection among wild rodents.
The researchers believe climate change may have played a role. One possible factor they cite is the so-called Great Renaissance Drought of 1540. Modern studies have shown that climate has a significant impact on the spread of plague among rodent populations, which serve as natural reservoirs for the disease.
"We found evidence that the plague repeatedly reached Estonia as early as the late 14th century and we identified several previously unknown genetic lineages of Yersinia pestis in both urban and rural areas," said Kristiina Tambets, one of the study's lead researchers and professor of archaeogenomics at the University of Tartu.
New method for dating historical outbreaks
One of the study's key innovations was the development of a method that allows ancient disease outbreaks to be placed on a timeline much more precisely. According to the authors, a comparison with the Covid-19 pandemic helps illustrate the method's significance.
Study author Marcel Keller said researchers tracked the spread of different variants of the virus during the coronavirus pandemic by analyzing their genomes. "Because the samples had precise dates, it was possible to reconstruct the spread of the virus almost in real time. With historical epidemics, such precise 'timestamps' are usually unavailable and dates obtained using the widely used radiocarbon dating method can span more than a century," Keller explained. This degree of uncertainty makes it difficult to link specific finds to particular historical disease outbreaks.
To address this problem, the research team developed a method that combines genetic and archaeological chronological information. Using an evolutionary tree constructed from plague bacterium genomes, the researchers were able to determine the age of many samples more precisely based on their position on older or younger branches of the tree. This also allowed the samples to be linked to specific historical events.
In addition to sequencing the new genomes, the researchers used the new method to analyze 64 previously published plague bacterium genomes. This is the first systematic attempt to link most known plague genomes from the 14th to 18th centuries to plague outbreaks documented in written sources.
The new approach allows ancient DNA data to be used much more effectively to study the spread of epidemics. It also makes it possible to reconstruct, with a high degree of chronological precision, events that affected Europe over centuries as successive waves of plague swept across the continent.
Wars help diseases spread
The findings also show how strongly human activity and historical events influenced the spread of the plague. The study also confirms that later plague outbreaks repeatedly reshaped the course of history.
The study adds to existing knowledge with new plague genomes linked to the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648) and epidemics during the Great Northern War (approximately 1700–1721). Genetic evidence suggests that the plague often spread as a result of wars and military campaigns.
"We can see how Yersinia pestis evolved during military conflicts, split into new lineages and traveled along the same routes as troops, refugees and trade," Marcel Keller said. During the 1710 siege of Tallinn, for example, the plague claimed lives on both sides, including Swedish and Russian soldiers as well as civilians.
More broadly, the study shows that the plague was not a single catastrophe but a recurring threat lasting for centuries, devastating cities and regions generation after generation.
Why plague research remains relevant
Although the plague no longer poses a significant health threat in Europe, the disease has not disappeared from the world. Yersinia pestis continues to persist in wild rodent populations in several parts of the world.
Understanding how the plague became established in Europe after the Black Death, persisted for centuries and eventually receded helps researchers better understand the long-term dynamics of infectious disease transmission. Such knowledge also supports modern efforts to monitor and prevent infectious diseases.
The study was the result of extensive international collaboration. Ancient DNA researchers worked closely with Estonian archaeologists and anthropologists studying the history of the plague in what is now Estonia, as well as researchers at the University of Cambridge and partners in the Netherlands and Switzerland.
The collaboration combined ancient DNA research, archaeological and historical data and radiocarbon dating to create the most comprehensive genetic picture of the second plague pandemic to date. It also provided new insights into how one of history's deadliest diseases shaped Europe's development over the course of centuries.
The study was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Syria's Suweida sees renewed international push for solution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:18:05 UTC
20:18:05 KST

Breadcrumb
Syria's Suweida moves toward a solution amid international push
Syria's province of Suweida appears to have entered a new phase of political and diplomatic activity after months of deadlock as control lines in the southern province became consolidated.
The renewed activity comes amid increasing US, Jordanian and Turkish engagement, alongside mounting pressure on Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri and a strong revival of discussion around the Syrian-Jordanian-US roadmap as the framework that could lead to a settlement ending the province's exceptional situation.
The activity indicates that Suweida is no longer an isolated domestic issue but has become part of broader regional arrangements concerning the future of the Syrian state and the balance between Damascus, Washington, Ankara and Tel Aviv.
Suweida in the spotlight
The Suweida file returned to the spotlight after al-Hijri's statements on 25 August, in which he said that the Druze "are an integral part of the State of Israel".
The remarks prompted objections from Druze figures and religious authorities in Syria, Lebanon and the Palestinian occupied territories, while also opening the door to internal conflicts, including pressure on voices opposing al-Hijri.
The most prominent development was the case of Atef Hanidi, one of Suweida's prominent figures, who issued a statement rejecting the linking of the Druze to Israel and criticised al-Hijri for monopolising representation of the province's residents.
After that, the Hijri-backed National Guard forces moved into the town of al-Majdal when Hanidi resides, forcing him to leave for Damascus. The Guard's leadership claim he had left at his own request.
Speaking to The New Arab, Wael Alwan, a researcher at Jusoor Centre, said the revival of the Suweida issue was primarily linked to al-Hijri's statements connecting the province's fate to Israel.
In his assessment, al-Hijri tried to capitalise on the Israeli political situation ahead of the Knesset elections scheduled for 27 October, hoping that Israel's spiritual leader of the Druze community, Mowafaq Tarif, would push Benjamin Netanyahu's government to offer gains to al-Hijri.
Alwan said the Syrian government, in return, had shown sufficient flexibility in dealing with the matter while maintaining national principles it considers necessary for stability.
He argues that Israeli pressure and al-Hijri's actions are inconsistent with consolidating internal stability in Syria, which is a shared Syrian, US and regional objective.
He pointed to the existence of an international roadmap based on Syrian sovereignty, alongside guarantees to prevent disruption of the settlement.
According to Alwan, Israeli involvement in Suweida may not continue in the same way after the Israeli elections, with time working in the Syrian state's favour, particularly given the need for a national solution within the province itself.
Journalist Fouad Azzam, who is from Suweida, echoes this view. He considers that the latest skirmish has forced the parties concerned to reaffirm the Syrian-US-Jordanian roadmap and push towards its implementation.
This was reflected in statements by US envoy Tom Barrack, as well as positions taken by the Syrian and Jordanian foreign ministers.
Azzam told The New Arab that the recent escalation began with students being prevented from sitting exams, the ceasefire lines on the western side being heated up, and al-Hijri's statements concerning Israel, culminating in the case of Atef Hanidi.
He pointed to growing discontent among residents over the security chaos and deteriorating conditions, leading to displacement towards Damascus or outside the country.
According to Azzam, the roadmap has taken steps towards implementation, and al-Hijri's rejection of it will not necessarily be enough to obstruct it, given the existence of national alternatives and declining confidence in him among part of the local community.
He also argued that Israel has begun to retreat on some of the issues, noting that Netanyahu has not repeated the "protection of the Druze" rhetoric in his latest statements. Instead, Azzam noted, Israeli discussion through Druze figures has shifted towards aid, which could indicate that the political use of the Suweida issue is being exhausted.
These developments have gained particular importance with intensified regional contacts.
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani discussed the implementation of the tripartite roadmap for Suweida with his Jordanian counterpart, Ayman Safadi, two days ago.
This came a day after Shaibani held meetings in Ankara with Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan and US envoy to Syria and Iraq Tom Barrack on Tuesday.
Barrack had reaffirmed Washington's commitment to the roadmap, considering it the only way to resolve the Suweida crisis.
He called for dialogue, understanding and cooperation between the Druze, tribes and neighbouring countries, warning that the alternative to dialogue is not victory but another round of mourning.
The roadmap stipulates that Suweida is part of Syria and calls for transitional arrangements that would ultimately reintegrate the province into state institutions.
It also includes investigating violations, holding those responsible to account, delivering aid, restoring services, compensating those affected and rebuilding damaged areas, returning displaced people, releasing detainees and revealing the fate of missing people.
On security, the plan proposes deploying Interior Ministry forces along the Damascus-Suweida road and withdrawing civilian fighters from the border, replacing them with regular police forces.
It also proposes forming a local police force that includes the province's different communities and is led by someone from Suweida.
The plan further proposes establishing a provincial council and reactivating civilian institutions, launching a reconciliation process between the Druze and tribes, and ending foreign intervention, alongside a Syrian-Jordanian-US mechanism to monitor implementation.
However, the main sticking point remains the issue of weapons and security decision-making.
The presence of a local armed force outside the official structure makes the dispute more than a question of administrative powers and raises the question of which side has the final decision-making authority in the province.
In this context, the US approach appears closer to a formula that combines maintaining Syrian sovereignty with granting the province broad local arrangements, rather than a return to a centralised model.
This explains the emphasis on local police, a local council, guarantees and accountability, alongside opposition to separation or the continuation of external spheres of influence.
Regionally, the calculations of Israel, Turkey and the United States are colliding in Suweida.
Israel views southern Syria from a security perspective linked to preventing the emergence of a strong Syrian state, while Turkey supports Syria's territorial unity and the capabilities of state institutions.
Washington, according to the information available, is pushing for a settlement that prevents a new explosion in the south, particularly as Syria's stability has become linked to broader regional calculations involving trade, energy and transport routes.
Between separation and accountability
Domestically, there are signs that opposition to any attempt to link Suweida to Israel is growing.
Academics and activists from the province have confirmed the existence of opposition to this approach, although fear of weapons and violence limits the ability of opponents to express themselves publicly.
Calls have also emerged to embrace the camp opposing separation and for Damascus to take practical measures to reassure the province's residents, foremost among them rebuilding damaged villages and continuing to hold those responsible for violations to account.
The question, therefore, appears to be how to reconstruct the internal balance in Suweida in a way that allows for a viable settlement.
If Damascus and Washington succeed in supporting local forces capable of representing the province's interests within the Syrian state, al-Hijri's monopoly over decision-making could weaken.
But if Damascus fails to provide convincing political, security and community guarantees, or returns to a heavy-handed security approach, tensions could flare and be exploited by forces opposed to any settlement.
The current activity therefore appears closer to an attempt to put the Suweida issue back on the path towards a solution, based on a US-Jordanian-Turkish convergence around the need to consolidate stability and make use of growing internal opposition to the status quo.
Yet the process's success remains linked to the parties' ability to address the root of the Suweida's crisis: combining Syrian sovereignty, justice and accountability, local guarantees and control of weapons, while preventing foreign intervention in a way that keeps the province from returning to a cycle of violence or becoming a permanent sphere of influence for any foreign party.
Article translated from Arabic by Afrah Almatwari. To read the original, click here.

ASHGABAT, September 11. /TASS/. Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) countries will continue to develop a joint air defense system and strengthen transport security, according to decisions made at a meeting of the CIS Economic Council in Turkmenistan’s capital of Ashgabat, a TASS correspondent reported.
In particular, the meeting’s participants signed a document on the allocation of funds for the establishment and development of a joint air defense system among CIS countries in 2027.
"Members of the Economic Council also approved an action plan to implement a strategy to ensure transport security in CIS member states when managing transport and international connections in 2026-2030. The document outlines a set of additional measures aimed at the practical implementation of coordinated approaches to regulating the field of transport security. <...> A report on the activities of the CIS Intergovernmental Council on the Agricultural Complex in 2023-2025 was presented during the meeting, as well as draft projects for the digital transformation of agricultural industries in CIS member states," CIS Secretary General Sergey Lebedev told reporters.
In addition, the meeting also addressed obstacles to trade within the CIS and recommendations on how to remove them.
CIS Economic Council
The CIS Economic Council meeting took place in Ashgabat on Friday as part of Turkmenistan’s 2026 CIS Chairmanship. Russian Ambassador to Ashgabat Ivan Volynkin said earlier that a meeting of the CIS Council of Heads of State would be held in the Turkmen city of Turkmenbasy on October 9. Russia will be represented by President Vladimir Putin.

Princess Diana’s ‘revenge dress’ expected to fetch up to $300,000 at auction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:16:59 UTC
20:16:59 KST

Dilara Hamit
11 September 2026•Update: 11 September 2026
The black evening dress worn by Princess Diana on the night her estranged husband, then-Prince Charles, now King Charles III, publicly acknowledged his infidelity is going up for auction for the first time.
The silk dress, designed by Christina Stambolian and widely known as Diana’s “revenge dress,” is expected to sell for between $150,000 and $300,000 at Sotheby’s in New York on Dec. 9, according to a press release.
Diana wore the dress to a fundraising dinner hosted by Vanity Fair at London’s Serpentine Gallery on June 29, 1994.
Her appearance came on the same evening that a nationally televised documentary aired in which Charles admitted that he had been unfaithful during their marriage.
The couple had been separated for nearly two years at the time.
Diana’s arrival in the fitted black dress before a crowd of photographers became one of the most widely recognized images of her and a defining moment in modern fashion history.
The outfit was soon dubbed the “revenge dress” by the media, with her decision to wear it seen as a public display of confidence at a time when details of her marriage were under intense scrutiny.
The off-the-shoulder dress features a pleated bodice, an asymmetric hemline and a dramatic chiffon train. Diana paired it with black heels and a clutch, as well as a pearl choker centered on an antique sapphire-and-diamond brooch given to her as a wedding gift by the Queen Mother.
Diana had owned the dress for three years but had previously considered it too daring for a public appearance. She reportedly made a last-minute wardrobe change ahead of the dinner, setting aside a more traditional Valentino gown.
According to her stylist at the time, Anna Harvey, Diana “wanted to look a million dollars.”
Morgane Halimi, Sotheby’s global head of handbags and fashion, said Diana understood that clothing could serve as a form of communication.
“On her own terms, Princess Diana turned the dress into one of the most powerful messages she ever made,” Halimi said.
The image helped establish the idea of “revenge dressing,” a term now used to describe clothing chosen to project confidence, transformation or independence after a breakup or personal crisis.
First auction appearance since 1997
Diana included the Stambolian dress among the 79 outfits she personally offered at a charity auction in June 1997, shortly before her death that August.
The sale raised funds for cancer and AIDS charities, and the dress was purchased by its current owners, who have kept it ever since.
A rare copy of the original 1997 auction catalogue, numbered and signed by Diana and Stambolian, will be sold with the dress. The catalogue credits Diana’s son, Prince William, with suggesting the original charity sale.
Part of the proceeds from the December auction will be donated to NHS Lothian Charity on behalf of the Royal Edinburgh Hospital.
Before the sale, the dress will go on an international exhibition tour. It will be displayed at Sotheby’s in London from Sept. 18 to 24 during London Fashion Week before traveling to Hong Kong and Geneva.
It will then be exhibited at Sotheby’s Breuer Building in New York from Dec. 2 ahead of the live auction on Dec. 9.
The original dress has not been displayed publicly for nearly 30 years, although replicas have appeared in exhibitions and television productions, including Netflix’s royal drama The Crown.

====================================================================================================

Hitler, horses and pigeons: Maurizio Cattelan explores power and darkness in Berlin exhibition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:14:40 UTC
20:14:40 KST

Italian artist Maurizio Cattelan has brought his provocative and often unsettling work to Berlin for his first major solo exhibition in Germany exploring power, violence, death, faith and uncertainty.
Night, at the Neue Nationalgalerie, brings together several of Maurizio Cattelan’s best-known works alongside pieces created more recently, transforming Germany's vast modernist Neue Nationalgalerie museum into a world of disturbing images and unexpected juxtapositions.
Hitler on his knees
Among the most striking works is Him, a 2001 sculpture depicting Adolf Hitler kneeling on the floor as if in prayer. From one angle, the figure appears to be a small, innocent-looking child. As visitors move around it, however, the face of Hitler is revealed.
Him was created more than two decades ago, and sold for €15 million at auction in 2016.
Night co-curator Lisa Botti says the work still has a lot to say about today's society: “The sculpture is actually from 2001, so it's not a recent one, but unfortunately it stays relevant in our times.”
Playful and provocative as ever, Cattelan deliberately leaves the meaning of the figure unresolved. “You don't really know if he's praying for forgiveness or not,” Botti added. “It stays in between. So it has this power that it shakes you, but it's not certainty.”
Berlin landmarks take on new meanings
The exhibition also plays with familiar symbols. In Purgatory, Cattelan presents a scaled-down version of Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate, while hundreds of stuffed pigeons appear to occupy the ceiling above visitors in People.
Another work, Novecento, shows an exhausted horse suspended from the ceiling. For Botti, the animal represents both the power associated with the 20th Century and its eventual collapse.
“Horses are always the symbol for nobility, for military, for winning,” she said. “But here it's the opposite. It's weak. It's exhausted.”
Outside the museum, a mechanical boy beats a drum on the roof in Never, a work inspired by Günter Grass's novel "The Tin Drum_"_. The image can be interpreted as a warning or a call to wake up.
From a golden toilet to a million-dollar banana
Cattelan has built his reputation on works that challenge conventional ideas about art, value and taste. His best-known pieces include Comedian, a banana duct-taped to a wall, which sold for €5.2m at auction in New York in 2024.
His gold toilet, America, meanwhile, was stolen in 2019 from Blenheim Palace in England. The work was presented as a satire of excessive wealth and had previously been displayed at the Guggenheim Museum in New York.
But Night takes a darker and more contemplative approach. Its title refers to darkness and a time for reflection, while also suggesting the promise of a new morning.
The exhibition runs at Berlin’s Neue Nationalgalerie until March 2027.

Türkiye releases archives documenting Greek army atrocities in Anatolia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:14:21 UTC
20:14:21 KST

The Turkish Foreign Ministry has released archival documents and photographs that it said documented atrocities committed by the Greek Army against Turkish civilians in Anatolia during the Greco-Turkish War of 1919-1922.
In a statement posted on X on Friday, the ministry said the material from its archives showed the destruction of villages and the killing of civilians during the Greek Army's occupation of Anatolia and subsequent retreat.
It said the records were evidence of a systematic policy of destruction that was recognised in the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne and by international reports.
"The documents and photographs we have released from our Ministry’s archives once again reveal the atrocities committed by the Greek Army in Anatolia between 1919 and 1922.
"During their occupation of Anatolia and subsequent retreat, Greek forces pursued a systematic policy of destruction — a fact recognised in the Lausanne Peace Treaty and various international reports.
"The records we are sharing hereby serve as a harrowing example of a massacre perpetrated against the Turkish civilian population in a village near Bursa."
Handwritten archival documents
The ministry's release included photographs attributed to a commission of inquiry, along with handwritten archival documents. The photographs show the remains of villages, civilian victims, and survivors of attacks in settlements near Bursa, in northwestern Türkiye.
One photograph depicts the village of Mashara Hasan after its destruction by fire. The accompanying caption says the village was among the settlements whose inhabitants were massacred by Greek forces during the Greek forces' retreat from Bursa.
Other images show the bodies of civilians, including women and children, and a group of injured survivors from Sogutpinar village in Mudanya.
The captions identify the photographs as records of alleged atrocities against Turkish civilians. The ministry said residents of Sogutpinar were forced into a local mosque, where some were killed and others were wounded by bayonets and gunfire.
Materials available in digital archives
The war began after Greek forces landed in Izmir on May 15 1919, and the conflict ended with the establishment of the Republic of Türkiye in 1923.
Article 59 of the Treaty of Lausanne, signed on July 24 1923, states that Greece recognised its obligation to make reparations for damage caused in Anatolia by acts of the Greek Army or administration that violated the laws of war.
The Turkish Foreign Ministry's Diplomatic Archives contain historical documents from the period, including records relating to the National War of Independence.
The ministry has made archival materials available through its digital archives and research facilities.

Spanish official resigns as questions grow over intelligence warnings ahead of Ceuta migrant influx
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:11:33 UTC
20:11:33 KST

Gonzalo Sanz's resignation comes just two days after the government made public 40 declassified reports containing communications involving the National Intelligence Centre, the Government Delegation in Ceuta and the Civil Guard.
The chief of staff to the Spanish government's delegate in Ceuta, Gonzalo Sanz, has resigned from his position, the latest episode in an ongoing controversy over what Spanish authorities may have known ahead of the mass arrival of migrants into the North African exclave in late July.
The resignation has not yet been officially confirmed by sources at the Government Delegation.
Sanz said he received a warning from the National Intelligence Centre (CNI) on 29 July, in which he was alerted to messages circulating on social media in groups with a combined 180,000 members. The warning came one day before the mass arrival of migrants into Ceuta from Morocco.
According to his account, Sanz passed that information on to the government's delegate, Miguel Ángel Pérez Triano, that same day.
He said there was an obvious "inconsistency" between this claim and the various statements the delegate has made to different media outlets, in which he insisted he was not aware of the warning until the government declassified the reports on the crisis.
Despite taking this step, the now former chief of staff made it clear that his decision was not motivated by any "bitterness" towards the delegate. According to Sanz, the Government Delegation worked "tirelessly" to obtain responses from the central government from the very first minute.
He added that there were reports documenting the warnings sent to the different ministries, and he expressed his hope that Ceuta "returns to normal as soon as possible."
Declassified reports
The resignation comes just two days after the government made public 40 declassified reports containing communications involving the CNI, the Government Delegation and the Civil Guard.
In those messages, sent via WhatsApp, an intelligence officer signalled his concern about calls detected on social networks for the following day, 30 July, and about the possibility of an "assault" by "sea and land" on the autonomous city.
The warning said that social media contained a call to take advantage of the Throne Day celebrations, when security forces would be occupied with the festivities.
After that message, there was an 11-minute phone call between the Government Delegation's office and the CNI agent. Shortly afterwards, Sanz replied to the intelligence officer, confirming that he had received the warning.
Differing accounts
Triano has said he had no knowledge of that conversation and has characterised the exchange as part of "an exchange of informational documents," never, according to him, linked to the possibility of a mass entry.
In a press conference, the delegate ruled out resigning over his handling of the crisis. He maintained that in the days leading up to the mass entry of 30 and 31 July, the authorities had only been warned of "a serious and complex migration situation," and that at no point had they been warned as to the scale of what would subsequently happen.
He also said he would not allow the work of the Government Delegation to be called into question, since, in his view, what happened on 30 July overwhelmed any measures that could have been adopted.
The government, for its part, has repeatedly denied that the CNI warned it that a mass entry could take place, a version of events that is now coming under scrutiny.

U.S. President Donald Trump has dismissed warnings that AI could pose an existential threat to humanity, after a wave of insiders at frontier labs Anthropic and OpenAI stepped up public warnings of risks from the technology.
When asked if he had concerns about AI leading to human extinction, Trump said, "No, I don't have any."
"I have concerns that if we don't win AI, we're going to be put in a very bad position," the president told reporters Thursday. "We are leading China right now by a pretty good period, I would say a year, which is, you know, considered a lot."
The U.S. and China are locked in a battle for AI supremacy, with tensions ratcheting up as Chinese AI models have become more advanced and their adoption grows across the globe.
Trump's comments came after a number of researchers at frontier AI labs, including OpenAI and Anthropic, sounded the alarm over the rapid pace of development of the tech.
Growing concerns
Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said Tuesday that he was quitting the company over concerns that Anthropic and rival OpenAI are "gambling with our lives."
He added that those building AI believed that it could "kill us all by the end of the decade" — a view which has since been echoed by other employees at the labs.
Many AI safety fears revolve around models developing the ability to improve their own performance, a technique known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI.
"It's hard to overstate how dangerous speeding towards RSI is," said Jasmine Wang, an OpenAI researcher working on alignment, on Wednesday evening.
OpenAI's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki said Saturday that he has a "strong expectation" that the speed of progress in AI could be sustained into recursive self-improvement. "I am concerned no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence."
Trump's comments come as some Republican lawmakers have joined Democrats in backing greater oversight of advanced AI systems.
In July, Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., and Rep. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., announced plans to introduce a bill called the FRONTIER Act, which aims to establish a framework for governing the deployment of advanced AI models.
"Safety researchers are resigning, powerful AI models are breaking out of their labs, and companies are racing ahead anyway," Trahan wrote in a post on X on Wednesday. "It's past time for Congress to get off the sidelines and do its job."
Earlier this month, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, introduced a bill called the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, which would temporarily pause advanced AI development until the federal government establishes safety rules.

Unknown

Demolition of historical building in Sabzevar draws heritage ministry’s legal action
TEHRAN - A historical building known as the Tumanian building, also referred to as the Padegan-e Rusha (“Russian barracks”) has recently been demolished in Sabzevar, northeastern Iran, prompting the Ministry of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts to blame the city’s municipality and pursue legal action.
The ministry has announced that the demolition was carried out without seeking an opinion from the local heritage authorities and was conducted so rapidly that little of the historical structure remains.
There was “no justification” for the demolition and that the case would be pursued through the courts, the ministry has underlined.
Moreover, in a note published following the incident, Roozbeh Kardooni, senior adviser to the minister of cultural heritage and tourism, has brough more light to the incident, saying that the building was not listed on Iran’s national heritage register. He cautioned, however, that this did not mean it had no historical value or could be demolished without restrictions.
According to Kardooni, the Tumanian building, dating to the first Pahlavi period, had been explicitly identified as a “historic-value” structure in the revised map of Sabzevar’s historical urban area, which was issued in November 2024.
He said the municipality was aware of the building’s status. Nevertheless, Sabzevar Municipality’s District 2 reportedly authorized the demolition of its southern and eastern walls before obtaining an opinion from the local heritage office.
Roozbeh Kardooni, senior adviser to the minister of cultural heritage and tourism
Kardooni said the Sabzevar heritage office had issued no permit for the demolition of the walls, entrance portal or historical fabric of the building. A proposal submitted in 2025 by Sabzevar University concerning the possible technical relocation of the entrance portal, he added, was only submitted for review and did not constitute authorization for demolition.
The official also rejected the argument that private ownership allowed the building to be demolished, saying property rights were subject to urban regulations.
Elsewhere in his remarks, Kardooni said it considers the demolition a violation of applicable regulations and has begun legal proceedings. It is also seeking to require the municipality to reconstruct and restore the building based on historical documentation.
The demolition has been halted, while the Sabzevar prosecutor’s office has opened a case.
Kardooni said parts of the building remain and that photographs, maps, aerial images and other historical documentation could provide a basis for emergency conservation, documentation and reconstruction of the demolished sections.
