Twenty-five years after 9/11: ‘I’ve never spoken about it until now’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Twenty-five years after 9/11: ‘I’ve never spoken about it until now’
On the morning of September 11, 2001, Swiss citizen Beat Reinhart was working directly opposite the Twin Towers. He witnessed the attacks first-hand. He has never spoken about it – until today. A testimony.
“I always keep the morning of September 11 free. There’s nothing in my diary, and it’s been that way for 25 years.
I never talk about September 11, 2001. Unless I absolutely have to. I had to come to terms with it for myself. It takes an incredible amount of time to come to terms with a trauma like that. It wasn’t just that one day, but the months that followed – the constant smell of smoke, working in a basement.
For me, the 25th anniversary is an opportunity to finally open up – even to my parents, who were sitting on the terrace of my flat in New Jersey on that day and watched the planes fly into the towers.
I remember the morning of September 11 very clearly. As always, I was in the office at 7am. By 7:10am, you were already running late at the trading desk. I was working for Commerzbank at the time.
I went into my office and thought to myself – this was before we had mobile phones – ‘Oh my God, today would have been the day to bring a camera into the office.’ The visibility was crystal clear; a real picture-perfect day. It’s never been that clear since.
I was working on the 32nd floor when I heard a noise – that’s how I imagine the sound of a rocket. That noise, like an engine. And then it just stopped. We didn’t hear an explosion in the traditional sense, more like an impact, and we felt a shockwave. Then all our phones in the trading floor went dead – including the brokers’ lines.
I knew which direction the sound had come from, so I went over to the east side to look up. I was absolutely stunned. For the second time. Because back in 1993, I’d already experienced a terrorist attack in the very same office – the explosion in the World Trade Center car park. I’d been spared then, too.
I stood at the window for at least a minute, watching a shower of paper pouring out of the building. How could there be so much paper up there? It just kept coming. It made no sense.
On September 11, 2001, terrorists hijacked four passenger aircraft. Two of them were flown into the towers of the World Trade Center in New York; a third struck the Pentagon near Washington. The fourth aircraft crashed in Pennsylvania. Almost 3,000 people died in the attacks.
The Swiss community was also affected. Two Swiss nationals lost their lives in the attacks in New York. In the days that followed, the foreign ministry sought to ascertain the whereabouts of hundreds of Swiss nationals in the US.
At that time, around 20,000 Swiss were living in the greater New York, New Jersey and Connecticut area. Today, over 26,000 Swiss nationals are registered in the region.
My second thought was that we’d never be able to travel freely again for the rest of our lives. They’ve done it again, and our freedom is gone.
Then I looked down – and I saw a person lying on the central reservation of the four-lane road. They weren’t moving. Why isn’t anyone calling an ambulance, I wondered.
I went back into the trading room. Everyone was trying, in one way or another, to get hold of their family members. I was worried about my mother.
My parents were visiting. They’d been living back in Switzerland for almost 20 years by then – they used to come and visit me every two or three years. My mother had said the night before that she wanted to go to the bookshop in the World Trade Center complex that morning.
I couldn’t get through to her on the phone. Shortly afterwards, we heard a massive explosion. The floor beneath me shook. The second plane had struck the South Tower from a different angle. It went deathly quiet. Nobody said a word.
I stood up and knew: we had to get out of there. I saw the petite Filipino woman in the back office, sitting at her desk, completely paralysed with fear. I took her by the hand and fled the building with her. Nobody said a word.
We ran down the fire escape. The emergency exit opposite the North Tower was closed. We were in the dark for a long time. I remember a long corridor, then we came out at the South Tower.
By then, we were a group of about seven people, and I was responsible for two young female interns from Germany.
Beat Reinhart, 62, has lived in the New York metropolitan area for decades. A dual Swiss-American national, he grew up in the US and Switzerland. His parents are from canton Thurgau and now live in Lausanne. After studying in the US, Germany and Switzerland, Reinhart pursued a career in the financial sector and now works for a major US financial firm. He has been actively involved in Swiss associations in New York for many years. He lives on a historic farm in New Jersey.
We decided to head for the ferry terminal. As luck would have it, the ferry was still running. It was the last crossing. I had to pay for every single person I took onto that boat.
We went to the upper deck. The Winter Garden, situated between the World Financial Center and the Twin Towers, was right in our line of sight. Behind it, the towers were ablaze, shrouded in a huge cloud of paper and smoke.
I wanted to take the people who were with me to my flat in Jersey City. We were walking up Montgomery Street when the chauffeur of a black saloon car asked me where we were coming from. The radio was blaring loudly from the car; the news was on. I replied, ‘From the World Trade Center.’ And he said, ‘They’re attacking everything.’
That was the first indication to me that it wasn’t just the World Trade Center that had been attacked.
We walked to my flat, where I’d been expecting my parents. I unlocked the door, went into the living room – no one was there. My heart stopped. But there was a staircase in the flat leading up to the roof terrace. And up there they all were: my mother, my father and my sister.
From there, we watched the towers collapse.
The sky was empty. Our souls were empty. Nothing but blue sky above the deserted streets.
Later, I heard that the collapse of the towers had blown out the windows of the lower 17 floors of my office block.
It took more than ten years before my parents, who are now 93, even mentioned that day. We never spoke about it. It was only this week, 25 years on, that we had perhaps the most open conversation we’ve ever had about it – and it lasted just two minutes.
They were sitting on my terrace that morning, having breakfast, when they saw the first aeroplane fly in right before their eyes. Just a mile away as the crow flies, with a completely unobstructed view.
It took 25 years for me to find out why my mother wasn’t at the World Trade Center that morning. At the last minute, my sister had said: ‘Oh come on, let’s just have a leisurely breakfast here on the terrace. I’ll pop down and get us some fresh bagels.’
The shock in the days that followed ran deep. Then there was that smell. The smell of fire. It didn’t smell of wood, or paper, or plastic. It was a distinct, acrid odour. Right up until Christmas, several times a week the wind would blow the smoke across the river straight into my flat in Jersey City.
About a month after the attacks, I fell ill – I had a severe case of shingles and was off work for two weeks. During that time, my colleagues attended one, two, three or more funerals every day. We mourned so many people: members of the New York Fire Department, relatives of colleagues and people with whom we had worked closely.
My family and I didn’t suffer the worst of it that day, but so many people around us lost everything.
In the months that followed, I commuted for several hours every day to our emergency operations centre in Connecticut, where we worked in a basement.
Today I work on the 39th floor of the rebuilt One World Trade Center – the so-called Freedom Tower. I followed the reconstruction from afar every day right from the start.
Even so, it took a very long time before I was able to set foot in this area again at all after it was completed. The fact that the Freedom Tower has been built and that life has returned there means more to me than any memorial. It shows that the city is alive.
Now that it’s being reported on everywhere again to mark the anniversary, I switch off the TV and the radio. I can’t bear to listen to it.
I know it’s pure fate, pure timing – whether a chunk of concrete falls on your head or whether someone says: ‘Let’s have a bagel first.’”
Edited by Balz Rigendinger. Translated from German, sub-edited by Thomas Stephens

International Day to Protect Education from Attack: Condemning US-Israeli aggression on Iran
Unknown

International Day to Protect Education from Attack: Condemning US-Israeli aggression on Iran
TEHRAN - September 9, the International Day to Protect Education from Attack, is a reminder of one of the most fundamental principles of international humanitarian law: schools, universities, teachers and students must be protected from the violence of war.
The recent war against Iran has highlighted a blatant violation of international law, with the United States and Israel carrying out attacks on Iran’s educational infrastructure, inflicting extensive damage to schools, universities, laboratories, research institutions, and other educational facilities, and killing many students and academics.
One of the most devastating incidents occurred on February 28 at the Shajareh Tayyebeh elementary school in Minab, Hormozgan Province. The school was struck as children between the ages of seven and twelve were beginning their lessons.
The collapse of the building trapped students and teachers under the rubble. Iranian authorities put the final death toll at 168, with at least 95 others wounded.
Whatever the ultimate findings regarding responsibility and the circumstances of the strike, the scale of the reported loss of civilian life underscores why the protection of educational spaces must be treated as an urgent international obligation.
The attacks did not end with schools. According to Hossein Simaei-Sarraf, the minister of science, research and technology, more than 30 universities across the country were directly attacked during the conflict.
He reported that five university professors and more than 60 students were killed. Officials have described attacks on scientific and educational infrastructure as crimes against humanity, arguing that scientific institutions were targeted because of their technological and research capabilities.
The Organization of Student Affairs has also said that legal proceedings were being pursued over attacks on universities, dormitories, schools and scientific centers.
According to its head, Saeed Habiba, a team of judicial experts was established to document the damage and assess its extent, while authorities are pursuing cases in domestic courts and international forums. Officials have further stated that 175 university students were killed in the attacks.
Specific university strikes have also been cited by Iran's ambassador to the United Nations, Amir Saeid Iravani. In letters to the UN Secretary-General and the Security Council, he said that attacks on scientific institutions constituted violations of international humanitarian law.
He referred, in particular, to damage caused to Sharif University of Technology, including facilities associated with civil and electrical engineering and research institutes, as well as an earlier strike affecting Shahid Beheshti University's Laser and Plasma Research Institute.
These crimes cannot simply be dismissed as another chapter in a geopolitical dispute. If educational institutions were deliberately targeted, or if attacks were conducted without adequate distinction between military objectives and protected civilian objects, the consequences under international law could be extremely serious.
The appropriate response is not political silence, but strong condemnation and impartial investigation based on evidence.
September 9 should therefore be more than a symbolic observance. It should be a demand for action: independent investigations into attacks on Iranian educational institutions; transparent assessment of civilian casualties and material damage; protection and reconstruction of damaged educational facilities; and accountability for anyone found to have violated international humanitarian law.
A classroom is not a battlefield. A university is not a legitimate target merely because it belongs to an adversary.
If the international community is serious about protecting education from attack, it must apply that commitment universally. The unlawful attacks on Iranian schools, universities and scientific institutions must be investigated, and those responsible must be held accountable.
Education is a right, not a target. And international law must mean the same thing for every child, everywhere.

Israel claims three Qassam Brigades members killed in Gaza strike
Unknown

The Israeli army has claimed killing three Palestinian commanders in Gaza, alleging they were part of the Qassam Brigades, the armed wing of Hamas.
“In a precise strike yesterday, Israeli forces and the Shin Bet security agency eliminated Mohammed al Yazouri in the Khan Younis area,” the army said in a statement on Friday. It claimed that al Yazouri served as commander of Hamas’ Khan Younis Brigade.
The army also claimed that Hudhaifa Muammar, a “company commander,” and Muhammad Bahjat Rashi, who it said was from Hamas’ military wing in the Khan Younis Brigade, were killed in the same strike.
There was no immediate comment from Hamas or the Qassam Brigades.
Since October 2023, Israel has been waging its genocidal war on Gaza, killing more than 73,000 Palestinians and injuring over 174,000 others, while destroying around 90 percent of the enclave’s infrastructure.
The attacks continue unabated despite a ceasefire in October 2025.

Gallery: ERR holds topping-out ceremony for new TV house
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:58:00 UTC
19:58:00 KST

Gallery: ERR holds topping-out ceremony for new TV house
The under-construction ERR TV House received a traditional Estonian topping-out ceremony on Thursday, with the Tallinn mayor and culture minister in attendance.
The building is due to be completed by the end of 2027 and, since the television house (Telemaja) has reached its full extent in terms of height, the topping-out ceremony (Sarikapidu) went ahead, replete with fir wreath placed at the highest point on the structure.
ERR board chair Erik Roose was joined for the ceremony among others by Mayor of Tallinn Mihhail Kõlvart (Center), Minister of Culture Heidy Purga (Reform) and Tarmo Pohlak, management board member of Nordecon, constructing the building.
Pohlak said the new build is a complex project due to its purpose, but beyond that the work as been much like any other city center construction project. The adjacent Radio House (Raadiomaja), built in the early 1970s also presented challenges.
"What was technically challenging was that the Radio House is right next door and has a shallow foundation — it sits on a slab — so we had to shore up that side to make sure the Radio House stayed in place," Pohlak explained.
The Cultural Endowment of Estonia (Kultuurkapital), financing the construction as one of several projects of national cultural importance, announced that its annual awards ceremony is set to take place at the TV house in early February 2028, concentrating minds on getting the project done by then.
"If they have invited themselves over, I think it would be hard for us to refuse. Otherwise, perhaps we won't get the final portion of the funding. I think that assuming it isn't 'raining knives' in February, which is possible, then yes, we'll start preparing," Roose commented.
While the new building will replace the somewhat dilapidated property on nearby Faehlmanni tänav, the latter building is being retained for one important room it contains: "It's a nuclear bunker. Back when the old television building was constructed, a nuclear shelter probably seemed more necessary, despite everything, than it does today. I hope we have assessed the security situation correctly," Roose said on this.
Background:
The new ETV TV house in Tallinn, designed by Kadarik Tüür Arhitektid, was funded by the Cultural Endowment after a 2024 law change and is being built by Nordecon. The total project cost was budgeted to remain within €77 million, funded by the Cultural Endowment, the sale of the old Gonsiori property, and the sale of another property belonging to ERR on Tuisu tänav in Tallinn. Construction began in 2025, involved demolishing the old TV mast foundations, and reached full height in September 2026. Completion is expected by the end of 2027, with ERR planning to move in during 2028.
What is a topping out ceremony?
The Sairkpidu is not unique to ERR's new TV house and fir wreaths can often be seen atop under-construction private residences and other buildings in Estonia.
The Estonian Open Air Museum explains a topping out (U.K.) or topping off (U.S.) ceremony is a tradition marking the moment a building's rafters are completed — the highest point of construction. In Estonia, builders place a wreath on the roof, and the owner is expected to bring it down and provide a meal for the workers. If the owner ignores it, the builders may replace the wreath with an old broom, trousers, or other objects as a humorous protest.
The custom has similar versions across Europe: Richtfest in Germany, Taklagsfest in Sweden, Rejsegilde in Denmark, and Kranselag in Norway. It likely reached Estonia through the Baltic German cultural space, with the earliest Estonian press mentions appearing in the 1850s and the tradition fully taking root among Estonians around a century ago.
In the 1930s, the wreath was often combined with the national flag, and sometimes decorated with tools or symbols. The tradition survived the Soviet era, though the accompanying partying was criticized in the Soviet press. Today, the topping out ceremony remains a widespread but simple way to mark a construction milestone and thank the workers.

IEA warns global oil refining system ‘stretched to the limit’ as Iran, Ukraine wars tighten market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:56:45 UTC
19:56:45 KST

The Iran and Ukraine wars are adding pressure to an oil refining system "stretched to the limit," the International Energy Agency warned Friday, as it once again cut its global supply and demand forecasts amid the ongoing energy shock.
In its closely monitored monthly oil report, the IEA further cut its global oil supply and demand projections for the remainder of the year, warning that a full recovery in flows from Middle East producers has been deferred until next year as the Iran war drags on.
The energy watchdog said it expects world oil supply to decline by 5.7 million barrels per day (bpd) in 2026, about 6% lower than 2025. The IEA previously forecast an annual drop of 4% in its last update in August.
Global oil demand, meanwhile, is seen falling more than expected as an impasse in diplomatic talks between the U.S. and Iran delays the prospect of a truce, amid renewed attacks in both the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea's Bab el-Mandeb choke point.
IEA significantly cuts its global oil demand forecast
The IEA said demand is expected to drop by 2.5 million bpd this year, significantly more than its August forecast of a 1.6 million bpd decline.
"Inventories have so far played a crucial role in balancing the market," the IEA said in its report.
"With buffers shrinking and the global refining system stretched to the limit, the need for progress in resolving the conflict in the Middle East – and the Russia-Ukraine war, which is now in its fifth year – is greater than ever to avoid further market tightening and demand destruction," the agency added.
The report comes at a time when oil prices have surged as the U.S. and Iran have exchanged attacks on tankers near the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz — and amid an escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.
Oil prices traded lower on Friday morning, but both major benchmarks could still end the week above $100 per barrel for the first time since mid-May.
International benchmark Brent crude futures with November expiry traded 3% lower at $104.44 per barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures with October expiry were last seen 2.6% lower at $99.86.

The co-author of the anti-corruption reform explained why involving foreigners will not change Ukraine&apos;s system: &quot;We need to take responsibility ourselves&quot;
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:56:22 EEST
19:56:22 KST

The co-author of the anti-corruption reform explained why involving foreigners will not change Ukraine's system: "We need to take responsibility ourselves"
Kyiv • UNN
Oksana Syroyid called on Ukraine to take responsibility for the functioning of its institutions itself. According to her, foreign experts are unable to change the system.
Oksana Syroyid, who participated in drafting anti-corruption legislation, spoke out against the practice of involving foreign experts in the formation and operation of Ukrainian institutions. In her view, Ukrainians must take responsibility for the functioning of government bodies rather than place it on representatives of other states. The former deputy chair of the Verkhovna Rada of the eighth convocation said this in an interview with the public initiative "Holka," published by "Glavkom," reports UNN.
Involving foreign experts in the process means relieving ourselves of responsibility. It is infantilism and an inferiority complex. As if to say, “Look, they are beating me, I’m a little girl. I’m not going to deal with this myself—I’ll go get a ‘big guy,’ bring him here, and he’ll hand everything out on my behalf.” At some point, you have to say: I’m an adult, and I take responsibility for myself
The former deputy speaker of parliament also cautioned against the belief that the foreign origins of specialists guarantee their integrity.
We should not think that people in Europe or America are born honest, while we are utterly corrupt. If they could make more profit without paying taxes, they would do so. It was not the state that forbade them from doing this; at the moment the state was created, they themselves agreed that it was better to pay taxes than evade them
According to Syroyid, Ukraine expends considerable effort trying to secure the participation of foreign specialists in the work of its own institutions, but this mechanism alone is incapable of changing the system.
We expend enormous effort lobbying Europeans, Americans, and the International Monetary Fund to appoint three—albeit highly respected—foreigners, hoping that they will make us happy. But as long as these people remain a foreign element, they will not change the system. Foreigners can be invited after we ourselves agree to act differently
Syroyid links the problem to the broader issue of responsibility for the work of state institutions. In her view, external participants cannot replace internal agreements on the rules by which the system should function.
As is known, Oksana Syroyid was a member of parliament of the eighth convocation and served as deputy chair of the Verkhovna Rada from 2014 to 2019. She participated in preparing the judicial reform and in the work of the Constitutional Commission, and was also the author of the idea to establish the Public Integrity Council. Syroyid is currently an officer in the Security and Defense Forces of Ukraine and serves in the 2nd Corps of the National Guard of Ukraine, "Khartia."
The Public Integrity Council is an independent civil society body in Ukraine that assists the High Qualification Commission of Judges (HQCJ) in checking judges and candidates for judicial positions for integrity, ethics, and the lawful origin of their assets.

For Tamer Nafar, music is no longer enough
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:56:02 UTC
19:56:02 KST

Breadcrumb
Palestinian rapper Tamer Nafar has lost faith in music's power to change the world. He keeps writing anyway
Tamer Nafar has spent more than two decades saying what others might hesitate to say. As a co-founder of DAM, the pioneering Palestinian hip-hop group, and one of the most recognisable voices in Arabic rap, he has built a career on confronting power, identity and the contradictions of Palestinian life with little interest in making anyone comfortable.
So when I sit down with the 47-year-old rapper and offer the most ordinary of pleasantries, "Hello, how are you?", his answer is anything but ordinary.
"I'm an Arab citizen of Israel," he replies, wearily.
In six words, Nafar gives an answer to a question that is rarely as simple as it sounds. It is a reminder that for him, even the most casual conversation is entangled with questions of identity, belonging and survival.
Two years ago, at this same festival, Nafar told The Guardian that music could not stop a war machine. Even then, however, he held on to something of Tupac's belief that an artist might spark the mind of the person who would eventually change the world.
Today, however, he has lost patience with that idea. When I ask whether he still believes that now, the idea does not survive the first minute of our conversation.
“F*** that," he says. "I said that before the genocide. What changes the world is oil deals."
It is a raw answer from an artist who has turned decades of blunt, hard-hitting lyrics into global hits and sold-out tours. He is not here to perform optimism, particularly when the facts offer so little reason for it.
"Oil deals change the world. Weapons and technology change it. Political choices change it"
Political leaders are not waiting to be persuaded by the right lyric. Their decisions are shaped by power, money, military relationships and technology.
Nafar knows he cannot overturn those forces simply by making something beautiful or politically compelling, but that does not mean he should abandon his art. It means being honest about its place in the hierarchy of change.
The law of the jungle
Nafar's performance at WOMAD comes at a strange moment for Palestinian music.
Palestinian artists are reaching new audiences across the world, selling out shows and claiming space on international stages.
There is a renewed interest in Palestinian music, culture and identity, but that attention has arrived amid, and often in response to, Israel's genocide in Gaza and the accelerating ethnic cleansing of the occupied West Bank.
How does Nafar feel about that bitter irony?
"That's the law of the jungle," he replies.
Palestinian culture is flourishing internationally at the same moment that Palestinian life is being destroyed. Music is carrying Palestinian stories across the world, yet the political forces determining their lives remain largely unmoved.
The contradiction hangs over our conversation. How should an artist understand success when it comes amid so much loss? What does it mean for the world to embrace Palestinian music while refusing to protect or defend Palestinian lives?
Nafar does not try to force a hopeful answer.
"There are three things we are fighting at once," he says.
"The genocide in Gaza, ethnic cleansing in the West Bank and Arab-on-Arab crime [in Israel]," he adds.
"It's about survival."
Nafar is from Lyd, one of several Palestinian towns where organised crime and violence have devastated communities amid accusations of systematic neglect by the Israeli authorities.
For him, the threats Palestinians face cannot be reduced to a single geography or one form of violence.
His answer moves between Gaza, the West Bank and Palestinian communities inside Israel because that is the political reality he inhabits.
Each crisis is distinct, but none can be separated from the wider structures governing Palestinian life.
He has moved away from the idea that music can reach the powerful and awaken something dormant within them. The problem is not that political leaders have failed to hear Palestinians clearly enough. The problem is power itself.
"Oil deals change the world. Weapons and technology change it. Political choices change it," he says.
A song, he knows, sits much further down that hierarchy. For Nafar, the task is to locate where he can still make art within it.
"I don't have the mindset that if only Donald Trump heard a moving song, he would suddenly decide to change his ways. That's bullshit."
He looks out across the festival site, dotted with Palestinian flags, keffiyehs, 'Make Peace Not War' paraphernalia, and plenty of glitter.
"But, you know, I am a little jigsaw piece in the puzzle of the world."
One small piece, trying to understand where his work fits and the limits of what it can do. In the world of festivals and grandiose gestures, it is a more modest claim for art than we are used to hearing, but a refreshingly honest one at that.
Nafar understands the world, recognises his place within it and knows the scale of the task ahead.
Overturning a genocidal government sustained by powerful imperial backers across the world, clearly, is going to take more than a few albums.
Different songs, different energy
Nafar helped pioneer Palestinian hip-hop as a co-founder of DAM, whose music brought the politics and daily realities of Palestinian life inside Israel to audiences around the world.
The group's work has never separated the political from the personal. Occupation, racism, poverty and violence sit alongside family, humour, self-criticism and the complicated reality of life in Palestinian towns.
Across a catalogue that has moved through Arabic, Hebrew and English, DAM developed a language for experiences that were either misrepresented or absent from mainstream culture.
Their music did not set out to explain Palestinians to the world politely; it documented the world in which they were already living.
Although Nafar is now developing his solo work, he is quick to stress that he is still performing with DAM.
The two projects require "different energy and different songs," he tells The New Arab. Moving between them means moving between different parts of himself and between music created at different political and personal moments.
It is not a clean break with his past, and DAM very much remains part of his present.
When asked which song is his favourite to perform, he chooses In the Name of the Father. It is one of his most personal works, using music to return to family, memory and the conversations that remain unfinished after somebody is gone.
The song does not attempt to persuade a president or redirect international politics; its world is altogether smaller and more intimate.
That does not make it apolitical. Nafar's music repeatedly returns to the places where public history enters private life: the car journey, the family home, the distance between a father and son.
If the machinery of political change operates through weapons, technology and oil deals, art can still document what that machinery does to the people living beneath it.
For Nafar, that is no longer the same as claiming music will stop it.
'I’m not a musician, I'm a writer'
Music is only one part of Nafar's work, and he is now writing a new novel, 3Gs, that spans three generations of his family.
When asked about the shift, he rejects the premise. "I'm not a musician," he says. "I've always been a writer." He describes 3Gs as an "archive of my thoughts," built from a lifetime of recording ideas.
"Someone told me to write a book, and I've always been writing things down, so I looked back and thought, you know what, I think I can make a book out of this. They asked for a specific number of pages, and I thought, yeah, I can do that."
It is an understated account of becoming a novelist: years of thoughts, a page count and the sudden realisation that the book was already there.
3Gs is an imagined memoir spanning three generations of the Nafar family: Fawzi, the father; Tamer, the son; and Shaden, the son's future daughter.
The novel gives him room to hold histories, relationships and memories that cannot always be contained within a song.
Moving between generations also allows Nafar to explore how Palestinian history enters a family, shaping those who experience its ruptures differently but remain bound together by them.
For a Palestinian writer, the act of building an archive is political. Palestinian history has repeatedly been narrated by those responsible for Palestinian dispossession, stripped of its intimacy and reduced to a dispute over territory, security or competing claims.
A family archive does something else. It preserves people as people: contradictory, funny, difficult, loving and shaped by histories they did not choose.
'I have to stay for my children'
When asked how home is, Nafar's answer is blunt. "Many people are leaving," he shares.
He is referring to the worsening conditions for Palestinian citizens of Israel living in cities such as Lyd and Haifa, both home to significant Palestinian communities.
Has he ever considered leaving himself?
"For me, of course, I would love to get out of there. But I have to stay for my children."
On his arm are the stick figures of a child's drawing, made permanent in ink. I ask whether his children drew them. Yes, he replies.
"That’s how they see me on stage, when I am under the lights," he shares.
This small and tender image reminds me of the public weight placed upon Palestinian artists and on Nafar himself.
Their work is expected to represent a people, preserve a culture, explain a political struggle and even change the minds of those responsible for their mass murder, occupation and oppression.
Nafar is also just a father holding a microphone, beneath the stage lights, as seen through the eyes of his children somewhere in the back of the crowd.
He no longer accepts the burden of changing the world. He will continue to write, perform with DAM, create songs with different energies, and build an archive of his thoughts.
But he will not pretend a song can do the work of political power.
"What changes the world is oil deals," he tells The New Arab. Music cannot end a genocide; Nafar is clear about that now.
Music may not change the course of the world, but it is one of the places where history is told and the realities that power would flatten or erase are preserved.
Nafar's work holds the many layers of Palestinian life — its violence and contradictions, but also its gallows humour, intimacy and joy.
He may not complete the puzzle, but he has added a vital piece: a pioneering artist, now an emerging literary figure, refusing to fit a mould or sugarcoat his life to suit anyone's narrative other than his own.
Tamer Nafar's first book, '3Gs', a prose memoir, is slated for release in 2026.
Frances Leach is a London-based writer covering human rights, global affairs and world culture

Yemen’s Houthis reach strategic island in Bab el-Mandeb Strait
The move potentially tightens the militants’ grip on a vital shipping route, further increasing the threat to energy markets
Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis reached the strategic island of Perim in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on Friday, four Yemeni government sources told Reuters, moving to tighten their grip on a vital global shipping route in the widening Middle East war.
Earlier, two sources from the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised Yemeni government said its forces had pulled out of Perim and that the Houthis had also taken the mainland Red Sea coastal town of Dhubab, which faces the island.
If the Houthis gain control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which is on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula from the Strait of Hormuz, it could give their backer Iran a critical advantage in its war with the US, reducing supplies through a second major transit corridor and sending oil prices surging.
Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest oil exporter and a close US ally, has relied on the Red Sea route since the Iran conflict effectively closed Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil used to flow.
In the wider war between Iran and the United States, the two sides have carried out a wave of tit-for-tat attacks this week on shipping in the Gulf, while President Donald Trump has jacked up economic pressure on Tehran. Diplomacy is largely stalled.
Iran confirmed on Friday that its representatives and those of Iraq and the Gulf Arab states would meet in Oman on Monday to resume discussions on safe commercial shipping routes in the Strait of Hormuz. The Financial Times originally reported the planned meeting.

Bank of Russia keeps key rate at 14% per annum

19:53:44 KST

MOSCOW, September 11. /TASS/. The Bank of Russia has decided to keep the key rate at 14% per annum, noting that current price pressures have increased in recent months, according to the regulator’s press release following its board meeting.
"On September 11, 2026, the Bank of Russia Board of Directors decided to keep the key rate at 14% per annum. The economy as a whole is growing at a moderate pace in 2026 Q3. Current price pressures have increased significantly in recent months," the regulator said.
The Bank of Russia added that it would make further key rate decisions based on the dynamics of inflation and inflation expectations as well as the analysis of risks posed by domestic and external conditions.
Underlying price growth has accelerated to 5-6% in annualized terms, primarily due to the impact of a temporary reduction in production capacities in certain sectors, the Central Bank added. "As these effects fade and aggregate demand grows moderately, underlying inflation will resume its decline. As of 7 September 2026, annual inflation stood at 6.3%," the press release said.
Inflation expectations of households, businesses, and financial market participants in Russia have changed diversely, remaining elevated though, which may impede a sustained slowdown in inflation, the regulator noted.
"According to high-frequency data, the economy is growing at a moderate pace in 2026 Q3. Growth in consumer demand is slowing but remains elevated. Investment activity continues to recover compared to the levels of early 2026," the document said.
The labor market tightness is gradually easing, according to the press release. "Survey results indicate that labor shortages continue to decrease. Wage growth is slowing and gradually converging with labor productivity growth, although the gap between them remains significant. Unemployment is near historic lows but has risen slightly in recent months," the regulator said.
Monetary conditions are assessed as moderately tight. Interest rates have changed diversely in various segments of the financial market. Taking into consideration the dynamics of inflation expectations, the overall tightness of monetary conditions has decreased slightly in real terms. Non-price bank lending conditions are still tight, the Bank of Russia said.
"Lending activity has been elevated in recent months, driven primarily by the corporate segment. The retail loan portfolio has been growing moderately. Households’ propensity to save has decreased slightly but remains high," the regulator noted.
Proinflationary risks have increased and prevail over disinflationary ones on the medium-term horizon, the Central Bank added. "Main proinflationary risks are associated with the supply-demand imbalances, driven by higher domestic demand and a longer contraction of production capacities in certain industries. Elevated inflation expectations may intensify the pass-through of costs to prices. Proinflationary risks associated with a long period of wage growth outpacing productivity growth as well as with a deterioration in the global economic outlook and rising global price pressures amid geopolitical tensions are still in place. Disinflationary risks involve a more significant slowdown in domestic demand," the press release said.
"The Bank of Russia’s July baseline scenario assumes a gradual decrease in the structural primary budget deficit to zero in 2029. Fiscal policy parameters, including the trajectory of returning to a zero structural balance, will be further detailed in the October forecast after the Government submits new medium-term budget projections to the State Duma. If these projections assume a higher structural primary budget deficit, a tighter monetary policy stance than stipulated in the baseline scenario may be required," the Bank of Russia concluded.

Russian Central Bank Holds Key Rate at 14%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:53:00 UTC
19:53:00 KST

Russia’s Central Bank kept its key interest rate at 14% on Friday, saying that rising fuel costs, driven by Ukrainian drone attacks on oil refineries, and a “temporary reduction in production capacities” are making it difficult to tame inflation.
The Central Bank reported that annual inflation hit 6.3% on Sept. 7. Policymakers maintained their full-year inflation forecast at 6% to 7%, and still expect price growth to fall toward the 4% target next year.
“In recent months, price dynamics have been considerably affected by volatile components, including motor fuel, fruit and vegetables,” the regulator said in a press release. “The rise in motor fuel prices has also affected underlying inflation dynamics.”
“Inflation expectations of households, businesses and financial market participants have changed diversely. Nevertheless, they remain elevated, which may impede a sustained slowdown in inflation,” it added.
The bank last lowered the key rate at its July 24 meeting, bringing it from 14.25% to 14%.
In a follow-up statement, Central Bank Governor Elvira Nabiullina warned that the effects of Russia’s fuel shortage are spilling into the broader economy. While the initial summer spike was limited to pump prices, she said, “second-round effects” are now taking hold as transportation costs push up prices across a wider range of goods and services.
Nabiullina also said Russia has been forced to increase imports of petroleum products to rebuild depleted stocks. That import surge, combined with export bottlenecks, weakened the ruble over the summer and further fueled inflation.
Inflation is a growing concern across the globe as the war in Iran drives up the price of oil, which has again risen above $100 per barrel due to renewed threats in the Strait of Hormuz. Earlier this week, the European Central Bank raised its benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point to 2.5%.
For Russia, sustained Ukrainian attacks against oil refineries and energy infrastructure are compounding the problem. Since the spring, drone strikes have halted or scaled back production at facilities that account for large shares of Russia’s gasoline output, leading to major fuel shortages across the country.
Yet at the same time, a long period of high borrowing costs has weighed down economic growth, leaving business leaders pressing for a lower key interest rate to stimulate investment.
GDP growth in Russia is projected at near-stagnant levels of 0% to 1% for this year.
On Friday, Nabiullina framed the decision to hold the key rate at 14% as a necessary “pause” in the bank’s rate-cutting cycle. She warned that further cuts are off the table until the bank sees clear evidence that underlying inflation is cooling and government budget plans for the coming year are finalized.
The Central Bank’s next rate meeting takes place on Oct. 23.

Senate continues work on election-law bill after controversy over preferences
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:52:30 CEST
19:52:30 KST

The Senate on Friday resumed work on
a bill presented by the parties of Premier Giorgia Meloni's
ruling coalition to bring in a new election law after a
controversial amendment on voter preferences was approved on
Thursday.
                                    
                                       
				The amendment, backed by Meloni's ruling alliance, gives voters
the option to express preferences for up to three candidates out
of six on a party list in which candidates names must alternate
according to gender.
                                    
                                       
				The opposition says that in reality this gives "fake
preferences" as the head of the ticket would always be
"blocked", arguing this was also be a step back for equality,
as, in theory, it would be possible for all the ticket heads to
be men.
                                    
                                       
				The current system does not give voters any option to express
preferences about which of the candidates on a party list they
want to represent them.
                                    
                                       
				The ruling coalition suffered an embarrassing defeat in a vote
on preferences when the bill was in the Lower House for its
first reading.
                                    
                                       
				The bill will see the current system, a mix of
first-past-the-post and proportional representation, replaced
with a proportional-representation system with bonus seats for
the coalition that obtains the most votes, as long as it reaches
a threshold of 42%, to ensure it has a working majority in
parliament.
                                    
                                       
				If no coalition reaches the threshold, or the votes for the
Lower House and the Senate produce different results, a purely
proportional system is used.
                                    
                                       
				The coalitions will have to name their candidate to be premier
before the election. The opposition has cried foul about the
drive to overhaul the electoral system, saying the ruling
alliance us changing it because it fears losing the general
election set to take place next year and wants to minimize the
chances of this happening.
                                    
                                       
				They have said, among other things, that the envisioned system
of bonus seats is unconstitutional.
                                    
                                       
				The Upper House is set to hold its final vote on the bill by
September 15 and the bill will move back to the floor of the
Lower House on September 28 for its third reading in parliament.

After election triumph, German far-right seeks allies to form state government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:51:04 UTC
19:51:04 KST

After election triumph, German far-right seeks allies to form state government
MAGDEBURG, Germany, Sept 11 - After its triumph in Sunday's state election in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany's far-right AfD needs to attract defectors from other parties or reach an agreement with the small far-left BSW party that is setting difficult conditions in return for its support.
Ulrich Siegmund, the 35-year-old AfD leader who is expected to become state premier, said there were discussions with both the BSW and individual members of other parties "to see if there is any common ground that could help secure a stable majority".
He said he wanted to form such a majority in the state legislature "as soon as possible". However, there is nothing unusual in German politics about coalition negotiations that last for weeks or even months before a government can be formed.
The discussions underline the political realities now facing Siegmund, who said repeatedly during the campaign that he wanted an absolute majority to be able to govern alone, only to fall just short, winning 39 seats in the 83-seat parliament.
Even if he secures an agreement with another party that would allow him to become premier, his majority is likely to be a slim one, making governing more complicated than his record score in the election might suggest.
AFD SHUNNED BY GERMANY'S MAINSTREAM PARTIES
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) is already the country's most popular party at the national level and is seeking to secure a foothold for advancing its agenda, which includes heavy restrictions on immigration, restoring ties with Russia, cutting support to Ukraine and quitting the euro.
However, all the other parties in Saxony-Anhalt's state parliament - as at the national level - have refused to join forces with the far-right party, with the exception of the BSW, a small far-left party that, like the AfD, wants to restrict immigration and restore ties with Russia.
The BSW, which won five seats in the state parliament, has said it is interested in working with the AfD, which the Saxony-Anhalt office of Germany's domestic security agency classifies as extremist far-right. But so far the BSW has said it does not want to enter a formal coalition and wants an independent state premier, a condition that Siegmund rejects.
"Just under 44% of people in Saxony-Anhalt voted for Alternative for Germany," Siegmund told reporters in Magdeburg, the state capital, on Thursday. "Naturally, our aim should be to be able to name the Minister-President."
If an agreement with the BSW cannot be reached, the most likely alternative would be to persuade some of the 15 members of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) in the state parliament to switch sides and back the AfD.
Opinion within the CDU is divided over the German mainstream parties' so-called "firewall" strategy to isolate the AfD and it may be possible to induce some to switch parties. But so far, no confirmed defectors have been identified.
If no agreement can be reached, Siegmund has even aired the prospect of calling a new election, saying it was "something we do not, in principle, shy away from".
"It would result from a situation where no one else is prepared to take on responsibility," he said. REUTERS

Russian air defence stocks significantly depleted
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:50:53 BST
19:50:53 KST

Russian long-range air defence interceptor stocks have been depleted to the point where Moscow is having to make serious decisions about where it deploys them, a Western official has told the UK Defence Journal.
We asked whether the assessment is that Russian air defence stocks are genuinely running down to a point that would leave Russian cities and infrastructure more vulnerable than they have been, or whether the decline reported by Ukrainian intelligence in S-300 and S-400 interceptor reserves is being offset by external supplies.
“No, absolutely, 100 per cent. They’ve been depleted,” the official said.
The explanation offered was that the stockpiles were never intended for this. Those reserves existed “for defence of Russia in a campaign from NATO, not some sort of regional conflict with Ukraine”, the official said, with the consequence that “absolutely those numbers are dwindling, and Russia is having to make some really serious prioritisation decisions about where they employ those air defence assets.”
The depletion was explained by reference to a series of Ukrainian operations that Russian planning had not anticipated. Reflecting on how much has changed, the official said an intelligence officer five years ago would not have thought the present situation realistic, and that the same applies looking at it from the Russian side. Ukrainian drone strikes reaching the vicinity of the St Petersburg International Economic Forum, and Russian oil refining capacity down by 40 per cent at its peak, were described as completely unforeseeable by Moscow.
One measure of how acute the problem became was legislative as Russia introduced a law to mobilise reservists specifically for the air defence of oil refineries, the official said, a step taken late last year in response to the success Ukraine was having against those targets.
On whether a point of exhaustion can be identified, the official was careful, telling me “I don’t think we’ll be in a position yet to say what that pivot point is,” they said, declining to predict a date by which reserves might run out while maintaining that Russia faces very difficult choices.
Officials described Russian use of North Korean KN-23 ballistic missiles as significant in itself. “The fact that Russia is having to use North Korean missiles is quite significant. It says a lot about Russia’s ability to resource its own conflict,” one official said, declining to give numbers.

Pro-Palestine groups 'blockade' UK insurers over Elbit ties
Unknown

2026-09-11

Breadcrumb
Pro-Palestine groups 'blockade' UK insurers over ties to Israeli arms firm Elbit
Pro-Palestine activists have carried out protests outside five UK offices belonging to two of the world's largest commercial insurance and reinsurance providers over their alleged links to Israeli arms manufacturer Elbit Systems.
Chubb and Sompo offices in Manchester, Glasgow, London and Maidstone faced disruption from campaigners who say that the insurers have provided underwriting for Elbit Systems and its subsidiary, UAV Engines, in Britain, as well as Elbit's US operations.
Elbit, Israel's largest arms manufacturer, supplies drones, surveillance systems and other weapons to the Israeli military, including during Israel's genocidal war on Gaza, which began on 7 October 2023.
According to the groups involved in the direct action, including Manchester-based Palestine Resistance Collective (PRC), Mothers Against Genocide Scotland and Boycott Bloody Insurance, protesters gathered outside Chubb's Glasgow office carrying banners and formed a 'red line' around the building while distributing leaflets to passers-by and office workers.
A speech was delivered inside the building's lobby, and a letter was handed to Chubb's management calling on the insurer to sever its relationship with Elbit.
In Manchester and London, protesters blockaded office entrances while making the same demand.
In a statement, Andrew Taylor, a member of Boycott Bloody Insurance, a campaign group calling on insurance companies to end their support for "destructive companies",, said: "Israel relies on Elbit’s weapons and technology to enact its genocide and occupation in Palestine – and Elbit wouldn’t be able to operate without insurance from Chubb."
He added: "People of conscience all over Britain will continue to reject Chubb’s complicity in war crimes until they see it come to an end."
Boycott Bloody Insurance has also accused Chubb of having significant exposure to companies it considers destructive, ranking it among the worst-performing insurers for underwriting weapons, fossil fuel and border detention and surveillance companies.
The group says this includes providing insurance to Lockheed Martin and several UK suppliers of components for F-35 fighter jets, which are also used by Israeli forces in military operations in the occupied Palestinian territories.
The latest action follows moves by two other insurance firms, Allianz and Aviva, to end underwriting for Israel's largest arms manufacturer following sustained direct action by banned activist group Palestine Action.
Allianz's coverage of Elbit Systems UK ended last November, while Aviva's employment liability insurance coverage for UAV Engines Ltd, an Elbit subsidiary, ended in last September.
Elbit Systems UK is now reportedly receiving employer's liability insurance from Aspen Insurance, while UAV Engines is insured by Chubb.

Smoke billows from an Israeli-controlled detonation in the village of Mansouri, as is seen from Hanniyeh village, southern Lebanon, Sept. 11, 2026. (AP Photo/Hussein Malla)
Israel has demolished key tunnels built by the Iran-backed Hezbollah group beneath the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge in southern Lebanon, triggering a 4.1 magnitude tremor.
AFP journalists in the area heard several explosions. In a video shared by Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz, a huge fireball can be seen rising into the night sky.
The explosion comes a few days after Israeli authorities claimed to have taken control of the Ali al-Taher ridge, saying that the pro-Iranian Hezbollah had dug numerous tunnels there, allowing it to attack Israel from this mountainous area.
Israeli troops occupy part of southern Lebanon, where Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says he wants to establish a “security zone” to prevent any attacks on the north of his country.
“This is strategic terrorist infrastructure that was built over two decades, with Iranian funding and planning,” Netanyahu and Katz said in a joint statement.
The destruction “completes the achievement of operational control over the Ali al-Taher ridge, above and below ground,” the statement added.
The United States Geological Survey reported a 4.1 magnitude tremor in the area, after Lebanon’s state-run National News Agency (NNA) reported that Israel carried out a “massive explosion” on the Ali al-Taher ridge in the Nabatieh region, “causing tremors and a powerful rumble.”
AFP journalists in south Lebanon also said they heard “huge explosions” on Sept. 10 evening.
“We were sitting there and everything shook,” Joelle Fares, who recently moved to Majayoun, told AFP.
Israel announced last week that it had captured the Ali al-Taher ridge.

Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has published a video of himself using a hammer to attack a monument in Poland dedicated to soldiers from the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a World War Two partisan formation that fought against the Soviet Union but was also responsible for massacring Poles.
Braun declared that the monument, which was also recently vandalised by other unknown perpetrators, should be removed as it “insults the memory of victims of the Ukrainian genocide against Poles” and “glorifies Nazism”.
The incident comes amid recent tensions between Warsaw and Kyiv over World War Two history, and in particular the fact that the UPA continues to be honoured in Ukraine.

The monument in question is located in the village of Liski, a few kilometres from the border with Ukraine, and marks the burial site of 41 UPA soldiers killed while fighting against the NKVD, the Soviet secret police, in 1946, in the aftermath of World War Two. The area previously had a large ethnic-Ukrainian population.
The memorial was vandalised last month, when it was sprayed with black paint and its arch was damaged. On Monday this week, further damage was discovered to the inscription on the monument.
Police announced that they had launched an investigation into vandalism, property damage and ethnic hatred, but had not yet identified the perpetrators, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP).
On Wednesday evening, Braun published a video showing himself and another man using a hammer to repeatedly strike the front of the monument, causing visible damage to the stone, which contains the names of the killed UPA soldiers. They also appear to attempt to remove a separate plaque.
During the video, Braun, who is a member of the European Parliament and finished fourth in last year’s Polish presidential election, claimed that local residents are “afraid they would be set on fire” if they attempted to remove the memorial themselves. It is not clear when the video was recorded.
Shortly after Braun published it, local police in Hrubieszów county, where the monument is located, issued a statement saying that officers were investigating damage to the monument. Interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka shared their statement and declared that “the perpetrators will not go unpunished”.

Braun regularly carries out stunts intended to demonstrate his anti-Ukrainian, antisemitic and anti-LGBT views, and is already facing multiple legal cases over such incidents.
He is currently on trial for attacking a celebration of the Jewish festival of Hanukkah in parliament using a fire extinguisher. Last month, he was charged with the crime of denying Nazi crimes for claiming that the gas chambers at Auschwitz are “fake”.

At the time of writing, there had been no response from Ukrainian authorities to Braun’s latest stunt. However, when the same monument was vandalised last month, the Ukrainian embassy in Warsaw issued a statement expressing its “deep indignation”.
“Regardless of the difficult and tragic chapters of our shared history, burial and memorial sites should remain outside the realm of political disputes and be treated with respect,” they wrote.
The embassy also expressed “particular concern that this incident occurs against the backdrop of a rising number of hostile acts toward Ukrainians in Poland, including reports of aggression and attacks on Ukrainian citizens”
“Any attempts to shift historical disputes into the realm of vandalism, intimidation or hostility toward modern Ukraine and Ukrainians are dangerous and must be met with an appropriate legal response,” they added.
Poland and Ukraine have been embroiled in a diplomatic dispute since May, when President Volodymyr Zelensky named a military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. His Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, responded by stripping Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour.
Tensions have since cooled, and Ukraine has made moves to defuse the crisis. However, significant differences remain, in particular over memory of the so-called Volhynia massacres, in which the UPA led the killing of around 100,000 Polish civilians.
Poland regards the episode as a genocide. Ukraine strongly rejects that label, and also continues to honour the UPA for its role in fighting against Moscow-imposed Soviet rule.
Recent months have also seen a rise in anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Poland, including a series of cases of verbal or physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are by far Poland’s largest immigrant group. Reported anti-Ukrainian hate crimes were up 30% in the first half of this year.
Demonstrations took place in 25 Polish cities on Sunday against the “growing wave of hate and violence” against Ukrainians, who are Poland’s largest immigrant group.
Reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland are up 30% this year https://t.co/gGAEc6QZWT

In 2017, Ukraine responded to the dismantling of a UPA monument in Poland by introducing a ban on exhumations of Polish victims of the Volhynia massacres on its territory. It is believed that tens of thousands still remain buried in unmarked mass graves.
However, last year, in a diplomatic breakthrough, Kyiv allowed such exhumations to resume, and since then the remains of dozens of victims have been found, researched and reburied.
Earlier this month, Poland also granted Ukraine permission to conduct a search for the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by Polish resistance fighters during World War Two.

Twenty five years on, US remembers lives cut short by 9/11 attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:48:00 UTC
19:48:00 KST

Americans marked the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks Friday, remembering nearly 3,000 lives lost and the sweeping consequences of al-Qaida's assault on the symbols of U.S. power and prosperity.
Friday's milestone anniversary will bring memorial rituals – wreath-laying, flag-flying, moments of silence, vigils and readings of victims' names – and volunteer projects in tribute to a day that about half of U.S. adults remember as the most historic event of their lifetime, according to a new poll .
For others it's an occasion for private reflection – or, in many schools, education – about the attack that unfolded in a single morning but left nearly 3,000 dead and a decadeslong trail of aftermath, from personal grief to far-flung wars.
Police Officer Casey Kloepfer plans to spend time Friday at the Brooklyn station house where his father, Officer Ronald Kloepfer, reported to work that day before being called to the World Trade Center. He didn't make it home.
Casey Kloepfer was only 4, but he grew up hearing about his father's affinity for helping people and for a job that enabled him to do so. He became an officer this past June.
"It's big footsteps to fill, but it's definitely something that I take very seriously and want to continue to honor him and be the best police officer I can," he said by phone this week.
The 29-year-old wears his father's badge number and even has joined the New York Police Department lacrosse team, which his dad founded.
On Sept. 11, 2001, al-Qaida terrorists hijacked four commercial jets and crashed them into New York's World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania.
The impacts brought down the World Trade Center's twin towers – icons of U.S. economic power, and among the tallest buildings on Earth – and blew a hole in the Pentagon, the U.S. military's fortress-like headquarters near Washington.
The fourth plane also was headed for the nation's capital, officials concluded, but the aircraft went down in Pennsylvania after passengers and crew members stormed the cockpit and fought the hijackers.
"In the course of history, there are a few moments that divide time into, really, what came before" and after, President Donald Trump said at a 9/11 remembrance in Washington this week. The Republican, who was in his native New York on Sept. 11 and has often recounted his memories, plans to attend the Pentagon's anniversary ceremony Friday.
Vice President JD Vance is expected at the observance at the National Sept. 11 Memorial in New York, while other administration officials are headed to the Flight 93 National Memorial in Pennsylvania.
Planned remembrances extend far beyond the attack sites, from beams of light projecting from New Hampshire's Mount Washington to a stair climb at Mississippi State University's football stadium to a ceremony at Honolulu's 9/11 memorial.
Traditionally, there are no political speeches at the New York commemoration, where relatives read all the victims' names, punctuated with moments of silence at key points in the attack timeline.
For the first time, this year's ceremony will add a silent moment to honor people who were exposed to the clouds of toxic dust released by the twin towers' fiery collapse and have since died of cancer and other illnesses. Questions remain about how many people developed health problems linked to the dust.
It's a reminder of how the attacks' long shadow has reached into many corners of life in the U.S. and beyond.
The U.S.-led global war on terrorism included invasions of Iraq and Afghanistan – the latter Washington's longest war – and detentions and harsh interrogation of terror suspects in an international network of secret CIA prisons.
The U.S. military found and killed al-Qaida leader Osama bin Laden in Pakistan in 2011, but accused 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed still awaits a trial 23 years after his capture.
The attacks changed U.S. air travel, prompted new federal surveillance and intelligence-gathering powers and banking regulations, and generated ongoing debate over the balance between security and freedom. The Department of Homeland Security, many state anti-terrorism laws and billions of dollars in state and local counterterrorism funding all are post-9/11 creations.
So, too, is the culture of individual vigilance summed up by the slogan "if you see something, say something."
Sept. 11 generated a wave of patriotism that propelled some Americans to join the military, fire departments, police forces or other public agencies. But amid the national unity that many remember, the attacks also fanned mistrust, prejudice and hate crimes directed at Muslims.
In the quarter-century since, Muslim Americans have played a growing role in public life from statehouses to Congress to New York City Hall, where Zohran Mamdani is the city's first Muslim mayor. Yet he is facing some criticism for planning to attend the anniversary ceremony at ground zero, something his predecessors have done for years.
Some complaints came from Republican ex-Gov. George Pataki and 9/11 victims' relatives, who cited among other things past remarks that some of Mamdani's political associates have made about the attacks. Former Mayor Rudy Giuliani, a Republican, also inveighed against Mamdani attending.
Mamdani, a Democrat, responded this week that he loves the city and country and wants the anniversary to focus on victims' families, first responders and New Yorkers who helped one another after the attacks, which he called a "horrific act of terror." The 34-year-old mayor was an elementary school student in New York on 9/11.
Sept. 11 isn't a federal holiday, but Congress has designated it both Patriot Day and a National Day of Service and Remembrance.
"One appropriate way to remember is by serving," says Jay Winuk, who lost his brother Glenn Winuk and then co-founded the volunteer organization 9/11 Day with friend David Paine. The group helps people find meal-packing and other volunteer opportunities and this year arranged for dozens of Times Square billboards to pause their advertising at 9:11 a.m. Friday.
Instead, they will simply display the time.

Mathernova: Russia acts in Ukraine just like terrorists did during Sept 11 attacks
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:47:30 EEST
19:47:30 KST

European Union Ambassador to Ukraine Katarína Mathernová believes that the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks—which destroyed the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center in New York—and Russia's terror in Ukraine share common features.
“The attacks have much in common. Terrorists and criminals are behind them. russia acts like a terrorist state in Ukraine,” Mathernova wrote in a post published on the social network X.
She noted that 25 years ago, she was in an office in Bratislava in front of a television screen and saw the second plane crash into the Twin Towers live on air.
“I saw the second plane crashing live on TV. The explosion. People desperately jumping from the burning towers. A huge cloud of dust engulfing New York City,” the ambassador said.
According to Mathernova, she did not think back then that she would ever again witness such horror in her life. Yet now, 25 years later, she is experiencing the same thing during Russian attacks on Kyiv.
“During the explosions of drones and missiles. The air stops moving for a moment when we run to shelters during the sirens and listen to the deafening explosions. Then I see images of dead bodies, bloodied people, and dust, rubble and emptiness everywhere,” Mathernova said.
She recalled that the September 11 terrorist attacks claimed the lives of 2,977 people.
“The attack on America united the democratic world in the belief that terrorism must never be appeased. In Ukraine, the UN has already officially verified the deaths of more than 16,800 civilians. According to the UN, the actual number is likely substantially higher,” the ambassador noted.
Mathernova emphasized that 25 years ago the world realized that terrorism is not the internal affair of a single country, and called for a renewed recognition of this fact.

NEW DELHI: The Congress on Friday attacked the government over a controversial US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) advertisement targeting “Mr Singh”. “Modi ji, who has been showcasing his international clout by calling Donald Trump his 'friend' and who even coined the slogan 'Abki Baar Trump Sarkar' among Indian-Americans, is now seeing continuous insults against Indians and people of Indian origin under his administration,” Ramesh said.“Yet, the Modi government is behaving as if it is a silent partner in this entire episode. An extremely offensive poster targeting 'Mr Singh' was issued from the official handle of the US Department of Homeland Security, in which a turbaned Indian was threatened with lines like 'Get off our roads' and 'Self-deport or find out',” he said in a post in Hindi on X.
Ramesh said the episode was not merely an insult to an individual or community but to “the dignity of all Indians”. He said the government should have strongly rebutted what he described as racial stereotyping and “this level of governmental rudeness”.The DHS later removed the advertisement following protests in the US, Ramesh said. However, he alleged that the department continued to defend the campaign and its language through other official posts.“The question is: Why has there been no strong public rebuttal from the Modi government on this insult to Indians?” Ramesh said.The Congress leader also linked the controversy to earlier instances in which he accused the government of failing to defend Indian interests before the US administration. He recalled the deportation of Indians on US military aircraft in handcuffs and leg shackles and the imposition of additional US tariffs on India.“Why has our diplomatic strength become so feeble during the tenure of the Modi government, which boasts of being the 'vishwaguru', that India's interests and sovereignty are facing one blow after another?” Ramesh said.“Why is the Modi government silent? Why does the Government of India keep proving itself weak time and again?” he said.Ramesh questioned whether the government's relationship with US President Donald Trump meant that Washington could continue to target Indians while India remained silent.“Friendship is important in foreign policy, but national interest, the dignity of Indians, and India's sovereignty are paramount, and there can be no compromise on them,” he said.The controversy erupted after DHS used AI-generated imagery as part of a campaign against unlicensed commercial drivers. The advertisement showed a brown-bearded man and referred specifically to “Mr Singh”.The reference drew criticism from advocacy groups, including the Hindu American Foundation (HAF) and Sikh Coalition, which accused the US agency of racial profiling.“Singhs are Hindu, they are Sikhs, they are American and they drive. Racist, un-American, anti-Indian profiling/trolling by @DHSgov should shock our nation's collective conscience,” the HAF said on X.“This is a discriminatory post by a federal agency that is far beyond political messaging, and we welcome an investigation,” the organisation said, tagging Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K Dhillon and FBI Director Kash Patel.The Sikh Coalition said the incident showed that Sikhs continued to face profiling based on their appearance.“Twenty-five years after 9/11, Sikhs are still being targeted and profiled for how we look,” it said.“Millions of Sikhs in the United States have the last name Singh, which means lion. We remain fearless in identifying as Sikhs even when our government portrays us as enemies,” the Sikh Coalition said.Other DHS posts as part of the campaign featured characters from the Transformers franchise. One video showed Megatron negotiating the release of truck drivers Harjinder Singh, Rajinder Kumar, Bekzhan Beishekeev, Akhror Bozorov and Jasveer Singh, who the agency said were involved in road accidents and other crimes.“If you approach this nation with hostile intent, know this. We will defend ourselves. We will defend Americanism. We will defend our home,” the DHS said in a post on X.
Another post featured Optimus Prime with a DHS arm patch confronting the brown-bearded man alongside the message: “Self-deport or find out”.The controversy comes amid the DHS campaign to promote its CBP Home programme, which allows eligible undocumented migrants to register their intention to leave the US voluntarily. Those opting for self-deportation can receive travel assistance and an exit bonus of USD 2,600, according to the DHS.

Military Court Centres
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher

11:47:16 BST

Military Court Centres
The Service Justice System is supported in the UK by two designated Military Court Centres at Bulford (Wiltshire) and Catterick (North Yorkshire).
Hearings at both court centres are open to the public unless directed otherwise by a Judge Advocate.
The courts are located on the perimeter of a military establishment. This design provides public access to the Service Courts. The public entrance is staffed by the personnel from Military Provost Guard Service who employ security screening checks as a condition of entry.
Each court centre has two court rooms with all courts holding the capability to manage any type of case within the Service Justice System. Case are listed between the hours of 9.30am to 4.30pm, Monday to Friday. The courts do not sit on Saturdays, Sundays and on public holidays.
Each court is fitted with the latest Digital Audio Recording technology, Assistive Listening devices, Digital AV/IP Evidential Presentation Systems and the latest Section 28 recording capability. We are leading the use of in-court technology for the Board members and defendants and are developing our use of AI court transcription technology throughout 2025.

Russia has threatened Lithuania with nuclear weapons as the Baltic nation is eyeing a lift of its nuclear weapons ban.
Lithuania’s parliamentary parties provisionally agreed to the constitutional amendments in July, and the parliamentary Committee on Legal Affairs voted 7-2 on the proposal on Wednesday, Sept. 9, paving the way for a final decision in early 2027.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The lifting of the ban would allow NATO, of which Lithuania has been a member of since 2004, to deploy nuclear forces on its territory.
On Friday, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov threatened Vilnius over the plan by saying the Baltic nation – once under Soviet occupation – will be “in the sights of our nuclear weapons.”
“And if there are nuclear weapons on the territory that are aimed at us, then the territory of this country will also be in the sights of our nuclear weapons,” Peskov told Russia’s Channel One on Friday, as reported by state media RIA Novosti.
Lithuania, one of Ukraine’s strongest backers in Europe, borders Russia’s exclave of Kaliningrad to the west and staunch Moscow ally Belarus to the south, with Vilnius a mere two-hour drive from Minsk, Belarus’s capital.
Russia began deploying nuclear weapons to Belarus, a non-nuclear nation, in June 2023. In December 2025, Russia also deployed its nuclear-capable Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missile (IRBM) to Belarus, whose combat use in Ukraine marked the first combat use of its kind in history.

In May, Belarus conducted a nuclear war drill with Russia, involving Belarusian military units tasked with the combat use of nuclear weapons and nuclear support operations.
In July, when discussions over the nuke ban gained traction in Vilnius’s parliament, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda attributed the need to changing geopolitical circumstances.
“The geopolitical situation is getting worse… Our constitution was written when geopolitical circumstances were totally different,” Nauseda said.

Houthis complete takeover of Bab al-Mandab area
Unknown
