Russia’s Recruitment of Foreign Fighters for Ukraine War ‘Amounts to Human Trafficking’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:23:24 UTC
19:23:24 KST

Russian military recruitment of foreign nationals to fight in Ukraine amounts to human trafficking with Kremlin recruiters using deceptive, coercive, and exploitative practices to fill out army ranks, human rights advocacy group Amnesty International said in a new report published on Thursday.Russia systematically lures individuals from abroad into the Russian Armed Forces under false pretences, and targets particularly vulnerable migrants and refugees already present in Russia who have traveled in from low-income countries of the Global South, the report said.
“Amnesty’s research demonstrates how Russia’s Armed Forces are…using them as cannon fodder,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General, in a published statement.
“The level of exploitation and coercion (by Russia) amounts to human trafficking as defined under the UN’s Palermo Protocol,” she added.
The Amnesty report was based on interviews with individuals from Brazil, Colombia, Cuba, Egypt, Sierra Leone, Sri Lanka, Somalia, and South Africa at two Ukrainian prisoner of war camps, between 2024 and 2026.
“Russian authorities have weaponized the irregular immigration status of those who overstay work-related visas and the precarious situation of foreigners accused of criminal offences, presenting enlistment as a favourable alternative to detention and deportation,” a co-published Amnesty statement said.
St. Petersburg Metro Prepares 9 Stations as Civil Defense Shelters
The International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) in a March 2026 report estimated that since invading Ukraine a second time in February 2022, Russia has recruited at least 27,000 foreign nationals from more than 130 countries.
According to that report, and Ukraine’s Coordination Center for the Treatment of POWs, some of those fighters are volunteers, but some are tricked into Russian army service. Recruitment of foreigners, voluntarily or coercively, to fight in a war of aggression constitutes a war crime, according to the report.
First-hand accounts published in Ukrainian media and reports from Ukrainian combat units that encountered foreign fighters on the battlefield reinforce Amnesty International’s findings that many foreigners joining the Russian army are recruited under false pretenses and misled by Russian authorities to bolster frontline manpower.
A 39-year-old Columbian man identifying himself as Basi (Basilio) Muñoz, told captors in Ukraine’s 63rd Mechanized Brigade that he had been hired by a Russian company to travel to Moscow and work as a military mechanic, signing a contract guaranteeing his job and specifically excluding him from front line duty.
“I couldn’t even imagine that there was even a chance I would get sent to the front with a rifle. But what can I tell you? They just lied to us. They just ran a big fraud with us,” Muñoz said in a June interview with his captors.
“Then they (Russian army commanders) treat you like the lowest order of trash. They took our passports and our telephones. They didn’t let us call our relatives. They always kept us locked up, and then they sent us to the front,” he added.
Muñoz was seriously wounded by a drone during an attack in the northern Donetsk region. He made his way to Ukrainian lines and was taken prisoner.
Soldiers from Ukraine’s 66th Mechanized Brigade, following a lethal August firefight, found that one of their dead opponents was Peruvian national Walter-Vicente, aged 60.
Documents found on Walter-Vicente’s body showed he spoke no Russian, had traveled to Russia for civilian work, and was forcibly transferred into a frontal assault attack unit despite his advanced age.
In May, a Ghanaian man profiled in the local news platform Joynews, in an hour long interview, said he was lured to Russia by an offer of work as a military steward. However, after arriving at the military camp, he was forced to sign a contract which he could not read, that obliged him to become a soldier and fight in Ukraine. According to him, Ghanaian businessmen cooperated with Russian recruiters in the scan and found that hundreds of Africans were similarly deceived.
The Ghanaian man was later severely wounded in a drone strike, but managed to leave Russian army service on medical grounds, the report said.
Kenyan Francis Ndung’u Ndarua, an electrical engineer, recorded a video sometime in early 2026 warning fellow Africans not to travel to Russia for supposedly civilian employment.
He claimed the Russian government was operating a world-wide forced recruitment network that tricks foreigners into traveling to Russia for work, after which by lies and under police pressure, they are forced to join the Russian army.
Ndarua’s case became widely-known after Russian troops, possibly as a joke, video-recorded him with an anti-tank mine strapped to his chest, while other soldiers laughed at him. His mother published the content in hopes of returning her son back home to Nairobi.
A 22-year-old citizen of Equatorial Guinea identified as Nchama, in content published by Polish Radio in mid-April, said he was recruited in late 2025 after being promised employment in Russia as a personal bodyguard. He was instead sent to fight in Ukraine, but deserted his Russian unit, found his country’s embassy, and returned home.
According to the Ukrainian government-sanctioned media group United24, “Russia deliberately exploits foreigners’ lack of language skills and knowledge of military contracts.”
Common Russian recruitment tactics reported by the group include false promises of rear area jobs, confiscation of passports, and use of minor violations of initial contract terms as grounds to force men into front line service.
The content published by United24 in August 2025 identified men from Ghana, Somalia, Sri Lanka, Egypt, and Togo as among those detained in Ukrainian prisoner camps.

Global trade at risk as Houthis capture Red Sea chokepoint under Iranian guidance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:23:11 UTC
19:23:11 KST

Officials with Yemen’s internationally recognized, Saudi-backed government acknowledged Friday that Iran-aligned Houthi forces had reached the coastal town of Dhubab and seized control of the Bab el-Mandab Strait.
Meanwhile, Yemeni government forces withdrew from the strategic island of Perim, also known as Mayyun, which sits in the middle of the southern entrance to the strait. The officials said control of Dhubab, adjacent to the waterway, and Perim was key to controlling Bab el-Mandab — and that the Houthis had now achieved it.
The development comes as fighting over the Strait of Hormuz has dragged on for months, raising fears that disruption at a second major Middle Eastern shipping chokepoint could send already elevated oil prices sharply higher.
A senior Israeli official called it a “negative development” but stressed: “If we are not attacked, we will not intervene.”
Axios reported that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called U.S. President Donald Trump twice Thursday and urged him to order strikes against the Houthis. Trump refused, according to the report.
Reuters reported that the latest Houthi campaign was carried out under direct guidance from Iran’s Revolutionary Guard. Two Iranian sources said Tehran instructed the Houthis last week to escalate attacks against Saudi Arabia and promised additional funding and weapons.
A regional diplomat briefed by Tehran said senior Revolutionary Guard officers had traveled to Yemen to oversee and command Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia following weeks of discussions over military strategy.
Citing intercepted communications and accounts from captured Houthi fighters, Yemeni military sources said they believed the Iranian effort was being led by Abdul Reza Shahlai, a senior Revolutionary Guard commander.
Iranian sources did not confirm the claim. Shahlai, a member of the Guard’s elite Quds Force, has previously been reported to have spent time in Yemen in recent years.
Bin Salman’s calls to Trump came after dramatic developments in Yemen, including the Houthi seizure of strategic Red Sea islands, the capture of the nearby port city of Mocha and mounting fears that the group could block or threaten traffic through Bab el-Mandab.
Trump rejected the request for U.S. strikes, and American officials said the administration does not currently intend to take direct military action against the Houthis.
The United States is increasingly concerned about the rapid escalation in Yemen and is stepping up support for Saudi Arabia while seeking to avoid direct military involvement, according to the report. Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command, traveled to Saudi Arabia on Thursday for urgent coordination meetings.
The Saudi-Houthi confrontation resumed in July after Riyadh prevented an Iranian aircraft carrying senior Houthi officials from landing in Yemen’s Houthi-controlled capital, Sanaa. The officials were returning from the funeral of Iran’s former supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
At the time, bin Salman sought Trump’s political backing for a Saudi strike on Sanaa airport but told Washington that Saudi Arabia did not need U.S. military assistance. Trump gave his support.
The Houthis responded by attacking Saudi tankers in the Red Sea, threatening a vital route for the kingdom’s oil exports. They later expanded their attacks to Saudi energy facilities. Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies responded with airstrikes and ground operations against Houthi positions.
Saudi Arabia’s latest request for direct U.S. military action represents a sharp shift from its position in July, when Riyadh told Washington it could deal with the Houthis on its own.
U.S. military and administration officials have told their Saudi counterparts in recent weeks that Trump’s directive is to keep American forces focused on Iran and the Strait of Hormuz and avoid opening another front.
American officials said that as Houthi forces advanced toward Mocha on Thursday and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces retreated, bin Salman called Trump to brief him on the deteriorating situation.
Several hours later, the crown prince called again and asked Trump to order strikes against the Houthis. Trump refused, but a U.S. official said Washington would provide Saudi Arabia with intelligence on the Houthis and targeting information.
A senior Trump administration official signaled that Washington’s priority is keeping the Red Sea open while leaving the broader campaign to regional partners.
“The United States is focused on protecting our core national security interests — such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea — while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges,” the official said. “We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen Government regarding regional stability.”
Houthis advance on key shipping chokepoint
Houthi forces launched a major ground offensive Thursday night, seizing large stretches of Yemen’s southwestern coastline from forces loyal to the internationally recognized government.
Reports said the Houthis also seized Perim during the offensive. The island sits in the middle of Bab el-Mandab at one of the strait’s narrowest points, making it strategically important for monitoring and potentially threatening maritime traffic.
The Houthis also reached the Hanish Islands, farther north in the southern Red Sea, and seized at least one of them. A military official said the Houthis launched missile attacks against Zuqar Island and sent boats carrying fighters there.
Bab el-Mandab, which connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and ultimately links Asia and Europe through the Suez Canal, is one of the world’s most important maritime trade routes.
Its importance has increased further since Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz at the start of its war with the United States in late February. Hormuz, on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula, is one of the world’s most important routes for oil and gas shipments.
The disruption at Hormuz has already driven oil prices sharply higher, and fears are mounting that increased Houthi control over Bab el-Mandab could deepen turmoil in global energy markets.
Amid those concerns, crude oil prices jumped at least 5% Thursday, with Brent crude, the international benchmark, reaching $106 a barrel.
Greater control of Bab el-Mandab by Iran’s allies could also strengthen Tehran’s bargaining position in negotiations with Trump and increase the pressure Iran is seeking to exert as it escalates attacks in an effort to end the U.S. blockade.
Regional communities fear fallout
The Houthi gains are also causing concern elsewhere in the region.
Members of the Sunni Afar community, which spans parts of the Horn of Africa, including Ethiopia, Eritrea and Djibouti, are worried about the Houthi advance toward Bab el-Mandab and its potential consequences for communities on the African side of the Red Sea.
“The developments could have direct consequences beyond Yemen, particularly for the Afar community in Eritrea’s Dankalia region,” an Afar representative told ynet. “Fishermen from the community depend on the Red Sea for their livelihoods and have longstanding fishing ties with the Yemeni coast.”
“The impact of the conflict in Yemen needs to be examined not only in terms of military and maritime security, but also in terms of livelihoods and the humanitarian consequences for fishing communities,” the representative said.
Iranian media celebrated reports of the Houthi advances Thursday. Iran’s Al-Alam television network claimed that the Houthis had also captured the “last stronghold” of the Saudi-backed Yemeni government’s forces along Yemen’s western coast.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry later said Tehran’s position “remains firm regarding the need to respect Yemen’s independence and end the illegal blockade on the country.”
“We emphasize the need to immediately resume dialogue based on the agreed road map for Yemen,” the ministry said.

Estonian National Library finishes moving 3.4 million items

Estonian National Library finishes moving 3.4 million items
The process of moving books, music and art collections, periodicals, sheet music, maps and other printed materials back into storage at the National Library of Estonia's Tõnismäe building has been completed.
"In total, we had to unpack more than 62,000 cardboard boxes of materials and fill 21 storage rooms, as well as move works from the art collection into a 22nd storage room," said Kaire Lass, chief custodian at the National Library of Estonia. She added that unpacking the cultural heritage collections took 158 days.
The rarest books were the last to be placed on the shelves. The collection comprises nearly 40,000 books, with the oldest dating from the late 15th century.
The materials were unpacked by National Library of Estonia staff and 60 volunteers. Lass said the next step will be to place the open-access collections on shelves.
At the same time as the collections were being moved into storage, preparations have been underway for the National Library of Estonia's new services and for furnishing the restored 45,000-square-meter building.
The National Library of Estonia will reopen on May 28, 2027.

Houthis seize key Red Sea island, take control of Bab al Mandeb area: goverment official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:21:37 UTC
19:21:37 KST

Yemen’s Houthis seized a key Red Sea island in the middle of the Bab al Mandeb Strait on Friday, completing a push to take control of a waterway crucial to Saudi oil exports, a local government official and eyewitnesses told AFP.
The Iran-backed Houthis, who have controlled large parts of northern Yemen for years, launched a large-scale offensive last week against Saudi-backed government forces, scoring a series of victories in fighting that has left hundreds dead.
Saudi Arabia has responded with dozens of air strikes, with the latest two hitting Mocha airport, Houthi media reported on Friday.
The fighting in Yemen has taken centre stage in the wider Middle East war, which erupted with US-Israeli strikes on Iran and prompted the Islamic Republic to blockade another waterway crucial to global energy flows, the Strait of Hormuz.
“Boats carrying armed Houthi fighters reached Mayyun Island after government forces withdrew from it yesterday,” the local government official told AFP, referring to an island also known as Perim.
“The Houthis have completed their takeover of the Bab al Mandeb area and Mayyun Island, which is located in the middle of the strait,” the official added, speaking on condition of anonymity.
An eyewitness said gunmen were “deploying along the Bab al Mandeb shore and driving around in military vehicles”.
Bab al Mandeb connects Asia and Europe via the Red Sea and the Suez Canal. It has gained importance as a transit route for oil exports from Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest oil exporter, since the Middle East war began.
Both Brent crude, the main international benchmark, and US West Texas Intermediate crude were trading above $100 on Friday.
‘Apocalyptic’
Before the offensive, the Houthis already controlled much of northern Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa, and the major Red Sea port city of Hudaida.
But they did not control any territory directly overlooking Bab al Mandeb.
The Houthis have previously used drones and missiles to disrupt shipping in the Red Sea.
Although Saudi Arabia has retaliated with air strikes, it has failed to halt the Houthis’ rapid advance.
“I think the Saudis have tried everything they can to avoid this war, but I don’t think they have any more choice by now,” said Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at the Chatham House think tank.
“The Houthis have pushed it to the limit, and whatever the cost in the Saudi mind thinking right now, it’s just cheaper than it will be in two years.”
The fighting in Yemen has killed more than 500 people since last week, mostly combatants, according to an AFP tally compiled from several sources.
It has also forced nearly 20,000 people to flee their homes, the International Organization for Migration said on Tuesday.
Mohamed, a 46-year-old Yemeni who fled Mocha in the middle of the night, told AFP there was an “apocalyptic” atmosphere in the port city.
Mujahid Tahami, who also fled towards Aden, said some families had fallen victim to “looting by gangs as they tried to flee”.
Humanitarian crisis
Yemen relapsed into war in July after years of relative calm punctuated by sporadic violence and deepening poverty.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said on Wednesday that the group had fired ballistic missiles and drones at several cities in southern Saudi Arabia.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on Thursday that Saudi Arabia had launched 64 strikes on Yemen over the previous 24 hours.
The UN Security Council met on Thursday to discuss the conflict. UN Special Envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg called for “the active investment of every member of this body to contain what could be the precipice for a far more dangerous conflict”.
The emergency meeting was convened by the United Kingdom, which called on the Security Council to “send a clear and consistent message: the Houthis must de-escalate, cease their attacks, and return to a path towards peace”.
The hostilities began in July when the Houthis allowed an Iranian aircraft to land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace.
The government retaliated by striking Sanaa airport, an attack the Houthis blamed on Saudi Arabia.
The continuing exchanges risk plunging Yemen back into a conflict that killed hundreds of thousands of people and triggered one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.
The Houthis seized Yemen’s capital and forced out the government before fighting the Saudi-led coalition from 2015 until a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022.

Trump and Musk super PACs unleash millions to boost Republicans in battleground races

Unknown Publisher

Trump and Musk super PACs unleash millions to boost Republicans in battleground races
NEW YORK, Sept 11 - The two biggest Republican money players in the 2026 midterm elections – U.S. President Donald Trump and billionaire Elon Musk – have finally turned on the spigot with less than eight weeks to go before Election Day.
With Republicans facing the prospect of losing control of at least one chamber of Congress, and polling showing Democrats more motivated to vote, a group connected to Trump has begun spending tens of millions of dollars to reserve blocks of TV ad time in close races.
Trump, whose approval rating is stuck at the lowest level of his political career, told reporters last week that he planned to allocate $400 million to $500 million to boost Republicans in the midterms.
The Trump-affiliated Republican political action committee No Going Back has locked in more than $24.9 million in ad time across six battleground states: Alaska, Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina, New Hampshire and Ohio, according to political ad research firm AdImpact.
Additionally, Musk’s America PAC and Trump's main fundraising arm MAGA Inc. have in recent days poured $2.4 million and $10 million respectively into the race for a U.S. Senate seat in Texas where state Attorney General Ken Paxton risks becoming the first Republican to lose to a Democrat in a state-wide election there in decades.
About $6.9 million of that money is being spent on attack ads against Democratic state lawmaker James Talarico who leads Paxton by 2.1 percentage points in an average of polls compiled by Nate Silver's Silver Bulletin.
"Republicans now must spend real money defending an expanded map," said Republican strategist Brad Dayspring of Purple Strategies in Alexandria, Virginia. “When you suddenly have to put millions into Texas, having President Trump and Musk open their wallets gives Republicans the ability to shore up vulnerable races without draining resources from the rest of the map."
Musk's America PAC expects to play a major role in Republican voter turnout efforts in key states, with spending on door knockers, digital advertising and direct-mail campaigns ahead of the November 3 election. He's already spent more than $7 million on digital advertising, text messages, voter calls, mailers and other printed materials, federal filings show. A spokesman for the PAC declined to comment.
NEW FUNDRAISING ARM
Trump's midterm war chest is supporting the new No Going Back super PAC, according to one person familiar with the matter who asked not to be identified. It is unclear how much of Trump's war chest will be allocated through this new group.
Though Trump's MAGA Inc. and No Going Back aren’t yet formally affiliated with each other, they share the same treasurer – Charles Gantt – phone number and address at the same firm in Massachusetts. Gantt, MAGA Inc. and No Going Back didn’t return requests for comment.
The New York Times reported that No Going Back spent $49 million reserving advertising on Tuesday and Wednesday alone.
It is not clear why the new PAC, which registered with the Federal Election Commission on September 1, was established but Republican strategist Ron Bonjean said it helps distance Trump and his MAGA movement from campaign donations as voters sour on the president.
Any advertising from the new PAC will be credited to No Going Back PAC instead of MAGA Inc., a name closely tied to Trump’s political brand.
"It’s a brilliant strategy because it takes MAGA out of the name. It takes any affiliation to Trump out of the name. It has an innocuous name that no one will care about as opposed to MAGA Inc., which could turn off independent voters right away," said Bonjean, a partner at bipartisan public affairs firm Rokk Solutions in Washington.
The new PAC has used some of the same vendors as MAGA Inc. to carry out its work and in August some officials from MAGA Inc. started telegraphing to Republicans their intention to create a new PAC, according to the person familiar with the operation.
The timing of No Going Back's registration will delay full disclosure of its donors until late October, according to FEC rules.
Trump capped the first day of his Republican Party's first-ever midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday by proposing to pay every U.S. adult a $5,000 "Trump dividend" if the party wins the congressional elections. It was not immediately clear how the $5,000 payments would work or whether they would be legal. REUTERS

The BEB reform has not changed its approach to business: companies continue to face pressure from the Bureau
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:19:10 EEST
19:19:10 KST

The BEB reform has not changed its approach to business: companies continue to face pressure from the Bureau
Kyiv • UNN
Despite the reform and change in the BEB leadership, businesses continue to complain about the Bureau’s actions. The situation involving airlines, against which criminal proceedings were opened due to the interpretation of leasing payments as royalties, is illustrative.
The reform of the Economic Security Bureau is ongoing; however, businesses’ complaints about the agency’s actions indicate that, so far, there has been no significant change in its operations. This creates additional risks for Ukrainian businesses and Ukraine’s investment climate. It raises the question of whether the reform will lead to real changes in the EСB’s approach to its work, or whether it will be limited to a change in leadership and a formal relaunch of the agency, UNN writes.
Details
Recently, a mission of the International Monetary Fund of Ukraine was working in Ukraine, among other things monitoring the fulfillment of structural benchmarks and overall reform progress. However, this time the mission left without making any public statement.
Despite the reform of the Economic Security Bureau, the number of business complaints about the agency’s work indicates that, so far, no significant changes have taken place in its operations.
Thus, according to data from the Business Ombudsman Council, almost one-third of business complaints about the actions of law enforcement agencies concern the work of the ESB. It is worth noting that this trend has persisted for the second year in a row. The problems entrepreneurs report include property seizures and questions regarding the admissibility of investigative actions.
Economist Viktor Halchynskyi noted in a comment to UNN that the ESB reform cannot be described as not being carried out at all: a competitive selection process for the leadership was conducted, and changes in the agency’s operations were launched. However, it is still too early to speak of a specific result.
As for businesses’ complaints about the ESB, I would refer here specifically to the wording from the IMF report—about the reforms "stalling"… As for the investment climate, this is, so to speak, one of the risks. Today, the main factor holding back investment is hostilities and life under martial law. There are high risks of businesses being destroyed and of operating in wartime conditions. But it is definitely one of the factors. If a business encounters unlawful or biased actions by law enforcement agencies, this affects its willingness to operate and invest in Ukraine
Problems involving pressure on businesses matter not only for individual companies. Member of Parliament Yaroslav Zhelezniak previously stated that unjustified investigative actions by law enforcement agencies are one of the main barriers to international investment in Ukraine. According to him, foreign investors are currently particularly interested in Ukraine’s defense industry.
An illustrative example of how the ESB’s work creates additional risks for businesses was the situation involving airlines. The ESB is investigating cases involving at least five airlines, including MAU, "Konstanta Airline," "Urga," H3Operations, and "Skyline," over the alleged failure to pay an additional 15% tax on nonresidents’ income to the Ukrainian budget under aircraft and helicopter leasing agreements. Investigators equate leasing payments with royalties and treat aircraft not as means of transport but as "equipment."
However, according to lawyers interviewed by UNN, during the investigation the investigators ignore the current international conventions on the avoidance of double taxation. Agreements with foreign states ratified by the Verkhovna Rada take precedence over national legislation and determine in which state and at what rate the relevant income of a nonresident may be taxed. Therefore, the automatic assessment of an additional 15% tax in Ukraine without taking into account the provisions of a specific convention is at least debatable, the experts emphasize.
As UNN reported, representatives of the aviation industry publicly stated that they were being pressured by the Economic Security Bureau because investigators interpret aircraft-leasing transactions as royalties, initiate criminal proceedings, and attempt to assess additional taxes for a seven-year period. According to them, civil aviation has come under threat of destruction due to the actions of state regulatory authorities, which could ultimately finish off companies that survived the closure of the airspace and relocation abroad because of the full-scale war.
For the aviation business, this means more than just legal disputes. Criminal proceedings create additional uncertainty for companies, their partners, lessors, and potential investors. And for an industry that depends to a significant extent on international financing and leasing mechanisms, the predictability of government policy is critically important.
That is why, in the opinion of economist Viktor Halchynskyi, the problem is not limited to who heads the BEB.
What could change the situation? I think it could work if the staff were completely replaced with motivated people who respect the new legislative framework governing the BEB's work. But we can see that this process is difficult. The system often does not know how to do much besides one very important thing—to protect itself. If the new head of the BEB manages to form a critical mass of a team made up of impartial people for whom the rule of law is not merely words but a working principle, then we will be able to speak of real change. The purpose of the reform is for the Bureau to genuinely protect the state's economic interests and the interests of honest and transparent businesses, rather than obstructing businesses that operate within the law
Ultimately, the BEB reform should be assessed not by whether a competition was held or the leadership changed, but by whether the agency's actual working practices have changed. For now, businesses continue to complain about the Bureau's actions, while certain industries, particularly aviation, are facing criminal proceedings over disputed tax matters.

General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, Inc. (GA-ASI), the company that introduced the world to unmanned warfare, has systematically transformed its aircraft lineup to address the defining requirements of modern high-technology warfare: range, persistence, payload, survivability, and scale against advanced adversaries.
The portfolio now spans from the company’s enhanced MQ-9B SkyGuardian and SeaGuardian platforms capable of long-range maritime strike, to the expeditionary Mojave STOL, to the Air Force’s newly selected FQ-42A Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) — its first uncrewed fighter — and, most recently, to the Wildfire Massed Modular Aircraft (MMA), a theater-range platform engineered for affordable, attrition-tolerant combat mass.
According to GA-ASI President David Alexander, the United States has entered an era where winning demands large, capable Uncrewed Aircraft Systems (UAS) that can operate from friendly airspace into contested environments affordably, without risking aircrews.
“We’ve never been a company that rested on its laurels,” said Alexander. “The conversation around uncrewed systems has changed, and frankly, it should. The battlefield has evolved, threats have evolved, and so have we.
“We’re keeping ahead of the game, and, in the case of our FQ-42A and Wildfire aircraft, we’ve designed them from the start to overmatch threats today and into the future.”
Physics Demands Large Airframes
Losses in contested environments have prompted some observers to suggest moving away from large UAS platforms. Alexander sees those same operations as validation for continued investment in evolved large UAS.
“Yes, we’ve seen combat losses,” he said. “We’ve also heard Pentagon leaders call our Reaper the ‘MVP’ of the campaign. That tells you something important. When a system consistently delivers decisive effects, you modernize it and build on it. And I believe that’s where the Department of War is headed.”
Alexander emphasized that Reaper was purpose-built to provide persistent surveillance, long endurance, and precision strike. MQ-9A delivers these capabilities at scale and at a fraction of the cost of manned platforms that put pilots’ lives at risk, he added.
The proliferation of small drones — quadcopters, gliders, and short-range rockets — doesn’t change fundamental operational requirements, he said.
Despite the hype, smaller platforms “can’t change physics,” Alexander noted.
“Long-range, high-payload, high-endurance missions require large, hefty airframes with significant wingspan, fuel capacity, and payload volume,” he continued. “If we are serious about surveilling and targeting across wide ocean areas, tracking mobile missile units, and holding adversary assets at risk from standoff distances, large UAS modernized for contested environments are the decisive advantage.”
Wildfire: Delivering Attritable Mass at Theater Range
Wildfire represents GA-ASI’s answer to a critical requirement: affordable combat mass that can sustain losses while maintaining operational pressure across contested theaters.
This theater-range, high-production UAS is designed specifically for high-threat environments:
Combat payload and range: Wildfire can carry two Long Range Anti-Ship Missiles (LRASM) or four Joint Strike Missiles (JSM) for meaningful combat distances and has a ferry range that exceeds 8,000 nautical miles. This enables delivery of weapons, sensors, electronic warfare capabilities, or communications relay deep into contested battlespace.
Modular architecture: Open interfaces and modular payload hard points enable modularity to support rapid mission reconfiguration, allowing commanders to adapt as threats and priorities shift during operations.
Volume production: Leveraging more than 5 million square feet of manufacturing capacity and advanced production processes, Wildfire is engineered to be built and fielded in numbers sufficient to absorb attrition while maintaining persistent theater-wide pressure.
Combined with Gambit Series capabilities, Wildfire delivers what defense leaders call “attritable mass”— large numbers of capable systems whose loss does not constitute strategic setback because they are affordable, uncrewed, and replaceable.
Gambit Series: Autonomous Combat Jets for Peer Threats
The Gambit Series represents GA-ASI’s family of autonomous jets for high-end contested operations. Built around a common core comprising roughly 70 percent of key components, the platform’s modular architecture drives down costs while simplifying production, logistics, and sustainment.
Recently selected by the U.S. Air Force for its CCA program, the FQ-42A — designed to fly alongside fighters like the F-22 — is a variant of GA-ASI’s Gambit 2.
Across six missionized Gambit variants, the architecture supports:
- Long-endurance ISR in contested airspace
- Air-to-air combat
- Adversary training for advanced threat replication
- Stealth reconnaissance in denied areas
- Carrier-based naval operations
- Penetrating air-to-ground strike and suppression of enemy air defenses
All Gambit aircraft are designed for human-machine teaming with advanced fighters and other UAS, extending sensors, adding weapons capacity, and imposing complex targeting dilemmas on adversary defenses — precisely the type of effects envisioned in modern Air Force operational concepts.
Mojave STOL: Airpower, Hold the Tarmac
Built on GA-ASI’s other pioneering aircraft, Mojave STOL addresses a critical vulnerability in modern combat: dependence on large runways.
Short Takeoff and Landing (STOL) capability: Mojave STOL operates from austere, unprepared locations — open fields, dry riverbeds, even amphibious assault ship decks — generating uncrewed combat airpower from sites adversaries cannot easily target or predict.
Advanced sensor integration: Controllable via human-portable, laptop-based ground control systems, Mojave STOL carries cutting-edge radar, electro-optical/infrared, and signals intelligence payloads, providing a comprehensive operational picture for precise targeting and situational awareness to support dispersed forces.
In a combat environment where large runways are vulnerable to adversary strikes, Mojave STOL establishes airfields without airports. Its rugged construction enables persistent ISR and strike capability sourced from improvised mobile launch and recovery sites.
MQ-9B: Evolved Flagship Platform for Standoff Operations
MQ-9B SkyGuardian and SeaGuardian remain GA-ASI’s flagship multi-mission ISR platforms, now upgraded for long-range contested operations and integration into distributed kill chains.
Long-range weapons integration: New pylons with 30-inch lug spacing accommodate larger standoff munitions, including LRASM and JSM. Combined with MQ-9B’s advanced ISR suite, this transforms the aircraft into a long-range strike and maritime interdiction platform capable of engaging far outside adversary standoff ranges.
Resilient communications: Integration with proliferated Low Earth Orbit (pLEO) satellite constellations provides low-latency, high-bandwidth, jam-resistant connectivity. In combination with DoD-standard cybersecurity, MQ-9B maintains secure command-and-control and sensor links globally, even under electronic attack.
For Air Force and joint planners, MQ-9B has evolved beyond counterinsurgency roots into a standoff sensor-shooter that functions as a resilient node in distributed operations.
Urgency Driven by Evolving Threats
Alexander noted that changing battlefield conditions have continually driven the company to advance its technology and operational concepts.
“When you look at the threats we’re seeing in Ukraine and Iran, we already knew our aircraft would need to evolve, and we’ve been pushing ahead there for years now,” he said. “But it seems like every morning the news puts fresh urgency behind delivering that vital combat capability while finding ways to strip out some of what drives up costs.”
That urgency is backed by unmatched operational experience. To date, GA-ASI has accumulated nearly 10 million flight hours, the vast majority in combat operations.
Taken as a whole, Alexander said, the aircraft portfolio shows that GA-ASI is serious about retaining its position as the leading provider of UAS to the United States and its allies.
“We know, to our core, what it takes to deliver relevant systems,” he said. “We have the people, infrastructure, and capacity in place, today, to do it at scale.
“GA-ASI is ready to answer the call.”

Algorithms should be able to explain reasoning behind decisions to customers: RBI Murmu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:18:26 UTC
19:18:26 KST

RBI deputy governor Shirish Chandra Murmu, speaking at the Global FinTech Fest in Mumbai on Friday, said digital lending should not merely make the process of extending credit faster.
Mumbai: The Reserve Bank of India wants lenders to ensure that algorithms used to make or materially influence credit decisions can explain why a borrower has been rejected, putting accountability and explainability at the centre of its expectations for technology-driven lending.RBI deputy governor Shirish Chandra Murmu, speaking at the Global FinTech Fest in Mumbai on Friday, said digital lending should not merely make the process of extending credit faster. Technology and better data should help lenders reach borrowers who have historically remained outside the formal financial system, making credit “better” as well as faster."The vendor with the printed QR code is now part of the formal financial system. The questions she faces next are harder ones. Will she be offered credit on terms she can understand? If an algorithm declines her 10 application, will anyone be able to tell her why? If her account is frozen by a frauddetection system, how long before she can trade again? Those questions are the real content of trusted innovation, and how we answer them will matter more than any technology we deploy," said Murmu.The deputy governor also cautioned institutions against being comfortable with their cryptographic dependencies.
He said that while quantum computing is not an immediate threat payment infrastructure has long tech cycles and migration to new standards takes years. "There is also the “harvest now, decrypt later” risk, under which encrypted information collected today becomes accessible as computing capability advance," said Murmu.The challenge is particularly relevant for India's millions of small merchants who have moved into the formal digital payments system. The RBI's concern is that algorithms can produce decisions that are statistically effective without being readily understandable. Murmu said well-designed models could identify creditworthy borrowers who might otherwise remain outside formal finance, but warned that the data used by such models could contain historical biases. Past relationships may not persist, a model may be economically inappropriate despite its statistical sophistication, and complex models may be difficult to explain to a customer whose application has been declined.The RBI's position is also that automation does not transfer responsibility from the lender to the technology. “The answer cannot be the algorithm,” Murmu said when asking who is accountable when an algorithm makes or materially influences a financial decision. Responsibility, he said, rests with the regulated institution, while boards and senior management must understand the models they deploy, their limitations and the consequences of using them.
This principle extends to the wider digital-lending ecosystem. Under the RBI's Digital Lending Directions, 2025, technology can change the channel through which credit is delivered but does not dilute the responsibility of the regulated lender. Borrowers must know who is lending to them, the cost of the loan and its terms, while technology should widen customer choice rather than steer borrowers towards unsuitable products. Even when lenders operate through partnerships, the regulated entity remains accountable for services delivered in its name.

Cilia Adela Flores de Maduro “is a 69-year-old woman who will need adequate time to recover from any procedures in a setting conducive to restoring her health,” her defense attorneys told the court in a filing Wednesday, arguing that the detention center cannot provide adequate post-operative care.
US forces captured Flores alongside her husband during a Jan. 3 military operation in Caracas, transporting both to New York to face federal cocaine importation and firearms charges, which they deny.
US law generally favors pretrial detention for defendants facing major narcotics charges. Flores' lawyers, however, argued that she should be released because of her family ties, status as an elected Venezuelan lawmaker and medical condition.
According to her lawyers, Flores previously managed a mitral valve prolapse with monthly injections that stopped after she was jailed. She now takes four medications, including a statin and beta-blocker, keeps nitroglycerin on hand and has lost more than 11.3 kilograms (25 pounds).
Her lawyers said recent medical tests showed severe abnormal heart rhythms and signs of reduced blood flow to the heart, raising the risk of sudden death.
Medical staff at the Brooklyn detention center recommended cardiac catheterization after a stress test was halted in April, according to the filing. Defense medical experts also said a severe 30-minute episode of chest pain on July 29 indicated that she may have suffered a minor heart attack.
The defense proposed home detention in New York with 24-hour armed monitoring by a private security firm, continuous GPS tracking and consensual monitoring of her phone calls.
US District Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein granted a motion to seal her detailed medical records on privacy grounds while keeping legal filings public. Prosecutors oppose her release request.
A US judge has scheduled the trial to begin June 1, 2027.

Scientists call for better protection of Swiss groundwater

Unknown Publisher

Scientists call for better protection of Swiss groundwater
The Swiss Academy of Sciences (SCNAT) has called for targeted measures to protect Switzerland’s groundwater reserves, strengthen infrastructure resilience and improve water management.
“Basically, groundwater is not doing so badly in Switzerland,” Christian Möck told Swiss public radio SRF on Thursday.
But as the summer of 2026 has demonstrated, increasingly frequent and extreme droughts are jeopardising the availability and quality of groundwater.
“Of course, this has extreme effects either locally or regionally, says Möck, head of the Swiss groundwater network at the Swiss Federal Institute of Aquatic Science and Technology (Eawag). He is also a member of an expert group at the Academy of Sciences, which aims to raise awareness about groundwater.
Groundwater has an impact on all areas of life and economy. Around 80% of drinking water comes from groundwater. It is also essential for agriculture, industry, and many ecosystems. It can act as a buffer during droughts: depending on its type and the season, groundwater contributes 30 to 80% to the total run-off of Swiss rivers and streams.
Swiss scientists at SCNAT are calling for a comprehensive strategy that allows groundwater to be renewed and maintained at good quality. In the future, dry periods or heavy precipitation are likely to become more frequent due to climate change.
More
Drought in Switzerland: Europe’s ‘water tower’ runs dry
Federal government works on water strategy
The government is currently working on a comprehensive water management strategy. “It is intended to help identify conflicts of use at an early stage, improve the data basis and manage the available water resources sustainably in the long term,” Katrin Schneeberger, director of the Federal Office for the Environment, said at the end of August.
She said Switzerland must preserve its waterways and wetlands, monitor water quality and explore how to store or retain water.
“On the one hand, it’s very much about raising awareness, but of course we also point out places where we feel there is still a need for action, where there may be gaps,” says Möck.

European bond yields hit multi-year highs as global sell-off continues

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11

19:16:15 KST

Long-term European government bond yields remain close to multi-decade highs, as inflation and interest-rate concerns keep driving the sell-off.
Government bond yields jumped again this week, with some reaching levels last recorded around the global financial crisis, as the escalating conflict in the Middle East threatens to keep energy prices and therefore inflation elevated.
With the conflict showing no sign of ending, investors are bracing for another surge in inflation that could put pressure on central banks to tighten monetary policy further, making borrowing more expensive.
The outlook for crude supplies has deteriorated further after Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels hit several Saudi energy targets and advanced towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The waterway is a key alternative route for global energy shipments while the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed and fighting between US forces and Iran shows no sign of easing.
International benchmark Brent crude has traded above $100 a barrel in recent days. On Friday morning, the front-month contract was trading just below $106 a barrel.
Government borrowing costs have risen rapidly in Europe, after the European Central Bank raised interest rates on Thursday, lifting its deposit rate from 2.25% to 2.5%, and warned that inflation could remain “well above target for an extended period”.
The higher inflation forecast and the ECB’s tougher-than-expected tone led investors to increase their expectations of further rate rises.
Germany’s 10-year Bund yield was around 3.5% on Friday morning. The equivalent French yield was about 94 basis points higher, at around 4.44%. Italian 10-year yields stood at approximately 4.37%, while their Spanish equivalents were around 3.96%.
The yield on the UK’s 10-year government bond eased towards 5.35% on Friday as energy prices retreated from Thursday’s highs ahead of an important US inflation report.
The 10-year gilt yield had reached 5.378% on Thursday, its highest level since 2007. Yields on 20- and 30-year gilts climbed to 5.895% and 5.948% respectively, their highest levels since 1998.
At the same time, long-term US Treasury yields reached new multi-year highs following data showing an increase in US wholesale inflation, fuelling expectations that the US Federal Reserve could raise interest rates next week.
The 30-year US Treasury yield climbed above 5.38% on Friday, its highest level since 2007. The US 10-year Treasury yield approached the closely watched 5% mark and was trading at around 4.95% on Friday morning in Europe, close to its highest level in three years.
Additional pressure came after the US Treasury bought back $5.2 billion (€4.5 billion) of bonds, below the operation’s $6 billion cap and less than half the $10.5 billion offered by investors.
In Asia, Japan’s 10-year government bond yield rose to around 2.98%, just below the 3% level it reached earlier this month for the first time since 1996.
AI-related debt competes for investor capital
Governments are seeking to attract investors at a time when enormous amounts of artificial intelligence-related debt are also coming onto global markets.
Major hyperscalers, including Alphabet and Amazon, have issued more than $200 billion (€172 billion) of debt so far in 2026, more than twice the amount raised during the whole of last year, according to LSEG data reported by Reuters.
A broader Goldman Sachs estimate, which includes debt connected to data centres and other AI infrastructure, put AI-related issuance at nearly $500 billion (€431 billion) by early August.
US technology companies are increasingly turning to the eurozone bond market to finance their investments. They are expected to require more than $1 trillion (€862 billion) in total capital expenditure by 2028, according to an ECB blog post published on 31 August.
The euro accounts for close to 10% of the outstanding bonds issued by these hyperscalers. Their arrival gives European bond investors greater exposure to technology companies.
This is particularly significant because technology makes up a much smaller proportion of eurozone bond indices: its weight is roughly one-third of that in comparable US indices.
ECB researchers said the growing presence of hyperscalers could eventually push up borrowing costs across different sectors. Investors may sell or avoid other bonds to make room in their portfolios for large technology-company issues, forcing competing borrowers to offer higher yields.
The researchers said this pressure could potentially spread to government and supranational bonds. However, they stressed that no such spillovers were evident in the eurozone at the time of their analysis, reflecting the still-limited scale of big-tech issuance and the resilience of sovereign bond markets.

====================================================================================================

Rosh Hashanah 2026: Recognizing God's presence in the world after a year of conflict, division
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:15:33 UTC
19:15:33 KST

Rosh Hashanah is the Day of Judgment. The fate of individuals is weighed, and the course of nations and empires is determined. We stand before God, examining our conduct, appealing for mercy, and praying to be inscribed in the Book of Life.
Yet Rosh Hashanah carries a wider significance. It marks the anniversary of Creation, when God brought the world into existence. By judging humanity, He reasserts His sovereignty over creation. We therefore turn beyond our own lives to the movement of history, asking how clearly God’s presence can be discerned in His world.
History begins with Creation and moves toward redemption. At the end of that journey, God’s presence will become unmistakable, as humanity comes to recognize Him.
Each Rosh Hashanah, as history advances along its difficult path toward that destination, we consider the year that has passed. Which developments have made God more visible, and which have pushed His presence further into concealment?
We cannot decode providence or confidently explain why particular events occur. Yet people of faith can still ask whether the broader movement of history has made God’s presence easier or harder to discern.
Rescue, victory, and divine intervention
Perhaps the most moving event in which we sensed divine intervention was the return of our hostages.
Their abduction was among the most agonizing elements of Oct. 7, compounded by the unimaginable suffering many endured in captivity.
For much of the war, the return of every hostage seemed beyond hope. We assumed Hamas would retain some as bargaining chips or human shields.
Yet 168 hostages were brought home alive, and ultimately every hostage who had been murdered or died in captivity was returned for burial in Israel. Again and again, we welcomed home people whose names and faces had become seared into our consciousness, and for whom we had prayed for months or even years.
Their return reminded people of faith that history is never limited by what appears possible at a particular moment.
We also continue to sense His hand guiding us through history as we return to our homeland and reclaim our place within the historical arena.
Over the past year, Israel achieved remarkable military successes. Iran, our most dangerous enemy, was severely weakened, while much of the “ring of fire” it had constructed around Israel through murderous proxies was dismantled or substantially degraded.
The contrast with the days following Oct. 7 is striking. Israel then appeared painfully vulnerable, surrounded by enemies and threatened on multiple fronts. Three years later, the strategic landscape of the Middle East has been dramatically altered.
None of this should obscure the terrible cost of the war or suggest that every danger has disappeared. Yet developments that once seemed improbable became reality, and for many of us the hand of God felt unusually close as the regional landscape was transformed.
Faith resurfaces after being tested
We have also witnessed renewed visibility of faith.
Israel today is very different from the country founded nearly eight decades ago. Even among Israelis who are not observant, many speak comfortably about faith, prayer, Jewish destiny, and God’s presence in our national story.
This shift had been developing for years, but Oct. 7 accelerated it dramatically. Faith has been tested under harsh conditions and has repeatedly surfaced in public life among soldiers, bereaved families, hostage families, and ordinary Israelis confronting fear and uncertainty. God has become a more explicit part of the language many Israelis use to understand their lives and the history unfolding around them.
These currents of faith in Israel have been mirrored by a strengthening of Jewish identity among Jews abroad. The hatred unleashed after Oct. 7 forced many Jews to reconsider identities they had previously worn lightly. Many became more conscious of their Jewishness, more attached to Israel, and more determined to display an identity they once kept private.
This awakening does not always take an explicitly religious form. Yet Jewish identity is never entirely detached from God. To identify more deeply with the Jewish people is to reconnect, even indirectly, with our people whose history and destiny were shaped by a divine covenant.
Every strengthening of Jewish consciousness creates another opening through which God can reenter Jewish life. Hopefully, this renewed peoplehood will mature into deeper spiritual and religious commitment.
Other developments, however, have obscured God’s presence. On Rosh Hashanah, we pray that these trends will be reversed.
An ancient hatred
Antisemitism is raging at levels unseen since the Holocaust. More disturbing, it has moved from the fringes toward the mainstream, voiced openly by prominent politicians, activists, and influencers.
Antisemitism has social, economic, political, and cultural causes, but beneath them lies a deeper spiritual impulse. We were chosen to represent God in history, and hostility toward God’s presence expresses itself toward our nation which carries His name. The resurgence of antisemitism therefore reflects a retreat of God’s presence from our world.
Yet, without romanticizing antisemitism, this hatred has clarified an important truth: the State of Israel lies at the heart of the Jewish future.
Much of today’s antisemitism is expressed through hostility toward Israel, extending beyond criticism of particular policies to denial of Israel’s legitimacy and right to exist. That hostility is directed at Jews regardless of whether they personally place Israel at the center of their identity.
Our enemies are teaching us a truth that some Jews have not yet fully embraced: the future of Israel and the future of every Jew are inseparably bound.
Fractures reappear between Jewish communities
Unfortunately, we have not preserved the unity that emerged immediately after Oct. 7. Many old divisions have returned, while new tensions, especially surrounding haredi non-enlistment, have deepened fractures within Israeli society.
When the Jewish people stands together, God’s presence is felt more powerfully among us. Our unity testifies that beneath our differences lie a deeper covenant and shared destiny.
When legitimate disagreements harden into bitterness and estrangement, that divine presence recedes. Rosh Hashanah should remind us that even deep disagreement cannot erase the covenant that binds us to one another.
The assault on truth
Finally, we live in a world in which truth itself is becoming difficult to discern. The rise of individualism has helped fuel moral relativism, in which truth and morality are reduced to perspective and context. Even acts of obvious evil are sometimes explained away by the setting in which they occurred.
God’s signature is truth, and when confidence in truth erodes, His presence becomes more obscured.
At the same time, artificial intelligence is making the distinction between fact and fabrication increasingly fragile. Photographs can be manufactured, videos fabricated, and voices reproduced with remarkable accuracy. We are entering a world in which seeing and hearing may no longer provide reliable evidence of what actually occurred.
It is therefore no surprise that AI-generated falsehoods have already been weaponized by those who demonize Israel and spread hatred of Jews.
The Jewish people represents God in history, and our return to our homeland is part of the divine drama of Jewish destiny.
Those who seek to delegitimize that return often distort not only our history but truth itself. There is something deeply troubling about this convergence. The assault on the people who carry God’s name is increasingly accompanied by an assault on truth, which is God’s own signature.
The year leaves us with a divided picture: God’s presence has felt startlingly close, even as it has grown more obscured in the moral and cultural world around us. The task of 5787 is to make His presence harder to miss.■
The writer is a rabbi and educator at Yeshivat Har Etzion (Gush). Find his latest book, Reclaiming Redemption, Vol. II: Faith, Identity, Peoplehood, and the Storms of War, at mtaraginbooks.com.

The last BRICS summit was held in Brazil last year, with China due to host the 2027 gathering.

EU approves EUR 6.1 bln support loan for drones, Patriot air defense missiles

The European Commission has officially approved providing Ukraine with a EUR 6.1 billion support loan to purchase drones and missiles for Patriot air defense systems, EU Commissioner for Defense and Space Andrius Kubilius said.
"Today I'll share news about our decisions under the Ukraine support loan. Today the European Commission officially approved allocating EUR 6.1 billion from this loan for the purchase of drones and missiles for Ukraine's air defense systems," he told reporters in Brussels on Friday.
Kubilius called this a genuinely important step forward, saying the Commission had worked hard with member states and Ukraine to reach this point, and that the decision formally allows Ukraine to purchase PAC-3 missiles for Patriot systems.
He explained that for EU funding to be used to purchase weapons from third countries, member states must adopt a separate decision. This package, financed under the Ukraine support loan, involves five departures from standard procurement eligibility rules, he said: three concern drones and components of Ukrainian manufacture whose cost exceeds set limits, and two concern equipment made in the United States, including PAC-3 missiles, among them procurement carried out through a joint purchasing mechanism coordinated by NATO.
The commissioner said Ukraine's military edge depends on the rapid availability of critical equipment in the necessary volumes and on very short timelines. Speeding up the delivery of needed equipment by drawing on existing stockpiles, reprioritizing orders and scaling up production remains a decisive task, he stressed, adding that today's decision means the full EUR 28.3 billion allocated this year from the Ukraine support loan has now been assigned to the country's defense needs.
He said the European Commission is currently processing payment requests worth EUR 4.7 billion, in addition to the EUR 8.3 billion already disbursed earlier. The disbursement process is therefore also moving forward, he said, noting that before transferring funds, the Commission verifies contracts to ensure they comply with the terms of the Ukraine support loan and with procurement rules agreed with member states.

Tamer Nafar on Palestine, genocide and the limits of music
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:14:29 UTC
19:14:29 KST

Breadcrumb
Palestinian rapper Tamer Nafar has lost faith in music's power to change the world. He keeps writing anyway
Tamer Nafar has spent more than two decades saying what others might hesitate to say. As a co-founder of DAM, the pioneering Palestinian hip-hop group, and one of the most recognisable voices in Arabic rap, he has built a career on confronting power, identity and the contradictions of Palestinian life with little interest in making anyone comfortable.
So when I sit down with the 47-year-old rapper and offer the most ordinary of pleasantries, "Hello, how are you?", his answer is anything but ordinary.
"I'm an Arab citizen of Israel," he replies, wearily.
In six words, Nafar gives an answer to a question that is rarely as simple as it sounds. It is a reminder that for him, even the most casual conversation is entangled with questions of identity, belonging and survival.
Two years ago, at this same festival, Nafar told The Guardian that music could not stop a war machine. Even then, however, he held on to something of Tupac's belief that an artist might spark the mind of the person who would eventually change the world.
Today, however, he has lost patience with that idea. When I ask whether he still believes that now, the idea does not survive the first minute of our conversation.
“F*** that," he says. "I said that before the genocide. What changes the world is oil deals."
It is a raw answer from an artist who has turned decades of blunt, hard-hitting lyrics into global hits and sold-out tours. He is not here to perform optimism, particularly when the facts offer so little reason for it.
"Oil deals change the world. Weapons and technology change it. Political choices change it"
Political leaders are not waiting to be persuaded by the right lyric. Their decisions are shaped by power, money, military relationships and technology.
Nafar knows he cannot overturn those forces simply by making something beautiful or politically compelling, but that does not mean he should abandon his art. It means being honest about its place in the hierarchy of change.
The law of the jungle
Nafar's performance at WOMAD comes at a strange moment for Palestinian music.
Palestinian artists are reaching new audiences across the world, selling out shows and claiming space on international stages.
There is a renewed interest in Palestinian music, culture and identity, but that attention has arrived amid, and often in response to, Israel's genocide in Gaza and the accelerating ethnic cleansing of the occupied West Bank.
How does Nafar feel about that bitter irony?
"That's the law of the jungle," he replies.
Palestinian culture is flourishing internationally at the same moment that Palestinian life is being destroyed. Music is carrying Palestinian stories across the world, yet the political forces determining their lives remain largely unmoved.
The contradiction hangs over our conversation. How should an artist understand success when it comes amid so much loss? What does it mean for the world to embrace Palestinian music while refusing to protect or defend Palestinian lives?
Nafar does not try to force a hopeful answer.
"There are three things we are fighting at once," he says.
"The genocide in Gaza, ethnic cleansing in the West Bank and Arab-on-Arab crime [in Israel]," he adds.
"It's about survival."
Nafar is from Lyd, one of several Palestinian towns where organised crime and violence have devastated communities amid accusations of systematic neglect by the Israeli authorities.
For him, the threats Palestinians face cannot be reduced to a single geography or one form of violence.
His answer moves between Gaza, the West Bank and Palestinian communities inside Israel because that is the political reality he inhabits.
Each crisis is distinct, but none can be separated from the wider structures governing Palestinian life.
He has moved away from the idea that music can reach the powerful and awaken something dormant within them. The problem is not that political leaders have failed to hear Palestinians clearly enough. The problem is power itself.
"Oil deals change the world. Weapons and technology change it. Political choices change it," he says.
A song, he knows, sits much further down that hierarchy. For Nafar, the task is to locate where he can still make art within it.
"I don't have the mindset that if only Donald Trump heard a moving song, he would suddenly decide to change his ways. That's bullshit."
He looks out across the festival site, dotted with Palestinian flags, keffiyehs, 'Make Peace Not War' paraphernalia, and plenty of glitter.
"But, you know, I am a little jigsaw piece in the puzzle of the world."
One small piece, trying to understand where his work fits and the limits of what it can do. In the world of festivals and grandiose gestures, it is a more modest claim for art than we are used to hearing, but a refreshingly honest one at that.
Nafar understands the world, recognises his place within it and knows the scale of the task ahead.
Overturning a genocidal government sustained by powerful imperial backers across the world, clearly, is going to take more than a few albums.
Different songs, different energy
Nafar helped pioneer Palestinian hip-hop as a co-founder of DAM, whose music brought the politics and daily realities of Palestinian life inside Israel to audiences around the world.
The group's work has never separated the political from the personal. Occupation, racism, poverty and violence sit alongside family, humour, self-criticism and the complicated reality of life in Palestinian towns.
Across a catalogue that has moved through Arabic, Hebrew and English, DAM developed a language for experiences that were either misrepresented or absent from mainstream culture.
Their music did not set out to explain Palestinians to the world politely; it documented the world in which they were already living.
Although Nafar is now developing his solo work, he is quick to stress that he is still performing with DAM.
The two projects require "different energy and different songs," he tells The New Arab. Moving between them means moving between different parts of himself and between music created at different political and personal moments.
It is not a clean break with his past, and DAM very much remains part of his present.
When asked which song is his favourite to perform, he chooses In the Name of the Father. It is one of his most personal works, using music to return to family, memory and the conversations that remain unfinished after somebody is gone.
The song does not attempt to persuade a president or redirect international politics; its world is altogether smaller and more intimate.
That does not make it apolitical. Nafar's music repeatedly returns to the places where public history enters private life: the car journey, the family home, the distance between a father and son.
If the machinery of political change operates through weapons, technology and oil deals, art can still document what that machinery does to the people living beneath it.
For Nafar, that is no longer the same as claiming music will stop it.
'I’m not a musician, I'm a writer'
Music is only one part of Nafar's work, and he is now writing a new novel, 3Gs, that spans three generations of his family.
When asked about the shift, he rejects the premise. "I'm not a musician," he says. "I've always been a writer." He describes 3Gs as an "archive of my thoughts," built from a lifetime of recording ideas.
"Someone told me to write a book, and I've always been writing things down, so I looked back and thought, you know what, I think I can make a book out of this. They asked for a specific number of pages, and I thought, yeah, I can do that."
It is an understated account of becoming a novelist: years of thoughts, a page count and the sudden realisation that the book was already there.
3Gs is an imagined memoir spanning three generations of the Nafar family: Fawzi, the father; Tamer, the son; and Shaden, the son's future daughter.
The novel gives him room to hold histories, relationships and memories that cannot always be contained within a song.
Moving between generations also allows Nafar to explore how Palestinian history enters a family, shaping those who experience its ruptures differently but remain bound together by them.
For a Palestinian writer, the act of building an archive is political. Palestinian history has repeatedly been narrated by those responsible for Palestinian dispossession, stripped of its intimacy and reduced to a dispute over territory, security or competing claims.
A family archive does something else. It preserves people as people: contradictory, funny, difficult, loving and shaped by histories they did not choose.
'I have to stay for my children'
When asked how home is, Nafar's answer is blunt. "Many people are leaving," he shares.
He is referring to the worsening conditions for Palestinian citizens of Israel living in cities such as Lyd and Haifa, both home to significant Palestinian communities.
Has he ever considered leaving himself?
"For me, of course, I would love to get out of there. But I have to stay for my children."
On his arm are the stick figures of a child's drawing, made permanent in ink. I ask whether his children drew them. Yes, he replies.
"That’s how they see me on stage, when I am under the lights," he shares.
This small and tender image reminds me of the public weight placed upon Palestinian artists and on Nafar himself.
Their work is expected to represent a people, preserve a culture, explain a political struggle and even change the minds of those responsible for their mass murder, occupation and oppression.
Nafar is also just a father holding a microphone, beneath the stage lights, as seen through the eyes of his children somewhere in the back of the crowd.
He no longer accepts the burden of changing the world. He will continue to write, perform with DAM, create songs with different energies, and build an archive of his thoughts.
But he will not pretend a song can do the work of political power.
"What changes the world is oil deals," he tells The New Arab. Music cannot end a genocide; Nafar is clear about that now.
Music may not change the course of the world, but it is one of the places where history is told and the realities that power would flatten or erase are preserved.
Nafar's work holds the many layers of Palestinian life — its violence and contradictions, but also its gallows humour, intimacy and joy.
He may not complete the puzzle, but he has added a vital piece: a pioneering artist, now an emerging literary figure, refusing to fit a mould or sugarcoat his life to suit anyone's narrative other than his own.
Tamer Nafar's first book, '3Gs', a prose memoir, is slated for release in 2026.
Frances Leach is a London-based writer covering human rights, global affairs and world culture
