Visible crises, invisible people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
08:31:43 UTC
17:31:43 KST

Share & more
On 24 July, The New Humanitarian (TNH) published an Instagram post recapping the third round of the war waged by the US against Iran. It named four American soldiers who had been killed in Iranian airstrikes in Iraq and Jordan. Missing from the post were the Iranians: 55 people killed in US strikes since 27 June and hundreds injured.
Why was this remarkable? Because TNH is not just any media outlet. It calls itself a “mission-driven, impact-seeking, decolonial organisation” and has made decolonising its journalism a strategic priority. Such claims create expectations.
Not one to stay silent, I raised this omission in the comments section, asking rather bluntly whether TNH considered Iranian casualties not worth mentioning. To its credit, TNH responded immediately, deleting the post within minutes and replacing it with one captioned: “Edited, Iranian casualties added to slide 2.”
The omission was probably not deliberate, but that is precisely why it matters. Nobody had to decide that Iranian deaths were unworthy of mention. Four American soldiers registered immediately, 55 Iranians did not. Adding them corrected the post, but it did not explain how a country with a population of over 90 million people under attack could initially be overlooked. If this can happen in a decolonial newsroom committed to centering people affected by crises, what should we expect from organisations without that commitment?
Iran is a textbook example of a country that is hyper-visible while its people are rendered invisible. I choose this example, not just because I’m Iranian-American, but because Iran is everywhere in the news: nuclear weapons, sanctions, security threats, regime change, and the never-ending Strait of Hormuz saga. Yet, Iranians are harder to find: civilians, political prisoners, journalists, women, queer and minoritised people, aid workers, Afghan migrants and refugees – people surviving and dying because of decisions they never made.
That invisibility matters far beyond whether a decolonial newsroom acknowledges deaths caused by an imperial power: When Trump threatens the annihilation of Iranian civilisation, the silence from media and humanitarian organisations makes these threats politically viable. The silence is therefore consequential.
The Iranian people are doubly invisible as a population caught between imperial violence and domestic repression, a bind that shapes what gets reported and funded. The Islamic Republic has become interchangeable with its population, erasing the population’s agency. After successive rounds of aggression by the United States and Israel, Iran has been exalted as the last bastion against imperialism. The dilemma is that though Iran is rightly aggrieved under international law, the Islamic Republic is also an autocratic theocracy that arrests and executes its own citizens daily.
The right sees only a regime to be overthrown, presenting the violent, illegal war as liberation. Trump’s own rhetoric already embodies this logic of annihilation recast as liberation. In doing so, it usurps Iranians’ role as authors of their own future.
Parts of the left demand a choice between condemning imperialist violence and condemning the regime, as if the two cannot coexist. Kamran Matin and Somayeh Rostampoor call this campism. It protects states, not people.
Iran’s right to resist imperialist aggression is real, and so is the war being fought against it. That is not in dispute. What campism does is take that one legitimate fact and use it to bury another: in this case, that this is a regime with a long record of authoritarian repression now using the war to deepen it. Campism recasts anyone resisting the regime as a foreign plot rather than a popular uprising, erasing the fact that they are the same people risking their lives against both the war and the regime.
Both positions narrow the stories journalists tell, the statements humanitarian leaders make, and the suffering donors will fund. Iranians disappear when they cannot fit neatly into either political camp.
Whose suffering is funded?
Visibility is not just a backdrop to humanitarian response; it is a determinant of it. Money follows attention, shaped by three actors: media deciding what counts as a story, humanitarian organisations deciding what counts as a crisis worth naming, and politicians deciding which victims are convenient to grieve.
Iran’s underfunding is what happens when all three fail at once. Attention does not mechanically dictate funding decisions, bureaucratic priorities and government interests shape them too; but it determines which crises get named as crises in the first place, and that naming is where the failure begins.
The scale should have made failure impossible: Iran has endured four rounds of war in just over a year. The 12-day air war in June 2025 killed more than 1,000 people. The second, beginning on 28 February 2026, killed nearly 3,500 people and injured more than 32,000. Millions fled, almost 150,000 civilian buildings were damaged. Two further rounds of US strikes have killed dozens more. During the most recent, a US missile struck a wedding in Kuhestak, killing four civilians and injuring dozens, including children.
Humanitarian leaders should defend the universality of aid, not allow donor politics determine whose suffering is recognised or funded.
At least nine Iranian Red Crescent Society staff and volunteers have been killed. I work in a sector that regularly insists aid workers are not targets, yet I recall no outrage over these nine colleagues. The contrast with responses elsewhere was flagrant: the same erasure that produced the TNH slide, now at sectoral scale.
International media was present in Iran throughout the strikes – filing, verifying, present on the ground. And even there, Iranian deaths still went uncounted. In Gaza, they aren’t present at all – barred from entering, while Palestinian journalists reporting the same deaths aren’t treated as credible enough to confirm them on their own. That exposes “we can’t confirm the casualties” as a hollow excuse: The only source treated as trustworthy is absent from Gaza and proved unreliable in Iran even when it was there.
Humanitarian leadership followed the same pattern of delay and euphemism. Tom Fletcher, the UN’s humanitarian chief, made his first (and so far only) public statement on Iran on 15 April 2026, after two wars had passed. It announced $12 million from the UN’s emergency fund. It said infrastructure had been destroyed and services disrupted, but it did not say by whom, nor whose lives were lost, nor that aid workers had been killed – the passive language made military violence sound like a natural disaster.
Fletcher is representative, not an outlier. Many of the humanitarian system’s largest donors are also waging or supporting the war against Iran. Humanitarian leaders should defend the universality of aid, not allow donor politics determine whose suffering is recognised or funded.
Politicians complete the circuit: They protect suffering that fits their alliances. Iranian civilians killed by US and Israeli strikes are inconvenient for governments allied with one or both; those imprisoned by their own state are inconvenient for anyone whose politics require a tidy narrative of resistance. Both categories need a political sponsor to be seen. Neither has one.
The funding record shows what these three compounded failures look like in dollars. The IFRC sought 120 million Swiss francs to help the Iranian Red Crescent Society reach 10 million people. By early August, it had received around 5%. The Norwegian Refugee Council received only $2 million of the $6 million it requested. UNHCR’s $140 million appeal for Iran was only 18% funded.
Not every missing dollar traces back to Iranian visibility, but the funding trend reflects donor interests, diplomatic relationships, and media attention. Iranian civilians did not fail to attract funding because the case was unclear: Media, humanitarian organisations, and politicians alike found them easy to look past.
From invisibility in reporting to invisibility in humanitarian response
Patrick Gathara calls the competition for attention between humanitarian emergencies, the “crisis roulette”, but the wheel is weighted by political decisions.
TNH’s slide showed how those decisions determine whose deaths get seen between and within crises. In Gathara’s “marketplace of suffering”, media and humanitarian organisations force affected populations into a dystopian contest for limited attention and funding. Both sectors invoke neutrality, but neutrality becomes obfuscation when it separates violence from its author or treats violence as the absence of a political choice rather than the exercise of one.
Neglect and disputed evidence look like opposite failures, but they are operations of the same wheel: one population loses when no one is watching, the other loses even while the whole world is.
Sudan has become known as the “forgotten crisis”, as though this were accidental. Media outlets moved on, humanitarian organisations failed to sustain attention, and governments withheld aid while continuing to arm those committing genocide.
Palestinians are rendered invisible even as they document the genocide in Gaza in real time; their lives and voices are erased, casualty figures disputed, and Israel’s responsibility obscured.
Neglect and disputed evidence look like opposite failures, but they are operations of the same wheel: one population loses when no one is watching, the other loses even while the whole world is.
Iran, Sudan, and Gaza are also routinely invoked against each other: Iran and Sudan are cited to diminish Gaza; and Gaza is invoked to silence Iranians. The same zero-sum logic resurfaces inside Iran’s own story, between condemning the war and condemning the regime.
Changing this requires more than correcting a slide. It means confronting the bias running across media and humanitarian organisations, determining whose suffering is named and funded. It also means rejecting the myth of scarcity on which the marketplace of suffering depends: that attention and humanitarian funding are inherently limited, even as far greater resources are found to wage and arm wars.
The scarcity is political, not inevitable, so too is the hierarchy it sustains. Media outlets and humanitarian organisations can treat different humanitarian crises as facets of one system of impunity, not rivals for a fixed share of attention.

Kapıkule Border Gate, Türkiye-Bulgaria border
Türkiye and Bulgaria are in talks to open a new border crossing designed as an alternative to Kapıkule, the country’s busiest border gate.
Kapıkule Border Gate, located on the Türkiye-Bulgaria border, is the largest land border crossing in Türkiye and Eastern Europe and the world’s second-busiest in terms of traffic volume. It serves as a key road corridor for trade and passenger traffic between Asia and Europe.
With thousands of vehicles passing through the crossing every day, the two countries are planning to open a new border gate north of the existing facility in a bid to ease congestion and increase the capacity of cross-border traffic.
The new customs crossing is planned to be established under the name “Kapıkule / Kapitan Andreevo – North.”
According to a statement issued by the Edirne Governor’s Office on Sept. 11, Turkish and Bulgarian delegations discussed planned works for the establishment of the new border crossing, as well as measures to increase the capacity of border crossings between the two countries.
Following the meeting, Edirne Gov. Yunus Sezer, Deputy Trade Minister Sezai Uçarmak and Bulgarian Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev inspected the area north of Kapıkule where the new border gate is planned to be built.
The delegation received information from officials about the works envisaged to be carried out in the area.
In 2025, more than 7.7 million passengers entered or exited Türkiye through Kapıkule. During the summer season alone, which saw the annual influx and return of Turkish expats, Kapıkule handled 2.5 million passengers and more than 600,000 vehicles.
Kapıkule also recorded one of the highest daily volumes of freight traffic in its history, processing a total of 3,442 commercial vehicles, 1,753 inbound and 1,689 outbound, in a single day on Dec. 7, 2025.

What Ukraine has that Japan and Taiwan lack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
08:30:06 UTC
17:30:06 KST

What Ukraine has that Japan and Taiwan lack
Ukraine’s former defence minister is launching a new venture that could offer more than drone technology. Asia should take notes
Six weeks before Karp’s name entered the picture, Fedorov had been Ukraine’s youngest-ever minister. The day after his July dismissal, Italy’s defence minister invited him to Rome as an adviser. Karp, whose firm is worth US$440 billion, reportedly soon called him to discuss working together. Neither was calling for Ukrainian hardware. What they presumably wanted was harder to manufacture: what Fedorov had learned running the system that produced that hardware.
That system was a loop: battlefield, failure, feedback, redesign, test, back to the battlefield. Brave1, the defence-tech cluster that was essentially Fedorov’s brainchild, is known for fast procurement – more than 500 grants in two years, prototypes certified in weeks. However, speed alone wasn’t the asset. Rather, the asset was the rapid feedback loop of real-world experience, which included soldiers dying when a tactic failed.
Military theorist John Boyd argued that combat is won by whoever cycles through observing, orienting, deciding and acting faster than the enemy can adapt. Ukraine didn’t just build weapons faster, it closed the loop between failure and correction faster than Russia could exploit the failure.
Covid-19 exposed a civilian version of the same mechanism: emergency conditions compressed vaccine development from years to months by running trials, manufacturing and regulatory review in parallel because immediate human costs were moving faster than ordinary institutions could tolerate.
In Ukraine, that loop was hard to contain within a conventional chain of command. An organisation built for rapid experimentation and discretionary procurement can collide with institutions built for command and accountability, even in a country fighting for survival.

Turkish combat drone gets a longer-range strike weapon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
08:28:15 UTC
17:28:15 KST

- Baykar has integrated Roketsan's new 300-ER air-launched ballistic missile onto its Akıncı combat drone, with a test launch expected soon.
- The missile can strike targets more than 500 km away and extends a family of shorter-range weapons already fired from the Akıncı.
Turkish drone maker Baykar has fitted its Akıncı unmanned combat aircraft with Roketsan’s new 300-ER air-launched ballistic missile, with a first launch from the drone expected soon, according to Ulusavunma.
Roketsan first showed the 300-ER publicly at the IDEF defense show in Istanbul in July 2025, presenting it as the longest-range weapon yet in a family of air-launched missiles that began with the shorter İHA-122 and İHA-230. The missile can hit targets more than 500 km (310 miles) away, depending on the altitude it is launched from.
The 300-ER measures about 5 meters (16 feet) long, weighs 900 kg (1,980 lb) and carries a warhead of more than 150 kg (330 lb) inside a 370 mm-diameter body. It navigates using GNSS and inertial guidance and switches to a TV camera seeker for the final approach to the target, a setup Roketsan says is built for precision strikes on radars, armored vehicles, air defense systems and command centers.
The missile extends a lineage Roketsan built from its ground-launched artillery rockets. The company adapted its 122 mm and 230 mm-class rockets into the air-launched İHA-122 and İHA-230, both of which Baykar has already test-fired from the Akıncı, hitting targets roughly 55 km and 100 km away in past trials. The 300-ER carries that same approach out to a much longer range, inside a larger airframe.
That range matters because it lets a large drone like the Akıncı release a weapon and turn away before coming within reach of many surface-to-air missile systems built to intercept aircraft rather than incoming ballistic threats. Roketsan has said the missile is also intended for use on fighter jets and on Baykar’s jet-powered Kızılelma combat drone.
Roketsan told Turkish media in April 2026 that it expected to complete initial test firings of the 300-ER and deliver the missile to the Turkish Armed Forces within the year. Baykar’s September 10 statement does not say whether that test launch has already taken place or specify a date for it, and neither company has disclosed when the missile might enter regular service.

(AA Photo)
Market participants slightly raised their year-end inflation expectations while trimming growth forecasts for the next two years, according to the Central Bank’s October Survey of Market Participants.
The survey, which tracks the expectations of decision-makers and experts from the financial and real sectors regarding key economic indicators, showed that the year-end consumer inflation (CPI) forecast rose to 29.61 percent from 29.43 percent in the previous survey period.
Expectations for inflation 12 months ahead were broadly unchanged at 23.7 percent, compared with 23.69 percent previously, while the 24-month-ahead inflation forecast increased to 18.32 percent from 18.03 percent.
Growth expectations were revised slightly lower. Participants now expect Türkiye’s economy to expand by 3 percent in 2026, down from a previous forecast of 3.1 percent.
The growth estimate for 2027 was also cut to 3.9 percent from 4 percent.
Meanwhile, expectations for the Turkish Lira remained mixed. The year-end U.S. dollar/lira forecast edged down to 51.57 from 51.66 in the previous survey. However, participants raised their 12-month exchange rate expectation to 58.60 liras per dollar from 57.43.

Major data center developments in Finland could hike electricity prices in Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
08:25:00 UTC
17:25:00 KST

Major data center developments in Finland could hike electricity prices in Estonia
If no new generation is added in either country, Google's Finnish data centers investment could hike the price of electricity by half a cent per kilowatt-hour in Estonia, experts warn.
Google is investing €13 billion in Finland to build large data centers there. The highly energy-intensive centers will buy half of the electricity generated by Finland's Loviisa nuclear power plant over the next 22 years. This could leave Finland with less surplus electricity that countries such as Estonia have been able to buy cheaply.
"This naturally means that prices there will rise, and if prices rise there, they will also rise for us during periods when we import electricity from Finland. Looking at this year, electricity consumption in Finland has actually increased by around 500 megawatts compared with 2025. There may be several factors behind that, but excluding the coldest winter months, the price in Finland has risen by €5 per megawatt-hour over the past year and that has also had an impact on us," said Tiit Hõbejõgi, a member of the management board of Eesti Energia subsidiary Enefit.
In that case, the price would rise by 0.5 cents per kilowatt-hour, although additional generating capacity is expected to come online in Finland.
"There will certainly be certain times when the surplus on the Finnish energy market, which has perhaps been one of its defining features, will be somewhat smaller. The average price will probably remain largely where it is today. Market volatility may increase, with some additional hours when electricity is very expensive. On the other hand, because this additional demand will also spur the construction of new power plants, there will also be quite a few hours when electricity prices are again very low because more cheap wind power has entered the market," said Timo Tatar, CEO of Ignitis Eesti.
In recent years, Estonia has imported 40 percent of the electricity it consumes from Finland and other Nordic countries. Estonia should not rely on how much surplus energy it can buy from its neighbors, transmission system operator Elering CEO Kalle Kilk said.
"If consumption increases and supply has not increased by the same amount, that clearly affects both security of supply and prices. We have to take into account that we in Estonia have been quite dependent on the situation in our neighboring countries. The main conclusion for us is that in the future we need to take somewhat greater responsibility ourselves for ensuring that we have enough electricity that can also be generated domestically," Kilk said.

Turkish Interior Minister Mustafa Çiftçi (AA Photo)
In a move to unify law enforcement across Central Asia and the Caucasus, Türkiye has proposed establishing “Türkpol” — a regional policing agency modeled on Europol for the Organization of Turkic States, Interior Minister Mustafa Çiftçi has announced following a meeting in Kazakhstan.
“One of the most important issues we addressed today was the establishment of a council for combating crime. The proposal we put forward for the establishment of this council was included in the joint declaration,” Çiftçi told reporters after the meeting in the Kazakh capital Astana on Sept. 10.
The proposed council will cover a range of issues, including combating organized crime, drug-related and terrorist offenses, irregular migration and illegal betting and gambling, he said.
“As a step beyond this, based on this founding agreement, I also put forward a proposal for the establishment of Türkpol, an organization among the Turkic states modeled on Europol and Aseanapol,” Çiftçi said.
He added that Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan gave positive signals to the proposal.
The meeting also addressed proposals to facilitate travel among member states by allowing their citizens to cross borders using only national identity cards, without passports.
Officials also discussed the possibility of establishing joint passport-control points at airports, allowing citizens of OTS member states to undergo passport checks at common control points.
A draft agreement incorporating all of these proposals is set for submission at the leaders’ summit in Ankara next month, Çiftçi added.
The organization was founded in 2009 by Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan as the Cooperation Council of Turkic-Speaking States, before being renamed the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) at a landmark summit in Istanbul in November 2021. The change was seen as a significant step in the evolution of Turkic integration, reflecting a growing ambition to turn longstanding cultural ties into greater geopolitical influence.
Türkiye is set to take over the OTS’ rotating presidency at a summit scheduled to be hosted in October.

Russia’s Digital Development Ministry announces 5G launch (only in 16 cities for now)
Russia has switched on its first commercial fifth-generation (5G) networks, the Digital Development Ministry announced.
The country’s “big four” mobile carriers — MTS, Beeline, MegaFon, and T2 — will offer 5G-based service in 16 cities, giving an estimated 10 million people access to 5G mobile internet, the ministry reported.
Android device owners in those cities will be able to use 5G “very soon,” the Digital Development Ministry noted, adding that access for iPhone owners depends on a decision by Apple.
The ministry stated it plans to expand 5G to 50 more cities by the end of 2026. Initially, the technology will run on LTE (4G) frequencies already allocated to carriers, which have also received new spectrum in the 4.63–4.99 GHz range.
In Russia, the Federal Security Service (FSB) and the Defense Ministry have traditionally controlled the 3.4–3.8 GHz frequency band used for 5G elsewhere in the world. Mobile carriers have long pushed to obtain these frequencies to build fifth-generation networks, but Vladimir Putin left them with the military in 2019 and has not reversed the decision since.

Pro-Palestine student suspended by King’s College London returns to campus
University lifts suspension amid criticism from student groups over crackdown on pro-Palestine sentiments.
London, United Kingdom – A 22-year-old Egyptian student suspended from King’s College London (KCL) last year after his involvement in pro-Palestine campus activism is returning to university.
KCL lifted Usama Ghanem’s suspension late last month, allowing him to return and complete the third and final year of his international studies degree.
“We won,” Ghanem said. “I was suspended because of my activism for Palestine … The injustices and the process that I’ve gone through have felt extremely bitter, but it also needed to be fought.”
According to a May 2025 letter addressed to Ghanem and seen by Al Jazeera, KCL accused him of several instances of non-academic misconduct, including “acting in an intimidating and hostile manner”, disrupting an event, “procedural breaches” and “causing a health and safety concern”.
The letter signed by university staff also stated: “You will need to return to your home country during this period of suspension.”
Ghanem’s visa was revoked as a result of the disciplinary action. But as he had previously been detained in Egypt over his activism, he had claimed that he risked persecution if he returned.
After taking legal action against the university and accepting delays to his studies, Ghanem told Al Jazeera: “I’m left with nothing but conviction, and the only regret I’ll ever have is that I didn’t do more for the Palestinian people.”
The campaign group Cage said, “This is a victory not just for Ghanem, but for every student at King’s, across London and beyond who has taken a stand for Palestine and for the right to protest.”
In July, Al Jazeera and Liberty Investigates reported that at least 26 students at KCL had faced disciplinary investigations after engaging in pro-Palestine protest activity between October 2023 and November 2025.
Since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began, several universities across the UK have faced criticism over their handling of Palestine solidarity protests on campus.
Earlier this year, the European Legal Support Center documented what it described as widespread repression of students, academics and teachers over their solidarity with Palestine, identifying educational institutions among those leading the crackdown.
KCL denies disciplining students for activism.
A university spokesperson told Al Jazeera that KCL had “upheld the original reasons” for Ghanem’s suspension but had determined that he “had met the conditions agreed for suspension and that re-enrolment was therefore the appropriate outcome”.
“We will always apply a fair approach to misconduct proceedings, and have a duty to act where behaviour breaches safeguarding and security regulations, or puts others at risk,” the spokesperson said.
They added that decisions on visa sponsorship are not made by KCL, but that the university “has a legal duty to notify (UK Visas & Immigration) of any change in student status”.
‘King’s overreached’
Al Jazeera has also seen evidence indicating that KCL used Horus, a private firm run by former military intelligence officials, to monitor protest activity.
In Ghanem’s case, the company appeared to have informed the university of upcoming demonstrations in support of the “expelled student”.
“They have specifically been engaged in surveilling me,” Ghanem said. “I think it’s crystal clear that King’s overreached.”
KCL denied monitoring Ghanem, saying “all information collated by Horus is already publicly available elsewhere.
“We use Horus as a horizon scanning tool for updates on events on or near our campuses, including protests on any subject,” the university said.
Hundreds of students and several academics supported Ghanem throughout his dispute with KCL, including the Association of Student Activism for Palestine (ASAP).
“KCL’s decision to reinstate Usama shows what happens when students and the wider community stand strong against the intimidation tactics of our universities,” ASAP told Al Jazeera.
“This victory has shown us the power that students and the wider movement holds when we stand on the side of justice unwaveringly.”

Emma Bonino has died, her More Europe party said on Friday. 
    The former Italian foreign minister and former European Commissioner was 78. 
    The historic Italian Radical bigwig and More Europe founder had been admitted to Rome's Santo Spirito hospital in code red on Sunday after suffering a respiratory crisis. 
    Sources close to her said Thursday that she had left Santo Spirito's intensive care and been taken to a private clinic. 
    Three years ago Bonino said she had gone into remission after suffering lung cancer. 
    Bonino was elected eight times to the Italian parliament, six times to the Lower House and twice to Senator, and served four times as an MEP. 
    She was at the heart of many of the Radical party's biggest civil-rights battles in Italy, including the campaigns for divorce and abortion in the 1970s. 
    She became one of the Italian women politicians best-known abroad thanks to her stint as the European Commissioner for Health and Consumer Protection between 1995 and 1999. 
    She was minister for trade and European affairs under Romano Prodi between 2006 and 2008 and foreign minister under Enrico Letta between 2013 and 2014.

"Another birthday": army officer Olena Rij injured during Russian attack on Pavlohrad
Army officer and Ukrainska Pravda 100 nominee Olena Rij has been injured during the Russian attack on Pavlohrad in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast.
Source: Olena Rij on Instagram Stories
Details: Olena sustained burns and is currently in hospital.
On 10 September, Russian forces attacked Pavlohrad with drones. The death toll stands at five, with 67 injured, including eight children.
Combat medic Olena Rij was in Pavlohrad that day. She said she was engulfed in flames after the final explosion, sustaining burns all over her body, and is now in hospital.
"Pavlohrad. Four Shahed drones. Another birthday. Burns. I survived and that is the main thing. My condolences to all who were killed and injured," Olena wrote.
She also noted that 10 September 2026 is her birthday.
"On 9 September 2023, an RPG round landed in the spot where I had crouched down just five to ten seconds before. Had it not been for that, my head would have been blown off," Olena recalled.
She also jokingly added that September bears a grudge against her.
Olena began her war journey as an active volunteer at the start of the full-scale invasion and subsequently joined the military as a combat medic and assault soldier in the 47th Separate Mechanised Brigade.
She saved lives in battles for Robotyne, Avdiivka, Chasiv Yar and elsewhere. She is currently an officer in the 412th Brigade Nemesis and was awarded the Order of Courage, Third Class.
In 2024, Olena Rij became the host of the video podcast Dumky na stil (Thoughts on the Table) on the Kharakter platform, interviewing military personnel, volunteers, their family members and activists.
Background: A girl named Viktoriia, who sustained injuries and multiple wounds during a Russian attack on a children's playground in Kherson, was previously discharged from hospital and is now trying to walk again.

Magyar vs. Moscow: Hungary toughens stance toward Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
08:20:00 UTC
17:20:00 KST

Magyar vs. Moscow: Hungary toughens stance toward Russia
September 11, 2026
While Viktor Orban was in power, no other EU member state was as pro-Russia as Hungary. Indeed, the prime minister's apparent eagerness to be of service to the Russian president earned him the nickname "Putin's pinscher" or "Kremlin agent."
For years, Hungary was seen as a security risk both in the EU and NATO. Russian spies were able to operate in the country largely unhindered for a long time.
In February, it came to light that Peter Szijjarto, Orban's foreign minister from 2014 to 2026, had passed on confidential information from EU meetings to his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov.
All this came to an end in May, when the government headed by Peter Magyar took office.
An unambiguous signal to Russia
In a clear departure from the government line under Orban, Hungary's new prime minister has already heavily criticized Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine several times.
The government also recently declared Russia a threat to Hungary's national security.
This week, it took its biggest step yet against the Kremlin, expelling 10 Russian diplomats for engaging in activities "that are unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention," as announced by Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orban (no relation to the former prime minister).
Although Orban did not provide any more details, the phrase is generally understood to mean that the diplomats in question were spies.
Orban said the decision "protects Hungary's security and sovereignty." She added: "It does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia. Hungary intends to continue the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and adherence to the rules."
Restoring old alliances
The minister's brief announcement immediately generated a huge number of headlines and comments — hardly surprising given that this was not only evidence of a 180-degree turn on the government's policy toward Russia but also one of the toughest diplomatic sanctions targeting Moscow since the collapse of communism in 1989/1990.
Speaking to Hungarian news website Index, secret service expert Peter Tarjani said this was "not a diplomatic conflict, but a serious secret service matter" and that with this decision, Hungary was simultaneously returning "to the mainstream of its allies' security policy."
Political scientist and leading Hungarian Russia expert Andras Racz told the Hungarian national news agency MTI that Hungary was the only EU and NATO member not to have made such an expulsion in recent years.
Racz said such a step "should really have been taken four and ahalf years ago." He added: "Hungary is now settling its old debt with its allies."
Reliance on Russian gas?
Under Viktor Orban, Hungary was the only EU country never to unreservedly condemn Russia's all-out war against Ukraine.
Indeed, during the final two years of his rule, Orban even blamed Ukraine and the West for Russia's aggression.
But long before that — even after he came to power back in 2010 — Viktor Orban took a markedly pro-Russia line, which he justified, among other things, with the claim that Hungary was more dependent on Russian energy supplies than almost any other country in the region.
His government's repeated assertion that Russian gas was cheaper has long been disproved. What's more, the expansion of the Paks nuclear power plant with Russian support will cost Hungary dearly for decades to come.
In the light of all this, Orban's close ties to Russia remain a mystery.
Absurd situations
For Hungary, this closeness to Russia often led to absurd situations in which the country's national security was put at risk. At the same time, Orban repeatedly told his critics that it was they who were a threat to Hungary's sovereignty.
For example, Russian secret service agents for years took part in military-style training exercises in the far-right scene right up until 2016.
Starting in 2012, Russian secret service operatives for years stole huge amounts of data from the Hungarian Foreign Ministry and other agencies without the government ever publicly condemning it.
In 2019, Russia got permission to move the headquarters of the International Investment Bank (IIB) to Budapest. The IIB was known as the "spy bank" because its leadership was made up of individuals linked to or associated with Russia's FSB intelligence service. It was only after the United States imposed sanctions on the bank in 2023 that it left Hungary again.
Investigative journalist Szabolcs Panyi has warned multiple times in recent years that Hungary had become a "logistical center and deployment zone for Russian secret services," thereby putting the whole region at risk.
Rejection of Orban's pro-Russia course
Orban's strictly pro-Russia course was laterally rejected by many Hungarians.
The decidedly pro-EU orientation of Peter Magyar and his Tisza party had a considerable role to play in the party's election victory earlier this year. The EU flag was often seen and spontaneous cries of "Russians, go home" were often heard at election rallies last spring.
Unlike Viktor Orban, Magyar and leading Tisza politicians are convinced that Hungary's place is exclusively in the European Union and that the country should only maintain pragmatic low-level relations with Russia.
Nevertheless, many observers and experts are surprised at how radically the Magyar government has turned away from Russia.
Andras Telkes, the former deputy head of Hungary's foreign intelligence service (IH), wrote in the newspaper Nepszava that the expulsion of diplomats shows that the presence of Russian secret services in Hungary obviously runs "very deep" and that the country has a serious problem.
Telkes said the expulsion of 10 diplomats would help rebuild trust in Hungary in the eyes of the secret services of its NATO allies.
He said the decision was significant. "Expelling two or three people would have been a sign," Telkes said. "Expelling 10 people already means war."
Telkes said the expulsions create a serious security problem for Hungary.
Will Moscow turn off the taps?
A spokeswoman for the Russian Foreign Ministry condemned the expulsion of the diplomats in strong terms. She spoke of a "Russophobe lobby in Budapest" and announced a "hard and painful" response.
Russian lawmaker Andrey Kolesnik, a member of the State Duma's Defense Committee, said the government would consider halting gas supplies to Hungary.
Foreign Minister Orban knows more about such Russian threats than anyone else in the new Hungarian government: In 2007, she wrote her doctoral thesis on Russia's energy policy in Central Europe. A year later, she published a book: "Power, Energy, and the New Russian Imperialism."
This article was originally published in German.

Two Azerbaijani sailors killed in Black Sea tugboat drone attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
08:19:01 UTC
17:19:01 KST

The Somali-flagged TEDY was hit near Odesa and struck twice more overnight, with two other crewmembers hospitalised with burns. Azerbaijan's foreign ministry did not attribute responsibility for the attack.
Two Azerbaijani sailors were killed when a tugboat was struck by drones in the Black Sea on Tuesday, in the latest attack on civilian shipping near the Ukrainian port of Odesa.
The Somali-flagged tugboat TEDY, owned by Mert Marine Corporation, was first hit near Odesa before coming under two further drone attacks overnight as it sailed toward the Romanian port of Constanta.
Azerbaijan's Foreign Ministry confirmed the deaths of crew members Aslan Aliyev and Asim Gasimov. Two other Azerbaijani sailors, Imran Novruzov and Rauf Aliyev, were hospitalised in the Ukrainian city of Chornomorsk with burn injuries. Six further crew members received treatment at the scene.
The vessel carried 10 crew members in total, including Azerbaijani, Turkish, German and Ukrainian nationals.
Azerbaijan's Foreign Ministry said it was coordinating with diplomatic missions and relevant authorities and was taking measures to repatriate the injured and carry out procedures relating to the deceased. It did not attribute responsibility for the attack.
Ukraine's Ministry for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport said Russia had carried out the attack, describing it as part of a sustained campaign against civilian vessels and port infrastructure.
Russia's Defence Ministry said on Wednesday it had struck two cargo vessels heading to Odesa and a tugboat, claiming the ships were carrying military supplies. Kyiv did not comment on the Russian claim.
Chornomorsk is a major Ukrainian commercial port on the Black Sea and one of the principal terminals for Ukrainian grain exports.
Following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, Kyiv and Moscow negotiated the Black Sea Grain Initiative, which allowed Ukrainian agricultural exports to resume under UN and Turkish supervision before Russia withdrew from the agreement in July 2023.
Russia has since targeted the port and its surrounding infrastructure repeatedly.
Attacks on civilian shipping in the Black Sea have intensified since July, when multiple merchant vessels flying the flags of third countries have been struck, raising concern about the risk to seafarers.
The attack on the TEDY is the latest in a series of incidents involving Azerbaijani sailors. Five Azerbaijani citizens were killed in attacks on two vessels in the Sea of Azov in June.

Uzbekistan gets its first C-390 military transport plane
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
08:18:44 UTC
17:18:44 KST

- Embraer presented Uzbekistan's first C-390 Millennium transport aircraft on September 10, 2026, making it the first Central Asian operator of the jet.
- Uzbekistan signed the two-aircraft order in December 2024, but Embraer did not name the customer until February 2026.
Embraer presented Uzbekistan’s first C-390 Millennium military transport aircraft on September 10, 2026, making the country the first C-390 operator in Central Asia. The Brazilian manufacturer confirmed the milestone in a social media post, without disclosing further details of the handover.
Embraer had kept the Uzbek order under wraps for more than a year before naming the buyer. The company signed the deal on December 27, 2024, but listed the customer only as undisclosed until it identified Uzbekistan at the Singapore Airshow on February 3, 2026. The order covers two C-390 aircraft.
“We officially welcome the Republic of Uzbekistan to the group of C-390 operators as the Uzbekistan Air Force modernizes its transport capabilities,” Bosco da Costa Junior, President and CEO of Embraer Defense & Security, said when the order was disclosed in February.
The C-390 Millennium can carry a payload of up to 26 tonnes and cruise at speeds up to 470 knots (870 km/h or 541 mph), figures Embraer says put it ahead of other medium-sized military transport aircraft. The jet handles cargo and troop transport, airdrops, medical evacuation, search and rescue, firefighting and humanitarian missions, and it can operate from unpaved or short runways. A tanker variant, designated KC-390, adds aerial refueling.
The aircraft fills a gap in Uzbekistan’s air transport fleet. The Uzbek Air Force currently flies four Airbus C295M-W light transports alongside older Soviet-era Ilyushin Il-76TD heavy airlifters, and the C-390 sits between those two types in size and range. The acquisition follows other recent additions of Western equipment to the fleet, including Airbus H125 and H215 helicopters, as Uzbekistan has moved to diversify a fleet built mostly around Soviet-legacy aircraft.
Uzbekistan becomes the eleventh country to operate or order the C-390, joining Brazil, Portugal, Hungary, South Korea, the Netherlands, Austria, the Czech Republic, Sweden, Slovakia and Lithuania. Embraer designed the aircraft to be interoperable with NATO systems even though most of its customers to date have been NATO members or close partners.
Uzbekistan has also been diversifying its air force with equipment from China. State television confirmed in August 2026 that Uzbekistan had taken delivery of Chengdu J-10CE fighter jets, becoming the second foreign operator of the type after Pakistan. Uzbekistan had reportedly agreed to buy 24 of the fighters for around $1 billion, though the government has not confirmed the total number delivered or the contract’s final value.

Algeria closes airspace to UAE after diplomatic break
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
08:18:39 UTC
17:18:39 KST

Breadcrumb
Algeria seals off airspace to UAE after diplomatic break
Algeria said Thursday it was closing its airspace to Emirati-registered civilian and military aircraft after cutting diplomatic ties with the Gulf country following years of tension.
In a statement announcing the severing of diplomatic relations, Algiers accused the Gulf country of "provocative and hostile acts", but it remained unclear what triggered the rupture.
The Algerian defence ministry said the airspace ban would go into effect Friday, with the exception of commercial flights to and from Algiers airport, which would continue until the end of 2026.
Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune has often referred to the UAE as a "micro-state" or "statelet" seeking to destabilise several countries in the region, citing Libya, Mali and Sudan.
The North African country, which has signalled for months a diplomatic break, said the decision came "after exhausting all avenues to preserve bilateral relations" with the UAE.
The Emirati foreign ministry later said it hoped the decision would be temporary so as to maintain "fraternal ties" with Algeria.
The Algerian foreign ministry said it had warned Abu Dhabi several times but the UAE "persisted in its actions, reaching a point where they could no longer be considered acceptable or tolerable".
"Algeria spared no effort to draw the Emirati side's attention to, and to warn it against, the dire consequences that could result from its regrettable and unjustified conduct," the ministry said.
In a televised interview in July, Tebboune again lashed out against Abu Dhabi, saying "wherever they set foot, blood flows".
"We want them to stay away, so that blood does not flow in our country," he added.
At that time, Tebboune said a diplomatic break "would have happened long ago" had Algeria not sought to avoid "deepening divisions" in the Arab world.
On Thursday, Algiers said it was giving the UAE ambassador 48 hours "to comply with the decision".
Sahel interference
Tensions between the two countries have been fuelled by several developments in recent years.
In the Sahel, Algeria was "striving to maintain some semblance of stability", whereas "the UAE was working directly counter to that", said Geoff Porter, an analyst with the North Africa Risk Consulting group.
"Algeria viewed the UAE's interference in North African and Sahelian affairs as not only contrary to Algeria's foreign policy principles, but as an indirect threat to Algerian security," he added.
Porter cited as points of contention Abu Dhabi's support for eastern Libya's military leader Khalifa Haftar, the backing of the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan, and a drone base in Mauritania, which neighbours Algeria.
Last year, Algerian state television denounced what it called a hostile media campaign after UAE-based broadcaster Sky News Arabia aired an interview with historian Mohamed Amine Belghit, who made controversial remarks questioning the existence of Algeria's indigenous Amazigh culture.
Belghit was jailed in Algeria but later pardoned by Tebboune.
Further divisions between Algiers and Abu Dhabi also stemmed from diverging diplomatic policies, including the UAE's normalisation of ties with Israel in 2020.

A large-scale production of counterfeit cosmetics worth more than UAH 235 million was exposed in Kharkiv
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:18:36 EEST
17:18:36 KST

A large-scale production of counterfeit cosmetics worth more than UAH 235 million was exposed in Kharkiv
Kyiv • UNN
In Kharkiv and Lviv, authorities seized 130 tonnes of counterfeit cosmetics, raw materials and equipment. About 50 people were involved in the scheme.
A large-scale operation producing counterfeit perfumes and cosmetics was uncovered in Kharkiv. During 14 searches in Kharkiv and Lviv, approximately 130 tonnes of finished products, raw materials and equipment with an estimated value of over UAH 235 million were seized. The Prosecutor General’s Office reports this, UNN writes.
Details
According to the investigation, the scheme’s participants organized a full cycle of illegal production—from manufacturing, bottling and packaging to applying the labels of well-known global brands and selling the goods through specially created websites.
About 50 people were involved in the illegal activity. Some of them were used as nominal heads of controlled enterprises.
According to the investigation, the organizers were two foreign nationals. After the start of russia’s full-scale invasion, they left Ukraine but continued to manage the business remotely.
The products were manufactured and stored in rented warehouse premises. A fully equipped workshop was set up in one of them. A private house was also used for storage.
To make the counterfeits look like original products, labels, markings and watermarks of well-known brands were applied to the packaging, while specialized equipment was used for bottling.
Perfumes, body mists and shimmers, hair sprays, aroma diffusers, shower gels, lotions, creams, cosmetic masks and other goods were sold as originals. Orders were sent to customers by mail.
During the searches, approximately 130 tonnes of products, raw materials and equipment, a Renault Trafic vehicle, almost UAH 1 million in cash, bank cards, phones, laptops, rough notes and other material evidence were seized.
Under the procedural guidance of the Kharkiv Regional Prosecutor’s Office and the Novobavarskyi District Prosecutor’s Office, a pre-trial investigation is ongoing under Part 3 of Article 229 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine—for the intentional infringement of rights to intellectual property objects that caused material damage on an especially large scale
After the necessary expert examinations are conducted and the exact amount of the damage caused is established, the issue of notifying the persons involved of suspicion will be decided. The possible presence of elements of other criminal offenses in their actions is also being examined.

How 9/11 helped Israel sell its war on Palestinians to America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
08:18:18 UTC
17:18:18 KST

How 9/11 helped Israel sell its war on Palestinians to America
The ‘war on terror’ made Israeli repression easier to present as part of a shared struggle against a common enemy.
For me, the New York City skyline was close to home. Quite literally. I grew up just across the Hudson River, with the famed skyline of America’s biggest city visible from my bedroom window. Being a Palestinian American living just outside of the world’s most famous city meant that I spent part of my summers as a tour guide for family visiting us from the Middle East, who, like so many people around the world, wanted to see the Big Apple that the movies and live broadcasts from Times Square on New Year’s Eve had made so famous.
I took visitors to the Statue of Liberty, the Empire State Building, Central Park and the World Trade Center. My last tour was in the final days of August 2001. We went to the observation deck of the World Trade Center known as “Top of the World”. Little did I know that two weeks later that deck, where we had stood looking out at the amazing metropolis below, would come crashing down along with the entire World Trade Center, killing thousands and instantly changing the world as we had known it.
By the time of the September 11 attacks, I was back in my dormitory at university in New England and huddled around a 10-inch television screen with floormates watching ABC’s Peter Jennings cover the horrific news as it was unfolding that Tuesday morning. Among the early reactions was one from Benjamin Netanyahu, then a former prime minister of Israel. Asked by The New York Times what the attack meant for relations between the United States and Israel, Netanyahu replied, “It’s very good.” Then he edited himself: “Well, not very good, but it will generate immediate sympathy,” adding that the attack would “strengthen the bond between our two peoples”. This was his response while ground zero was still smouldering after an attack that had killed nearly 3,000 people.
It immediately hit me that not only was the world about to change, but my life in the US as a Palestinian American was about to become far, far more complicated. The US was about to embark on military engagement in the Middle East, and Netanyahu was excited by the opportunity this presented Israel.
To better understand the impact this moment had on US-Israel relations, it is crucial to consider the preceding context. I have argued elsewhere that the period between the end of the Cold War and 9/11 was a complicated one for US-Israel relations. For most of the history of the US-Israel relationship, the Cold War was the defining paradigm in international relations. For Israel, this was an easy paradigm to navigate. It billed itself to Americans as a like-minded, US-aligned democracy confronting Soviet-backed satellite states in the Arab world.
But as the Cold War ended, the political landscape shifted. The Berlin Wall fell, democratisation swept Eastern Europe, and apartheid ended in South Africa, while Israel was brutally repressing the first Palestinian Intifada. Suddenly, Israel did not fit so comfortably in this new world order. It was during this period that the US made its greatest investments in Israeli-Palestinian peacemaking, however flawed, and used some leverage to press the Israeli government on settlement building.
September 11 and the ensuing global “war on terror” changed all of this. With the second Palestinian Intifada under way, the September 11 attacks on the US provided an opportunity to once again put Israel and the US on the same side of a new defining global divide. Instead of communism, the new global bad guy was radical Islam.
Netanyahu and his allies understood this very well, just as he made clear to The New York Times 25 years ago this week. A wounded America was primed for Islamophobic narratives, and pro-Israel voices were often happy to provide them, as they understood that an America obsessed with “counterterrorism” would have to stay close to Israel.
There are numerous areas where we see the impact of this over time: enhanced US-Israel intelligence collaboration, growing US financial support for Israel and legislative initiatives supported by Israel’s backers in the US that used broadened anti-terror authorities to crack down on Palestinians, to name a few.
The narratives that helped support these outcomes also went beyond simply linking Israel and the US through a common “terrorist threat”. Palestinians were also more easily turned into a “security problem” to American audiences. Instead of asking why Palestinians were resisting oppression, American audiences were pushed to see Israeli repression as self-defence similar to US behaviour. Muslims were often cast as one of two types in American discourse: moderate or extremist, and those criticising Israel were routinely placed in the latter category, which led to stigma and a chilling effect.
Israeli military practices could be cast as useful for America as well. Surveillance, counterinsurgency, targeted killings and other tactics Israel had used in the West Bank and Gaza, which had occasionally been criticised by Washington, were used by American forces in Iraq and Afghanistan and thus increasingly legitimised before American audiences.
Some of the greatest purveyors of the Islamophobic narratives that characterised much of the post-9/11 period in the United States included David Horowitz, who consistently sought to connect Palestinians with terrorism and called for profiling to make Palestinian identity itself a security concern; Daniel Pipes, who often characterised Muslim organisations as potentially or secretly militant, casting suspicion on Muslim advocacy; Steven Emerson, who sought to popularise infiltration narratives to try to turn mainstream Muslim organisations into security subjects; Brigitte Gabriel, who regularly framed Islamism as a civilisational threat, thus casting Israel as a front-line defender of the West; and David Yerushalmi, who sought to expand the threat narrative to Sharia law and Muslim political influence, thus casting Muslim political participation as potentially subversive.
The general logic of these narratives was that terrorism was effectively synonymous with all things Palestinian/Arab/Muslim and thus Israel’s security model should be seen as legitimate, if not ideal, by Americans.
It is important 25 years later to reflect on the dangerous political opportunism that spewed hate into American discourse to cast Israel and Israeli policy in a favourable light. A quarter-century later, the US is once again embroiled in a seemingly intractable quagmire, this time in Iran, a losing effort that has already cost Americans more than $100bn through higher petrol and diesel prices. Given all of this, Americans today should be quick to question Islamophobic narratives, the dangerous paths they lead down and the real motives of those who spread them.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Philippines ferry fire: Search continues for dozens missing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11

17:18:00 KST

Philippines ferry fire: Search continues for dozens missing
September 11, 2026
Philippine firefighters on Friday managed to enter a smoldering ferry in a search for dozens of people still unaccounted for after the vessel caught fire on Wednesday evening, with rescue work complicated by heavy smoke and extreme heat.
The Philippines Coast Guard said that rescuers recovered 30 bodies from a ferry, raising the death toll from the incident to 35.
Earlier, firefighters reported that five people had died, 43 had been rescued, and more than 80 were missing.
On Friday, Coast Guard spokesperson Commodore Noemi Cayabyab said that charred remains had been found in the economy accommodation area, but added that the exact number of those found would need to wait for police forensic investigators to examine the remains for recovery and identification.
"We can't provide exact numbers yet on what we saw today," Cayabyab told AFP news agency.
"We will be providing it once we conduct retrieval and recovery," she added.
The ferry "MV June Aster" had originated in Manila, and was nearing its destination, the tourist hotspot of Coron in the western Philippine province of Palawan, when it caught fire just off the coast.
The Philippine Coast Guard updated the number of missing people from 86 to 84 after confirming that two people originally listed on the manifest had not been on board.
Ferry fire spread 'in seconds'
Cayabyab told a radio interview earlier Friday that the fire broke out in "seconds."
"From the time that they heard the loud explosion, the appearance of smoke, and then fire. It spread very quickly," she said, citing survivor accounts.
Cayabyab said some of those who made it off the ship did not have time to put on life jackets.
The Coast Guard has deployed several vessels and divers to the incident, while army rescue boats, fishermen and private resort
owners have also provided assistance in the search. 
Investigation ongoing
The fire began in the cargo hold, and may have moved even more rapidly due to strong winds, Cayabyab added later.
Although the exact cause of the accident has yet to be officially determined, survivors reported hearing explosions inside the ship.
They later said that a small fire quickly escalated and engulfed the vessel.
Some passengers jumped into the sea, where they remained afloat until they were rescued. The vessel caught fire some 7 kilometers (4.5 miles) off the village of Turda.
The ferry was carrying electric cars, motorcycles, cargo, and heavy-duty equipment, as well as provisions for the crew and passengers.
Ferries are one of the most widely used forms of transport in the Philippines, an archipelago made up of 7,600 islands.
The country has a history of maritime accidents, some of which are caused by overcrowding, adverse sailing conditions, and lax safety standards.

Five killed in Dutch coach crash in Swiss Alps
Five people were killed and 40 others injured, some seriously, after a coach carrying a Dutch tour group crashed in a remote part of southeastern Switzerland on Thursday, Graubünden cantonal police said on Friday.
According to the Graubünden cantonal police, this was a single-vehicle accident. The coach was travelling from Zernez towards Susch in canton Graubünden when it veered off the road and overturned near the village of Less, in a roadworks area.

India news: Putin, Modi to hold talks ahead of BRICS Summit

BRICS Summit 2026: Putin, Modi reaffirm partnership
Published September 11, 2026last updated September 11, 2026
What you need to know
Here is a roundup of some of the top headlines from the BRICS Summit 2026 in India.
- Putin and Modi discussed a wide range of issues including the Ukraine-Russia conflict, energy cooperation and trade across several sectors
- In the evening, Modi is expected to hold bilateral talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Iran facing 'critical, dangerous' pressure — Pezeshkian
Iranis currently experiencing "critical, dangerous" levels of pressure, President Masoud Pezeshkian said.
The pressure comes as a result of the US sanctions on the country, according to Pezeshkian.
"Iran has been subjected to heavy sanctions in recent years," the Iranian leader said ahead of the BRICS summit in India.
"This pressure has reached critical and dangerous stage in recent months following the military aggression by the US and Israel," he added.
Pezeshkian also said that the world is going through a period of "unprecedented complexity."
Putin blames West for attempting to reclaim 'former leadership'
RussianPresident Vladimir Putin blamed Western countries for attempting to reclaim their "former leadership" in an "unseemly" fashion,
According to Russia's leader, the West is focusing on destroying facilities and pipelines, as well as seizing vessels, in an attempt to maintain its economic leadership.
Putin made these comments while speaking at the BRICS business forum in India.
Modi, Putin reaffirm partnership on issues of mutual interest
Indian PM Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin held bilateral talks on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit that will begin on Saturday.
The two leaders "exchanged views on India-Russia engagement in the multilateral sphere, in particular in BRICS under India’s Chairship for 2026," a statement by India's Ministry of External Affairs said.
In the meeting, the leaders also exchanged views on "key regional and global issues of mutual interest, including the conflicts in West Asia and the Black Sea region which have impacted maritime trade and the safety and security of Indian seafarers."
Reaffirming their ties, the two leaders committed to "remain engaged in an effort to strengthen further the Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership between the two countries," the statement added.
Pezeshkian arrives for BRICS Summit
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian landed in Delhi to attend the BRICS Summit.
This is the first visit by an Iranian President to India in over eight years.
Pezeshkian is scheduled to hold bilateral talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi at 6.15 p.m. local time Friday to advance two-way trade and strengthen overall ties.
His participation at the BRICS Summit and bilateral talks with Modi holds significance as it comes at a time when tensions are rife in the Middle East and energy market disruptions have shaken the economy worldwide.
WATCH — India's difficult BRICS chairship
With BRICS nations now representing nearly 3.7 billion people and close to 40% of global GDP, leaders are meeting amid rising geopolitical tensions, trade disputes and energy challenges.
While the expanded bloc is seeking a stronger voice in the global economy, disagreements over an alternative payment system and China's dominant role could test unity. Renewable energy and green infrastructure financing are emerging as key areas to watch.
Former UN diplomat: BRICS is 'voice of Global South,' but 'contradictions remain'
Speaking to DW about the BRICS Summit, former UN diplomat Shashi Tharoor said that the expansion of the bloc has made it the voice of the Global South.
The BRICS coalition started out with four member countries; Brazil, Russia, India and China but now has 11 members and partner countries after the economic bloc decided to open up membership for more countries in 2023.
Tharoor noted that while Iran joined the coalition, US strategic partners Egypt and Ethiopia also joined
"The expansion that took place in Johannesburg turned out to be one in which both sets of geopolitical points of view were accommodated," Tharoor noted in an interview with DW.
He argued that, "in some ways the expansion has made it much more the voice of the global south."
However, he also said that while the majority of the world is represented in the new 11-member BRICS, the chances of having a consensus has also decreased.
"I would say that BRICS is functioning, but the contradictions remain, and some contradictions have become even more apparent," he said.
He said that when BRICS leaders met this year, they "could not agree on any particular language, and so the chair, India, issued a chair statement instead… it wasn't just Iran, it was also Ukraine that they couldn't agree on."
Tharoor noted that the bloc has a "built-in set of geopolitical divergences which will crop up whenever issues divide the members."
Piyush Goyal proposes 'borderless' digital trade at BRICS
Indian Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal on Friday urged BRICS member countries to link their payment systems, encourage trade in local currencies, and make digital trade more accessible globally.
Addressing the opening ceremony of the BRICS Business Forum on Friday, Goyal highlighted India's digital payments ecosystem, including the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), as a potential foundation for deeper cross-border financial cooperation among BRICS economies.
"Today, it is also accepted in 11 countries and I would urge the Brics member countries and partner countries to link our payment systems, trade in each other's local currencies, make digital trade global and build together for the future emerging technologies," Goyal said as reported by Indian newspaper Deccan Herald.
Modi, Putin to meet on the sidelines of BRICS
Russian President Vladimir Putin landed in Delhi on Friday to attend the BRICS Summit being held at the Bharat Mandapam on September 12 and 13.
He will be meeting Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in the afternoon. Talks are expected to focus on enhancing cooperation in a range of areas, including defence, energy, technology, pharmaceuticals and people-to-people exchanges.
"Warmly welcome President Vladimir Putin of Russia for the 18th BRICS Summit. He was received by MoS K V Singh at the airport. India and Russia share multifaceted and longstanding ties anchored in Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership," Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said in a post on X.
This is Putin's first in-person participation at a BRICS Summit held outside Russia since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Later in the evening, Modi will also be holding a bilateral talk with Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian.
Welcome to our coverage
Hello! This is Midhat from the New Delhi bureau, bringing you the biggest headlines emerging from across India.
With just one day to go before the BRICS Summit kicks off, Delhi is all geared up and welcoming the dignitaries — several of whom have already arrived in the capital, including Russian President Vladimir Putin.
From Friday onwards, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi will be holding bilateral talks with several leaders, including China's Xi Jinping, Iran's Masoud Pezeshkian and Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.
Security in the capital has been intensified with thousands of personnel deployed. All schools in Delhi, including government, and private schools will remain closed on September 11 due to the BRICS Summit.
Commuters in Delhi will see traffic restrictions and diversions over the bext three days. Authorities have advised travelers to plan journeys and use the Metro where possible.
Stay tuned as we bring you more on the BRICS Summit and everything else making a buzz in the country.

Canada announces new aid for Ukraine to strengthen energy infrastructure ahead of winter
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:16:31 EEST
17:16:31 KST

Canada has announced new support to help Ukraine repair and strengthen its energy infrastructure ahead of another winter under Russian attacks.
The announcements came during President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's visit to Canada and his meeting with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.
According to the Canadian prime minister's office, Canada will provide the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development with new credit guarantees worth nearly CAD 435 million to support energy security, including winter gas purchases and secondary power generators for electricity production during shortages.
Canada is allocating CAD 200 million in concessional loans through Export Development Canada to support Ukraine's reconstruction. The prime minister's office said this will help Ukraine repair critical infrastructure while giving Canadian companies the opportunity to support critical projects.
The support package also includes an additional CAD 10 million for the Energy Support Fund for Ukraine, bringing the total to $100 million, to support Ukraine's energy infrastructure, including the procurement and delivery of critical energy equipment to strengthen Ukrainians' resilience to energy shocks.
In addition, Canada announced CAD 2 million for the International Energy Agency's (IEA) Joint Working Programme to support the development of Ukraine's energy resources. This funding will strengthen Ukraine's energy resilience, provide regulatory support, and advance clean energy projects.

IEA further cuts Russian oil output forecasts on Ukrainian attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

17:16:03 KST

IEA further cuts Russian oil output forecasts on Ukrainian attacks
MOSCOW, Sept 11 - The International Energy Agency said on Friday it again revised down the outlook for Russia's oil production due to ongoing Ukrainian drone attacks on energy infrastructure.
Crude output in Russia, the world's third-largest oil producer, has been declining amid Ukraine's strikes on the country's energy infrastructure, including oil refineries.
The Paris-based IEA said in its monthly review that Russia's crude forecast was cut by 125,000 barrels per day to 8.7 million bpd in 2026 and by 235,000 bpd in 2027, when it is expected to average 8.6 million bpd.
A government draft forecast seen by Reuters last week showed Russia had downgraded the oil output outlook for this year to a 17-year low and revised the fuel exports outlook for 2026 and 2027 due to the conflict with Ukraine.
According to the IEA, Russia's oil production declined last month by 200,000 barrels per day from July to 8.36 million bpd.
That is a steep 940,000 bpd lower than the January 2026 peak of 9.3 million bpd and 695,000 bpd below year-ago levels, the IEA said.
Russia stopped publishing data on oil output in April 2023, a little more than a year after the start of the conflict in Ukraine.
The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries said on Thursday that Russia's oil production declined by 160,000 bpd in August from July to 8.718 million bpd. REUTERS

Australia sees record share of workers holding multiple jobs
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:14:16 CST
17:14:16 KST

CANBERRA, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- The number of Australians working more than one job reached 1 million in June 2026, accounting for a record 6.9 percent of employed people, official data showed on Friday.
The number of multiple job-holders increased 6.6 percent from 984,200 in March, while 14.1 million people held a single job, according to data released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).
Women were more likely than men to work multiple jobs, with 7.7 percent of employed women holding more than one job, compared with 6.2 percent of men, the ABS said.
Workers aged 20-24 had the highest rate of multiple job-holding at 11.2 percent, while only 3.1 percent of employed people aged 65 and over held multiple jobs, statistics showed.
The multiple job-holding rate remained between 5 and 6 percent from 1994 to 2019 before falling sharply during the COVID-19 pandemic, the department said, adding that it has since risen to a record 6.9 percent and remained at or above 6.4 percent since June 2022.
In March, multiple job-holders worked an average of 39.3 hours per week across their jobs, compared with 34.8 hours for single job-holders, it said, adding that multiple job-holding was more common in regional areas than capital cities. ■

Column: BRICS, a path toward a more equitable, multipolar world
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:13:50 CST
17:13:50 KST

by Dr. Diaa Helmy
The world today faces growing economic, political and trade challenges amid rising unilateralism and protectionism. In this context, I believe BRICS, especially following its expansion into "BRICS Plus," has become an important platform for building a more equitable and multipolar world.
The past decades have shown that hegemony and unilateralism often fuel conflicts and tensions rather than promote stability and development. It is against this backdrop that the concept of "a shared future for humanity" takes on particular significance, emphasizing cooperation and mutual benefit as a basis for building a more equitable global order.
BRICS was initially formed by Brazil, Russia, India and China, later expanding with the addition of South Africa and, subsequently, new members including Egypt in early 2024. This expansion has strengthened Global South representation and increased the grouping's economic and political weight.
BRICS EXPANSION BOOSTS GLOBAL SOUTH VOICE
BRICS expansion gives Global South countries greater space to express their interests and opens new avenues for economic, technological, industrial and cultural cooperation. Today, BRICS countries account for around half of the world's population, representing nearly half of global consumers and consumer markets, giving the grouping considerable economic weight.
The geographical and demographic diversity of BRICS countries, along with their natural resources, is a source of strength and an opportunity for greater integration.
At the same time, BRICS is not directed against any particular country, currency or party; it aims to support member states' legitimate rights to development, progress and prosperity within a more equitable and balanced framework for international cooperation.
This approach is particularly relevant as global trade faces growing challenges from unilateral tariffs and excessive protectionism. In my view, high tariffs can harm not only the targeted country but also the country imposing them, by pushing markets toward alternatives and restricting free trade.
China's opening-up policy offers certainty to the world economy. China not only exports its products but also opens its market to products from other countries. For instance, the China International Import Expo in Shanghai provides developing countries and those of the Global South with access to the Chinese market and new trade opportunities.
BRICS can build on this approach by expanding trade among its members, increasing exchanges of technology, information and expertise.
EGYPT, CHINA AND BRICS: A PARTNERSHIP IN ACTION
For Egypt, joining BRICS represents an important opportunity to expand cooperation in the economic, trade, industrial, cultural and political spheres, creating greater opportunities for trade, technology transfer and investment with other member states.
China is a leading example of this cooperation. Egypt-China trade reached about 20.79 billion U.S. dollars in 2025, while cumulative Chinese investment in Egypt has exceeded 10 billion dollars, alongside thousands of jobs created for Egyptian youth by Chinese projects.
These figures reflect not only growth in economic relations but also a qualitative shift in cooperation, particularly in technology transfer and industrial localization. Supported by the political will of the two countries' leaderships, the Egypt-China comprehensive strategic partnership has helped transfer technology and expertise and support Egypt's efforts to localize industry.
The Belt and Road Initiative proposed by China is, in my view, one of the most important initiatives of the 21st century. Its scope extends beyond economics to trade, culture, tourism and civilizational exchanges. Similarly, the Shanghai-based New Development Bank supports BRICS countries through a financial framework based on mutual respect and national sovereignty.
Egypt has further opportunities to benefit from cooperation with China and other BRICS countries, particularly in manufacturing and exports. Its strategic location and access to African and Arab markets could enable it to become a base for joint production and exports.
BRICS will undoubtedly face challenges and pressures, especially from parties that view the grouping's growing strength as a threat to their interests. I believe greater cooperation among member states is the best way to strengthen the grouping's ability to withstand such pressures and challenges.
What is needed is to expand trade and investment among BRICS countries, organize regular joint economic exhibitions and conferences, encourage exchanges of experts and information, and turn ideas into projects with tangible benefits for people.
The strength of BRICS lies in its ability to offer a model of integration instead of conflict, and cooperation instead of hegemony. In a world of growing uncertainty, I believe greater cooperation is the most realistic path. Egypt and China, with their shared will and vision, can play an important role in advancing this course.
Editor's note: Diaa Helmy is the founder and secretary-general of the Egyptian-Chinese Chamber of Commerce in Cairo, a member of the Asia Committee at the Egyptian Council for Foreign Affairs, and a member of the Egyptian-Chinese Friendship Association in Cairo.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect those of Xinhua News Agency.
