S. Korea's fiscal deficit narrows to 5-year low through July on solid tax revenues
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:13:47 CST
17:13:47 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's fiscal deficit through July narrowed to a five-year low, driven by solid tax revenues, government data showed Friday.
The consolidated fiscal balance, or gross revenue minus gross expenditure, posted a deficit of 20.1 trillion won (14.9 billion U.S. dollars) in the January-July period, down from a deficit of 57.5 trillion won tallied in the same period of last year, according to the Ministry of Planning and Budget.
The managed fiscal balance, which excludes social security funds to offer a more precise picture of the fiscal health, recorded a deficit of 64.8 trillion won in the first seven months of 2026, marking the smallest cumulative deficit for the period since 2021.
Gross revenue, including tax and non-tax revenues, jumped 71.1 trillion won from a year earlier to 456.1 trillion won in the seven-month period.
Tax revenue served as the primary driver, surging 41.4 trillion won to 274.0 trillion won.
Income tax collections expanded by 12.2 trillion won, fueled by higher earned income tax from performance bonuses and increased capital gains tax from rebounding real estate transactions.
Corporate tax grew by 4.4 trillion won on improved corporate earnings, and value-added tax advanced by 8.1 trillion won due to growth in private consumption and imports.
Securities transaction tax mounted by 6.4 trillion won on the back of higher stock trading volume.
Gross expenditure through July reached 476.2 trillion won, up from 442.5 trillion won logged a year earlier.
As a result of cumulative fiscal spending, central government debt stood at 1,354.2 trillion won at the end of July, up 15.7 trillion won from a month earlier. ■

Saudi-backed Yemen forces face second setback this year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
08:13:47 UTC
17:13:47 KST

- A Southern Transitional Council offensive briefly seized roughly half of Yemen in December 2025 before collapsing by January 9, 2026.
- Saudi Arabia has scaled back, not abandoned, its Neom megaproject in 2026 amid budget pressure and a broader Vision 2030 review.
The Houthi seizure of Mocha this week lands on top of a difficult year for Saudi Arabia’s position in Yemen, one that already saw its allied government nearly collapse under a separate rebellion months earlier.
A offensive by the UAE-backed Southern Transitional Council swept across southern Yemen in December 2025, briefly seizing roughly half the country’s territory before a Saudi-backed counteroffensive reversed those gains and the group announced its own dissolution on January 9, 2026.
That earlier crisis pitted two of the internationally recognized government’s own backers against each other. STC forces, drawing on support from the United Arab Emirates, took the oil-producing Hadramawt and al-Mahra governorates from Saudi-aligned units in a matter of days, driving toward Aden before Saudi airstrikes and a government counteroffensive pushed them back. STC leader Aidarus al-Zoubaidi was removed from Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council on charges of treason and fled to the UAE as his forces’ resistance collapsed.
French Middle East analyst Clément Molin, writing on social media, described the STC’s December offensive as an early warning sign for Saudi-backed forces in Yemen and argued that this week’s fall of Mocha extends a run of setbacks for Riyadh in 2026. Molin’s characterization is his own assessment rather than an official one, and it comes alongside broader claims about Saudi Arabia’s finances and its posture toward Iran that carry more nuance than a single social media post can capture.
One part of that picture is well documented: Saudi Arabia has scaled back its flagship Neom megacity project this year, not abandoned it as some social media commentary has suggested. The Financial Times reported in January that Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s office was preparing a significantly smaller and redesigned version of Neom after a year-long internal review found delays and cost overruns, with the project’s centerpiece, The Line, expected to be reworked well below its original 170 km (106 mile) design. Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund said in April that it had reshuffled Vision 2030 priorities toward artificial-intelligence investment and away from large-scale tourism spending.
Saudi Arabia has also weathered direct attacks tied to the wider war that began after U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28, 2026. Iran launched hundreds of missiles and drones at Saudi targets in the weeks that followed, striking the Ras Tanura oil refinery and damaging the U.S. embassy in Riyadh, among other sites; Saudi air defenses intercepted the large majority of the incoming fire. Whether Saudi Arabia struck back is less settled than Molin’s post suggests. At least one account of the conflict describes Saudi forces quietly hitting Iranian missile and drone-launch sites and Iranian-backed militias in Iraq in response, though Riyadh has not publicly confirmed any retaliatory strikes on Iranian territory. Molin also raised the possibility that the UAE could reassert itself in southern Yemen, pointing to continued pro-STC sentiment even after the group’s formal dissolution. That remains speculation rather than a documented plan; neither the UAE nor STC remnants have announced any renewed push since al-Zoubaidi’s departure in January.
Mocha’s fall does not reopen the STC-Saudi rift directly, since the fighting this week pitted the Houthis against the Saudi-backed government’s National Resistance Forces in the country’s northwest, far from the STC’s former territory in the south and east. But the two episodes, seven months apart, point to the same underlying problem for Riyadh: the coalition it has backed against the Houthis since 2015 has struggled to hold ground even when it is not the Houthis doing the attacking.

Southeast Asia growth resilient as AI boom offsets risks: Moody's

17:13:44 KST

SINGAPORE, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- Southeast Asia's economy has proved more resilient than expected this year, supported by an artificial intelligence (AI)-driven boom in exports and investment, although mounting external risks could weigh on the outlook, Moody's Analytics said on Thursday.
The AI boom is lifting the region unevenly, favoring economies that are more closely integrated into the global technology supply chain, the agency said in a note.
"Higher energy prices, evolving U.S. tariffs and soft domestic demand threatened to widen growth disparities, yet an AI-driven boom in exports and investment has kept the region on a firmer footing than headlines suggest," it said.
For ASEAN, Moody's September baseline projects growth to ease slightly to 4.8 percent this year and 4.6 percent in 2027, from 4.9 percent in 2025.
While the front-loading of orders seen last year has normalized, the AI boom continues to support growth, particularly through data center investment and electronics exports.
Moody's said most Southeast Asian economies are performing better than expected when comparing its January and September forecasts, with the AI boom accounting for much of the upward revisions.
However, the outlook faces increasing risks from elevated U.S. tariffs. Moody's expects effective U.S. tariff rates to remain high through 2028, with risks tilted towards further escalation.
"The carve-out for semiconductor chips is shielding major Southeast Asian tech exporters such as Singapore, Malaysia, and Vietnam from higher effective tariff rates, although this could soon land on the chopping block," it said. ■

Koizumi made the remarks at a press conference when asked about whether Japan should possess nuclear submarines, the report said.

However, the moves have drawn opposition in Japan. In July, several civic groups and relevant individuals issued a statement criticizing the plan, saying that Japan has long advocated the abolition of nuclear weapons and that the country's Atomic Energy Basic Act stipulates that the use of nuclear energy shall be limited to peaceful purposes. Possessing nuclear-powered submarines, they said, would amount to Japan denying its own longstanding position. ■

Across China: China-U.S. researchers rebuild extinct ancient horse in 3D
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:13:39 CST
17:13:39 KST

This undated file image provided by Jilin University in northeast China's Jilin Province shows a reconstructed 3D image of Equus ovodovi, an extinct ancient horse. (Jilin University/Handout via Xinhua)
CHANGCHUN, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- The year 2026 is the Year of the Horse in the Chinese zodiac, and scientists have welcomed a long-lost relative back to the horse family tree.
A China-U.S. research team has, for the first time, reconstructed the full appearance of an extinct ancient horse, known as Equus ovodovi, giving a face to a species that had puzzled scientists for over a century.
Jilin University in northeast China on Thursday unveiled a 3D image of the animal, a brown-furred creature about the size of a donkey. According to the university, using ancient DNA data and comparative anatomy, its bioarchaeology laboratory carried out the reconstruction in collaboration with U.S. company Evolutio LLC.
This joint work fills a gap in terms of what this animal looked like, and establishes a complete research chain from ancient DNA to visual reconstruction, the university told Xinhua.
The horse fossils, dating back roughly 40,000 years, were first found in a cave in southwestern Siberia in Russia. Initially, only broken jawbones and teeth were discovered, without a complete skull. Over the years, related fossils have also been unearthed in North America, Africa, Siberia and northeast China. However, because the bones were scattered fragments, the animal's true appearance had remained a mystery for more than a hundred years.
In 2022, Chinese researchers at Jilin University and Northwest A&F University in northwest China's Shaanxi Province successfully extracted high-quality gene data from the fossils. Building on that work, they worked with American researchers in 2026, comparing the fossil data with living species, such as the Asian wild donkey and domestic horse. They reconstructed the skeleton, built up muscle structure, and eventually recreated the animal's full appearance.
The study shows that the "returned horse" is a fourth independent lineage of the horse family tree, alongside horses, zebras and donkeys. It split off roughly 2.7 million to 2.3 million years ago. Genetically, it is more closely related to donkeys and zebras than to domestic horses. It noted that this horse survived into the Bronze Age before eventually going extinct.
Lead researcher Cai Dawei, at Jilin University in Jilin Province, said that gene data can only tell what this animal was and when it disappeared, but together with evidence from its bones and body shape "scientists can understand this extinct species as a complete organism, from its skeleton to its physical appearance."
Evolutio LLC said every stage of the workflow was grounded in verifiable scientific data, and the resulting model can be used for both research and science education.
The research team expects that the reconstruction will enable the public to gain an intuitive understanding of an extinct horse that once coexisted with humans. ■

Emma Bonino, Italy’s activist commissioner, dies at 78
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
08:11:49 UTC
17:11:49 KST

Indefatigable Italian rights activist and European heavyweight Emma Bonino died aged 78, her party Più Europa announced on Friday.
A former European commissioner and member of the European Parliament, Bonino held a series of senior positions at home, serving as lawmaker, senator and two-time minister, in a career that straddled Brussels and Rome.
For the EU, she was chief among the voices who helped establish the bloc as a defender of international human rights and became a passionate advocate for European federalism. For Italy, she was a radical liberal who refused to neatly fit into her country’s entrenched left-right divide, garnering respect across ideological lines without abandoning her activist roots.
Advertisement
“To me, power can be good or bad according to what you do with it,” Bonino said. “Power is having the responsibility to change things to the best of your abilities.”
Lifelong campaigner
Born in rural Piedmont, Bonino decided to dedicate her life to political activism after having an illegal abortion in 1974 — an experience that inspired her to join the feminist movement and launch civil-disobedience demonstrations.
Two years later, the then-28-year-old was elected to parliament as part of the libertarian-left Radical Party. Young, female and radical, she refused to adapt to her surroundings, using the hemicycle as a platform for campaigns to legalize abortion and divorce, ban nuclear power and secularize Italy.
Bonino quickly learned to leverage the bloc’s power dynamics, using her MEP status to take her human rights work global, and was repeatedly arrested while campaigning beyond the bloc’s borders.
Poland’s Communist regime briefly imprisoned her for participating in a pro-democracy demonstration in Warsaw in 1987, and she was detained in New York two years later for distributing sterile syringes to drug users in protest of America’s AIDS-prevention policies.
Advertisement
The combative commissioner
The complexity of politics in Rome propelled Bonino to global prominence.
Following Italy’s 1994 elections, the late center-right politician Silvio Berlusconi needed the Radical Party’s support to become prime minister. In exchange for the group’s backing, he agreed to nominate her as Italy’s European commissioner.
Bonino said she was initially “unhappy” with the appointment to what she considered “too much of a bureaucratic role.” She also regarded her portfolio — humanitarian aid, consumer policy and fisheries — as “crumbs.” But she soon warmed to the job, finding “the ideas that I supported on the street and as a militant can be better pursued on a transnational level.”
Bonino threw herself into aid work, traveling to conflict zones including the Balkans, Rwanda and Zaire to show the EU was actively confronting crises beyond its borders. Italian journalist Marco Zatterin, who served as her spokesperson in 1995, told POLITICO her hands-on approach and willingness to speak with “literally anyone” raised eyebrows in Brussels.
“She was nothing like the commissioners that had come before her,” he said. “The EU is disliked by most people because it often projects its status through bureaucratic norms that are removed from the world everyone else lives in, and she was the opposite of that.”
“Politicians tend to think of themselves as gods,” Zatterin noted, “but she was a listener.”
Advertisement
When Bonino spoke, however, she was direct and often unabashedly critical, taking aim at governments she believed were failing to respond to crises and capitals that continued doing business with dictatorships.
But her “straight talk” made her enemies across the bloc too, Zatterin said. It also became an issue when the EU found itself embroiled in the 1995 “Turbot War” with Canada, which saw Bonino accusing Ottawa of “piracy” after it seized a Spanish fishing trawler in international waters. It later came to light the European fleets Bonino was defending were overfishing and misreporting catches.
The commissioner’s critics also cheered when a 1998 fraud probe was launched into €2.4 million of fictitious humanitarian aid contracts awarded by the EU. Although investigators found no evidence of her involvement, Bonino’s time as commissioner still ended abruptly the following March, when Jacques Santer’s entire College resigned amid broader allegations of fraud and mismanagement surrounding France’s Édith Cresson.
But Bonino was swiftly able to resume her work, reelected to the Parliament just three months later.
The stateswoman
In her later years, Bonino expressed frustration with an EU that, she said,“such as it is, doesn’t work.”
She also called for progress toward a “political union” that would allow Europe to “become a big dog like China and the USA” — though she firmly rejected the idea of a “European super-state,” pressing for an EU with strength in limited competences.
Advertisement
Bonino eventually returned to Italian politics in 2006, serving as minister European affairs in Romano Prodi’s center-left government, before becoming senate vice president. Her willingness to work across the aisle made her an outlier in Rome, and paved the way for her appointment as foreign minister under then-Prime Minsiter Enrico Letta in 2013. It is also what had her under repeat consideration for the presidency.
The respect Bonino garnered throughout her career also forged unusual personal relationships, like her friendship with Pope Francis. Despite being ideologically opposed on issues like abortion, the two bonded over their shared support for migrants, with the pontiff hailing the fiercely anticlerical politician as an “example of freedom and resistance.”
Zatterin noted Bonino was always willing to work with governments of all ideological backgrounds, as she believed being in power gave her a better chance of advancing the causes she believed in.
“She was never an opportunist,” he said. “Her priorities were her causes.”
CORRECTION: An earlier version of this article misstated the number of times Emma Bonino held a ministerial position in Italy. She was a minister twice.

Emma Bonino, Italian politician who fought for abortion access, dies aged 78
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
08:11:03 UTC
17:11:03 KST

Emma Bonino, Italian politician who fought for abortion access, dies aged 78
ROME, Sept 11 - Emma Bonino's life in politics began with a crime. In 1974, at a time when abortion was illegal in Italy, she travelled to a clandestine clinic in Florence to terminate an unplanned pregnancy.
"Coming back by train at night, I decided that never, never, never again should anyone have to suffer this humiliation," she later recalled. A year later, determined to drag abortion out of the shadows, she handed herself in to the police, turning her private "offence" into a public act of defiance.
The arrest made headlines, fueling a campaign that eventually led to the legalisation of abortion in 1978. It also launched Bonino into parliament with the Radical Party, a small but relentless force for civil rights.
Direct and diminutive, Bonino was a passionate advocate for social justice and gender equality who deliberately courted controversy to advance her many causes at home and abroad.
"I have been fighting for rights all my life, warning people to defend them, because they don't last forever," she told state broadcaster Rai in 2024.
In a dynamic career spanning five decades, Bonino won repeated election to both the Italian and European parliaments and served as a foreign minister and European affairs minister in Rome. She was also a high-profile European Commissioner in Brussels.
She remained in frontline politics well into her 70s, overcoming lung cancer despite refusing to give up smoking.
Underscoring her high standing in Italy, and belying Roman Catholic disapproval of her stance on abortion, the then Pope Francis made an unusual trip outside the Vatican in November 2024 to visit her in her home after an acute health scare.
She died on Friday aged 78, her spokesperson said.
On Monday, Bonino was hospitalized in a serious condition, but was taken out of intensive care on Thursday and transferred to a private clinic.
BRINGING COLOUR TO A GREY BRUSSELS
Founded by Bonino's mentor, Marco Pannella, the Radical Party helped redraw Italian society, promoting an array of causes through acts of civil disobedience, hunger strikes and dozens of referendums.
Some battles they won, such as banning nuclear power. In other campaigns, including a push to legalise cannabis, they fell short.
To widespread surprise, Bonino was appointed to the European Commission in 1994, thanks to the backing of the then Italian Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi. There she took charge of a disparate group of dossiers that no-one else had claimed - fisheries, consumer policy and the European Community's humanitarian office.
She was the first woman ever to wear trousers at a meeting of the male-dominated Commission, and proved herself to be one of the most colourful politicians in an often grey Brussels.
Accomplished and confident before the television cameras, she quickly drew media interest by riding Spanish fishing boats on the high seas during the EU's "fish war" with Canada. Not one to mince her words, she accused Canada of piracy, which that country's government denied.
'I DO NOT THINK WOMEN ARE A CATEGORY'
In 1997 she was briefly detained by Taliban militia during a visit to Afghanistan after people in her party took pictures in a women's hospital - an offence under Taliban regulations.
She condemned the international community's silence over the fate of Afghan women under the Taliban but told Reuters in 1996 that she did not see herself as a traditional feminist.
"I do not want and I do not think that we women are a category," she said. "If we think we are a category to be protected, I think we will lose our fight."
After her stint in Brussels, she pursued a broad mix of causes, including the campaign against female genital mutilation, pension equality in Italy and migrant rights.
She also promoted closer integration across the European Union, founding the +Europa (More Europe) party in 2017.
While she herself regularly scored well in popularity polls, her new party fared poorly at the ballot box, failing to win any seats at the 2019 and 2024 European parliamentary elections, while picking up just two seats at the 2022 national polls.
Bonino, who was born in northwest Italy in 1948, never married and did not have children.
"I didn't have them out of choice," she told Io Donna magazine in a 2018 interview. "You need a lot of courage (to have children). With a child you need to say 'for ever'. I never managed that."
For more obituaries, click here. REUTERS

2026-09-11

17:09:33 KST

A major chemical plant in Russia’s Perm region was reportedly targeted by Ukrainian drones on the morning of Sept. 11, with footage appearing to show a drone diving toward the facility.
The reported target was the Azot plant in Berezniki, owned by Russian chemical giant Uralchem and one of the country’s largest chemical-industry enterprises, according to Ukrainian monitoring channels citing footage from local residents.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The reports could not be independently verified, and Russian authorities had not publicly confirmed a strike on the plant at the time of publication.
Several videos circulating online appear to show a drone approaching the industrial site. Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova reported gunfire and a column of smoke “in the area of the chemical plant.”
Residents in local online groups also reported repeated explosions and drones flying over the city.
“Something has been flying into Berezniki all day, since this morning. They’re flying right over our heads,” one resident wrote.
Classes canceled as drone alert hits Perm
The reported attack prompted a “drone threat” alert across Perm region.
Several universities and colleges reportedly canceled classes and evacuated students, including Perm State University, Perm Polytechnic University, Oniks, and the Perm Institute of Railway Transport.
Russian authorities had not reported casualties or confirmed damage to the Azot plant.
Russia Hits Kyiv Gas Stations for Second Straight Day, 2 Killed
Azot produces ammonium nitrate, ammonia water, urea, nitric acid, and other chemicals, some of which are used in the production of explosives. It is also reportedly Russia’s only producer of sodium nitrate and crystalline sodium nitrite.
The plant was previously targeted by Ukrainian drones in October 2025. At the time, Perm Governor Dmitry Makhonin said the attack caused a “brief halt in the technological cycle” at Azot. Local residents reported several powerful explosions at the facility.
Part of wider Ukrainian drone campaign
The reported attack came amid a broader wave of overnight Ukrainian drone strikes against Russian industrial infrastructure.
In Saratov, a fire was reported at the Rosneft-owned Saratov Oil Refinery, while an Ozon logistics center also reportedly caught fire.
In Volgograd, regional authorities reported damage to an industrial facility and an apartment building, with two people hospitalized.
Ozon logistics hubs have increasingly been targeted since late August. Seven warehouses have reportedly been hit across Samara, Rostov, and Belgorod oblasts, Krasnodar Krai, Bashkortostan, and Dagestan.
The attacks also come as Ukraine continues to target Russia’s oil-refining sector. Ukrainian drones have struck Russian refineries at least 70 times since the beginning of 2026, according to Bloomberg, contributing to a sharp decline in refining output and growing gasoline shortages.
At least 17 Russian regions have introduced restrictions on fuel sales, while Russia has increasingly turned to imports from India, Morocco, Turkey, and Belarus to cover the shortfall.
The Russian defense ministry had not released a tally of intercepted drones from the latest wave, while Ukraine had not officially claimed responsibility for the reported attacks.

Anthropic warns of bids to use AI to build biological weapons
Experts urge stricter access to AI models as Anthropic reports rising misuse cases, including biological research risks.
Anthropic has disrupted several attempts to use its artificial intelligence models for research that could help develop biological weapons, the United States technology company has reported.
The firm listed the cases in a report issued on Thursday outlining misuse of its models, including the chatbot Claude, over the past eight months. Concern continues to rise over the potential dangers posed by AI development.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3AI researcher quits Anthropic saying AI race ‘could kill us all’
- list 2 of 3Anthropic discloses 4th AI hacking incident as researcher quits over safety
- list 3 of 3Anthropic claims Claude AI used for missile projects, global espionage
Anthropic said it could not determine whether the research was legitimate or malicious, as inquiry that leads to vaccines can also help engineer dangerous pathogens. The company said it erred on the side of caution.
In one case in May, a scientist sought help with a grant application to engineer mutations to chikungunya – a mosquito-borne virus similar to malaria – to make it more harmful in live animals.
Anthropic said the case was worrying in part because it could tell the work was intended for a military research institute. It banned the accounts involved.
“What we don’t know is if the research was meant to be weaponised,” Jacob Klein, Anthropic’s head of threat intelligence, told The New York Times.
Andrew Weber of the Council on Strategic Risks, who reviewed the report before its release, told the newspaper that access to such models should be limited to trusted researchers.
Anthropic said evaluations of its older models last year found they could not meaningfully assist dangerous biological research, but newer models can complete complex scientific work.
The same report set out bids to use Claude for missile projects and espionage. Two days before the report, a researcher quit Anthropic, saying the race to develop AI could wipe out humanity.
President Donald Trump late on Thursday dismissed the rising concerns regarding the technology.
Speaking to reporters, Trump said he is concerned that the US will be in a “very bad position” if it does not lead the AI race.
Asked if he has concerns that AI could lead to human extinction, he said: “No, I don’t have any.”

Greece reports record annual West Nile virus cases as death toll hits 30
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
08:06:19 UTC
17:06:19 KST

Greece has recorded 324 locally acquired West Nile virus cases this year, the highest annual total on record, with 30 deaths reported.
The figure surpassed the previous record of 317 cases in 2018, the daily Kathimerini reported on Thursday, citing data from the National Public Health Organization.
Authorities recorded 34 new cases and six additional deaths over the past week. Of the total cases this year, 217 involved complications affecting the central nervous system.
68 people remain in hospital, including 32 in intensive care.
Actual figure may be higher
The Attica region, which includes the capital Athens, accounted for 56.8 percent of reported exposures.
Health experts believe the actual number of infections is considerably higher, as fewer than one percent of those infected develop severe symptoms.
Despite widespread mosquito activity across Europe, Greek authorities believe the outbreak has already passed its peak.
West Nile virus is transmitted primarily through the bites of infected mosquitoes. People over 50 and those with weakened immune systems face a greater risk of severe illness.

Asian hornet sightings surge across Switzerland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
08:03:24 UTC
17:03:24 KST

Asian hornet sightings surge across Switzerland
The Asian hornet is continuing to spread across Switzerland, with the country's reporting platform receiving between 150 and 250 reports a day, its operators told the Keystone-ATS news agency.
“The Asian hornet is one of the most invasive species Switzerland has ever seen,” says Carine Vogel, a biologist responsible for processing reports on the frelonasiatique.ch platform.
But it is not yet possible to present a full overview for 2026, as “we are in the middle of hornet season”. A large proportion of the reports submitted via the platform turn out to be Asian hornets after verification.
As in recent years, cantons Vaud and Geneva are heavily affected areas. But other cantons, such as Jura, the two Basel cantons, Aargau, Solothurn and Bern, are increasingly being impacted, according to Vogel.
It is still too early to assess the impact of this summer’s heatwave on the species. Vogel points out, however, that the Asian hornet “does not particularly suffer from the heat”, as it has been adapting for several years in the south of France, Spain and Portugal.
“What will be interesting to find out is whether the summer of 2026 had a negative impact on our native species,” the biologist adds.
More
Can the spread of invasive quagga mussels be stopped in Switzerland?
Hornets fitted with radio transmitters
This invasive insect species feeds mainly on honeybees and other insects. For this reason, sometimes considerable efforts are made to locate the nests of this invasive species. Among those involved in the fight against this species is the Geneva-based beekeeper Kévin Golay, co-founder of the Pollinea Action association.
To search for Asian hornet nests, Kévin Golay and his team use telemetry: they capture the hornets one by one and fit them with radio transmitters. When the insects return to their nest, it is possible to track the signal and locate the nest. This method is essential as the nests are often perched high up in trees and hidden by foliage.
“Once the nest has been pinpointed, our investigative work is complete and the specialists responsible for its removal can take over,” explains Golay.

Former China ambassador warns Beijing is becoming 'smug' and closed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
08:01:45 UTC
17:01:45 KST

Former China ambassador says Coalition 'delighted' in Beijing's coercion
In short:
The former Morrison government's response to Beijing's coercion has been criticised by a former Australian ambassador to China.
Graham Fletcher says some Coalition MPs seemed "almost delighted" in being targeted in a podcast hosted by an Australian National University academic.
He was Australia's ambassador in Beijing from 2019 to 2023.
A former ambassador to China has sharply critiqued elements of the Morrison government's response to Beijing's coercion, saying some in the Coalition "almost delighted" in being targeted and "paraded" the famous list of 14 grievances handed over by Chinese diplomats.
Graham Fletcher has also delivered a blunt critique of China's direction under President Xi Jinping, saying it is increasingly "smug" and closed off to new ideas, while warning that ideological fixations risk sapping the country's entrepreneurial drive.
Mr Fletcher is one of Australia's most experienced China hands and was ambassador in Beijing from 2019 to 2023, a period which spanned both the collapse of bilateral ties in 2020-21 and the relationship's "stabilisation" after Labor's 2022 election victory.
Beijing responded furiously when the then-foreign minister Marise Payne called for an international inquiry into the origin of the COVID-19 pandemic, cutting off all contact with Morrison government ministers and imposing tariffs and trade barriers on Australian exports worth billions.
At the height of the dispute, Chinese embassy officials handed a list of "14 grievances" to an Australian journalist, complaining about blocks on Chinese investments, government funding for think tanks criticising China, new laws targeting foreign interference in Australia and a host of other issues.
Mr Fletcher told the Australia in the World podcast, hosted by Australian National University academic Darren Lim, that China kicked on "own goal" by issuing the demands.
"It was like a free kick for us to say, 'Don't be silly; you're asking us to change who we are,'" he said.
"That won't happen, and that's unreasonable."
But he also said it was not a formal list of demands from the Chinese government, and that they were "overplayed" by Australian commentators and politicians who revelled in the conflict rather than seeking a diplomatic resolution.
"There was a sense in which some in the previous government almost delighted [in] being the victim, or at least paraded it,"
"And my view was: well, we are where we are. And I would prefer we're not but now that we are, let's not stay here.
"And let's not keep digging ourselves further."
Mr Fletcher did not name Scott Morrison but appeared to take aim at the former prime minister, who repeatedly showed other world leaders a copy of the 14 demands at bilateral and multilateral meetings overseas.
"I heard one of our government members laminated the list and would give it to people when that person was overseas," he said.
"That digs you in deeper to where you don't really want to stay."
Mr Fletcher said the ALP's election in 2022 created a circuit breaker, allowing both sides to reset the relationship without losing face.
He said that required compromise on both sides, including in Australia.
"There were people on our side who wanted to win, that wanted China to be shamed, embarrassed, defeated," he told the podcast.
"For them to admit, and apologise. Just like China wanted us to [apologise] — it's just not going to happen!"
The former ambassador also reflected on the increasingly authoritarian political climate in China, suggesting that the government's ideological fixations were damaging its prospects.
"They're kind of locking themselves into a fairly narrow channel of thought when it comes to development and the political conditions, and certainly their society," he said.
Mr Fletcher said when he first served in China in the 1980s, while the country was opening up its economy, Chinese officials were "very much open to new ideas" and keen to talk to outsiders.
He contrasted that to the current political moment in China, telling the podcast that Xi Jinping's fixation on ideological control and state control over the economy "comes at a cost".
"That satisfaction, or smugness even, in terms of their own progress — which has been remarkable — leads them to be a bit too satisfied with the status quo," he said.
"Most thoughtful observers of China would recommend that they continue to challenge their own assumptions … they could be doing a lot better, if only they were prepared to be more open in their own minds."
Mr Fletcher said while there was still dynamism and energy in Chinese society and the economy, the ideological rigidity was also becoming a "drag on their system and growth".
"That's the downside of so much emphasis on propaganda and ideology is that it boxes people in," he said.
"Officials and state-owned enterprises and private entrepreneurs are more risk averse because they can see the downside of getting out of line."

Hong Kong court hands stiff jail sentences to Tiananmen vigil activists
Convictions came under the draconian national security law that Beijing imposed on Hong Kong in 2020 following huge pro-democracy protests.
A Hong Kong court has sentenced three activists to five to seven years in prison for their roles in organising a vigil marking the anniversary of the Tiananmen Square massacre.
Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, and Chow Hang-tung, 41, were both sentenced on Friday to seven years for inciting subversion. Albert Ho, 74, was sentenced to five years and two months, having pleaded guilty in January.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong pleads guilty in national security case
- list 2 of 4China’s support for Iran shows its limits as US ramps up pressure on Tehran
- list 3 of 4Why are Hong Kong’s Tiananmen vigil organisers facing prison?
- list 4 of 4Hong Kong court rules Dow Jones tried to stop journalist taking union role
The United Nations, rights groups, and foreign governments condemned the convictions under the draconian national security law that Beijing imposed on Hong Kong following huge pro-democracy protests in 2020, which has suppressed civil liberties in the city that previously enjoyed greater freedoms than in mainland China.
Judges highlighted that the defendants, part of a group that organised annual commemorations marking Beijing’s 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown on pro-democracy protesters, had breached the Chinese constitution by calling for an “end to one-party dictatorship”.
The verdict read that although the case did not involve violence, and the defendants had not put forward a timetable for that objective, their offence was still of “a serious nature”.
The court judgement added that the now-disbanded Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China faces a fine of 1.5 million Hong Kong dollars ($191,000).
Lee is the former chair of the Hong Kong Alliance. Chow is a former vice-chair. Both have been in custody since pleading not guilty in 2021.
Ho is another former chair of the vigil group and was a leading figure in the opposition Democratic Party. The sentences are expected to include time already served.
Public commemorations of the 1989 civil unrest used to be legal and tolerated in Hong Kong and were seen as a symbol of the city’s relative freedoms compared with mainland China.
However, they were outlawed in 2020 when the National Security Law came into force after mass protests in 2019, when the last vigil took place.
Lee’s wife Elizabeth Tang told the Reuters news agency that he would “definitely appeal” his sentence. Chow, a barrister who represented herself, told a hearing last month that she had “nothing to repent for”.
Taiwan’s government condemned the verdicts, saying that pursuing democracy and human rights is not a crime. Its China-policy-making Mainland Affairs Council said in a statement that authorities have “fabricated charges and conducted political trials in the name of national security to shield an authoritarian regime”.

Russia strikes 2 gas stations, kills 2, injures 5 in Kyiv during morning rush hour

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
07:59:41 UTC
16:59:41 KST

'There might be nothing left tomorrow' — Russia ramps up attacks on Kyiv's gas stations
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Russian drones struck two gas stations in Kyiv on Sept. 11, killing two people and injuring 12 others, including a child, local authorities said.
An air raid siren sounded in the capital at around 9:10 a.m. local time. About half an hour later, explosions were heard across the city, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground.
Five people were hospitalized, while one was treated at the scene, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko. At 11:45 a.m. local time, Klitschko said two of the injured had died in hospital.
The number of people injured rose to 12 by around 3 p.m. local time, including a 12-year-old boy, the Kyiv City Military Administration (KMVA) said.
As of 3 p.m. local time, seven people remained hospitalized, according to the mayor.
One emergency responder was among the injured in the Russian attacks on the gas stations, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said.
Klitschko said Russian drones struck gas stations in the Dniprovskyi and Obolonskyi districts, with debris damaging a car in the latter. The KMVA later clarified that Russia carried out a double-tap attack on the gas station in the Obolonskyi district.
The recent Russian attacks have raised concerns among Kyiv residents and commercial gas station chains over the worsening security situation.
Artem, 25, a refueling technician who asked to be identified by his first name only, said the station previously closed only during "red-level" air raid alerts, which signal a potential missile attack. Following a series of strikes on the city, the station also began closing during "yellow-level" alerts on Sept. 11, which indicate a drone attack, he added.
Artem added that amid the recent attacks, customers have also started buying more fuel, filling their car tanks and storing additional gasoline in personal jerry cans.
"It's scary that there might be nothing left tomorrow," the refueling technician said.
Rita Shvets, a cook at a gas station operated by the national OKKO chain, told the Kyiv Independent that as Russian drone attacks on the capital have intensified, the company has strengthened its threat-monitoring system and alerts employees when they need to leave their workplaces for safety.
"We have time to run to the metro. If we don't, there's a basement nearby where we take shelter," Shvets said.
"I've been working (through the war) for four years now, so I've somehow adapted."
Valeriia, 32, a project manager at an American IT company who asked to be identified by her first name only, told the Kyiv Independent that the recent Russian attacks have made her more concerned about potential damage to her apartment and car. Refueling the car has also become more difficult in Kyiv.
"I'd rather avoid going to gas stations and shopping malls during air alerts. And now they're so often that probably should avoid it all the time," she said.
"I'd rather keep my tank full and avoid going (to gas stations) pretty often."
Russia has been expanding its campaign against Ukrainian gas stations. This summer, Russian forces deliberately targeted facilities in regions near the front line in the east and south, gradually expanding the geographic scope of their strikes to central and northern Ukraine.
Russia first struck a gas station in Kyiv on Sept. 10, with attacks on Sept. 11 bringing the number of damaged stations in the capital to three. All three are operated by state-owned Ukrnafta, Ukraine's largest oil and natural gas producer.
A new series of explosions was reported in the capital at around 12:30 p.m. local time during an ongoing Russian drone attack.
A Russian drone hit an office building in the Podilskyi district, damaging the building and starting a fire on the fourth floor, while a neighboring one-story non-residential building also caught fire, Klitschko said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky later said the building of Ukrainian mobile operator Kyivstar was damaged in the Russian daytime attack.
"Russia's escalation with jet-powered "shaheds" is gradually becoming increasingly terrorist in nature," Zelensky wrote on X.
"We cannot simply wait while Russia hones its repertoire of killing," Zelensky said. "Right now, maximum attention must be focused on protecting the skies, finding solutions to protect people, and scaling up countermeasures against Russian drones."
The Sept. 11 attacks came as Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski arrived at Kyiv's main train station. The exact agenda of his visit is not known, but it comes amid growing tensions between Poland and Ukraine.

All you need is a Beatles lyric, TU Delft researchers find
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
07:58:23 UTC
16:58:23 KST

All you need is a Beatles lyric, TU Delft researchers find
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Researchers at TU Delft have found Beatles lyrics and song titles in more than 3,000 titles of scientific articles, according to a new paper in the open-access journal PLOS One.
Gabriel Budel and Rob Kooij of TU Delft teamed up with Michiel Tjepkema, co-host of the Dutch Beatles podcast Fab4Cast, to look for the lyrics here, there and everywhere across the scientific disciplines.
They identified 2,237 exact references and 963 examples of creative wordplay in data from the academic database Scopus.
The most used songs were “The Long and Winding Road” (798 mentions), “With a Little Help from My Friends” (209) and “Here, There and Everywhere” (129). The most cited paper was “Attention is all you need”, the 2017 paper that introduced the architecture behind ChatGPT – and a play on “All You Need Is Love”.
According to Budel, it’s not all too much. “Some of these are genuinely brilliant. ‘The lung and winding road’ is a paper on long Covid that changes one vowel,” he said in a statement.
The undertaking was not a hard day’s night. The team used a large language model to identify the lyrics, but they couldn’t just let it be. “The three of us then went through every selected title by hand to determine if it really was a Beatles pun,” Budel said.
The group didn’t stop until they got enough. They also found lyrics from Michael Jackson and Elvis Presley, though far fewer than the Beatles.
The researchers weren’t all shook up by their findings. Pop culture references can help reach a wider audience and improve readability, they said.

Owners of dogs that died after receiving Russian vaccine Multikan-8 were offered payouts for dropped claims and silence
Vetbiokhim, the maker of the Russian vaccine Multikan-8, has drawn up settlement agreements with owners of dogs that died after being vaccinated with the drug, the news outlet Ostorozhno, Moskva reported, citing posts in private chats used by those affected.
The company is offering to reimburse verified expenses and pay separate compensation for emotional distress. Those affected say the payments range from 200,000-300,000 rubles.
Under the agreement, an owner whose dog died must waive any further claims against the company and keep the circumstances of the case and the compensation amount confidential. It also bars them from discussing what happened to their pet with the media, on social media, or in messaging apps without the company’s consent.
Vetbiokhim does not directly acknowledge any link between the vaccine and the animals’ deaths: the document instead refers to “the animal’s death, possibly following vaccination.” The authenticity of the published document has not been confirmed.
One of the largest chats for people affected by Multikan-8 was deleted from the Max messenger amid reports of Vetbiokhim’s settlement offer, the independent Russian media outlet Takie Dela reported. Dog owners had used the chat since mid-August to describe the aftermath of their pets’ vaccinations.
Vetbiokhim confirmed to the Russian business news outlet RBC that its agreements “on providing financial assistance to owners” of dogs that died include a confidentiality clause. The agreements vary individually in content, and the confidentiality provision reflects “standard legal practice,” a company representative said.
Reports of mass deaths among dogs vaccinated with the Russian-made vaccine Multikan-8 first surfaced in mid-August. At least 300 animals are known to have died. Their owners, among other things, asked deputies in the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, to look into what happened.
The manufacturer says its investigation into the deaths is ongoing. Some owners of the dogs that died linked the deaths to contamination of the Multikan-8 vaccine with the virus that causes Aujeszky’s disease (pseudorabies), though Vetbiokhim says its own research found no such contamination. The company recalled four batches of the Multikan vaccine after the first reports of dog deaths.
Imported veterinary drugs, including vaccines, disappeared from the Russian market after Western sanctions and corporate withdrawals followed Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Veterinary clinics now mostly carry Russian-made drugs.

European defense giant KNDS rolls out new heavy vehicle mobility kit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
07:54:38 UTC
16:54:38 KST

- KNDS Mobility launched Celeris 8x8, a modular mobility kit for armored vehicles up to 36 tonnes, at MSPO 2026 in Kielce, Poland.
- The 8x8 kit builds on Celeris 4x4, already used in Finland's SCATA MK1 armored personnel carrier and vehicle programs in four other countries.
KNDS Mobility unveiled Celeris 8×8, a new mobility kit for heavy wheeled combat vehicles, at the MSPO defense trade show in Kielce, Poland, on September 10, 2026.
The kit is not a finished vehicle. It is a complete set of engineered components, engine, transmission, axles, suspension and onboard electronics, that vehicle makers and armed forces can build a custom armored vehicle around, for platforms weighing up to 36 tonnes.
The 8×8 version extends a platform KNDS Mobility already sells in 4×4 form. That smaller Celeris kit has been picked for vehicle programs in five countries, according to the company, including Finland, where the domestic firm SCATA has used it as the mobility base for its MK1 armored personnel carrier.
KNDS Mobility was formerly known as Texelis Defense, a French mobility-systems specialist based in Limoges and Roanne. KNDS France completed its acquisition of the company on April 2, 2026, and renamed it KNDS Mobility. Before the deal, Texelis had already supplied chassis and mobility components for the French Army’s Serval troop carrier, Singapore’s Terrex 8×8 and Serbia’s Lazar 3 8×8, work that KNDS says gives the new unit’s engineering team direct experience across the 4×4 to 8×8 weight range.
KNDS says the kit-based approach lets a manufacturer skip years of chassis development and get a new, locally built vehicle to the field in as little as one year from the start of a program. The company says Celeris 8×8 can support both chassis-based and monocoque hull designs, opening it to infantry fighting vehicles, armored personnel carriers, amphibious variants and heavy logistics trucks.
KNDS has not named a customer for Celeris 8×8 or announced a signed contract built on the new kit. The company also has not disclosed pricing or a timeline for when the first vehicle using the platform might reach a customer.
KNDS, the parent company formed from the merger of France’s Nexter and Germany’s Krauss-Maffei Wegmann, employs close to 11,000 people and reported 4.4 billion euros (roughly $5.11 billion) in revenue in 2025. The company said its order backlog stood at 33.1 billion euros (roughly $38.4 billion) as of December 31, 2025, and that more than 40 armed forces use its equipment worldwide, including 24 in Europe.

ECHR declares application against Ukraine regarding Donetsk shelling inadmissible
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:54:03 EEST
16:54:03 KST

The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has declared inadmissible a complaint against Ukraine filed in connection with the destruction of the applicant's apartment in Donetsk during shelling on August 9, 2014.
The Court released the ruling on September 10, 2026. A three-judge committee unanimously declared the complaint inadmissible.
"The applicant, a resident of Donetsk, claimed that on August 9, 2014, artillery shelling by Ukrainian government forces destroyed the apartment she owned and lived in. In support of her claim, she provided copies of her passport, a certificate of inheritance, a certificate of ownership, a household register, a damage report, and photographs," said Margaryta Sokorenko, the Government Agent before the ECHR, in a Facebook post.
The applicant also lodged a complaint under Articles 6 § 1 and 13 of the Convention, claiming she was unable to exercise her rights due to the suspension of state institutions in eastern Ukraine—specifically courts, which had been relocated to Ukrainian government-controlled territory.
Furthermore, the woman claimed that the destruction of her property forced her to relocate. However, she did not specify exactly where she had moved, nor did she provide evidence of such relocation.
The ECHR dismissed all complaints on the grounds of non-exhaustion of domestic remedies, in accordance with Article 35 § 1 and 4 of the Convention.
The Court noted that the principle of subsidiarity entails an obligation for the applicant to first give national authorities the opportunity to examine the alleged violation. In this context, the ECHR referred to its previous rulings in the cases of A, B and C v. Ireland and Vučković and Others v. Serbia.
At the same time, the Court, citing the judgment in Ryashentseva and Others v. Ukraine of September 9, 2025, noted that Ukraine had established legal mechanisms and specialized units capable of investigating shelling incidents similar to the one described by the applicant.
Furthermore, the ECHR noted that the applicant had not applied to Ukrainian courts, even though—as documented—she regularly traveled from Donetsk to government-controlled territory, and the Court had previously acknowledged the accessibility and functioning of courts relocated from Donetsk. Moreover, upon receiving the complaint, Ukrainian investigative authorities initiated criminal proceedings on their own initiative; however, the applicant failed to cooperate with the investigation or provide materials that could have aided the inquiry.
"The Court’s conclusion: the alleged ineffectiveness of the investigation cannot be attributed to the State, as it stemmed primarily from the applicant’s own inaction—specifically, a lack of due diligence in her dealings with the authorities (mutatis mutandis, Bekoyeva and Others v. Georgia). Finally, the Court dismissed the complaint regarding forced displacement as unfounded," Sokorenko emphasized.
As Sokorenko noted, this judgment upholds the ECtHR’s established case law regarding the accessibility of relocated Ukrainian courts as a domestic legal remedy.
"Strasbourg sees what Ukraine is doing to ensure access to justice, even under unprecedented conditions. And it consistently acknowledges this," the ECHR Agent emphasized.

Taiwan orchestra pairs Korngold’s return to classical music with Prokofiev’s ‘Romeo and Juliet’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
07:53:00 UTC
16:53:00 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — From a composer’s return to classical music after a career in Hollywood to a tragic tale of star-crossed lovers, Taiwan’s National Symphony Orchestra will bring both stories to the stage this week.
Under the baton of music director Jun Markl, the orchestra will perform a program featuring works by Austrian composer Erich Wolfgang Korngold and Russian composer Sergei Prokofiev. The concerts will be held at the National Concert Hall in Taipei on Friday and Kaohsiung’s Weiwuying on Sunday.
The first half will feature violinist Paul Huang (黃俊文) performing Korngold’s “Violin Concerto in D major, Op. 35.” The second half will turn to Prokofiev’s “Romeo and Juliet” Suites No. 1 and No. 2, based on William Shakespeare’s famous tragedy.
Austrian-born Korngold fled to the US after the Nazis came to power in Europe, where he went on to build a successful career composing music for Hollywood films. He wrote original scores for 18 films, adapting the orchestral sound and romantic style of European classical music for the cinema.
Korngold’s success in Hollywood brought him two Oscars, but his return to concert music after World War II came at a difficult time. The romantic style that had defined his work had fallen out of favor in concert halls, and he died in 1957 believing that his music had been forgotten, according to the Society of Composers & Lyricists and BBC Music.
Korngold’s “Violin Concerto in D major,” which will be featured in this week’s concerts, marked his return to classical music. Markl said the piece may not be among Korngold’s best-known works, but is “one of the most beautiful pieces.” For violinist Huang, the concerto is less a symbol of a difficult era than “a magnificent beginning.”
The program then moves to Prokofiev’s “Romeo and Juliet.” Written in the 1930s, the ballet has become one of the composer’s best-known works and one of the major works of 20th-century classical music.
Prokofiev’s score brings the story’s drama to life through music, moving between the tenderness of the lovers and the conflict surrounding them. Its dramatic force has also allowed individual excerpts to stand on their own, according to Opera North.

Von Sandrart served in the German Bundeswehr for more than four decades. During his military career, he held various senior positions within NATO and German structures, including the commander’s position at one of the Bundeswehr’s main land formations, Germany’s 1st Panzer Division.

Lai calls for stronger Taiwan unmanned combat capabilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
07:52:03 UTC
16:52:03 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The government will continue investing in unmanned systems research, training, and combat capabilities as new technology rapidly reshapes modern warfare, President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) said Friday.
Speaking during a visit to the Army Unmanned Systems Training Command, Lai said drones can help troops gather information and carry out reconnaissance, surveillance, and precision strikes. He added that they can also improve military operations when linked with command systems and other units, CNA reported.
Lai said unmanned systems are important for strengthening defense resilience and asymmetric capabilities. He stressed, however, that advanced equipment can become effective combat power only when personnel know how to use it properly.
Troops must be able to operate drones and coordinate with other units on the battlefield, the president noted. Tactics must also be adjusted quickly as new countermeasures emerge, per CTEE.
Lai said the Army Unmanned Systems Training Command should go beyond training operators. It should turn battlefield experience, military needs, and new technology into tactics that can be used in actual operations.
He said the military must now move from building training capacity to testing operational combat capability. Success should be measured not only by the number of operators trained or flights completed, but also by whether troops can carry out missions in contested electronic environments.
Lai said procurement, training, doctrine, and testing must be developed together so new equipment can be integrated effectively with other military units and combat systems, per UDN.
The defense ministry is introducing emerging technologies through small-scale testing and troop use before expanding deployment, he said. The approach allows the military to identify problems, make adjustments, and improve systems through practical experience, per Economic Daily News.
The president also said the military should learn from recent overseas conflicts while developing unmanned-system tactics suited to local terrain, operating conditions, and defense needs. Repeated training, testing, and exercises will help build stronger unmanned combat capabilities, he added.

€1,000 Shot: Estonia Develops Tempterno CP260 Multi-Target Mini-Rocket
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
07:50:05 UTC
16:50:05 KST

Estonian company Tempterno Defence has developed the Tempterno CP260 multi-mission, multi-target unguided mini-rocket designed to destroy aerial and ground targets.
The new development was unveiled at the MSPO international defense exhibition in Poland, Militarnyi reports.
The about 1-kg munition has a maximum range of up to 2.5 km and an effective range of 200 to 500 meters. The developers cite its low cost per shot, at around €1,000, as one of its main advantages.
The rocket can be launched from multicopters, fixed-wing UAVs, ground launchers, or manually from the shoulder. The launcher for the missile is being developed by another Estonian company.
In its air defense configuration, the rocket uses a proximity fuze that detonates at a distance from the target, creating a cloud of tungsten pellets.
Естонська компанія Tempterno Defence розробила легку багатоцільову мініракету Tempterno CP260 pic.twitter.com/SYhBv6ZXJB
— Владислав (@Vladislav110528) September 10, 2026
For engaging ground targets, including personnel and vehicles, high-explosive, inflaming, and anti-armor warheads are being developed.
“Instead of simply using a kamikaze drone to destroy a single target, you can arm a UAV with rockets and destroy several targets in a single flight,” a Tempterno Defence representative said.
The missile is currently guided manually using a camera mounted on the launcher, but the developers are working to automate target detection and acquisition with artificial intelligence.
The company is already in contact with Ukrainian enterprises regarding cooperation on integrating warheads and software for automated target acquisition.
The rocket itself is already ready and undergoing test flights, while development and testing of the warhead lineup are expected to be completed by the end of this year or early next year.
As Militarnyi previously reported, the Estonian-Ukrainian company DoD Solution and Estonian company Defsecintel will develop joint systems for detecting and intercepting drones.
Also in December 2025, Latvia successfully tested a similar Estonian Mark 1 micro-missile designed to counter drones.

Lawmakers seek smart glasses ban in Zurich pools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
07:49:31 UTC
16:49:31 KST

Lawmakers seek smart glasses ban in Zurich pools
The Zurich government is set to examine a ban on so-called smart glasses in swimming pools and other public facilities following a cross-party motion aimed at preventing covert filming through cameras embedded in the eyewear.
Smart glasses are increasingly being misused, for example to film women at outdoor swimming pools without their knowledge or consent, members of Zurich’s cantonal parliament declared in a question published on Thursday.
In some cases, such recordings are even circulated on the internet. Covert filming and the circulation of such recordings constitute serious infringements of the personal rights of the individuals concerned.
Existing ban is not enough
In the view of the members of the cantonal council, the existing bans on photography and filming, as applied in some Zurich swimming pools, do not go far enough when it comes to smart glasses. Because the integrated cameras and microphones are barely recognisable, they argue that it is essential to ban such devices or prevent them from being brought onto the premises.
Members of the cantonal parliament have asked the government what steps it considers appropriate to introduce such a ban in indoor and outdoor swimming pools, saunas, gyms or similar facilities. They also ask whether such a ban could be extended to privately run but publicly accessible facilities such as fitness centres or nurseries.
Finally, they also ask whether a ban on the sale of such products would be appropriate. If so, the cantonal government should set out what options it sees for advocating for corresponding regulations at federal level.
Resistance in other regions too
Resistance to smart glasses is also growing in other towns and municipalities. In Bern, for example, a motion seeks to ban the wearing of such glasses in the city’s indoor and outdoor swimming pools. The ban on wearing and using smart glasses is to be enshrined in the city’s swimming regulations.
In Lucerne, Wil and Basel, parliamentary motions are calling for clear rules on smart glasses.

Social minister: Money leaking out of the healthcare system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
07:49:00 UTC
16:49:00 KST

Social minister: Money leaking out of the healthcare system
As the Estonian Health Insurance Fund seeks to balance its budget, it does not plan to cut the volume of medical care, but instead sees regional adjustments to services as the solution, said Minister of Social Affairs Karmen Joller.
Joller stressed that while technological development helps cut costs in the healthcare system, no additional money can be put into the system until the areas where funds are "leaking out" have been addressed and rejected using reserves to cover permanent costs.
According to Joller, the root problem with healthcare funding lies in inefficiencies and leaks in the current system.
"My message from the very beginning of my term has been that if we put more money into a system that has holes in it, allowing the money to flow out, then that money will not buy us better health, but something else," Joller said, explaining the system's shortcomings. She said there are losses under the current system that may not be apparent to people outside the medical sector.
"I am an expert and I understand that someone who does not work in healthcare cannot see the places where money simply leaks out of the system," Joller said, referring to fellow "Reporteritund" radio show guest and former social affairs minister Tanel Kiik (SDE).
Joller said the Estonian Health Insurance Fund's reserves should not be tapped to cover deficits or permanent expenses such as sustained pay increases for medical professionals. "The Health Insurance Fund's reserve is intended for times when, for example, unemployment rises, the economy declines in some way or there is a new pandemic," Joller said, explaining the reserve's actual purpose. "By its very nature, it is not appropriate to use the reserve for permanent costs, such as pay increases. That is not sustainable."
Kiik, for his part, expressed concern that leaving the reserves untouched could reduce access to medical care.
"There is, in fact, still an expectation within the sector for additional funding or at the very least that the Health Insurance Fund's existing reserves can be used both to ensure pay increases and to cover other healthcare costs," Kiik said, disagreeing with Joller.
Kiik warned that failing to put more money into the system would have direct consequences for patients: "If the Health Insurance Fund's supervisory board has now decided to move toward balancing the budget without doing so, then the inevitable question is what will have to give. /.../ If there is no additional capacity, diagnoses will be delayed and treatment will be delayed. Ultimately, that simply means even more expensive treatment and potentially additional costs in the social care sector and elsewhere," Kiik said.
Despite the need to optimize spending, Joller said reducing medical services is not the answer. "Experience around the world shows that cutting services can have very serious consequences, which is why the Health Insurance Fund's position is that services will remain unchanged," he said.
Instead, savings are being sought in areas where advances in medicine have reduced costs over time, including laboratory services where prices can now be lowered.
"Laboratory services have changed enormously over time, which is why laboratory service rates were cut and that alone saved €24 million," Joller said. She added that new technologies have significantly reduced laboratories' staffing needs over the decades, making it possible to lower prices.
The ministry is also reviewing hospital network funding models with the aim of linking the services purchased to the actual medical needs of each region.
"We are not simply taking services away. Instead, we are looking at what residents of a particular region need most — for example, people in Ida-Viru County have more respiratory problems, while Southeast Estonia may have other issues," Joller said, explaining the planned changes.
Joller added that in the future, hospital funding will be more closely tailored to local health needs.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski, Mari Peegel
Source: "Reporteritund"

Growth: France lags behind its European neighbours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
07:48:39 UTC
16:48:39 KST

It comes after France's national statistics office lowered its forecast for 2026 growth from 0.7% to 0.4% and warned that the French economy was "losing ground."
France's government has cut its forecast for economic growth in 2026 from 0.7% to 0.5%, as weak activity in the first half of the year weighs on the outlook.
Economy Minister Roland Lescure announced the downgrade on Friday after the French economy contracted by 0.2% in the first quarter and stagnated in the second, putting the nation increasingly at odds with some of its main European neighbours.
Germany, Italy, Spain, and the UK all recorded growth during the first two quarters of the year. Germany posted growth of 0.4% and 0.3%, Italy 0.3% and 0.2%, Spain 0.6% and 0.7%, and the UK 0.6% and 0.4%.
The new forecasts come a day after even more pessimistic projections from INSEE, the French statistics office. It lowered its forecast for 2026 growth from 0.7% to 0.4%, warning that the French economy was "losing ground."
Lescure nevertheless forecast growth of 1% in 2027. He added that he expected inflation to reach 2.1% in 2026 and 1.8% next year.
The downward revision makes the government’s budget equation more complicated. Weaker growth is likely to weigh more heavily on public finances, even though the government had set itself the goal of bringing the deficit down to 5% of GDP in 2026, from 5.1% in 2025. French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu had already admitted he was not "very optimistic" about hitting that target.
French economy 'stalled'
According to INSEE, "all the engines of domestic demand" are "stalled."
Household consumption remains weak and investment is falling, hit by a slowdown in public projects linked to the municipal electoral cycle.
The institute also highlights the impact of heatwaves, which are particularly severe for agriculture. For its part, the government estimates that, if nothing is done, climate change could shave 3.6% off French GDP by 2050.
INSEE also reports that the labour market is "more degraded than elsewhere in Europe," with rising unemployment and sluggish wage growth.
Deteriorating public finances are also limiting budgetary support for the economy.
Activity is nonetheless expected to pick up slightly in the second half of the year. INSEE is forecasting growth of 0.1% in the third quarter and 0.2% in the fourth. For the year as a whole, however, the expansion of the French economy would remain roughly three times weaker than that of its neighbours in the eurozone and the UK.
Rising inflation, falling purchasing power
Another piece of bad news for households is that inflation is expected to keep rising, reaching 2.9% at the end of the year, compared with 2.4% in August.
In this context, purchasing power is set to fall by 0.4% over the year as a whole, due in particular to the decline in paid employment and rising prices.
"A large share of households" is likely to be affected, according to INSEE.
Household consumption, traditionally a key driver of the French economy, would therefore grow by only 0.3% in 2026. Households are also expected to dip further into their savings, with the savings rate falling from 17.8% of gross income in 2025 to 17.3% this year.
Business investment, for its part, would fall by 0.3%, while household investment would drop by 1.3%.
INSEE nevertheless stresses that "some uncertainties remain," notably regarding the impact of heatwaves on activity in the third quarter and developments in the situation in the Middle East.

Croatia signs deal for 18 rocket launchers from South Korea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
07:46:51 UTC
16:46:51 KST

- Hanwha Aerospace signed a $478 million contract on September 10, 2026, to supply Croatia with 18 K239 Chunmoo rocket launchers.
- Croatia is the fourth European country to order Chunmoo, joining Poland, Estonia and Norway, with deliveries running through 2030.
South Korea’s Hanwha Aerospace signed a contract with Croatia’s Ministry of Defence on September 10, 2026, to supply 18 K239 Chunmoo multiple rocket launcher systems, the company’s first defense deal with Croatia.
The contract is worth 411.8 million euros (roughly $478 million).
The signing ceremony took place at the Office of the Prime Minister in Zagreb and drew senior officials from both governments: Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković, Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Ivan Anušić, South Korean National Defense Minister Ahn Gyu-back, Defense Acquisition Program Administration Minister Lee Yong-cheol, South Korean Ambassador to Croatia Lee Seung-bum, and Hanwha Aerospace’s Head of Business Operations Billy Boo-hwan Lee.
The deal covers 18 Chunmoo launchers along with ammunition carriers, fire-direction command vehicles and integrated logistics support. It also includes several types of precision-guided rockets for short-, medium- and long-range missions, plus training and lifecycle support. Deliveries are scheduled to run through 2030.
“Today’s signing marks the beginning of Hanwha Aerospace’s long-term defence partnership with Croatia,” said Billy Boo-hwan Lee, Head of Business Operations at Hanwha Aerospace. “We are honored that Chunmoo has been selected to support the modernization of the Croatian Armed Forces, and we look forward to delivering proven capabilities, reliable lifecycle support and enduring partnership for many years to come.”
“This is one of the largest investments in the equipment and modernization of the Croatian Armed Forces,” said Andrej Plenković, Prime Minister of the Republic of Croatia. “With the Chunmoo system, the Croatian Armed Forces acquire a new strategic capability for fast and precise action, with high-value targets at distances from approximately 30 to 300 kilometers.”
Chunmoo is an 8×8 wheeled rocket launcher that carries two rocket pods at a time and can fire different types of guided munitions depending on the target’s range. Its modular design lets buyers mix rocket types and link the launcher to their own command-and-control systems rather than adopting South Korea’s setup wholesale.
Croatia’s launchers will run on the Topaz battlefield management system built by Poland’s WB Group, the same system Poland uses to network its own Chunmoo fleet. Hanwha said the shared system will help Croatia’s launchers operate alongside other European Chunmoo users.
Croatia becomes the fourth European country to buy Chunmoo, following Poland, Estonia and Norway. Poland has ordered 290 launchers across two contracts, the largest Chunmoo order to date, while Norway signed a $922 million deal for 16 units in February 2026. Estonia bought an initial batch in October 2025 and added three more launchers in a follow-on order this past May. Hanwha has also committed $115.5 million to build a sustainment and repair center and an ammunition factory in Estonia, part of a broader push to build local industrial ties alongside its export sales.
Hanwha said it plans to launch a formal Chunmoo User Club in 2027, following a workshop for the system’s European operators held in Estonia on September 3.

Russian Forces Strike Pavlohrad, Leaving Four Dead and Over 60 Injured
At least four people were killed and 60 others were injured, including three children, following a strike by Russian forces on Pavlohrad in the Dnipropetrovsk region on September 10.
The attack on Pavlohrad occurred at approximately 4:25 p.m. using drones, according to the Office of the Prosecutor General of Ukraine. The strike caused damage to commercial pavilions and vehicles in the area, as reported by Deutsche Welle.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

The blast occurred at approximately 10:25 a.m., shortly after Ukraine's Air Force had issued a warning regarding a high-speed target heading toward the city.
The casualty count steadily climbed throughout the day as officials updated the initial reports, eventually confirming four fatalities and 21 injured individuals, with five men remaining in serious condition under medical care.

Ukraine Seals Off 1-Kilometer Strip Along Russia, Belarus Borders Under Special Regime
Ukraine has imposed a special border regime along a one-kilometer strip running the length of its state frontier with Russia and Belarus, barring free entry. Residence, movement, and any work unrelated to defense or border protection for the duration of martial law.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
This was announced on the government's official website on September 10, which confirmed that the measure had already entered into force and that border-protection agencies had begun implementing the new rules.
The government explained that the restrictions respond to "the need to resolve urgent issues related to strengthening the state's defense capability" amid Russia's continuing armed aggression and the possible use of Belarusian territory for reconnaissance and subversive activity. It emphasized that the limits are temporary and will apply exclusively during the martial law regime.
Within the designated zone, the resolution prohibits free entry, stay, residence, and movement of persons, as well as any work not connected to repelling armed aggression, defense, or the protection of the state border. The government noted that the restrictions extend to all land plots within the one-kilometer strip along the border.
Officials framed the measure as a response to risks, including the destabilization of the social and political situation in border regions and the creation of conditions that could threaten Ukraine's national interests. The government also cited the goal of avoiding danger to civilians in these areas and minimizing the risks of unauthorized presence along the frontier.
The restrictions build on measures introduced at the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion. On February 26, 2022, the Ukrainian government temporarily closed all border crossing points with Russia and Belarus after Russian forces attacked Ukraine from both countries, while allowing Ukrainian citizens to return home through the border.
This move fits a wider pattern of states hardening the frontier facing Russia and Belarus, while Finland has completed roughly 200 kilometers of new fencing along selected sections of its border with Russia. The project launched in 2023 at a cost of approximately $413 million.
The barrier comprises metal mesh, surveillance cameras, lighting, and loudspeakers, along with a dedicated patrol road.
The same border pressures have driven neighboring states to build physical defenses of their own. Lithuania has approved counter-mobility zones and engineering barriers along its frontiers with Belarus and Russia's Kaliningrad region, including a 20-meter-wide strip and the restoration of wetlands to slow the movement of heavy military equipment, with the measures phased in through the end of the decade.
