Mapping Narratives: What the UN Map Reveals About Symbolic Reparations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

This article is part of our new Opinion section, a format for argument-driven essays on critical questions shaping our field.
For centuries, most of the world has looked at itself through a 16th-century instrument of spatial representation. On September 4, the United Nations General Assembly voted to change that, adopting a resolution that asks governments, schools, media organizations, and technology companies to retire the Mercator projection wherever the relative size of countries actually matters, in favor of equal-area alternatives like the 2018 Equal Earth projection. The vote passed 164 to 1. The United States was the sole vote against.
The resolution, sponsored by Togo and backed by the African Union, is non-binding, and it leaves Mercator's actual function untouched: the projection remains, as it was designed to be in 1569, a reliable tool for maritime and aerial navigation. What the vote targets is its afterlife: the nearly two hundred years in which a map built to solve a navigation problem became the default image of the planet in classrooms, atlases, and now browser tabs.
The distortion itself is not in question. Mercator's projection is conformal: it preserves angles and shapes at the cost of area, which enlarges with distance from the equator. Greenland and Africa read as roughly equivalent on a Mercator map; Africa is actually about fourteen times larger. Alaska appears close to the size of Australia, which is four and a half times bigger. Put more legibly: the United States, China, India, Mexico, Japan, and most of Europe would fit inside Africa's outline, with room left over.
France broke from Mercator days before the vote, opting for the equal-area Eckert IV. Togo's government says it hopes to revise its school geography materials by the end of the year. On the other hand, the United States, through its UN representative, called the resolution a distraction from "genuine problems of international peace, prosperity, or good relations" and accused the body of pushing an "ideological agenda."
That a map — a fixture of classroom walls, atlases, and browser tabs, largely unquestioned for nearly five centuries — could produce this kind of disagreement at the United Nations is itself worth noting. Nobody at the General Assembly disputed the underlying geometry; equal-area projections are not a matter of interpretation. What was being contested was something else entirely.
Not the Territory
"The map is not the territory," the semanticist Alfred Korzybski wrote in 1931. Any representation, however useful, is always an abstraction, a reduction of something larger than itself. Jorge Luis Borges pushed the idea to its logical, absurd conclusion in the tale On Exactitude in Science: an empire's cartographers, striving for total accuracy, eventually produce a map the exact size of the empire itself, coinciding with it point for point. The map is useless. A perfect map, Borges suggests, is not a more truthful one — it is simply redundant. Representation only works by leaving things out.
What gets left out, and what gets kept, is never a neutral choice. Italo Calvino explored this idea in an essay written after visiting the 1980 exhibition Cartes et figures de la terre at the Centre Pompidou. Calvino's argument runs against the intuition that the aerial, top-down map, the one in every atlas, is the natural or original form of a map. The earliest maps were records of journeys: Roman itinerary scrolls, medieval strip maps, a seventeenth-century Japanese scroll charting the road from Tokyo to Kyoto in unbroken, ground-level detail. These are linear, embodied, built from the perspective of someone moving through space, one step at a time, closer to a narrative than to a diagram.
The god's-eye view came later, and it came from somewhere specific: Calvino notes that the representation of the globe only began once the coordinate system already used to map the heavens (poles, equator, meridians) was transposed onto the Earth. The map of the world, in other words, was never simply observed. It was inherited from the sky, and centered wherever its makers happened to stand.
That inheritance carries its own history of shrinking self-importance. Roman maps, Calvino writes, folded the known world into the outline of the Empire. However, by 1459, Fra Mauro's planisphere, informed by Marco Polo's travels and the first circumnavigations of Africa, already shows Europe visibly smaller against the rest of the world, and its cardinal points inverted: the reversal of scale matched by a reversal of orientation. Cartography, read this way, is not a story of objectivity. It is a negotiation over how much of the frame a civilization gets to occupy.
Gerardus Mercator entered that negotiation in 1569 to solve a problem that had nothing to do with size. His projection is conformal — it preserves angles and shapes — which meant a sailor could plot a straight compass course, a rhumb line, across an ocean and trust it. That was a genuine, difficult problem, and Mercator managed to solve it. But he understood the area distortion his method produced well enough to use, himself, a different, equal-area projection when he needed to compare landmasses rather than to navigate between them. The projection that would carry his name took nearly two more centuries to become fully usable at sea, once the marine chronometer solved the parallel problem of longitude. It took even longer, well into the nineteenth century, at the height of formal European empire, to become the default general-purpose map of the world, in atlases, classrooms, and eventually newsrooms — contexts for which it was never built and in which its distortions cost nothing to shape but a great deal to perception.
The British cartographer George Kellaway, in his book Map Projections (1946), described the consequence with precision. He declined to ascribe any "imperialistic motive" to Mercator or to the mapmakers who followed him, as the projection was not designed as propaganda. But its popularity, he argued, owed something real to the fact that it made the British Empire look considerably larger than it was, and by then several generations had grown up seeing that inflated scale as simply how the world looked. "For them", he wrote, "any other map is a distorted and meaningless hieroglyphic." A map built to solve a sailor's problem had become, for people who would never plot a course by it, the only image of the world that felt true.
Counter-Cartographies
If cartography has always been a negotiation over whose frame the world gets read through, it also holds the possibility to negotiate back — or to transgress its frame. In The Mapping Journey Project, the French-Moroccan artist Bouchra Khalili filmed eight people who had made clandestine migrations across the Mediterranean, each recounting their journey while tracing it, in real time, on a geopolitical map. The camera never leaves the map and the moving hand; there are no faces, no interviews, no casting. Khalili gave the participants the map itself and let them author their own account of crossing it. What results is not a documentary illustration of migration but a redrawing of the map's authority: the same paper that states where borders fall becomes, in a stranger's hand, the register of a route no border was built to permit. Memory here does not recount a closed past; it produces space, in the present, on the same surface the state uses to deny it.
Working from the opposite premise, Scottish-Nigerian architect and artist Dele Adeyemo doesn't overwrite the official map, but refuses its logic altogether. In The Cosmogony of (Racial) Capitalism, he juxtaposes the Cantino planisphere — an early-sixteenth-century Portuguese map that renders territory as something to be claimed and extracted — against spatial diagrams drawn from West African material culture, building what he calls a "trans-cosmological cosmogram." The contrast turns on a single shared symbol. In European cartography, a cross marks a point: a coordinate, a claim, a site of conquest. In the Yoruba cosmology Adeyemo draws on, a cross inside a circle marks something else entirely: the intersection of the material and immaterial worlds, reached not by measurement but through dance, divination, ritual movement.
It is not a more accurate map of the same territory. It is a different account of what territory is, one in which land was never reducible to a plotted coordinate in the first place — which is precisely what colonialism and capitalism needed it to become.
These artistic practices suggest that the corrective to a distorted map is not always a more accurate one. Sometimes it is a map that insists on being authored from below; sometimes it is the recognition that the grid itself was never the only way to hold space. Both are forms of the same refusal: to let territory remain something drawn from above, by others, on someone else's behalf. That refusal, however, doesn't only land in galleries. On September 4, it reached the UN General Assembly.
Size, Symbolically
What a map enlarges, it also elevates. Mercator's math was never in dispute, but its centuries-long run as the default image of the planet was never only mathematical: it consistently inflated the imperialist nations and compressed the colonized countries. Equal Earth projection performs a similar operation in reverse. Correct the distortion, and Africa, Latin America, and Southeast Asia grow, on the page, into something closer to their actual weight in the world. The countries that Mercator shrank are, with almost no exceptions, the countries the resolution enlarges.
Togo's foreign minister, Robert Dussey, was careful to frame the campaign as scientific rather than political. He is right: equal-area projections are settled cartography, not opinion. But the framing is also strategic: anchoring the correction in irrefutable math is precisely what makes its symbolic weight impossible to wave away as ideology. Jean-Noël Barrot, announcing France's own break from Mercator, said directly: "Changing the map obviously doesn't change the world. But correcting a representation that distorts it is already an act of truth." Moky Makura, of the advocacy group Africa No Filter, went further, framing the stakes as narrative rather than geometric: "If we got something as basic as Africa's size wrong for this long, what else about Africa have we simply accepted without questioning? Africa doesn't need to be made bigger. It needs to be seen accurately."
The United States' objection, read against this, is more revealing than it first appears. Yaryna Ferencevych accused the General Assembly of relitigating "map projects from the 16th Century" in the name of "reparations and 'cognitive justice.'" The remark was meant to dismiss the resolution as trivial. Instead, it names what's actually at stake: scale is being treated here as a question of justice, and nobody — not even the US — is disputing the math behind it.
But why does depicting the exploited countries and continents — the periphery of capitalism — in their actual size bother so much? There is a longer theoretical thread underneath this. Geography is never produced from a neutral vantage point; it is always read from somewhere, and that somewhere sits in a structural relation, of center and periphery, to everywhere else. In that framework, the periphery's condition is not simply a matter of scarcity or underdevelopment; it is a deprivation of the capacity to narrate one's own place in the world on equal terms. A map is one of the most literal instruments through which that narration happens or fails to happen. For nearly five hundred years, and more strongly in the last two centuries, that instrument told one story. Equal Earth tells a different one on purpose — not because the periphery has grown, but because, for the first time at this scale, an institution has agreed to draw it at the size it actually is.

Ukrainian companies increasingly integrating AI into missiles
Several Ukrainian companies are working on missile systems that use artificial intelligence, Brave1 CEO Andrii Hrytseniuk told Business Insider.

Details: According to Hrytseniuk, AI is now "increasingly being integrated into missile systems as well".
"...although this has not yet reached the scale of hundreds of solutions that we see in the drone sector, we are already seeing the first successes and many developments that are currently under way," the Brave1 chief said.
Ukrainian companies are already widely integrating artificial intelligence into drones and combat robots, including for decision-making, navigation and targeting.

Efforts to integrate AI into missiles appear to have intensified as Ukraine invests in developing long-range strike weapons, which are frequently used to attack military and energy facilities in Russia.
It is currently unclear exactly how Ukrainian companies are using artificial intelligence in missiles or how far the relevant developments have progressed. Brave1 said the technology would expand Ukraine's capabilities but would not remove humans from the process entirely.

- Ukrainska Pravda reported that the Ruta Block 2 missile, developed with support from Brave1, is undergoing flight testing in Ukraine. For the prospective Ruta Block 3, the developers say it will feature autonomous navigation in degraded GNSS environments and a terminal guidance system.

Singapore's ministers get a bump to already world-leading salaries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
07:28:46 UTC
16:28:46 KST

Singapore's famously well-paid politicians are getting a pay bump.
Prime Minister Lawrence Wong — who already had the highest official salary of any world leader — will have his annual remuneration package increase from $S2.2 million ($2.4 million) to $S3.6 million, including bonuses.
That's more than six times as much as Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.
So why are Singapore's pollies on such a good wicket and why are they now getting a raise?
Why are Singapore's politicians paid so much?
Singapore has historically paid its politicians and public servants well to attract the best and brightest — and discourage corruption.
The city state uses the median income of the top 1,000 Singaporean earners as a benchmark, as their qualities and abilities "reflect the desired calibre of the people whom Singapore needs for good government", Singapore's Public Service Division says on its website.
Gillian Koh, from the National University of Singapore's Institute of Policy Studies, said the ministerial pay benchmark was 40 per cent less than the private sector's to "reflect the commitment to public service which is maintained".
But she said the salaries were still high enough to curb corruption.
"Singapore's record on corruption is a consistently, incontrovertibly positive one," she said, pointing to the case of former minister S Iswaran — who was jailed for accepting hundreds of thousands of dollars in gifts — as the "exception that proved the rule".
However, it was unclear whether the low levels of corruption were due to the generous pay or tough enforcement, said Chong Ja Ian, a political scientist at the National University of Singapore.
"Cases of official corruption do exist among senior civil servants and politicians regardless of pay and enforcement, so the system is not foolproof,"
Dr Chong said Singapore's political remuneration system did have drawbacks.
Pegging political appointee salaries and bonuses to the private sector incomes fed a perception that public service was "transactional", he said.
"There is also an impression that political appointees in Singapore associate more with high levels of wealth than with ordinary people."
Performance bonuses
Under the new pay scale, an entry-level Singapore minister's salary will increase from $S1.1 million a year to up to $S1.8 million a year.
Sixty-five per cent of the salary is fixed, while the other 35 per cent will be dependent on personal performance and a "national bonus" related to things like GDP, national wages growth and unemployment.
Mr Wong said ministers would start with a one-off salary increase of up to 9 per cent, and go up incrementally rather than jump immediately to $S1.8 million.
By the end of this term of government, most entry-level ministers would earn about $S1.35 million and those who did well could "move higher", he said.
The salary package for the prime minister, president, speaker and deputy speaker would immediately be raised to the new benchmark and were not dependent on achieving personal performance goals, said Dr Koh.
Why the pay increase now?
Mr Wong made the announcement on Tuesday in line with a decision by an independent review committee, with the pay increase to take effect on October 15.
The last time the city-state's ministerial pay was amended was in 2012 when it was reduced, with the prime minister's going down by 36 per cent.
Still, the announcement this week has proven controversial in Singapore, where the median wage worker made $S5,775 a month last year.
"The sums involved are more than what most citizens earn, so I understand why Singaporeans scrutinise them closely and why many feel strongly about the matter," Mr Wong said.
Mr Wong said it would have been "easier politically" for him to leave things as they were but that "would not be the right thing to do" as salaries in the private sector, civil service, judicial service and public sector had increased since 2012.
He said he planned to donate his own pay top-up to charity for the next five years.
What are other world leaders paid?
According to data from non-profit PoliticalSalaries.com, the Hong Kong chief executive is the second-highest earner globally with $HK5,633,940 ($1,003,000) annually, followed by the Swiss president at 490,168 Swiss francs ($842,000).
US President Donald Trump earns $US400,000 ($559,000) while Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is on $622,100.
ABC/Reuters

Ukrainian hacker jailed in Switzerland over ransomware attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
07:26:56 UTC
16:26:56 KST

Ukrainian hacker jailed in Switzerland over ransomware attacks
A Ukrainian IT specialist was sentenced in Zurich to 12 years and nine months in prison and banned from Switzerland for ten years for his role in ransomware attacks on several firms, including Stadler Rail. Prosecutors put the damage at around CHF100 million ($123 million).
In its judgement handed down on Thursday, the Zurich District Court went further than the prosecution, which had sought a prison sentence of twelve years for the 52-year-old IT specialist. The man, who was living in canton Basel Country, has been in pre-trial detention since October 2021.
The court found that the defendant had played a key role in cyberattacks against companies such as Stadler Rail, Meier Tobler and Crealogix with the aim of extorting ransoms. He is regarded as the lead developer of the Lockergoga, Megacortex and Nefilim malware programmes, which were used to encrypt data belonging to the targeted companies.
More
Hackers demand millions in ransom for stolen Stadler Rail documents
During the attack on Stadler Rail, the defendant stole around 500 gigabytes of confidential data and threatened to publish it online. Stadler Rail refused to pay the ransom demanded. Other companies, however, accepted. In total, the losses incurred are estimated at CHF100 million.
Merely a “consultant”
The judge said the Ukrainian was not the mastermind behind the operations, but developed the malware and passed it on to instigators who remain unknown. These people then targeted companies in Switzerland and abroad and coordinated the extortion attempts.
More
Cyberattackers demand CHF10m from Swiss train maker Stadler
The defendant has consistently denied being aware of the criminal use of his software. He maintained that he had simply been working as a consultant for an unknown client in the field of IT security, which was why the source codes had been found at his home. But the court did not believe him as extortion messages were also found among his data.
Mysterious death in Moscow
During the trial in August, certain revelations by the prosecution caused a stir. The accused’s alleged instigator is said to have cooperated with the Russian secret services before dying after falling from a window in Moscow in November 2022. He was reportedly a Ukrainian hacker, for whom the United States had offered a bounty, who was using a false identity provided by the Russian intelligence services.
More
Up to 200 Swiss companies targeted by ransomware hacker group
The prosecutor had also linked these cyber-attacks to Russia’s strategy of sowing disorder in the West and causing economic damage. The interests of criminal hackers and state actors overlap in this regard. Moscow tolerates, or even encourages, such activities, he argued. But there is no evidence to suggest that the defendant himself had any direct links with the Russian secret services.
The defence lawyer called for his client’s full acquittal and compensation for wrongful detention. In his view, all the seized data storage media should be declared inadmissible, as the defendant had not been sufficiently informed, during the searches, of his right to have the data sealed.
The judgement is not final and may be subject to an appeal.

The U.S.-Ukrainian company Swarmer has entered into an agreement to acquire unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) manufacturer Ratel Robotics for up to $224 million.
The U.S. company said Swarmer will integrate Ratel’s line of combat ground drones with its own software for autonomous control of unmanned systems.
Ratel Robotics manufactures modular ground platforms for logistics, casualty evacuation, reconnaissance, mine clearance, and drone deployment.
Since the beginning of 2026, the company has signed contracts worth $86 million and accounted for approximately 37% of all unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) procurements for the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
Upon completion of the acquisition, more than 300 employees of the Ukrainian manufacturer will join Swarmer, while the company’s founder, Taras Ostapchuk, will remain as CEO.
The combined company plans to scale up UGV production and begin supplying the systems to NATO countries under the Build With Ukraine initiative.
Ratel Robotics announced the start of serial production of the modified NURSE TB20 UGV, designed to support infantry operations.

5G communication launched in Russia
Unknown

07:21:19 UTC
16:21:19 KST

MOSCOW, September 11. /TASS/. 5G communication has officially been launched in Russia on the instructions of President Vladimir Putin, the Ministry of Digital Development, Communications and Mass Media reported.
"5G technology is a comprehensive ecosystem designed for digital transformation of the economy. Its implementation will contribute not only to boosting mobile internet speeds," the ministry said.
This new communications standard can be used to control autonomous vehicles and robotic systems, to advance telemedicine, digitize industry, and serve other purposes.
The first stage involves 5G operation on frequencies previously assigned to operators for the LTE standard. Telecom companies have also received the 4.63-4.99 GHz frequency band for the fifth-generation standard. The band was allocated free of charge and in equal shares.
"[This] makes it possible to maintain a high level of competition and guarantee affordable tariffs," the ministry noted.

S. Korea's ex-president Yoon acquitted of harboring suspect
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:20:19 CST
16:20:19 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's former President Yoon Suk-yeol was acquitted of abusing his presidential power to harbor a criminal suspect, according to Yonhap news agency on Friday.
The Seoul Central District Court delivered the verdict, ruling that it cannot be definitively concluded that there was an intent to obstruct the investigations into a marine's death.
The team of independent counsel Lee Myeong-hyeon, who led investigations into the marine's death, sought a five-year prison term on charges of aiding the criminal suspect's flight and abusing presidential power.
Yoon was accused of ordering the appointment of former Defense Minister Lee Jong-sup as ambassador to Australia to help him flee the country in November 2023, about four months after the marine's death.
The special counsel team alleged that Yoon helped Lee, a primary suspect at the time, flee the country through the appointment to cover up the marine's death.
The court handed down blanket acquittals for several former top-ranking officials involved in lifting Lee's travel ban and fast-tracking his appointment.
Yoon was sentenced to life in prison in February for the insurrection stemming from his martial law declaration and 30 years in prison in June for the general treason relevant to the infiltration of drones into the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.
The emergency martial law was declared by Yoon on the night of Dec. 3, 2024, but it was revoked hours later by the National Assembly.
He was indicted under detention in January 2025 as a suspected ringleader of the insurrection, becoming the first sitting president to be arrested and indicted. ■

China looks to AI to sharpen software sector's competitive edge
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:19:56 CST
16:19:56 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- China has unveiled a dedicated action plan to accelerate the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into its software and information technology services industry, aiming to reshape the sector's core competitiveness.
The plan, released by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, sets out a two-stage roadmap.
By 2028, China aims to significantly raise the intelligence level of its software industry, by cultivating high-standard coding tools and development platforms, and extending their use to more than 20,000 major software enterprises.
Meanwhile, the plan also calls for building 100 benchmark applications for agent-based software across key industries and incubating at least five high-quality open-source projects.
The plan envisions a step-change in the integration of AI with the software sector, with full intelligent upgrades across critical software systems by 2030. AI-powered programming, agent software and intelligent services are expected to emerge as new growth engines, supported by internationally competitive open-source communities and industrial clusters.
Currently, AI is fundamentally transforming how software is developed, what products look like and how services are delivered, making it the core engine driving industrial upgrading.
The action plan is the latest in a series of policy moves as China races to embed AI across its economy.
The government work report has deployed the "AI Plus" initiative for three consecutive years, and this year in particular called for "creating new forms of smart economy" for the first time.
AI has evolved from a supporting tool into a core engine of economic transformation, one that will systematically reshape the foundations of how the economy operates, analysts said.
Authorities predict China's AI-related sectors will surpass 10 trillion yuan in combined scale by 2030. ■

China's top economic planner invites private investment in 36 projects

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:19:56 CST
16:19:56 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- China's National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) has recommended 36 investment projects to private enterprises in a bid to further stimulate private investment.
These 36 projects, spanning transportation, logistics, water conservancy and energy, were presented at a recent NDRC symposium involving private enterprises and industry associations.
The projects have a combined estimated investment of 61.4 billion yuan (about 9.06 billion U.S. dollars) and are expected to attract 15.6 billion yuan in private capital. They cover railways, warehousing, wind power, energy storage, charging facilities and water diversion projects, among others.
Private capital can participate through wholly-owned investment, controlling stakes, or equity participation in relevant companies.
The NDRC said it will make full use of its regular communication and problem-solving mechanism in working with private enterprises. It will also work with relevant parties to improve services, strengthen the supply of capital, land and other factors of production, and coordinate efforts to resolve key issues to ensure early implementation of the projects.
It will also establish a regular project recommendation mechanism to expand opportunities for private enterprises to participate in high-quality projects and better facilitate private investment growth.
This project recommendation endeavor comes after official data showed that fixed-asset investment in China fell 6.7 percent year on year in the first seven months of 2026, while private investment dropped by 9.4 percent. Excluding real estate development, private investment declined 5.7 percent in this period. ■

Economic Watch: CIFIT highlights expanding China-Saudi investment and trade cooperation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:19:37 CST
16:19:37 KST

XIAMEN, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- China-Saudi Arabia cooperation is expanding into more fields, with green transformation, tourism and cutting-edge digital technologies becoming new growth areas, as showcased at the ongoing 26th China International Fair for Investment and Trade (CIFIT) in Xiamen, east China's Fujian Province.
As a guest country of honor of this year's CIFIT, Saudi Arabia has sent a large economic delegation to the fair, which opened Tuesday. The Saudi Pavilion showcases the country's investment environment, highlighting priority opportunities from petrochemicals and energy to advanced manufacturing and digital infrastructure, as well as capital markets and financial technology.
"We are focusing not only on the scale of investment, but also on the expansion and diversification of the investment scope," said Saudi Assistant Minister of Investment Ibrahim Al-Mubarak at the opening ceremony of the fair.
ROBUST TWO-WAY INVESTMENT
Often viewed as a barometer of China's outbound investment and inbound foreign direct investment, the CIFIT has served as an important platform to promote two-way investment, connect industrial chains, and showcase cooperation opportunities.
The 2026 CIFIT attracted more than 1,200 delegations from 129 countries and regions, and 30 international organizations, including government agencies, businesses, and other entities.
During the 2023 CIFIT, Chinese and Saudi companies reached an agreement to invest in an industrial gas center, which complements the Gulei Ethylene Project. Located in Zhangzhou, Fujian Province, the project is another joint venture between Chinese and Saudi companies backed by a total joint investment of 44.8 billion yuan (about 6.7 billion U.S. dollars).
The ethylene project, which is expected to produce 1.5 million tonnes of gas -- 3.6 percent of China's total output in 2025 -- employs nine proprietary techniques from Saudi Basic Industries Corporation. These techniques feature high feedstock flexibility, superior energy efficiency, and ultra-low emissions, placing them at the forefront of global ethylene technology.
While Saudi companies boost industrial efficiency in China, their Chinese counterparts also help drive Saudi Arabia's shift toward sustainable development.
In the desert south of Jeddah, Saudi Arabia's second-largest city, a 2.6-gigawatt photovoltaic power station has been in full commercial operation since May 2025. Contracted by China Energy Engineering Group Co., Ltd., the Al Shuaibah solar project is the largest of its kind in the Middle East. The power station is expected to reduce carbon dioxide emissions by 245 million tonnes in 35 years, equivalent to planting 545 million trees, according to the contractor.
Data from the Ministry of Commerce show that Saudi investment in China in the first seven months has shown remarkable growth momentum, surging by 343.7 percent year on year. Meanwhile, by the end of 2025, China's stock of direct investment in Saudi Arabia reached 4.26 billion U.S. dollars, with approximately 750 Chinese companies operating in the country.
"Our Chinese partners have brought us green electricity-related technologies such as solar energy, batteries, and power transmission," said Saleh Khabti, executive vice president of ACWA Power and president of ACWA China on Wednesday. ACWA Power is a Saudi power generation and water desalination company.
EXPANDING COOPERATION IN EMERGING SECTORS
Beyond the petrochemical industries, China-Saudi Arabia cooperation has expanded to tourism and cutting-edge digital technologies.
Saudi firm Man3 made its CIFIT debut this year, hoping to help Chinese companies invest safely and successfully in Saudi Arabia. Its head, Abdulmajeed Alfaifi, told reporters that China's advances in AI and robotics, and its supply-chain strengths, are exactly the resources Saudi Arabia hopes to connect with. "We want to link the two sides' businesses and unlock cooperation between them," he said.
Saudi Arabia is also promoting special economic zones which welcome Chinese investors in sectors covering automobile, food, advanced manufacturing, and IT. "We are ready to accommodate you all," said Edwin Lammers, an official with the Economic Cities and Special Zones Authority of Saudi Arabia.
Chinese AI companies have been providing cutting-edge algorithms, large language models, and smart-city solutions for various Saudi mega-projects, from urban management to healthcare. Saudi Arabia is seeking to build technical partnerships with leading Chinese companies and institutions, according to Majid Alshehry, spokesperson of the Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority.
Saudi Arabia's tourism transformation also involves Chinese firms. In Diriyah, home to the UNESCO-listed At-Turaif district, Chinese construction firms are helping turn a centuries-old oasis settlement into a global tourist destination under Saudi Vision 2030, with residential, entertainment and educational functions.
The cooperation model between the two countries offers an example that could be applied to other parts of the Middle East, Africa and other emerging economies, helping foster broader multilateral cooperative frameworks, according to Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan. ■

Unknown Publisher

by Xinhua writers Pang Mengxia, Sui Lixi and Wu Jianfeng
XIAMEN, China, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- The 26th China International Fair for Investment and Trade (CIFIT), being held from Sept. 8 to 11 in Xiamen, southeast China's Fujian Province, has drawn exhibitors and delegations from 129 countries and regions to its 14 themed exhibition areas.
Beyond the deals on display, executives say the event is increasingly serving as a barometer of where global capital sees opportunities in China.
At Hall 5 of the Xiamen International Expo Center, the booth of Yihai Kerry Arawana Holdings Co., Ltd. -- the China unit of Singapore-listed agribusiness group Wilmar International -- was packed with visitors. Products on display included low-GI, high-fiber oats, black highland barley and tartary buckwheat -- a lineup the company says is aimed at China's booming "big health" market.
"We have observed new changes in the Chinese market, and the most prominent is the upgrading of health demand," Mu Yankui, president of Yihai Kerry Arawana, told Xinhua.
Noting that China's elderly population has reached 300 million and that young people are showing growing personalized health needs, he said national health demand is driving the company to keep pace with the times in developing "big health" products.
Mu said the company has invested a total of roughly 100 billion yuan (about 14.9 billion U.S. dollars) in China, of which around 60 billion yuan (about 8.95 billion U.S. dollars) was invested in just the past eight years.
"Going forward, we will firmly continue to invest in China and help the country's agriculture transform from 'big' to 'strong,'" he said.
China has grown into the world's second-largest consumer market, with household consumption shifting from "whether there is enough" to "whether it is good enough." In recent years, the structural opportunities created by consumption upgrading have drawn global investors to vote with real money.
Decathlon, the French sporting goods brand, feels this trend keenly.
"China's sports market enjoys vast room for growth," said Zhao Jie, public relations and media communications director at Decathlon China. To meet consumers' increasingly diverse, segmented and specialized sports needs, Decathlon is advancing product innovation, local research and development, and sports service upgrades, offering more than 8,000 products in China covering more than 80 sports.
"China boasts a complete and efficient manufacturing and supply chain system. Over 94 percent of the products Decathlon sells in China are made locally, enabling faster response to local demand. Meanwhile, the fast-developing tech ecosystem and rich consumer scenarios allow the company to stay closer to consumers' real needs and connect more quickly with frontier technologies, product R&D and industrial resources," Zhao said.
Beyond the livelihood opportunities brought by consumption upgrading, new industrial openings under the green and low-carbon transition are also drawing global capital.
Guided by the "dual carbon" goals, new sectors such as energy conservation and environmental protection, resource recycling, and low-carbon smart manufacturing are emerging rapidly, with a "green China" becoming a "new blue ocean" for multinational companies.
Veolia, the French environmental services group founded in 1853, entered the Chinese market in the early 1990s. It now invests in and operates more than 100 projects in over 40 Chinese cities, serving more than 650 project sites, with businesses covering water supply and wastewater treatment, liquid and hazardous waste treatment and recycling, and solid waste recovery and reuse.
"Phrases such as 'green, low-carbon and circular economy system,' 'zero-carbon industrial parks' and 'expanding the scale of recycled material use' appear frequently in localities' plans for the 15th Five-Year Plan period," noted Huang Xiaojun, global senior vice president of Veolia China. "This is exactly one of the key areas where we hope to deepen cooperation," he said at CIFIT.
From selling products to building ecosystems, and from expanding markets to pursuing co-innovation, for many foreign businesses, China today is no longer merely a sales market, but an innovation system integrating R&D, manufacturing and commercialization.
"In the past, many multinational companies introduced innovative products into China. Today, that notion is far outdated. Companies need to place greater importance on innovative R&D systems, commercialized operation systems, and production and supply chain systems," said Wayne Shi, president of Sanofi Greater China.
China, Shi noted, has made remarkable progress in life sciences over the past decade and more. "The growing pool of outstanding research talent and biotech companies, higher-level clinical research capabilities, and the accelerating integration of artificial intelligence and digital technologies with life sciences means China is not only an important global pharmaceutical market, but is also becoming an important part of the global pharmaceutical innovation landscape," he said.
Data from China's Ministry of Commerce show that nearly 4,800 foreign-invested enterprises increased their investment in China in the first half of this year, while more than 37,700 new foreign-invested enterprises were established in the first seven months, up 4.4 percent year on year, and foreign investment actually utilized in high-tech industries surged 32.7 percent. The 2026 Kearney Foreign Direct Investment Confidence Index shows China rose to fourth place globally.
Ling Ji, China's vice minister of commerce and deputy China international trade representative, said at a press conference of the State Council Information Office earlier that foreign investors in China are no longer focusing solely on traditional factor costs such as labor and land.
"They are now paying more attention to an efficient industrial ecosystem, superior infrastructure -- especially the supply of new production factors such as green power and computing capacity -- an efficient supply chain system, a vibrant innovation ecosystem and a high-caliber talent pool," Ling said.
"In our exchanges with executives of many multinational companies, we often hear them say, 'If you can succeed in the Chinese market, you can achieve even greater success in the rest of the world,'" Ling added. ■

‘Free and happy. That is our victory’: ex-hostage Matan Angrest's first Rosh Hashanah back home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
07:18:29 UTC
16:18:29 KST

Last year, Anat and Hagai Angrest did not buy groceries for the holiday, plan a meal or know where they would spend Rosh Hashanah eve.
“We don’t have a holiday. We don’t have dates,” they said at the time, while their son, Matan, was still being held hostage by Hamas in Gaza.
This year, the dining table at the Angrest family home is being extended once again, and Matan returned especially from a trip to South America to celebrate the Jewish New Year with his family.
“Last year, I tried to hold on to the hope that one day I would get out and celebrate the holiday with my family,” he said. “It’s hard for me to describe the depth of the sadness and pain, surviving those days while at the same time feeling such a strong connection to my parents and my three siblings, remembering the white holiday table, the family atmosphere and the laughter that belongs only to us.
“My mind is only now processing, as I hear all the preparations for the holiday, that tonight it is really happening. Thank God, I’m here a year later, celebrating Rosh Hashanah for the first time with everyone close to me. Free and happy. That is our victory — and my personal victory.”
A year ago, the Angrest home, which had always filled with family, friends, cooking pots and tables being extended from the afternoon onward during the holidays, was quiet.
“We’re stuck on Oct. 7,” Hagai said then. “We don’t have a holiday. We don’t have dates. When everyone else is celebrating, those are our hardest hours.”
A year has passed, and Anat is once again thinking about holiday shopping, what she will cook, how the table will look and who will be there.
“It’s emotional,” she said. “Everyone wants to come. This will be the first time Matan has been here for the holiday since Oct. 7.”
Only in hindsight do they know how close they were at the time to the end of his captivity.
“We had already learned to protect ourselves emotionally and not get disappointed,” Anat said. “There was constant talk — there’s a deal, there isn’t a deal, these people agreed, those people didn’t. And suddenly, things began to develop.”
For Matan’s parents, every report of a possible hostage deal carried another fear. Matan was an Israeli soldier when he was abducted, and they worried that even if some hostages were released, their son might be left behind.
“There was always this dilemma — whether to support a partial deal that saves people or fear that afterward it could take a very long time to get the others out,” Anat said. “Those are incredibly cruel decisions.”
Only now, the family says, are they beginning to process what they endured.
“I give talks about my journey as a mother, and suddenly, when I talk about my family and show the videos, I realize that this is actually our personal story,” Anat said. “That we are part of this national story. Only now do we have the space to understand what happened here. Throughout that entire period, we were on autopilot.”
The joy of having her son home does not diminish the scale of the tragedy, she said.
“We constantly live with the sadness for those who did not get to come back, for those who were murdered and for those who were alive there but were not brought home in time,” Anat said. “Even during this holiday, my thoughts wander to those families.
“We learned how to be happy and how to be sad at the same time. I didn’t even know that was possible.”
At her first reunion with Matan, Anat said, all she wanted was to look into his eyes and hear his first words.
“From that, I knew I would be able to tell whether he had returned mentally broken or in a condition that would allow him to recover,” she said. “And when he said to me, ‘Mom, it’s me, Matan,’ I knew that from there we would recover. That the same kid had come back. He came back even more resilient, even tougher.”
Matan spent five months traveling in South America before returning to Israel ahead of Rosh Hashanah eve.
“It was important to me to come back and spend the holidays from beginning to end with my family here in Israel,” he said.
For the new year, he said his main wish is “to continue my recovery. To be close to my family, keep making up for lost time and be with my friends.”
Anat added with a smile that perhaps it is also time for him to “get on some kind of path” and begin studying.
Anat said that although the family tries to stay out of politics, she hopes the coming year will bring change in Israel.
“As much as we try not to get into politics, I wish for all of us that there will be change here, and it has to begin with investigating what happened here so that it does not happen again,” she said.
“I hope Israeli society will look like the young people who enlist in the military, where all they care about is being together and defending this country. I am the daughter of a Holocaust survivor, from the generation that built the country and taught me how important it is and how important it is to defend it, and that was passed on to Matan as well.
“I hope those values become part of Israeli society — togetherness, mutual responsibility, one for all and all for one.”
A year ago, when Matan was not there to hear them, Anat and Hagai sent their son a message: Do not lose hope, stay strong and know that the people of Israel want you home.
This year, Matan can answer them himself.
“Happy holiday to everyone,” he said, “and may this new beginning be a successful one, God willing.”

On 9 September, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski visited Latvia. During the visit, the chief of the Polish MFA met with Polish soldiers and talked with foreign ministers of Latvia, Finland, Ireland, and Hungary.
While in Latvia, Deputy Prime Minister Radosław Sikorski and Latvia’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Baiba Braže visited the Ādaži military base hosting NATO’s multinational brigade. During the meeting, the Polish MFA head highlighted that Poland and Latvia face similar threats and challenges in the security domain.
Both of our countries have recently been experiencing airspace violations caused by Russia, weaponized artificial migration pressure on our borders, and various other hostile sabotage actions
- said Deputy Prime Minister Radosław Sikorski and pointed out that Poland and Latvia are leaders within NATO in terms of defence spending, which accounts for 4.8 and 4.7 per cent of their GDPs respectively.
Deputy Prime Minister Sikorski emphasised that the military base in Ādaži is a symbol of Polish–Latvian defence cooperation. The Canadian-led Combat Group that stations at the base comprises about 2,850 troops, including over 230 soldiers from Poland. Most of the 19th rotation of the Polish Military Contingent Latvia is made up of the 11th Lubuska Armoured Cavalry Division soldiers from Żagań. Deputy Prime Minister Sikorski met with Polish soldiers and took part in a presentation of military equipment.
While in Latvia, Deputy Prime Minister Radosław Sikorski also participated in a meeting with the heads of diplomacy of Latvia, Finland, Ireland, and Hungary. The ministers discussed hybrid threats in Europe. The head of Polish diplomacy spoke about an intensification of Russia’s hostile hybrid activities targeting NATO and EU members, in particular countries on the eastern flank. He emphasised the need for close cooperation to counteract such activities.
The ministers also talked about the enlargement of the European Union, especially progress made to date by Ukraine, Moldova, and Western Balkan countries. Deputy Prime Minister Sikorski pointed out the need for an in-depth discussion on the EU’s functioning in its future, enlarged form.
The talks also covered the situation in the Strait of Hormuz. The ministers highlighted the need to work towards a dyplomatic resolution of the conflict and to restore free and safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz.
They also laid flowers at the Freedom Monument in Riga, which commemorates soldiers fallen during the Latvian War of Independence in 1918–1920.

UN monitoring findings point to continued al-Qaeda activity 25 years after 9/11 - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
07:14:35 UTC
16:14:35 KST

Twenty-five years after 9/11, the United States killed Osama bin Laden, decimated Al-Qaeda’s founding leadership, and spent two decades and trillions of dollars fighting a war in Afghanistan.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Yet the network responsible for the September 11, 2001, attacks has not been eliminated.
Although Al-Qaeda’s senior leadership is marginalized and its capability and intent to conduct external operations remain unclear, the organization has survived through adaptation. It decentralized its command structure and embedded itself in regional conflicts, fragile states, and allied armed groups.
The attacks, which killed nearly 3,000 people, transformed global security and triggered the US-led “War on Terror.”
Beginning with the invasion of Afghanistan and the overthrow of the Taliban, the campaign evolved into a two-decade war that reshaped US foreign policy, military strategy, and geopolitics across the Middle East and South Asia.
US military forces severely weakened Al-Qaeda’s central leadership, culminating in the 2011 raid that killed bin Laden in Pakistan. The organization, though, was not eliminated.
It reorganized through decentralized networks and regional affiliates across Africa, the Middle East, and Asia.
US withdrawal revives concerns over terrorist groups in Afghanistan
The US withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021 and the Taliban’s return to power revived a central post-9/11 concern: whether Afghanistan could again offer an environment in which terrorist organizations could regroup, recruit, and assist allied networks.
One enduring consequence of the war is the unresolved case against Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, whom US authorities describe as the alleged mastermind of the attacks.
Captured in Pakistan in 2003 and transferred to Guantanamo Bay in 2006, Mohammed has spent more than two decades in detention without trial. A military judge has scheduled his trial, alongside three co-defendants, to begin on June 5, 2028, nearly 27 years after 9/11.
The delay reflects the legal and political complications of the post-9/11 detention system.
Prosecutors recently declined to appeal a ruling excluding statements Mohammed made after years of Central Intelligence Agency detention and interrogation, choosing instead to preserve the 2028 trial schedule.
Recent UN assessments indicate that Al-Qaeda maintains a persistent presence in Afghanistan under Taliban rule. The UN Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team said in its August 10 report that Al-Qaeda’s status and strength in Afghanistan remained unchanged.
The report said the terrorist threat emanating from Afghanistan also remained largely unchanged and that the ability of numerous terrorist groups to operate there posed an enduring threat to neighboring countries and Central Asia.
Al-Qaeda aided TTP in insurgency against Pakistan, UN says
Al-Qaeda provided ideological guidance, training, and support to Tehrik-e Taliban Pakistan (TTP) in its insurgency against Pakistan, according to the report.
The UN report said Al-Qaeda’s official media arm, As-Sahab Media Foundation, published a statement on April 28 supporting the Taliban and, for the first time, TTP in operations against Pakistan.
Al-Qaeda in the Indian Subcontinent (AQIS) has evolved from a fragmented group into a regional terrorist entity, according to the UN assessment. The report said AQIS had established logistical and financial networks that operated through decentralized, scattered cells rather than large units.
The report said AQIS leaders remained in Kabul and had been issued Afghan identity documents, known as tazkiras, suggesting close cooperation between the Taliban and AQIS.
Alex Mishra, a Washington-area policy analyst focusing on Afghanistan, Al-Qaeda, and geopolitical alignments, told The Media Line that “25 years after 9/11, Al-Qaeda has a larger territorial presence across three continents than at any point since [its] founding.”
Mishra argued that the group’s lower profile should not be mistaken for disappearance or defeat.
Asif Durrani, Pakistan’s former special representative for Afghanistan and a former ambassador to Iran and the United Arab Emirates, offered a different assessment. He told The Media Line that “there was relatively little to discuss about Al-Qaeda,” which he described as an organization that had “lost its teeth and appeal.”
According to Durrani, the Islamic State (ISIS), also known as Daesh, has displaced Al-Qaeda as the more prominent jihadist threat. ISIS once controlled large areas of Iraq and Syria at the height of its power.
“Terrorism in its known form has lost its importance; the [term] ... ‘war on terror’ is no longer a currency in international politics,” Durrani said.
Durrani pointed to the case of Ahmed al-Sharaa, Syria’s president, noting that he was once associated with jihadist groups but, in his current political role, has gained acceptance from President Donald Trump and several European leaders.
Kamal Alam, formerly a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and an expert on Afghan affairs, took a more cautionary view. He told The Media Line that “Al-Qaeda’s presence in Afghanistan is at its highest level since the Taliban’s return to power in 2021 and the group’s expulsion by US Special Forces.”
Alam said the killing of Al-Qaeda leader Ayman al-Zawahiri in Kabul after the Taliban takeover demonstrated the group’s continued presence in Afghanistan.
The Taliban publicly denies hosting terrorist groups, but Alam said UN agencies and independent assessments have documented the presence of Al-Qaeda, ISIS, and other regional and transnational armed groups in the country.
While describing Al-Qaeda as more decentralized and competing with ISIS for influence, he said the broader threat extends beyond the two groups and involves armed networks linked to Syria, Iraq, and Africa.
“The key concern is not the label, Al-Qaeda or ISIS, but the growing network of groups with regional and international connections,” Alam said.
Atlanta-based geopolitical analyst Erik Lehmkuhle told The Media Line that “the Taliban’s return to power had given Al-Qaeda a permissive environment to operate.”
Lehmkuhle cautioned against interpreting Al-Qaeda’s reduced visibility abroad as weakness or compliance, saying the group was pursuing “a deliberate strategy of operational patience.”
Andy Vermaut, a Brussels-based human rights activist and counterextremism expert, said the unresolved Mohammed prosecution remains one of the most serious failures of the post-9/11 system.
“A quarter-century after 9/11, the inability to try alleged mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed is still a major outstanding problem,” Vermaut told The Media Line.
Vermaut said torture, including waterboarding, and the exclusion of statements obtained under coercion have undermined the prosecution and prolonged the case. He argued that the United States should have pursued a public trial under ordinary law rather than creating a system that has left the case unresolved for two decades.
Thaliban denies Afghan responsibility for 9/11
Afghan Taliban chief spokesman Zabiullah Mujahid rejected Afghan responsibility for the 9/11 attacks, saying the plotters received training, housing, and logistical backing outside Afghanistan and that no domestic infrastructure or complicity was involved.
“There was no such arrangement or infrastructure in Afghanistan at that time,” he told The Media Line.
Mujahid argued that Afghanistan had since undergone significant changes following “20 years of American aggression,” after which the Islamic Emirate and Islamic rule were established in the country.
He insisted that the government neither permits foreign armed factions to operate within its borders nor harbors foreign organizations, dismissing warnings of terrorist safe havens as foreign propaganda.
Without naming Al-Qaeda, Mujahid further claimed that such groups now have broader opportunities to live and operate in “Arab countries.” He did not identify the countries to which he was referring.

US declines Saudi call for strikes on Houthis, offers intelligence support: Axios
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
07:12:51 UTC
16:12:51 KST

The US declined Saudi Arabia’s appeals to launch direct military strikes against Houthis in Yemen following their capture of the strategic coastal city of Mocha, the Axios news website reported on Thursday.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman contacted US President Donald Trump twice in quick succession to request American air operations as the Houthis advanced towards the Bab al Mandeb Strait, according to the report.
The crown prince initially described the retreat of allied Yemeni forces before formally requesting direct military intervention hours later.
Trump rejected the request to maintain Washington’s focus on Iran and the Strait of Hormuz and avoid opening another combat theatre, sources familiar with the matter told Axios.
While ruling out direct air strikes, the White House agreed to provide non-combat assistance, authorising the transfer of actionable intelligence and targeting information to Saudi forces.
The intelligence-sharing comes in addition to around 200 US military personnel stationed in the kingdom in advisory and liaison roles.
Washington also sent US Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper to Saudi Arabia on Thursday for consultations with senior Saudi defence officials.
The developments come amid rising tensions between Riyadh and the Houthis. Addressing the UN Security Council on Thursday, Saudi Ambassador Abdulaziz Alwasil said the kingdom would take “all measures necessary” after Houthi strikes on civilian sites in southern Saudi cities earlier this week wounded 73 people.
Control of Mocha and the surrounding coastline is strategically important because of its proximity to the Bab al Mandeb Strait, a vital shipping route connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.
Yemen has seen renewed fighting between government forces and the Houthis since early July, following years of relative calm under a truce that began in April 2022.
The Houthis have controlled the capital, Sanaa, and large parts of northern and western Yemen since September 2014, while the internationally recognised government and allied forces hold areas in the south and east.
Saudi Arabia has led a coalition supporting Yemen’s government against the Iran-aligned Houthis since March 2015.

Swiss city returns remains of indigenous ancestors to Chile

Swiss city returns remains of indigenous ancestors to Chile
Canton Basel City is returning two skeletons and a skull of Kawésqar ancestors to Chile. On Thursday, Government President Conradin Cramer received a delegation from the Indigenous community at City Hall to mark the restitution.
The Basel government had decided to proceed with this restitution following a joint application from the Natural History Museum, the Museum Commission and the Rectorate of the University of Basel, the Presidential Department announced. The Cantonal Museums Act stipulates that such a joint application is required.
Provenance research carried out at the Natural History Museum Basel clarified the history of the human remains’ origins.
Basel collectors Arnold Masarey (1881–1953) and Ludwig Paravicini (1868–1953) acquired them in Patagonia in the early 20th century. They donated them to what was then the Museum of Ethnology. Today, the bones are housed at the Natural History Museum.
More
Swiss museums contain human remains from colonial times
In collaboration with indigenous partners, the research team was able to establish the circumstances of their colonial appropriation, a press release stated. They were also able to prove that the indigenous communities did not give their consent to the purchase at the time. In the eyes of the Kawésqar, these are not merely human remains, but individuals who, even today, maintain an ongoing spiritual connection with their descendants.
Restoring dignity
Canton Basel City will transfer the remains to Punta Arenas in consultation with the indigenous communities. There, the descendants will decide on a suitable final resting place.
More
Swiss take steps to ‘decolonise’ cultural artefacts
For the indigenous families concerned, this restitution represents not only the return of their ancestors, but also an “important step towards restoring their dignity”, recognising the continued existence of the Kawésqar and “building a lasting relationship of trust with the institutions involved”, said the presidential department.
The Kawésqar’s history spans over 6,000 years. They are a community of maritime nomads in the channels and fjords of the “Kawésqar Wæs”, known since colonisation as western Patagonia in present-day Chile. The Kawésqar were severely decimated as a result of colonisation.

Taiwan's Unique Opto-Electronics expands into CPO supply chain with glass blanks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
07:06:51 UTC
16:06:51 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Optical glass blank supplier Unique Opto-Electronics Co. is expanding into the co-packaged optics supply chain by supplying glass blanks for the technology.
The company said Thursday that it has secured orders and recently begun shipments. Revenue from these products is expected to account for about 10% of total revenue, with shipments projected to increase gradually next year, according to CTEE.
Unique Opto-Electronics mainly supplies optical glass blanks to the automotive, robotics, and medical sectors. The blanks are produced by melting and mixing raw materials at high temperatures, using ultrasonic stirring to remove air bubbles before cooling the material, according to Sinotrade.
They are subsequently processed into optical lenses, including those used in CPO. CPO is a packaging technology that integrates light-based components with computing chips in the same package, shortening signal paths to reduce power consumption and transmission delays.
Unique Opto-Electronics Chair Chen Chung-cheng (陳忠政) said CPO requires optical glass materials with high refractive indices and strict quality standards. This leaves only a limited range of materials that meet the requirements.
The company has secured access to raw materials from major international manufacturers, including Germany's Schott and Japan's Ohara. Chen said its glass-processing capabilities also allow it to produce glass blanks according to customer specifications.
Meanwhile, the company's order intake this year has exceeded expectations, driven by orders from European optical companies and stronger business in robotics and drones. Unique Opto-Electronics had originally forecast full-year revenue growth of about 10%, but revenue for the first eight months reached NT$351 million, up 28.24% year-on-year.

Umno seeks early Malaysian election to cement conservative Malay bloc
Umno is deepening ties with PAS, buoyed by recent state victories and growing talk of a new alignment to consolidate the Malay vote
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Malaysia’s once-dominant Umno party has given its clearest indication yet that it will break with the country’s current ruling alliance, after its president called on Friday for a general election to be held immediately.
The call comes as the United Malays National Organisation deepens ties with opposition Islamist party the Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS), buoyed by recent state victories and growing talk of a new alignment to consolidate the Malay vote.
“The time has come for the [national election] to be held immediately. Agree?” Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi told delegates during the party’s general assembly at the World Trade Centre in Kuala Lumpur. “Since we are already fighting, let us fight. Fight all the way.”
The demand represented a much tougher line from Zahid, who only last week said Umno-led Barisan Nasional (BN) was open to an early election but was prepared to let parliament run its full term. Malaysia does not have to hold its next general election until early 2028.
Zahid, deputy prime minister in Anwar Ibrahim’s government, also warned against betrayal in future political deals but did not name any of Umno’s current government partners.

Guava season in Gaza: surviving trees struggle to bear fruit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
07:06:15 UTC
16:06:15 KST

Breadcrumb
Guava season in Gaza: surviving trees struggle to bear fruit amid Israel's genocide
In al-Mawasi area in the southern coastal enclave of the Gaza Strip, the guava season has arrived on land where orchards once stretched across thousands of dunams.
But much of that landscape has disappeared under Israeli bombardment and bulldozing, while other parts are now occupied by tents housing displaced Palestinians amid three years of an Israeli genocide.
Among the trees that remain, farmer Khaled Al-Najjar moves carefully through his land, checking the guavas that have ripened and are ready to be picked. This year's harvest is less about abundance than salvaging whatever the war has left behind, he says.
"This land used to be full of trees and workers, but today, some parts are inaccessible, while others have become shelters for displaced people. We are no longer farming the way we used to. We are simply trying to find whatever space is still available to work," the 56-year-old father of eight told The New Arab.
Before the Israeli genocidal war, Al-Najjar cultivated around 3,000 dunams in Al-Mawasi, Khan Yunis. That area has now fallen to roughly 500 dunams that can still be used for cultivation.
Losing farmland is only part of the problem. The trees that survived the destruction are struggling with shortages of water, fertilisers, pesticides and fuel, leaving farmers unable to provide the care needed to maintain production.
"Even the trees that survived need to be saved," al-Najjar said. "Without water and agricultural supplies, it is becoming harder to care for them. When the trees produce less, farmers lose money and workers lose the days they depend on."
He has no clear idea when the damaged areas will become usable again. For now, his attention remains fixed on the surviving trees and the small amount of fruit that can still reach Gaza's markets.
"We are not asking for the land to be restored overnight," he added. "What matters now is stopping the losses and allowing us to reach our land again. The land knows its owners, but what happened has made it impossible for us to care for it as we once did."
Season of scarcity
For Khan Younis-based agricultural worker Ibrahim Shehadeh, the difference between this year's guava season and those before the war is visible in the number of people working in the fields.
"In previous seasons, we worked in large groups because the land needed many hands during harvest […] Now there is much less work, and every farmer is trying to get whatever he can from the trees that remain," he told TNA.
Even small quantities of fruit are being collected, with farmers reluctant to leave anything behind at a time when every kilogram can bring much-needed income.
The guava season in Gaza normally runs from September through December. But the war has disrupted almost every stage of production, from reaching farmland and maintaining trees to harvesting, transporting and selling the crop.
The consequences are also being felt by consumers.
At a market in Khan Yunis, Maysaa Abu Khalil examines the price of guavas before deciding how much she can afford to take home.
She found each kilogram was sold for US$10, which is expensive for her.
"Before the war, we used to buy it for less than one dollar […] Unfortunately, fruit has become something we buy only when the household budget allows. When prices are high, we either buy a small amount or leave it altogether," she told TNA.
With food prices rising and household incomes under severe pressure, the decline in local agricultural production has created another burden for families already struggling to secure basic necessities.
Agriculture under attack
"The fate of Gaza's guava crop reflects the broader collapse of the territory's agricultural sector," Hossam Qasim, an agricultural researcher, told TNA.
Before the war, around 1,700 dunams were planted with guava in Gaza. That figure has now fallen to less than 100 dunams, according to Qasim.
"Replanting trees is possible in principle, but the damage is much more serious than the loss of trees. The land itself has been damaged, along with water networks and irrigation sources, while accessing agricultural areas has become increasingly difficult," he added.
Water has emerged as another major threat, particularly in al-Mawasi. Qasim explained that salinity in some water sources has risen from around 400 parts per million to between 4,000 and 5,000 parts per million.
Such levels can reduce productivity and threaten the long-term survival of trees, he explains, which means that restoring Gaza's orchards will require more than just planting new trees.
"The water crisis has to be addressed alongside the rehabilitation of the land," he continued.
The damage to Gaza's agricultural sector extends far beyond individual orchards.
Raafat Asaliya, a spokesperson for Gaza's Ministry of Agriculture, estimates the sector's total damage and losses at around US$3 billion, including approximately US$1.49 billion in direct damage and US$1.59 billion in indirect losses.
Around 8,700 agricultural water wells have been rendered inoperable due to Israel, according to the ministry, while 3,828 agricultural water ponds have been damaged and around 1,371 kilometres of agricultural water transmission lines were destroyed by Israeli bombardment.

Swedish PM Kristersson seeks new term and backing for partnership with far right

Unknown Publisher

Swedish PM Kristersson seeks new term and backing for partnership with far right
STOCKHOLM, Sept 11 - When Ulf Kristersson promised Holocaust survivor Hedi Fried his Moderates would never cooperate with the far-right Sweden Democrats back in 2018, the party was still treated as a political outcast by much of Sweden's right wing.
Four years later, the party's support helped carry Kristersson into office, lending its votes to the three-party right-wing minority government he leads and propelling his journey of shifting Sweden's politics to focus on tougher policies on immigration and crime.
Now, if the right wins Sunday's election, Kristersson has said he will include the Sweden Democrats in his new government, which would be the first time it would join a cabinet.
Kristersson's government has already abolished permanent residency for asylum seekers and ramped up expulsions. It had to drop a bill to lock up the most violent 13-year-old criminals, settling for offenders one year older, but has imposed stiffer sentencing and expanded police powers.
MANAGERIAL STYLE
"There were fundamental things that just weren't working in Sweden," Kristersson, a 62-year-old father of three, said at the launch of his party's manifesto in August.
Asylum numbers have dropped to a 40-year low and shooting deaths are down 75%.
Things looked bleak for Kristersson - who as head of the Moderates' youth wing espoused open borders - when he took over as party leader in 2017.
The centre right was split over whether to work with the Sweden Democrats and had no way back to power.
Prioritising pragmatism over principles, Kristersson broke the taboo, clearing the way for a centre-right victory in 2022 and four years of stable government - a rarity in recent years.
His unflappable leadership and managerial style have smoothed personal frictions with his coalition and helped him shake off questions about his judgment in picking advisers, including one accused of leaving secret documents in a hotel.
"He talks about being the adult in the room, and, by and large, he has succeeded in being that," Jenny Madestam, political scientist at Sodertorn University, said.
CRITICS POINT TO MOVE FURTHER RIGHT
To critics, however, Kristersson's pursuit of power risks cementing the far right's anti-immigration agenda at the heart of Swedish politics and a further move to the right.
"I've lived in Donald Trump's USA the last few years and I've seen how fast it can go in the wrong direction," Birgitta Ohlsson, of the opposition Centre Party and a former EU minister, said.
Polls show the left and right blocs running neck and neck.
If Swedes do pick the right bloc, Kristersson's pragmatism could still face a test. The Sweden Democrats could get more votes than the Moderates. Most analysts expect Kristersson would soldier on as prime minister, but his authority would be weak.
"The Sweden Democrats would be in control, in practice," said Marie Demker, professor of political science at Gothenburg University. REUTERS

Swedish PM-hopeful Andersson preaches unity but needs to heal opposition split
STOCKHOLM, Sept 11 - Cooperation rather than conflict is the promise Swedish Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson is offering voters as she seeks a return to the prime minister's office in Sunday's election.
A former national level swimmer who colleagues describe as hardworking and demanding, Andersson became Sweden's first female prime minister in 2021.
She holds the record for the shortest period in office — resigning after less than 12 hours as prime minister when her coalition partner quit — although ultimately completed a 10-month term, starting again days later as the head of a single-party minority government.
As prime minister, she had to negotiate Sweden's response to the COVID pandemic and NATO application in the wake of Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Despite being voted out of office in 2022, polls still show her as the politician most trusted by Swedes.
Andersson, 59, has portrayed herself as a unifying force after four years during which the centre right, backed by the far-right Sweden Democrats, have cracked down on immigration and turned away from the liberal, inclusive politics that have characterised Sweden for decades.
"Either I lead the government and bring the country together ... or you have a government where the Sweden Democrats use their platform to create division," she told reporters earlier this month.
BLOC DIFFERENCES OVER ENERGY AND TAX
Yet the message of unity masks tensions within her left-wing bloc, with parties differing on issues ranging from energy policy to taxation.
Andersson is more technocrat than torch-bearer: she carries a boiled egg in her handbag in case she gets hungry and told Swedish radio earlier this year she could not tell Hollywood actors Brad Pitt and Tom Hanks apart.
After graduating from Stockholm's prestigious School of Economics, she spent her early career in the finance department before becoming deputy director-general of Sweden's Tax Agency, returning to politics as finance minister from 2014 to 2021.
Playing on traditional Social Democratic strengths, Andersson is promising voters more spending on welfare, a fairer tax system and a focus on social cohesion.
Polls show the centre-left bloc's 10-point lead during the summer has melted away, partly over concerns about how Andersson can square the circle of ruling with parties that refuse to cooperate with each other.
If Andersson does win office she is "probably doomed to hold together a quartet that includes parties that loathe each other, but which just about loathe the Sweden Democrats more", Nick Aylott, senior lecturer in political science at Sodertorn University, said. REUTERS
