Reinventing the battlefield
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
06:39:18 UTC
15:39:18 KST

Israel’s defense-tech ecosystem is undergoing one of the most significant transformations in its history.
For decades, Israel's three major defense contractors developed everything from missiles and radar systems to satellites and armored vehicle protection, while the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) served as both customer and proving ground.
It was a tightly held domain that has increasingly expanded into a sprawling, multilayered innovation network of start-ups, research centers, dual-use technology companies, and military-industry partnerships that are building technologies that are redefining how wars are fought.
The ecosystem’s rise comes at a moment when global demand for advanced defense technology is surging. Israel’s defense-tech landscape is not only reshaping the country’s security posture but also redefining its economic trajectory, industrial priorities, and global influence.
Unlike many countries where defense innovation is concentrated within a handful of large contractors, Israel's ecosystem has always been closely connected to its broader technology sector. Engineers frequently move between military service, commercial start-ups, and established defense companies, carrying operational knowledge with them.
Rather than competing with Israel's established defense primes, the start-up companies are increasingly becoming partners, supplying niche technologies that can be integrated into larger weapon systems or rapidly deployed to meet emerging operational requirements.
This start-up culture has become particularly important as warfare itself changes.
The proliferation of inexpensive unmanned aircraft, artificial intelligence (AI), electronic warfare (EW), and software-defined operations has lowered barriers to innovation. Modern militaries increasingly require software updates measured in weeks rather than hardware upgrades measured in decades. Israeli start-ups, accustomed to rapid product iteration, are well positioned to deliver those capabilities.
Yet the country's established defense contractors remain indispensable.
The backbone of the ecosystem
Israel Aerospace Industries-IAI, Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, and Elbit Systems continue to anchor Israel's defense industry, providing manufacturing capacity, systems integration, global supply chains, and decades of engineering expertise that few start-ups could replicate.
IAI, the country’s largest defense contractor, has been long regarded as Israel's aerospace powerhouse. It combines satellite manufacturing, UAV development and manufacturing, missile defense, and intelligence systems under one organization. Its solutions have been central during the last three years of multifront war that Israel has been fighting – from its Arrow defense system that has intercepted countless Iranian missile barrages to its UAVs striking targets far from the country’s borders.
IAI’s growing collaboration with smaller companies, particularly in autonomous systems and AI-driven mission management, shows how even the largest players are adapting to a more distributed innovation model.
“We are always trying to look two generations ahead. We don’t have the luxury to wake up one morning and have something ready the next day; we look for the answers decades ahead of time,” Boaz Levy, chairman of IAI, told Defense & Tech by The Jerusalem Post in an interview.
Rafael remains synonymous with layered air defense. The company's role in developing the Iron Dome and the Iron Beam directed energy system has made it one of the world's most recognized missile defense companies. The company has repeatedly produced the technologies that redefine Israel’s strategic posture. The Trophy Active Protection System, Spike missiles, advanced electro-optics, and cutting-edge EW systems have all emerged from Rafael’s labs.
According to foreign reports, Rafael’s Spike missiles were one of the platforms used to destroy Iranian ballistic missiles and their launchers in the opening round of Operation Rising Lion in June 2025.
But Rafael's strategy increasingly extends beyond internal research. The company has expanded collaboration with younger firms developing AI-enabled targeting, advanced sensing, and autonomous capabilities, recognizing that software innovation often occurs faster outside traditional corporate structures.
Elbit Systems, meanwhile, has evolved into one of the world's most diversified defense technology companies. Rather than specializing in one domain, the company built a portfolio that spans air, land, sea, cyber, EW, and C4I. This breadth gives the company a unique vantage point – it sees how technologies intersect, how operational needs evolve, and where gaps emerge.
One of its most influential contributions to Israel’s defense-tech identity is its work on soldier modernization. Its soldier systems are used by militaries around the world, but their influence inside Israel is even more profound. They shape how the IDF trains, fights, and adapts to new threats. And they create a natural bridge to start-ups working on computer vision, autonomy, and electro-optics, many of which build technologies that plug directly into Elbit’s soldier ecosystem.
Elbit is one of Israel’s most successful defense exporters, with customers in more than 30 countries. Its relationships with foreign militaries allow it to identify emerging global needs and feed that intelligence back into Israel’s innovation ecosystem.
Together, the three companies remain the industrial backbone of Israeli defense. Yet these primes no longer operate in isolation. They are increasingly intertwined with start-ups that bring agility, software expertise, and fresh operational perspectives.
Winning the drone war
Few technologies illustrate Israel's innovation ecosystem better than autonomous aerial systems.
The country has been a pioneer in unmanned aircraft for decades but today a new generation of companies is pushing autonomy beyond surveillance into logistics, maneuver, and collaborative operations.
Aeronautics, now part of Rafael, continues to expand its portfolio of tactical unmanned systems, providing intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) capabilities for military customers around the world. Its integration into Rafael also demonstrates another defining characteristic of Israel's ecosystem: Promising companies often become part of larger industrial groups while retaining their innovative culture.
A different approach comes from XTEND, whose intuitive operating systems enable personnel to control drones in complex environments with minimal training.
Founded in 2018 by Aviv Shapira, Matteo Shapira, Rubi Liani, and Adir Tubi as a gaming company, since October 7, the company has shifted its focus to specialize in human-guided autonomous machine systems for defense applications. The company has gained international recognition for combining immersive control technologies with autonomous capabilities, allowing operators to conduct reconnaissance, inspect hazardous locations, or perform tactical missions while remaining outside immediate danger.
The company’s platforms have been used in the Israel-Hamas War, Operation Rising Lion, and during the deadly earthquake in Venezuela. “Other companies are still testing their products, but we are proving ours during wartime,” Aviv Shapira told D&T.
Aero Sentinel, a boutique Israeli drone manufacturer specializing in covert intelligence-gathering drones, is rapidly gaining traction among elite military units and international customers. The platforms are short- and medium-range drones that are optimized for tactical operations, border patrol, and other sensitive surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) missions.
The platforms are built for environments where traditional drones struggle, such as GPS-denied zones, urban canyons, or areas saturated with RF interference, where many UAVs lose stability or fail entirely. Aero Sentinel’s systems are engineered to adapt, relying on multisensor fusion and onboard decision-making to maintain flight integrity.
The company’s platforms were used in covert missions during Operation Rising Lion, and its headquarters were struck by an Iranian ballistic missile during Operation Roaring Lion.
“The fact that we were targeted as a high-value strategic objective speaks for itself. It reflects the quality, relevance, and operational importance of the systems we provide,” the company told D&T.
C-UAS
As low-cost drones become an increasingly common feature of modern battlefields, systems that improve infantry effectiveness without requiring entirely new weapons have attracted growing international attention.
Conflicts around the world have demonstrated how inexpensive unmanned aircraft can conduct reconnaissance, deliver precision strikes, disrupt logistics, and overwhelm traditional air defense systems. Their widespread use has created an equally urgent demand for technologies capable of detecting, identifying, and defeating them.
Israel has responded by developing one of the world's most diverse counter-UAS industries.
D-Fend’s flagship technology uses cyber-based takeover methods to safely control hostile drones without jamming or kinetic fire. This approach is increasingly favored in civilian environments where collateral damage is unacceptable.
Founded in 2017 in the garage of CEO and chairman Zohar Halachmi, along with CTO and vice president Assaf Monsa and chief product officer and president Yaniv Benbenisti, the software-driven company has built its reputation on the simple but demanding premise of neutralizing rogue drones cleanly, quietly, and without jamming half the city or blowing anything out of the sky.
“Commercialized drones or the DIY ones are causing 90% of the incidents… Small drones can be very problematic,” Halachmi told D&T. “This is a sensitive, surgical system.”
Sentrycs pursued a similarly sophisticated strategy. Instead of relying primarily on radar or kinetic defeat, its systems analyze communication protocols between drones and their operators, enabling precise detection and disruption while minimizing interference with nearby wireless networks.
The company provides militaries and civilian infrastructure such as airports and even sporting events like FIFA World Cup with the ability to classify drones in real time. Its systems distinguish between friendly and hostile UAS, which is a critical capability as drone usage expands.
In November 2025, the company was acquired by the American defense conglomerate Ondas Holdings in a deal valued at approximately $224.6 million. The acquisition combined Sentrycs’s cyber-over-RF technology with Ondas’s broader autonomous systems, creating a more comprehensive layered solution for military, homeland security, and critical infrastructure customers worldwide.
Meanwhile, SmartShooter has approached the drone challenge from the perspective of the soldier on the ground. Its fire-control technologies combine electro-optics, computer vision, and target tracking to increase the probability of successfully engaging small aerial threats.
“Part of the beauty is that we can use the same core technology for different applications. We can continuously upgrade the software and provide it on various platforms in our broad portfolio,” Shir Ahuvia, VP of product told D&T. “That’s the magic.”
Seeing more, seeing less
Information has always been a decisive military advantage, but the challenge today is not collecting data – it’s processing it quickly enough to support operational decisions. Electro-optical technologies remain one of Israel's greatest strengths, supported by decades of expertise in sensors, thermal imaging, laser systems, and advanced optics.
Asio Technologies has specialized in portable situational-awareness solutions that combine navigation, mapping, and sensor fusion for military and security forces operating in complex terrain. These systems enable dismounted personnel to understand their surroundings more effectively while reducing reliance on traditional GPS navigation alone.
Its battle-hardened and operationally proven technology has been in the hands of IDF troops and commanders for close to a decade, allowing the company to provide the necessary upgrades and changes for troops in the field.
“We focus on bringing innovation so that troops can do their work and be tactically independent,” CEO Tomer Malchi told D&T, adding that the company’s goal is to “make their day-to-day life on the battlefield clearer. We want to deliver the right amount of data, without any overkill.”
SpectralX represents the growing role of advanced imaging and artificial intelligence in modern defense sensing. The company develops technologies focused on analyzing complex visual data and extracting actionable intelligence from sensor inputs.
As militaries collect increasing volumes of imagery from drones, cameras, and other platforms, the ability to rapidly interpret that information has become as important as the sensors themselves.
“The main challenge is finding the right balance between stealth, movement, and protection,” Asaf Picciotto told D&T. “We deny detection on the battlefield.”
ThirdEye Systems develops thermal imaging and advanced vision technologies designed to improve detection under low-visibility conditions. As militaries increasingly operate around the clock and across diverse environments, demand for sophisticated electro-optical sensing continues to grow.
The rise of defense AI
Few technologies have altered the battlefield more rapidly than AI. If the last era of defense innovation was defined by hardware, the next is defined by software. And Israel’s defense-AI sector is one of the fastest growing in the world.
Kela’s AI-driven intelligence platforms fuse data from multiple sources to identify threats, track adversaries, and support operational planning. In an age where information overload can paralyze decision-making, Kela’s systems provide clarity at machine speed. Its tools are used globally for counterterrorism, border security, and cyber-intelligence operations.
Kela’s systems are engineered to be flexible, mobile, and operable by a single soldier, an approach shaped by the lessons of October 7, which underscored the need for rapid-response capabilities and seamless integration with advanced sensors. The company’s platforms are designed to incorporate both civilian and military technologies without dependence on a single manufacturer or the need to replace existing infrastructure.
Axon Vision specializes in automatic target recognition and situational awareness for armored vehicles and ground forces. Its AI systems classify threats in real time, giving soldiers the ability to process complex environments faster than human cognition alone allows. The company provides AI-driven computer vision and situational awareness solutions for defense and security applications. Its EDGE ClearSky solution supports rapid detection and identification of aerial threats through thermal sensing and AI-driven real-time processing.
Built on an open, platform-agnostic architecture, Axon Vision solutions integrate sensors and effectors across existing military platforms. The systems are integrated onto platforms of various militaries around the world, including the IDF, through partnerships with multinational defense companies.
Airwayz builds AI-powered UAS traffic management systems that allow multiple drones to operate autonomously in shared airspace. Its technology enables coordinated missions, swarm behavior, and safe integration with manned aircraft.
“OVERWATCH brings the ability to control the airspace, to understand which aircraft flies where and where to broadcast, like a control tower,” Airwayz CEO Eyal Zor told D&T. “The chaotic environment of drones in the lower skies – from 400 feet or 7,000 feet – showed us the outcome of non-controlled airspace and the missed potential to utilize drones. The new airspace control is all about drones and autonomous systems.”
As drone usage expands, Airwayz’s systems are becoming essential for both military and civilian operations.
EW & RF: The invisible battlefield
If drones have become the most visible symbols of modern warfare, the electromagnetic spectrum has become one of its least visible but most fiercely contested domains. Protecting communications, disrupting enemy networks, detecting radio-frequency (RF) emissions, and enabling resilient command-and-control systems are now essential functions across every branch of modern militaries.
Tenna Systems is one of Israel’s emerging leaders in RF analytics, spectrum monitoring, and EW support tools. Its technology helps militaries detect, classify, and respond to electronic threats in real time.
Originally founded as Tip & Cue Inc. just months before the October 7, 2023, massacre in southern Israel, Tenna Systems aims to build the world’s first dynamic, unified map of the electromagnetic spectrum. Its battlefield-tested software is designed to safeguard wireless-dependent systems across defense, aerospace, and mobility sectors – domains where connectivity has become both indispensable and dangerously vulnerable.
“For semi-autonomous systems, drones, munitions, maritime autonomous systems, ISR systems, and more, connectivity is their lifeline,” Tenna CEO Avner Bendheim told D&T. “We can’t afford to be blind.”
Ground robotics: the next frontier
While aerial drones dominate headlines, ground robotics is quietly becoming another important area of innovation. Modern armed forces face growing demand for unmanned systems capable of conducting reconnaissance, transporting equipment, inspecting hazardous environments, and supporting soldiers in contested terrain.
Robotican develops autonomous aerial and ground robotic systems designed for military, homeland security, and industrial applications. Its portfolio spans hybrid aerial-ground drones, unmanned ground vehicles, autonomous interceptors, and advanced simulation tools used for training and research.
The company’s technologies emphasize operational flexibility, allowing unmanned platforms to function in environments where conventional vehicles may face significant risks.
“It’s the era of robots,” Robotican CEO Hagai Balshai told D&T.
Shifters is emerging as one of Israel’s most promising ground-autonomy companies, building rugged unmanned vehicles designed to patrol borders, secure critical infrastructure, and operate in terrain where human presence is risky or resource-intensive. Its robots navigate complex environments using multisensor fusion, real-time obstacle detection, and GPS-denied autonomy – capabilities that make them reliable in the kinds of contested zones where traditional UGVs struggle.
Shifters’ main solutions are TRUST – Tactical Robot for Unmanned Safety & Security Tasks – a family of rugged AI-native autonomous quadruped robots, and RITA – Robotic Intent to Action – a software stack that powers TRUST with four layers: locomotion, navigation, perception, and action.
“The first asset into a dangerous environment should increasingly be a robot, not a person,” CEO Ofer Ballin told D&T.
Looking down from space
Israel's defense ecosystem extends well beyond the atmosphere. Satellite imagery, communications, and space-based intelligence have become indispensable components of modern military operations, supporting everything from strategic planning to disaster response.
ImageSat International specializes in satellite imagery and geospatial intelligence services, delivering analytical products that assist governments and commercial organizations in monitoring developments around the world.
High-resolution imagery, combined with increasingly sophisticated analytics, enables decision-makers to identify changes, monitor infrastructure, and support intelligence assessments with greater speed. Operating high-resolution imaging satellites and providing intelligence services to governments and commercial clients, its capabilities give Israel strategic reach far beyond its borders.
Orbit Technologies, meanwhile, develops advanced communications systems for maritime, airborne, and satellite applications. As military operations become increasingly networked across domains, secure and reliable communications remain essential to ensuring that information collected from space can be transmitted rapidly to commanders on the ground.
The continued expansion of commercial space capabilities also reflects another defining trend: Technologies once reserved for major governments are increasingly being developed by agile private companies capable of serving both defense and civilian customers.
The next chapter of Israel's defense industry
The rise of Israel's defense-tech ecosystem is not simply a story about start-ups. It’s about how an established defense industry has adapted to a rapidly changing technological landscape.
Rather than replacing the legacy primes, the start-ups are expanding the country's innovation capacity. The primes continue to provide manufacturing expertise, certification, systems integration, and global customer relationships, while start-ups contribute speed, software, and highly specialized technologies that can evolve far more rapidly than traditional hardware programs.
Warfare is becoming increasingly autonomous, data-driven, and dependent on commercial innovation. Space and cyber domains are now as central as land, sea, and air. The ability to iterate quickly – to update software, adapt tactics, and deploy new systems – often matters more than the size of a nation’s arsenal.
Recent industry mapping has shown that Israel’s defense-tech sector has nearly doubled in size since October 7, growing from roughly 160 companies in 2024 to over 330 active start-ups today. And those start-ups have had orders that have reached approximately $330 million in exports – representing double the amount registered in the same period of 2025.
“Defense-tech is part of the State of Israel's unique advantage, built on combat-proven capabilities that Israeli talent has successfully demonstrated on the battlefield time and again,” said Defense Ministry Director-General Maj.-Gen. (res.) Amir Baram.
For a country known as the “Start-Up Nation,” the surge is striking, and for the defense establishment, it is becoming indispensable.
Israel is now the Defense-Tech Nation.

Hiking routes in Paran Regional Brigade sector opens to hikers during holidays, IDF announces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
06:38:26 UTC
15:38:26 KST

Route 10 in the Paran Regional Brigade sector near the western border will open to hikers for the holidays, starting on Friday, the IDF announced.
For Rosh Hashanah, the route will open between Ezuz and Har Harif from 8:30 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. on Friday and between the Bar-Lev Lookout and the 10/12 Checkpoint from 8:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. on Saturday and Sunday.
For the Sukkot holiday, the route between Ezuz and Har Harif will be open from 8:30 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. on September 25. Additionally, the area from the Bar-Lev Lookout to the 10/12 Checkpoint will be open from 8:30 am to 4:00 p.m. from September 26 to October 3.
To enter the routes, you must present an ID card and register at the entrance. No prior coordination is required.
Training exercises to continue in the south and north
The IDF emphasized that training exercises in live-fire zones in the south and the north will continue over the weekends, and those areas will remain closed to hikers.
The public is urged to avoid restricted areas to allow security forces to continue carrying out their missions.

Thai PM Anutin under fire over US$90,000 amulet linked to disgraced monk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
06:31:06 UTC
15:31:06 KST

Thai PM Anutin’s US$90,000 amulet back in spotlight after disgraced monk’s arrest
Photos have resurfaced of the prime minister wearing the rare pendant as a senior abbot is disrobed and arrested for embezzlement
The photos were taken in October 2023 while Anutin – then serving as deputy prime minister and interior minister – was leading a group of Bhumjaithai Party MPs to watch the hit horror-comedy The Undertaker, local outlet ThaiRath reported. Anutin publicly displayed the Thai Buddhist amulet to reporters, praising it as an example of Thai “soft power”.
The amulet in question is a rare 2006 Jatukam Ramathep gold edition from the collectible Nuea Duang (Elevating Fate) series, valued at around 3 million baht (US$90,700). Produced by Wat Phutthaisawan in Ayutthaya province, the pendant is prized among disciples and collectors who believe it brings good fortune, wealth and elevated social status.
The item returned to national headlines after the arrest of the temple’s abbot early Thursday morning.
Phra Wachirayan Wi, also known as Luang Pho Atichot Dhammawaro, was arrested on allegations of embezzling over 92 million baht from the temple, according to The Nation. Authorities also detained Punyawee “Ae” Rungrueang, a 47-year-old lay follower believed to be the 66-year-old monk’s romantic partner.
CCTV footage from inside the abbot’s private quarters showed the pair engaging in sexual acts on a dining table inside the temple compound, Bangkok Post reported. A group of the monk’s followers had given the videos to police, saying they “could no longer tolerate his behaviour”.

General Staff: Russia has lost 1,503,880 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
06:30:18 UTC
15:30:18 KST

Ukrainian soldiers of the 47th Separate Mechanized Brigade, operating under the call signs "Mahura" and "Hrek", return to the battalion command post after visiting forward infantry positions near the border with Russia in Sumy Region, Ukraine, on Aug. 28, 2026. (Kostiantyn Liberov/Libkos/Getty Images)
Russia has lost around 1,503,880 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Sept. 11.
The figure includes 1,490 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,441 tanks, 25,312 armored combat vehicles, 147,211 vehicles and fuel tanks, 49,516 artillery systems, 2,109 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,622 air defense systems, 441 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,573 unmanned ground systems, 510,130 aerial drones, 5,103 cruise missiles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to a lot more missing in action (MIAs).

MAD Reveals Design to Transform 1923 Warehouse Into Danshuis in Rotterdam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

MAD, the architecture studio founded by Ma Yansong, has revealed the designs for Danshuis, a new dance center planned for Rotterdam, the Netherlands. Located on a landmark site in the city's historic docklands, adjacent to the Fenix Museum of Migration, also designed by MAD, the project is expected to open in 2030. The 9,500-square-meter center will transform an Art Deco warehouse dating from 1923 on the south bank of the River Maas. Planned as a center for the production, development, and practice of dance across different styles, Danshuis aims to bring together professional and amateur programs for different ages and levels of experience.
The project will introduce 14 dance studios alongside an open podium, gym, exhibition space, and café. A rooftop Salle des Fêtes will accommodate large-scale public programs, while providing views across Rotterdam's historic harbor. The building's different levels will be connected by a vertical foyer extending through the structure and linking the main spaces with the rooftop venue. Extensive outdoor areas are also planned along the riverfront. The design positions movement and public activity as key elements of the building's relationship with its surroundings, creating a connection between Danshuis and the adjacent Fenix Museum.
The plans are being developed by Rotterdam-based Droom en Daad Foundation, which has been involved in several cultural developments in the city, including the Fenix Museum of Migration, which opened in 2025. The center will provide spaces for dance education, production, rehearsal, performance, exhibitions, and public programming, with the aim of connecting local communities and international dance professionals within a single venue.

"Movement goes beyond architecture, becoming part of the character of the district. The beauty of human movement and the moments of dance will resonate with Fenix, creating a continuous dialogue between the two," said Ma Yansong, founder and principal partner of MAD. The design extends the cultural program already established around the Fenix Museum, adding a building centered on movement and performance to the waterfront district.
Other recent project news include Stefano Boeri Architetti's winning proposal for approximately 190 affordable rental apartments in Ibiza, AART's competition-winning design for a 1,300-square-meter underground extension to Copenhagen's Rosenborg Castle, and MVRDV's newly revealed WOMA development in Miami's Wynwood Norte. UN meeting on Iran nuclear file abuse of process
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
06:29:15 UTC
15:29:15 KST

Gholamhossein Darzi, Iran's chargé d'affaires at the UN, made the remarks in a letter to France's permanent representative, which holds the Security Council presidency this month. He said the meeting on what is called the "1737 Committee's activity" is a clear abuse of the Council's procedure and authority.
Darzi said Iran's position is clear, continuous and formally registered in official correspondence with the Secretary-General and the Council president. He said Resolution 2231 expired on 18 October 2025, and that from that date, all provisions, measures and restrictions related to the nuclear issue were permanently terminated. The Security Council ended its consideration of Iran's nuclear issue, and the "non-proliferation" agenda item was removed from the Council's agenda.
He said the so-called snapback mechanism was never triggered by the three European countries because they lacked the legal standing to invoke it, having failed to meet their own obligations under the JCPOA and Resolution 2231.
Darzi said the root causes of the current situation lie primarily in the illegal attacks by the United States and the Israeli regime against Iran's peaceful, safeguarded nuclear facilities. Over the past two years, while Iran was moving actively and in good faith on the path of negotiation and diplomacy, the U.S. and the Israeli regime carried out illegal and criminal acts of aggression against Iran's civilian infrastructure, including its safeguarded nuclear facilities. These, he said, constitute acts of aggression and flagrant violations of the UN Charter and the peremptory prohibition on the use or threat of force.
He said the repeated accusations against Iran's nuclear programme are political. Iran has been a committed member of the NPT since 1970, and its nuclear programme has been under extensive IAEA supervision for nearly 25 years. The agency has never reported any diversion of nuclear material in Iran. That record should be evaluated objectively and impartially, he said.
Darzi said the failure to properly address illegal attacks on Iran's safeguarded nuclear facilities, including in the IAEA Board of Governors' recent resolution, raises serious concerns about the agency's institutional balance and credibility. Political pressure cannot replace an objective assessment of safeguards.
He said the non-consensual resolution adopted by the IAEA Board of Governors on 9 September 2026 was driven by U.S. and E3 political considerations and lacks the requirements of objectivity and impartiality. Like previous resolutions, it remained silent on the illegal and criminal attacks by the U.S. and the Israeli regime on Iran's safeguarded nuclear facilities.
Darzi said Security Council meetings and procedures must not be abused to raise political or unproven accusations against member states, or to provide political cover for illegal actions. Formal and procedural action alone cannot lend legitimacy to unsupported claims.
Iran called on the Security Council to fully abide by the UN Charter and international law, and to reject opportunistic and deliberate attempts by the U.S. and some members to politicise or instrumentalise its procedures, meetings and mechanisms.

China Focus: Global experts chart cooperation on cultural heritage digitization
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:29:02 CST
15:29:02 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- A diverse cohort of officials, scholars and industry leaders from more than 20 countries and regions gathered in Beijing to discuss a common challenge: how to harness digital technology to preserve cultural heritage through collaborative efforts.
The 8th International Symposium on Cultural Heritage Conservation by Digitization (CHCD) kicked off on Wednesday in the capital. The four-day event was hosted by Tsinghua University, which has been exploring digital heritage since its pioneering "Digital Yuanmingyuan (Old Summer Palace)" project in 1998.
"Science history tells us that landmark breakthroughs rarely happen at the center of a discipline -- they emerge where disciplines collide," said Bai Benfeng, vice president of Tsinghua University. "Cultural heritage digitization is exactly such a crossroads. It needs deep roots in history, archaeology, architecture and the arts, alongside continuous advances in computing, artificial intelligence (AI) and spatial information technology."
Launched as a joint initiative in 2010, the CHCD has continued to broaden and deepen its international exchanges and cooperation, Bai added.
Greece participated as the guest country of honor for this year's symposium. Over the past two decades since China and Greece established a comprehensive strategic partnership, bilateral cooperation in cultural heritage and other fields has become increasingly substantive.
In 2021, the National Archaeological Museum in Athens launched a digital Terracotta Warriors exhibition during the China-Greece Year of Culture and Tourism. The following year, "RE Olympia," a China-Greece cultural exchange exhibition in Beijing, brought the ancient Olympic civilization to Chinese audiences through cutting-edge digital technology.
Building on this momentum, 2024 saw the signing of the Sino-Hellenic Digital Heritage Joint Laboratory at the 7th CHCD by top heritage research institutions from both countries -- the first international joint laboratory dedicated to digital heritage.
That same year, Konstantinos Eleftheriadis, director of the Institute of Nuclear and Radiological Sciences and Technology, Energy and Safety at Greece's National Centre for Scientific Research (NCSR) Demokritos, joined a Greek scholars' delegation on a visit to Beijing's Shougang Park, a flagship example of adaptive reuse for industrial heritage in China.
He hopes to apply the digital technologies developed at Shougang to Greece's GRR1 research nuclear reactor, a key piece of the country's nuclear energy industrial heritage. "Our challenge is how to preserve, document and showcase the historical and technological heritage of the nuclear reactor over the past decades. It deserves to be better understood by the public," he said.
His wish came true at this year's symposium, where the joint laboratory's flagship project was unveiled -- the Digital Revitalization Project of NCSR's GRR1 Nuclear Energy Industrial Heritage -- marking a major step forward in bilateral cooperation from institutional framework-building to tangible project implementation.
"We are proud not only because this joint laboratory has yielded significant results and is attracting more partners, but also because Greece and China have more than one partnership to showcase in this field," said Evgenios Kalpyris, ambassador of Greece to China.
The symposium also included a special session focused on Greece, where Chinese and Greek experts discussed and shared experiences on precision heritage mapping, digital twin applications, and smart heritage information systems.
During a separate session, Fulvio Rinaudo, president of CIPA (Comité International de la Photogrammétrie Architecturale) Heritage Documentation and professor at the Polytechnic University of Turin, spoke about the challenge of documenting cultural heritage in the age of AI. "The strongest future is not AI replacing human intelligence (HI), but HI and AI working as a cognitive partnership," he said.
The professor noted that HI brings purpose, ethics, empathy and judgment, while AI contributes speed, scale, memory and pattern recognition. "Together, they enable augmented intelligence," he added, urging young people to "study the theory more deeply to be able to spot errors and correct them."
A signing ceremony for a China-Italy digital cultural tourism collaboration was also held during the symposium, with the Xanadu Site in China's northern Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region serving as the central cultural anchor of the initiative. Italian explorer Marco Polo (1254-1324) described Xanadu in his book "The Travels of Marco Polo." The site was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2012.
As early as June last year, the Tsinghua Heritage Institute for Digitalization, one of the CHCD's executive organizers, signed a memorandum of cooperation with Civita, an Italian company specializing in cultural exhibitions and museum management, to deepen bilateral collaboration in digital heritage. The partnership involves inviting Italian experts to serve as technical advisors and curatorial consultants for the digital recreation of Yuanmingyuan's grandeur, as well as using digital technology to showcase Italian culture and art at Shougang Park.
"Cultural heritage is fragile. Digital technology can help ensure its sustainable transmission and preservation, giving traditional cultural heritage new vitality and greater international reach," said Elisa Messina, cultural attache at the Italian Embassy in China.
Liu Yuzhu, chairman of the China Foundation for Cultural Heritage Conservation, was also involved in China-Greece digital heritage exchanges in the early years and is pleased to see the joint laboratory moving steadily forward.
"I have also witnessed China-Italy cooperation on the restitution of lost cultural relics. In the future, both sides can further explore 'digital return' as a way to comprehensively document and present dispersed artifacts," he said, adding that the foundation will step up support for international exchanges in heritage digitization and promote mutual learning between China and other countries.
"The protection of cultural heritage is no longer a purely local matter or the responsibility of any single country," said Ashraf Al-Azzazi, secretary-general of Egypt's Supreme Council of Culture. "It has become a shared responsibility of humanity, requiring concerted efforts, the exchange of knowledge, and stronger cooperation among countries around the world."
He believes that cooperation among great civilizations such as China, Egypt, Greece and Austria "can provide the foundation for building a shared global model for the protection of human heritage, one that makes technology an instrument for bringing peoples closer together, rather than merely a means of technological advancement." ■

Economic Watch: Smart, digital transformation revitalizes China's old industrial base
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:28:53 CST
15:28:53 KST

SHENYANG, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- A four-legged inspection robot showcased its agility to navigate challenging terrain as it effortlessly scaled a steep slope, while another robot fitted with flexible, articulated arms demonstrated tasks designed for hazardous high-voltage industrial environments.
The robots, built and displayed by Nanjing-based YIJIAHE Technology Co., Ltd., were among the exhibits drawing attention at the 2026 Global Industrial Internet Conference in Shenyang, capital of northeast China's Liaoning Province.
The three-day event, which concluded on Thursday, brought together guests from political, business, academic and other sectors to discuss innovation and development of the industrial internet. Powered by technologies involving 5G and AI, the industrial internet connects people, machines and other production resources, allowing manufacturers to better coordinate and optimize production.
Northeast China is one of the country's traditional industrial bases, with deep industrial roots and a well-established industrial system. The region also faces challenges in upgrading equipment and shifting growth drivers. In recent years, smart and digital transformation has become an important part of its efforts to upgrade the manufacturing sector.
The opportunities created are attracting companies from outside the region.
YIJIAHE, headquartered in Nanjing, east China's Jiangsu Province, established its Northeast Asia international innovation center in Shenyang last month, focusing on the development of intelligent robots for healthcare, power and firefighting.
"Liaoning boasts a wide range of industrial scenarios," said Zhang Jiachun, head of solutions at the company. "We hope to explore diversified real-world applications here and support the smart and digital transformation of the old industrial base."
Local companies are also tapping into Liaoning's industrial resources. At the conference, the Liaoning branch of China Mobile displayed industrial large models for sectors that include petrochemicals, electric power and equipment manufacturing.
Factories across Liaoning have accumulated large amounts of production data over the years, much of which has yet to be fully utilized, according to Tang Dianbo, deputy head of the company's industrial innovation research institute.
At Genertec Shenyang Machine Tool Co., Ltd., AI is being applied directly to machining. With its self-developed numerical control system, 5G private network and industrial internet platform, AI can fine-tune the machining process in real time based on changes in materials and tool wear, automatically correct machining errors and provide early warnings of potential equipment problems.
The transformation is not limited to heavy industry. At Dayang Group Co., Ltd. in Liaoning's port city of Dalian, after customers upload body measurement, fabric selection and pattern design through the company's industrial internet platform for customized clothing, its system generates production instructions and enables the production line to switch between different products with minimal adjustments.
By linking measurements, design, cutting and production data, customized orders can move through the same production system, allowing the company to combine large-scale production with personalized demand.
"Before the digital upgrade, even the most experienced pattern makers needed around two hours to turn measurements into a pattern. The process now takes just two seconds," said Hu Dongmei, general manager of the company, adding that a customized suit can now be completed in as few as three days.
Similar applications are emerging across Liaoning, with major manufacturers working with local software service providers in areas such as equipment-failure prediction, adaptive optimization of machining processes and intelligent quality control in steel production.
In April, the province launched a three-year action plan for the smart and digital transformation of manufacturing, aiming to develop more than 600 industrial 5G private network projects and cultivate 150 provincial-level industrial internet platforms by the end of 2028.
Similar policy support has been introduced elsewhere in northeast China. In Jilin Province, financial incentives are provided for smart and digital transformation projects, while Heilongjiang Province has organized experts to offer one-on-one assessments for enterprises, while helping to connect companies with digital service providers.
The regional push is part of China's wider development of the industrial internet. Data from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology shows that the country's core industrial internet industry exceeded 1.6 trillion yuan (about 236 billion U.S. dollars) in 2025, while the number of industrial 5G private networks topped 26,000.
The industrial internet is now applied across all major sectors in China, with 100 advanced 5G-enabled factories meeting global leading standards, according to the ministry. These facilities reported a 25 percent increase in average production capacity, a 21 percent improvement in product quality and a 19 percent reduction in operating costs.
A think tank report released at the conference said northeast China's experience in applying smart and digital technologies to its well-established heavy industrial system could provide pointers for the upgrading of other traditional industrial cities in China and offer insights for similar industrial regions elsewhere in the world. ■

MACAO, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- Shenzhen municipal government issued 1 billion yuan (approximately 147.6 million U.S. dollars) in offshore sustainability bonds in China's Macao Special Administrative Region on Thursday, the Monetary Authority of Macao (AMCM) said.
The three-year bonds, offered to professional investors, carry a coupon rate of 1.41 percent. The issue was oversubscribed, it said.
Proceeds will fund water management, health care and other projects. The bonds received pre-issuance certification from the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency.
The sale marked Shenzhen's second consecutive year of issuing offshore yuan-denominated government bonds in Macao and its first offering there of sustainability bonds themed around the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area.
The AMCM noted the sale reflected closer financial cooperation between Shenzhen and Macao. It said the issuance would help attract more issuers to Macao's bond market and support green and sustainable finance in the Greater Bay Area.
Macao will continue developing its bond market under its third five-year plan as part of efforts to develop its financial sector and diversify its economy, it added. ■

Australia records 710,980 short-term visitor arrivals in July

15:28:36 KST

CANBERRA, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- Australia recorded 710,980 short-term visitor arrivals in July 2026, down 4.3 percent from the same month a year earlier, official data showed on Friday.
The number of short-term visitor arrivals was 10 percent lower than the pre-COVID level recorded in July 2019, according to data released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).
New Zealand was the largest source of visitors, accounting for 18.9 percent of all short-term visitor arrivals, followed by China and the United States, the ABS said.
The state of New South Wales recorded the highest number of short-term visitor arrivals among Australia's states and territories, with 247,410 trips, while the island state of Tasmania recorded the fewest, at 4,320, statistics showed.
Meanwhile, more than 1.25 million short-term resident return trips were recorded in July, an increase of 3.8 percent from a year earlier and 11.4 percent above the July 2019 level, the department said.
Indonesia was the most popular destination for Australian residents returning from short-term overseas trips, accounting for 15.1 percent of all returns, followed by New Zealand and the United Kingdom, it said. ■

====================================================================================================

Across China: Dinosaur fossil found deep underground in drill core in north China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:28:34 CST
15:28:34 KST

This undated file photo provided by Xing Lida, a dinosaur expert from China University of Geosciences (Beijing), shows a dinosaur fossil unearthed inside a drill core from a copper mineral resources survey in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. (Xinhua)
BEIJING, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- Scientists have discovered a dinosaur fossil buried hundreds of meters underground, not at a traditional excavation site but inside a drill core from a copper mineral resources survey in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region.
A research team of members from the nuclear industry and paleontology research institutions published the finding online Thursday in the journal Earth History and Biodiversity. According to the study, the dinosaur bones were found 473.2 meters down in a drill core in 2023. They were preserved in the upper part of the Bayan Gobi Formation, a geological layer of ancient sediment dating to the Early Cretaceous, about 120 million years ago.
Dinosaur fossils found in drill cores are extremely rare worldwide, said co-author Xing Lida, a dinosaur expert from China University of Geosciences (Beijing). One of the most famous cases occurred in 1997, when an exploration well at the Snorre oil field in the northern North Sea struck a crushed limb bone in a drill core about 2,256 meters below the seabed. Scientists later identified it as a plant-eating dinosaur. The discovery showed that the area was then a vast alluvial plain crossed by rivers, not the seabed.
Like the Norwegian one, the fossil found in north China is "a reminder that drill cores deep underground, seemingly relevant only to mining, can also hold keys to the ancient world," Xing said.
According to the study, the specimen includes part of a rib, four tail vertebrae and six bony arches from the tail. The bones had not yet fused, suggesting the dinosaur was a juvenile when it died.
The research team then ran a detailed comparison of the new specimen's tail bones with those of more than 20 other bird-hipped dinosaurs. The tail bones turned out to look most like those of Psittacosaurus, a small plant-eating dinosaur known for its parrot-like beak. The dinosaur species lived in the Early Cretaceous of East Asia, measured about 1 to 2 meters long and walked on its hind legs. It is one of the most common dinosaurs in the region, with fossils found in China, Mongolia and Siberia.
However, because the fossil material is limited, the researchers did not list it to a specific genus or species. They left it as an unidentified bird-hipped dinosaur.
The specimen also has a surprising feature: a row of tiny holes on its tail bones. Such holes have not been reported before in other bird-hipped dinosaurs. The researchers think they were probably normal openings for blood vessels and nerves. But because the dinosaur may have been young, it is still unclear whether the holes were a sign of species differences, individual variation or a temporary stage of growth.
The Bayan Gobi Formation is an important Early Cretaceous dinosaur site in north China. Many fossils of different dinosaur species have been found there before. This new find offers fresh information about the range of body shapes and features of dinosaurs in the formation, Xing noted.
He added that the specimen was collected at the Inner Mongolia Museum of Natural History, and it will soon go on public display. ■
This image provided by Xing Lida, a dinosaur expert from China University of Geosciences (Beijing), shows a restoration drawing of the dinosaurs based on a fossil unearthed inside a drill core from a copper mineral resources survey in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. (Xinhua)

S. Korea-born giant panda cub named Shu Bao on 100th day
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:28:29 CST
15:28:29 KST

Giant panda cub Shu Bao is pictured at Everland in Yongin, South Korea, Sept. 11, 2026. A giant panda cub born in South Korea made its first public appearance on Friday at Everland, the country's largest theme park in Yongin, about 40 km south of the capital Seoul. Everland also announced the 100-day-old cub's name on the same day, naming it "Shu Bao." Shu Bao's parents, Le Bao and Ai Bao, arrived in South Korea in 2016 and began a 15-year stay at Panda World at Everland. (Xinhua/Yao Qilin)
SEOUL, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- A giant panda cub born in South Korea made its first public appearance on Friday at Everland, the country's largest theme park in Yongin, about 40 km south of the capital Seoul.
Everland also announced the 100-day-old cub's name on the same day, naming it "Shu Bao."
Kang Cheol-won, a giant panda keeper at Everland, said that following Fu Bao, Rui Bao and Hui Bao, Shu Bao is the fourth giant panda born in South Korea, expressing hope that it will bring joy to more people, just as its older sisters have done.
Visitor Jeong Da-hyeon said she had been following the growth of the panda family and was delighted to witness the arrival of a new member.
Shu Bao's parents, Le Bao and Ai Bao, arrived in South Korea in 2016 and began a 15-year stay at Panda World at Everland.
Shu Bao was born on June 3, weighing 171 grams. It is the third successful natural breeding of giant pandas in South Korea, following the birth of Fu Bao in 2020 and twin cubs Rui Bao and Hui Bao in 2023. ■

Video: Is Google's €13bn investment good news for Finland?
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
09:28:00 EEST
15:28:00 KST

Earlier this week, search engine giant Google unveiled its plans to invest some 13 billion euros in Finland over the next two years.
The money will be used to build data centres as well as supporting infrastructure in three different locations around the Oulu and Kajaani regions, and the outlay represents Google's largest single investment in Europe to date.
Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo (NCP) lauded the move, telling a press conference on Wednesday that the expansion of Google's operations in Finland will create thousands of jobs and "generate significant tax revenues for municipalities and central government".
According to Google's own figures, the construction phase alone will "contribute an annual average of 3.6 billion euros to Finland's GDP and support more than 37,000 jobs nationwide".
Sakari Lähdemäki, a senior researcher at economic research think tank Etla, described Google's projected figures as "optimistic" in an interview with Yle. He also questioned the long-term benefit for Finland's jobs market.
"With data centres, the fear has been that they do employ people during the construction phase, but after that they are quite automated, and thus the employment effect later remains smaller," Lähdemäki noted.
Aside from the economic effects, data centres in general have become a controversial topic in many parts of the world, as critics say they drain local resources and exacerbate the climate crisis.

====================================================================================================

Germany's connection to the September 11 attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
06:26:00 UTC
15:26:00 KST

Germany's connection to the 9/11 attacks
September 11, 2026
"This day has changed the world," German President Johannes Rau said. He had watched in shock as the burning twin towers of the World Trade Center collapsed in New York.
Nearly 3,000 people were killed on September 11, 2001, when Islamist terrorists hijacked four passenger planes and turned them into deadly weapons.
Eleven Germans among the 9/11 victims
Germany’s head of state struggled to find the right words: "We do not know what political or social consequences what happened today will have — what we have watched unfold on our television screens in shock, barely able to comprehend or even reflect on it."
It soon emerged that the victims include people from 92 countries, among them 11 Germans.
The following day, a rapidly spreading rumor was confirmed: Three of the four suspected hijackers had recently lived in Hamburg. The Islamist terrorists were thought to have been led by Egyptian-born Mohammed Atta, who had come to the northern German city in the early 1990s to study.
Mohammed Atta and the Hamburg cell
At some point, the young man became radicalized, particularly at Hamburg's Al-Quds Mosque, which was later closed by German security authorities. He spent the final three years of his life in an apartment shared with two other suspected attackers in the Harburg district.
The so-called Hamburg terrorist cell was believed to have included six men, among them Moroccan national Mounir al-Motassadeq. He was charged as an accomplice in the world's first trial related to the September 11, 2001, attacks. In 2003, the Hanseatic Higher Regional Court sentenced him to the maximum 15-year prison term for aiding and abetting thousands of murders and for membership in a terrorist organization.
German-born Murat Kurnaz held at Guantanamo
After serving his sentence, al-Motassadeq was deported to his native Morocco. Another suspected attacker from the circle around pilot Mohammed Atta was Ramzi Binalshibh, who was born in Yemen and had been held without trial at the US detention facility at Guantanamo Bay since 2006.
The United States detained hundreds of suspects at the prison, which human rights groups and international bodies have described as contrary to international law. Among them was Murat Kurnaz, who was born in Bremen. He was released in August 2006 after nearly five years without evidence establishing his involvement in the terrorist attacks.
Kurnaz later recounted his experience in a book that was adapted into a film in 2013.
Frank-Walter Steinmeier before investigative committee
Meanwhile, investigative committees in the German Bundestag sought to determine why Kurnaz and other suspects had wrongly come under the scrutiny of US and German intelligence agencies. Among those called to testify was then-Foreign Minister and current German PresidentFrank-Walter Steinmeier.
At the center of the inquiry was the question of why German security authorities rejected the possible return in 2002 of the German-born detainee, who held a Turkish passport.
"No one doubts, and neither do I, that Mr. Kurnaz suffered terribly in Guantanamo," Steinmeier said. "That is why we also sought to ensure that he was treated in accordance with the rule of law. But at the same time, please understand that we were also obliged to ensure security in our own country."
Gerhard Schröder voiced 'unconditional solidarity'
The Kurnaz case illustrated the pressure on German policymakers in the aftermath of the terrorist attacks in the US. Chancellor Gerhard Schröder addressed parliament the following day.
"Yesterday, September 11, 2001, will go down in history as a dark day for all of us," the Social Democrat said.
He said he had expressed to the American president the deeply felt condolences of the entire German people.
"I also assured him of Germany's unconditional — I emphasize: unconditional — solidarity," Schröder said.
Germany, he added, would offer the US any assistance they requested, "of course, also by identifying and pursuing those responsible for and behind these despicable attacks."
Germany's Bundestag passes anti-terror laws
Schröder's remarks set the tone and opened the door for a series of tougher laws. Just weeks after the attacks, the governing coalition of Social Democrats and Greens unveiled its first so-called security package, involving more funding, more personnel as well as greater powers for police and intelligence agencies.
Religious organizations that had previously been granted special protection could now be banned like other associations if their activities were directed against the Basic Law, Germany's constitutional order based on freedom and democracy, or if they pursued other criminal aims. Less than four months after the terrorist attacks in the US, Germany's Anti-Terrorism Act took effect.
Intelligence agencies were given access to personal data held by banks, airlines and telecommunications companies. Immigration laws were tightened.
Through data-mining searches, in which large amounts of data were cross-checked without any specific suspicion, authorities sought to identify so-called sleeper agents — people like Mohammed Atta from the Hamburg terrorist cell, who had not been identified by security agencies in time.
The Federal Constitutional Court brought an end to the legally questionable practice. Such searches were permissible only when there was a specific threat, the court said in a 2006 ruling. Seven years later, Germany's highest court also ruled that parts of the country's anti-terrorism database were unconstitutional.
Germany joins the war in Afghanistan
The Islamist terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, also had far-reaching and lasting military consequences. The US launched attacks on the Taliban in Afghanistan as early as October 2001. The Taliban had refused to hand over Osama bin Laden, the head of the al-Qaeda terrorist network and suspected mastermind of the attacks.
Germany joined the US-led war in December 2001. The conflict lasted 20 years and ended in August 2021 with the Taliban's return to power. Around 3,600 soldiers from the international forces were killed, including 59 members of Germany's Bundeswehr. Three German police officers also died.
The words spoken by German President Johannes Rau on Sept. 11, 2001, in the aftermath of the Islamist terrorist attacks in the US, still resonate today: "This day has changed the world."
This article was originally published in German.

Ukraine, Canada sign declaration on 100-year partnership
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
09:25:38 EEST
15:25:38 KST

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney signed a Declaration on a 100-Year Partnership, setting out the two countries' intent to elevate bilateral relations to a comprehensive strategic partnership.
This is according to a joint statement by the Canadian prime minister and the Ukrainian president, posted Thursday on the Canadian government's website.
The leaders affirmed that Ukraine's security is an integral part of Euro-Atlantic security and that Ukraine's future lies in NATO, and stressed the importance of continued Ukrainian reforms on the path to full EU and NATO membership.
"Canada will continue to meet Ukraine’s most pressing military needs and sustain Operation UNIFIER, now extended to 2029. Canada will continue to strengthen Ukraine’s Armed Forces, with a particular focus on urgently needed air defence capabilities and interceptors, while continuing to provide training, military equipment, ammunition, and other critical military support. The two countries will deepen cooperation in intelligence, cyber defence, counter-drone and electronic disruption capabilities, and in countering hybrid threats and foreign information manipulation. Canada will continue to work with partners on a framework of politically and legally binding security guarantees to prevent any future aggression by the Russian Federation." the statement said.
Canada and Ukraine will also deepen cooperation in intelligence, cyber defense, counter-drone and electronic warfare capabilities, as well as in countering hybrid threats and foreign information manipulation.
The countries will establish a long-term defense-industrial partnership for the joint production of unmanned systems, counter-drone capabilities, electronic warfare equipment and ammunition. The partnership will build on the Letter of Intent on joint production signed in Kyiv on August 24, 2025, and will include research and technology transfer.
The two sides will also facilitate predictable procurement of jointly produced equipment and will work with partners to establish a Defense, Security and Resilience Bank.
Canada will also maintain and increase economic pressure on Russia, and will work with G7 partners to explore ways of using the full value of Russia's frozen sovereign assets for Ukraine's benefit.
"There can be no decisions about Ukraine without Ukraine," the declaration states.
The two sides also agreed to work toward concluding a comprehensive Strategic Partnership Agreement built on three pillars: defense innovation, economic growth and recovery, and people-to-people ties.

PrivatBank launches subscription service for customers
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
09:23:44 EEST
15:23:44 KST

PrivatBank has launched a "Subscriptions" service for retail customers, offering a free basic tier and two paid packages with additional terms on banking and partner services, the bank's press service said.
Customers can choose between the "Pryvat PRO" package, priced at UAH 129 a month, and "Spilna PRO," at UAH 297 a month, the latter designed for up to five users. The first month of "Pryvat PRO" is free.
The free basic tier includes, among other things, no fee for transfers between the bank's cards for subscribers and free top-ups for payout cards linked to the service.
The paid packages include cashback and discounts on select digital and postal services, fuel, supermarket purchases and medical services. For digital services, cashback of up to UAH 200 a month is offered, and for postal services, up to UAH 100. For fuel, an additional discount of up to UAH 3 per liter applies, with a monthly limit of up to 200 liters under the largest package.
The medical component includes up to five teleconsultations a month, emergency medical assistance, and a medical concierge service, with an annual limit of up to UAH 10,000 for "Pryvat PRO" and up to UAH 30,000 for "Spilna PRO."
For paid package holders, the bank has also set separate terms for using credit limits and an increased rate on funds held in "Envelopes" savings accounts, of up to 7% per annum.
According to PrivatBank, the combined benefit from using the service could reach UAH 1,000 a month, exceeding the subscription cost for 95% of active users.
PrivatBank said that in developing the service, it analyzed active customers' spending patterns: 91% buy groceries, 51% spend on medicine, 33% on postal services, 32% on digital services, and 26% on fuel.
"We created special offers specifically for these key categories, so you keep buying what you bought before, but with real savings," said Dmytro Musiienko, PrivatBank board member for retail business.
The bank will not automatically switch customers onto subscriptions. Customers can activate their chosen tier via Privat24 or at a branch, and can also select the relevant package when issuing or reissuing a card.
Under "Spilna PRO," the primary user can invite up to four additional people to the package.
PrivatBank is Ukraine's largest state-owned bank. According to the National Bank, the bank's total assets stood at UAH 979.31 billion as of August 1, 2026, or 22.7% of the sector's total.
For the first half of 2026, the bank had 18 million active retail customers, 13.7 million Privat24 users, and 950,000 business customers.

In the Verkhovna Rada, they propose continuing sessions in the shelter during air raids
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
09:22:37 EEST
15:22:37 KST

In the Verkhovna Rada, they propose continuing sessions in the shelter during air raids
Kyiv • UNN
Members of Parliament propose continuing plenary sessions in the shelter at 5 Hrushevskoho Street after 10 minutes of an air raid alert. Voting will be electronic.
A group of members of parliament proposes establishing a new working procedure for the Verkhovna Rada when an air raid alert is announced. In particular, after the alert is announced, lawmakers would have to go to a shelter, where they would continue voting electronically. UNN reports this with reference to Draft Resolution No. 16059.
Details
According to the draft resolution, in the event of an air raid alert and/or the receipt of information about an increased threat, it is planned to establish that the plenary session of the Verkhovna Rada will resume after a break and be held in the shelter of the building at 5 Hrushevskoho Street.
A plenary session that has already begun may be continued in the shelter 10 minutes after an air raid alert is announced or information about an increased threat is received, following an oral announcement by the presiding officer.
Voting on draft laws and draft resolutions is planned to be conducted using the electronic system.
If the air raid alert ends while agenda items are being considered during a plenary session in the shelter, their consideration may continue at that location until all agenda items have been considered.
As stated in the explanatory note, the systematic announcement of air raid alerts in Kyiv leads to the forced interruption of plenary sessions of the Verkhovna Rada, effectively creating a threat of paralysis of the legislative process.
Under Ukrainian law, during an air raid alert, members of parliament and employees of the Secretariat are required to immediately proceed to a safe shelter.
Regular lengthy breaks take up a significant amount of productive time needed for parliament to exercise its constitutional powers to ensure the country's defense capability, economic stability, and the protection of citizens. In view of this, there is an urgent need to regulate a mechanism for the uninterrupted operation of the Verkhovna Rada by allowing an ongoing plenary session to continue directly in a shelter equipped with security measures
Supplement
According to the resolution of the Verkhovna Rada "On Certain Issues Regarding the Organization of the Work of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine of the Ninth Convocation Under Martial Law," during martial law, the Verkhovna Rada of the ninth convocation operates in the format of a single plenary session that continues until the day martial law in Ukraine is terminated or lifted.
It should be noted that on September 1, the Verkhovna Rada opened a record-breaking 16th session.
Previously
Members of parliament began testing the voting system in the Verkhovna Rada’s shelter.

Several killed in Dutch coach crash in Swiss Alps

Several killed in Dutch coach crash in Swiss Alps
A Dutch tourist coach crashed in the southeastern Swiss Alps on Thursday afternoon, leaving several people dead and others injured, police say.
The Graubünden cantonal police have not provided a precise toll. A press conference is expected on Friday.
The coach, which belongs to the tour operator Oad, was carrying 48 passengers, the Dutch Federation of Travel Agencies (ANVR) told the AFP news agency.
All the passengers were Dutch citizens on a tour. The passengers had set off from the Netherlands on Monday and were on a day trip to Switzerland from Austria.
Coach hit crash barrier
The accident occurred at around 4:45 pm. The vehicle was travelling from Zernez towards Susch in canton Graubünden when it collided with the crash barrier. It then left the road and overturned on its side below the carriageway, said Roman Rüegg, spokesperson for the cantonal police, speaking to the media at the scene that evening.
Numerous emergency services were mobilised, including helicopters. A hotline has been set up for relatives and consulates in connection with the accident. The contact number is 081 256 56 56 at the Graubünden Cantonal Police operations centre.
Gateway to national park
Swiss President Guy Parmelin said he was “deeply shocked”. His thoughts are with the victims and their loved ones.
On the social media platform X, Parmelin also thanked the many rescue workers for their efforts. The relevant Swiss authorities will ensure that a comprehensive and thorough investigation is carried out to shed light on all the circumstances of the accident, Parmelin added.
Following the accident, the road between Zernez and Susch was closed. The police have not specified when this route might reopen. Zernez is the gateway to the Swiss national park, a vast, largely unspoilt Alpine area covering approximately 170 km².

Firefighters board burned Philippine ferry as 84 remain missing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
06:21:13 UTC
15:21:13 KST

The Philippine Coast Guard has discovered bodies aboard a ferry engulfed by fire, with the death toll expected to rise as dozens of people remain missing
Coast guard spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said on Friday that the bodies were found in the economy accommodation area of the M/V June Aster, which caught fire on Wednesday night during a voyage from Manila to the western province of Palawan.
Five people had been confirmed dead before the discovery, while 84 remained missing and 43 had been rescued.
“We can't provide exact numbers yet on what we saw today,” Cayabyab said in a phone call.
“We will be providing it once we conduct retrieval and recovery,” she added, saying a meeting was under way to determine the proper protocols for the operation.
Cayabyab confirmed that the entire ship had now been searched. Earlier on Friday, she told a radio station that the fire began in the cargo hold and swept through the vessel within seconds.
The ferry ran aground near the tourist hotspot of Coron, Palawan, after the blaze erupted.
Thick smoke, extreme heat delayed access
Earlier on Friday, firefighters boarded the vessel after thick smoke and extreme heat delayed access.
The coast guard revised the number of missing from 86 to 84 after verifying that two people listed on the manifest had not been aboard. A total of 43 people have been rescued.
The manifest listed 117 passengers and 17 crew members aboard the ferry.
Aerial footage showed a Coast Guard helicopter hovering above the burned ferry, whose upper decks were blackened by fire. While light smoke continued to rise from parts of the vessel, it was noticeably thinner than the thick plumes seen a day earlier. Two firefighters could be seen on an upper deck.
Richard Marceliano, one of the survivors, told GMA News he saw a small amount of smoke that quickly turned into a raging fire and spread through the ferry within seconds. He said he and other passengers spent nearly two hours floating in the sea before they were rescued.
Meanwhile, relatives of missing passengers gathered outside the Manila office of shipowner Atienza Inter-Island Ferries, seeking information after their calls to the company went unanswered.
Evelyn Umpad, 64, said she was waiting for news of her son and daughter-in-law, who had been travelling to Taytay in Palawan to buy land.
"We kept calling but nobody was answering. They took my number and said they would call back, but no one contacted us, so we came here ourselves to find out the situation," she said.
"My appeal is for them to take action and keep us updated."
The ferry company has said it is fully cooperating with government authorities investigating the incident.
Cause remains unclear
The Coast Guard has deployed five vessels and divers to the area, with army rescue boats, fishermen and private resort owners also helping in the search, which began on Wednesday night. Coast Guard spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said a larger vessel would also be deployed.
The cause of the blaze remains unclear. The ferry was nearing the end of its more than 20-hour voyage to Coron, a popular tourist destination in northern Palawan, when the fire broke out.
The Maritime Industry Authority (MARINA), citing survivors’ accounts, said two successive explosions were heard inside the vessel before the fire erupted.
The ferry had a capacity of 330 people and was also transporting cargo, including five motorcycles, an electric vehicle, a forklift and a pickup truck, according to the Coast Guard.
Ferries are a vital means of transport in the Philippines, an archipelago of more than 7,600 islands, where millions rely on boats to travel between provinces.
The country has a poor maritime safety record, with previous ferry disasters linked to overcrowding, rough weather and weak enforcement of safety regulations.

Researchers eye AI revolution in natural disaster forecasts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
06:20:24 UTC
15:20:24 KST

Swiss National Supercomputing Centre (CSCS) director Thomas Schulthess (R) discuss with professor of climate physics at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zurich (ETH Zurich) Reto Knutti next to the Alps supercomputer, at the CSCS, in Lugano, southern Switzerland, on August 27, 2026. (AFP Photo)
A revolution in forecasting natural disasters is underway, say researchers in Switzerland who are training AI models on vast troves of NASA climate data to produce potentially-lifesaving data at lightning speed.
They are feeding the NASA file stash into one of the world's most powerful supercomputers so artificial intelligence can speed up and expand vital weather and climate forecasting, and spot patterns scientists could not have seen.
AI models are increasingly used in weather and climate forecasting and for early detection of natural hazards.
As well as speed, they carry the promise of spotting previously imperceptible patterns in satellite and other data, potentially making it possible to flag in advance disasters like Nepal's devastating flood, which last month left thousands dead or missing.
But training such AI models requires vast amounts of high-quality climate and Earth observation data, and significant computing power.
Researchers at Switzerland's Federal Institute of Technology Zurich (ETH) say they now have both, after copying around 100 petabytes of publicly available NASA data onto servers adjacent to one of the world's most powerful supercomputers, known as Alps.
"This is a huge scientific opportunity," said Thomas Schulthess, an ETH computational physics professor and head of the Swiss National Supercomputing Centre (CSCS) in the southern city of Lugano.
"It's really enabling scientists to do things we would not even have thought of before," he said.
It took approximately a year to copy the roughly six billion NASA files onto servers connected to the supercomputer, said Reto Knutti, a climate physics professor who heads ETH's Center for Climate Systems Modeling (C2SM).
That is equivalent to around 20 million feature-length films in terms of data volume, or around a million times the storage on a typical computer.
Now the researchers are using the mass of information to develop AI models that can speed up and expand vital weather and climate forecasting.
"Data is essentially everything," Knutti said.
"The next step will be making sense of the data".
That is where the proximity to the massive computing power of Alps comes in, Schulthess said.
"It matters whether you can move the data within a few seconds or whether you have to wait days for the data to come," he said.
New AI-generated statistical models are far faster than the traditional process of using mathematically equations to simulate the complex processes taking place in the oceans and atmosphere.
There is "a revolution in weather forecasting," Knutti said, describing the statistical models as "really, really powerful" and "incredibly fast."
Instead of the hours traditionally needed to produce a forecast, a statistical model based on pattern recognition "can run a global weather forecast for multiple days — the whole globe — in a minute or so", he pointed out.
And while expensive to train, the models are "cheap to run," he said, meaning "you can do more iterations, maybe every few minutes, to see if some specific weather pattern exists."
"That allows us to do early warning systems to save lives."
