analysis
Hanson's overreach on Hastie kicks Liberals into gear
Pauline Hanson declared in a recent News24 documentary: "I don't back down."
This week, Ms Hanson and her party followed through with two high-risk demonstrations, heels firmly dug in.
In the face of demands from Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie, Ms Hanson refused to withdraw one of her Please Explain animated cartoons that depicts (in multiple mentions) the decorated former soldier as a "traitor".
On a very different front, One Nation is toughing out a controversy around Warren Pickering, its leader for the November Victorian election, after his admissions — following allegations from his former partner — of extensive drug use as a young man.
The battle with Mr Hastie is highly consequential not only for One Nation, but also for the Liberal Party.
Ms Hanson's animated cartoons, edgy and popular, have been among One Nation's savviest political tactics.
This one, however, not only went over the top but poked a political bear who — given his background in the SAS — defaults to fight, not flight, when his reputation is impugned.
Mr Hastie began on Wednesday by calling Ms Hanson (and One Nation's treasury spokesman Barnaby Joyce) "lying cowards"; by Thursday he was describing her as "weak and glass-jawed".
Ms Hanson and Mr Hastie have been targeting each other for months, with One Nation chasing Mr Hastie's Western Australian seat of Canning.
The party's recent win in the state by-election for Secret Harbour, mainly inside Canning, only intensified things.
One Nation's antagonism towards Mr Hastie is particularly driven by his giving evidence against Victoria Cross winner Ben Roberts-Smith in the latter's failed defamation case.
He'll probably have to do so again in the coming trial of Roberts-Smith, accused of war crimes in Afghanistan, where both men served.
Mr Hastie has previously publicly called out those Liberals inclined to accommodate the insurgent party, especially WA leader Basil Zempilas, in the by-election.
Loading
But this escalation of the Hanson-Hastie confrontation is changing the dynamic.
Several of Mr Hastie's Coalition colleagues quickly backed him.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said Ms Hanson should take down the video.
If the episode is pushing the Liberals together in their response to One Nation (although that may not last), it is also pointing to underlying divisions among the Hansonites.
Mr Joyce has been clearly uncomfortable. After saying on Wednesday he hadn't been aware of the offending cartoon, he later texted Mr Hastie, inviting him to make contact.
Mr Joyce has to do a lot of cleaning up after Ms Hanson, but this is too much.
Ms Hanson was on the back foot. Her line that she had not called Mr Hastie a traitor and respected his war service was an implausible defence.
She authorised the cartoon (which went live in July). Her claim this was just "satire" also didn't wash.
Regardless, Ms Hanson opened a new front against Mr Hastie on Thursday, with Ben Roberts-Smith in mind.
Referencing a 2024 change to Australia's war crimes legislation, which was backdated, Ms Hanson tweeted the law had passed on the votes "so we don't know where Hastie stood".
Journalists should ask Mr Hastie, "Do you support retrospectively changing criminal law to make prosecutions of veterans easier?"
She later tried unsuccessfully to move an amendment to the legislation in the Senate.
The latest polls have One Nation's national number strong; subsequent polling will indicate whether the party's supporters are concerned about the attacks on Mr Hastie.
On one level, the Victorian election is a side hustle for Ms Hanson; on another, it is a significant judgement moment.
So how to respond to the public revelations about Mr Pickering was an important strategic decision, especially for the party's national campaign director James Ashby, formerly Hanson's chief of staff.
As commentators have observed, if this had been a Labor or Liberal leader, they would probably have been on their bikes.
But One Nation, obviously previously aware of the allegations, was sticking by its man. In her not-backing-down mode, when asked about Mr Pickering, Ms Hanson said on Monday: "It is a personal situation. He said he denies the false allegations that have been made against him."
This dismissal wouldn't hold up.
By Tuesday, One Nation unveiled an elaborate response to the Pickering problem. Mr Pickering's story became one of redemption.
A news conference was called, with Mr Ashby, Mr Pickering, his daughter Jhett and his stepson Johnny.
Adopting the demeanour of a lawyer acting for his client, Mr Ashby outlined Mr Pickering's background with his former partner.
Mr Pickering then spoke about his past extensive drug habit and turning his life around. Johnny and Jhett supported him.
Mr Pickering, 43, told the media conference:
"I'm proud of the man I am today. I sure as hell would not have run for office four times in the last five years if I wasn't firmly in my convictions and comfortable with who I am today.
"I'd like to provide an example to people that intend to turn their lives around, that have maybe done it a little rough or made some mistakes when they were younger."
Apart from whatever appeal the redemption narrative might have, One Nation is seeking to cut through with the fact that after all his personal issues, the defence force accepted Mr Pickering and he served some years in it.
One Nation hardliners predict voters will be split over Mr Pickering, with his background putting off some people while others empathise with him.
Some Victorian Liberals fear Mr Pickering's story could increase the One Nation state vote.
Amid the pyrotechnics, One Nation this week challenged government and opposition on the policy front, releasing a plan to allow homebuyers and renters access to some of their superannuation.
This caught out the opposition, which has itself been flirting with potential changes to superannuation arrangements.
The government unsurprisingly hit the nuclear response button, projecting how much worse off future retirees would be under One Nation's plan.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers declared this was an "existential moment" for Australian superannuation.
Probably not quite that, but it's likely that how Australia's landmark superannuation scheme should operate will be one of the major issues in the 2028 election.
Michelle Grattan is a professorial fellow at the University of Canberra and chief political correspondent at The Conversation, where this article first appeared.

It's an odd time for Labor to play politics as usual with federal grants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
18:56:10 UTC
03:56:10 KST

analysis
It's an odd time for Labor to play politics as usual with federal grants
Standing inside the "Royal Marrickville" clubhouse, Anthony Albanese joked in front of a group of a few dozen supporters and some local media about his association with the club.
"I've got a couple of things I need to put on the record so that … people who oppose the club can put it online: I declare an interest," Albanese said to members in a video recorded back in 2019 by his one-time golf coach.
"I've been coming here for decades and using this club."
Before that video cuts off, the member for Grayndler begins another "confession": that despite his coach's best efforts, he hasn't become much of a golfer.
When the prime minister promised $6 million to the Marrickville Golf Club during the 2025 election campaign, it wasn't because someone at the club was slipping him a $20 note every fortnight.
And Albanese is not using his honorary membership, given 15 years ago and not declared, to skip the club's $1,100 annual fee to hit the links every weekend; the PM's preference for tennis is well known.
But his golf club was the only golf club on a list of 220 projects given public money — a place that he lived around the corner from and frequented, that hosted Labor candidate launches he joined, and to which he had promised money at least twice before — and, by his own words, had an "interest" in.
When there is such a clear relationship, and when Labor hand-picked the projects that got money from its "invitation-only" program, it is hard for the public to believe other worthy projects in seats not of interest to Labor are getting a fair go.
As old as ancient Greece
The Centre for Public Integrity's conclusion from its examination of that $560 million grant scheme under which the Marrickville Golf Club was funded was inescapable: Three-quarters of the money went to Labor-held seats, or close to 90 per cent of the whole program to safe Labor seats and marginals where the party was competitive.
The defence being mounted by Labor, apparently, is that it is fine for that $560 million to favour the party, because everybody does it sometimes.
"In elections, members of parliament, candidates running for election make promises. If you win, if you form government, then you fund those promises, and that's what this is," frontbencher Jason Clare said this week.
"I think this is probably as old as ancient Greece. You know, all politics is local."
The fact that this is same-old politics is why this matters.
Voters are rejecting a tradition as old as ancient Greece: spending public money on partisan interests.
There are half a dozen independent MPs who rode into parliament on a wave of desire for politics to be done differently, including on integrity issues like pork-barrelling.
There is a belief inside the major parties that independents are simply unhappy that there isn't enough room at the trough to stick their noses in, too, given they don't want grants abolished; just opened up to everyone.
And there is an argument that MPs, who are accountable, should make decisions, not faceless, disconnected bureaucrats in Canberra.
But the major parties also know there are a seat-flipping number of voters willing to turf out MPs seen as putting their own interests, or those of the party, ahead of the public.
That sentiment has handed Liberal heartland to teal MPs, and polls now say more than a quarter of voters are prepared to abandon the major parties for One Nation, some frustrated by a system they feel is stacked against them.
In 2019 and 2020, Labor pursued the Coalition's "sports rorts" relentlessly, an issue something Albanese said "stinks more than a bucket of prawn heads that you left out on a hot day".
It was a central campaign line of Labor's that it would "end the waste" and "end the rorts".
The government tightened the grant rules and guidelines, including a requirement that ministers approving grants hand over the decision to a colleague if the grant application was in their electorate.
That doesn't matter much if the projects were already identified and a funding amount committed before the list of projects ever reached the minister.
Sports grants cause trouble again — again
The $100 million sports grants scandal that engulfed the former Morrison ministry eventually forced the resignation of then-sports minister Bridget McKenzie, who had signed off on a grant to a gun club where she was an honorary member.
The senator said it was a membership worth about $30 and that she didn't know she had it. In the end, she agreed the "personal interest" breached the ministerial code.
More than 30 years ago, the Keating government kicked off the first "sports rorts affair", when its then-sports minister, Ros Kelly, could not explain the distribution of $30 million in sporting grants to marginal electorates.
Kelly's resignation followed her revelation that funding had been arranged using a shortlist made on a whiteboard in her office, of which there was no record since it had been wiped clean.
In both cases, the Keating and Morrison governments denied bias in the awarding of grants, which in both cases had been levelled by the auditor-general.
During Question Time on Wednesday, Albanese denied knowledge of his honorary membership, but he was also unapologetic about the grant to Marrickville Golf Club and grants to a women's health centre and women's shelter.
"I support every one of the grants as a local member, and I am proud to defend my electorate, the inner west of Sydney," he said.
"If you're a good local member, a whole lot of people will give you honorary membership of things. If you're a good local member who stands up for your electorate, that will occur," he later added.
Discussing the Centre for Public Integrity's report, its chair Anthony Whealy told the ABC he feared voters were becoming immune to pork-barrelling.
"I think that unfortunately Australians have now become almost anaesthetised to the problems of the improper allocation of public monies," the former justice said.
"It happens so often, it happens so frequently, and it's business as usual. I think we've got to jolt the public consciousness to say this isn't good enough, we don't want this, we want a proper system that's merit-based, transparent and accountable."
The Coalition drove an entertaining Question Time this week, pushing on the issue.
But it also planned to use the people's cash on local projects. Whether that would have been spent fairly won't be known, since the Coalition didn't win.
Albanese made that exact point in Question Time on Thursday.
"I looked through the list of Coalition election commitments from 2025, and there were over 1,000 projects worth $1.2 billion. I looked for anything in Grayndler and, of the thousand projects, there wasn't a single one in the inner west, not one."
The prime minister complained that the Coalition's promises would leave his seat out, while the Major and Local Community Infrastructure Program left 45 electorates off the list.
Some of the poorest seats in the country missed out on a grant, with no way to even ask for a slice of the $560 million pie.
It seems a messy way of doing things, where the people of Page must wait for Kevin Hogan to become PM, or the people in Wannon for Dan Tehan to take the top job, for grant money to swing back their way.
Pork-barrelling may not even work, according to Labor's own assistant minister Andrew Leigh.
A 2022 paper he co-authored examined the Coalition's "sports rorts", and found they had no significant effect on voter intentions, bringing seemingly no benefit to the Coalition.
Leigh and his co-author concluded pork-barrelling did not work, even if politicians believed it did.
What it did do, they said, was erode the public's trust.

El Niño fuels wildfires in Indonesia, sickening some 100,000 people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
18:55:25 UTC
03:55:25 KST

El Niño conditions are helping to fuel wildfires across Indonesia, leaving some 100,000 people ill or injured, according to the country’s health officials. This year’s looming El Niño is predicted to be among the most powerful or perhaps the strongest ever.
El Niño is a climate event associated with warming waters in the Pacific shifting toward the east—this affects global wind patterns and sea levels, fueling storms in some areas but also unusually small amounts of rain in others. This year's El Niño began to form in June. Because of where in the Pacific El Niño forms, Indonesia is often particularly affected.
A spokesperson for the country’s health ministry told media outlets on Thursday that, as of September 9, the number of people who had been treated for respiratory conditions tied to the fires had reached 113,336, more than double the case load since the start of the month, according to Reuters. More than 12.5 million people have been exposed to haze caused by the fires, officials said.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The fires are particularly dangerous to human health because they are concentrated in peatlands—these wetland ecosystems can generate higher levels of particulates and other harmful substances when they are burned. Meanwhile toxic haze has spread beyond Indonesia to Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines.
In addition to the health effects, the fires have also caused an enormous surge in carbon emissions from Indonesia, according to Fire Emissions Watch. The country has already accounted for 12.82 megatons of carbon emitted into the atmosphere by wildfires in 2026; that’s nearly 100 times as much as was emitted in all of 2025.
El Niño conditions have triggered massive wildfires in Indonesia in the past, including in 1997 and 2015. During the latter, smoke from more than 100,000 peatland fires led half a million people to be hospitalized for respiratory, eye and skin ailments.
The current severe drought conditions in Indonesia resemble those seen in 2015—another El Niño year—according to NASA data. That aridness allows the fires to spread in underground peat deposits more easily, and the drought is likely to continue until the rainy season begins in October or November.

How Russia Is Targeting Ukraine’s Food Chain, From Factories to Store Shelves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
18:54:14 UTC
03:54:14 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
How Russia Is Targeting Ukraine’s Food Chain, From Factories to Store Shelves
Russian strikes on Ukraine's food production and logistics are increasingly reaching supermarket shelves, where shortages have begun to surface. What began as attacks on distant warehouses is now registering at the checkout, in thinner produce aisles and in new limits on how much shoppers can buy.
The retail chain ATB, among Ukraine's largest supermarket networks, has introduced temporary purchase limits on several categories of goods. Customers can buy no more than six units or kilograms of groceries, eggs, and bulk products in a single transaction, the company reported on Facebook.
It attributed the limit to the fallout from Russian strikes and a surge in speculative buying, describing resellers who make wholesale purchases in stores and pile additional pressure on already-stretched logistics. ATB stressed that the restrictions are temporary and that it is doing everything possible to keep shelves supplied.
The squeeze is visible in Kyiv, where fresh fruit, vegetables, sugar and dairy have intermittently vanished from some supermarkets as strikes disrupt the depots that feed them.
Ninety percent of food retail logistics is destroyed
The pressure on retailers follows weeks of intensifying attacks on warehousing and delivery infrastructure. Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi, cited by Reuters, told reporters in Kyiv that roughly 90% of the food logistics run by retail chains had been wiped out.
"As of today, roughly speaking, 90% of food logistics operated by retail chains have been destroyed, but that doesn't mean Ukrainians will be left without food," Vysotskyi noted.
Both sides have stepped up strikes on economic targets in recent weeks, with Russia concentrating on warehouses tied to Ukraine's leading supermarkets, its top postal service and home-goods stores. The blows have rippled beyond food: a wave of attacks delayed trains across several regions and left passengers stranded, while Kyiv spent close to 15 hours under air-raid alert on a single day.
Food producers are hit directly
The strikes have repeatedly struck food producers themselves. In Dnipro, Mayor Borys Filatov reported on Telegram that a recent attack had damaged, for the second time in the full-scale war, an oil-extraction plant belonging to the US agribusiness Bunge, maker of the Oleina cooking-oil brand.
Filatov emphasized that the plant stands in the city center and that US Senator Richard Blumenthal had visited it shortly before the strike.
On September 8, a Russian drone hit a food plant operated by Euro Food Service in Bila Tserkva, south of Kyiv. The company stated on LinkedIn that its production and storage facilities had been significantly damaged and that manufacturing and shipments were halted. No staff were injured, and the firm indicated it was working to keep its products on store shelves while it assessed the destruction.
American-owned plants in the crosshairs
American-owned facilities have featured prominently in the campaign. On September 3, Russian drones set fire to a Coca-Cola plant outside Kyiv, near Brovary, an attack President Volodymyr Zelenskyy framed as a message to Washington.
"It's a clear Russian signal to America. The Russians cannot be unaware that this is an American facility," Zelenskyy declared in his nightly video address. The strikes on Bunge and Coca-Cola, together with the senator's earlier visit, have sharpened Ukrainian appeals for a firmer US response.
The disruption now reaches ordinary consumers. McDonald's reported on September 10 that frequent, prolonged air-raid alerts and delivery delays had forced some Ukrainian outlets to reduce their menus, with items to be restored as supply stabilizes.
Couriers, retailers and aid stockpiles
The wider wave has swept up couriers, retailers and humanitarian stockpiles alike. Reuters reported that recent strikes destroyed Nova Poshta sorting centers near Kyiv and in Sumy, wounded at least four people at an Epicenter home-improvement store in Zaporizhzhia, and gutted a warehouse shipping thousands of book titles a day.
A shopping center in Kharkiv was struck for the second time in two days, while drone attacks on the Kyiv region damaged more than a dozen warehouses and killed one person.
Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi wrote on Telegram that 16 people had been killed across Ukraine in a single day of attacks. "They are hitting civilian businesses, food warehouses, hypermarkets, postal terminals, warehouses where books are stored," he added.
The World Health Organization (WHO), cited by Reuters, confirmed that one of its main medical-supply warehouses in the Kyiv region was struck overnight in early September.
Spokesperson Christian Lindmeier told reporters in Geneva that at least 20 attacks had hit warehouses storing humanitarian supplies during 2026, 15 of them holding health-related goods. An earlier August strike on a WHO depot in Dnipro destroyed half the supplies intended for an estimated 225,000 people in front-line areas.
A deliberate strategy, officials contend
Ukrainian officials have characterized the campaign as a deliberate effort to grind down daily life rather than a run of stray hits. Andriyy Kovalenko, who heads Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation, described waves of jet-powered drones aimed at paralyzing the capital and exhausting its defenders and residents.
"The aim—to wear down the air defenses and the population," he indicated. The choice of food depots, hypermarkets and postal terminals, in Vyhivskyi's account, points to civilian supply as the intended pressure point.
What shoppers are being told
Authorities are also advising residents to prepare for potential supply and utility disruptions. Kyiv has begun stockpiling essential food and drinking water ahead of possible prolonged winter blackouts, while maintaining emergency reserves for vulnerable residents and Points of Invincibility.
The city can currently provide hot meals for up to 25,000 people and plans to purchase another 20,000 emergency food kits as Russia continues targeting critical infrastructure.
Vysotskyi has urged households to keep a modest one-week food reserve while ruling out any need for month-long stockpiling, warning that wartime disruptions could recur. Even so, he maintained that goods that are interrupted on the shelf tend to reappear once logistics adapt.

Qantas changes tune over broken wheelchair after ABC questions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
18:54:12 UTC
03:54:12 KST

Qantas backflips to fund broken wheelchair after ABC questions
In short:
A prominent disability advocate is furious with the national airline over the difficulty of getting compensation for a wheelchair that was broken on one of its flights.
Akii Ngo was travelling with Qantas in June when, after exiting the aircraft, they found their powered wheelchair had been damaged beyond repair.
What's next?
This comes amid consultation on the federal government's proposed standards to improve air travel for people with disability, announced two years ago.
Qantas has backflipped and says it is now planning to replace an expensive powered wheelchair broken beyond repair on one of its flights, after questions from the ABC.
Akii Ngo was travelling from Sydney to Melbourne on June 28 after attending a disability conference.
Ngo said when they exited the aircraft and tried to put batteries back in the chair, it began beeping strangely and would not turn on.
It then began to malfunction while Ngo was sitting in it and suddenly took off, almost slamming them into the side of the aerobridge.
Ngo, who lives with multiple disabilities and travels regularly for work, said their wheelchair had been damaged many times before on flights operated by Qantas and other airlines.
"I just thought, the wheelchair Russian roulette has struck again," Ngo said.
"Sometimes I'm lucky; I land, and my wheelchair is fine. There might be a few scratches or cracks, and I ignore it, but this time I couldn't use it.
"Without my chair, I can't leave the house for paid work or see friends … I can't be independent."
An 'exhausting' ordeal
Ngo asked Qantas to pay to replace the wheelchair.
An independent mobility aid supplier assessed the chair, determining it "beyond repair", and quoted a replacement at almost $6,000.
But in communications seen by the ABC, Qantas said according to the Aviation Civil (Carriers' Liability) Act 1959, it would only reimburse Ngo up to $3,000.
"To finalise this matter, we have processed the amount of AUD$3000 towards a replacement mobility aid," an email sent by Qantas on August 19 said.
Ngo said it was "ridiculous" the airline was relying on a 67-year-old law introduced when smoking was still allowed on board.
The 33-year-old is not alone in having their wheelchair broken on flights, with the ABC reporting similar cases across all airlines.
People with disability have also long complained of discrimination and having to shoulder extra costs during air travel.
Since the incident in June, Ngo has continued flying for work and has had to hire second-hand wheelchairs, which they said risked giving them pressure sores, and often struggled to grip the ground and move up slight inclines.
The ABC asked Qantas a series of questions last Thursday, including whether it would cover the full cost of a new power wheelchair and reimburse Ngo for the full amount spent hiring temporary ones.
It responded on Monday afternoon, and the ABC understands the airline is now planning to provide Ngo with a new replacement wheelchair.
According to time stamps on emails sent to the ABC and Ngo on Monday, Qantas had not informed Ngo of that development when it responded to the ABC's questions.
In its statement, Qantas said it sincerely apologised to Ngo for the damage caused to their wheelchair.
"We … understand how upsetting this experience has been," the statement read.
"We are in contact with them and are working to replace their wheelchair as soon as possible."
Ngo said they were grateful for the outcome and believed it only happened because they went to the media, but acknowledged not everyone could pursue these sorts of issues.
"I'm in a privileged position where I'm able to advocate for myself, but someone shouldn't have to go to the media to expose how poorly people with disability can be treated," they said.
"It's exhausting to have to continue demonstrating how invaluable mobility aids are … I can't believe the drastic measures I had to take to get this sorted."
Ngo said the saga had taken a major toll on them.
They said Qantas's official forms and communications listed their chair as a "damaged bag" throughout the ordeal, and it made them feel the company did not understand how critical wheelchairs were for users.
"Losing luggage is an inconvenience. Losing or breaking a mobility aid changes the way in which you live your life."
Draft standards released
Ngo's case comes as the federal government releases draft standards for the aviation sector to better support passengers with disability, two years after they were recommended in 2024's Aviation White Paper.
Consultation on the draft guidelines closes on October 2.
A spokesperson for Transport Minister Catherine King said the treatment of people with disability by airlines and airports had not been good enough.
"The Australian government is committed to an aviation industry where everyone, including passengers with disability, can plan, book their travel, and fly safely and comfortably," the spokesperson said.
People with disability have expressed frustration at the speed of the process, given air travel has thrown up issues for so long.
"This process has taken time, but it has proven vital to identifying key priorities for the new standards, such as the need to include people with disability in airport and airline decisions on accessibility matters, the importance of consistency across every air travel journey, the need for comprehensive staff training in disability awareness, and greater transparency on what people with disability can expect at all points of their aviation journey," the minister's spokesperson said.
In May, the government also announced it would set up an Aviation Consumer Protection Authority to strengthen passengers' rights, a body advocates have long called for and a concept that exists in other countries.
The legislation, which would pave the way for this body, is before parliament.

Ukrainian Company KORT Presents Hunter Killer Drone Lineup
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
18:53:54 UTC
03:53:54 KST

The Ukrainian company KORT has unveiled its lineup of modular Hunter Killer strike and reconnaissance UAVs.
A KORT representative shared this information with a Militarnyi correspondent during the MSPO exhibition in Poland.
According to him, the company offers a wide range of unmanned platforms — from 7-inch quadcopters to 23-inch relay drones.
One of the company’s main products is the Hunter Killer 3 UAV, which is available in several variants and can perform reconnaissance, strike, and interception missions.
The platform features a standardized fuselage, the configuration of which varies depending on the aircraft’s mission.
The Hunter Killer 3 can be equipped with various communication systems, including the Starlink satellite system or the company’s proprietary telemetry system. The strike version of the drone is capable of carrying a payload weighing approximately 3 kg.
Separately, the company offers the Hunter Killer 3S and Hunter Killer 3M variants, which are positioned as middle-strike-class drones. Their stated operational range is 100 km or more, and their cruising speed is 100-105 km/h.
The next-largest platform is the Hunter Killer 10. This drone can carry a payload of 10 to 15 kg, depending on the operator’s requirements.
In a configuration with a 15-kilogram warhead, its stated range is approximately 300-400 km.
A deep strike version has also been developed based on the Hunter Killer 10. By reducing the warhead’s weight to 10 kg and increasing the fuel capacity to 18 liters, the drone’s flight range can exceed 700 km.
The Hunter Killer 10 is built with a pusher-configuration engine located in the nose of the aircraft.
At the same time, the company is finalizing work on the larger Hunter Killer 15 platform. The first prototypes of the drone have already been manufactured and are undergoing final testing. Unlike the Hunter Killer 10, the Hunter Killer 15’s engine has been moved to the tail section.
The largest of the projects presented by the company is the Hunter Killer 50 prototype, which is in the final stages of refinement and testing.
In its guided strike configuration, the drone is designed to carry a payload weighing up to 60 kg and strike targets at a range of up to 600 km. The drone will be controlled and video signals transmitted via the Starlink satellite channel.
Based on the same airframe, the company plans to develop a Deep Strike variant with a range of up to 1,200 km and a payload weighing approximately 50 kg.
KORT was founded in 2015 and currently collaborates with Poland, Latvia, the Czech Republic, and Denmark.

The Planet Mercury Has Been Shrinking—More Than Scientists Expected
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
18:53:04 UTC
03:53:04 KST

Mercury is nobody’s idea of a big cosmic deal. The solar system’s smallest planet, it measures just 3,023 miles across—or barely 3.6% of the 88,846 mi. diameter of Jupiter, the solar system’s largest. Saturn’s moon Titan and Jupiter’s Ganymede both also have greater diameters than Mercury. And according to a new study in Geophysical Research Letters, Mercury has actually put in the work to get as small as it is, spending part of the past 4.5 billion years shrinking—significantly more than planetologists once thought.
That matters. Figuring out the history of Mercury provides clues to how all rocky worlds like the moon and Mars formed. And what happens in our solar system surely happens in ones much farther afield in space.
How did scientists measure Mercury’s shrinking?
The findings come courtesy of data gathered by the Mercury MESSENGER spacecraft—a ship whose name was derived from the decidedly clumsy acronym “MErcury Surface, Space ENvironment, GEochemistry, and Ranging.” MESSENGER launched in August 2004; reached Mercury in March 2011; and completed 4,105 orbits of the planet before running out of fuel and crashing into the surface on April 30, 2015. In those four-plus years on the job, MESSENGER did a lot of work, studying Mercury with seven different scientific instruments—including its Mercury Laser Altimeter, a ranging tool that could measure surface features to within one meter; and a dual imaging system that used two cameras to map the surface in wide- and narrow-angle and black and white and color.
Scientists have known for a long time that Mercury has gotten steadily smaller since its birth. The planet was formed when dust, gas, rocks, and asteroids left over from the formation of the sun collided and collected, coalescing into a discrete body and generating enormous amounts of heat in the process. Over the eons much of that heat dissipated, causing Mercury to contract by what astronomers estimated to be 2.5 miles to 10 miles in diameter.
To confirm that conclusion, MESSENGER scientists used the spacecraft’s laser altimeter and dual-imager to scan the planet looking for so-called shortening structures, which are distortions in the surface made up of wrinkles, ridges, and what are known as lobate scarps—cliff-like structures that form when the crust pushes rock upward along a fault. Shortening structures form when a planet contracts; the greater the number of those surface features, the greater the planetary shrinkage has been.
MESSENGER did its best to map shortening structures across the entirety of the planet, but two things made that job a challenge. For starters, the more powerful of its two imaging systems, the laser altimeter, could not operate effectively if the spacecraft was more than 930 miles away from the planet—a proximity it reached only when it was over Mercury’s north polar region during its sweeping elliptical orbits; at other points it was as much as 9,500 miles distant. The dual-imaging system could survey the surface during those more remote approaches, but it did not produce the detailed three-dimensional pictures the laser altimeter did.
Then too, there is the condition of Mercury’s surface itself. The shortening structures formed early in the planet’s history, and in the eons since, Mercury has been steadily pounded by incoming asteroids, gouging out craters and scattering debris, obscuring the telltale scars of planetary contraction. It’s possible to read through that rubble—tracing shortening structures until they are covered up by craters or rocks and estimating what their course and reach was—but that takes planet-wide three-dimensional maps, something that MESSENGER did not provide. There was, however, a way to create them.
With the cooperation of NASA, the custodian of the MESSENGER images, a team led by Gaku Nishiyama, a planetary scientist at the German Aerospace Center Institute of Space Research and the lead author of the new paper, harvested two-dimensional pictures taken by the spacecraft’s dual-imaging system and combined them in such a way that every patch of surveyed land was captured twice—from slightly different angles each time.
“We used a digital terrain model generated through so-called stereophotogrammetric technique,” says Nishiyama. “Combining two images taken at different viewing angles [is similar to the way] human beings recognize stuff with both eyes. So two-dimensional images are combined to derive three-dimensional topography.”
With the help of that detailed terrain map, Nishiyama and his colleagues were able to study the entirety of Mercury with a resolution never before achieved. That helped the team infer the location and reach of shortening structures that were otherwise covered up over time, and that, in turn, led them to conclude that previous calculations of Mercury’s historical shrinkage were underestimates.
“We find a lack of shortening structures in rough regions,” the researchers wrote, “suggesting that roughness-related processes obscure pre-existing structures. This biases previous contraction estimates downward… implying that Mercury’s contraction is up to 30% larger than previously thought.”
What can Mercury’s shrinking teach us about the planet and our solar system?
That 30% factors out to about 4.5 miles more contraction than earlier calculations—small even on the scale of a world as modest as Mercury, but significant all the same. Increased shrinkage means planetologists have to rethink what they previously believed about the chemical composition and temperature of Mercury’s core, with lower sulfur or silicon content than previously believed, leading to faster cooling and more contraction. It could also suggest that Mercury’s core started out hotter than suspected, which resulted in a more dramatic volume change when it finally did cool down.
“More shrinking means Mercury could have a larger metal core, less light elements like silicon mixed into the metal core, or a higher starting temperature,” said Nishiyama in a statement that accompanied the release of the study.
What Nishiyama and his colleagues learned about Mercury’s cooling and shrinking could have implications for the study of other rocky worlds like the moon and Mars. The moon has more craters and other rough features than Mercury, making it more important to try to interpret the shortening structures that did survive in order to estimate potential lunar shrinkage—learning if what happened on Mercury indeed happened on the moon and perhaps Mars. If so, says Nishiyama, all three worlds are likely to be contracting still, as heat continues to escape from their interiors into space.
Meantime, Mercury will get a closer look soon. In 2018, the European and Japanese space agencies launched the BepiColombo spacecraft on an eight-year journey to Mercury. The ship will arrive in December and begin science operations in April 2027. BepiColombo has a significantly more powerful laser altimeter than MESSENGER’s, able to resolve surface changes as small as 20 centimeters (8 in.). The spacecraft will also be in a less eccentric orbit than MESSENGER, putting more of Mercury’s surface within its crosshairs.
“New data from BepiColombo will open a door for understanding how Mercury has been shaped up to now,” says Nishiyama.

2030 Winter Olympics boss departs amid turmoil
- Published
Edgar Grospiron has left his position as president of the organising committee for the 2030 French Alps Winter Olympics just 18 months after his appointment.
The departure of Grospiron, the 1992 Olympic moguls champion, was confirmed at a meeting of the committee's executive board on Thursday, marking the latest setback in the event's troubled governance.
In a statement, the organising committee said: "His decision to leave the presidency is part of a deliberate, organised and fully assumed transition, taken in the interests of the project and its governance.
"It reflects a shared desire with stakeholders to enable the organisation to quickly enter this new operational phase."
Confirming his departure via a post on LinkedIn, Grospiron said his decision followed "months of tension".
"I draw the conclusion that the conditions are not met for me to continue this," he wrote.
Grospiron's tenure, which began in February 2025, has been plagued by internal turmoil and logistical challenges.
In February 2026, chief executive officer Cyril Linette left the committee, citing "insurmountable disagreements" with Grospiron.
Linette's departure followed a number of other high-profile resignations, including chief operating officer Anne Murac and communications director Arthur Richer.
Budget cuts have plagued the planning process, with Grospiron admitting in February they had "little time, little money".
However, he remained confident he could "deliver a Games that will honour our vision and ambition" provided there was "serenity" and "continuity" from the organising committee.
In May, the committee was forced to shelve the Games' 'ice sports hub' in Nice after the city's mayor, Eric Ciotti, refused to allow OGC Nice's Allianz Riviera Stadium to be converted into a temporary ice rink.
The ice events will now be hosted in Lyon, with the exception of speed skating, which will take place in Heerenveen in the Netherlands.
Two months later, following a tense board meeting in July, French Olympic Committee president Amelie Oudea-Castera told La Tribune Dimanche, external that they were "once again facing governance problems".
Despite another departure from the organising committee, French sports minister Marina Ferrari says there is "no concern about what comes next".
"The bid is continuing to move forward," she told reporters. "Our teams are mobilised and working. We are confident about the future of the Alpes project."
The International Olympic Committee praised Grospiron's "crucial work in laying the foundations for the success" of the Games.
"The IOC will continue working in close collaboration with the organising committee to build on the solid foundations that Mr Grospiron has laid," the statement added.

Algeria to close airspace to UAE aircraft after diplomatic break

Algeria will close its airspace to all United Arab Emirates-registered civilian and military aircraft from Friday, the North African nation announced Thursday following a decision to sever diplomatic relations with the Gulf country.
UAE commercial flights to and from Algiers will be exempt from the ban until the end of 2026, when the current contract expires, its Defense Ministry said.
The UAE, meanwhile, later Thursday said it hoped Algeria's decision to cut diplomatic relations was temporary.
Algeria accused Abu Dhabi of interfering in national and regional affairs and said it was giving the UAE ambassador 48 hours "to comply with the decision."
In an official statement, Algiers accused the Gulf country of "provocative and hostile acts," but it remained unclear what triggered the rupture.
Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune has often referred to the UAE as a "micro-state" or "statelet" seeking to destabilize several countries in the region, citing Libya, Mali and Sudan.
The North African country, which has signaled for months a diplomatic break, said the decision came "after exhausting all avenues to preserve bilateral relations" with the UAE.
The Algerian Foreign Ministry said it had warned Abu Dhabi several times, but the UAE "persisted in its actions, reaching a point where they could no longer be considered acceptable or tolerable."
"Algeria spared no effort to draw the Emirati side's attention to, and to warn it against, the dire consequences that could result from its regrettable and unjustified conduct," the ministry said.
In a televised interview in July, Tebboune again lashed out at Abu Dhabi, saying "wherever they set foot, blood flows."
"We want them to stay away, so that blood does not flow in our country," he added.
At that time, Tebboune said a diplomatic break "would have happened long ago" had Algeria not sought to avoid "deepening divisions" in the Arab world.
Tensions between the two countries have been fueled by several developments in recent years.
Last year, Algerian state television denounced what it called a hostile media campaign after UAE-based broadcaster Sky News Arabia aired an interview with historian Mohamed Amine Belghit, who made controversial remarks questioning the existence of Algeria's indigenous Amazigh culture.
Belghit was jailed in Algeria but later pardoned by Tebboune.
Further divisions between Algiers and Abu Dhabi also stemmed from diverging diplomatic policies, including the UAE's normalization of ties with Israel in 2020.

Canada will allocate $253 million for American air defense interceptors for Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
21:45:10 EEST
03:45:10 KST

Canada will allocate $253 million for American air defense interceptors for Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Canada will finance the purchase of American interceptor missiles for Ukraine through the JUMPSTART mechanism. The type and delivery timeline have not yet been disclosed.
Canada will allocate approximately 350 million Canadian dollars (approximately 253 million US dollars) to purchase critically needed air defense equipment for Ukraine through the US JUMPSTART mechanism. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said this on September 10 after a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, reports UNN.
According to the Canadian government, the funds will be used to purchase interceptor missiles to strengthen Ukraine’s air defenses. The decision was made amid an intensification of Russian air attacks and Ukraine’s growing need for means of protecting civilians and critical infrastructure.
At the same time, the Canadian side has not yet disclosed which specific missiles or what quantities will be purchased, nor has it announced specific timelines for their transfer to Ukraine.
What the JUMPSTART mechanism provides for
JUMPSTART is a US mechanism that enables allies and partners to finance the purchase of US weapons for Ukraine through the Foreign Military Sales (FMS) system. The scheme provides that the partner country allocates the funds, after which the United States organizes the purchase and delivery of the relevant weapons to Ukraine. Therefore, it is important to understand that the 350 million Canadian dollars announced by Canada do not mean the transfer of missiles to Ukraine from Canadian military stocks. It is specifically funding for the purchase of US air defense systems.
What official Kyiv previously asked Ottawa for
Canada’s decision is directly linked to previous negotiations between Kyiv and Ottawa. In June 2026, Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov discussed with his Canadian counterpart David McGuinty the possibility of purchasing PAC-3 interceptor missiles for Ukraine through the JUMPSTART mechanism.
PAC-3 is one of the key types of interceptors used by Patriot systems to counter ballistic missiles. The need for such munitions remains one of Ukraine’s priorities, as partners’ stocks of highly effective interceptors are limited and their production takes time.
However, as of September 10, the Canadian government is officially speaking only of critically needed air defense interceptors. Therefore, it is premature to claim that all 350 million Canadian dollars will be spent specifically on PAC-3 missiles.
It should be noted that Canada has already financed US weapons for Ukraine. The current agreement is part of Canada’s broader support for Ukraine’s air defenses.
Earlier, official Ottawa allocated funds to purchase US weapons for Ukraine through other mechanisms, including PURL. In August 2025, Ottawa announced the allocation of approximately 680 million Canadian dollars for a corresponding military aid package that included air defense systems. Through mechanisms of this type, Ukraine’s allies can pay for weapons manufactured in the United States without transferring their own stocks to Ukraine.
Other partners of Ukraine also joined JUMPSTART. In particular, Germany announced funding for the purchase of additional PAC-3 interceptors, while Norway and other European countries used the mechanism to finance US weapons for Ukraine.
Canada expands its defense partnership with Ukraine
The decision to finance air defense became part of a broader package of agreements announced during Zelenskyy’s visit to Canada. The two countries agreed to develop a long-term defense-industrial partnership, particularly in the areas of drone production, counter-drone systems, electronic warfare equipment, and munitions.
The Canadian authorities also announced their intention to provide Ukraine with one-third of the drones produced by Canadian companies. Separately, a partnership was announced between Canada’s General Dynamics Mission Systems-Canada and Ukraine’s Green Tech Harvest in the development and production of unmanned systems.
In addition, Ottawa plans to provide nearly 435 million Canadian dollars in guarantees to the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development to support Ukraine’s energy security, including the purchase of gas ahead of the heating season.
Context
During the meeting, Carney and Zelenskyy signed a declaration on a 100-year partnership between Canada and Ukraine. The document provides for deepening cooperation in the areas of defense, security, the Ukrainian recovery, technology, and people-to-people ties.
The Canadian side separately reaffirmed its continued support for Ukraine in the area of air defense and the supply of interceptors.
Ottawa also announced its support for Ukraine’s FREYJA program, aimed at developing a more affordable and mass-produced interceptor to counter Russian ballistic missiles.

25 years after 9/11, the story of American-Israeli tech pioneer Danny Lewin: The first victim after fighting terrorists aboard Flight 11
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
18:44:50 UTC
03:44:50 KST

- i24NEWS
- International
- US / Canada
- The incredible story and legacy of Daniel Lewin, the first man to die on 9/11
The incredible story and legacy of Daniel Lewin, the first man to die on 9/11
Crammed into his short life, Daniel Lewin started a company that changed the internet, was a captain in an elite IDF unit, and died trying to stop the deadliest terror attack in history
Twenty-five years ago, on the morning of September 11, 2001, American Airlines Flight 11 was hijacked by five al-Qaeda terrorists and crashed into the North Tower of the World Trade Center.
It was the first of four planes that would be turned into weapons that day, striking the South Tower, the Pentagon, and a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, killing nearly 3,000 people.
Seated in business class on that first plane, directly behind hijacker Mohamed Atta, was Daniel “Danny” Lewin, a 31-year-old American-Israeli entrepreneur, mathematician, and former captain in the IDF’s elite Sayeret Matkal unit. Evidence from flight attendant calls and a 2002 FAA memo indicates that Lewin was stabbed to death while attempting to stop the hijackers, making him the first person killed in the 9/11 attacks, nearly 20 minutes before the plane hit the tower.
This is the story of Danny Lewin: the soldier, the scientist, the co-founder of Akamai Technologies, and the man whose final act was to fight back.
O captain, my captain
“When I first met Danny, within a few months, I said, ‘Danny, you’re either going to be the future Prime Minister of Israel, or the next Bill Gates at Microsoft, or both.’ That’s how incredibly formidable Danny was,” recalled Marco Greenberg, a close friend of Lewin.
Born in Denver, Colorado, in 1970, Lewin moved to Israel with his family at age 14. After high school, he enlisted in the Israel Defense Forces, joining Sayeret Matkal, the IDF’s most elite counterterrorism unit, and rising to the rank of captain. Friends remembered him as a rare blend of physical strength and intellectual brilliance: a “Mr. Teenage Israel” bodybuilding champion who was also a star student, warm, socially aware, and deeply humane.
“He was an absolute character… incredibly articulate, intellectually curious, socially aware… someone that would give high fives and back slapping and fist bumps and hugs,” Greenberg said. “It wasn’t just his intellectual abilities and later his feats in Sayeret Matkal… it was also his humanity and his character that really distinguished him.”
From the Technion to MIT
After his military service, Lewin studied mathematics and electrical engineering at the Technion in Haifa, graduating summa cum laude in 1995 with both a BA and a BS. He worked part-time for IBM Israel, rising to project leader and research fellow while helping develop the Genesys-Pro tool.
In 1996, he moved to the United States to pursue a Ph.D. at MIT, where he was accepted by multiple top schools but chose MIT to work with Professor Tom Leighton, a leading expert in theoretical computer science and applied mathematics
“I met Danny for the first time when he came to MIT as a graduate student in algorithms and theoretical computer science,” Leighton recalled. “I selected him as my teaching assistant and got to know him as an incredibly smart and hard-working person, and we started working on research together.”
Solving the “World Wide Wait”
Together, Leighton and Lewin developed algorithms to speed up internet traffic, which in the 1990s often buckled under heavy strain. Their work formed the basis of Lewin’s award-winning thesis and, in 1998, the foundation for Akamai Technologies, the company they co-founded with Jonathan Seelig and Randall Kaplan.
“You know, initially ‘www’ stood for ‘worldwide wait’ because when there was popular content, a lot of people would be stuck waiting,” Leighton explained. “The algorithms that we developed would make the web work so we could scale… and then when we started Akamai, things grew pretty quickly because the web was really just starting to scale up.”
Akamai rode the dot-com boom but was hit hard by the market crash that followed. By September 2001, the company was struggling, and Lewin was traveling frequently to Los Angeles to help devise a turnaround plan.
“I remember the night before 9/11, Danny and I were up very late at night working on a large-scale reduction in force because…a lot of our customers were going broke,” Leighton said. “We weren’t able to raise money, and the stock value had declined a lot. And then, of course, the horrible tragedy on 9/11.”
The Morning of September 11
On September 11, 2001, Lewin boarded American Airlines Flight 11 at Boston’s Logan Airport, bound for Los Angeles. The flight took off at 7:59 a.m. and was hijacked shortly thereafter.
According to the 9/11 Commission Report and FAA records, Lewin was seated in 9B, directly behind Mohamed Atta, the ringleader of the hijacking. When two terrorists moved toward the cockpit, Lewin got up to confront them. A third hijacker, Satam al-Suqami, seated behind him, slashed his throat.
“It was reported live by the stewardess from the back of the plane that… the person in Danny’s seat had gotten up and tried to fight off the terrorists and was killed in the process of trying to defend the stewardesses in the cockpit,” Leighton said. “Danny, obviously, fluent in Arabic, highly skilled operative…there’s no question he would have gotten up and done everything in his power to stop the attack.”
Greenberg added: “The fact that Danny, who was seated in business class and was armed with nothing but a BlackBerry, a laptop, a pair of jeans, T-shirt, and sneakers… decided to rise up and fight back against the ringleader of 9/11 along with five other terrorists surprised no one that knew him. We knew that instinctively that’s what Danny would do.”
Lewin was killed at age 31, leaving behind his wife and two sons, both under the age of 7.
Legacy: The Company That Kept the Web Running
Akamai survived the dot-com crash and the loss of its co-founder. Twenty-five years later, it remains a cornerstone of the internet, with a market capitalization of roughly $15 billion and its technology still used by most major websites to deliver content quickly and reliably.
In a painful irony, 9/11 became the ultimate test of the very technology Lewin helped create. “One of the ironies of this story, the painful, tragic ironies, is that Akamai proved its value during the most frenetic and heavily trafficked news day of that era, which was 9/11,” Greenberg said. “Akamai’s job was to keep all these websites up and running… that was the biggest test of the technology that Danny developed.”
Leighton, who became Akamai’s CEO in 2013, has called Lewin the “heart and soul of the company” and “my best friend.” In 2017 Lewin was posthumously inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame for inventing the content delivery network that solved the “World Wide Wait.”
“The Ultimate Poster Boy for What Being an American-Israeli Is All About”
For those who knew him, Lewin embodied the best of both American and Israeli culture: a proud American citizen and an ardent Zionist, a decorated commando and a brilliant mathematician, a devoted family man and a visionary entrepreneur.
“Danny was a very proud American citizen, but he was an ardent Zionist,” Greenberg said. “One of the reasons I think Danny would want his story told is that he would want people seeing Israel in an accurate and positive light. He was the best of both American culture and Israeli culture. He was the ultimate poster boy for what being an American-Israeli is all about.”
Twenty-five years after his death, Danny Lewin’s legacy endures; not only in the infrastructure of the internet he helped build, but in the courage he showed in his final moments, trying to stop the deadliest terrorist attack in history.

Switzerland publishes 200-page dossier on Nazi doctor Mengele, known as ‘Angel of Death’
The war criminal was infamous for carrying out horrific medical experiments on inmates at Auschwitz
The Swiss federal intelligence service on Thursday published a 200-page dossier on the notorious Nazi war criminal Josef Mengele, the German doctor known as the “Angel of Death” for conducting horrific medical experiments on prisoners at Auschwitz.
During World War II, Mengele served at the Auschwitz extermination camp in Nazi-occupied Poland, where about 1.1 million people were killed, around 1 million of them Jews.
He became infamous for carrying out brutal medical experiments on inmates, including children, under the guise of scientific research.
After the war, Mengele obtained a Red Cross travel document under a false identity, allowing him to leave Europe. Like many former Nazi officials, he spent years in hiding in Latin America while being pursued internationally for his crimes. He drowned in 1979 while swimming on the coast of Brazil.
The documents released by Swiss authorities include material provided to police suggesting that Mengele may have returned to Switzerland after initially fleeing Germany, or may have been planning to enter the country under a false name, according to the German news agency dpa.
Historians seeking to establish whether Mengele spent time in Switzerland while being pursued as a war criminal, without Swiss authorities catching him, had long sought access to the files.

German state could face EU fund freeze after AfD win – media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
18:36:05 UTC
03:36:05 KST

German state could face EU fund freeze after AfD win – media
The eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt could face an EU funding freeze after the right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) scored a landslide victory in regional elections last week, German broadcaster ARD has reported.
The party, which won 43.8% of the vote, has long challenged Berlin and Brussels on migration. The EU previously resorted to funding freezes in its disputes with dissenting governments, including those in Hungary and Poland.
Saxony-Anhalt is set to receive €2.95 billion ($3.43 billion) from the EU’s 2021-2027 budget, to fund projects ranging from school and daycare renovations to modern medical equipment for hospitals. According to ARD, it gets more EU regional funding per capita than any other German state.
According to Green MEP Daniel Freund, the scheme could soon be suspended if the AfD forms a regional government and upsets Brussels in any way. The lawmaker described the right-wing party as a political group that acts against “the European project,” adding that “if necessary, the European Commission would have to withhold funds.”
Freund, who had previously actively supported similar measures against Hungary under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, described the move as a good way to rein in dissenting national governments, particularly in Hungary and Poland.
“We saw in both countries that after the freezing of EU funds, there were changes of government, and that the new governments had a significantly better relationship with the European institutions,” he told ARD. Now, the same approach could potentially be applied in Saxony-Anhalt, he added.
Brussels froze assistance funds for Warsaw and Budapest on several occasions over the past years, accusing both nations of rule of law violations. Hungary and Poland described the moves as political persecution linked to their opposition to the EU policies.
In Hungary’s case, funds were frozen in 2022 when the European Commission accused Orban – a long-time critic of EU migration policies and Ukraine aid – and his government of corruption and rule-of-law violations. The money was only partially released this year after Orban lost an election to his rival Peter Magyar and his Tisza Party.
Saxony-Anhalt could lose up to €500 million a year as part of a similar scenario, according to Luise Quaritsch from the Jacques Delors Centre think tank branch in Berlin. Such a decision would “significantly impact regional and economic development and thus also have a negative impact on the state government,” she warned.
The AfD has described this scenario as a form of “undemocratic” pressure. “We laugh at our party opponents who are now trying to disadvantage us undemocratically at the EU level as well. Because they are long since defenseless against us in political competition,” said Bernd Baumann, the AfD federal parliamentary faction’s chief whip.
The federal government in Germany was also working on its own plan to put constraints on a potential AfD-led regional government. Defense Minister Boris Pistorius recently stated that Berlin was preparing mechanisms to cut it off from some federal resources, such as the intelligence-sharing network. The Telegraph and Die Welt reported in July that a “secret plan” was being developed to prevent any “obstructionism” on the part of the regional authorities, particularly if the government would need to facilitate a large NATO troop movement through German territory, potentially towards the Russian borders.
Despite being the strongest faction in the regional legislature by a wide margin, the AfD is still a few seats short of claiming the absolute majority needed to form a single-party government. It will either need to enter a coalition, which could be difficult due to virtually all other parties refusing to cooperate with it, or secure enough votes to form a minority cabinet.

Ukraine and Canada agree on 100-year partnership: declaration signed
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney have signed a declaration establishing a 100-year partnership, which sets out the two countries' intention to raise bilateral relations to the level of a comprehensive strategic partnership in various spheres, including defence and assistance to Ukraine's armed forces.
Source: European Pravda, with reference to a joint statement by Carney and Zelenskyy
Details: In the statement, the leaders condemned Russia's war in Ukraine and paid tribute to the courage of the Ukrainian people and their defenders.
Both leaders stressed the importance of continuing reforms in Ukraine on the path to full membership of the European Union and NATO.
"Canada remains a committed partner in supporting these efforts," the statement emphasised.
The statement stressed that Canada will continue to "meet Ukraine's most pressing military needs and sustain Operation UNIFIER, now extended until 2029".
Canada will also continue to strengthen the Armed Forces of Ukraine, paying particular attention to "urgently needed air defence capabilities and interceptors, while continuing to provide training, military equipment, ammunition and other critical military support".
"The two countries will deepen cooperation in the areas of intelligence, cyber defence, counter-drone and electronic disruption capabilities, and in countering hybrid threats and foreign information manipulation. Canada will continue to work with partners on a framework of politically and legally binding security guarantees to prevent any future aggression by the Russian Federation," the statement said.
The statement also notes that Canada and Ukraine will establish a long-term defence industry partnership for the joint production of unmanned systems, counter-drone and electronic jamming systems, as well as ammunition.
In addition, the countries will expand trade and investment under the modernised Free Trade Agreement, promote the development of public-private partnerships and mobilise capital and risk-mitigation solutions needed to support Ukraine's recovery and reconstruction.
Separately, Canada and Ukraine agreed to deepen cooperation in the areas of energy security and critical minerals, industry and sustainable forest resource management, and will strengthen ties between innovators and researchers in the fields of AI, cybersecurity, space, biotechnology and digital governance.
The countries will also cooperate to ensure reliable and safe navigation in the Black Sea, as well as to further disrupt and deter the activities of Russia's shadow fleet.
In addition, Canada has pledged to maintain and intensify economic pressure on Russia.
Background:
- Zelenskyy is on a three-day visit to Canada together with First Lady Olena Zelenska.

Global energy market shock not over yet — IMF
Unknown

WASHINGTON, September 10. /TASS/. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) believes that the energy shock in global markets, triggered by the war involving the US, Israel, and Iran, has not yet been overcome, IMF Spokesperson Julie Kozack said at a regular press briefing.
"As the managing director (Kristalina Georgieva - TASS) has said, the energy shock is not over," Kozack noted.
"Oil and gas prices remain elevated. Prices of refined products such as diesel and jet fuel are also very high. Ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is only 1/10 of pre-war levels, and we know that there's been a use of strategic oil and gas reserves in some countries, but those will need restocking at some point," the IMF spokesperson noted.
"At the same time, we know that the AI boom is increasing demand for energy in some countries, and we also know that the Northern Hemisphere winter is now coming, and that will create additional energy demands," Kozack added.
As the IMF warned in an analytical note published in mid-July, a significant portion of the capacity to mitigate the global energy crisis sparked by the war involving the US, Israel, and Iran has already been exhausted. IMF Chief Economist Pierre-Olivier Gourinchas had previously emphasized that a US-Israeli military operation against Iran could trigger an "energy crisis of unprecedented scale."

What to watch in September, from Australian docos to British thrillers
Welcome to what to watch, where we take you through what's on the box in September.
This month brings a heartbreaking documentary about a dark part of Australian history, and the first local show from international streamer AppleTV. Plus, a madcap variety show like you've never seen, and the newest dramedy from Bad Sisters creator Sharon Horgan.
Here's what we're watching this month.
The Cage
What's it about? Casino co-workers Matty (Michael Socha) and Leanne (Sheridan Smith) couldn't live more different lives. She's a widowed single mother responsible for two teens and a dementia-riddled Nanna, who is ironically the only reason they have a roof over their heads. Once she moves into an assisted living centre, Leanne and her kids will be evicted from their council housing.
Matty's a former drug addict and current gambling addict whose mornings consist of a phone full of lost sports bets and a punch in the head from his (admittedly quite kindly) bookie after missing another pay day.
Matty and Leanne's desperation leads them to the same place: cooking the books and stealing money from the casino, which also happens to be their employer. But catching each other in the act is merely the beginning of their troubles when a drug kingpin who is laundering money through the casino figures out his profit is a little light.
Like many thrillers where bad things consistently happen to mostly good people, The Cage can be a tough watch at times but it's the deep, lived-in performances of its main duo which make it endlessly compelling.
Perfect for: A fake crime story you can be obsessed with without feeling guilty
Where to watch: The first episode of The Cage is streaming on ABC iview now
Last Seen
What's it about? Ian (Patrick Brammall; Colin from Accounts) isn't doing well. He's barely holding onto his sobriety, with help from his friend and sponsor Donald (Daniel Henshall; ABC TV's The Newsreader). His marriage to Debbie (Jessica Wren; Devil's Playground) has long ended, he's estranged from his son Dean (Tobias Muhafidin; Bali 2002), and he's working as an emergency dispatcher after giving up a career in the police force.
At least Ian is very good at keeping strangers calm at times of crisis, offering the kind of empathy you wish he'd extend to himself and the people close to him. But he's too wracked by grief to do that, following the disappearance of his three-year-old daughter Maggie more than a decade ago.
When police find the remains of a girl near the port-side town where he lives, Ian is thrust back into that grief — but this time, he's hell-bent on finding out what happened to his daughter.
It leads him into the path of the similarly stubborn Henry (Brendan Cowell; Love My Way) who lives off-grid with his wife Jenna (Maxine Peake; Say Nothing) and daughter Sarah (newcomer Chloe Jean Lourdes), who is about the same age Maggie would be now.
At first, Last Seen slowly teases out the true relationships between the characters, before it transforms into a fast-paced thriller, complete with a car chase, more than one shoot-out, and Colin Friels (Water Rats) as a fundamentalist patriarch.
Perfect for: Lovers of twisty but emotional crime shows set in Australia, like Black Snow and Troppo
Where to watch: Last Seen is streaming on Apple TV now
Stamptown
What's it about? How to describe Stamptown, the mutant travelling circus brought together by comedian Jack Tucker (professional clown Zack Zucker). Zucker has been assaulting audiences around the world with his high-octane variety show, but capturing the sprightly, slightly unhinged essence of the live show on a recorded format was always going to be a challenge.
Zucker and his troupe of performers more than rise to the occasion with a full hour of nonstop comedy clownery.
Don't worry if the beaming safety vest dance of Norwegian clown Viggo Venn isn't tickling your funny bone because in the next second the dangerously high-heeled Vanessa 5000 (LA comedian Courtney Pauroso) will be here to chat cryptocurrency with unsuspecting male audience members. Meanwhile, Nate-luminary Natalie Palamides is already out here telling jokes as the original nepo baby (complete with still-attached umbilical cord).
For some, Stamptown will be too much (there are multiple penises), but for the right crowd it's an absolute delight to join in on the breathless fun — even if it's through a screen.
Perfect for: When you want to be surprised at every turn
Where to watch: Stamptown is streaming on Netflix now
Tampa: The Turning Point
What's it about? In late August 2001, a leaky boat carrying 433 asylum seekers bound for Australia's Christmas Island broke down in the middle of the open ocean.
All hope seemed lost until two days later, the Norwegian freighter MV Tampa responded to a distress call and rescued the mostly Hazara men, women and children, who were from Afghanistan.
Then Australia refused them entry.
At the time, then-prime minister John Howard was gearing up for an election. The asylum seekers on board the Tampa offered an opportunity to demonstrate his tough border stance, kickstarting an eight-day standoff.
His management of the situation, which would see some of the Tampa survivors sent to New Zealand and others to an offshore detention centre in Nauru, initially prompted international condemnation.
But the public's perception of the immigration measures shifted dramatically after 9/11.
In the wake of the terror attacks, many Australians became increasingly concerned with security, controlled borders and terror threats, lending support for the Howard government's hardline measures. And in the decades since, our hardline policy has been adopted in countries around the world.
Now it's time to reflect.
This gripping three-part docuseries hands the microphone to the people at the centre of the story — some of whom were children when they were rescued by the Tampa. Their recollections are juxtaposed with testimonies from legal and migration experts, media and politicians of the day. Then and now, John Howard is front and centre.
Perfect for: Anyone who wants a holistic and balanced view of how we got here
Where to watch: All episodes of Tampa: The Turning Point are streaming now on ABC iview
Youth
What's it about? From Phoebe Waller-Bridge's Fleabag to Aisling Bea's This Way Up, the last decade has been a boon for the female-led, warts-and-all, realities-of-life dramedy. Irish actor Sharon Horgan has already cut her teeth in the genre on both ends of the spectrum with accidental baby sitcom Catastrophe and the darker Bad Sisters, for which she scored two Emmy nominations for Best Lead Actress in a Comedy.
Now Horgan is Alex, a 50-year-old divorcee with an apathetic adult teen, a dead-end publishing job (one of the three professions fictional women can apparently hold) and an absent ex.
She can barely muster the mental effort to find her sexuality, let alone put it to any good use. It's a stage of life when she should finally be making space for herself, but Alex more often finds herself trying to help 18-year-old Ruari (Aran Murphy) launch out of arrested development and, more importantly, her house. Her boss/friend Sam is a good sparring partner but has a bad habit of pushing work she'd rather avoid on Alex.
Despite Alex saying she's not looking for anything serious romantically, her situationship with Patrick (Rupert Friend) grows more entangled every time they meet. Sporting some sparkling cameos from UK favourites, it's Horgan's inextinguishable light which keeps Youth bright and tight.
Perfect for: Fans of a quick quip and a messy situation
Where to watch: Youth premieres on HBO Max on Monday September 21

No. 6: Miriam Adelson: The Rothschild of our times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
18:29:44 UTC
03:29:44 KST

US President Donald Trump was in the middle of his Knesset speech when he stopped to thank a woman sitting in the room. She loves Israel, he said. She has $60 billion in the bank. Then he told the Israeli parliament that she had shaped some of the decisions he made about their country.
That was last October, and nobody flinched. A few years ago, we would have.
Miriam Adelson was No. 26 on this list last year. She is in the top five now, and her fortune did not move. What moved was us.
For two decades, we filed her under politics. She and Sheldon were donors, Israel Hayom was Netanyahu’s paper, and every check they wrote got read backward from there. It was a convenient way to avoid thinking about her.
Then the hostages.
While the government briefed and the talks stalled, Adelson worked the one phone line in the world that mattered. Channel 12 named her. Hostage families named her. In the end, Trump named her out loud, from our own parliament. Nobody here had to guess anymore.
Herzog gave her the Presidential Medal of Honor that same month, and she used her remarks, delivered on behalf of all the recipients, to talk about the hostages. In May, the Israeli-American Council gave her a lifetime award in Los Angeles. She said the day they all came home was the best day of her life, that it fell near her birthday, and that God had handed it to her.
The politics have not softened. Forbes puts the family at close to $38b. She is still the largest individual donor in Republican politics, and at the White House Hanukkah reception in December, she was reported to have pushed Trump toward a third term with another $250 million behind it. Six months later, her own paper ran an open letter telling him he had failed on Iran.
Anyone still calling Israel Hayom a PR sheet has not read it recently
Both of those are true about the same woman. Anyone still calling Israel Hayom a public relations sheet has not read it lately.
Now the part Israelis skipped for 20 years.
The Adelsons came into Birthright in 2011 because they heard that 10,000 young Jews were sitting on a waiting list every year for lack of money. They paid for the list. The list doubled. They paid for that, too. A quarter of a billion dollars by 2015, and that is one program. There is also the medical faculty at Ariel, Yad Vashem, the IAC, and the addiction clinics.
I asked them why, in 2020, for Makor Rishon. She did not give me a speech. She gave me a girl.
On the last day of a trip, at Independence Hall, a participant told Adelson she knew there was no such thing as a free lunch and asked what the family wanted back. Adelson told her that if Israel is ever in danger, she will fight for it, and she will go to the White House and shout. Then she told her the investment had already been repaid, because she had shown up.
In June, she wrote about Elie Wiesel, 10 years gone, a friend of hers. Wiesel’s pulpit, she wrote, was his pen.
Baron Rothschild paid for the first moshavim, the early farming villages, and Jews resented him for it while he was alive. We do this. We take the money and mistrust the hand.
Adelson is the most consequential Jewish philanthropist alive. She is also a private line between Jerusalem and the Oval Office. This year, we finally said so.
