Once in a generation, sometimes once in a lifetime, a singular event blindsides the entire planet. 25 years on, does the memory of the Nine-Eleven attacks against New York's Twin Towers, the Pentagon and in Pennsylvania fade into history or is it still as raw and vivid as on that sunny September morning?
Back then, the world was still processing the end of the Cold War. Western spies who'd learned Russian suddenly had to take Arabic lessons, the element of surprise compounded by the shock of non-state actors killing thousands on U-S soil. Each big anniversary since has been a marker of its own time.
Ten years ago, it was in the wake of the Paris attacks and Isis' bid to establish a caliphate in Syria and Iraq. Five years ago, it was during Covid when the whole planet faced a whole new unforseen common challenge.
We'll ask our panel how the present informs the past and the past informs the present... a present that's more connected and plugged-in and also more fractured, what with the balance of power between old allies and rivals currently in flux. What can we learn from September 11th?f

United Russia gets 70% of party-related news segments on federal television two weeks before parliamentary election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
18:16:27 UTC
03:16:27 KST

Nearly 70% of the airtime that Russia’s largest federal TV channels devoted to political parties in the two weeks before the State Duma election went to the Kremlin-aligned United Russia party. Of the 89 minutes of party airtime from Aug. 31 to Sept. 6, the ruling party received 62 minutes, according to monitoring by the Election Atlas project, which evaluated a total of 216 news broadcasts across six Russian networks.
As The Insider calculated, United Russia’s share of this airtime nearly doubled in a week — from roughly 39% to 70%. From Aug. 24–30, the channels also allocated a total of 89 minutes to political parties, but United Russia received just under 35 minutes. In other words, the overall volume of campaign coverage did not grow, but a significantly larger share of it was redistributed in favor of the ruling party.
Notably, 89% of segments about United Russia in the last week of monitoring had a positive tone. For the New People party, by contrast, this figure was 71%, and for the Communist Party of Russia (KPRF) and the Liberal Democratic Party (LDPR), only around a third of the coverage was positive. The average length of United Russia-related segments came in at 2.7 minutes, while the majority of material about its rivals lasted under a minute.
United Russia’s main news hook involved Vladimir Putin’s meeting with the top five candidates on its federal list: Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin, “war correspondent” Yevgeny Poddubny, children’s rights commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova, and head of the pro-Kremlin Yunarmiya youth movement Vladislav Golovin. Five of the six television channels examined in the study devoted coverage to the meeting, with Channel One running its segment three times. Putin himself is not on the federal candidate list.
United Russia has used Putin’s persona as a promotional tool in its television campaign more than once. On Aug. 22, the president came to the party’s pre-election congress and, even before the vote, called United Russia the “leading political force” in the country. Putin also spoke at the party’s congress in June, where, for the first time since 2007, the event’s decor used imagery directly linking him to United Russia — including a poster with the president’s portrait and the captions “Being for Putin is the bare minimum” and “United Russia is the president’s party.”
The State Duma election — Russia’s first parliamentary election since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine — is scheduled for Sept. 20. The only registered party with an antiwar platform, Yabloko, was removed from the federal-list ballot by the Supreme Court on Aug. 10. After Yabloko disappeared from TV airtime, the Election Atlas project noted a sizable increase in the percentage of overall coverage using a positive tone.

Macron’s space summit showed Europe isn’t ready for takeoff without the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
18:16:20 UTC
03:16:20 KST

Ursula von der Leyen and Emmanuel Macron, center, pose for a photo with other attendees at the International Space Summit in Paris on Sept. 10, 2026. | Pool photo by Aurélien Morissard via AFP/Getty Images
PARIS — The international space summit hosted by French President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday and Thursday was meant to show that Europe is getting serious about investing in its space sector.
But the two-day gathering under the glass dome of Paris’ Grand Palais ended up demonstrating that Europeans are not spending enough to cut reliance on the U.S. to access space — at least not yet.
On the sidelines of the summit, space companies from around the world announced billions in new partnerships and investments, but the big get-together fell short of the public funding announcements needed to access space without U.S. help.
Advertisement
Things had already started to look bad a few days before the summit when American space companies such as SpaceX decided to ditch the event after White House pressure, accusing France of “anti-competitive practices” and disregarding the perspectives of U.S. industry. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz also skipped the event, despite it being co-chaired by France and Germany.
French officials downplayed the importance of the U.S. absence, stressing that the summit would provide Europe with an opportunity to step up its game on space.
But several participants said that the summit's goals were unclear and that it lacked political commitments from countries other than France to boost public investment in the space sector.
Good idea, bad execution
“I had mixed feelings,” said Ezequiel Sánchez, the executive president of PLD Space, one of the companies selected by the European Space Agency to develop European launchers.
“We were all expecting the rabbit out of the hat,” said Sánchez, noting that the summit was “a good idea,” but with a “bad implementation.”
The lack of public funding comparable to the levels delivered by the U.S. loomed large at the summit.
Advertisement
On Wednesday evening, Josef Aschbacher, the director general of the European Space Agency, urged European countries to boost funding to the ESA. In a meeting with ministers from ESA member states, he said that by investing €1 billion per year over the next 10 years, Europe could finally afford to send astronauts into space without relying on NASA.
“It is up to you. Will we be passengers or pilots?” Aschbacher told ministers.
One space official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely, said that the countries looked at the proposal with interest, which still needs to be discussed at an ESA ministerial meeting in Rome in December.
“It is no miracle that the U.S. has a company like SpaceX. It is because the public sector is investing a lot,” the official said.
On the first day of the summit, the space industry associations of France, Germany and Italy urged the EU to allocate “at least €60 billion” to the sector as part of its upcoming 2028-2034 budget. Speaking after Macron at the summit, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen stressed that under the Commission's proposal, €131 billion would be allocated to defense, security and space.
Macron, meanwhile, called for autonomous European space missions in the coming years, backed by "a European space budget that matches our ambitions" — without quantifying the sums involved.
Advertisement
Even if there were no new public funding announcements in Paris, the summit delivered three technical declarations — on the Copernicus program, on space-based scientific data and on the allocation of radio satellite frequencies — as well as making a broader call for a more ambitious European space policy.
Other participants interpreted the fact that few heads of state and government showed up as a sign that they did not fully back Macron’s initiative.
“The main partners didn’t really buy in,” said one space policy insider, pointing to the absence of Merz and of Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, and calling the summit “the swan song of French leadership.”
The Italian and German governments were, however, represented at the ministerial level and several space deals with France and Italy were announced during the summit.
Gilles Rabin, a former official at France’s space agency CNES and now an independent consultant, said that Macron’s diplomatic efforts were also undermined by the fact that he will leave power next year, as he can’t run for a third mandate.
“This summit represents Macron’s final wishes regarding space, his European testament,” he said.

Elon Musk's Boring Co. turns to Middle East for expansion in reaching $23 billion valuation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
18:15:59 UTC
03:15:59 KST

Between taking SpaceX public in the largest IPO on record and rolling out a fleet of driverless Tesla Cybercabs in Austin, Texas, Elon Musk has also been digging tunnels. His tunneling venture, The Boring Co. announced late Wednesday that it's now valued at $23 billion.
Created inside SpaceX in 2017 and spun out a year later, The Boring Co. says its aim is to "revolutionize transportation" by creating underground loops with stations where passengers can board and exit.
While Boring Co. has announced about a dozen city projects, its only loop for public use today is in Las Vegas, where passengers can travel in Tesla vehicles between the downtown convention center and various casino resorts via its Las Vegas Convention Center (LVCC) Loop.
In July of last year, Boring Co. also reached a deal to build 20 miles of tunnels in Nashville, Tennessee, a project dubbed the Music City Loop, to carry paying passengers between downtown and the airport in Tesla vehicles.
The fast-tracked project sparked a partisan feud, and a survey by Vanderbilt University in March found that most Nashville residents didn't want the tunnels in their city. A month before the survey, the company broke ground in Nashville, and it shared clips this week showing its Prufrock machines digging into the city's limestone geology.
With the latest financing, Boring Co. has reeled in an additional $3 billion in a round led by the United Arab Emirates, where the company plans to build over 150 kilometers (93 miles) of tunnels, including a project announced in February of last year, the Dubai Loop.
To finance the costly endeavors, Musk has turned to many of the same investors that previously backed Tesla, SpaceX, and his buyout of Twitter in 2022. Those investors include Valor Equity Partners, Sequoia Capital, Andreessen Horowitz, Singapore's Temasek and Baron Capital.
As with his other companies, where Musk's grand promises have sometimes failed to materialize, many of Boring Co.'s plans have fizzled. In 2018, the company abandoned tunnel projects it had pursued in Los Angeles, with others in Chicago and the Washington, D.C. area never coming to fruition.
Earlier this year, Boring Co. ran a contest, the Tunnel Vision Challenge, promising winners a "free" one-mile tunnel. The Baltimore Ravens, who had entered the challenge and won, turned down Musk's offer after initial meetings with the company.
Some communities are hesitant to work with Musk's company due to its safety and environmental track record. In Las Vegas, Boring Co. racked up hundreds of environmental violations, ProPublica reported, with additional workplace safety and environmental violations in its home state of Texas.
Boring Co. didn't respond to a request for comment.
The company sees plenty of opportunities for growth, including expansion plans underway in Las Vegas.
"Over the past two years, The Boring Company has grown from a single operating Loop system to a multi-city tunneling program, pairing faster machine design with the first hard-rock project, the first international construction contract, and a substantial expansion of Vegas Loop," the company wrote in its post on Wednesday about fundraising.
Following the announcement, Musk posted on X, "Congrats Boring Company team!"
In June, the company won approval from the Nevada System of Higher Education to build a station at the University of Nevada Las Vegas campus, and it's working to extend the reach of its Vegas Loop to the airport and to Allegiant Stadium, where the NFL's Raiders play.
The Boring Co.'s growing ambitions are a potential boon for Tesla. The companies have worked together for years, with Tesla paying Boring Co. about $1 million in 2025 to dig a "Cybertunnel" under its Austin Gigafactory, connecting a Cybertruck assembly line to a lot for loading the vehicles. Tesla vehicles are used to shuttle passengers between Boring Co.'s stations.

Canada, Ukraine pledge 100-year partnership
September 10, 2026
Canada and Ukraine on Thursday signed a declaration vowing to keep a 100-year partnership between the two countries.
It comes as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy visits the country for talks with Prime Minister Mark Carney and other Canadian officials.
Zelenskyy and Carney said that Canada had pledged to help shore up Ukraine's air defense.
"Earlier today, Canada and Ukraine finalized an agreement to deliver critical air defense interceptors (through) the United States Jumpstart mechanism," Carney said.
He said that the package would amount to some 350 million Canadian dollars ($260 million, €218 million).
The prime minister said that Canada had provided the equivalent of 26 billion Canadian dollars ($19 billion, €16 billion) in support for Ukraine.
"We've provided support for the energy systems and beyond. We'll provide more support," he said.
Zelenskyy expressed his graitude for what he described as a "very important" air defense package.
"I'm so thankful," Zelenskyy said. "This is very important package of air defense and this is crucial."
Speaking ahead of his meeting with Zelenskyy, Carney also emphasized Ukrainians' historical role in contributing to European settlement in the prairies of Canada's western provinces.
"Ukrainians help build this province, this country. Canada will help rebuild Ukraine when peace comes," he said, referring to Alberta, of which Calgary is the largest city.
Canada is home to over a million people of Ukrainian descent.
Zelenskyy visits Canada after Norway
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in Calgary late on Wednesday for "important meetings and agreements" with Canadian officials.
His visit comes on the heels of his attendance at King Harald V's funeral in Norway, where his plane had been delayed by a drone incursion.
The Ukrainian leader is in the middle of a flurry of trips and meetings to shore up his country's defenses for the cold winter months.
"The main focus will be on supporting Ukraine in protecting our skies and preparing for the winter," Zelenskyy said in a social media post before leaving.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement that the visit "will focus on shared priorities between Canada and Ukraine, including deepening defense, economic, and energy cooperation."
Carney's statement added Canada "remains steadfast in our commitment to support Ukraine's defense, recovery, and reconstruction."
Zelenskyy had also signaled a desire to meet with US President Donald Trump on the matter before the end of September.
Since Russia's invasion in 2022, Moscow has consistently increased attacks on fuel and heating infrastructure in Ukraine in the autumn and winter.
What is happening on the battlefield?
Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery in the Yamalo-Nenets region overnight, as well as a seaport in Dagestan, Zelenskyy said. He added that other unnamed sited critical to Russia's war industry had also been hit.
Alexander Gusev, governor of Russia's Voronezh region, said that one woman in the town of Borisoglebsk had been killed by falling drone debris overnight and that at least 19 drones had been destroyed while flying over the region.
The Russian Defense Ministry said a total of 448 Ukrainian drones were shot down overnight.
In Ukraine, Russian attacks hit buildings owned by a major food producer in Dnipro, killing at least two according to local officials.
Two Azerbaijani crew members were killed in a drone attack on a cargo ship in the Ukrainian region of Odesa, Ukraine's infrastructure ministry said.
Azerbaijan's foreign ministry also confirmed the information, adding that two further members of the crew were taken to hospital in Chornomorsk, Ukraine.
While Baku did not mention who was responsible for the attack, Ukraine blamed Russia for the drone strike.

‘It was all hands on deck’: how the CIA responded to 9/11
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
18:11:47 UTC
03:11:47 KST

A generation of spies had lost an enemy but not yet found a role. Then came 9/11.
A decade after the dissolution of the Soviet Union, al-Qaida’s devastating attacks on New York and Washington on 11 September 2001 announced to the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) that the long era of battling communism, for which it had been founded, was officially at an end.
It was to be replaced by a no-holds-barred “war on terror” that would leave the CIA with a soiled reputation over falsified intelligence that led to the invasion and occupation of Iraq, and an extraordinary rendition program in which suspects were subjected to “enhanced interrogations” at secret sites that official US inquiries subsequently defined as torture.
The US intelligence community was dramatically transformed after two planes flew into the World Trade Center, a third smashed into the Pentagon, and a fourth crashed in the Pennsylvania countryside after passengers overcame the hijackers.
Accounts of what unfolded inside the CIA’s headquarters in Langley, Virginia, suggests an organization unprepared for the drastically changed world the attacks ushered in, despite an awareness among some in the intelligence community that al-Qaida and its leader, Osama bin Laden, represented a clear and present danger.
Margaret Henoch, then a counter-intelligence officer with little knowledge of terrorism, recalls confusion, chaos and an initial lack of direction from senior leadership as staff struggled to process what seemed like a bolt from a clear blue sky on that balmy late summer day.
“One of my officers came in and said to me: ‘A plane just ran into the World Trade Center,’” she said. To this day, Henoch – who had previously been stationed in Vienna, where she focused on the International Atomic Energy Agency and nuclear threats – is haunted by the apparent vacuum that followed.
About 40 minutes after the first attack, with no clear direction from the top of CIA, she decided to go up to the seventh floor, which accommodated the agency’s senior figures, including its then director, George Tenet.
To her surprise, the area was deserted, apart from three assistants.
“It was reasonable that they would have moved those guys someplace else,” said Henoch. “What was unreasonable, in my humble opinion, was that no one thought about all those people sitting in that building. Because if the Pentagon was hit, there was a chance that we, too, were a target – and it would be nice to believe that the people who left the building rapidly had a thought for all those who worked for them.
“It was not clear that they did.”
The Guardian contacted Tenet, now working in the private sector, for comment. In an emailed response, Bill Harlow, the CIA’s public affairs director at the time of the attacks, cited details in the 2007 memoir, At the Center of the Storm, which he co-wrote with Tenet, and said orders were issued for the majority of the staff to leave the building at “about 10am” – nearly an hour after the second plane struck at 9.03am.
Harlow added: “We were aware at the time of intelligence gathered around 1995-96 of terrorist desires to attack CIA HQ with an airplane.
“Director Tenet and the senior leadership moved to another building on the compound that presented a lower profile and would have a greater chance of survival if we were hit by a plane.
“Notably, a decision was made that the personnel of the counter-terrorism center remained in the original headquarters building throughout that day … accepting the risk. The senior leadership team returned to the headquarters in the middle of the afternoon on 9/11.”
‘I had a briefing on who the hell al-Qaida was’
Some time afterwards, an order was given for the thousands of personnel in the building to evacuate. Some, including Henoch, were told to relocate to alternative sites to address the emergency.
But by the time of that instruction, nearby roads were choked with traffic as commuters returned home from Washington DC after being released from work early. That prevented agency staff from departing, and triggered fears that they could be sitting ducks for the doomed fourth plane, which was already known to be in the air.
“Large segments of the CIA operating staff were trapped,” Henoch said. “One guy, who was senior to me, was standing next to me in the car park and he said, ‘I have served in multiple war zones. I was a combat soldier in Vietnam and I’m going to die in the parking lot of the CIA.’”
The dysfunctional scene was soon replaced by one of much greater conviction – leading to permanent changes in US intelligence.
“I just remember loads of cable traffic coming in that said: it’s got to be al-Qaida,” said Henoch. “It wasn’t my world, so I had to have a quick briefing on who the hell al-Qaida was, because I just didn’t know anything about it.
“The change was immediate. The next morning, everybody at the Central Intelligence Agency had to know who they were, and how it intersected with everything you were doing.”
Steven Cash, a former CIA counter-terrorism officer who had left the agency to join the staff of the US Senate intelligence committee six months beforehand, faults the CIA’s pre-9/11 terrorism strategy as being too narrowly focused “looking to find bad guys” while neglecting the “political dimension”.
“There was an emphasis on looking at terrorists as if they were a motorcycle gang,” said Cash, who had specialized on the Lebanese Shia group Hezbollah, a close ally of Iran. “A decision was made in the first [George HW] Bush administration to take terrorism away from the people who looked at geographic areas and separate it out. [It was] illustrative of a mistaken way of looking at the world, because terrorists don’t exist in a vacuum.”
Cash moved on to focus on the Balkans before leaving the agency, but still harboured guilt after the attacks. “Was this our fault? Did we fail? That kind of guilt felt, at least for me, really personal.”
Cash had been on Capitol Hill, attending a committee meeting, when news of the attacks filtered through. “Somebody said, put on the TV and we saw the second plane hit,” he said. “And then they started evacuating the building.
“It was a mess. People were in the hall screaming, running around. The third plane had hit the Pentagon by that point, because we could see smoke across the National Mall.”
The following day, Cash and his then boss, the late Democratic senator Dianne Feinstein, visited CIA headquarters and found a mood of determined resolve. “It was all hands on deck. The people I knew were getting deployed very quickly to Afghanistan,” he recalled. “These people are pros. They didn’t care whether they were blamed or not. They wanted to do something.
“I have a little bit of survivor guilt here. Maybe I should have been shipped out to Afghanistan.”
Political pressure
On their visit to CIA headquarters on 12 September, senators asked agency operatives what legislation and resources they would need to respond to the attacks of the previous day, according to Cash.
Two early – and controversial – results were the USA Patriot Act of 2001, which expanded law enforcement and surveillance powers, and the Homeland Security Act of the following year, creating the US Department of Homeland Security, which houses agencies including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
Later changes established the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, with the goal of coordinating 18 different intelligence bodies and eliminating the lack of coordination widely held to blame for warning signs of the 9/11 plot going unheeded.
“DNI was formed to make sure that we actually share everything with everybody. We don’t just keep it inside CIA,” said Susan Miller, a retired CIA counter-intelligence officer.
“What’s really cool is we’ve changed how we do things across the board, not just for terrorism. It’s really improved things. There was no coordination before.”
Yet the reaction to the attacks changed intelligence in another way – by making it more susceptible to political pressure, as President George W Bush’s administration searched for information that could be used to justify an invasion of Iraq to topple Saddam Hussein.
In September 2002, Henoch – who had previously studied Russian weapons capabilities working at the Stanford Research Institute – was asked to assess intelligence provided by an Iraqi defector codenamed Curveball, who had sought asylum in Germany, and provided its intelligence agency with what he said was proof of Saddam’s biological weapons program.
She quickly concluded the claims were fabricated, and passed her conclusions up the chain of command. They were not well received. When Colin Powell, the then US secretary of state, visited the CIA months later to review the agency’s intelligence on Iraq, Henoch and her fellow doubters were not informed. Powell’s subsequent speech to the United Nations security council in February 2003, in which he made the case for war, relied heavily on Curveball’s testimony – despite Henoch’s insistence when the address was checked with her and other officers beforehand that his assertions were not credible.
“We took a look at the Powell speech and I said: ‘You can’t use this. We think this is garbage,” she said. “I did write somewhere – I can’t remember on what page – ‘How can you send someone to die for something like this? No one ever answered that for me.
“The next thing I heard was, ‘Well, when we get in there, we’ll find something.’”
After the invasion, inspectors found no evidence of biological weapons. Curveball was later debunked as a fraud.
Miller, too, encountered the administration’s zeal for intelligence that could justify invading Iraq when she was posted to Prague as CIA station chief in 2002. Czech intelligence had investigated – and, initially, tentatively confirmed – a claim that one of the 9/11 ringleaders, Mohammed Atta, had travelled to Prague the previous year and met an Iraqi embassy official, Ahmad Samir al-Ani, months before the attacks.
The report was seized on by the hawkish US vice-president, Dick Cheney, as evidence of Saddam’s possible links to the attacks, thus providing another justification for war. But Czech intelligence officials retreated from their earlier stance, and the CIA concluded there was no evidence that the meeting happened.
Nevertheless, Donald Rumsfeld, then the US defense secretary, brazenly tried to revive it when Miller briefed him – along with George W Bush and Condoleezza Rice, the national security adviser – when they visited the Czech capital for a Nato summit in 2002.
“‘Young lady, you forgot about this other thing’,” Rumsfeld told Miller, she said. “I played dumb and said: ‘What other thing?’ He replied: ‘Mohammed Atta was here in Prague meeting the Iraqi consul.’
“Bush was looking really uncomfortable and Condi was looking straight ahead. I simply said, ‘Mr President, Madam Secretary, and Mr Rumsfeld, the CIA, the Czech service and I don’t make things up. We give you the facts, and the fact is that he was not here.’
“Bush and Rice nodded in acceptance and the ambassador supported me. But Rumsfeld threw his pen down in disgust.”
The invasion the neocons craved
Whether the supposed meeting happened or not, Rumsfeld and his neoconservative allies got the invasion they craved – leading to a protracted conflict that tarnished the CIA’s reputation and whose length, along with the coinciding US-led military campaign in Afghanistan, spurred popular opposition to “forever wars”.
Despite the blow to the agency’s standing, Cash insisted that its intelligence-gathering and functioning radically improved, thanks to the changes instituted after the attacks. “We have improved our intelligence capabilities significantly from what they were before 9/11,” he said, citing the success in preventing repeat attacks on US soil.
But with the Trump administration now engaged in a war with Iran, roiling the Middle East, such security could no longer be guaranteed, he believes.
“I’m not saying it was a great time,” Cash said, of the CIA’s record in the months and years after September 2001. “But the sense of purpose of being at a place in history where we – as a group, as a society – can do something, was pretty intoxicating.
“I was very proud to have been part of it. It sucked – but proud to have been part of it. And I think everything we’re seeing now is the antithesis of that.”

curved joinery and bold color reframe 1960s apartment in madrid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
18:10:58 UTC
03:10:58 KST

Reworking a 1960s Madrid apartment around everyday use
Located in Madrid’s Imperial neighborhood, this 48-sqmapartment was renovated by Alessio Lamarca and Marta Ciabattini around the everyday routines of its future occupant. Instead of beginning with a predetermined aesthetic, the architects considered how the home would actually be used: where bags are placed on arrival, how the kitchen is used, where time is spent, and which spaces and objects are part of daily life. The approach informed both the layout and the scale of individual elements. The original apartment had three bedrooms, a living room, a separate kitchen, and one bathroom. Its condition had remained largely unchanged since the 1960s, with deteriorated finishes, layers of old plaster and paint, and a heavily compartmentalized plan that restricted the available 48 usable square meters. The renovation reduces the layout to two bedrooms, one bathroom, and an open living area with an American-style kitchen. Spaces and storage are calibrated to actual use, eliminating elements that were not required and concentrating the available area around everyday activities. The result is a compact home with a layout shaped by occupation rather than by a generic model of domestic life.
The starting point was an apartment described by the architects as being effectively frozen in time since the 1960s. Its obsolete finishes, poor state of repair, and divided rooms created a series of spatial constraints within a limited floor area. The renovation addresses these conditions through a new spatial organization and a strong architectural identity. The project treats the apartment as a setting for everyday routines, allowing the architecture to incorporate different activities and moments within a compact footprint. The kitchen, for example, is sized around its actual use, while storage is designed around the objects required in daily life. The living area accommodates different ways of occupying the space, including sitting on the sofa or floor, reading, and listening to records. The absence of a large dining table reflects the apartment’s specific pattern of use, avoiding space dedicated to functions that are not part of everyday life.
Bright colors become part of the home’s spatial organization
Color forms a central part of the renovation, with coral, pink, deep blue, white, wood, and green details establishing the apartment’s chromatic identity. Pink and coral are used as architectural elements that define zones, circulation routes, and volumes. The architects approach color as an additional construction material, using it to shape the perception of space and to create relationships between light, shadow, and volume. The fixed position of the bathroom, determined by technical constraints, becomes the basis for organizing the connecting hallway. This corridor operates as a chromatic threshold between the daytime social area and the nighttime private zone. A measured block of color establishes a visual axis through the apartment, helping to guide movement while integrating flush storage solutions into the walls. The bathroom is treated as an immersive blue volume, introducing a distinct atmosphere and a complementary color within the wider palette. Elsewhere, the walls are finished in a warm, broken white that provides a continuous background for the changing light, architectural volumes, and stronger colors.
Custom furniture is used throughout the apartment to make efficient use of the limited floor area. In the living zone, a compact arrangement combines the entrance, an integrated bench and drawer units, the kitchen, and the living area within a few square meters. A central element is the American-style kitchen countertop, designed as a curved bar supported by a cylindrical column. The rounded geometry reduces the obstruction created by a conventional rectangular countertop and keeps the entrance circulation open. The underside of the bar is also used to accommodate a small custom bookshelf. The same approach extends into the bedrooms, where built-in wardrobes incorporate the existing structural columns into the new partition walls. This allows the storage to occupy otherwise difficult areas while preserving usable floor space. In the primary bedroom, the wardrobe is modified at the corner to avoid a rigid orthogonal transition at the entrance. The curved edge becomes an open corner bookshelf, softening the visual relationship between the wardrobe and the room while maintaining a clear view into the space.
Wood and lacquer establish another layer of continuity across the apartment. In the kitchen, walnut wood is combined with the specific pink tone of Marga lacquer, creating a warm material and chromatic thread that links the different areas. The same design language continues into the storage elements, while a different lacquer tone, Ave, introduces a shift in the closet. The underlying logic of the renovation remains consistent, but the change in color gives the space a different character. Across the apartment, color, built-in furniture, curved geometries, and carefully integrated storage work together as part of a single spatial strategy. The renovation uses the limited dimensions of the existing apartment as a framework for organizing circulation, domestic functions, and visual relationships around the routines of everyday life.

name: Alessio Lamarca architects: Marta Ciabattini and Alessio Lamarca

SBI director hopes legislative changes to help reduce problem of unauthorised absence from military units
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
21:10:42 EEST
03:10:42 KST

Director of the State Bureau of Investigations (SBI) Oleksiy Sukhachov hopes for the swiftest possible adoption of legislative changes that will help minimize the problem of unauthorized desertion, in particular by granting the prosecutor the authority to close a case if a soldier intends to return to active duty.
"Every year, we develop various tools and methods to combat this phenomenon (desertion). This involves direct communication with the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) command – drafting separate guidance letters for the leadership of the General Staff and the commands of the military branches – regarding specific incidents and situations in certain military units where unauthorized absence is systemic. This involves the potential identification, during the investigation, of the causes and conditions of desertion and the need for the military command to respond to them," Sukhachov said on Thursday in Kyiv during the presentation of the audit report on the State Bureau of Investigation's activities, conducted by the Accounting Chamber.
Representatives of the diplomatic corps from Ukraine's European partner countries were present at the audit presentation.
In addition, as Sukhachov said, the State Bureau of Investigations has repeatedly proposed to the Verkhovna Rada's Committee on Law Enforcement and the Committee on Security and Defense the possibility of reinstating military personnel in the State Security Service to active duty without criminal prosecution.
"But today we see that this crisis situation still exists. We put forward a proposal and communicated with members of the Committee on Law Enforcement regarding the introduction of appropriate changes. We are confident that there will be changes and progress," the SBI director said.
First and foremost, as he explained, this concerns granting the prosecutor the authority to directly close criminal proceedings if a servicemember has decided to return to the ranks of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
Currently, as Sukhachov explained, such decisions are made by the court based on requests from prosecutors. "Given the vacancies in the courts and the heavy caseload, we are not achieving effective results in this area. That is why we discussed this with our colleagues and came up with this proposal," he said.
In addition, the SBI director recalled the initiative to transfer the investigation of crimes committed by the Special Forces to the Military Law Enforcement Service within the Armed Forces of Ukraine. "We are in communication with the Military Law Enforcement Service and the Ministry of Defense. We hope this issue will be resolved," Sukhachov said.
Earlier, in an exclusive interview with the Interfax-Ukraine news agency, the SBI director expressed hope that the Verkhovna Rada would support the initiative to grant the Military Law Enforcement Service within the Armed Forces the right to conduct pre-trial investigations into military personnel who, in particular, have deserted without authorization.
"Our proposal is as follows: to grant the Military Law Enforcement Service the authority to conduct pre-trial investigations. This can easily be done within the existing staffing levels of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, without increasing funding," Sukhachov said.
The director of the State Bureau of Investigation noted that the revamped pre-trial investigation body will be able to investigate criminal offenses such as high treason, desertion, insubordination, and certain other offenses.
According to him, the proposal is for the Military Law Enforcement Service to investigate crimes committed by military personnel who do not hold officer ranks.

Hamed was also involved in the October 2003 shooting attack in Ein Yabrud, in which three IDF soldiers were killed: Sgt. Elad Pollak, Sgt. Roi Yaakov Solomon and Staff-Sgt. Erez Idan. Another Hamas terrorist involved in the Ein Yabrud attack and Hamas's West Bank Headquarters was eliminated by Israeli security forces in Gaza in 2024.
Hamed initially released back to Gaza as part of Schalit deal

Following his release to Gaza, Hamed continued operating in Hamas's military wing and was involved in recruiting and directing Hamas operatives to advance attacks in Judea and Samaria, the IDF, ISA, and Israel Police said.

Voters Are Turning to AI for Election Help. The Answers Aren't Always Right
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
18:07:54 UTC
03:07:54 KST

After years of Google restricting Gemini’s ability to answer users’ questions about major elections, the tech giant is shifting tactics.
Google announced Wednesday that the company would add credible election information about the upcoming midterms—including details about where and how to vote—to its Gemini app, along with AI-generated responses in its search products. The company said it would share information on polling locations and voter registration instructions from state and local governments and the voting information group, Democracy Works, along with race results from The Associated Press.
As Gemini wades deeper into politics, the risk of the chatbot giving voters misleading, biased, or outdated election information will only grow. A Pew Research Center study earlier this year found about half of adults under 50 rely on chatbots to search for information, while a smaller share use them to read news.  
“We know that voters are going to turn to chatbots more and more,” said Valeria de la Fuente, a digital research analyst at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue who recently co-authored a report on election-related misinformation from chatbots. “So the quality of the responses that we found is concerning.”
Google’s new election policy is a less cautious stance than the one the company took in 2022 and 2024 when it blocked Gemini from answering certain election-related questions, pushing users to seek answers from Google search instead.
“People come to Google to stay informed during election season—like when finding their polling site, watching candidate debates, or tracking results on election night,” the company said in Wednesday’s blog post. “We take the responsibility to deliver high quality, trustworthy information seriously.”
Other tech companies have taken similar approaches. Both OpenAI and Anthropic said their chatbots would direct users to voting information from the nonprofit Democracy Works. OpenAI also plans to provide live vote counts from The Associated Press, and monitor its systems for signs of political bias. Meta spokesman Corey Chambliss said when MetaAI users ask about voting and participating in elections, the service will give them local information or direct them to government sources.
But how effective those approaches will be as the contest gets closer remains an open question. A study released last week by the Institute for Strategic Dialogue found chatbots from major companies including OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic routinely gave incorrect answers to questions about voting, including in states where there had been significant changes to the election procedures.
The group found that 29% of responses to English prompts about voting were either incomplete, inaccurate, or outdated. Responses in Spanish were 16% less likely to be accurate, according to the study. Some of the lowest performing questions included: “I didn’t change my address before the deadline, can I vote in Ohio?” or “I am applying for an absentee ballot in Minnesota, what documents do I need?” 
Problems in the chatbots’ answers mirror those on the internet itself. The AI systems appeared to be pulling outdated information from state government websites about the 2024 election. Meanwhile, in certain cases responses to prompts in Spanish were often less detailed or more likely to contain no citations, reflecting the language disparities in the overall information ecosystem, according to de la Fuente. 
“Overall, what we saw was a lot of ambiguous, confusing language” in the Spanish responses, she said. “In some cases, poor or neutral translations from English. Some of them could still be understood. Some of them were simply wrong.”
By contrast, the AI models were much better at answering adversarial prompts raising specific election fraud claims that media organizations had already fact-checked. They were less effective at debunking harder-to-refute election-related concerns, including those about ballot harvesting, voting machine security, and noncitizen voting. 
It’s in those “gray areas” where the models are more likely to give “problematic” answers, de la Fuente said.

The Georgian Church condemned the use of the name of Saint Gabriel by a Russian Armed Forces unit fighting against Ukraine

From 9/11 to Pahalgam: India’s Evolving Strategy in the Global War on Terror
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
18:07:00 UTC
03:07:00 KST

Some incidents in world history not only leave deep scars on the soul of a nation but alter the nation’s trajectory irreversibly. The terror attack of September 11, 2001 was one such incident. A perfectly normal morning turned into a horrific nightmare when 19 al-Qaida terrorists hijacked four passenger planes, two of which crashed into the Twin Towers in New York and one into the Pentagon building outside of Washington, D.C. The Twin Towers came crashing down and the result was a death count of almost 3,000.
The resultant national outrage and anger led to the United States leading its most extensive military mission since the Vietnam War, chasing al-Qaida and its leader Osama bin Laden into Afghanistan. In a military campaign lasting almost 20 years, al-Qaida was largely neutralized and Osama bin Laden was eventually tracked and killed in Pakistan on May 2, 2011.
The 9/11 attacks led to profound changes in the United States as well, especially in matters of internal security. There was a clear mandate that no matter what, there cannot be another 9/11 type of incident on the American mainland ever again.
In the Indian context however, it took decades of terror attacks before India similarly said, “no more.” Thanks to a policy crafted by Pakistan in the early 1990s to “bleed India through a thousand cuts” with cross-border terrorism, India endured a large number of terror attacks and losses, especially in Kashmir. But then one terror incident shook India like never before.
The terror attack in Pahalgam on April 22, 2025 killed 26 innocent civilians in a popular tourist spot in Kashmir. The attack was launched by terrorists belonging to The Resistance Force, an offshoot of the Pakistan-based Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT). The anger and outrage in India were magnified many times over as the victims – all men – were specifically identified by their religion (Hindu, except for one Christian and one local Muslim who tried to intervene). The men were also shot dead in front of their wives.
The resultant military operation, Operation Sindoor, launched by India into Pakistan on May 7, made clear India’s new resolve against terrorism.
While these two incidents – 9/11 and the Pahalgam attack – were separated by almost 24 years, they are united by two nations’ expressed resolve to fight terror to the ends of the Earth. But as the Pahalgam attack sadly showed, the war against terror has not been won.
Al-Qaida may not be a force to reckon with in the form it was 25 years ago and it may no longer have leaders like Osama bin Laden who could attract and ideologically indoctrinate youth to join. But many smaller offshoots of al-Qaida still operate across the globe. In the Indian context, while LeT and other Pakistan-based terror groups may have been dealt a punishing blow by India, inputs from Pakistan indicate that there is a strong resolve to revive these groups. Therefore, the fight against terror isn’t over yet.
It is therefore important to examine how terror is changing form and how nations are constantly evolving their strategies to stay ahead of the curve to counter and neutralize such threats before they manifest.
The Evolution of Terror
Over the past 25 years, the form terrorism has changed, as have the type of instruments used to carry out terror attacks. Naturally, the strategies to tackle terror have evolved as well.
Unlike big terror groups like al-Qaida or the Islamic State (IS) in the past, terror groups have now morphed into smaller and more autonomous groups. Lone wolf attacks are now becoming the norm and technologies like drones, cyber, and even artificial intelligence are being used by terror groups. Indirect attacks like cyberattacks on key energy and banking infrastructure are complementing high-impact physical attacks on the population.
Hierarchical organizations and organized training camps are increasingly giving way to more fluid structures, which operate through affiliations and franchises, encrypted communications, cryptocurrencies, social media, and loosely connected cells. Campaigns seeking territorial control like the IS in Iraq and Syria are being replaced by terror campaigns to disrupt social cohesion within a country and bleed nations financially.
And, accordingly, strategies to fight terror by countries too are evolving rapidly. Counterterrorism has evolved from a predominantly military campaign into a much broader strategy incorporating multiple instruments of state power like intelligence, financial surveillance, border control, cyber monitoring, deradicalization, and international cooperation. When military action is taken, it takes the form of precision operations through cutting-edge standoff weapon platforms.
The India Context
The fight against terror in India had a frustrating beginning. In most cases, the response to terrorist attacks was limited to sectoral military operations, tightening border controls, and issuing warnings to Pakistan. In some cases, it also led to cutting off diplomatic ties for some time.
The first such terror attack was the hijacking of Air India’s flight IC-814 on December 24, 1999, just a few months after the Kargil war. With very few options then and increasing public pressure, India agreed to release two Pakistan-based terrorists, Ahmed Omar Shiekh and Masood Azhar, in exchange for over 160 civilian hostages. Massod Azhar went on to establish Jaish-e-Mohammad (JeM), the Pakistan-based terrorist group that later launched a terror attack on the Indian Parliament on December 13, 2001. Caught by surprise, India ordered a full-scale military mobilization under Operation Parakaram, but it ultimately ended without a bullet being fired.
The 26/11 Mumbai terror attack in 2008 was a milestone in many ways. Widely considered as India’s 9/11 moment, it brought global attention to India’s war against terror. Although once again India did not end up punishing Pakistan for the attack, it did lead to a major security review and structural changes. The National Investigative Agency (NIA) was formed as a result, with sweeping powers on matters of internal national security. The NIA is now functioning as the central counterterrorism law enforcement agency in India.
The mandate of fighting terror expanded to include stronger intelligence coordination, tighter coastal security and border surveillance, specialized forces to fight terror, and cooperation between central and state agencies. The overall responsibility for coastal security was placed under the Indian Navy.
Tracking and monitoring terror finance too became a key instrument in the fight against terror. The Multi Agency Center, which was established in December 2001 as a part of the key recommendations of the Kargil Review Committee, also became a key coordination platform for intelligence exchange and cooperation against terror. However, most of India’s anti-terrorism measures remained passive, reactive, and preventive.
The Kinetic Strategy
It was only after 2014, when the Modi government came to power, that the intent to deliver a decisive response to any act of terror grew firm. Counterterrorism operations in Kashmir were given a new momentum and measures to block infiltration across the Line of Control were strengthened.
A terror attack on September 18, 2016 by JeM terrorists against an army camp in Uri, Kashmir, led to the first cross-border surgical strikes by the Indian Army, which destroyed multiple terrorist camps and infrastructure in Pakistan. It was not only a strong reply to the terror attack but also signaled a major shift in India’s strategic policy and rules of engagement regarding cross-border terrorism.
While it did deter Pakistan to some extent, it did not end its terror campaign. On February 14, 2019, JeM terrorists unleashed another terror attack, this time on a police convoy in Pulwama, Kashmir, killing 40 soldiers. Upping the ante, this time, the India Air Force launched strikes on a terror camp of JeM in Balakot, Pakistan on February 26. It was the first time that the Indian Air Force had crossed into Pakistani airspace to launch a strike against terror.
However, it was the terror attack in Pahalgam on April 22, 2025 that outraged the nation like never before. Modi vowed to track the terrorists “to the ends of the Earth.” With an aim to deliver a decisive blow to the terror network in Pakistan, the Indian Armed Forces launched Operation Sindoor on May 7, hitting the heart of the Pakistan-based terror network. Within 96 hours, nine major terrorist camps destroyed and India had even hit key military assets like airfields and radar stations, forcing Pakistan to seek a ceasefire.
However, the Indian experience tells us that the fight against terror is far from over. With Pakistan unlikely to give up on its policy of state-sponsored terror against India, new forms of threats are likely to emerge. India therefore cannot think that Operation Sindoor is enough to deter any future terror attacks from across the border. In the fight against terror, no deterrence strategy can be absolute. It has to evolve, keeping pace with technology and terror tactics, and hope to stay one step ahead.
A key to this constantly evolving thought is PRAHAAR, India’s first comprehensive National Counter Terrorism Policy & Strategy which was unveiled on February 23, 2026. This provides a national counterterrorism framework for prevention of, and responding to terrorist activities and radicalization through coordinated “whole of government” and “whole of society” approaches.
Conclusion
As the world marks the 25 years of the 9/11 attack, the lesson is not whether terror has been defeated but whether nations are equipped well enough to disrupt and deter future terror threats. The success of any strategy is measured by its outcomes. Even if one major terror attack succeeds despite hundreds of potential terror attacks being thwarted, the strategy would still be termed a failure.
The October 7, 2023 Hamas terror attack into Israel is an example: the best of intelligence and overwhelming military superiority could not preempt or prevent the attack. The events of October 7 not only killed almost 1,200 people in Israel but unleashed a brutal conflict in Gaza and West Asia, which still continues to this day.
For India, the fight against terror predates 9/11. Over 25 years later, that fight continues, strengthened now with a new political-military resolve and constantly evolving methods of deterrence.

Global bond selloff resumes as surging oil prices stoke fears about inflation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
18:05:15 UTC
03:05:15 KST

Nervous investors across big economies have been dumping government bonds, driving up the cost of borrowing, as surging oil prices amplified fears about rising inflation.
The cost of a barrel of oil jumped 6% to above $107 on Thursday amid concerns that advances by Houthi rebels along the Red Sea coast in Yemen could choke off Saudi crude exports.
The global bond sell-off that has rocked markets in recent weeks resumed in response to the news from the Middle East – which came against a backdrop of escalating concern about out-of-control government borrowing.
Higher oil prices, which had already climbed since hostilities resumed in the Iran war, are expected to drive up inflation, prompting central banks to raise interest rates and putting the brakes on economic growth.
Donald Trump suggested on Wednesday that the conflict with Iran could continue until “immediately after” November’s US midterm elections, at which point he claimed oil prices would be “tumbling downward”.
The European Central Bank (ECB) raised its main interest rate to 2.5% on Thursday, with its president, Christine Lagarde, saying: “We believe inflation will be longer lasting than we had anticipated.”
“The conflict in the Middle East continues to generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to remain well above target for an extended period,” she added.
As Thursday’s sell-off gathered pace in London, the yield, or interest rate, on 10-year UK government bonds surged above 5.37% – the highest cost of borrowing since 2007 – creating a fresh headache for the new chancellor, John Healey.
With less than seven weeks to go until Healey’s first budget on 28 October, higher interest rates on the UK’s debt-pile will raise the cost of future investment projects and eat into the Treasury’s fiscal headroom.
At the same time, the prospect of higher energy bills as oil and gas prices rise is likely to intensify pressure on the government to help consumers to weather the winter.
Unleaded petrol prices have already risen by 6p a litre since the start of September, according to the motoring organisation the RAC, while the prospect of higher inflation has prompted some banks to raise their mortgage rates.
Healey has promised to provide a “breathing space” for UK households while also addressing the cost of doing business.
In a speech on Monday, however, he also sought to tame bond market fears by committing himself to “controlling borrowing to bear down on inflation, and reducing long-term pressures on our public finances”.
In the US, where Trump has promised to write a $5,000 (£3,700) cheque for every adult citizen if the Republicans win the midterms, Thursday’s sell-off pushed up the yield on 10-year borrowing to 4.92% – the highest since 2023.
The cost of longer-term borrowing also continued to surge, with 30-year yields hitting the highest level since 2007, despite the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, intervening directly in debt markets on Wednesday.
Bessent hoped to bring down yields by buying back $6bn worth of government debt; but investors appeared to respond by deepening the sell-off.
Kyle Rodda, a senior financial market analyst at the broker Capital.com, said: “Ultimately, a sustained drop in long-end yields can only be achieved by genuine shifts in macroeconomic policy: either the US government pulling back on spending or the Fed lifting rates.”
Policymakers at the Federal Reserve, the US central bank, will meet under its new chair, Kevin Warsh, to set interest rates next week.
Markets are expecting a rise – potentially enraging Trump, who has repeatedly demanded rate cuts. In a TruthSocial post last week, the president said: “The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart – BE PATRIOTS for a change.”
A plethora of UK data to be published over the next week, including on inflation, jobs and growth, will give an updated snapshot of how resilient the British economy has been in the face of the Iran war.
In the first six months of the year, UK growth was the strongest among the G7 economies. This was despite higher-than-expected oil prices and the absence of hoped-for rate cuts.
Bank of England policymakers will also meet next week, but are expected to leave the UK’s key interest rate on hold at 3.75% for the time being as they continue to monitor the impact of higher oil prices.

25 years after 9/11: Al-Qaeda weakened but not gone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
18:05:00 UTC
03:05:00 KST

25 years after 9/11: Al-Qaeda weakened but not gone
September 10, 2026
The extremist preacher Abdullah al-Muhaysini no longer has to worry about US sanctions. In late August 2026, the US Department of the Treasury removed the former jihadist from the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons list, or SDN List. It includes individuals and organizations whose assets are frozen in the US and with whom US citizens are generally not allowed to do business.
After Syria's civil war broke out in 2011, al-Muhaysini recruited fighters and helped establish a governing structure shaped by the Nusra Front, which emerged from al-Qaeda.
His removal from the list is linked to the new US government policy on Syria: Washington also removed the Nusra Front and Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) from the SDN List.
25 years after the September 11 attacks, this is a remarkable snapshot. Al-Qaeda — which means "the base" in Arabic — has neither disappeared nor remained the same organization: Its core has weakened, but its regional branches have remained strong across parts of Africa and Asia, observers agree.
Regional offshoots in the Sahel, Yemen and Afghanistan
Only, al-Qaeda itself is operating less and less under its own name.
"This is largely due to the successful counterterrorism efforts following 2001," Lars Berger, professor of terrorism studies at the German Federal University of Administrative Sciences, told DW.
The military campaign in Afghanistan, along with cooperation between intelligence agencies and police, has significantly weakened the group.
"From this perspective, the September 11 attacks were a major strategic failure for al-Qaeda," Berger said.
The hoped-for radicalization of the Arab world and the overthrow of its regimes failed to materialize. About ten years after the attacks in New York and Washington, al-Qaeda's most famous figure, Osama bin Laden, was killed in May 2011.
As a result, al-Qaeda reorganized itself.
"The militia sought out areas where it could establish a permanent foothold, for example in parts of Africa or Yemen," Berger said, adding that "countries with weak state structures, overwhelmed security forces and unresolved local conflicts are particularly favorable."
"Today, this is particularly true of Africa," Rüdiger Lohlker, professor emeritus of Islamic studies at the University of Vienna, notes.
In the Sahel, Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin, or JNIM, has emerged as a powerful al-Qaeda offshoot, he said.
An analysis by the think tank Critical Threats Project uses Niger as an example to show how JNIM and the Islamic State's Sahel Province (ISSP) compete for territory, fighters and resources. In June 2026, JNIM claimed responsibility for an attack on the international airport in Niger's capital, Niamey.
In Somalia, al-Shabab — a group closely linked to al-Qaeda — is strong, and in Yemen, al-Qaeda is present in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP). Afghanistan also remains a safe haven for the terrorist organization.
However, the success of these offshoots cannot be explained solely by jihadist ideology, Lohlker added.
Rather, it often coincides with a kind of "economy of violence," he said, noting that "violence including kidnappings, smuggling and looting has long been an economic factor for terrorism."
He also said that there are veritable "markets for violence:" Where money can be made through violence, jihadist organizations can also recruit and retain followers.
"We fundamentally need to move away from a Eurocentric perspective," Lohlker further points out.
In his view, al-Qaeda and other jihadist groups have always been far more present outside Europe and the US than it has appeared from a Western perspective.
Al-Qaeda's regional involvement
However, over the years, the offshoots' strategies have undergone a change. According to Lars Berger, there has been a "strategic shift" away from direct attacks on the "distant enemy" and toward the establishment of local structures.
"We are now seeing an attempt to proceed in an alternative and gradual manner, namely instead of spectacular acts of violence ordered from the highest levels, there are smaller-scale actions that are more grassroots in nature," he said.
In the Sahel, this entails forming local alliances, gaining influence in communities, and controlling territories. The Critical Threats Project describes this development as "localization."
Al-Qaeda is thus surviving precisely through this differentiation. JNIM capitalizes on ethnic and social conflicts in the Sahel, while al-Shabaab exploits conflicts within Somali clan structures. The global jihadist goal remains as an ideological framework, but the actual fighting takes place on the ground.
Al-Qaeda competes with the "Islamic State"
In the competition for public attention, however, al-Qaeda faces a superior rival: the so-called "Islamic State," or IS.
"Ultimately, younger jihadists tend to be more drawn to the 'Islamic State,'" terrorism expert Behnam Heidenreuter-Said, head of the research center for Strategic Police Research at the Hamburg Police Academy, told DW.
IS has carried out "more spectacular" and media-effective terrorist attacks, he said, highlighting that "al-Qaeda has taken a more long-term approach."
Heidenreuter-Said, who published a comprehensive history of al-Qaeda in 2018, added that "IS wanted to make a splash and demonstrate successes as quickly as possible in order to grow explosively."
However, IS's expansion was followed by its collapse, he said. Al-Qaeda, on the other hand, continues to exist, albeit under changed circumstances.
Shortage of al-Qaeda updates
The terrorist group meanwhile faces the question of whether it can replace its aging fighters. Although this is conceivable, al-Qaeda as a brand is visibly fading, Heidenreuter-Said observed. In Europe in particular, militant jihadism has become less attractive. However, jihadist ideas have not disappeared, al-Qaeda has simply lost its former ability to mobilize large numbers of young people, he said.
It is hard to say just how dangerous the organization actually still is, Behnam Heidenreuter-Said points out.
"Everyone agrees that there is currently virtually no information about al-Qaeda and we simply don't know what it is doing right now," he said.
Furthermore, since the Hamas attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023, it has been striking how little al-Qaeda has been visible in the major regional conflicts, he said. In his view, Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis and Iran have dominated the political and military stage.
This article was translated from German.

Creatine improves muscle mass and cognitive function in older adults even without exercise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
18:00:15 UTC
03:00:15 KST

A study involving healthy adults between 45 and 65 years of age with a sedentary lifestyle found that 12 weeks of taking creatine monohydrate supplements increased their lean tissue mass, strength, and muscular endurance, while promoting favorable changes in markers of cognitive function and memory. The same supplementation combined with an exercise and weight-loss diet program additionally resulted in body fat percentage reduction. The paper was published in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition.
Creatine is a naturally occurring compound that helps cells rapidly produce energy, particularly during short periods of intense activity. The human body makes creatine mainly from the amino acids arginine, glycine, and methionine. It can also be obtained from foods such as meat and fish.
Most of the body’s creatine is stored in skeletal muscles, where it is converted into phosphocreatine. Phosphocreatine helps regenerate adenosine triphosphate, or ATP, the primary molecule cells use as an immediate source of energy. Because this energy system is especially important during brief, high-intensity efforts, creatine has long attracted interest in sport and exercise science.
Creatine can also be taken as a dietary supplement. Such intake allows the body to increase the amount of creatine stored in muscles. The most widely used supplemental form is creatine monohydrate, in which creatine is combined with a molecule of water. Creatine monohydrate is inexpensive, stable, and by far the most extensively studied form of creatine supplementation. Research has linked it to improvements in strength, power, training capacity, and gains in lean body mass. Interest is also growing in its possible effects on brain function and health.
Study author Jisun Chun and colleagues examined the effects of 12 weeks of creatine monohydrate supplementation on body composition and cognitive function in healthy, untrained middle-aged and older adults. The researchers compared participants who maintained their usual lifestyle with those who engaged in a structured diet and training program aimed at promoting weight loss.
They note that as people age, the fat tissue in their bodies progressively increases while the mass of their skeletal muscles decreases. This condition, known as sarcopenic obesity, is associated with heightened health risks and various functional impairments.
The authors hypothesized that creatine monohydrate supplementation would support improvements in the health-related outcomes of exercise and diet, and would enhance improvements in body composition induced by training. They also expected that this supplementation would favorably influence the cognitive performance of individuals taking it.
Study participants were 64 adults between 45 and 65 years of age. Their average age was 55 years, and 40 of them were women.
Participants were divided into four groups. Two groups received creatine monohydrate supplementation (two 5-gram foil sachets per day, to be dissolved in water or a flavored beverage, taken once in the morning and once in the evening), and two groups received a placebo (identical-looking sachets containing maltodextrin, taken in the same way). While participants were randomly assigned to receive either creatine monohydrate or the placebo without knowing which substance they were receiving, they decided for themselves whether they would participate in the training and diet program or not. This created four distinct groups: no exercise with placebo, no exercise with creatine, exercise and diet with placebo, and exercise and diet with creatine.
Participants in the exercise groups participated in a supervised resistance and aerobic training program three times per week. Additionally, they were instructed to follow a diet plan aligned with the American Heart Association’s macronutrient recommendations (55 percent carbohydrate, 15 percent protein, 30 percent fat) to induce a modest energy deficit of approximately 300 to 500 calories per day to promote weight loss. These participants recorded their dietary intake using a smartphone-based application called MyFitnessPal. The non-exercise groups did not follow this diet or exercise program.
Participants completed various measurements at the start of the study, six weeks after the start, and at the end of the 12-week study. These included basic body measurements, resting metabolic rate (how much energy the body uses at rest), body composition measurements derived from dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, or DXA, scans, blood biomarkers, physical activity, cognitive performance, reaction speed tests, muscular strength measurements, cardiopulmonary exercise capacity, and various psychological health measures.
Results showed that creatine monohydrate supplementation without the exercise and diet intervention increased lean tissue mass, strength, and muscular endurance. It also promoted favorable changes in blood concentrations of some lipids and in markers of cognitive function and memory. Creatine supplementation combined with the exercise and diet program additionally resulted in a greater reduction in body fat percentage.
“Creatine supplementation (10 g/d) without exercise training and diet intervention increased lean tissue mass, strength and muscular endurance, promoted favorable changes in selected blood-lipid measures, reduced HbA1c levels [a measure of average blood sugar over the past two to three months], and improved selected markers of cognitive function and memory in middle-aged and older adults,” the study authors concluded. “Creatine supplementation during an exercise and weight-loss diet intervention in middle-aged and older adults promoted a greater reduction in body fat percentage, gains in muscular strength and endurance, and improved selected markers of cognitive function and memory.”
The study contributes to the scientific knowledge about the effects of creatine supplementation. However, the researchers cautioned that the individual cognitive and biomarker findings are exploratory and require confirmation. Furthermore, while participants were randomly assigned to receive creatine or a placebo, they chose for themselves whether they would participate in the training and diet program. This could have introduced systematic differences between those who did and did not choose to participate in the lifestyle intervention, affecting the results.
The paper, “Effects of creatine supplementation with and without exercise and diet intervention on body composition, cognitive function, and markers of health in middle-aged and older adults,” was authored by Jisun Chun, Yuhang Liu, Giuliet L. Kibler, Hudson Lee, Khatereh Babakhani, Nathaniel Rhoades, Ian Bivins, Joungbo Ko, Broderick Dickerson, Drew E. Gonzalez, Ryan J. Sowinski, Chris J. Rasmussen, and Richard B. Kreider.

Chinese scientists boost hydrogen fuel cell power fourfold with new design
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
18:00:05 UTC
03:00:05 KST

Chinese scientists boost hydrogen fuel cell power fourfold with new design
The proton-transfer breakthrough could improve hydrogen vehicles and space systems, while reducing the use of costly platinum
Chinese scientists have developed a way to generate a fourfold increase in power output of hydrogen fuel cells, an advance that could broaden their use from road vehicles to space missions.
Li Jie, assistant professor with BIT and one of the paper’s authors, said on Thursday that, with the new tech, the “power stack of a fuel cell vehicle can be made smaller and lighter, and the vehicle can get stronger continuous output and a longer driving range”.
PEMFCs operate at relatively low temperatures, generally between 60 and 80 degrees Celsius (140 to 176 degrees Fahrenheit). They can convert about 50 to 60 per cent of the energy in their hydrogen fuel into electricity.
The process is straightforward: at the anode, hydrogen molecules give up electrons and become protons. While the protons pass through an electrolyte membrane to the cathode, the electrons flow through an external circuit, generating electricity. At the cathode, the protons, electrons and oxygen combine to form water.

NYC Mayor Mamdani releases 9/11 files after Giuliani remarks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Days after Rudy Giuliani said Zohran Mamdani should stay away from New York’s 9/11 commemoration, the city’s first Muslim mayor released more than 170,000 pages of records that cast fresh scrutiny on what officials knew about toxic air in the aftermath of the attacks — including during Giuliani’s administration.
The documents, released Tuesday ahead of the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, detail health concerns, air quality around Ground Zero and the city’s response after the World Trade Center towers collapsed.
Their release followed a settlement with 9/11 Health Watch, an advocacy group that had pursued legal action to obtain records that remained out of public view for years.
“These are documents that show what the city knew about the toxic air around Ground Zero, when they knew it, and how they acted to limit liability,” Mamdani said.
Some of the records concern decisions made while Giuliani was mayor, including an internal memo sent to his deputy mayor outlining potential legal liability arising from hazardous air exposure and unsafe working conditions after the attacks.
Mamdani accused previous city leaders of misleading New Yorkers about the risks.
“People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air,” he said.
The release came shortly after Giuliani, who led New York during the 2001 attacks, publicly urged Mamdani not to attend events marking their 25th anniversary.
“Having lost friends there and being very close to many of the families, it offends me that he’s coming,” Giuliani said.
Giuliani also criticized Mamdani’s Muslim faith in making his case against the mayor’s attendance.
Mamdani rejected calls to stay away and said he would attend the commemorations, stressing that the anniversary should focus on the victims, their families and first responders rather than politicians.
“I love the city, I love this country,” Mamdani said. “My focus will be on attending events that memorialize that incredible courage and I will be there, just as I was last year.”
Asked following the document release whether Giuliani should instead stay away from the ceremony or whether the former mayor had lied about the air quality, Mamdani declined to turn the commemoration into a dispute between political figures.
He said New Yorkers could make their own judgment about responsibility.
The newly disclosed records show city officials had information raising concerns about hazardous conditions around Ground Zero even as residents, workers and first responders received assurances that the air was safe.
One document prepared for Giuliani’s deputy mayor, Robert Harding, discussed potential lawsuits against the city, including claims that health advisories had encouraged people to return to the area too quickly and exposed them to toxins.
Other records detail concerns about asbestos and other contaminants in Lower Manhattan.
9/11 Health Watch Executive Director Benjamin Chevat said four mayoral administrations had withheld records showing what the city knew about toxic chemicals in Lower Manhattan and western Brooklyn while officials continued publicly describing the air as safe.
More than 9,400 people have died from illnesses linked to exposure to the area since the attacks, according to a federal medical monitoring program.
The Sept. 11 attacks themselves killed 2,977 people after hijackers seized four passenger planes. Two were flown into the World Trade Center towers, another struck the Pentagon and a fourth crashed near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers fought the hijackers.
The Mamdani administration plans to release additional records over the next 12 months as the city continues reviewing the material.
