Forgetful Farage shares rose-tinted memories of Reform’s party conference | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
17:33:08 UTC
02:33:08 KST

Which one of us has not dreamed of getting a personal email from Nigel Farage? So imagine the excitement that Reform supporters must have felt when a message from their leader dropped into their inboxes late on Wednesday night. And mine. Could he also be about to offer everyone in the country £5,000 in return for electing a Reform government?
Sadly not. Even Honest Bob’s planned welfare cuts won’t cover that. Instead, Nige was treating us all to his reflections on his party conference that had just ended. The only drawback was that there appeared to be some gaps in his memory. Let’s be kind and assume he was pushed for space. So let’s help him fill in the blanks.
Dear John. ‘Wow.’ That’s what I kept thinking as our conference closed. Good start, Nige. Because that’s what I was thinking too. It’s not every party conference that is completely derailed by an undercover investigation into allegations of illegal sources of party funding. And it came completely out of the blue. Who would have thought that a party leader under investigation over a £5m gift from a Thai crypto billionaire, and a party whose main funder is Ben Delo – who was convicted in the US for failing to comply with legislation against money laundering – might be implicated in possible wrongdoing?
But we can all admire the sheer professionalism with which you handled the crisis. It was a stroke of genius to dismiss two of your oldest muckers as mere contractors. After all, Dan Jukes had only been your right-hand fixer for 10 years and James Orr, the Cambridge professor of ethics – nice touch that – was your head of policy. Of course it was all “loose pub talk”. Everyone goes to the pub to discuss how they plan to break the law. And you definitely “hadn’t been listening”. We could tell that by the way you appeared to join in the conversation. Such bad luck it’s all ended up in yet another police investigation. It’s obviously massively reassuring that you say you can’t be bought. But you can clearly be rented.
6,000 of us packed in Birmingham’s National Exhibition Centre. And may I say how pleasing it was that none of you felt you needed to come in a balaclava. What this country needs are patriots who are prepared to stand up and be counted. Who can be relied on to protest against the arrival of foreigners arriving by small boats. From now on, it will be Reform policy that the RNLI should be disbanded.
We can’t have a country of volunteers who are prepared to jeopardise their own lives to save others. They are nothing less than traitors and send all the wrong messages to the rest of the world. I know I speak for everyone when I say that all Brits would rather drown than have one more foreigner step ashore in Portsmouth. I was also immensely proud to see so many in the audience at your conference speech who were willing to assault a female protester. Making England Great Again. Robert Jenrick nailed it when he said: “Boohoo.”
We got Starmer out and are still neck and neck with Labour in the polls. Er, yes. That’s one way of putting it. Another is that you were at least eight points ahead of Labour only a few months ago. Your popularity may have peaked. The more people get to see of you the less they like you. It also seems that voters much prefer a leader who doesn’t require a minimum of £1m a year to get out of bed and a party that doesn’t seem to lurch from one financial scandal to the next.
Zia Yusuf and I will put the Royal Navy in the Channel and stop the boats. This is the Zia Yusuf who is so unpopular that everyone in your inner circle privately refers to him as “the wanker” and is so disliked that no constituency wants him to stand as their Reform candidate. Yet he insists on referring to himself as the “shadow home secretary” when he remains outside Westminster. But let’s indulge you. Let’s pretend that Zia is elected an MP. Do you really think the Royal Navy is going to participate in operations to turn back the small boats that could result in the deaths of dozens of migrants?
You saw the odds-on next prime minister of France, Jordan Bardella, sign a historic memorandum of understanding with us to make this happen. Or the memorandum of misunderstanding as we prefer to call it. Still, it gave us a huge laugh to see you pull the wool over the “wet behind the ears” Jordan. It’s so good to see Reform turn over its political allies abroad. A reminder to Johnny Frenchman that when we left the EU it was to put some distance between us and him.
It was a masterstroke to write the memorandum in both English and French, and sneakily adding a clause in English agreeing that France would take back all migrants who had arrived in England. And as Jordan’s English was not that good, he never noticed! Chapeau! Or perhaps he’s a bit thick. Either way, he’s a lot less odds-on to be the next prime minister because Marine Le Pen is furious with him and there’s an almighty row going on in the National Rally party.
In our first 100 days, Richard Tice pledged to cut £250 off your energy bill by scrapping the mad levies on them. No one thinks Dicky is going to do anything. Everyone inside the party thinks he is just an afternoon TV presenter from the 1980s. A man born to be your hype person. Who owes his entire existence to you. The same goes for Robert Jenrick and Suella Braverman. Politicians too mediocre even for the Tory party.
It’s looking like we’ll need 10,000 candidates for the general and local elections. Recruiting that many candidates will be a mammoth task. So I need more of you than ever to step forward. It goes without saying that the 6,000 of you in Birmingham are already on the list. But we still need 4,000 more. So, please, I beg you, delete your Facebook and other social media accounts, where you might accidentally have liked something racist or spread idiotic conspiracy theories, and sign up. That includes you, Matt Goodwin. Your country needs you.
Yours, Nigel Farage

Bolivian president demands investigation following deadly military base blasts

Laura Gamba
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz asked the Public Prosecutor's Office on Thursday to investigate whether last week’s deadly explosions at the Bolivar Artillery Regiment in Viacha were the result of a deliberate attack.
He said hostile political factions are seeking to destabilize his administration.
The disaster, which unfolded last Friday at the military facility near La Paz, has left nine dead, more than 80 injured, and five reported missing as rescue workers continue sifting through the rubble.
“I ask the Prosecutor's Office to thoroughly investigate the Viacha incident -- I don't know if it was an attack,” he told reporters in Cochabamba. “They should investigate the possibility of an attack; there are people who want the government to fail because they want to return to power, and they are willing to do anything.”
The Public Prosecutor's Office has opened a formal inquiry into the blasts under preliminary charges of negligent homicide, negligent injury, and property destruction.
Investigators have determined that the first explosion originated from stored black powder and pyrotechnic material, according to Defense Minister Ernesto Justiniano. The cause of a second, far more destructive secondary blast, however, remains under active investigation. Military-grade explosives, grenades and confiscated pyrotechnics were housed at the site.
Maj. Gen. Hector Alejandro Alarcon, the army’s commanding general, noted that while the regiment has an active roster of approximately 240 personnel, a significantly lower number of troops were on-site at the time of the explosion, a factor that prevented an even higher casualty count.
At the Forensic Investigations Institute, operations remain focused on victim identification. Authorities confirmed that rescue teams have recovered 48 bags containing fragmented human remains from the debris, which are currently housed at a La Paz morgue. Biological samples are being collected from families of the missing to conduct DNA matching.
Paz assumed the presidency in November, concluding nearly two decades of continuous governance by the Movement for Socialism (MAS) under former Presidents Evo Morales, who ruled from 2006 to 2019, and Luis Arce from 2020 - 2025. He previously accused Morales and his political allies of orchestrating efforts to destabilize his administration.

Switzerland said Thursday it shares concerns over the situation in Gaza and the West Bank following plans by 12 countries to introduce trade restrictions targeting illegal Israeli settlements, but stressed that Swiss law does not allow it to impose such sanctions independently.
“Switzerland has taken note of the declarations of intent from certain countries and is closely monitoring the situation,” Francoise Tschanz, spokesperson for Switzerland's State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO), told Anadolu in a written statement.
“The Federal Council shares the concerns regarding the situation in Gaza and the West Bank,” Tschanz said.
Asked whether Switzerland was considering similar national restrictions, Tschanz pointed to the country's Embargo Act.
Under the law, Switzerland can implement sanctions adopted by the UN, the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), or its main trading partners, which “in practice” means the European Union, she said.
“The law does not allow for the adoption of measures independently,” Tschanz added.
In its January 2025 analysis of the ICJ's July 2024 advisory opinion on Israel's policies and practices in the occupied Palestinian territory, the Swiss Foreign Ministry said Switzerland does not support economic activities related to illegal Israeli settlements and advises individuals and companies against supporting settlement activities.
France, the UK, Canada, Denmark, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Iceland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, and Sweden pledged on Tuesday to impose national restrictions on trade in goods from illegal Israeli settlements or support European restrictions.
The joint declaration reaffirmed that the 12 countries are "seriously considering" adopting such restrictions or other measures in accordance with their national procedures.
“We firmly oppose any action resulting in the annexation of Palestinian land and the forced displacement of Palestinian populations,” the joint statement read.
Since taking office in late 2022, the current government led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has approved the establishment of 104 new settlements, while 160 agricultural settlement outposts have been established in the West Bank, according to Palestinian data.
In the first half of 2026, Israeli occupiers carried out 3,488 attacks in the West Bank, according to the Palestinian government’s Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission.
The attacks killed 17 Palestinians and fully or partially displaced 26 Bedouin and pastoral communities, while 42 new settlement outposts were established, the commission said.
Around 750,000 Israeli occupiers live in 194 illegal settlements and 400 illegal outposts across the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, according to Palestinian figures.
Israel has occupied the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since 1967. The international community considers Israeli settlements in the occupied territories illegal under international law, a position Israel rejects.

The Guardian view on falling birthrates: cash alone cannot buy belonging | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
17:30:19 UTC
02:30:19 KST

Why are people in one of the world’s richest, safest countries having so few children? Singapore is asking that question. In 2000, its fertility rate matched America’s at 1.6 children per woman. By 2025, it had dropped to 0.87 – almost half the US rate. Singapore’s leaders, worried about population collapse, have reached for the chequebook. Each child, including those born to unmarried parents, will get $55,000 in government support by the time they turn 17. Yet a quarter of Singaporeans say they do not intend to have children. Wealth and security, clearly, don’t guarantee more babies.
UN data shows that global fertility fell from 5.3 births per woman in 1963 to 2.2 in 2023. But this masks a growing divide. In some poor sub-Saharan African countries there are around six births per woman. Compare this with England and Wales, where the figure is just 1.39. More than half of the world – including a billion women in India and China – have a fertility rate below the global 2.1 “replacement level” needed to sustain populations without migration. But even in poor countries with high mortality rates and consequently higher replacement rates, births outpace deaths. In Nigeria, for example, the fertility rate of 4.4 exceeds its replacement rate of 2.6 children per woman.
To understand this phenomenon, the UN asked 100,000 18- to 39-year-olds from 73 nations their views on relationships and having children. The results, released in July, were striking: two-thirds said they want to marry or live with a partner. Those who did not have children overwhelmingly wanted them. Yet about a quarter of those aged 25 to 39 said they wanted a partner but were single and not dating – a status reported more by men than women. More than half said the biggest barriers to a durable relationship were economic constraints. Young people want partnership and parenthood, but questioned achieving the “emotional and financial” stability needed for a shared life.
The Nordic region – consisting of five states and three territories – is viewed as a good place to have children thanks to generous parental leave and subsidised childcare. Yet fertility rates have fallen by up to third since 2010, against 12% across the EU. The Polish sociologist Anna Gromada wrote in the Guardian that despite her country’s economic success, its fertility rate was 1.05. While the state transfers cash worth 10% of the median wage for every child born each month, Poland’s population is shrinking. Prof Gromada argues that people are not just deciding against children; many never form lasting relationships in which the question arises. Almost half of under-30s are single. Cash paid after a family exists cannot create the togetherness needed for a family in the first place.
The world is not running out of people. The UN expects today’s 8.2 billion people to become 10.3 billion by the mid-2080s. What is emerging is a demographic divide between ageing, shrinking rich societies and population growth in poorer ones. Getting richer seems to mean lower fertility. The baby bust may indicate a wealthy country’s failure to reproduce itself socially as well as biologically. People ask not only whether they can afford children, but whether they fit in, can trust each other and believe in a future. This loss of confident belonging poses questions that politics across the rich world has yet to tackle.

Former PE teacher faces lengthy jail term for sexually abusing pupils

A former PE teacher is facing a lengthy jail sentence for grooming and sexually abusing three pupils at two schools.
Bronwen James, 30, admitted offences against two girls at schools in Hampshire and Wiltshire and was found guilty by a jury of charges involving a boy.
The Crown Prosecution Service described James’s crimes as “a sustained pattern of predatory behaviour against children in her care” and praised the teenagers she targeted for coming forward.
Judge James Bromige asked for reports to be prepared on James so that he could assess the danger she posed when sentencing her later this year. Her defence team said she knew she faced a significant jail sentence.
During her trial at Winchester crown court, jurors were told that James, from Chippenham in Wiltshire, flirted with a 16-year-old boy in class at a school in Southampton.
They began exchanging Snapchat messages and arranged for her to drive him to a promenade, where they kissed in her car.
Later they went to her house where they cuddled while watching the Wimbledon tennis championships on the television before going to her bedroom where they had sex. She told him she loved him and wanted him to move away with her.
Edward Culver, prosecuting, told the trial the school was made aware of the incident after another student showed a teacher some text messages apparently sent between the James and the complainant.
He said: “They suggested a sexually charged relationship. He [the boy] was named as ‘number 8’ in the messages as a cover. She acted not only in an unprofessional and overfamiliar way, but failed to recognise any boundaries, exploiting her position to engage in sexual activity with one of her young students.”
In a police interview, the boy said he had been “groomed” by the defendant.
James was convicted of three counts of sexual activity with a child by a person in a position of trust.
Before the trial, James pleaded guilty to offences against two girls. One was a pupil at the same Southampton school as the boy, the other attended a school in Wiltshire that James had also taught at.
The offences included sexual activity with a child, sexual communication with a child and making an indecent photograph of a child. The victims were 13 and 14 at the time.
During legal argument, which can now be reported, it also emerged that at the start of her career, James received a warning while she was teaching at the private Seaford college in West Sussex for giving her personal mobile number to a pupil.
Bethany Adams, of the CPS, said: “Bronwen James was trusted to educate and protect children. Instead, she used that trust to groom and sexually abuse three students.
“James manipulated her victims with calculated precision, exploiting her position of authority to isolate them and normalise the abuse.
“This was not a lapse in judgment; it was a sustained pattern of predatory behaviour against children in her care.
“The courage shown by James’s victims in coming forward has been instrumental in securing this conviction. I hope it gives them, and their families, some measure of justice.”

Canada has reached a C$350 million ($250 million) agreement with Ukraine to supply Kyiv with air defense interceptors, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday as he met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Zelenskyy announced the assistance during a visit to Canada for talks with Prime Minister Mark Carney, with strengthening Ukraine's air defenses and preparing its energy infrastructure for winter among the main issues on the agenda.
"This is a very important package of air defense. This is crucial," Zelenskyy told reporters, thanking Canada for its continued support.
He did not provide details on the weapons or equipment included in the package or specify the extent of Canada's planned assistance for Ukraine's energy sector.

Carney said Canada had already provided approximately 26 billion Canadian dollars ($19 billion) in support to Ukraine since Russia launched its invasion in February 2022 and pledged further assistance.
"We've provided support for the energy systems and beyond. We'll provide more support," Carney said.
Canada has committed more than 25.5 billion Canadian dollars in overall assistance to Ukraine, including about 8.5 billion Canadian dollars in military aid.
Carney also reaffirmed Ottawa's backing for Ukraine's efforts to join NATO and the European Union and said Canada would continue supporting the country after the war.
"Ukrainians helped build this province, this country. Canada will help rebuild Ukraine when peace comes," he said.
Canada has one of the world's largest Ukrainian diasporas, with an estimated 1.3 million to 1.4 million people of Ukrainian descent.
Zelenskyy had said upon arriving in Canada that strengthening air defenses and securing support for Ukraine's preparations for winter would be the primary focus of his visit.

The U.S. government is going after a Michigan labor union over its Palestine activism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
17:26:59 UTC
02:26:59 KST

On June 10, 2026, the FBI raided the homes of activists involved in Palestine solidarity activism at the University of Michigan (UM), who are now known as the “Michigan 8.” In a show of force, federal agents in military gear broke through the door of a home in Ypsilanti, MI, to arrest a couple of individuals. That day, the FBI also arrested individuals connected to UM Palestine activism in Illinois and Wisconsin. The Justice Department indicted these activists on wildly exaggerated “conspiracy” charges. They could face decades in prison.
The government is now targeting a pro-Palestinian campus labor union involved in defending the Michigan 8.
Last month, August 2026, the Graduate Employees’ Organization (GEO), which represents over 4,000 UM graduate student workers, was served a subpoena signed by the Justice Department’s attorney on the Michigan 8 case. This came shortly after UM and a local prosecutor tried – but failed – to bring down GEO’s President using baseless “embezzlement” charges. The August subpoena requests extensive information about GEO, including a list of current and former members, meeting minutes, and financial records, dating back to 2023.
This is a clear criminalization of ordinary labor organizing. It’s also a “fishing expedition” that is meant to help the government’s case against Palestine solidarity activists.
The developments in Michigan closely follow those in Minnesota, where certain anti-ICE organizers (the “Minnesota 15”) were also indicted on “conspiracy” charges in June 2026, and where federal agents had spied on unions and used a subpoena to obtain union financial records.
The federal government understands that our struggles are connected. It’s time all labor unions realize it too, and refuse to separate Palestine solidarity or migrant justice organizing from labor organizing.
Criminalizing a pro-Palestinian labor union by targeting its president
The University of Michigan has been working with the local and federal governments to attack GEO. In recent years, GEO, which is Local 3550 of the American Federation of Teachers (AFT), has won concessions. In April 2023, it went on the longest strike in the University’s history, which resulted in better pay and health care for graduate workers. And while big labor unions have historically been on the side of U.S. imperialism (AFT’s current President Randi Weingarten is a staunch Zionist), some union locals, such as GEO, have embraced Palestine solidarity.
Recognizing this emerging alliance between labor and Palestine solidarity organizing, the University turned to the legal system to criminalize the union. This past summer, they went after GEO’s President, Hiab Teshome, an MD-PhD student at UM.
On June 15, 2026, just five days after the FBI raids on the Michigan 8, Detective Sergeant Ryan Cavanaugh of the University of Michigan Police Department called Teshome on her personal phone to say there was a warrant for her arrest and that she would soon be charged with “embezzlement” and “false pretenses.” According to Teshome, he said he wanted to talk about the logistics of her turning herself in to the police. Cavanaugh is well-known to the campus Palestine solidarity movement: he has pepper-sprayed some protesters in the past, allegedly tackled others, and also attended the September 9, 2026, court hearing for the Michigan 8, where we saw him speaking with the U.S. government attorneys. Organizers, including Teshome, also report that Cavanaugh has a history of harassing them. In February and April of 2026, Cavanaugh had called Teshome to tell her she was being investigated for “embezzlement,” but without giving specifics. Teshome says she referred Cavanaugh to her lawyer, but he failed to respond to her lawyer’s calls. Instead, he continued to call, text, and email Teshome directly, and even visited her former residence, believing it was her current home.
It turned out that the “embezzlement” charges concerned purchases made by a student group in which Teshome was the designated co-signer. UM claimed the purchases weren’t properly accounted for – yet Teshome did not make these purchases herself and was no longer involved in the group. She was implicated simply by being a co-signer, on paper.
Rather than try to resolve this bureaucratic matter internally with its own students, UM took the unprecedented step of turning to the local county prosecutor, Eli Savit (who calls himself a “progressive prosecutor” and is currently running for Michigan Attorney General). Using the narrative and information provided by Cavanaugh, Savit then pressed felony charges against Teshome for embezzlement and false pretenses.
At Teshome’s arraignment on June 26, 2026, an Ann Arbor judge noted that the University had requested that Teshome be banned from campus as part of the bond conditions. Such a ban would have prevented Teshome from participating in the union’s bargaining with the University. The judge refused that request, but instead banned Teshome from the University’s administration building and specifically noted she must stay away from the UM Regents. The Regents, who set the University’s major policies, have been targeted by campus activists with calls to divest from Israel. This bond condition shows that the attack on Teshome was also meant to stifle such divestment campaigns.
In response, many showed solidarity with Teshome. An open letter in support of Teshome was signed by hundreds of individuals and several organizations, including the Harvard Graduate Students Union (HGSU-UAW Local 5118) and the Huron Valley DSA. Yet conspicuously absent from the signatories was Michigan’s labor union establishment, which did not seem to grasp the political significance of the attack on a union president. This is the same labor establishment that had failed to heed a call by Palestinian trade unions, following October 7, 2023, to disrupt the entities enabling Israel’s genocide in Gaza.
Nonetheless, the grassroots prevailed. On August 6 2026, activists and community members packed the court for Teshome’s probable cause conference. The judge, Cedric Simpson, dismissed the charges within minutes. The court, Simpson said, “is certainly not getting involved in that.”
Criminalizing the whole union
After the effort to bring down Teshome failed, the next target became the union as a whole.
The federal government served a grand jury subpoena, dated August 6: the day that the charges against Teshome were dismissed by the court. The subpoena – signed by the Justice Department Attorney Maggie Smith from the Michigan 8 case and by Detroit office FBI agent Kara Phipps – asks for the following information, dating back to January 1, 2023:
“1. Collective bargaining agreements;
2. Constitution and By-laws;
3. All disbursement records and receipts journals pertaining to union officials;
4. All union employee personnel records, to include all payroll records, W-2 Forms, W-4 Forms, 1099’s, etc;
5. All associated membership agreements;
6. Listing of all active and former union members;
7. Complete listing of all officers and executive board members, to include position.
8. All minutes of membership meetings and Executive Board meetings” [emphasis added].
“The University of Michigan and the federal government are attacking our union and the broader labor and Palestine solidarity movement because we are powerful and because we are challenging the University’s material investments in genocide,” said GEO President Hiab Teshome. GEO’s lawyers are currently attempting to get the subpoena quashed on the grounds that it is too broad in scope and violates the union members’ rights to free speech.
The attacks on this Michigan labor union closely parallel the federal government’s tactics against the anti-ICE movement in Minnesota, following the January 2026 murders of Alex Pretti and Renée Good by ICE agents. As part of their investigation into “domestic terrorist financing,” federal agents used subpoenas to obtain several years’ worth of wire transfers made by the Service Employees International Union, which largely represents health care workers. The individuals who so far have been singled out by the government, the Minnesota 15, may now face decades in prison, just like the Michigan 8.
“What is happening to our labor union and other unions across the country is extreme acts of workplace repression by our employer collaborating with the state and the federal government to weaken labor organizing and violate our right to collective action,” Teshome noted.
The major labor unions can no longer keep pretending like workers’ struggles can be separated from Palestine solidarity or from the struggle against ICE and policing. No one should stay neutral on this moving train.
Ways to support the Michigan 8 and Minnesota 15
- Donate to the Michigan 8 legal fund and visit defendmichigan8.org
- Donate to the Minnesota 15 legal fund and visit minnesota15.org

products.

Thursday, September 17.
                                    
                                       
				The measure was introduced to mitigate the effects of the Iran
war in helping push fuel prices higher.
                                    
                                       
				Critics have said the government should include petrol duties
too.
                                    
                                       
				The cut in excise duties "was extended again today to keep the
cost of petrol and diesel under control, pending new measures
arriving next week," said Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni in a
video message posted on social media following the cabinet
meeting.
                                    
                                       
				Meloni said the decree also includes measures to accelerate oil
and gas production and new commissioners would help regions
fast-track permits for research, exploration, and extraction.
                                    
                                       
				"We want to move forward with increasing domestic oil and gas
production, because it makes little sense to buy this energy
from abroad when we can produce it right here in Italy. That is
the goal of the measure approved today by the Council of
Ministers," said Meloni in the video.
                                    
                                       
				The meeting passed a decree containing "urgent provisions
regarding oil prices linked to the ongoing crisis in
international markets, as well as strategic energy
infrastructure and activities.
                                    
                                       
				"It will allow the State," Meloni explained, "to appoint
commissioners to help the regions cut red tape and issue permits
and concessions for hydrocarbon research, exploration, and
extraction on our territory much more quickly. Because Italy
cannot afford to wait decades to unblock a concession."

A year of saving lives: Magen David Adom answered an emergency every 16.5 seconds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
17:24:14 UTC
02:24:14 KST

Magen David Adom emergency crews were dispatched 1,911,412 times during the Hebrew year 5786, equivalent to one response every 16.5 seconds on average, according to annual figures released by the organization ahead of Rosh Hashanah.
MDA said its 101 emergency hotline received more than 2 million calls during the year, with an average response time of up to two seconds.
The organization, which marked 96 years of activity, said it now has about 39,200 employees, volunteers, national service participants and civil service members, including some 16,500 teenagers. Volunteers contributed more than 6.3 million hours over the course of the year.
MDA medics and paramedics treated 67,624 people injured in road accidents and assisted 1,399 women who gave birth at home or on the way to the hospital. During the current swimming season, teams have so far treated 229 people following drowning incidents.
Its emergency fleet includes hundreds of ambulances, mobile intensive care units and motorcycles, as well as specialized vehicles for mass-casualty events, four-wheel-drive ambulances, intensive care buses and protected command vehicles. MDA also operates sea ambulances on the Sea of Galilee and in Eilat, as well as five medical helicopters in cooperation with partner organizations.
The organization said its blood services collected 281,917 units during the year, including more than 46,000 donations from first-time donors. Its National Human Milk Bank supplied about 5,700 liters of breast milk to premature infants, hospitalized newborns and medically vulnerable infants at home.
MDA also expanded training programs in the wake of the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks. More than 17,800 civilians have now been trained through its Magen Project to provide initial medical care during emergencies, including local rapid-response team members, municipal workers, doctors and paramedics.
About 500,000 people completed first-aid and resuscitation courses during the year, while the organization certified 401 new paramedics.
MDA Director-General Eli Bin said the organization had continued to expand its technological and operational capabilities while providing emergency medical care and collecting blood for hospitals and the IDF.
“About 39,200 volunteers and employees of the organization worked over the past year for the health of the residents of the State of Israel, day and night, in the air, at sea and on land,” Bin said.
“Magen David Adom teams continued to work under fire and at risk to their lives, with heroism and courage, in order to save lives in the best possible way,” he added. “In 5787, too, we will continue to do everything in our power and spare no effort for the health of the citizens of the State of Israel.”

PARIS - France’s interior minister on Sept 10 warned of criminal proceedings if a French television channel allows back on air a Russian commentator who was expelled over claims that she is a Kremlin agent.

Any return to air “directly contravenes the expulsion and asset-freezing measures imposed and is liable to give rise to several criminal charges”, he said in the letter revealed by Le Monde daily and seen by AFP.
Fedorova is the former head of the French arm of RT, which was banned in France after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.
She then became a commentator for outlets within conservative French billionaire Vincent Bollore’s group of broadcasting outlets, including Cnews.
Fedorova, who has decried the accusations as “censorship”, has said she was outside France on holiday when the deportation order went into effect so was never physically deported. AFP

Ukraine and Canada signed a declaration on a 100-year partnership
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10

02:23:29 KST

Ukraine and Canada signed a declaration on a 100-year partnership
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine and Canada agreed to jointly produce drones, electronic warfare systems, and ammunition. The parties are also preparing a Drone Deal and defense supplies.
Prime Minister of Canada Mark Carney and President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed the "Declaration on a 100-Year Partnership," which provides for a long-term partnership in the defense industry to jointly produce unmanned systems, counter-drone and electronic-warfare capabilities, as well as ammunition. The parties are also working on the Drone Deal. This was reported by the Government of Canada, according to UNN.
"On September 10, 2026, Prime Minister of Canada Mark Carney and President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy met in Calgary and signed the "Declaration on a 100-Year Partnership," in which they expressed their intention to elevate relations between their countries to the level of a comprehensive strategic partnership and confirmed their alignment," the statement said.
It is noted that, based on the Letter of Intent on joint production signed in Kyiv on August 24, 2025, Canada and Ukraine will establish a long-term partnership in the defense industry to jointly produce unmanned systems, counter-drone and electronic-warfare capabilities, as well as ammunition, supported by scientific research and technology transfers.
"They will promote predictable procurement of jointly produced equipment and work with partners to establish a Defense, Security and Resilience Bank. Canada and Ukraine will expand trade and investment under a modernized Free Trade Agreement, promote the development of public-private partnerships, and mobilize the capital and risk-mitigation solutions necessary to support Ukraine's recovery and reconstruction. Canada will cooperate with the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development to support macroeconomic stability and mobilize private capital," the Canadian government said.
It is also noted that both countries will deepen cooperation in the areas of energy security and critical minerals, industry and sustainable forest-resource management, as well as strengthen ties between innovators and researchers in the fields of artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, space, biotechnology, and digital governance.
Zelenskyy said that, together with Prime Minister Carney, they had discussed opportunities to ensure Ukraine's financial resilience for this year and the next.
"Thank you for your willingness to help find the funding necessary for the needs of the budget and our soldiers. I also spoke about Russia's virtually constant ballistic missile and drone strikes. Mark assured me that Canada is ready to join our European FREYJA anti-ballistic program with its technologies. This is a necessary and timely step. There will also be additional defense supplies. Of course, we also had a substantive discussion of promising bilateral projects in defense and the economy. In particular, our teams are currently working on the Drone Deal. We expect that in the near future we will be able to reach a full-fledged agreement," Zelenskyy said.
It should be recalled
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that Canada had decided on a "very important package of assistance for air defense".

Global Strike ‘Campaign’ Aims to Speed Up B-1, B-52 Maintenance, Parts Supply
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
17:18:55 UTC
02:18:55 KST

One year into a new campaign to boost readiness rates for the B-1B Lancer and B-52H Stratofortress bombers, Air Force Global Strike Command is claiming some early wins and planning to forge ahead with more improvements.
The North Star Readiness Campaign, launched in summer 2025, is mostly focused on coordinating maintenance and supply logistics for two of the most in-demand but stressed fleets in the Air Force. AFGSC is teaming up with Air Force Materiel Command and the Defense Logistics Agency in an effort to streamline the supply of spare parts and engineering support, break down logistical barriers, and improve how depots operate to allow B-1s and B-52s to be repaired and maintained faster.
The drive to improve readiness is needed, officials say, to help keep the B-1 flying through 2037 and the B-52 even longer than that while the Air Force builds out its new fleet of B-21 Raiders. The B-1 fleet’s average age is approaching 40 years old, and the B-52 fleet average is past 60 years old. What’s more, the Air Force has had more and more trouble over the years keeping the jets mission capable.
The Air Force no longer releases statistics on airframes’ mission-capable rates—the percentage of time an aircraft is available and able to carry out its mission—but in 2024, B-52s were available 54 percent of the time, and B-1s were even lower at 43 percent. Both had been on a steady downward trend.
“The North Star Readiness Campaign is our commitment to ensuring the warfighter has the nation’s bomber force ready to go at a moment’s notice,” Global Strike commander Gen. S.L. Davis said in a Sept. 8 statement from the Air Force. “This is a team effort. It brings together the operators at Air Force Global Strike Command, the acquisition and sustainment experts at Air Force Materiel Command, and our logistics partners at the Defense Logistics Agency to focus on one thing: operational readiness.”
In its Sept. 8 release, Global Strike did not detail new mission capable rates for the bomber fleets. But the command did note some progress.
The B-1, for example, has frequently suffered from “mission-impacting part problems.” MICAPs, as they are known, occur when a part that is necessary for an aircraft to be mission capable fails, and the spare or repair part is not available. At the start of the North Star Readiness Campaign, the B-1 fleet had more than 450 MICAPs, the Air Force release states. Now, that figure is down to about 160.
This has allowed maintainers to spend less time working on immediate emergencies on the B-1 and instead concentrate more on high-priority backorders and emerging trends on failures on the aircraft.
Another sign of progress are daily meetings between DLA representatives, supply chain officials, logistics readiness squadrons at the base level, and flightline maintainers to figure out which parts are being delayed and fix problems faster. By clearing procedural logjams, the release states, the command has been able to speed up some shipment timelines from more than a week to two or three days.
The campaign is unfolding at Air Force is increasingly worried about its ability to keep enough bombers in the air—and as some of its key platforms are showing their age.
The B-1 fleet, which now numbers 45 aircraft, was flown extremely heavily and worn out during the Global War on Terror. Over the last five years, the Air Force retired 17 of its most exhausted B-1s, in part to allow maintenance Airmen to concentrate on the healthiest Lancers.
The B-52, meanwhile, is famed for its longevity but is increasingly showing its age. The 75-aircraft fleet’s Pratt & Whitney-made TF33 engines are original, dating back to when the bombers rolled off the production lines, and commonly break. Many of the companies that made spare parts for the B-52 have closed or otherwise stopped making them, forcing the service to find other sources for parts—and even cannibalize other non-flying Stratofortresses for usable parts.
The Air Force is now in the midst of a massive modernization effort for the B-52, which will ultimately see its engines, avionics, radar, cockpit displays, and other key components replaced. This upgrade, which is extensive enough the Air Force will redub the bomber the B-52J, is intended to keep the bombers flying into at least the 2050s.
The Air Force said insight from maintainers who work on these planes every day is crucial to the readiness campaign. Flightline maintainers are providing information that is helping to refine maintenance processes and more quickly move critical parts to where they need to be, the Air Force said.
Chief Master Sgt. Shane Anderson, change management lead for the North Star Readiness Campaign, said one example was the way Airmen built a playbook to allow the “phase maintenance” process—or an extensive maintenance overhaul regularly scheduled for when an aircraft flies a certain number of hours—to be performed much more efficiently, without compromising safety or security.
“The [readiness campaign] started as a concept at the strategic level, but we have also received ideas directly from the flight line,” Anderson said. “They are the ones with the hands-on experience, and we would be remiss if we didn’t leverage their expertise to drive these improvements.”
The campaign also aims to expedite the parts availability for critical B-1 structural and avionics components, while working with AFMC and DLA to “streamline depot-level maintenance cycles.”
“These targeted efforts are designed to maximize the B-1’s operational readiness, ensuring it remains a lethal and highly visible conventional global strike option,” the Air Force said.
The Air Force also said the campaign is helping leaders anticipate future issues that might hurt the bombers’ readiness before they flare up into problems that grind missions to a halt.
The unified approach to improving maintenance is crucial to make sure the strategic bomber fleet remains able to project airpower, the release states.
“By modernizing these incredible platforms and ensuring our maintainers have the parts and support they need, we are sending a clear message to our adversaries and allies alike that the United States’ long-range penetrating strike capability is, and will remain, second to none,” Davis said.

Ukrainian Intelligence Warns of Russian False Flag Terror Attacks During State Duma Elections
The Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine (SZRU) has warned that Russian secret services are highly likely to orchestrate false-flag terrorist attacks and high-profile provocations in the temporarily occupied territories during the Russian State Duma elections scheduled for September 18–20, 2026.
According to the SZRU, the Kremlin’s primary objective is to artificially escalate the war, discredit Ukraine, and derail the US-mediated peace process by convincing Western partners that diplomatic tracks are futile.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The intelligence agency noted that Moscow also aims to use these provocations to justify repressive policies against the local population and create a pretext for a new wave of military mobilization within Russia.
The SZRU highlighted a historical pattern of Russian authorities staging bloody provocations during elections or key political dates to exert psychological pressure and legitimize aggressive policies.
The agency cited the 1999 apartment bombings in Russia, the 2002 Dubrovka (“Nord-Ost”) hostage crisis, and the 2004 Beslan school siege as examples where the Kremlin used terrorist attacks to justify restricting civil liberties, centralizing state power, and bolstering Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s support.
Furthermore, the intelligence service pointed to regular provocations in the occupied Donetsk and Luhansk regions between 2014 and 2024, where puppet administrations staged car bombings and “assassination attempts” ahead of important diplomatic negotiations to blame Ukraine.
During the upcoming voting days in the temporarily occupied Zaporizhzhia, Kherson, Donetsk, Luhansk, and Crimea regions, the SZRU predicts three likely scenarios:
- Bombings of polling stations or ballot collection points outside of business hours are designed to secure images of “destroyed” polling stations while avoiding mass casualties among key Russian propagandists.
- Sabotage of transport or infrastructure used to move election commission members could be followed by immediate accusations against Ukrainian drones or sabotage groups.
- Assassination attempts on collaborators could specifically target heads of occupying election commissions or parliamentary candidates who publicly demonstrate their loyalty to Moscow.
“Russian secret services do not hesitate to cause civilian casualties if it serves their current political objectives,” the SZRU warned.
To protect their lives and health, the Foreign Intelligence Service strongly advised residents of the temporarily occupied territories to avoid gathering places, including polling stations, administrative buildings, and Russian military infrastructure, between September 17 and 21.
The threat of false flag operations comes as the Kremlin tightly controls a stifled political atmosphere ahead of the vote. Russian political parties have previously drastically cut spending for the State Duma elections, leading strategists to label it the most underfunded campaign of the millennium.
Regional officials stated that standard campaigning is meaningless while the country faces drone strikes and fuel shortages, and candidates are barred from discussing the war. The Kremlin is reportedly suppressing voter turnout to minimize political risk, using the staged vote as a precursor to a planned mobilization drive.

Ukrainian FP-1 Drones Fly Record 3,200 km to Strike Russian Gas Processing Plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
17:16:39 UTC
02:16:39 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukrainian FP-1 Drones Fly Record 3,200 km to Strike Russian Gas Processing Plant
Ukrainian FP-1 long-range drones traveled more than 3,200 kilometers to strike a gas condensate processing facility in Russia’s Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug, setting a new reported distance record for the drone, according to Ukrainian defense company Fire Point and the CyberBoroshno OSINT project.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Fire Point said the target was the Novy Urengoy Condensate Preparation for Transport Plant, one of Russia’s largest facilities for processing gas condensate.
The strike also marks a significant increase in the FP-1’s reported reach. The drone initially had a maximum range of about 700 kilometers, compared with the more than 3,200 kilometers covered in the latest operation, substantially expanding the depth at which targets inside Russia can potentially be reached.
“We are erasing the deep rear doctrine from the Russian military vocabulary,” Fire Point CEO Iryna Terekh said at MSPO 2026 according to a UNITED24 Media correspondent.
CyberBoroshno reported that the drones specifically struck a de-ethanization gas treatment unit at the facility, operated by Gazprom Pererabotka and located about 18 kilometers from Novy Urengoy.
According to the OSINT project, FP-1 drones reached the Yamalo-Nenets region for the first time, making the facility the most distant target from Ukraine’s state border to have been struck since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Unlike oil refineries frequently targeted in Ukrainian long-range operations, the Novy Urengoy facility is part of Russia’s gas-processing industry. It handles the initial processing of unstable gas condensate into marketable products and receives feedstock from fields in the Nadym-Pur-Taz region, Russia’s largest gas-condensate basin. The plant has a design capacity of approximately 19.5 million tons of feedstock annually.
The unit targeted in the strike processes gases released during the de-ethanization of condensate. These gases contain ethane, a key feedstock for producing ethylene and polyethylene, and are intended to supply the Novy Urengoy Gas Chemical Complex.
The gas chemical complex has a planned production capacity of up to 400,000 tons of low-density polyethylene per year. CyberBoroshno estimated that this represents roughly 10% of Russia’s combined polyethylene and polypropylene production capacity.
According to the OSINT project, damage to the de-ethanization gas treatment unit could disrupt the broader production chain from gas condensate to polyethylene. Without gas treatment, ethane supplies to the Novy Urengoy Gas Chemical Complex could be interrupted, potentially affecting the production of ethylene and polyethylene.
CyberBoroshno noted that even if the plant’s condensate de-ethanization units remain operational, disruption to the gas treatment infrastructure could prevent the resulting gases from being processed and transferred further along the production chain.
The record-range FP-1 strike comes as Fire Point continues to expand its portfolio of domestically developed long-range weapons. The company has also advanced its FP-7 ballistic missile to military trials after completing two earlier rounds of testing, moving the system closer to potential operational deployment.

“Weeks, Not Months”: Ukraine’s FP-7 Ballistic Missile Nears Battlefield Debut
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

- Category
- Defense Tech
“Weeks, Not Months”: Ukraine’s FP-7 Ballistic Missile Nears Battlefield Debut
Ukraine’s FP-7 ballistic missile is now in military trials and could enter operational use within weeks, while its longer-range FP-9 may ultimately have to prove itself the hard way—against real Russian targets.
Ukrainian defense company Fire Point has moved its FP-7 ballistic missile into military trials after successfully completing two earlier stages of testing, bringing the weapon potentially within weeks of operational use.
Fire Point CEO Iryna Terekh announced the milestone during the 34th International Defense Industry Exhibition MSPO, according to a UNITED24 Media correspondent on September 10.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Terekh, the FP-7 has already passed its first two testing phases and is now undergoing military evaluation, which is also part of the missile’s formal codification process.
The earlier stages included ground and laboratory testing, during which individual systems and subsystems were evaluated separately, including the rocket engine and navigation equipment.
“We are erasing the deep rear doctrine from the Russian military vocabulary,” said Terekh.
Flight testing followed, allowing engineers to collect data on the missile’s behavior in the air and determine how closely its actual performance matched design calculations.
The FP-7 has now advanced beyond those stages.
“We’re talking weeks, not months,” Terekh said when asked how soon the missile could move toward operational use.
Fire Point is simultaneously developing the longer-range FP-9 ballistic missile, which is currently undergoing flight testing and remains one stage behind the FP-7.
Testing the FP-9 presents a very different challenge because of its greater range.
According to the developers, the missile has a minimum distance required for ballistic flight. Once it passes a certain point in its trajectory, the test can no longer simply be terminated through software.
That makes conducting a complete test entirely within Ukrainian territory difficult.
As a result, once the current flight-testing phase is completed, the FP-9 could potentially move from testing into military evaluation through actual employment against Russian targets rather than following the same conventional test sequence as the shorter-range FP-7.
Earlier, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed hope that the US will support implementing the FREYJA anti-ballistic missile program, with the interceptor missile being built based on the Fire Point FP-7 ballistic missile.
“We are preparing our own FREYJA program. We very much hope that the Americans will support this program as well. But nevertheless, with the Europeans we will definitely achieve the desired result,” Zelenskyy said.

Iranian arms and advice helped Yemen's Houthis seize key Red Sea city - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
17:15:28 UTC
02:15:28 KST

The lightning Houthi advance down Yemen's Red Sea coast this week came with direct guidance from Iran's Revolutionary Guards seeking to open a new front in Iran's war with the US, according to Yemeni government, Iranian, and regional sources.
By seizing the southwestern port city of Mocha, the Houthis have strengthened their chokehold on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key waterway whose disruption further constricts global energy supplies after Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
Six months into the wider regional conflict between the Houthis' Iranian allies and the United States, the group now looks focused on consolidating that grip on the strait even as opposing government forces backed by Saudi Arabia focus on an offensive in the north.
Iran told the Houthis last week to escalate their attacks on Saudi Arabia, a close US ally, and promised more funding, weapons and senior officers to help them do so, two Iranian sources said.
While Iran describes the Houthis as an ally, it publicly denies giving them military direction, saying they are "not a proxy."
How did the IRGC help the Houthis take over Yemen's Mocha Port?
Several senior Revolutionary Guards commanders had already traveled to Yemen to oversee and command Houthi attacks directed against Saudi Arabia after weeks of discussions over military strategy, a regional diplomat briefed by Tehran said.
A third Iranian source, an official, said Iran had held several meetings with allies including the Houthis and that the move on Mocha was a Houthi rather than Iranian decision. However, it had helped Iran by putting upward pressure on oil prices and hurting the United States and Saudi Arabia, the official added.
Inside Yemen, five military sources from the Saudi-backed and internationally recognized government said the Revolutionary Guards had directed the new Houthi campaign along the Red Sea coast, a flat, narrow plain known as the Tihama, starting with a blitz of rocket fire.
Citing communications intercepts and the accounts of captured Houthi prisoners, the Yemeni military sources said they believed the Iranian effort was being directed by Abdolreza Shahlaei, a top Revolutionary Guards commander.
Iranian sources could not immediately confirm that, though they had previously described Shahlaei, who is in the Guards' specialist Quds Force unit, as having spent time in Yemen in recent years.
The Guards were still able to move weapons and personnel in and out of Yemen despite an aerial and maritime blockade of Houthi areas, the Iranian sources said without elaborating on how they did so.
"If we look at their offensive on the west coast, it's not something prepared just last week or last month," said Ahmed Nagi, a Yemen analyst at the International Crisis Group, describing the seizure of Mocha as a significant milestone in the war.
"The evolution of the Houthis was basically because of the new weapons they gained, either through the Iranians directly or through the different smuggling networks that they are counting on," Nagi said, pointing specifically at their use of drones in the latest offensive.
As the Houthis began an advance towards Mocha last week, Yemen's government requested more air support and other help from the Saudis, two more Yemeni officials said.
It was seeking a Saudi air campaign against Houthi targets in the Houthi heartland, including Sanaa and key strategic assets such as oil depots, they said.
However, the kingdom stuck to providing logistical, armament and intelligence support, with only limited air strikes focused on northern battlefronts in Jawf and Marib provinces, areas the government regarded as less important.
Saudis fear escalation with IRGC-backed Houthis as war with Iran rages on
The officials' own assessment was that Riyadh was anxious to avoid a major escalation with the Houthis for fear of provoking heavier drone strikes on Saudi territory.
Saudi officials did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment on Riyadh's military focus on the northern front rather than the Red Sea coast and other big Houthi targets.
The overall military situation in Yemen is hard to gauge after a years-long pause in major warfare since a ceasefire was agreed in 2022. Both Iran and Saudi Arabia have invested in forces they back there. But the pro-government coalition has suffered from internal splits.
Although previous rounds of warfare in the Tihama had produced sudden advances and retreats, it remains unclear if Saudi-backed forces can easily dislodge the Houthis this time, Nagi said.
"Maybe we can see some advances from the government if they get the necessary support from the Saudis. But that could be a bit difficult this time," he said.

Mayoral candidates and community members gathered for a debate on antisemitism and community safety, proceeding in the absence of Mayor Olivia Chow on Tuesday at a synagogue in Toronto.
The forum, hosted by the Jewish Lawyers of Canada, was organized to allow candidates to present their strategies for tackling antisemitism, protecting community institutions, and strengthening public safety in the city. The event's location was not announced publicly because of security concerns, but it was provided to registered participants.
Mayor Chow opted out of the event; her campaign team told local outlets she would not take part in any debates before her re-election campaign officially launches.
Journalist and podcaster Jesse Brown, the debate moderator, addressed the audience regarding the mayor's absence and the surrounding communication. Brown noted that organizers were left without answers for weeks before being told last week that the event could not be attended because Chow's campaign does not officially start until September 9. Brown added that when organizers offered to move the date to September 9 instead, they received no reply.
Chow's primary challengers attended the event: Brad Bradford, a city councilor seeking to unseat the incumbent, and Chris Alexander, a former federal cabinet minister and diplomat pitching a fresh approach from outside municipal hall.
Taking the stage, Bradford opened by addressing the mayor's absence, stating, "I'm disappointed that the mayor wasn't here tonight because... we're not having a real conversation about antisemitism, about Jew-hatred, that's festered like an infection in the city over the past three years." Emphasizing that leadership requires direct engagement, he added, "And the mayor's job is to be the mayor for everybody. And that means you've got to show up."
Bradford contrasted this by committing to active leadership on public safety oversight, explaining, "the first thing I'm going to do... is I'm going to sit on the police board." He noted that previous mayors served on the board, pointing out that "Olivia Chow chose not to."
Bradford: 'If the city is not safe, then the city is not free'
Bradford addressed the pervasive nature of the security crisis facing the community, noting that incidents have impacted schools, synagogues, and local businesses. "If your kids go to a faith-based school and it's Jewish, well you've seen it shot up," Bradford told the audience. He stressed that the alarming rise in hate incidents affects the entire city, concluding, "If the city is not safe, then the city is not free. And that is what I'm going to be laser-focused on, of course, correcting."
Chris Alexander told the audience that having strong candidates with different kinds of experience working to end antisemitism and hate crimes was vital for the city.
When pressed on what separates him from Bradford, Alexander contrasted his municipal rival with his own federal cabinet and diplomatic experience, explaining, "The biggest difference is that I'm looking at these things with fresh eyes. I'm coming from outside of council... at the cabinet table in Ottawa, in diplomacy, managing complex issues like a very difficult international community, international military presence, Afghan government in Kabul, and the Department of Immigration."
Expanding on how his background equips him to handle local safety and community threats, Alexander emphasized his record of tackling global security challenges head-on. "I've actually been working on these issues of counter-terrorism, standing up to Iranian aggression, recognizing who their proxies are, and thinking about the pressures on Canada that come from places far from our borders for my entire career," Alexander told the audience.
He argued that municipal leaders must recognize how international threats intersect with local security, adding, "We are in a dangerous, a more dangerous world. It's no longer a cliché or throwaway statement to say that. It's literally true... And we are not responsible for foreign policy in City Hall, but what we do on issues like this will determine, will set the tone and determine the direction of Canada for years to come."
Emphasizing that the fight against hate is deeply personal, Alexander noted his lifelong ties to the local community and his family's history in the area, stating, "I was born here, I grew up here, my parents have always lived here, I've always been close to the Jewish community."
He framed the challenge as an existential priority for the city's future, adding, "This is existential for me. Tackling this issue, being part of a Toronto that heals itself, that puts itself back on the right track... I'm bringing my expertise, I'm bringing my commitment, I'm bringing energy to this race."
Toronto city councilor emphasizes broad stakes of the municipal election
Toronto City Councilor Mike Colle also addressed the audience during the event, emphasizing the broader stakes of the municipal election beyond everyday civic issues.
"This is a time like no other time in Toronto's history," Colle stated. "This is just not an election about property taxes, congestion, bike lanes."
Colle stressed that voters must look at the bigger picture regarding leadership and moral conviction, warning, "This is really a seminal time in Toronto's history when the future of this city and the direction of this city will be decided, because the direction we're going in right now, without leadership to deal with these problems and without moral persuasion, we are not going to combat this ongoing assault on the Jewish community."

Iran is producing new missiles in limited quantities from existing components - report
Unknown

17:15:16 UTC
02:15:16 KST

Iran has resumed producing ballistic missiles from existing components while working in underground facilities, the Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday, citing officials from the United States and the Middle East.
The renewed production threatens to undo what the US and Israel have described as one of the significant achievements of the war, following heavy attacks on Iranian missile sites and industrial infrastructure during its initial phase, according to the report.
Despite the damage to those facilities, Iran has been assembling both liquid-propellant and solid-propellant ballistic missiles, some of the officials told the WSJ.
Liquid-propellant missiles must generally be fueled shortly before launch, while solid-propellant missiles can be stored in a launch-ready state, allowing them to be fired more rapidly.
Reported rebuild became major focus of Israeli operations
The reported rebuilding effort comes after Iran's missile arsenal and production infrastructure became a major focus of Israeli operations.
Israel has previously carried out strikes on targets across Iran in response to Iranian missile attacks, while Tehran has continued to demonstrate its ability to launch ballistic missiles across the region.
Taken together, the developments underscore two continuing challenges facing Washington and its regional partners: efforts to dismantle Hezbollah's independent military infrastructure in Lebanon, and attempts to limit Iran's ability to restore missile capabilities damaged during the war.

Twenty-five years after the September 11 attacks, what has happened to al-Qaeda? - explainer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
17:14:53 UTC
02:14:53 KST

In the 25 years since al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked passenger jets and flew them into New York's World Trade Center towers and the Pentagon, the group founded by Osama bin Laden has spawned affiliates and inspired attacks around the world.
While it has suffered setbacks, notably bin Laden's killing in 2011 by US forces and the emergence of Islamic State as a rival, experts say al-Qaeda still serves as a source of support and inspiration for terrorists in many regions, particularly in Africa.
What is al-Qaeda?
Al-Qaeda emerged as a transnational jihadist network in the late 1980s under the leadership of bin Laden, a wealthy Saudi-born militant who had helped recruit and funnel support to Arab volunteers fighting the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan after 1979 and fought there himself.
Al-Qaeda became a magnet for terrorists who aspired to establish hardline Islamist rule and who shared common hostility to the United States, Israel, and US-allied governments in the region.
Bin Laden was stripped of his Saudi citizenship in 1994 and expelled from Sudan in 1996, taking sanctuary in Afghanistan.
He began organizing attacks on US interests long before arriving in Afghanistan. The first recognized by the United States was a 1992 al-Qaeda bombing of two hotels in Yemen intended to kill Somalia-bound US troops who had already left or were staying elsewhere.
In Afghanistan, he supported training camps and established an elite brigade of foreign fighters.
In 1996, he declared jihad against US forces he described as occupying Saudi Arabia.
This was followed in 1998 by the announcement of a "World Islamic Front" for jihad against "Jews and Crusaders," and a declaration that it was a duty for Muslims to kill Americans and their allies, whether civilian or military.
Later that year, al-Qaeda truck bombings against the US embassies in Kenya and Tanzania killed 224 people.
The September 11 attacks were carried out by 19 hijackers, 15 of them from Saudi Arabia. They hijacked four jets, the fourth of which crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after passengers stormed the cockpit. The attacks killed nearly 3,000 people.
What happened to al-Qaeda's leaders after 9/11?
The United States invaded Afghanistan in October 2001, toppling the Taliban and driving al-Qaeda from its base of operations.
Anti-Taliban forces overran al-Qaeda's base in the Tora Bora mountains in December 2001, but bin Laden evaded capture for a decade, periodically releasing messages until US special forces killed him in a raid on his compound in Abbottabad, Pakistan, in 2011.
The self-professed mastermind of September 11, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, was captured in Pakistan in 2003. In 2007, Mohammed said he planned the attack "from A to Z," according to a transcript of a military hearing released by the Pentagon.
A judge recently ordered Mohammed, who is held in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, and three co-defendants to stand trial before a military tribunal in June 2028, following two decades of legal deadlock.
Bin Laden's successor, Ayman al-Zawahri, was killed by a US drone strike in Kabul in 2022.
Egyptian militant Seif al-Adel is believed to be al-Qaeda's de facto leader today.
How did al-Qaeda's influence spread after 9/11?
While al-Qaeda's leaders scattered, terrorists linked to al-Qaeda or inspired by its ideology carried out numerous attacks.
The deadliest included a 2002 attack on a nightclub district in Bali that killed 202 people, bombings that killed more than 190 people on trains in Madrid in 2004, and suicide bombings that killed 52 people on London underground trains and a bus in 2005.
Al-Qaeda affiliates sprang up in the Middle East and beyond. One of the most powerful was in Iraq, where al-Qaeda fought US-led forces following the 2003 invasion.
A branch emerged in North Africa in 2007 and another in the Arabian Peninsula in 2009. After 2011, al-Qaeda's Nusra Front became a force in Syria's civil war.
In Africa, al-Qaeda affiliates include Al Shabaab in Somalia and Jama'at Nusrat al‑Islam wal‑Muslimin (JNIM) in the Sahel region. al-Qaeda also has ties to Tehrik-e Taliban Pakistan (TTP), also known as the Pakistani Taliban, which is waging an insurgency against Islamabad.
Antonio Giustozzi, a senior research fellow at the RUSI think-tank in London, said that while al-Qaeda suffered losses and dislocation after the invasion of Afghanistan, its profile rose and it expanded massively in the years that followed. Its influence peaked around 2013 before its Iraqi branch broke away to form Islamic State, he said.
How was al-Qaeda affected by the rise of ISIS?
Islamic State founder Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi split from al-Qaeda and declared a "caliphate" across large parts of Syria and Iraq in 2014, sparking conflict with the Nusra Front.
Though Islamic State was eventually beaten out of its territory in Syria and Iraq, in a reversal for jihadism, its rivalry with al-Qaeda continues, particularly in West Africa, where affiliates of the two groups regularly clash as they compete for territory and influence.
Another blow came in 2016 when the Nusra Front broke away. Its leader Ahmed al-Sharaa, then known by his nom de guerre Abu Mohammed al-Golani, went on to topple Bashar al-Assad in 2024. He became Syrian president and made Damascus a Western ally.
Where is al-Qaeda most active today?
Somalia and West Africa's Sahel region are the main theaters in Africa where al-Qaeda-aligned groups are expanding their influence and governing across swathes of territory.
TTP has expanded its insurgency in northwestern Pakistan. It has received ideological guidance, training and support from al-Qaeda, according to a UN report published last month.
Pakistan says the TTP leadership and many of its fighters are based in Afghanistan, where the Taliban returned to power in 2021 after the US withdrew.
In February, another UN report said al-Qaeda "continued to enjoy the patronage of the de facto authorities" in Afghanistan, a reference to the Taliban government, and that its "appetite for external operations" remained "undiminished."
Kabul denies that al-Qaeda operates in Afghanistan, or that it allows militant attacks on Pakistan from its territory.
Giustozzi said that while al-Qaeda was past its peak, "they're still remarkably influential."
It had evolved to be less dependent on specific individuals, relying instead on a cadre of low-profile operatives who are "much more difficult to target and identify," he said.

Declaration for a sustainable use of outer space for all.
France
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
19:10:00 CEST
02:10:00 KST

Signature : Armenia, Australia, Austria, Bahrein, Belgium, Brazil, Bulgaria, Cambodia, Canada, Chile, Costa Rica, Croatia, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Denmark, Djibouti, Ecuador, Estonia, Finland, France, Georgia, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, Ireland, Israel, Italy, Japan, Jordan, Kazakhstan, Latvia, Luxembourg, Malta, Mauritius, Mexico, Morocco, Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Philippines, Poland, Romania, Rwanda, Saudi Arabia, Serbia, Singapore, Slovakia, Slovenia, South Korea, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey, United Arab Emirates, United Kingdom, European Space Agency (ESA), UN Office of Outer Space Affairs (UNOOSA)
We, participants of the International Space Summit held in Paris in September 2026 :
-    Affirm our common and overarching goal to ensure a peaceful, secure, safe, stable and sustainable use of outer space, for all humanity.
-    Reaffirm the importance of the widest possible adherence to and full compliance with the 1967 Outer Space Treaty.
-    Note that the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS) and its subcommittees retain an important role in fostering discussions related to current and emerging issues related to the safe and sustainable use of space and promoting consensus on effective and practical international cooperation in the peaceful exploration and use of outer space.
-    Reaffirm that there is a need for international coordination to foster transparency, clarity and consistency of relevant policies, guidelines and recommendations across the various existing fora and initiatives, in order to effectively address and promote the safety and sustainability of space activities at large.
-    Support a gradual and pragmatic approach to international space issues, based on dialogue, transparency and reciprocity.
-    Underline the necessity of ensuring long-term sustainability of outer space activities.
Therefore, we :
-    Call on all nations to join and participate actively in the work of COPUOS and its subcommittees.
-    Support consideration by COPUOS, on the basis of consensus, of the organization of a UNISPACE IV conference. 
-    Encourage the implementation of best practices and guidelines to encourage the safe and transparent use of outer space activities, emphasizing that such measures are complementary to, and not a substitute for, efforts to negotiate legally binding instruments in this regard.
-    Advocate for the continued implementation of the Guidelines for the long-term sustainability of outer space activities adopted by COPUOS in 2019.
-    Welcome the creation of the Expert Group on Space Situational Awareness (SSA) under the COPUOS as the most appropriate international forum to address this key issue ; and support its work in accordance with its agreed mandate, terms of reference and work plan. Call on the Expert Group on SSA to study measures for enhanced international coordination and report to COPUOS for consideration and decision by consensus.
-    Call for the adoption by COPUOS of the voluntary recommendations of the Expert Group on SSA, advancing a shared understanding of information important for timely and effective coordination ; with consideration of the possible establishment of an information sharing and international coordination framework under COPUOS on SSA enabling spacecraft operators to share, maintain and make available up-to-date points of contact without prejudice to respective national regulatory framework, whose secretariat could be assured by UNOOSA.
