Syphilis cases rise 3% through August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:38:00 UTC
01:38:00 KST

Syphilis cases in Taiwan rose by 3 percent year-on-year in the first eight months of this year, driven by a 4 percent increase among women and young adults, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said in a statement yesterday.
The CDC said that 78 percent of cases in the period were male, while 70 percent were aged 15 to 44.
Reported cases among women and people aged 15 to 24 were 1,538 and 1,340 respectively, both up 4 percent from the same period last year, it said.
Photo: Chen Chien-chih, Taipei Times
CDC Deputy Director-General Lin Min-cheng (林明誠) said there were 68 reported cases of congenital syphilis during the period, highlighting the need for measures to control the disease.
Infants can contract congenital syphilis if their mother was diagnosed with the disease while pregnant, but they must be monitored for up to 15 months before a definitive diagnosis can be made, Lin said.
The number of reported cases does not necessarily correspond to the number of diagnoses, she said, adding that some cases might be attributed to false-positive test results of mothers, with subsequent testing confirming that they did not have the disease.
If pregnant women diagnosed with syphilis do not seek timely treatment, it could lead to stillbirth, miscarriage or premature birth, she said.
Benzathine penicillin G is the only effective treatment for preventing mother-to-child transmission, she added.
Syphilis can be difficult to diagnose definitively, as it can be asymptomatic and can cause a variety of symptoms that might easily be mistaken for a common cold or other skin conditions, Lin said.
Symptoms can also temporarily subside without treatment, leading people to delay seeking medical care and assume that the infection has gone away, she said.
However, Treponema pallidum — the bacteria that causes the disease — can spread and remain transmissible in the body, potentially progressing to severe tertiary syphilis and allowing an unseen chain of transmission to persist, Lin said.
Early diagnosis and appropriate treatment are vital to stopping the spread, she said.
If pregnant women test positive in an initial rapid plasma reagin or venereal disease screening during prenatal care, the same blood sample can be used for a T pallidum particle agglutination or T Pallidum hemagglutination assay confirmatory test, eliminating the need for a return visit and helping speed diagnosis, reporting and treatment, the CDC said.
Pregnant women with positive initial screening results should undergo confirmatory testing as soon as possible and, if diagnosed with syphilis, undergo appropriate treatment promptly, it said.
When reporting cases involving pregnant women, medical professionals should also record the pregnancy and gestational age to facilitate follow-up by public health authorities, it added.

Asian Games open with Qatar win

16:37:58 UTC
01:37:58 KST

The Asian Games began in Japan yesterday when Qatar beat Iran in the men’s basketball opening group game, the first action in the continental multisport showpiece that has more participants than the Olympics.
More than 17,000 athletes and officials are expected to take part in 43 sports at the Nagoya-Aichi Games — which do not officially start until the opening ceremony on Saturday next week and runs through Oct. 4.
Several events such as basketball, soccer, cricket, hockey and modern pentathlon are to get under way before the opening ceremony.
Photo: AFP
Qatar held off a comeback from Iran to win their Group B encounter 59-35 at the Aichi International Arena in Nagoya in the first match of a men’s basketball competition that would hold medal finals on Sept. 20, the day after the opening ceremony.
Los Angeles 2028 Olympics qualifying spots are up for grabs in several sports at the Asian Games, which are returning to Japan for the first time since 1994.
Organizers hope the athletes would have a “unique experience” staying in eye-catching accommodation ranging from a cruise liner and wooden containers to standard hotel rooms.

Europe’s center fears nationalist wave after AfD victory, but only has itself to blame
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:54 UTC
01:37:54 KST

The numbers speak for themselves: Alternative for Germany (AfD), a party that dabbles in Nazi imagery, distinguishes between “biological” and “passport” Germans, and is too extreme even for Marine le Pen, leader of the National Rally in France, nearly doubled its score in Sunday’s state election in Saxony-Anhalt to 43.8 percent of the vote.
Meanwhile, the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz collapsed to 17.2 percent, less than half its total in the same race five years ago and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) — Germany’s other main party of government for the past 60-odd years — scraped 9.3 percent.
The least that can be said is that the center did not hold.
Illustration: Mountain People
It is not yet clear whether the AfD, whose local branch in the east German state of Saxony-Anhalt is officially classified by the country’s domestic intelligence service as “confirmed right-wing extremist,” will be able to form a government. It has 39 lawmakers in the 83-member parliament, just short of an outright majority.
However, the score is the party’s strongest-ever state result and puts it closer to governing a German state than any far-right party since World War II. It has sent shock waves around Europe, with nationalists cheering a “historic win” that is “just the beginning” and mainstream leaders warning of a “grave moment” for Europe.
Sweden holds legislative elections next weekend. France faces a crunch presidential ballot next spring. Key parliamentary races will follow there, as well as in Italy, Spain and Poland later in the year. Far-right parties are polling strongly in all of them and Europe’s center fears a continent-wide nationalist wave.
It would be wise not to read too much into one election result in one quite particular German state. Saxony-Anhalt, analysts say, is home to barely 1.8 million voters and has long been a far-right stronghold. In federal and state elections over the past decade, support for the AfD there has consistently been double the national average.
“A far-right party winning a regional election in Germany is not more scary than a far-right party winning a regional election in France, the UK or the Netherlands,” said Tarik Abou-Chadi, a professor of European politics at Oxford University. “Saxony-Anhalt should not be the basis for sweeping conclusions about the electoral sociology of the AfD.”
Nonetheless, the AfD leads in national polls. It is also ahead — although in a far tighter race, with the SPD — in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where state elections are due later this month, and it is lying second even in liberal Berlin. Its rise is part of a decade-long march by far-right parties across Europe.
Almost one in four voters in Europe now cast their ballot for far-right parties, according to research led by Matthijs Rooduijn, a political scientist at the University of Amsterdam, a proportion that has grown nearly fivefold since the mid-1990s and climbed particularly steeply over the past three years.
This analysis, by more than 150 political scientists in 31 countries, found that the proportion of Europeans voting for a far-right party in their country’s most recent national elections had risen this year to more than 23 percent, from about 10 percent a decade ago and roughly 5 percent in 1995.
Far-right populist parties are now in government as part of ruling coalitions in Croatia, the Czech Republic, Italy and Finland, propping up a right-wing minority government in Sweden, and leading in the polls in Austria, Belgium, France and Germany (and, until very recently, the UK).
They have also suffered recent defeats, including in the Netherlands, where Geert Wilders’ Freedom party (PVV) lost nearly one-third of its seats to finish second last year, and Hungary, where former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orban’s Fidesz was comprehensively beaten by his center-right rival in April.
However, the trend seems clear.
As Cas Mudde of the University of Georgia, a leading expert on Europe’s far right, put it after Orban’s defeat: “The far right is here to stay and many of its parties are as established as the [former] ‘mainstream’ parties. Like other parties, their electoral support fluctuates.”
That steady electoral advance has been achieved, despite a refusal by mainstream parties in countries such as France and Germany to collaborate with far-right parties, prompting some commentators to argue that the “cordon sanitaire” or “firewall” has now failed, or even been counterproductive.
By keeping the AfD out, they argue, Germany’s mainstream parties have actually boosted it. The party has been protected from the compromises and failures inherent in government. At the same time, the center has been “hollowed-out” — forced into uncomfortable, unstable alliances that agree on and, vitally, accomplish little, further frustrating voters and driving support for the extremes.
“There’s a self-reinforcing political dynamic that feeds the AfD’s rise,” said Mujtaba Rahman of the Eurasia Group risk consultancy. “The weaker the election results, the less common ground in the coalition, the fewer the policy results. The fewer results, the bigger the frustration in the electorate, the bigger the AfD’s share of the vote.”
However, many political scientists say that blaming the firewall is an excuse, and data suggest that far-right parties do not in any case get weaker when they are in government, but become stronger. One recent study of more than 1,300 different governments in 57 countries found far-right parties that entered government averaged a score 6 percentage points higher in the next election.
Besides the persistent inability of mainstream governments to deliver for disillusioned voters hit by a spiraling cost of living crisis, it is above all the gradual mainstreaming and normalization of the far right’s ideas that has driven — and continues to drive — its steady advance, political scientists argue.
Research suggests voter attitudes toward core far-right themes such as immigration have not changed significantly, but have become much more significant in their voting decisions: Normalization by the media and by mainstream parties that readily embrace far-right framing have legitimized far-right views.
“The entire debate about whether the cordon sanitaire is ‘successful’ or contributes to strengthening the far right completely misses the point,” said Gabriela Greilinger, an Austrian-Hungarian political scientist. “Far-right politics and policies already constantly take center stage, whether or not the far right is in power. There is no cordon around their ideas.”
Well, sort of. Tomorrow is the seventy-fifth anniversary of the San Francisco Peace Treaty, signed by forty-nine nations on September 8, 1951. The Republic of China wasn’t one of them. Article 2(b) of the Treaty reads: “Japan renounces all right, title and claim to Formosa and the Pescadores.” So, tomorrow would be the Diamond Jubilee of Formosa’s freedom from Japanese sovereignty. As my good friend and former Examination Yuan President Yao Chia-wen (姚嘉文) voiced in these pages last year (“San Francisco treaty should be taught: adviser”, Sept. 7, 2025), the Japan peace treaty should be taught in all Taiwan schools to
Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) was under constant fire last month over the city government’s questionable public works projects and child protection issues, and last week he sparked another controversy involving his son. Chiang on Monday last week confirmed that his eldest son, who was recently admitted to Taipei Municipal Chien Kuo Senior High School, would take a leave of absence to participate in a year-long exchange program in the US. The exchange program Chiang’s son was selected for is funded by the Taipei City Government, and is limited to 25 spots for eligible junior-high and high-school students. Chiang was accused

The Guatemalan embassy yesterday celebrated the Central American country’s 205th independence day at a reception in Taipei attended by Taiwanese officials and members of the diplomatic community.
Guatemalan Ambassador to Taiwan Luis Raul Estevez Lopez said his country’s political, social and cultural experiences since gaining independence from Spain on Sept. 15, 1821, have shaped the democracy Guatemala is today.
Turning to bilateral relations, Estevez said that cooperation between Guatemala and Taiwan has continued to deepen across diplomatic, commercial, defense, cultural and technological fields.
Photo: CNA
He cited increases in Guatemalan exports to Taiwan, additional scholarships for Guatemalan students and efforts launched after Guatemalan President Bernardo Arevalo’s visit to Taiwan in June last year, to help Guatemala play a role in the semiconductor supply chain.
Meanwhile, Guatemala has consistently supported Taiwan’s participation in international organizations, Estevez said.
The two countries would mark 92 years of uninterrupted diplomatic relations in December, he added.
Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Ger Baushuan (葛葆萱) congratulated Guatemala and praised bilateral cooperation in public health, infrastructure, personnel training and trade.
Ger cited joint projects including Guatemala’s first public specialized cancer hospital, modernization of La Aurora International Airport and a cloud backup data center aimed at improving government cybersecurity.
"Two-way trade and investment remain a cornerstone of our bilateral relations," Ger said, adding that Guatemala’s annual exports to Taiwan totaled US$130 million over the past two years.
Taiwan would encourage more companies to establish operations in Guatemala and use the country as a hub for expansion into the Americas, contributing to industrial development and job creation, Ger added.

City unveils GS safe pet product certification
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:53 UTC
01:37:53 KST

The New Taipei City Government on Tuesday unveiled a GS safety certificate system for pet products in collaboration with private enterprises in the industry.
Incidents involving animal harm by unsafe pet products prompted the city’s Animal Protection and Health Inspection Office to develop a safety labeling system based on policies that foreign countries successfully implemented, office Deputy Commissioner Liu Hsu-fen (劉淑芬) told a news conference.
Pet products using substandard materials or of poor construction pose a danger to pets, Liu said.
Photo courtesy of the New Taipei City Animal Protection and Health Inspection Office
A trolleys’ weight-bearing capacity, small components or sharp edges on toys and escape-proof fences are some of the design features that the GS standard evaluates before certifying a product, she said.
Establishing safety standards and inspection protocols helps manufacturers to design better products and identify potential flaws to prevent harm, said Huang Hsien-ping (黃獻平), chairman of the Taipei-based China Pet Products Development Association.
The GS standard obliges manufacturers to report unsafe products to the association for recall and comply with measures should a major safety incident occur, Huang said.
Office Director Yang Shu-fang (楊淑方) said pet owners should think carefully about their pet’s size, physical condition, age and habits before buying products.
Protecting the welfare of pets requires a regulatory system that provides comprehensive oversight from design to safety evaluation before products are released to the consumer market, an office spokesperson said.
New Taipei City Government officials and association representatives at the news conference demonstrated how to check the suitability of a product for pets.

Army to conduct another Tianma exercise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:53 UTC
01:37:53 KST

The 6th Army Command is to conduct live-fire anti-armor drills in Hsinchu County from Wednesday to Friday next week for the second consecutive month of its “Tianma” (天馬) exercise as Taiwan’s anti-armor units step up training with newly fielded TOW 2B missiles.
Taiwan has received the full package it procured under its High-Performance Anti-Armor Missile Program, which includes 1,700 TOW 2B RF anti-armor missiles, 100 Improved Target Acquisition Systems and 100 M1167 High Mobility Multipurpose Wheeled Vehicles, the Ministry of National Defense said.
The NT$11.815 billion (US$374.51 million) program, launched in 2018, aimed to bolster Taiwan’s asymmetric warfare capabilities.
Photo courtesy of the Military News Agency
The equipment has been distributed to military units, which have begun training and familiarizing themselves with the new systems, contributing to a higher tempo of live-fire exercises in recent months.
The Tianma exercise is the military’s major anti-armor live-fire exercise, and typically features TOW and Javelin missiles.
The exercises are usually conducted at coastal firing areas in Pingtung County, such as Fangshan (枋山), Jioupeng (九鵬) and Jialyutang (加祿堂), due to range and safety restrictions.
In line with the ministry’s push for combat-oriented training, the exercise this year was conducted at tactical positions within each combatant command’s area of responsibility, allowing troops to train in their designated operational areas and familiarize themselves with local terrain.
The command’s latest exercise is to be held at Fongkeng Beach (鳳坑海灘) in Hsinchu County’s Sinfong Township (新豐) from 8am to noon every day.
That follows the army’s Tianma exercise at the Kengzinkou Range (坑子口訓場) on Aug. 27, underscoring the increased training tempo of northern Taiwan’s anti-armor units.
The nation has conducted exercises since March, when the Second Combat Area in eastern Taiwan reopened a firing range at the mouth of Taitung County’s Taimali River (太麻里溪) for the first time in 30 years.
In June, the 6th Army Command conducted a live-fire drone and Tianma exercise in Yilan County, with an anti-armor platoon from the army’s 584th Combined Arms Brigade conducting qualification firing with TOW 2A missiles and validation firing with TOW 2B missiles.
The TOW 2B RF uses radio-frequency guidance rather than the wire guidance employed by the older TOW 2A, giving it a maximum range of 4,500m.
Its key feature is its top-attack capability: The missile flies above the target’s line of sight before detonating over an enemy tank and directing its warhead downward against the vehicle’s more vulnerable roof armor.
The command’s intensive top-attack drills at Fongkeng Beach are intended to bolster northern Taiwan’s coastal defenses and improve its ability to counter armored vehicles attempting an amphibious landing.

INDONESIA
Japan helps fight wildfires
A Japanese military transport ship yesterday docked on the island of Borneo as part of a disaster relief mission to help fight wildfires that are causing a toxic haze impacting people’s health in other countries. Japan deployed 300 crew members, landing ship JS Kunisaki and three CH-47 helicopters, which arrived in Kalimantan. The mission marked the first known overseas firefighting operation carried out by the Japan Self-Defense Forces. “To this end, we will learn from the Indonesian military’s operational experience and work in coordination and cooperation with them, striving to ensure that the Indonesian people can lead stable lives as soon as possible,” Japanese Colonel Syunji Nakahara, the commander of the disaster relief activities, said at a port in Mempawah District.
Photo: Reuters
NORTH KOREA
Kim could have another child
Leader Kim Jong-un’s daughter and apparent successor is believed to have a younger sibling, the South Korean National Intelligence Service said yesterday, offering a more detailed view of the ruling family’s line of succession. The spy agency has previously said Kim is thought to have three children, but some uncertainty remains on the number of offspring as well as the order of their birth. Kim’s daughter, Kim Ju-ae, was first introduced to the public in 2022 when she accompanied her father to the launch of an intercontinental ballistic missile. Seoul had initially indicated that Kim Jong-un and his wife, Ri Sol-ju, had their first child, a boy, in 2010, and that Kim Ju-ae was their second child, but in 2023, Seoul said it was “unable to confirm” the existence of the son. The Taiwan Football Premier League (TFPL) is to start on Sunday, with four matches on the day, as clubs seek to dethrone Tainan City TSG as defending champions.
Eight teams are contesting the 10th season of Taiwan’s top men’s competition, with the Kaohsiung Attackers added to the roster after they won the second-division title last season, earning promotion to the top flight.
New Taipei Hang Yuan host TSG in the first game at the Fu Jen University Soccer Stadium in New Taipei City, while hosts Taichung Futuro take on the Tatung Taiwan Leopard Cats at Situn Soccer Stadium in Taichung.
Photo: CNA
Elsewhere, Taipower FC host Sunny Bank AC Taipei at the Nanzhih Soccer Stadium in Kaohsiung and the Attackers face Taichung Rock FC at the same ground in the evening match.
Players, coaches and officials of the Chinese Taipei Football Association (CTFA) governing body at a news conference on Tuesday last week unveiled the new season of 21 regular-season rounds, or 84 games, through May next year.
Officials said that the slogan for the season was “Beyond Limits.”
“This is an important milestone for the TFPL reaching its 10th year and we hope it will usher in a new era for Taiwan soccer,” CTFA chairman Michael Chang told the news conference.
The top men’s competition was once the national soccer league before turning semi-professional in the 1980s with the Enterprise Football League and rebranding as the Intercity Football League in 2007-2008. The TFPL launched in 2017-2018.
Chang said that the CTFA would push for more reforms, initiate new programs and plan for expansion of the TFPL.
“We are working toward adding two new teams to the current format so that 10 clubs are competing in the TFPL’s 2027-2028 season,” he said. “The plan is for each club to operate at its own home ground so it will be a full home-and-away competition,” he added.
The TFPL’s eight clubs are based in five major urban centers. Taipei (formerly the Leopard Cats), New Taipei City, Taichung, Tainan, and Kaohsiung (Taipower).
“Expanding would improve the competition and provide more opportunities for players,” Chang said. “Taiwan has many youngsters who are gaining experience at international tournaments, so the top-league TFPL is the stage for them to grow, cultivate and hone their skills, and challenge for higher honors.”
“That is the way Taiwan can sustain the future generations of soccer talent,” he added.
However, there are barriers, Chang said.
“Among the most urgent issues is the lack of fields that are up to the standard for a top-flight competition,” he said. “We must address this important task now, which requires the CTFA and all clubs to work toward upgrading pitches.”
Chang said that the sport needs more resources and funding from local governments, as well as more corporate sponsorship, citing the cost of booking certified soccer stadiums.
The Ministry of Sports should plan new stadiums dedicated to soccer, and provide more resources and funding to underwrite ground rental to reduce the financial burden on clubs, he said.
“Overall, we need more certified soccer grounds throughout Taiwan, for the men’s and women’s top-flight competitions, and also so we can host international tournaments,” he said.

The High Court yesterday sentenced businessman Cheng Ming-chia (鄭明嘉) to 10 years and six months in prison for developing an organization for the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) "united front" authorities.
Retired Executive Yuan official Hu Peng-nien (胡鵬年) was sentenced to five years for attempting to do the same.
The ruling can be appealed.
Photo: CNA
From 2021 to last year, Cheng helped Chinese "united front" officials approach and attempt to recruit targets in Taiwan by providing contact information and arranging meetings in China, the court said.
He recruited Hu as a potential operative, while his efforts to recruit another individual surnamed Huang (黃) failed after Huang did not respond.
Treating Cheng’s actions as a continuous offense, the court sentenced him to 10 years and six months in prison.
Meanwhile, Hu used the same methods from 2021 to 2024 to try to recruit three people, prosecutors said.
None responded, leading the court to convict him of attempting to develop an organization. It sentenced him to five years in prison.
Hu admitted to the offenses, while Cheng denied wrongdoing throughout the investigation and trial, the court said .
It said the evidence against Cheng was clear and rejected his defense.
Both defendants followed instructions from CCP personnel to facilitate the recruitment of new targets, the court said.
Hu also transported a communications device supplied by the Chinese authorities into Taiwan and handed it to another person, conduct that the court said significantly aided Beijing’s “united front” efforts.
Cheng recruited Hu — then teaching in China — after becoming involved with CCP-affiliated "united front" organizations in Guangzhou, and arranged for him to take direction from CCP Taiwan affairs personnel in identifying contacts and recruits in Taiwan, a January indictment by the High Prosecutors’ Office said.
Hu targeted current and retired military personnel, political workers, wardens, retired civil servants and defense contractors, seeking military-related information and insights into government and legislative operations, although most recruitment efforts failed, prosecutors said.
Cheng and Hu have remained in detention since their arrest following raids in September last year, and both were absent from yesterday's sentencing.

Photo: Reuters
“Apple’s pricing was one of the most impressive parts. Keeping the iPhone Duo just under the US$2,000 mark, at US$1,999, and only about US$100 above the Galaxy Z Fold 8 looks like a pretty bold move by Apple,” Counterpoint Research associate director Liz Lee said.

CWA warns of potentially deadly waves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:46 UTC
01:37:46 KST

The Central Weather Administration (CWA) yesterday warned the public of potentially deadly hazards posed by swells, known locally as “crazy dog waves,” which have claimed more than 770 lives in the past 25 years.
From 2000 to November last year, the CWA recorded 445 incidents involving freak waves along Taiwan’s coasts, resulting in 778 people falling into the sea.
Offshore abnormal wave events were also reported, with 206 incidents recorded from 2000 to June 2023 involving 936 people, CWA data showed.
Photo: CNA
Lin Fang-ju (林芳如), a specialist in marine meteorological technology at the CWA’s Marine Meteorology and Climate Division, said long-period waves, or swells, can sometimes become hazardous.
The CWA has established separate warning systems for abnormal waves in coastal waters and the open ocean.
Wave conditions are primarily affected by wind speed, the size of the area over which the wind blows and the duration of the wind, Lin said.
Stronger winds blowing over a wider area for a longer period produce larger waves with greater energy, she said.
Wind waves are generated locally by winds blowing across the sea surface, while swells are generated by strong winds farther away and continue to travel after leaving the area affected by the winds, she added.
Swells are also known as long-period waves, Lin said.
Because swells have longer periods and travel faster than normal waves, they can reach speeds of more than 100kph, she said.
By comparison, typhoons generally move at about 5kph to 20kph. As a result, swells generated by a distant typhoon can reach Taiwan’s shores one or two days before the storm itself, she added.
When swells enter shallow waters, coastal topography can cause high waves that break and crash, creating dangerous conditions, she said, adding that unusually large waves despite calm local winds could indicate severe weather systems offshore.
The CWA provides real-time swell information when wave heights reach at least 1.5m and periods are eight seconds or longer, except during typhoon warnings.
In cooperation with National Cheng Kung University’s Coastal Hydraulics Center, the CWA has developed a Coastal Abnormal Wave Warning System to improve warnings of dangerous waves near shore.
The Ocean Abnormal Wave Warning System uses nonlinear wave theory and wave models to provide the probability of abnormal waves occurring in the following 24, 36 and 48 hours.
The CWA also uses data from buoys to monitor waves, currents, water temperatures, wind, air temperatures and atmospheric pressure.
The solar-powered buoys generally collect observations hourly when sufficient power is available, although fishing nets, ship collisions and ropes tied to the buoys can affect data quality.
In cooperation with Kenting National Park, the CWA provides warnings when forecast wave heights reach specified levels, and forecasts of high and low tide lines to help prevent people from becoming stranded on beaches or sandbars.

====================================================================================================

Bronze Age hoard, Egyptian diamonds: String of museum heists throughout August shake Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:44 UTC
01:37:44 KST

Nearly a year after the infamous Louvre heist shocked the world, a new series of museum thefts across Europe has raised concerns in the art and antiquities world about the rising phenomenon.
On Tuesday, four paintings were stolen from the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer on the French Riviera, and in mid-August, four paintings by Renaissance master Antonello da Messina were stolen from the Museo Regionale di Messina in the painter’s hometown.
Last month, the pan-European police body Europol said that art thieves in Europe are committing more violent robberies and specialist gangs have been replaced by ad hoc opportunists recruited through social media.
But the recent heists have not only been of priceless paintings, but of artifacts as well.
Treasure of Villena
On August 27, thieves in Spain entered the Villena Museum (MUVI) and stole the majority of the Treasure of Villena, a collection of Bronze Age artifacts often described as one of the most significant prehistoric European finds.
The collection is made up of 66 artifacts of gold, silver, iron and amber. The gold artifacts including 11 bowls, three bottles and 28 bracelets.
It was originally discovered in 1963 by Spanish archaeologist José María Soler.
The theft happened “in a matter of minutes,” Villena Mayor Fulgencio Cerdán said during a press conference following the robbery.
He explained that the robbery took place around 5:20 a.m., with the thieves believed to have left the museum approximately four minutes later.
While most of the treasure had been taken, Cerdán noted that three silver vessels, a bracelet, some ornamentation of the bastón del reyezuelo, and the “Kingfisher staff.”
The stolen gold pieces are estimated to be worth €1.7 million, according to media reports.
“We are absolutely devastated,” Cerdán said. “I am shaking. The truth is that, for those of us from Villena, this destroys us. It is part of our heritage and part of our wealth and of what we feel proud of.”
Following the theft, MUVI stated in a social media post that it has temporarily closed its doors to the public, but will announce a reopening date as soon as possible.
“The MUVI's pieces and collections are not just heritage: they are shared memory, part of everyone's history,” the museum wrote. “We have full confidence in the ongoing investigations and the professionalism of the State Security Forces.”
Queen Nazli’s diamond necklace
That same day, two unmasked men smashed a display case at Vienna's Museum of Applied Arts (MAK) and stolen a diamond necklace worth over $4 million.
It had been featured at the MAK as part of an exhibition titled “GLANZSTÜCKE: Van Cleef & Arpels High Jewelry × Masterpieces from the MAK Collection.”
According to Austrian state broadcaster ORT, the unmasked thieves bought tickets to the exhibit prior to the robbery and commited the theft during the museum’s opening hours.
Police added that the two then “fled with the piece of jewelry in an unknown direction.”
Photographs and CCTV footage of the suspects have been shared by police, and has since been added to INTERPOL’s Stolen Works of Art database.
The museum noted in an August statement that it would not be sharing information regarding the investigation into the robbery.
Belonging once to Queen Nazli of Egypt (1913-1936), the second wife of King Fuad I, the necklace is adorned with 673 diamonds and weighs about 200 carats.
It, and a matching tiara, had been commissioned by Nazli for the wedding of her daughter Fawzia to, the at the time Iranian Crown Prince and later Shah, Mohammed Reza Pahlavi.
Reuters contributed to this report.

Australia jails man who compiled reports for China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:42 UTC
01:37:42 KST

An Australian man convicted of reckless foreign interference for compiling reports for Chinese intelligence was yesterday sentenced to more than three years in jail by a Sydney court.
Marketing executive Alexander Csergo, 58, was arrested in Sydney by Australian police in 2023, shortly after he returned from living in Shanghai.
He was accused of accepting cash from Chinese intelligence agents to write reports on topics including Australia’s AUKUS nuclear submarine partnership with the US and the UK, and critical minerals.
Photo: Bianca De Marchi, AAP Image via AP
Sydney’s district court sentenced Csergo to three years and six months in jail, eligible for parole from next month, a court official said.
“Foreign interference is an assault on Australian sovereignty,” Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Director-General of Security Mike Burgess said, responding to the sentencing.
“In this case, the spies wanted the Australian to target individuals in Australia’s intelligence community, Prime Minister’s Office, defense sector, judiciary and think tanks,” he added.
Csergo is the second person to be convicted under foreign interference laws introduced in 2018 to criminalize activity that helps a foreign power interfere with Australia’s sovereignty or national interest.
He is the first person sentenced for reckless foreign interference.
The court heard that Csergo had met two suspected Chinese agents, known to him as Ken and Evelyn, in Shanghai after they made contact on professional networking platform LinkedIn.
He met the pair in empty cafes in Shanghai, where he suspected the venues had been cleared for their meetings.
He returned to Australia in 2023 with a “shopping list” of topics Ken wanted information collected on.
The police discovered the list three weeks after Csergo arrived in Australia to live with his family at Bondi Beach.
The court heard that Csergo exchanged thousands of WeChat messages with the pair between 2021 and 2023, and accepted cash in envelopes.
Csergo, found guilty by the court in March, had said that much of the information in the reports was publicly available.
The Australian Federal Police Assistant Commissioner Cyber and Special Investigations Sandra Booth said the best defense against foreign interference was community awareness.
“Often foreign powers will use covert, deceptive or coercive activities to influence political processes, harm national security or threaten communities,” she said.

PAINSTAKING PROCESS: Ice makers freeze water for up to 72 hours, replace tainted water with a fresh batch once freezing begins, and are constantly stirring In the historic Japanese city of Kanazawa, craftsmen painstakingly shape and slice blocks of ice destined to chill negronis in some of the world’s trendiest bars. The men work for Kuramoto Ice, a century-old company in Ishikawa on the Sea of Japan coast and one of dozens of Japanese firms producing ultra-clear, premium ice. Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:39 UTC
01:37:39 KST

The Executive Yuan yesterday approved expanded subsidies for residents of long-term care facilities, allocating NT$16.62 billion (US$526.82 million) to the plan expected to benefit about 105,000 people.
Under the new plan, the maximum monthly subsidy for people with moderate to severe disabilities residing in long-term care facilities would rise from NT$10,000 to NT$15,000, while the annual cap would increase from NT$120,000 to NT$180,000, the Cabinet said.
The program would accept applications under the updated scheme from Monday next week, with the subsidy adjustments applying retroactively from Jan. 1, it said.
Photo: CNA
The central government also plans to provide a monthly accommodation subsidy of NT$5,000 for people with moderate to severe physical or mental disabilities living in specialized disability care facilities, the Cabinet said.
Previously, eligibility for the program was assessed on an annual basis, with beneficiaries required to stay in a facility for more than 180 days to receive a full year’s subsidy. Those who stayed for fewer than 180 days were not eligible.
Under the revised scheme, subsidies would be calculated monthly, with applicants eligible for one month’s subsidy if they reside in a facility for at least half of the calendar days in a given month, the Cabinet said.
Eligible facilities include nursing homes, psychiatric nursing homes, senior welfare institutions, disability welfare institutions, veterans’ homes and long-term care service facilities.
The government would also shorten reimbursement times by increasing the disbursement schedule to twice a year, the Cabinet said.
Application, review and disbursement procedures have been streamlined to ensure faster and more stable payments, Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) said.
The Ministry of Health and Welfare and local governments have been instructed to complete administrative preparations as soon as possible, and step up public outreach to ensure applications and reviews proceed smoothly and subsidies can be disbursed at the earliest opportunity, he said.
Taiwan has become a “super-aged” society, with the number of people aged 65 or older exceeding 4.77 million as of the end of July, accounting for 20.5 percent of the population, Cho said.
Of those 4.77 million, 16.47 percent have disabilities and 7.99 percent have dementia, Deputy Minister of Health and Welfare Lu Chien-te (呂建德) said.
To meet rapidly growing long-term care needs, the government this year launched the Long-Term Care 3.0 program, investing NT$115.3 billion in its first year, Cho said.
The program aims to enhance coordination between medical and care services, while expanding support for people with moderate to severe disabilities and their families, he said.
The health ministry’s revised scheme would focus on reducing financial burdens and streamlining administrative procedures, he added.

Cabinet approves draft for NT$100bn MSME program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:39 UTC
01:37:39 KST

The Executive Yuan yesterday approved a draft proposal for an eight-year, NT$100 billion (US$3.17 billion) program to support the development of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) through expanded tax breaks, relaxed investment thresholds and targeted loans.
More than 4,000 MSMEs are expected to benefit from the initiative, generating more than NT$50 billion in investment, the Ministry of Economic Affairs said.
A notice to commence a period of public comments for the proposal was announced yesterday, with public hearings to be held to gather feedback from business owners.
Photo: Chung Li-hua, Taipei Times
It is expected to be submitted to the Executive Yuan for approval next month before being forwarded to the legislature for review.
According to the government’s White Paper on Small and Medium Enterprises last year, Taiwan has 1.716 million MSMEs, accounting for 98.9 percent of all businesses and employing nearly 80 percent of the workforce, or about 9.194 million people.
The draft plans to extend government assistance to 1.029 million microbusinesses, including sole proprietorships and partnerships, which account for about 60 percent of all businesses.
The program would also cover commercial districts, public markets, local specialty industries, agricultural enterprises, tourism businesses and start-ups.
It includes measures to improve the business environment in 353 commercial districts and 1,030 public markets.
A chapter dedicated to start-up development discussed encouraging large corporations and venture capital firms to nurture start-ups, and creating an environment for innovation and experimentation. Larger companies would be encouraged to help MSMEs connect with high-tech supply chains and digital platforms.
For businesses with fewer than 30 employees, the government would provide simplified loan applications, project-based loans and short-term interest subsidies, while expanding credit guarantee coverage.
A Small and Medium Enterprise Credit Guarantee Fund would also increase its risk coverage to help smaller businesses that lack substantial collateral to obtain financing for transformation.
Businesses could obtain additional credit guarantee coverage if funds are used to raise employee wages, the ministry said.
The program would significantly expand tax incentives for equipment investment, and research and development (R&D), and lower the minimum investment required to qualify for tax credits on smart machinery, artificial intelligence, digital transformation and net zero equipment from NT$1 million to NT$250,000, under the Industrial Innovation Act (產業創新條例).
Digital management systems needed by service businesses and outsourced R&D spending would also qualify for the first time, while the R&D tax credit rate would rise to 20 percent.
Tax incentives for hiring would be expanded, with the eligible age range widened from 24 or younger and 65 or older to 29 or younger and 55 or older.
The additional tax deduction for wage increases would rise from 175 to 200 percent.

2026-09-10
16:37:37 UTC

The death toll from a fire that erupted yesterday on a foreign-flagged cargo ship docked in a Chinese port has risen to 25, including five people who had been listed as missing, state media said.
The bulk carrier, moored in the eastern shipping hub of Qingdao, had 42 people on board when the fire broke out, state broadcaster China Central Television (CCTV) reported.
Seventeen of those were evacuated, including five who were injured.
Photo: Qingdaowolin via AP
However, by yesterday evening “all 25 missing persons had been found, none showing signs of life,” CCTV said.
“The open flames were extinguished” by about 2:30pm, it said.
Xinhua news agency said earlier that the fire broke out at about 11:15am during the ship’s port call for maintenance, without specifying the cause of the fire.
A witness from a neighboring residential compound said he saw thick smoke coming from the ship, but did not hear an explosion.
“I saw the smoke from the ship by chance, but there was no visible fire,” he said. “I didn’t hear an explosion or smell anything.”
Xinhua shared a video of the scene showing a large ship called the Ocean Melody docked at Beihai Shipbuilding Co (中國船舶集團青島北海造船), with dozens of rescuers swarming its decks and entering the vessel.
Several fire trucks and ambulances were stationed on the dock in front of the ship.
Ocean Melody is a 190m-long bulk carrier sailing under the Liberian flag, according to the vessel-tracking Web site MarineTraffic, which located the ship as moored in Qingdao.
The Beihai Shipbuilding yard operates as a subsidiary of China State Shipbuilding Corp (中國船舶集團).
Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) “stressed the need to ... strictly hold those responsible to account,” Xinhua reported.
“All regions and relevant departments must draw profound lessons from this incident, thoroughly investigate and rectify all types of fire hazards,” Xi said.
There have been several major industrial accidents in China over the past year, where safety regulations are often lax.
An explosion and ensuing fire at a shipyard in China’s Fujian Province last month killed one fire and rescue worker and injured 12 others, state media reported.
China launched a campaign against fire hazards in high-rise buildings in November last year after a huge blaze engulfed several residential tower blocks in Hong Kong, killing 168 people.
A blast at a fireworks factory in central China killed 37 people in May, marking one of the nation’s deadliest industrial accidents in years.
A fire in a shoe factory in Fujian in July killed at least 28 people.

Japanese baseball legend Isao Harimoto, who survived the atomic bombing of Hiroshima and became the first player from his country to reach 3,000 hits, has died aged 86, reports said yesterday. Born to Korean parents in Japan, Harimoto learned to play left-handed when an accident at the age of four left him with severe burns and limited mobility in his right hand. Building beyond Bilingual 2030
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:37 UTC
01:37:37 KST

Recent discussions about Bilingual 2030 have produced no shortage of disagreement. Educators do not always agree about education. More interesting is what happens when we look beyond those disagreements and consider what each perspective adds to the conversation.
Nigel Daly (“Taiwan wants bilingual, AI-ready graduates — but tests for yesteryear,” June 3, page 12) questioned whether assessment reflects the capabilities students increasingly need. Jye Smallwood (“Basic Misunderstanding of EMI,” Aug. 9, page 8) examined the pedagogical demands of English-medium instruction. Gerhard Erasmus (“Bilingual 2030: time’s up for opinions,” Sept. 5, page 8) emphasized rigorous research, stronger evidence and the need to adjust policy as that evidence emerges. My own contributions have focused on classroom experience and the connections between learning, assessment and teacher development.
Taken together, these perspectives begin to look less like competing diagnoses and more like different parts of the same education system.
Assessment matters, because what measure inevitably influences what students and teachers prioritize. As artificial intelligence (AI) changes the value of information retrieval and routine language production, greater attention to communication, judgement and the ability to use knowledge becomes increasingly important. Assessment can help signal those priorities while providing evidence of whether students are developing them.
The discussion around English as a medium of instruction (EMI) brings us closer to what happens when educational ambitions reach classrooms. Teaching academic content using English requires more than subject expertise or English-language proficiency. Teachers also need the pedagogical skills to make complex ideas accessible, check understanding and create opportunities for students to engage meaningfully with language and content.
If we expect classroom practice to evolve, teachers need opportunities to develop alongside the expectations placed upon them. Professional development can connect broader education goals with the daily decisions teachers make about tasks, interaction, feedback and learning.
Classroom experience and research provide evidence. Some of it can inform immediate adjustments; other patterns require systematic study over time. Evidence becomes most valuable when it can travel through the system and help inform what happens next.
These elements can reinforce one another. Stronger assessment can provide better information about learning. Teacher development can help educators respond to that information. Better-prepared teachers can create richer learning experiences. Classroom experience and research can then reveal where further development or adjustment might help.
An education system cannot communicate in only one direction. Policy travels from ministries toward schools, but classroom experience must also travel back through the system. Researchers, teachers, students, schools and policymakers each see something that others might not.
This raises a larger question about Bilingual 2030 itself. Governments need deadlines. Education needs direction.
The year 2030 is a useful milestone for setting goals, focusing investment and evaluating progress, but learning would continue long after it passes. A child entering elementary school today would still be in the education system after 2030. A teacher beginning a career now might still be teaching in the 2050s. AI, internationalization and changing workplaces would continue reshaping how English is learned and used.
Perhaps the most important legacy of Bilingual 2030 is not a final verdict on whether every ambition was achieved by a particular date. It is the education capacity Taiwan builds along the way.
The nation has already invested substantially in many of these areas. Bilingual 2030 has generated years of experimentation, professional development, classroom experience and public discussion from which to learn. Each contribution to that discussion helps illuminate another part of a complex picture.
None of these perspectives needs to contain the whole answer. Their value lies precisely in what becomes possible when we put them together.
The deadline 2030 would arrive soon enough. The larger opportunity is to ensure that everything Taiwan learns on the way helps its teachers, students and education system become even more capable in 2031, 2035 and beyond.
Daniel Eyrich is director of English studies at CenYing English in Keelung and has more than 15 years of experience in English-language teaching, assessment and teacher development in Taiwan.

Photo: CNA

Based on feedback he has collected, many Taipei residents also have strong feelings about the reduced number of public trash cans, which has caused inconvenience while also failing to reduce the number of rat sightings, Shen said.

August hottest month ever recorded
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:36 UTC
01:37:36 KST

The EU’s climate monitor yesterday said that last month was the hottest single month ever recorded globally, with ocean temperatures also reaching unprecedented highs as western Europe capped its warmest summer.
In response to the assessment by the Copernicus Climate Change Service, the UN said that until humanity weaned off fossil fuels, the planet would only push deeper into uncharted territory.
Copernicus observations go back to 1940, but other evidence — such as ice cores, tree rings and coral skeletons — allow scientists to place today’s climate against a much longer historical context.
Photo: AFP
“Humans haven’t seen temperatures as hot as today for, arguably, at least the last 100,000 years,” European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts strategic lead for climate Samantha Burgess said.
The center oversees Copernicus.
Global average air temperatures last month were 16.96°C, Copernicus said — surpassing by 0.01°C the previous all-time monthly record set in July 2023.
Copernicus said it considered the two months joint-highest given the narrow difference.
Scientists say that human activity — primarily the burning of coal, oil and gas — has warmed the planet by about 1.4°C since preindustrial times and increased the severity and likelihood of extreme weather.
Yet heat-trapping greenhouse gas emissions rose to new highs last year.
“The evidence is irrefutable: This is the spiraling price of humanity’s fossil fuel addiction, and the global climate crisis it is fueling,” UN Framework Convention on Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell said of the Copernicus report.
Global sea surface temperatures also set a new daily high and tied equal-hottest for August, extending a three-month streak of record-breaking warmth across the world’s oceans.
More than 90 percent of excess heat trapped by greenhouse gas emissions has been absorbed by the oceans, sparing land from warming, but at severe cost to marine life, reefs and coastal communities.
Records tumbled in overheated basins such as the Atlantic and Mediterranean and also the tropical Pacific, where the strongest El Nino weather pattern in the modern era is fast accumulating strength.
These events are marked by unusually warm Pacific waters but raise the odds of wild weather thousands of miles away, from floods in Peru to droughts in Africa and wildfires in Australia.
The warmer phase of a natural climate cycle, El Nino episodes usually deliver a spike in global temperatures already elevated by long-term background warming.
Scientists expect records to keep falling in the months ahead as this “super” El Nino approaches peak intensity around December and for next year — and maybe even this year — to become the hottest years ever observed.
“Climate change makes every El Nino hotter, and until we stop burning coal, oil, and gas these record-shattering months will simply keep on coming,” Imperial College London climate scientist Friederike Otto said.
Last month also “marked the end of western Europe’s warmest summer” that surpassed the long-standing record set in 2003, Copernicus said.
Elsewhere, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration on Wednesday said the contiguous US has endured its hottest summer on record.
Regions home to about 900 million people lived through the hottest July ever observed, an analysis of Copernicus data showed.
“We’ve had an exceptional summer — not only in Europe, but other parts of the world where records that have existed for close to a century have fallen,” Burgess said.
The climate would “continue to get more extreme unless we turn off the tap to global emissions,” she added.

The move to hold Lin I-chun (林怡君) and current chief of staff Chen Chih-huang (陳智葟) in custody came four days after Chang, indicted on corruption charges, cut off his electronic monitoring wristband and jumped bail.
The High Prosecutors’ Office said that it believes Chang had developed a Chinese spy ring, which might have operated for more than a decade, with funding from China, and that Lin and Chen were suspected of being involved.
Photo: CNA
The High Court approved prosecutors’ application to detain Lin and Chen with communications restrictions to prevent collusion, evidence tampering and flight, it said.
Investigators believe that Chang has been recruiting and organizing Chinese agents in Taiwan, and are examining the sources and destinations of funding, the office said.
Prosecutors have not determined whether Chin was complicit in spying, or knew of Chang’s role in funneling illicit funds from China, it added.
Chang allegedly had personal relationships with pro-unification and indigenous groups that had dealings with China’s Taiwan Affairs Office (TAO) and National Ethnic Affairs Commission before becoming Chin’s chief of staff in 2002, the Chinese-language Liberty Times (the Taipei Times’ sister paper) reported.
At Chin’s office, Chang was considered the person in charge of China affairs and a core member of the lawmaker’s inner circle, it said.
Chang accompanied Chin on her many visits to China, which allowed him to opportunities to contact officials linked to the TAO and commission, it said.
In 2009, Chin visited then-Chinese president Hu Jintao (胡錦濤) in Beijing to raise funds for victims of Typhoon Morakot, obtaining 20 million yuan (US$2.98 million), it said.
Chang was also intimately involved with Chin’s founding of the Taiwan Indigenous Peoples’ Multi-Ethnic Cultural Exchange Association, an organization that engaged in unofficial cross-strait interactions, it said.
Separately, Lin and Chen have also been named codefendants in an ongoing trial over Chin’s alleged embezzlement of NT$545,917 (US$17,304) from public funds allotted for legislative aides’ salaries.
The Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office in June indicted Chin and 23 people connected to her office on charges linked to alleged embezzlement, forgery, money laundering and illegal imports of COVID-19 rapid test kits from China.
Chang and Chen were among the indicted defendants.
Staffers in Chin’s office were allegedly directed to create records of non-existent aides for Chin to benefit from their payrolls, the office said in the indictment.
Prosecutors also accused Chen of defrauding the national labor insurance of NT$158,040 by falsely claiming unpaid parental leave when he was still working and receiving compensation.
Chen has confessed to that part of the charges, the office said.
Prosecutors are seeking a prison sentence of more than 16 years for Chang, who was granted bail at NT$10 million before absconding.
The court has issued a warrant for his arrest.

EDITORIAL: PIF presence step in right direction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:34 UTC
01:37:34 KST

The Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) took place from Aug. 30 to Friday last week in Palau. Unlike last year, Taiwan this time had a strong presence at the event, in a diplomatic setback to China.
While Taiwan-China tensions featured prominently at the forum, Beijing’s disruption of the meeting with its “wolf warrior” diplomacy was the focus.
Ahead of the event, the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs asked the PIF and Palau to adhere to the “one China” principle in handling Taiwan’s participation. Then, in retaliation against Ngerulmud’s decision to invite Taipei, the Chinese Ministry of Culture and Tourism warned its citizens to be wary of traveling to Palau.
Chinese Special Envoy for Pacific Island Countries Affairs Qian Bo (錢波) even said: “There will be consequences when China is unhappy.”
As Palauan President Surangel Whipps Jr had insisted on the forum’s autonomous right to invite non-member partners, Taiwan sent a large delegation, led by Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍). They were warmly welcomed during “Taiwan night.” Lin was also invited to make a rare appearance at the opening ceremony of the PIF leaders’ summit.
Taiwan and its three diplomatic allies in the region — Palau, Tuvalu and the Marshall Islands — signed a joint statement pledging to work more closely. The US also announced that it is working with Taiwan and other partners to support the development of hospitals and drinking water sampling facilities in Palau.
In another diplomatic setback for China, the leaders’ summit released a joint communique expressing concerns over Beijing firing an intercontinental ballistic missile that fell into South Pacific waters without adequate notice, saying that such tests should “ensure transparency and eliminate doubts, including by providing at least 24 hours’ notice in accordance with international practice.”
Despite these setbacks, China’s growing influence in the region cannot be overlooked. Over the past few years, Beijing has caused divisions and geopolitical rivalry in the region, testing the solidarity of Pacific island nations.
For example, the PIF’s host country last year, the Solomon Islands, barred all non-member countries from the event after Beijing pressured it to block Taipei’s participation. That risked the loss of international support for the PIF and infringed on the sovereignty of countries in the region.
Additionally, Nauru opposed the joint communique criticizing China’s missile test, while Kiribati did not attend the negotiations, which showed that the two nations’ expanding ties with Beijing is undermining the unity of Pacific island countries in safeguarding regional security and stability.
China’s deepening cooperation with Pacific island nations in policing, security and infrastructure has also alerted Western democracies that the Pacific region — which is home to strategic facilities and resources such as ports, submarine cables, fisheries, maritime surveillance, seabed minerals and military corridors — has become the front line of strategic jockeying in the Indo-Pacific region.
During the PIF, the US in a statement pledged its commitment to the security and prosperity of Pacific island nations. US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau also announced more than US$150 million in funding to support nations in the region.
Meanwhile, Australia pledged a A$600 million (US$432.54 million) package to help Pacific island nations combat transnational drug trafficking, and signed defense and cooperation agreements with countries in the region to limit China’s influence.
As for Taiwan, the PIF this year showed that Taipei’s status as “development partner” since 1993 remained unchanged, and it is set to be included in next year’s forum in New Zealand. China would likely ramp up efforts to pressure nations into obstructing Taiwan’s international participation.
As most nations grapple with more imminent threats such as rising sea levels, extreme weather, inadequate healthcare and fragile national finances, Taiwan should use its soft power and help Pacific island countries achieve sustainable development goals, and establish a replicable and scalable model of cooperation that could solidify more mutually beneficial relations in the region.
Taiwan cannot compete with China in terms of financial diplomacy or military coercion. Taipei should instead offer help that would not cause small countries to lose autonomy, make allies feel the value of cooperation and show the world that Taiwan could be a partner in Pacific governance.

Army holds first voluntary marksmanship program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:32 UTC
01:37:32 KST

The army’s first voluntary live-fire shooting program for reservists, with newly relaxed eligibility rules, took place in Taichung on Monday, allowing those who were discharged more than a decade ago to refresh their combat skills with T91 assault rifles.
The Taichung Reserve Command held the exercise amid Taiwan’s efforts to incorporate reserve infantry brigades in its war plans.
The drill was among the first to be held after the Ministry of National Defense lifted a restriction limiting participation in marksmanship refresher training to soldiers who left the service less than 12 years ago.
Photo: CNA
A reporter said 35 former service members took part in the target practice at Chenggong Ling (成功嶺) military training camp.
The participants included former draftees and retired professional soldiers, with many of the latter wearing their old helmets, uniforms, boots and other accoutrements.
Of the participants, 10 were former soldiers who had served more than 12 years ago, including one man whose service dated to two decades ago. Two were retired professional soldiers and some were former conscripts.
The reservists were required to hand over their mobile devices before donning current-issue helmets, body armor with ballistic plate inserts and T91 rifles.
The marksmanship exercise consisted of two parts — a virtual reality training component and a live-fire component — to ease them into weapons handling.
A command sergeant major of a Taichung-based reserve brigade walked the reservists through the design and handling of the unfamiliar rifles in the virtual reality training facility.
They simulated shooting in prone, half-kneel and standing positions for realistic training.
The senior non-commissioned officer supervised the live-fire component of the exercise, during which the reservists zeroed their rifles at 25m, then fired 30 rounds loaded in three magazines at a 175m silhouette target.
The reservists also fired three rounds each in the prone, half-kneel and standing positions behind a barricade at a 175m silhouette target.
Loading only a few rounds in each rifle magazine helped the trainee practice reloading magazines as they shoot, a military spokesperson said.
A new spotting scope enabled the instructor and trainee to observe hits and misses without inspecting the target up close, which would have taken more time than necessary, they said.
Casing catchers were installed on the rifles to protect instructors and trainees on the range, allowing them to focus on shooting instead of dodging hot empty shells, the spokesperson said.
A reservist in his late 40s said shooting a T91 “felt like entering in a new age,” as his issued weapons were the much older T57 and T65K.

AI and industrial sector gap widens: ratings firm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:32 UTC
01:37:32 KST

Taiwan’s artificial intelligence (AI) boom is widening the divide across its industrial economy, with technology companies benefiting from surging global investment while steel and petrochemical producers struggle with Chinese overcapacity, geopolitical risks and growing trade barriers, Taiwan Ratings Corp (中華信評) said on Wednesday.
AI has become the biggest source of revenue for Taiwan’s technology hardware companies, with continued capital spending by US cloud-service providers driving growth across the supply chain, the ratings agency said.
The gains are spreading beyond semiconductor and electronics manufacturers to power supplies, substrates and passive components, creating a broader technology investment cycle, it said.
Photo: Wu Hsin-tien, Taipei Times
“AI has become the most important revenue source for Taiwan’s technology hardware companies,” Taiwan Ratings chief analyst Raymond Hsu (許智清) told a news conference in Taipei.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電), Hon Hai Precision Industry Co (鴻海), Delta Electronics Inc (台達電) and Unimicron Technology Corp (欣興) have received ratings outlook upgrades on expectations of AI-related revenue growth, he said.
The boom is also benefiting Yageo Corp (國巨), the world’s third-largest multilayer ceramic capacitor supplier, Taiwan Ratings deputy chief analyst Anne Kuo (郭彥煒) said.
Yageo’s business has accelerated over the past two or three quarters as demand rises for high-end passive components used in AI applications, while supply constraints have also pushed up prices for lower-end products, Kuo said.
Strong AI demand has helped manufacturers absorb higher costs from building factories in the US and Southeast Asia, Kuo said.
At the same time, tight supply in the AI ecosystem has given companies pricing power to pass much of the increase on to customers, she added.
The technology sector could remain resilient even if AI investment slows, Taiwan Ratings said.
Under a stress scenario in which cloud AI revenue falls 50 percent, earnings margins decline 30 percent and cash-conversion cycles lengthen 10 percent, technology companies would still maintain relatively solid earnings, Hsu said.
The outlook is weaker for traditional industries, the agency said.
Taiwan’s steel and petrochemical producers are facing earnings below previous cyclical troughs as Chinese overcapacity weighs on prices and margins, it said.
Rising trade barriers aimed at containing Chinese exports are adding pressure to Taiwan’s export-dependent producers, while geopolitical tensions could raise energy costs and squeeze margins, Taiwan Ratings analyst Irene Lai (賴冠?) said.
Companies with greater exposure to specialty chemicals, vertical integration and diversified businesses are better positioned to weather the downturn, Lai said.
Steelmakers face similar challenges, she said. Although demand is growing in Southeast Asia, new capacity is coming online, limiting the prospect of meaningful improvement in global supply and demand, she added.

Street acrobats entertain motorists stuck in the Kenyan capital’s notorious traffic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:31 UTC
01:37:31 KST

As the light turns red at a busy intersection in the Kenyan capital, a young man costumed in leopard print emerges into the street to perform somersaults. He is joined by five others, dressed similarly, as they execute a combination of acrobatic stunts.
One of them, juggling woven hats, breaks away and approaches the drivers of vehicles that have come to a halt. He’s hoping for generous tips as he presents his hat to driver after driver while his mates continue their routine. The group breaks away as soon as the traffic lights turn green.
Nairobi’s street acrobats first began appearing in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic, and they have since become normalized at traffic stops in and around the city, with acrobats taking advantage of gridlocks to perform in exchange for cash tips. It is how they earn a living.
Photo: AP
Mohammed Nyale, 22, said he started doing acrobatics hoping for a life-changing occupation.
“I have always loved acrobatics since I started performing at 15 years old,” he said.
He and others left their homes on the Kenyan coast with dreams of on-stage careers and sold-out theaters, but they have so far settled for the streets, performing their stunts for motorists in Nairobi’s never-ending traffic.
Nyale’s group gathers in the early mornings in an abandoned field in Nairobi’s impoverished neighborhood of Kawangware to rehearse their routines. Next, they move into the streets as traffic starts to build up during the morning rush hour.
“We say a prayer before changing into our costumes,” Nyale said.
They usually perform until noon, taking turns to collect tips from motorists. The amounts given tend to be small, usually no more than 50 shillings (about 40 US cents). Because many Kenyans keep money in mobile wallets, the acrobats also hand out slips of paper with their phone numbers to which tips can be sent.
On a good day they might each earn roughly US$6, enough to look after their basic needs, though on some days they make more.
That is equal to the daily wage of most casual laborers in construction or agriculture in a country where unemployment is widespread. The youth unemployment rate stood between 4.9 percent and 9.9 percent in 2024, according to figures from the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics.
Earning money from street performances “is what enables us to live in Nairobi because we moved here from quite far and no one is helping us to pay rent,” Nyale said.
They have rivals. Acrobatic troupes have materialized in other parts of the city. Across town, a group including 28-year-old Jackson Okoth entertained motorists along Lang’ata Road.
“There are no opportunities for us that we can go to, so we like it when we are here because it keeps us busy and it keeps us fit also,” Okoth said. “Instead of staying at home and doing reckless things, we decided to come here and perform for motorists and pedestrians.”
Okoth dreams of playing in a professional circus and touring the world.
“I am still on my way, I am still trying, I am still working hard so that one day things might go well and I may find myself in Europe performing in a circus show,” he said.
Some motorists see the acrobats as a nuisance. Others welcome the distraction.
“They are a source of entertainment here on the road. They entertain us and we feel good,” said Geoffrey Kioi, a Nairobi entrepreneur who regularly gives tips to the acrobats. “They are young people. They need to hustle. They are like my sons.”

Unknown Publisher

National Tsing Hua University (NTHU) president John Kao (高為元) yesterday apologized for applying to become chancellor of a US university just three days after being confirmed for a second term at the Taiwanese institution in May, vowing to donate his monthly salary every May for the remainder of his term to refurbish student dormitories and make amends.
Kao was not offered the position at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, despite being shortlisted with two other candidates.
He apologized over the incident in front of about 300 faculty members and students attending an explanatory session on campus, but it drew mixed reactions.
Photo: Hung Mei-hsiu, Taipei Times
Lin Burn-jeng (林本堅), dean of the Semiconductor Research College, and Huang Yi-long (黃一農), a professor of history, said that what Kao did was a matter of trust and honesty, which are now in question.
As the issue could affect NTHU’s operations, its administrators should reconsider Kao’s qualifications for the post so that the university can move forward from the incident, Lin and Huang said.
Former NTHU president Tai Nyan-hwa (戴念華) and other professors and alumni defended Kao and affirmed his contributions to the university during his first term, saying that his job search in the US was a private matter.
Whether Kao is honest and trustworthy should be judged by the way he handles NTHU affairs, rather than how he conducts personal matters, they said.
NTHU chief secretary Chan Hung-lin (詹鴻霖) and vice president Lu Ping-chiang (呂平江) said that the university would convene supervisory board and university council meetings to determine whether Kao should continue serving as president.
The next university council meeting is scheduled for Oct. 20.
Kao’s application for the position in the US sparked criticism following a report by the Liberty Times (sister paper of the Taipei Times) in July.
Prior to yesterday’s session, Kao issued a letter last month, in which he said that he was deeply sorry for the inconvenience and unease caused by the news of his job hunting in the US and the public discussion of the matter.
“Recruitment and headhunting are common in higher education and in the business sector. However, it is rare for a university overseas to seek out a sitting university president in Taiwan. When such an opportunity arose, it did pique my curiosity. This reflected my insufficient understanding of the differences between workplace cultures in the East and the West,” he said in the letter.
In his speech yesterday, Kao again apologized, saying that he had experienced the most difficult time in his academic career in the past month.
He said that his failure to think matters through carefully has hurt those who believe in him and made the university the subject of gossip.
He let people in the NTHU community down by overlooking the distinctiveness of his duty as president and by beginning to seek other career possibilities during just the initial stage of the second term, he said.
His visit to the Manoa campus was to learn more about the US university’s expectations of him and vice versa, he said, adding that there was no further development afterward, nor did the UH Manoa hold a final vote on whether he should be recruited.
“NTHU did not know I would be given a job offer from another university when they voted to confirm my second term,” Kao said. “I cannot simply ask for your understanding and forgiveness with excuses of curiosity and cultural differences. My previous response to this incident was short and disappointing. This university is where people have dreams and aspirations, and one cannot simply come and go as they please.”
He would fully cooperate with the NTHU investigation, he added.

Spain approves citizenship for Sahrawis born under Spanish rule

Spain approves citizenship for Sahrawis born under Spanish rule
MADRID, Sept 10 - Spain's lower house voted on Thursday to grant citizenship to Sahrawis born when Madrid administered the North African territory of Western Sahara as a colony, a move that could inflame delicate relations with Morocco.
The legislation, which a statement from parliament said was approved with 168 votes in favour, 31 against and 145 abstentions, would also allow descendants of those granted citizenship to acquire it.
Some 70,000 to 110,000 Sahrawis could be eligible for Spanish citizenship, according to local media.
Spain's ruling Socialist Party and its junior left-wing partner Sumar, which filed the initiative, were among those who supported the bill, while the opposition conservative People's Party abstained and far-right Vox voted against it.
"With the adoption of this legislation, we are restoring – and I emphasise, restoring – the Spanish national identity card to those Sahrawis who once held it and from whom this state took it away," said Tesh Sidi of the leftist Sumar coalition, the first woman of Sahrawi origin to serve in parliament.
TENSIONS WITH MOROCCO
Tensions have grown between Spain and Morocco following the mass arrival of at least 70,000 migrants in Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta in July.
Spain controlled Western Sahara under various administrative arrangements from 1884 until 1976. Morocco claims sovereignty over Western Sahara and began asserting control over the territory after Spanish rule ended.
The Algerian-backed Polisario Front independence movement seeks recognition of an independent state called the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic.
Many Sahrawis live in refugee camps in Tindouf, Algeria, or elsewhere abroad, while others remain in Western Sahara.
Spain had supported a referendum in the territory — in line with United Nations resolutions — until Sanchez's government reversed course in 2022 and backed Morocco's position.
Tensions eased somewhat after that shift, with Madrid describing Rabat's autonomy proposal for Western Sahara as "serious, credible and realistic". REUTERS
