Russia cut oil production by 160,000 bpd month-on-month in August — OPEC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:17:25 UTC
01:17:25 KST

MOSCOW, September 10. /TASS/. In August 2026, Russia reduced its oil production by 160,000 barrels per day (bpd) month-on-month to 8.718 million bpd, according to a report by the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC).
In August, Russia's quota under the OPEC+ deal stood at 9.887 million bpd, including all voluntary restrictions. Thus, Russia's oil production for the month was 1.169 million bpd below the quota (excluding the compensation schedule).
Currently, Russian oil production is limited by the OPEC+ agreement. From the beginning of 2024 through March 2025, Russia's baseline production quota, including voluntary restrictions, was 8.978 million bpd. This figure did not account for obligations to compensate for overproduction during the period of voluntary cuts.
Starting in April 2025, Russia began increasing production in accordance with the OPEC+ plan, with output rising gradually month by month. In September 2025 – a year ahead of schedule – OPEC+ nations completed the phase-out of voluntary cuts totaling 2.2 million bpd and began phasing out the 1.65 million bpd cut, bringing the curtailed volumes back to the market.

Pro-Israel rally outside Downing Street calls to ‘Sanction Terror Not Judea and Samaria’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:17:08 UTC
01:17:08 KST

Demonstrators gathered outside 10 Downing Street on Wednesday evening to protest the British government’s recent policy measures regarding Israel.
The rally, titled Sanction Terror, Not Judea and Samaria,” was organized by Stop the Hate UK, a Jewish-led direct action campaign group, to protest the British government’s announcement of sanctions targeting Israeli settlements.
The rally drew activists who displayed banners and signs reading “Sanction terror, not Judea and Samaria” and “Israel is an ally, not an enemy.” Participants criticized the government following announcements of restrictions targeting Israeli settlements.
Stop the Hate UK founder and CEO Itai Galmudy addressed the demonstrators, focusing heavily on what he termed the double standards applied to the Jewish state. Galmudy questioned why the British government deploys sweeping regional trade bans and blanket economic measures against Israel while maintaining bilateral trade frameworks and economic agreements with other conflict-ridden countries.
Pointing to nations such as Yemen, where large swaths of land are dominated by the Houthis, and southern Lebanon, where Hezbollah exerts immense pressure, Galmudy noted that Britain handles those regions with targeted responses rather than sweeping economic isolation.
“What makes those measures so deeply frustrating is the undeniable double standard. Where is the same sweeping economic approach when it comes to other conflict zones, rife with terror?” Galmudy asked the crowd, asserting that this singles out Israel, holding it to a standard no other country faces, and risks alienating key democratic allies.
Mark Birbeck, founder of the grassroots campaign Our Fight, a group challenging British antisemitism, took to the microphone to warn about the rising prevalence of anti-Israel sentiment, explaining that leaders often search for a moral framework to fill a void and that “the framework that they are reaching out for now is anti-Israel.”
Birbeck: Antisemitic ideology 'made its way into parliament'
Birbeck said that this ideology has “made its way into Number 10 and it’s made its way into parliament,” adding that “the technocrats have become dangerous because they are now the instigators and the propagators of the most dangerous idea in British politics now, that Israel is the source of the world’s problems, and that to be virtuous and to be good and to be moral, you need to be against Israel.”
Birbeck further emphasized the severity of the shift, telling the crowd, “this is a dark, dark time that’s coming, and we need to rally our forces; we need to find those people who understand the seriousness of what we are facing because this anti-Israel prejudice, this anti-Israel bigotry, is now becoming an ideology.”
Comedian Josh Howie also spoke at the demonstration, delivering a sharp critique of the government’s motives and policy decisions.
He argued that the boycott of goods from Judea and Samaria would “achieve nothing,” noting that it fails to bring about peace, threatens thousands of Palestinian jobs, and pushes a two-state solution further away.
Howie contended that the policy served as a political crusade for votes rather than a moral stance, warning attendees, “This is no moral crusade for peace; this is a crusade for votes from the far-left and Muslims.”
Reform UK Deputy Leader Richard Tice also attended and addressed the crowd, sharply criticizing the Labour government over the policy shifts.
Tice: Labour policy shifts a 'grave mistake'
Tice highlighted the immediate hostility faced on the streets during the gathering, pointing out that cyclists had just gone past and spat at the demonstrators. He argued that the government’s actions effectively embolden antisemites and damage key strategic relationships with allies such as the United States and Israel, describing the measures as a grave mistake.”
“I think the foreign secretary is playing purpose to this. He is making a grave mistake that has damaged international relations, that has frankly damaged the respect and trust that everybody in Israel feels about the United Kingdom,” Tice said.
Concluding his remarks, Tice said he hoped a general election would take place within the next three years, bringing the moment when the prime minister and the foreign secretary are punished for their grave and grievous judgments.

The critics saw hassidim, but the White House saw American Jewish leaders - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:17:05 UTC
01:17:05 KST

Last Thursday, for the first time since 1979, a delegation of hassidic leaders came to the White House to meet the president of the United States.
They spent an hour with senior officials on the needs of their communities, then half an hour with US President Donald Trump himself. Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio dropped in unannounced.
The grand rabbis of Satmar, Bobov, and Vizhnitz came, along with a representative of Skver and the head of Beth Midrash Govoha, the great yeshiva of Lakewood, New Jersey. The community had come to Washington to talk about conditions of federal prisons, the future of Maimonides Medical Center in Brooklyn, and housing assistance for large families.
On that last point the vice president, who walked over after his press briefing, had some standing. Hassidim, he joked, are the only people with bigger families than his. Rabbi Teitelbaum led the delegation in the blessing for kings - the prayer Jews have said over emperors and presidents for centuries - and left the president a leather-bound copy.
Before the rabbis had even arrived, the meeting was being argued over online. Satmar teaches that a Jewish state must wait for the Messiah. Some of the president's own supporters said men who believe that had no business standing next to him.
As antisemitism abounds, White House opens its door to Jews
The argument, however loud, missed the point. Most Americans cannot tell a Satmar hasid from a Bobov one. What they saw was simpler and far more important. A week before Rosh Hashanah, the most powerful man in the world sat with a room full of bearded men in long coats and black hats - visibly and unmistakably Jewish - and gave them his attention.
We live in a moment when a young couple leaving a Jewish museum in Washington can be shot dead on the sidewalk and marchers for the hostages can be set on fire in Colorado. When the regime in Tehran chants death to America and death to Israel in the same breath, and antisemitism rises here and abroad. When synagogues have a budget for armed guards. When a man in a fur hat and long black coat thinks twice before walking home alone. Against all that, the door to the Oval Office opened. America and the world saw it open, and saw a president who cares.
At a briefing just before he joined the rabbis, the vice president said you can disagree with someone and still be friends, because the republic depends on people of different views being able to talk to one another. A plain idea, and an American one.
Trump knows he must serve all Jewish communities
The fight over who belonged in that room is a family fight, and it is ours to have. No single White House meeting will settle it. A president who grasps that he serves the whole family, including the branch that argues with the rest, has understood something about this country.
Consider what the delegation came to discuss: prisons, housing, a hospital. Ordinary matters, brought by citizens to their government. For decades, Washington treated hassidic communities as a curiosity when it noticed them at all. On Thursday they were treated as constituents. That is the whole purpose of the White House Faith Office, and of the decision to seat the administration's liaison to the Jewish community inside it for the first time. That liaison spent months arranging Thursday’s visit.
The record behind the picture is real. This president has treated antisemitism on college campuses as something to confront rather than manage. He has defended religious schools and the parents who choose them. He has made the safety of Jews a matter of federal policy. He won a larger share of the Jewish vote than any Republican since 1988, and hassidic precincts voted for him nearly as one. The rabbis in the Oval Office thanked him for all of it. So do I. And the vice president deserves his own thanks for walking in when he could have walked past.
One more thing happened on Thursday. The two Satmar rebbes are brothers who lead rival factions and have been estranged for two decades, since their father’s death in 2006. They shook hands and spoke face to face. One congratulated the other on a grandson’s engagement. The visit took more than a year to arrange, and it landed in the days before Rosh Hashanah, when Jews wish one another a happy, healthy and sweet new year and set about repairing what is broken between people. That two brothers reconciled in the room where world leaders meet and make their hardest decisions fits the season’s spirit.
It also suggests a wish for the year ahead. Wherever we live, in Israel or America, however we vote, however we pray, we are one people. We can disagree, and we will, but we will still be able to wish each other a Shana tova.
The writer is the former chairman of the United States Commission for the Preservation of America’s Heritage Abroad.

====================================================================================================

Russians about Goethe-Institut: 'Hostage to politics'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:17:00 UTC
01:17:00 KST

Russians about Goethe-Institut: 'Hostage to politics'
September 10, 2026
Germany's Goethe-Institut will close all Russian branches by September 13 amid one of the worst spats in the history of relations between Russia and Germany.
The Russian foreign ministry ordered the closure of the German cultural centers in Moscow, St. Petersburg and Novosibirsk in response to Berlin's reaction to the attempteddrone attackat Leipzig airport in early August. The German authorities blamed Moscow for organizing the attack and announced sanctions. They include closing the Russian culture and education center in Berlin, known as the Russian House, and the Russian Consulate General in Bonn, as well tightening visa restrictions for Russian citizens.
"All employees must cease their work in Russia as of September 13, 2026," Secretary General of the Goethe-Institut Gitte Zschoch said in a statement. "No more books can be borrowed from our libraries, and no further training can be offered. German language teachers are losing an important source of professional training and support. For people in Russia, this further restricts access to the German language, culture and reliable information from and about Germany."
DW asked its users in Russia to share how the closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect them personally. The responses received do not constitute a representative survey. All users shared their stories on conditions of anonymity. Russian authorities labeled DW an "undesirable organization" making every cooperation with the media company a criminal offense.
'We'll have to travel to another country' for German exams
Many DW readers fear that, after the closure of the Goethe-Institut branches, they or their relatives will no longer be able to take exams in Russia for internationally recognized German language certificates.
Some readers pointed out that closing the Goethe-Institut in Russia will hit ethnic Germans willing to relocate back to Germany, or late repatriates, especially hard.
"I no longer live in Russia, having emigrated as a late repatriate, but my parents are still in Russia and were planning to take exams at the Goethe-Institut this fall or winter before submitting their resettlement documents. It looks like they'll have to take the exams in another country, which means additional stress and expenses for them," one reader said.
DW also received responses from parents whose children are learning German and plan to continue their education in Germany.
"My son attends a German school, and now we won't be able to take the exam in Russia. We'll have to travel to another country," one message said.
It remains unclear whether exams, language courses and educational programs will continue in Russia in another format or through partner organizations. Several readers expressed hope that at least some services will remain available online.
Goethe-Institute closures hit teachers hard
The closure of the institute will affect not only those planning to move to Germany or enroll at a German university. A German language teacher from the Moscow region told DW that her school had cooperated with the Goethe-Institut for more than 15 years.
"This partnership was one of the most important pillars of our work. The institute supported us with high-quality teaching materials and provided modern books and publications about life in Germany, helping us make lessons engaging and relevant. Our students attended additional courses, and many successfully passed the Goethe certificate exams," she wrote.
"I teach German and can't find a job in Russia," another teacher told DW.
"It's terrible. I'm a German teacher, and I feel professionally stranded and lost," a third wrote.
Despite the restrictions imposed since the beginning of Russia's war in Ukraine in 2022, demand for the institute's services remained high. According to the Goethe-Institut, around 10,000 people studied German through its programs and partnerships in 2025. Before 2023, that number used to stand at around 16,000 people. The institute administered roughly 22,000 exams, and its libraries were visited by 6,700 people in 2025.
'Culture has become a hostage to political decisions'
Many readers perceive what is happening as another stage in the destruction of ties between Russia and Germany.
"We would like cultural relations between the Russian Federation and Germany not to be destroyed," one DW user responded. "It is sad to realize that culture has become a hostage to political decisions. The closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect people who have no way of influencing politicians."
Some DW readers from Russia specifically draw attention to the responsibility of politicians. One reader called the decision to close the institutes another step toward isolating the country and wondered why its consequences affect ordinary citizens rather than the Russian politicians who make such decisions.
"Why can the people making decisions to isolate Russia from Europe simultaneously provide their own children and close relatives with a European education and a European way of life?" a DW user asked, proposing a ban on the education of the children and close relatives of members of Russia's top leadership at universities in Germany and other EU countries.
Part of the audience considers Moscow's decision expected.
"The closure of the branches looks like a logical response to the closure of the Russian House in Germany. Could it have been otherwise? It is a pity that cultural and humanitarian ties between the countries are becoming hostages to politics," one reader wrote.
Some Russians hold Germany responsible for deteriorating relationship
Some Russians however believe that closing the Goethe-Institut branches in Russia was the right step and blame Germany for the recent escalation of the conflict with Russia.
"German authorities have buried cultural cooperation with Russia by shutting down the Russian House. The responsibility lies entirely with the German side, " said one of the survey participants.
A bilateral intergovernmental agreement between Russia and Germany from 2011 regulates the work of the Russian House in Berlin and the Goethe-Institut's branches in Russia. It obliges both countries, on the basis of reciprocity, to ensure conditions necessary for the operation of their cultural centers. However, it does not in any way provide for the automatic closure of one country's cultural centers in response to the other country doing so.
President of the Goethe-Institut Gesche Joost called the closure of its branches in Russia "the end of an era in German-Russian cultural relations."
According to its website, the Goethe-Institut has 154 branches in 100 countries. This number includes the three branches in Russia that are now being closed.

"No more books can be borrowed from our libraries, and no further training can be offered. German language teachers are losing an important source of professional training and support. For people in Russia, this further restricts access to the German language, culture and reliable information from and about Germany."
DW asked its users in Russia to share how the closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect them personally. The responses received do not constitute a representative survey. All users shared their stories on conditions of anonymity. Russian authorities labeled DW an "undesirable organization" making every cooperation with the media company a criminal offense.
'We'll have to travel to another country' for German exams
Many DW readers fear that, after the closure of the Goethe-Institut branches, they or their relatives will no longer be able to take exams in Russia for internationally recognized German language certificates.
Some readers pointed out that closing the Goethe-Institut in Russia will hit ethnic Germans willing to relocate back to Germany, or late repatriates, especially hard.
"I no longer live in Russia, having emigrated as a late repatriate, but my parents are still in Russia and were planning to take exams at the Goethe-Institut this fall or winter before submitting their resettlement documents. It looks like they'll have to take the exams in another country, which means additional stress and expenses for them," one reader said.
DW also received responses from parents whose children are learning German and plan to continue their education in Germany.
"My son attends a German school, and now we won't be able to take the exam in Russia. We'll have to travel to another country," one message said.
It remains unclear whether exams, language courses and educational programs will continue in Russia in another format or through partner organizations. Several readers expressed hope that at least some services will remain available online.
Goethe-Institute closures hit teachers hard
The closure of the institute will affect not only those planning to move to Germany or enroll at a German university. A German language teacher from the Moscow region told DW that her school had cooperated with the Goethe-Institut for more than 15 years.
"This partnership was one of the most important pillars of our work. The institute supported us with high-quality teaching materials and provided modern books and publications about life in Germany, helping us make lessons engaging and relevant. Our students attended additional courses, and many successfully passed the Goethe certificate exams," she wrote.
"I teach German and can't find a job in Russia," another teacher told DW.
"It's terrible. I'm a German teacher, and I feel professionally stranded and lost," a third wrote.
Despite the restrictions imposed since the beginning of Russia's war in Ukraine in 2022, demand for the institute's services remained high. According to the Goethe-Institut, around 10,000 people studied German through its programs and partnerships in 2025. Before 2023, that number used to stand at around 16,000 people. The institute administered roughly 22,000 exams, and its libraries were visited by 6,700 people in 2025.
'Culture has become a hostage to political decisions'
Many readers perceive what is happening as another stage in the destruction of ties between Russia and Germany.
"We would like cultural relations between the Russian Federation and Germany not to be destroyed," one DW user responded. "It is sad to realize that culture has become a hostage to political decisions. The closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect people who have no way of influencing politicians."
Some DW readers from Russia specifically draw attention to the responsibility of politicians. One reader called the decision to close the institutes another step toward isolating the country and wondered why its consequences affect ordinary citizens rather than the Russian politicians who make such decisions.
"Why can the people making decisions to isolate Russia from Europe simultaneously provide their own children and close relatives with a European education and a European way of life?" a DW user asked, proposing a ban on the education of the children and close relatives of members of Russia's top leadership at universities in Germany and other EU countries.
Part of the audience considers Moscow's decision expected.
"The closure of the branches looks like a logical response to the closure of the Russian House in Germany. Could it have been otherwise? It is a pity that cultural and humanitarian ties between the countries are becoming hostages to politics," one reader wrote.
Some Russians hold Germany responsible for deteriorating relationship
Some Russians however believe that closing the Goethe-Institut branches in Russia was the right step and blame Germany for the recent escalation of the conflict with Russia.
"German authorities have buried cultural cooperation with Russia by shutting down the Russian House. The responsibility lies entirely with the German side, " said one of the survey participants.
A bilateral intergovernmental agreement between Russia and Germany from 2011 regulates the work of the Russian House in Berlin and the Goethe-Institut's branches in Russia. It obliges both countries, on the basis of reciprocity, to ensure conditions necessary for the operation of their cultural centers. However, it does not in any way provide for the automatic closure of one country's cultural centers in response to the other country doing so.
President of the Goethe-Institut Gesche Joost called the closure of its branches in Russia "the end of an era in German-Russian cultural relations."
According to its website, the Goethe-Institut has 154 branches in 100 countries. This number includes the three branches in Russia that are now being closed.

The pro-Israel mayor of Providence, Rhode Island, lost his reelection campaign Wednesday to a progressive pro-Palestinian challenger in the latest demonstration of how Israeli politics are seeping into local US elections.
Incumbent Brett Smiley, who converted to Judaism in 2024 while in office, was bested by state Sen. David Morales in the Democratic primary in this deep blue city. Morales, a democratic socialist, carried endorsements from leading progressives, including Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders and California Rep. Ro Khanna. With 99% of ballots counted, Morales had garnered 52.5% of the vote to Smiley’s 47.5%.
During the campaign, pro-Smiley flyers were defaced with Hitler mustaches and devil horns, acts which his opponent condemned.
The city’s Democratic primary also previews a significant general election vote on divestment. In November, Providence will become the largest American city to cast a vote on a measure that, despite not naming Israel directly, could stop the city from investing in companies linked to Israel.
Morales supports the binding divestment vote, while Smiley and local Jewish and pro-Israel groups have opposed it. The mayor called the ordinance “both unenforceable and likely in violation of existing state law” in a statement to Jewish Insider.
Morales criticized Smiley for participation in CAM summit during campaign
During the campaign, Morales criticized Smiley for participating in a mayoral summit run by the Combat Antisemitism Movement, where Smiley serves in a leadership role. Morales accused the group of suppressing pro-Palestinian speech and not being transparent about its funders.
The Rhode Island-Israel Collaborative, which promotes business ties between the state and Israel, opposes both the ballot initiative and Morales. Avi Nevel, the group’s founder, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency prior to the primary that Morales was “fueled by pro-Palestinians and Israeli haters.”
It was a night of overthrowing incumbents in the state, as Rhode Island’s sitting governor also lost his primary to an intra-party challenger. That race, however, did not pivot on Israel: Gov. Daniel McKee’s popularity in the state has sunk following a scandal involving the closure of a major bridge.

OpenAI covered up scale of rogue agent security breaches – Reuters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:14:27 UTC
01:14:27 KST

OpenAI covered up scale of rogue agent security breaches – Reuters
Rogue AI agents developed by OpenAI bypassed restrictions on posting online and used more than ten previously undisclosed websites to communicate with one another, Reuters reported on Wednesday, adding that the company kept the unauthorized activity quiet for months.
An AI agent is a software system that can independently carry out tasks on a user’s behalf, making decisions and taking actions with limited human supervision. The findings raise concerns that increasingly autonomous AI systems can find ways around safeguards and take actions their developers did not authorize or anticipate.
Reuters reviewed findings from six independent investigators or research groups, which suggested that the activity was far more widespread than previously known. Researcher Andrew Yoon identified 18 previously undisclosed sites used from May to July, while a team led by Sydney Von Arx found evidence across 23.
”We have no idea how much is out there,” Von Arx said, warning that the estimates are incomplete.
OpenAI did not directly answer Reuters’ questions about how many sites were affected or why the activity was kept under wraps for months. The company said it was conducting a broader review.
The agents reportedly repurposed old wikis, online text-storage services, and university link shorteners as makeshift message boards while carrying out research tasks. Although permitted to search the web for information, they were not supposed to post content, but found ways to leave messages for one another using editable pages and other website features.
The findings expand on an incident revealed last week involving DseWiki, a German programming wiki where researchers attributed more than 15,000 edits to OpenAI agents. The systems reportedly used the site to exchange tactics for completing tasks, circumventing restrictions, and avoiding detection.
Researchers said some discussed using Tor, which allows users to browse the internet anonymously, and created backup pages after a moderator began deleting their messages.
The incidents follow a more serious breach in July, when OpenAI agents circumvented safeguards during cybersecurity testing, reached the open internet, and gained unauthorized access to systems belonging to Hugging Face, a major platform for hosting and sharing AI models.
OpenAI later acknowledged that its agents exploited vulnerabilities and accessed parts of Hugging Face’s infrastructure without authorization, describing the episode as a “warning shot” about the risks posed by increasingly capable autonomous systems.
The company told Reuters that it found no additional activity matching the “severity or scale” of the Hugging Face breach. OpenAI said it was reviewing broader agent activity and developing a framework for reporting AI “misalignment” during model training, evaluation, and deployment.

What internal exclusion really means for school pupils | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:13:41 UTC
01:13:41 KST

Your article quotes Tom Bennett, “a leading expert in behaviour management”, suggesting that internal exclusions are “a form of inclusion” (‘Internal exclusion’ of England secondary school students almost triples in three years, 3 September). That does not reflect my own experience. If a student is internally excluded, it must be as a last resort. I spent several months in the isolation room at my secondary school, and it didn’t feel inclusive to me.
Like many of the students disproportionately affected by internal exclusion, I was from a disadvantaged background. I also had undiagnosed dyslexia. For me, internal exclusion meant I was unable to learn alongside other students – I’d simply get a printed handout from a teacher of the lesson notes and was told to read them.
I finished my education in a pupil referral unit, but was able to go on to college thanks to the support of one of my teachers, who also mentored me. I am now in my final year of studying neuroscience at university, and I am working as a youth adviser with Lewis Hamilton’s charity, Mission 44. We are calling for internal exclusion to be properly recorded and scrutinised, alongside suspensions and permanent exclusions.
Schools must also have sufficient resources and clear guidance on what good internal exclusion looks like, as well as how to address the causes of poor behaviour, so they can intervene before a young person reaches crisis point and is removed from the classroom.
Faysal Yusuf
London
You have to experience being in a classroom when significant disruption takes place. It is devastating. It wrecks the learning of the pupils who want to learn. It ruins the confidence of teachers who want to impart a love of their subject and enable their pupils to progress. It takes up valuable senior leadership time when a pupil has to be extracted. Dysregulated and verbally or physically disruptive children are not the product of schools. They are often the product of severely challenged family units.
In such cases, internal isolation, as a strategy, has the best outcome. Pupils and teachers can resume learning and teaching in a calm atmosphere. The internally isolated pupil has a chance to recognise what triggered their outburst, and can resume learning in a fresh classroom climate that can include attention to their specific needs. And they are still safe on the school premises.
Authorities and commentators should therefore not start to demonise internal isolations in schools without examining the deep-rooted socioeconomic and political causes behind them. 
Jo West
Former secondary school headteacher, Virginia Water, Surrey
Imagine if, at work today, you had to commit at all times to looking at the boss (never out of the window or at the floor), to nodding, to walking corridors in silence and to asking questions at least five times a day. Pupils in secondary schools can be banished to internal detention for failing to do these things, among other reasons.
The government’s special educational needs and disabilities reforms are based on making mainstream schools more inclusive. To achieve that, it must accept that the tyranny of rigid, non-evidenced rules does not work for 21st-century children. That doesn’t mean a reduction in standards – it means better and less harmful interventions to manage behaviour.
Jane Harris
Vice-chair, Disabled Children’s Partnership 
We were pleased to see you draw the public’s attention to the new data showing that poorer pupils and those with special educational needs and disabilities are disproportionately affected by internal exclusions in secondary schools.
We are very concerned that the government remains mute on this and is not doing more to promote practices that are trauma-informed and grounded in modern neuroscience. Some schools are already managing to do this, investing in staff training to use relational and restorative approaches that balance both high challenge and high support. Plenty of organisations are ready to provide this training.
But real change needs leadership from the very top of government. Too often, poor behaviour is still seen as deliberate defiance for its own sake. We need to see it instead as a symptom of a system that fails to promote empathy, understanding and taking responsibility for how our actions affect others.
Ben Harper
Peacebuilding in schools coordinator, Quakers in Britain

Retailers test operations during yellow air raid alerts
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
19:13:41 EEST
01:13:41 KST

Shopping centers and retailers are analyzing the possibility of operating during a yellow air raid alert level, companies said.
Starting September 10, guided by government resolution No. 1092 of September 4, 2026, "Certain issues of optimizing population protection and responding to air attack threats," a number of Kyiv shopping centers switched to an updated regime during air raid alerts. At the yellow level (drone threat), River Mall, Retroville, Piramida, and DREAM shopping centers continue operating, as they announced on their social media pages. At the same time, during the yellow threat level, stores that gave voluntary consent remain open. Meanwhile, each seller can independently decide to close a store if they feel unsafe.
DREAM shopping center additionally reported that the list of tenants terminating operations during the yellow level will be published in stories and on the shopping center's website.
Some of the surveyed shopping centers have not yet made a decision on changing their operating mode. In particular, Lavina and Blockbuster Mall management companies told Interfax-Ukraine they are in the risk assessment stage. Respublika Park, near where a gas station was hit on Thursday during a drone alert, expectedly refused to comment.
Regarding anchor tenants, cinema chains reported readiness to continue operating under the conditions prescribed by the resolution (including the presence of shelters in shopping centers or creating them within the next 3 months). "We operate during 'yellow' alerts. But we warn everyone about the threat, and those who wish can go to the shelter," Planeta Kino cinema chain CEO Nataliya Baidan said. Multiplex Holding CEO Roman Romanchuk provided a similar response.
COMFY specified that 95% of the chain's stores are located in shopping centers, so in matters of safety and operating mode, particularly during the yellow level, the company adheres to the rules of the specific shopping center, taking into account the situation in the region. If a shopping center decides to stop operations or evacuate during an air raid alert, COMFY acts in accordance with that decision. At the same time, in cases where store operations can continue, safety must be ensured primarily by the availability of an accessible shelter nearby.
Fozzy Group said it is still working on decisions regarding the operating mode during the yellow level.
Auchan Ukraine told Interfax-Ukraine that currently only 1 hypermarket operates during an air raid alert – the capital's Auchan Lybidska in Ocean Plaza. Even though the shopping center closes during alerts, the hypermarket operates because it is located on the minus 1 floor.
International home goods chain JYSK has not changed its rules since 2022: all stores in all regions close during an alert, regardless of its degree or the decisions of individual shopping centers, JYSK Country Director in Ukraine Yevhen Ivanytsia emphasized in a comment. At the same time, the company continues to invest in creating shelters near some stores (primarily referring to frontline regions).
Earlier, McDonald's Ukraine Ltd., which develops the fast food restaurant chain in Ukraine, also reported the continued application of expanded security rules.
As reported, the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine with resolution No. 1092 of September 4 regulated that during a yellow-level air threat, business entities can carry out activities, and the presence of visitors in establishments is at their own discretion.
According to the resolution, the "Air Raid" signal in the nationwide automated centralized alert system, based on information from the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, is differentiated according to the classification of air attack threat levels: red level – missile or missile-drone threat, or massive drone threat; yellow level – drone threat.
It is noted that in the event of a yellow threat level, business entities regardless of ownership form can conduct activities in premises, buildings, structures, or territories where temporary or permanent shelters for staff and visitors are available. Where temporary or permanent shelters are absent, activities are possible in coordination with the labor team until a shelter is equipped, but for no longer than 3 months from the date this resolution enters into force.

Zoe Williams may be right to describe Keir Starmer as a poor politician, but what did we expect (Farewell Keir Starmer, a terrible politician whom we desperately wanted to be something more, 2 September)? Equally troubling was his approach to criticism. Many longstanding Labour supporters, including elderly members who opposed the war, felt ignored or dismissed. Leadership requires engagement with dissent, not contempt for it.

Long-range strikes alone cannot win a war; they are a means of coercion that is effective only in conjunction with other forms of combat operations, Head of the President's Office of Ukraine Kyrylo Budanov said.
"Deep strikes cannot win a war. Deep strikes cannot kill everyone. Look at the example of the United States in Iran. Deep strikes are a form of support and a means of influence and coercion. "In other words, jet-powered drones are now competing against interceptor drones. This is a standard competition. We are following the same path by creating high-speed small interceptor drones," Budanov said.

The Arab films hoping to make the cut at the 2027 Oscars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:10:26 UTC
01:10:26 KST

Breadcrumb
The Arab films hoping to make the cut at the 2027 Oscars
Several Arab films have been submitted for the 2027 Academy Awards in the Best International Feature Film category ahead of the 30 September deadline.
The selection of Arab films has garnered widespread praise, in what has been seen as a major win for the region and its film industry.
All international feature films submitted must be more than 40 minutes long, be produced outside the US and have more than 50% of their dialogue in a language other than English. Eligible films must also have been released between 1 October 2025 and 30 September 2026.
Here, The New Arab looks at some of the submissions from the Middle East.
1. Morocco: La Mas Dulce
Morocco’s submission is La Mas Dulce, known internationally as Strawberries, which follows two young women who travel to Andalusia to work as strawberry pickers in a bid to improve their living conditions and economic prospects.
The film explores the exploitation and harassment they face, as well as the emotional turmoil of deciding whether to endure the harsh conditions or speak out against them.
2. Palestine: Citizen Osama
Citizen Osama is a documentary filmed in northern Gaza amid Israel’s brutal genocide, which began in October 2023.
It follows the daily life of Osama al-Ashi, an artistic photographer who became a war photographer as a result of the devastating circumstances in the enclave.
In the 69-minute film, he is shown going to great lengths to protect his newborn child and wife from the devastation and heavy Israeli bombardment.
The film delves into his experiences, as well as those of other civilians who have faced loss, starvation and displacement in Gaza.
3. Iraq: No Paradise if You are Killed by a Woman
Iraq’s selected film, by Kurdish-Norwegian filmmaker Halkawt Mustafa, follows a female sniper who suppresses her emotions after years of war.
It follows her discovery that her younger sister, who disappeared during an Islamic State (IS) assault in 2014, may still be alive, and her subsequent journey to find her.
Mustafa said the film was inspired by Kurdish women who fought IS, as well as several meetings he had with female Peshmerga fighters on the front line in 2014.
The 15-film shortlist is set to be announced on 15 December, with the final nominees to be revealed on 21 January.
The 99th Academy Awards will take place in Los Angeles on 14 March 2027.

Explainer: What’s happened to Al-Qaeda in the 25 years since 9/11?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:07:32 UTC
01:07:32 KST

Explainer: What’s happened to Al-Qaeda in the 25 years since 9/11?
Sept 10 - In the 25 years since Al-Qaeda militants hijacked passenger jets and flew them into New York's World Trade Center towers and the Pentagon, the group founded by Osama bin Laden has spawned affiliates and inspired attacks around the world.
While it has suffered setbacks, notably bin Laden's killing in 2011 by U.S. forces and the emergence of Islamic State as a rival, experts say Al-Qaeda still serves as a source of support and inspiration for militants in many regions, particularly in Africa.
WHAT IS AL-QAEDA?
Al-Qaeda emerged as a transnational jihadist network in the late 1980s under the leadership of bin Laden, a wealthy Saudi-born militant who had helped recruit and funnel support to Arab volunteers fighting the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan after 1979 and fought there himself.
Al-Qaeda became a magnet for militants who aspired to establish hardline Islamist rule and who shared common hostility to the United States, Israel and U.S.-allied governments in the region.
Bin Laden was stripped of his Saudi citizenship in 1994 and expelled from Sudan in 1996, taking sanctuary in Afghanistan.
He began organising attacks on U.S. interests long before arriving in Afghanistan. The first recognized by the United States was a 1992 Al-Qaeda bombing of two hotels in Yemen intended to kill Somalia-bound U.S. troops who had already left or were staying elsewhere.
In Afghanistan, he supported training camps and established an elite brigade of foreign fighters.
In 1996, he declared jihad against U.S. forces he described as occupying Saudi Arabia.
This was followed in 1998 by the announcement of a "World Islamic Front" for jihad against "Jews and Crusaders", and a declaration that it was a duty for Muslims to kill Americans and their allies, whether civilian or military.
Later that year, Al-Qaeda truck bombings against the U.S. embassies in Kenya and Tanzania killed 224 people.
The September 11 attacks were carried out by 19 hijackers, 15 of them from Saudi Arabia. They hijacked four jets, the fourth of which crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after passengers stormed the cockpit. The attacks killed nearly 3,000 people.
WHAT HAPPENED TO AL-QAEDA'S LEADERS AFTER 9/11?
The United States invaded Afghanistan in October 2001, toppling the Taliban and driving Al-Qaeda from its base of operations.
Anti-Taliban forces overran Al-Qaeda’s base in the Tora Bora mountains in December 2001, but bin Laden evaded capture for a decade, periodically releasing messages until U.S. special forces killed him in a raid on his compound in Abbottabad, Pakistan, in 2011.
The self-professed mastermind of September 11, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, was captured in Pakistan in 2003. In 2007, Mohammed said he planned the attack "from A to Z", according to a transcript of a military hearing released by the Pentagon.
A judge recently ordered Mohammed, who is held in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, and three co-defendants to stand trial before a military tribunal in June 2028, following two decades of legal deadlock.
Bin Laden's successor, Ayman al-Zawahri, was killed by a U.S. drone strike in Kabul in 2022.
Egyptian militant Seif al-Adel is believed to be Al-Qaeda's de facto leader today.
HOW DID ITS INFLUENCE SPREAD AFTER 9/11?
While Al-Qaeda's leaders scattered, militants linked to Al-Qaeda or inspired by its ideology carried out numerous attacks.
The deadliest included a 2002 attack on a nightclub district in Bali that killed 202 people, bombings that killed more than 190 people on trains in Madrid in 2004, and suicide bombings that killed 52 people on London underground trains and a bus in 2005.
Al-Qaeda affiliates sprang up in the Middle East and beyond. One of the most powerful was in Iraq, where Al-Qaeda fought U.S.-led forces following the 2003 invasion.
A branch emerged in North Africa in 2007 and another in the Arabian Peninsula in 2009. After 2011, Al-Qaeda's Nusra Front became a force in Syria's civil war.
In Africa, Al-Qaeda affiliates include Al Shabaab in Somalia and Jama'at Nusrat al‑Islam wal‑Muslimin (JNIM) in the Sahel region. Al-Qaeda also has ties to Tehrik-e Taliban Pakistan (TTP), also known as Pakistani Taliban, which is waging an insurgency against Islamabad.
Antonio Giustozzi, a senior research fellow at the RUSI think-tank in London, said that while Al-Qaeda suffered losses and dislocation after the invasion of Afghanistan, its profile rose and it expanded massively in the years that followed. Its influence peaked around 2013 before its Iraqi branch broke away to form Islamic State, he said.
HOW WAS AL-QAEDA AFFECTED BY THE RISE OF ISLAMIC STATE?
Islamic State founder Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi split from Al-Qaeda and declared a "caliphate" across large parts of Syria and Iraq in 2014, sparking conflict with the Nusra Front.
Though Islamic State was eventually beaten out of its territory in Syria and Iraq, in a reversal for jihadism, its rivalry with Al-Qaeda continues, particularly in West Africa where affiliates of the two groups regularly clash as they compete for territory and influence.
Another blow came in 2016 when the Nusra Front broke away. Its leader Ahmed al-Sharaa, then known by his nom de guerre Abu Mohammed al-Golani, went on to topple Bashar al-Assad in 2024. He became Syrian president and made Damascus a Western ally.
WHERE IS AL-QAEDA MOST ACTIVE TODAY?
Somalia and West Africa's Sahel region are the main theatres in Africa where Al-Qaeda-aligned groups are expanding their influence and governing across swathes of territory.
TTP has expanded its insurgency in northwestern Pakistan. It has received ideological guidance, training and support from Al-Qaeda, according to a U.N. report published last month.
Pakistan says the TTP leadership and many of its fighters are based in Afghanistan, where the Taliban returned to power in 2021 after the U.S. withdrew.
In February, another U.N. report said Al-Qaeda "continued to enjoy the patronage of the de facto authorities" in Afghanistan — a reference to the Taliban government — and that its "appetite for external operations" remained "undiminished".
Kabul denies that Al-Qaeda operates in Afghanistan, or that it allows militant attacks on Pakistan from its territory.
Giustozzi said that while Al-Qaeda was past its peak "they're still remarkably influential".
It had evolved to be less dependent on specific individuals, relying instead on a cadre of low-profile operatives who are "much more difficult to target and identify", he said. REUTERS

What Russia Is Really Up To in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:07:17 UTC
01:07:17 KST

Russia’s Real Strategy in Europe
Moscow doesn’t want a conventional war, but it is busy fighting a hybrid one.
On Russian state television, the Kremlin’s propagandists have for years threatened to bomb European capitals, even while the country’s diplomats insist that no such war is imminent. Lately, the denials have gotten hard to sustain, as European intelligence agencies have ascribed hundreds of clandestine sabotage operations—cyberattacks in Italy, arson in the United Kingdom, undersea-cable ruptures in the Baltic, severed pig heads left outside French mosques—to Russia.
U.S. intelligence assessments conclude that a conventional Russian attack on a NATO country is likely to happen sometime from this fall to 2029. But another possibility is that Moscow will remain content with sabotage and intimidation. This hybrid campaign is all the war Russia wants or needs—and stoking fear that Moscow just might directly strike Ukraine’s European allies is part of it.
If this is what Russian President Vladimir Putin is really up to in Europe, then he was telling the truth when he assured Trump this week that Russia has “no aggressive intentions against European statehood.” Moscow has not massed troops on any NATO member’s border. Rather, it has been sending a carefully calibrated message meant to persuade Europe to stop supporting Ukraine.
For Moscow, this has been a summer of setbacks in Ukraine. Russia stalled on the battlefield and sustained damage from thousands of Ukrainian long-range drones that plunged the country into fuel shortages. And so it escalated elsewhere in Europe: Fires broke out at ammunition plants in Italy, Bulgaria, and Estonia last month, and explosive-laden drones were discovered near a German power plant and at an airport in Leipzig, apparently intended to destroy Ukrainian cargo planes.
From the Kremlin’s point of view, Europe has been deepening its involvement in Ukraine. At the beginning of the full-scale war, Europe donated weapons to Ukraine from its own stocks. Within two years, European governments were paying Ukrainian factories to manufacture arms. Last year, Fire Point, a Ukrainian missile-and-drone manufacturer, announced that it would establish a solid-fuel production plant in Denmark, making it the first such arms company to expand production abroad. Today, Europe provides the bulk of financial assistance to Kyiv. It has also become Ukraine’s secure production base—Ukrainian weapons are manufactured in Germany, Britain, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, France, Romania, and Spain.
Because Kyiv is attacking Russia’s rear, it’s logical to worry that Moscow will attack Ukraine’s. Russian security services are almost certainly capable of carrying out a lethal attack on European soil. And Western war games have entertained many possibilities along those lines. Among them are a limited Russian incursion into a small Baltic town that has a Russian-speaking population; a full-scale invasion of the Baltic states, launched simultaneously from Belarus and Kaliningrad, Russia’s European exclave, to cut them off from the rest of Europe; the rapid creation of an impenetrable drone “kill zone” on European soil; and a strategic blockade of the Baltic Sea. Some of these scenarios are plausible; others would require hundreds of thousands of Russian troops to crisscross Europe.
Russia has not visibly prepared for any such scenario, however. Instead, it continues to wage its hybrid war—which European security services continue to thwart. Such are the headlines: Drones carrying explosives are discovered in Leipzig, improvised explosive devices are found near a German power plant, and flying objects are spotted near airports.
Moscow may not much care that these operations get foiled. In a way, the effect is similar to that of Russia’s harassment of journalists and embassy workers stationed in Moscow: Things in their apartment get rearranged, signs of eavesdropping are deliberately made obvious, or a window is left open in the middle of winter. Such interference conveys a sinister message: We’re watching you. We have access to you. You are not in control. But it’s still different from blowing up the apartment.
Putin has generally chosen to fully engage the Russian military only in conflicts that he feels (rightly or, in the case of Ukraine, wrongly) assured of winning. This does not describe any hypothetical attack on the Baltic states, which have heavily fortified borders, conduct regular military exercises, and spend 5 percent of their GDP on defense.
That’s not to mention the thousands of British, German, and Canadian troops stationed near the Baltics as part of NATO’s Enhanced Forward Presence. Moscow may be willing to wager that the United States won’t intervene should Russia attack Estonia. But Russia would then find itself at war with numerous European states armed with submarines, aircraft carriers, fifth-generation fighter jets, long-range cruise missiles, and even nuclear weapons—all while it was still fighting in Ukraine.
Russia’s hybrid war has not succeeded in its likely purpose: stopping weapons, money, and intelligence from flowing into Ukraine from Europe. Kyiv has more arms, funds, and—judging by its strikes on Russian soil—intelligence than ever before. Neither has the Russian campaign taken out a European satellite that supplies Ukraine with intelligence, say, or destroyed a shipment of Patriot missiles.
But Putin persists in this campaign for a reason. Through inexpensive means, expendable operatives, and a steady stream of chilling leaks, the Kremlin has millions of Westerners braced for it to wage a full-scale war against Europe. Regardless of whether that war is likely, Putin will be demanding concessions in exchange for bringing it to an end.

Houthi blitz reaches Bab al-Mandab as rebels reportedly seize strategic Red Sea island
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:04:48 UTC
01:04:48 KST

The Houthis’ sweeping offensive across western Yemen reached the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait on Thursday, with a report claiming the Iran-backed rebels had seized Perim Island, a tiny but potentially crucial position at the narrowest point of one of the world’s most important shipping routes.
Qatar-based Al-Araby reported that the Houthis captured Perim, also known as Mayyun, as part of the blitz that saw them seize large stretches of Yemen’s southwestern coast from forces aligned with the internationally recognized, Saudi-backed government. The claim has not been independently confirmed and remains the only specific report that Perim itself has fallen.
But separate reports indicate that Houthi forces have reached several other strategically important islands nearby. Reuters, citing military sources in Yemen’s internationally recognized government, reported that the rebels had reached the Hanish Islands after capturing the nearby port city of Al-Mokha earlier Thursday. The report did not say whether Zuqar, Greater Hanish or Lesser Hanish had been taken. A military source quoted by AFP said the Houthis had captured at least Zuqar after firing missiles at the island and sending fighters there by boat.
Perim’s location gives the report particular significance. The roughly 13-square-kilometer island lies in the middle of Bab al-Mandab, separating the waterway into two channels between Yemen and the Horn of Africa. Control of the island could allow the Houthis to monitor shipping more closely and potentially threaten vessels passing through the strait without relying solely on the long-range missiles and drones they have used in previous attacks.
Opponents of the Houthis have also warned that a permanent presence there could give the group greater ability to mine the waterway, potentially forcing an extensive international naval operation to remove them.
Bab al-Mandab links the Indian Ocean and Asia to the Red Sea, Suez Canal and Europe, making it a critical artery for global trade. Its importance has increased further since Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz after its war with the United States began in late February.
The possibility that Tehran’s Houthi allies could strengthen their position around a second major maritime chokepoint has added pressure to already volatile energy markets. Brent crude rose at least 4% Thursday to around $105 a barrel amid fears that shipping through Bab al-Mandab could face greater disruption.
The gains could also strengthen Iran’s hand in its confrontation with U.S. President Donald Trump, giving Tehran another potential source of leverage as it seeks relief from an American blockade that has severely restricted its oil exports.
Iranian media celebrated the Houthi advance. Iran’s Al-Alam television claimed the rebels had captured Dhubab, which it described as the last major Saudi-backed government stronghold on Yemen’s western coast, as well as nearby Zuqar Island.
“Bab al-Mandab is under the control of the forces after the complete capture of Dhubab,” the channel reported.
The Houthis later described their operations as “defensive” and pledged that international freedom of navigation through Bab al-Mandab would continue. At the same time, the group is enforcing what it calls a “naval blockade” against Saudi Arabia and has attacked Saudi tankers and other vessels in recent weeks.
Yemen’s internationally recognized government accused Tehran of driving the offensive.
“Iran seeks to give the Houthis the ability to influence the Bab al-Mandab Strait and the Red Sea,” said Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council. “Attempts to change the military situation near the Bab al-Mandab Strait cannot be treated as a purely internal Yemeni matter.”
“Any threat to the Bab al-Mandab Strait directly affects the Red Sea, the Suez Canal and global trade,” he added, arguing that restoring government control over Yemen’s coastline and territorial waters was a shared international interest.
Al-Mokha falls as thousands flee
The latest advance came after government officials acknowledged Thursday morning that their forces had withdrawn from the strategic port city of Al-Mokha, roughly 80 kilometers from Perim.
Witnesses told AFP that Houthi fighters entered the city chanting “Death to America, death to Israel.”
The forces opposing the Houthis are divided among several factions. Al-Mokha had been held by the National Resistance Forces led by Gen. Tareq Saleh, which fight alongside the internationally recognized government. Saleh said Thursday that he had moved his command center to “a safe location” and acknowledged that his forces and their allies had paid “a heavy price in recent days.” He also accused Iran of planning and supporting the offensive.
At least 20,000 people had already been displaced by the latest fighting in several areas before the fall of Al-Mokha, with reports suggesting the number rose sharply overnight as residents fled toward Aden, the seat of the internationally recognized government.
One 46-year-old resident who fled Al-Mokha during the night described an “apocalyptic” atmosphere to AFP. Another said families were robbed by gangs while trying to escape.
AFP reported earlier this week that at least 500 people had been killed in the renewed fighting, most of them combatants but including dozens of civilians. The toll is believed to have risen as the Houthi offensive expanded.
Saudi oil facilities also under attack
The Houthi blitz comes amid the sharpest escalation in Yemen in years. Earlier this week, government forces said they had captured territory from the rebels in the northern province of Al-Jawf, while the Houthis launched a major missile and drone attack against oil facilities in southern Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis said the strikes were retaliation for Saudi attacks. Riyadh reported at least 73 people wounded and several energy facilities damaged and temporarily knocked out of operation.
Saudi Arabia has responded with extensive airstrikes across Yemen in support of government forces. Houthi officials claimed Riyadh carried out around 40 strikes on Thursday morning alone in areas including Taiz, Hodeidah, Al-Jawf and Marib.
Yemen’s civil war began in 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, after exploiting the weakness of the government established following the Arab Spring upheaval. Saudi Arabia intervened the following year at the head of an Arab coalition seeking to restore the internationally recognized government.
The coalition prevented the Houthis from conquering the entire country but failed to defeat them. The rebels retained control over most of northwestern Yemen and repeatedly launched missiles and drones at Saudi cities, airports and oil infrastructure.
Saudi Arabia later shifted course, reaching a truce with the Houthis in 2022 and restoring diplomatic relations with Iran the following year. That relative calm began breaking down again in July, when Saudi Arabia struck Sanaa airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing in the Houthi-controlled capital.
The Houthis subsequently stepped up attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and shipping and declared their naval blockade against the kingdom. In recent days, that confrontation has expanded into major ground fighting.
Saudi Arabia’s new alliance faces its first test
The crisis is also testing the trilateral defense alliance Saudi Arabia signed with Turkey and Pakistan last month.
The agreement, dubbed the “Mecca Alliance” after the city where it was signed, contains a mutual-defense provision. Both Ankara and Islamabad have condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia but have so far taken no significant military action on Riyadh’s behalf.
Reuters reported earlier this week that Pakistan relayed a Saudi warning to Tehran calling on Iran to restrain the Houthis before the confrontation spiraled further. A senior Iranian official responded that “Iran does not control the Houthis.”
Danny Citrinowicz, a former head of the Iran branch in Israeli military intelligence’s research division and now a senior researcher at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies, said the fighting represented the alliance’s first major strategic test.
“The importance of an alliance is not measured by the declarations made when it is established, but by what its members are willing to do when one of them is attacked,” he wrote on X.
The question, he said, was whether the Mecca Alliance would develop into a genuine regional security architecture or become a “paper tiger” precisely when Saudi Arabia needed it.
For Washington, he added, the crisis also exposes the gap between encouraging Middle Eastern partners to take greater responsibility for their own security and creating alliances whose members are willing to share risks when deterrence fails.
“An alliance that works only in peacetime,” he wrote, “is not a real alliance.”

Forensics officers dressed in blue overalls and a crime scene photographer were coming and going from a branch of KFC, where locals said the incident occurred, and there were evidence markers visible on the floor.
Abandoned food could still be seen on the tables as evening drew in, suggestive of the haste in which people left the restaurant amid the incident. “I heard a really loud bang and people running from KFC,” said George Ioannou, who was working in Antonio’s Male Grooming next door to the KFC.
“An elderly woman ran into the shop and I had to lock the door to shelter her until it calmed down. She was crying. About five minutes later, we heard the sirens.” Other shop workers nearby said the incident was quick and that it was over in moments.
The KFC has an alleyway down one side – along which people ran as they passed the male grooming shop – and faces on to Bromley’s High Street. Part of the latter was still closed to the public on Thursday evening. It is a busy thoroughfare, with a large shopping centre at one end and a train station taking commuters between Kent, south-east London and the capital’s centre at the other. Those and the parade of shops lining the high street draw large numbers of people from the surrounding area. About 15 bus routes were diverted, including the 61, 208 and 119.
The London ambulance service said ambulance crews, a paramedic in a fast-response car, an incident response officer, an advanced paramedic and London’s air ambulance were dispatched to the scene.
Four patients were treated at the scene before being taken to hospital, the service added.
The Bromley and Biggin Hill MP Peter Fortune said: “I am aware of the incident on Bromley High Street this afternoon and I know that residents will have safety concerns. The police are in attendance and have made a number of arrests. I will remain in close contact with the police as they continue to investigate this incident.”
A picture shared on social media on Thursday afternoon appeared to show a section of Bromley High Street cordoned off, with an emergency vehicle on site. The Met asked anyone with information to contact the police on 101.

Mother of imprisoned UK Palestine Action activist tells TNA of mortgage rejection over 'reputational risk'
The mother of a jailed Palestine Action activist has told The New Arab that Lloyds Bank rejected her mortgage application over what her broker said was a "reputational risk", adding to scrutiny of the bank over accusations of politically motivated debanking.
Emma Kamio said the decision came in June, six weeks into a mortgage application she had pursued under a tight deadline as she sought to raise money after years spent campaigning for her daughter, Leona "Ellie" Kamio.
Documents seen by Novara suggest the application was rejected over "adverse media", at a time when Ellie Kamio was being held on remand over a Palestine Action protest.
Lloyds told The New Arab that it does not close accounts or make lending decisions on the basis of political or personal beliefs, and said its decisions are instead governed by laws, regulations, account conditions and lending requirements.
Emma Kamio said she had been trying to remortgage one of her properties after her work as a homoeopath and Pilates instructor suffered while she devoted much of the past two years to campaigning for her daughter.
"As a small business owner, just fighting for my family's life for the last two years, the business has definitely been affected," Kamio told The New Arab.
Ellie Kamio, one of a group known as the "Filton 4", was sentenced to six years in prison in June after being convicted of criminal damage over a direct-action protest at an Elbit Systems factory in Filton, England.
Her mother said she had informed her mortgage broker about her own arrest while protesting against the proscription of Palestine Action. She was later found not guilty.
But after weeks of progressing through the mortgage application, she said she was told Lloyds would not proceed.
"Six weeks down the track, it wasn't just like within days. I was under a time bracket, which put me under a lot of stress," Kamio said.
Kamio, who described herself as a longstanding Lloyds customer, said the mortgage rejection was not the family's first unexplained difficulty with the bank.
While Ellie was being held on remand and before her conviction, Kamio said Lloyds closed her daughter's account without providing an explanation.
"A letter came to my house saying that she needed to find alternative ways of paying for her mobile bill," she said.
Lloyds declined to comment on the individual cases.
"Our decisions are based on relevant laws, regulations, account conditions, or lending requirements," a spokesperson told The New Arab. "We do not close customer accounts or make lending decisions based on political or personal beliefs."
'I've lost the property'
Kamio eventually secured another mortgage provider, but said the stress surrounding the process, combined with her daughter's imprisonment, had taken a severe toll on her health.
She said she developed high blood pressure, post-traumatic stress disorder and eczema, eventually prompting her to hand the property over to her sister.
"I've developed high blood pressure, PTSD, eczema - that's a new one - my face," Kamio said.
"We've lost another sister 20 years ago to cancer, and so my sister said to me, 'I can't lose another sister with your blood pressure the way it is', and she's just taken it off my hands, so I've lost the property."
"That's all the stress that goes with it, to be honest."
The Kamio family's experience comes amid wider accusations that Lloyds has debanked other customers associated with left-wing politics or activism without adequate explanation.
The bank came under scrutiny in June after left-wing news outlet The Canary said it had been unable to pay staff after Lloyds closed its business account following almost a decade as a customer.
The Canary finances in doubt after Lloyds shuts account
British politician George Galloway also threatened legal action against Bank of Scotland, which is owned by Lloyds Banking Group, after saying his account had been closed without warning or an adequate explanation.
Kamio said her experiences over the past two years had fundamentally altered her view of powerful institutions in Britain.
"I would say that what I've learned over the last two years is much like the government; they have the power to penalise and silence voices that don't agree with their support of the genocide or the financing of the arms industry," she said.
"But I believe that this will now change as we begin to experience what the Muslim community have been subjected to all this time."
Kamio said she believed the expanding use of terrorism legislation would ultimately affect people far beyond Palestine solidarity activists.
"The abuse of the terrorism laws and its wide-reaching consequences will begin to affect us all, and the upside of that, hopefully, is that it will unite the divide."

====================================================================================================

Getting a smartphone before age 13 linked to worse mental health in young adulthood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:00:50 UTC
01:00:50 KST

New research provides evidence that receiving a smartphone early in childhood is associated with poorer psychological well-being in young adulthood. The findings indicate that these negative outcomes are largely tied to early access to social media, which opens the door to cyberbullying, poor family relationships, and disrupted sleep. The study was published in Journal of Human Development and Capabilities.
Scientists and policymakers have expressed growing concern over the modern digital landscape. Smartphones operate as gateways into algorithmically curated digital environments. These algorithms are designed by artificial intelligence (AI) programs to maximize user engagement, often by presenting content that keeps users scrolling.
When young children navigate these spaces, they face unique challenges. According to a 2026 review, adolescent brains undergo biological changes that heighten their sensitivity to social feedback and variable rewards, like notifications and likes. This makes young minds particularly vulnerable to the design features of modern digital platforms.
Efforts to manage this issue have been mixed. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2026 evaluated the concurrent impact of restricting phone use during secondary school hours and noted little to no mental health improvement from daytime bans alone. With inconsistent findings across the scientific literature, questions remain regarding the long-term impact of digital exposure starting in early childhood.
The authors of the new study focused on the concept of mind health, which they distinguish from traditional clinical categories like depression and anxiety. Mind health encompasses the full complement of emotional, social, and cognitive capacities that allow a person to navigate life’s challenges and function productively.
The research, led by Tara C. Thiagarajan, founder and chief scientist of Sapien Labs, aimed to determine the population-level developmental consequences of owning a smartphone during childhood. They sought to understand how the age at which a child receives their first smartphone correlates with their mind health as a young adult.
“We are a nonprofit tracking mind health across the globe and exploring how different aspects of the environment contribute to the decline across each younger generation,” Thiagarajan told PsyPost. “One of the most significant environmental shifts that tracks with this trajectory is the advent of smartphones. We wanted to understand the cumulative effect of having a smartphone in childhood on development rather than just the immediate effect of using it.”
To explore this, the researchers analyzed data from the Global Mind Project, a large-scale data acquisition initiative. Their sample included over 100,000 young adults between the ages of 18 and 24, spanning 163 countries and various cultural backgrounds. Participants completed an online assessment tool called the Mind Health Quotient.
The Mind Health Quotient captures 47 different functions and symptoms, generating a score that reflects a person’s overall mental well-being on a spectrum from distressed to thriving. The survey also collected contextual information, including the age at which each participant received their first smartphone and when they first created social media accounts. The researchers used regression analysis to identify associations between early phone ownership, potential mediating factors, and current mind health.
The results showed a consistent pattern across different regions and languages. Receiving a smartphone before the age of 13 was associated with progressively lower mind health scores in early adulthood. For example, the average Mind Health Quotient score was 30 for individuals who acquired their first smartphone at age 13, but it dropped to just 1 for those who received one at age five.
“That the younger a child got a phone, the worse their mental health is likely to be in adulthood,” Thiagarajan explained. “This relationship is particularly steep before age 13. That means that every successive year before 13 makes it even worse.”
The percentage of young adults considered distressed or struggling was higher among those who acquired smartphones earlier. Compared to those who received a phone later in adolescence, females who obtained a smartphone at a very young age experienced a 9.5 percent higher rate of severe struggles, while males showed a 7.0 percent higher rate.
Specific symptoms also varied based on the age of first smartphone ownership. Among female participants who received a smartphone at age five or six, 48 percent reported severe suicidal thoughts as young adults, compared to 28 percent of those who received their first phone at age 13. Among males, the figures were 31 percent for early adopters and 20 percent for those who waited until age 13. Participants who owned phones earlier also reported higher rates of aggression, feelings of detachment from reality, and diminished emotional resilience.
“We were surprised that the specific aspects that early smartphone exposure effects after controlling for other factors are things like suicidal thoughts, aggression towards others and detachment from reality and not the typically discussed anxiety and depression,” the researcher noted.
To understand why this association exists, the researchers looked at several potential contributing factors. Globally, the age at which participants first accessed social media accounted for about 40 percent of the link between early smartphone ownership and poorer adult mind health.
Other factors played a role, but they were often tied to social media use. Cyberbullying and poor family relationships were linked to early smartphone ownership, and the researchers found that these issues were largely downstream effects of accessing social media at a young age. On the other hand, early smartphone use was also associated with disrupted sleep, but this sleep disruption appeared to happen independently of social media access, suggesting it might stem from other screen activities like gaming or watching videos.
The study highlighted regional differences, particularly in developed, English-speaking countries. Young adults in these countries reported receiving smartphones at an average age of 11, compared to ages 14 to 16 in parts of Africa, South Asia, and the Middle East.
In these English-speaking nations, the age of social media access explained up to 70 percent of the negative mind health associations linked to early smartphone ownership. In this region, experiences of cyberbullying and poor family relationships were almost entirely downstream of early social media access. For females in these countries, early social media access was also linked to an increased likelihood of experiencing sexual abuse, which in turn predicted poorer mental health outcomes.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2026, which found that youth social media engagement is consistently linked to poorer emotional well-being and diminished self-worth. It is worth noting, however, that the earlier study examined ongoing digital usage during childhood rather than the specific age of first smartphone ownership on young adult outcomes.
The findings are in tension with an earlier study regarding whether adolescent phone use impairs long-term psychological development. That previous study specifically tracked self-control over time in teenagers in South Korea, whereas the new study relied on retrospective reports of first smartphone ownership and broader adult mental health outcomes.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relies on observational data, meaning it can show links between early phone ownership and later mental health, but it cannot establish that one directly causes the other. Participants were also asked to recall events from their childhood, which can introduce memory errors.
“These results reflect the population level effects,” Thiagarajan said. “What that means is that they reflect having phones in a world where almost everyone else has one too. If you are the only one without a phone, it doesn’t mean you will easily have better outcomes. In fact it could even be more isolating.”
“On the other hand if an entire group doesn’t have phones it will change the social dynamic and behaviors in positive ways,” she added. “So the more impactful solutions are likely to be population level – bans until 13 at the school or societal level.”
The researchers did not measure the total amount of time participants spent on screens during childhood. The study also lacked data on the specific types of online content the individuals interacted with as they grew up. The findings reflect broad patterns across large populations and do not predict the exact outcome for every child who receives a smartphone at a young age.
“We are working on understanding if these cumulative effects can be reversed and how,” Thiagarajan said. “One example is this recently published camp study.”
The study, “Protecting the Developing Mind in a Digital Age: A Global Policy Imperative,” was authored by Tara C. Thiagarajan, Jennifer Jane Newson, and Shailender Swaminathan.

community-led cultural hub provides permanent home for black creative education in new orleans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
