01:00:46 KST

The Black Schoolhouse takes shape in New Orleans’ Seventh Ward
The Black School has created The Black Schoolhouse, a 185.8-square-meter community arts center in New Orleans’ historic Seventh Ward that brings creative education, cultural exchange, and neighborhood resources together under one roof. Located at 1660 N. Roman Street, the center is shaped by an 18-month design process with local residents and incorporates climate-resilient strategies alongside references to Black architectural traditions and local cultural memory. The Schoolhouse is scheduled to open to the public on October 10th, 2026, marking The Black School’s 10th anniversary.
The Black School developed the project through door-to-door surveys, imagination workshops, and community design charrettes. Residents identified access to creative skills, technology, youth and family gathering spaces, wellness resources, and architecture that reflected the identity of the Seventh Ward as priorities. The building includes a gallery, classrooms, computer lab, makerspace, library and meditation room, community kitchen, and garden.
all images by Neil Alexander
Community design shapes the Schoolhouse’s program
Founded in New York City in 2016 by artists and educators Joseph Cuillier and Shani Peters Cuillier, The Black School relocated to New Orleans in 2021, eventually purchasing land in the Seventh Ward, where Cuillier’s family has lived for more than a century.
Before construction began, The Black School used the site for a community garden and Garden School workshop series, healing circles led by local teaching artists, and public programs including Black Love Fest and the Creative Change Trip. The building consolidates these activities while adding facilities for making, learning, exhibitions, and professional development.
The organization has also developed a model that connects education with pathways into creative work. Through The Black School: Design Studio, it has graduated 39 Design Apprentices and employed 35 Junior Designers. The new building provides a physical base for those education and apprenticeship programs while expanding the capacity of the organization for creative production and neighborhood programming.
openings in the upper shipping containers create shaded, operable facades across
Climate resilience meets Black architectural memory
The Schoolhouse also places environmental performance alongside cultural identity. Its design incorporates repurposed shipping containers, solar energy systems, and rainwater-management infrastructure, although the supplied project material does not specify the individual systems or their performance figures. These elements position climate resilience as part of the building’s everyday infrastructure rather than as a separate technical layer.
The cultural dimension is equally important. The Black School places the Schoolhouse within a lineage of Black-led educational infrastructure that includes Rosenwald Schools, Freedom Schools, and the Black Panther Liberation Schools. Those precedents combined education with community organization and self-determination; here, that lineage is adapted to a contemporary arts and design context.
This makes the project particularly relevant to a broader question around community infrastructure: what happens when cultural buildings are conceived not simply as places to display or consume culture, but as places where skills, relationships, resources, and collective memory are produced?
The Schoolhouse represents approximately $1.7 million in investment, including major support from the Mellon Foundation alongside community supporters, philanthropic partners, and donors. Its opening marks a shift in The Black School’s work from temporary programming and design research toward a permanent physical presence in the Seventh Ward.

Farage donor scandal turns spotlight on UK polling industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

LONDON — Questions are swirling around the British polling industry — and piling up for the company implicated in a Reform UK party scandal that prompted the resignation of two senior party aides.
The scandal hinged on donations from undercover reporters posing as a wealthy American benefactor and his son that were used to pay for a real set of high-impact polls that were released without disclosing the funding source.
These polls were carried out by the influential opinion research firm JL Partners, which has become a fixture of the British polling landscape since it was founded seven years ago by James Johnson, who served as an adviser to Theresa May when she was prime minister.
Advertisement
Since the sting video first aired last week, former employees and clients of JL Partners have told POLITICO that the company carried out other polls where the funder was not declared — while similar lapses have occurred at other well-known British polling companies.
Rules set out by the British Polling Council, the industry watchdog, specify that all research carried out by pollsters which enters the public domain “must include reference to the… client commissioning the survey” as well as dates, methodology and sample size.
JL Partners did not respond to requests for comment on these fresh claims. The company told Channel 4 News in response to the report about their work for Reform UK last week: “Despite there being no concern about the accuracy of our work, the report did reveal weaknesses in our procedures.”
The British Polling Council said in a statement about the Channel 4 News report that it was “clear there have been breaches” of the watchdog’s rules, adding: “We are seeking further information from the BPC member concerned.”
Reform UK denies any wrongdoing in relation to the sting, which is now under investigation by the Met Police.
Tory leadership races
Johnson’s firm conducted polls on three occasions during the Tory leadership elections in 2022 and 2024 which received press coverage without disclosing who paid for them either in the media reports or in the company’s published tables.
Advertisement
JL Partners conducted internal research for Rishi Sunak’s 2022 bid for the leadership and Tom Tugendhat’s 2024 campaign and Johnson had personal ties to both camps, according to two people linked to the pollster and three people linked the Conservative Party, who were granted anonymity to speak candidly.
Two of these people went further, and claimed allies of the candidates had arranged polls without it ever being disclosed. These polls produced positive findings for the candidates in question and were subsequently shared with the media, the same people said. There is no suggestion the findings were manipulated.
An ally of Sunak denied that his campaign had commissioned the poll in question. Tugendhat declined to comment.
Rishi Sunak leaves No. 10 Downing St. in London in November 2023. | Leon Neal/Getty Images
A JL Partners poll conducted in 2022, which was picked up by the Telegraph, showed Rishi Sunak was rated most highly by Tory voters asked who would make a good prime minister, but did not mention who was behind the poll.
A person familiar with the Telegraph’s publication process said they didn’t have any record of being given any more information than what was published.
Another survey carried out by JL Partners in 2024, covered by the Daily Express, quoted Johnson as saying it was “a good poll for Suella Braverman and Tom Tugendhat” without any mention of who commissioned it. Reach PLC declined to comment on behalf of the Express.
Advertisement
A news item on BBC Radio 5Live in the same year concentrated on a focus group with broadly positive findings for Tugendhat. The focus group was commissioned by the BBC, but it is not known who paid for it.
Dominic Cummings, former chief of staff to Boris Johnson, questioned the BBC Radio 5Live feature at the time, posting on X: “Pollsters should make clear when they are being paid by campaigns. And a media company that cared about honesty to their audience would insist on this.”
A BBC spokesperson told POLITICO: “This focus group was commissioned by BBC Radio 5Live from JL Partners at no cost to the BBC. The BBC understood that no third party had funded or commissioned the work and the programme made clear that the focus group was not representative of wider public opinion.”
Questions for industry
POLITICO also discovered several instances of other pollsters failing to cite their clients.
JL Partners director Johnson wrote an op-ed in the Telegraph earlier this year discussing a shift in public opinion against assisted dying without mentioning the poll cited in the piecewas paid for by the Christian lobbying group CARE.
Johnson, the firm’s founder, has also contributed opinion columns to POLITICO in the past, in some cases citing his polling without disclosing who paid for it.
Advertisement
A recent Opinium poll carried by the website Guido Fawkes which highlighted Londoners would rather have an entrepreneur than an ex-minister as mayor did not state the poll was commissioned by London mayoral hopeful Festus Akinbusoye. While this information was included in an Evening Standard write-up of the poll, it was only published belatedly by Opinium.
A spokesperson for Opinium said: “We take our responsibilities as a member of the British Polling Council seriously and are committed to meeting the requirements that apply when polling enters the public domain.”
They added they had rectified the way the tables were labeled, which they said was due to an “administrative oversight.”
Liberal Democrat placards are stacked against a tree in Surrey, England on March 24, 2026. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images
In another case in January 2023, the Liberal Democrats commissioned Savanta to ask voters who was responsible for the problems the country faces. The respondents were asked to choose between three named Conservative prime ministers, the Conservative Party itself, and the COVID pandemic and the Ukraine war, with no other answers available.
The poll was private until some of its results were briefed to the Observer newspaper, which brought it under the British Polling Council’s transparency rules. Despite this, Savanta did not upload the full tables — confirming the client, sample size and details of the questions and answers — until POLITICO contacted the firm this week.
A Savanta spokesperson said the failure to upload the tables was “an oversight on our part.”
Transparency campaigners have said it is time that polling firms were held to tougher standards.
Tim Picton from the campaign group Spotlight on Corruption said: “These alarming revelations suggest that this is a long-standing issue that goes beyond just one polling company. It is vital that the British Polling Council now investigates these cases and assesses if there is a wider culture of polling companies working hand in glove with political parties while not declaring the relationship.”

Morocco, Spain joust over 2030 World Cup final amid Ceuta crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10

Breadcrumb
Morocco and Spain joust over which will host 2030 World Cup final amid border crisis
Morocco and Spain are arguing over the right to host the 2030 World Cup final — with besieged FIFA boss Gianni Infantino hovering backstage.
FIFA has yet to officially announce which country will host the biggest match of the biggest event in soccer. And even though the 2026 edition just finished with Spain winning the title this summer, Moroccan and Spanish officials are staking their claim on the next final.
The tussle over the soccer match also comes with Spain still reeling from a massive border crossing by tens of thousands of migrants who pushed through the frontier from Morocco into the north African Spanish enclave of Ceuta in late July.
One big game for two proud countries 
The head of Moroccan soccer boasted that his country had it locked up on Thursday.
"The city of Ben Slimane will host the World Cup final. Hate it or love it, and if anyone wants to talk on top of that, let them talk," Moroccan federation president Fouzi Lakjaa told a political rally.
"The city is Ben Slimane, the Hassan II stadium is the stadium, and I hope that Morocco will be playing it," he added.
But FIFA responded to the claim and said that decision has not been made yet, telling multiple news outlets that a host venue for the final will be decided upon "in due course."
This week, the head of the Spanish soccer federation, Rafael Louzán, insisted it was Spain that deserved the game, while acknowledging that it has not been guaranteed that honour.
"We all signed to accept the candidacy … it’s too bad that, regarding the final, it wasn’t made clear, totally clear, where it is to be played," Louzán said. "Spain, as world champion both in men’s and women’s soccer, must host the final."
European soccer officials believe that the sprawling, multi-nation 2030 event, which includes Portugal and even a handful of games in South America, should be considered a European event with the final on the continent.
In a request for comment by the Associated Press on Thursday, FIFA said its decision will be made “in due course."
Infantino has found support in Morocco 
The dispute over the final comes with Infantino under intense pressure after UEFA, the umbrella organisation of European soccer federations, led a successful revolt to scuttle his plan to sell stakes in the World Cup.
By contrast, six Arab nation federations, including Morocco’s, have backed him since that fiasco.
The King Hassan II Stadium is being built in Ben Slimane, a town outside Casablanca. It is planned to seat 115,000 spectators. Spain can offer the home stadiums of Real Madrid or Barcelona as potential sites for the final.
Infantino has recently made two trips to Morocco, meeting with King Mohammed VI during annual celebrations of his ascent to the throne in July and then holding a FIFA crisis meeting there in August.
World Cup final spat among other tensions 
When confirmed three years ago, the joint candidacy between Spain, Portugal and Morocco looked like a perfect event to bridge Europe and Africa and strengthen bonds between the western Mediterranean neighbours.
But the dispute over the final comes with diplomatic tensions between Madrid and Rabat already frayed over who was responsible when tens of thousands of mostly Moroccans driven by posts on social media pushed into the small Spanish enclave of Ceuta that borders Morocco. Spain's prime minister said 140 people died in the crossing.
Spain’s government has been under political pressure at home to get tough on Morocco, which it has said acted in good faith in the border crisis. Spanish police assessments couldn’t rule out complicity by Moroccan security forces but said that it was unlikely the Moroccan government had intentionally orchestrated it.

Thousands of Food-Packaging Chemicals Lack Safety Data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:57:48 UTC
00:57:48 KST

We don’t often look with suspicion at the plastic wrapping a block of cheddar, the waxed carton containing milk, or the plastic bottle of ketchup. We expect food packaging to be more or less inert—breakfast isn’t supposed to come with a side of chemicals, after all.
But evidence suggests that many food-contact materials, as food packaging is known, leach chemicals into the products they house. The most famous of these is likely bisphenol A (BPA), an ingredient in plastic that is a potent endocrine disrupter. In 2025, the E.U. banned BPA’s use in food-contact materials, and in the U.S. it’s banned in baby bottles, sippy cups, and formula packaging.
But when one chemical is demonized, its replacement may not be any safer, says Helene Weisinger, a chemist at the Swiss nonprofit Food Packaging Forum. (BPA, for instance, is often replaced with BPS, which turns out to have similar issues.) It’s “chemical whack-a-mole,” Weisinger says.
In a recent paper in Environmental Science and Technology, she and her colleagues propose a new system for avoiding this situation, in which chemically similar substances are grouped together and may be banned or regulated together, rather than one by one—an idea that could simplify what’s proving to be a difficult process.
A lack of safety information about food packaging
The chemicals we encounter in daily life aren’t well understood. “There's 350,000 chemicals that are put on global markets, and for a lot of those, we have relatively little information about their toxicity. They've not been exhaustively tested,” says Olwenn Martin, an associate professor in health and environment at University College London who was not involved in the new research. “That's something that, in my world, is well known, and probably for the general public would come as a bit of a shock.”
Chemicals used in food packaging are little different; the health effects of relatively few are well-understood. Out of about 15,000 chemicals used in food-contact materials, 1,222 have known major health risks, the researchers state in the new paper, while there is little information on most of the others. “People kept asking us, ‘We can't do measurements for 15,000 chemicals. What should we really be concerned about?’ And that is kind of how we started off with the study,” says Weisinger.
The team sorted known food-contact chemicals into structurally related groups, identifying 38 groups where many of the members had clear health risks. Each group contained numerous compounds whose health effects are still a question mark, which the researchers point out should be addressed in future studies. But even in the absence of further toxicological work, says Martin, this information could be used to regulate similar chemicals en masse, helping to avoid chemical whack-a-mole.
“The backlog is such that it would take hundreds, if not thousands, of years to test all of these chemicals at current rates, and even regulatory bodies are looking at different ways of doing this,” she says. “One of the ways is by grouping chemicals: looking at chemicals that are fairly similar—structurally or through other means—to be able to make assumptions about chemicals in this group and regulate them as a group.”
Regulating chemicals can make a big difference in reducing people’s exposure, if done correctly, says Martin Wagner, a biologist at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology who studies the health effects of plastics and who was not involved in the new research. As a result of stricter rules in Europe against BPA and other dangerous substances, “we're seeing in European populations that levels of exposure to phthalates and to regulated bisphenols, BPA and so on, are dropping, which is a good thing, “ he says. “But at the same time, we see that the level of exposure in Europeans to all these alternative chemicals is increasing.” Banning entire groups of chemicals might stop this kind of unfortunate substitution.
The push to put safety first
Even if governments grouped chemicals to lighten the regulatory load, there are still many substances to be assessed—some of them that even the people making the materials may not know about. “The problem with food-contact materials and with plastics is that these are really incredibly complex materials, and our research in the lab is showing they contain a lot of unknown chemicals,” says Wagner.
Plastics manufacturing, for instance, involves chemical steps that are known to generate other products, and contaminants are not uncommon in the materials used to make food-contact materials. “We call them non-intentionally added substances,” says Wagner. “We have no way of making sure that all these compounds are safe. Yet we know that these are leaching into food, into water. So people are very likely to be exposed to that complex mixture of compounds with very little oversight.”

46 days before Israel election, neither bloc assured of forming government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:57:07 UTC
00:57:07 KST

With 46 days to go before Israel’s general election, the country faces a political deadlock as opinion polls show neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition securing enough seats to form the next government.
Polls show the opposition Yashar party, led by former Israeli army chief Gadi Eisenkot, ahead of Netanyahu’s Likud.
Eisenkot also leads Netanyahu in polls asking who is better suited to serve as prime minister, but that does not guarantee that he could form a government.
Israel’s prime minister is not directly elected. Instead, the task of forming a government is entrusted to the politician who can secure the support of at least 61 lawmakers in the 120-seat Knesset.
Israel’s general election is scheduled for Oct. 27, with Netanyahu’s bloc competing against the opposition parties.
Blocs tied
A poll published by Israel’s public broadcaster KAN on Wednesday evening showed Netanyahu’s bloc and the opposition each winning 52 seats if elections were held that day, while Arab lawmakers would take 12 seats and an alliance led by Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha would win four.
Hendel, who is identified with the political right, has not said which bloc he would support in forming a government.
The four seats projected for his alliance would also be insufficient on their own to give either camp the 61-seats needed to form a government.
A similar picture emerged from a poll published by Israel’s Channel 13 on Wednesday evening.
According to the results, Netanyahu’s bloc and the opposition would each win 53 seats, while Arab lawmakers would secure 14.
Arab lawmakers
Based on these figures, the Jewish opposition could theoretically reach an understanding with Arab lawmakers that would allow it to form an alternative government, but significant political obstacles remain.
Most leaders of Jewish opposition parties reject the idea of relying on Arab lawmakers to form a government, while Netanyahu and his allies have focused their campaign on warning against a government that depends on their support.
Any agreement by Arab lawmakers to support the opposition would also come with demands, particularly regarding the needs of Arab citizens in Israel and Palestinian rights in the occupied territories.
Netanyahu has focused heavily in his election rhetoric on the possibility that the opposition could rely on Arab lawmakers, particularly the United Arab List headed by Mansour Abbas, which helped establish the so-called change government led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid in 2021.
That marked the first time an Israeli government was formed with the support of an Arab party, and Netanyahu is seeking to prevent a repeat of that scenario in the upcoming election.
Possibility of another election
If the political map remains unchanged, Israel could once again face multiple elections until one of the blocs manages to secure enough support to form a government.
Israel previously held three successive elections in April 2019, September 2019 and March 2020 before a government was eventually formed in 2021.
Israeli observers do not rule out a similar scenario if the Oct. 27 vote fails to produce a clear majority.
Such a possibility would be significant for Netanyahu because, in the event of another election, he would remain prime minister of a caretaker government until an alternative government could be formed.
Observers say Netanyahu would prefer either to form the next government himself, even as part of a national unity government, or at least to prevent the opposition from establishing an alternative coalition.
Concerns over accepting results
Alongside concerns over a potential inability to form a government, there are also fears in Israel that some groups could refuse to accept the election results if their side is defeated.
The Israel Democracy Institute said in a poll published Wednesday that 56% of Israelis believe there is a high likelihood that some elements on the “losing side” would refuse to accept the declared results and resort to force in an attempt to alter them.
According to the institute, the proportion holding this view was similar among Jewish and Arab respondents.
An analysis of Jewish respondents by political affiliation found that a clear majority of centrists, and an even larger majority of those on the left, viewed such a scenario as possible.
The figure was lower among right-wing respondents but still slightly more than half.
The upcoming election is widely seen as critical to the political future of Netanyahu and the far-right parties participating in his government.
Netanyahu has led the current government since late December 2022, which is widely described as the most right-wing government in Israel’s history.
He has also been the subject of an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court since 2024 over war crimes against Palestinians in Gaza.
Netanyahu has refused to accept responsibility for the failures preceding the Oct. 7 events, instead placing responsibility on the military and security agencies, while his opponents have demanded that he accept political responsibility.

Bayeux Tapestry ‘mania’ sweeps UK as sold-out exhibition of 1,000-year-old medieval artwork opens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:56:12 UTC
00:56:12 KST

Bayeux Tapestry ‘mania’ sweeps UK as sold-out exhibition of 1,000-year-old medieval artwork opens
- The Bayeux Tapestry, depicting the 1066 Norman conquest, is on display in London for the first time outside France, attracting huge public excitement and selling 100,000 tickets.
- The exhibition is a symbolic gesture of renewed UK-France relations post-Brexit, featuring animations and careful conservation of the nearly 1,000-year-old tapestry.
- The event has sparked widespread cultural interest, inspiring themed products, school trips, and increased tourism at related historical sites across the UK.
AI generated
LONDON - London’s Bayeux Tapestry exhibition opened on Sept 10 to a British public gripped by “mania” over the medieval artwork depicting the Norman conquest of England, on display outside France for the first time.
Excited visitors who had tickets for the first day of the sold-out exhibition queued outside the British Museum ahead of the opening, where some staff had donned period costumes.
“It is back here for the first time in 950 years!” 46-year-old Catherine Pitt told AFP in the queue outside the museum entrance.
“It is like a big bang moment in our history,” she added.
The unprecedented loan from France, the result of years of diplomacy and set to last until July 2027, has been hailed as a symbol of renewed cross-Channel ties following the rancour of Brexit.
The Times newspaper called the exhibition a “spine-shivering experience” that has sparked “Tapestry-mania” in Britain, while The Economist dubbed it the “hottest ticket” around.
Depicting the 1066 Battle of Hastings and the invasion by William the Conqueror’s Norman army, the 70m-long tapestry has shadowy origins.
It is widely thought to have been made in England almost 1,000 years ago before being transferred to Bayeux in France.
“I am amazed it is in such a good condition. It has survived all these years,” retiree John Heys, 74, told AFP after seeing the exhibition.
Fifty-two-year-old Jenny said it was “moving”, perusing the museum shop stocked with tapestry-themed mugs, dish towels and puzzles.
“It is quite brutal. It is real people in a battle, with death on both sides,” she added, not wanting to share her last name.
The British Museum has so far sold a record 100,000 tickets, which cost £25-£33 (S$42-S$56) for adults.
‘Emotional’
King Charles III said the temporary transfer was “a precious symbol of trust at a time when trust seems sadly to be in short supply between nations”.
“The colours are beautiful. Illustrations look very modern. For the younger generation it is going to spark interest, more than some history lessons!” said Mela Prasens, 58, after viewing the exhibition.
“It was beautiful, an emotional experience,” added Prasens, who lives in New York.
Around the country, students who learn about the artwork in history classes are gearing up for school trips, while businesses are bidding to capitalise on some of the fervour.
Luxury store Liberty has released cushions inspired by the artwork, priced at £165 each, while budget bakery chain Greggs has unveiled its own embroidered “Ta-Pastry”.
A museum in Reading, west of London, is enjoying a flurry of attention for its little-known Victorian replica of the tapestry, and in the south-east, the Battle of Hastings site anticipated greater footfall from those who missed out on exhibition tickets.
In the heart of the capital, near the British Museum, a pub has hung up an 8m embroidered “Beer Tapestry” recounting the history of brewing in a playful tribute to the more violent original.
“I think it’s quite hard to explain to French people the excitement in the UK. I think the French don’t realise what a big treasure they’ve got,” exhibition curator Michael Lewis told AFP during a preview.
“The British are kind of completely crazy about this object because it’s such a fundamentally important object for our history.”
‘Processional experience’
Plans to loan the tapestry to London had been considered twice before, but both were aborted – in 1953 for the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II, and in 1966 for the 900th anniversary of the Battle of Hastings.
In what is believed to be its first time travelling outside France, the tapestry depicting 627 figures and more than 700 animals has been laid flat in a raised glass cabinet.
In its home in Bayeux, it is displayed hanging vertically.
Animations projected on the wall accompany the tapestry, zooming in on details and key events in the artwork, which is replete with gore and drama.
“It’s quite a processional experience because people have to go bit by bit through the tapestry,” Lewis said.
Ticket-holders have 40 minutes to spend inside the exhibition once they enter.
Conservators watched nervously as the delicate, 11th-century artwork was transported by truck in a risky operation from its home in northern France to the British capital in July.
France said last week that two broken threads were spotted during a full condition check.
However, the British Museum said the embroidery was “virtually unchanged”, with thread breaks, measuring a few millimetres at most, not considered significant damage. AFP

Ahmed Hassan and Lina Altawell
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
Moroccan Football Federation President Fouzi Lekjaa said Thursday that the 2030 FIFA World Cup final will be held at the Hassan II Stadium that is under construction in Ben Slimane province, near Casablanca.
“Ben Slimane province will have the honor of hosting the 2030 World Cup final,” Lekjaa said on the sidelines of an event in Bouznika.
“I hope the final will be between Morocco and France, so we can settle the score,” he added.
Morocco lost 2-0 to France in the semifinals of the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, before the two teams again met in the quarterfinals of the 2026 tournament. France also won that match by the same scoreline.
Morocco will co-host the 2030 World Cup with Spain and Portugal. The tournament’s first three matches will be held in Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay to mark 100 years since the first World Cup.
FIFA has not announced which city will host the final, with Morocco and Spain showing interest in staging the match.
Ben Slimane province is around 55 kilometers (34 miles) from Casablanca, and is currently witnessing construction on Hassan II Stadium, which is expected to have a capacity of around 115,000 spectators, making it one of the world’s largest football stadiums once completed.
Spanish Football Federation President Rafael Louzan had earlier expressed his country’s desire to host the final, saying Spain believes it has the capabilities to stage the major event.
Last month, FIFA said media reports claiming that President Gianni Infantino had made any promise in relation to Morocco hosting the final were “false and misleading,” stressing that no decision has been made by the world football governing body.
The 2030 World Cup will be held during the centenary of the tournament, after Uruguay hosted the first edition in 1930.

Statement on support for ITU's regulatory framework for frequency management.
France
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
17:55:00 CEST
00:55:00 KST

Signatures : Angola, Armenia, Austria, Bahrain, Belgium, Bulgaria, Cambodia, Croatia, Cyprus, Djibouti, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Finland, France, Georgia, Germany, Hungary, Iceland, Ireland, Israel, Italy, Japan, Kazakhstan, Latvia, Luxembourg, Madagascar, Malta, Monaco, Netherlands, Norway, Philippines, Poland, Rwanda, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey, United Kingdom, European Space Agency (ESA).
The International Telecommunications Union (ITU) plays a fundamental role in maintaining the international framework for the use of the radio frequency spectrum and associated satellite orbits. It supports interference-managed environment for radiocommunication systems worldwide - a crucial issue for space services. This ITU framework is based on the Radio Regulations, a binding international treaty, revised every four years at World Radiocommunication Conferences (WRC), which set out rules and procedures governing the registration, coordination and protection of ITU Member States’ rights of use, in particular for space assignments.
We support the role of ITU as the primary global entity responsible for the efficient and sustainable use of the radio frequency spectrum and associated orbit. We acknowledge that the ITU has successfully accommodated and facilitated the development of satellite systems including large constellations and a wide range of new-space applications. We are confident that the Radio Regulations will continue to evolve to adapt to new scientific and technological development and that the ITU will continue to implement this framework in a fair, transparent and effective manner.
In an evolving geopolitical context, we firmly believe that adherence to the ITU global governance of radio frequency spectrum and satellite orbits, rooted in a multilateralism based on international Law and the ITU constitution and convention, is the essential foundation for nations for the coordination of radiocommunication systems to prevent harmful interference between satellite systems and for the development of their space radiocommunication policy while avoiding harmful interference between satellites.
The frequency registration procedures managed by the ITU foster equitable access to spectrum and associated orbits, with, today, all 194 ITU Member States having national resources in the ITU Space Plan and more than 100 administrations having additional satellite assignments, including 56 for geostationary orbit. The ITU allows many developing countries to develop their own satellite capabilities free from harmful radio interference, in order to meet the connectivity needs of their populations. This equitable access to spectrum and orbit resources, particularly to developing countries, supports the broader goal of reducing the digital divide, as pursued through the ITU’s development mandate.
We note that studies relating to the framework established in the Radio Regulations for the protection of geostationary networks (GSO) from non-geostationary (NGSO) constellations will be reported to WRC-27. In this context, it will be important to ensure conducive environment for both technologies and to maintain a reliable protection of geostationary networks with clear, measurable and predictable interference environment, particularly in the Ku and Ka bands, while ensuring that NGSO systems are not unduly constrained. Any future evolution of the radio regulation should remain proportionate, evidence-based and technology-neutral, ensuring effective protection of GSO networks while facilitating the development and deployment of NGSO systems. WRC-27 will also consider the topic of satellite Direct-to-Device communications, taking into account aspects such as supporting innovation and resilient coverage, protecting terrestrial networks, and preserving technology neutrality and spectrum efficiency.
We stress the importance for any satellite system to strictly comply with Radio Regulations rules governing the protection of GSO networks as well as with the coordination procedures applicable to constellations using the same frequency bands. This is essential to ensure the continuity of satellite services that support public space services and governmental satellite services, while also enabling the efficient deployment and operation of NGSO constellations within a technology neutral framework that fosters innovation and access to spectrum.
Based on ITU rules and procedures, we remain firmly committed to protecting our satellite systems from harmful interference.
This statement is not a legally binding document and does not create legal rights or obligations under domestic or international law.

TV presenter v secret son: the succession dispute engulfing a Ugandan kingdom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:53:29 UTC
00:53:29 KST

A traditional Ugandan kingdom has become engulfed in a bitter succession dispute after the family of a king who recently died rejected the selection of a television news anchor as his successor.
King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who became the world’s youngest reigning monarch when he took the throne in the kingdom of Tooro in 1995 at the age of three, died on 27 August in the US, where he was receiving cancer treatment.
On Wednesday, the royal clan’s succession committee announced it had chosen Oyo’s cousin Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, a news anchor and editor at the public broadcaster UBC, as crown prince.
However, at a press conference held later the same day, Oyo’s sister, Princess Ruth Nsemere Komuntale, said that according to her brother’s will, a son whose existence had not been publicly known until his death should succeed him.
The kingdom’s spokesperson shared a section of the document, which says: “I hereby declare and direct that if, at the date of my death, I am survived by a son lawfully recognised as my biological son, I appoint him as my heir to the throne of the kingdom of Tooro.”
In a statement on Thursday, Oyo’s mother, Queen Mother Best Kemigisa Akiiki, denounced a “self-appointed group of clan members” who had selected a new king despite having had the will read to them hours earlier.
She also claimed that the royal family had been put under house arrest. Troops had “removed the royal guards without notice, and ... were deployed around the palace,” she said. “We cannot leave or receive people freely.”
Oyo was unmarried and was not known to have any children. The Tooro kingdom’s prime minister, Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki, revealed the existence of a son in a social media post on 27 August when announcing Oyo’s death.
“His majesty leaves behind a prince as his heir, whose identity will be formally revealed at the appropriate time, in accordance with the traditions and customs of Tooro kingdom,” he said.
Another contender had been Prince George Desmond-Kamurasi, who plays for the London amateur football club South East Dons. According to the committee, the goalkeeper had declined the offer of the throne because of his other responsibilities.
The Tooro king is selected by a succession committee appointed by the royal clan. A committee member told the local NTV station that a royal child must be officially introduced to elders in order to be considered for leadership.
Andrew Mwenda, a prominent Ugandan journalist and relative of the royal family, wrote on X on Thursday that Oyo’s family had not been able to produce a photo of the purported son, and declined to disclose details about the family of the boy’s mother. He added that, in Tooro, a king’s son could only succeed him if he were born to a queen officially married to the king.
The prime minister called for restraint on Thursday. “There will be time to examine the will, to hear those advancing a different position, and to consider our customs, the applicable law and the proper institutions through which succession should be determined,” he said in a social media post.
“That process should take place calmly and credibly, not through competing announcements, confrontation, or attempts to establish facts on the ground while our king still awaits burial.”
Edward, a popular TV news presenter, is the son of Prince Christopher Paul Kijanangoma and a grandson of the former king George David Rukidi III.
Oyo, who was crowned after his father’s death, will be buried on Saturday at the Karambi royal tombs in the kingdom’s capital of Fort Portal in western Uganda.
Uganda has several ancient kingdoms that lack formal sovereignty, but whose leaders are revered as symbols of tradition and wield vast social influence. Tooro is one of five that are recognised by the government. Their monarchs have no political authority and are legally barred from engaging in partisan politics.
In 1967 Uganda’s then president, Milton Obote, abolished the kingdoms, saying he wanted to unify the country. They were restored by the current president, Yoweri Museveni, in 1993.
The Tooro are the latest African royal family to become mired in a succession dispute. King Misuzulu Sinqobile kaZwelithini, the reigning king of the Zulu people in South Africa, waited 15 months for his coronation after the death of his father because of a bitter feud involving accusations of forgery and poisoning.
Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

Cabinet approves decree, diesel tax cut extended by one week
The measure will remain in effect until Thursday, September 17
ROME,
10 September 2026, 17:50
ANSA English Desk
Share
Link copiato
- ALL RIGHTS RESERVED
The Italian cabinet on Thursday
approved a new decree-law addressing high fuel prices, extending
a 17 cent per litre cut in excise duties on diesel—which was
otherwise set to expire at midnight—by one week.
The measure will therefore remain in effect until Thursday,
September 17.
The measure was introduced to mitigate the effects of the Iran
war in helping push fuel prices higher.
Critics have said the government should include petrol duties
too.

International declaration on space-based scientific data.
France
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
17:50:00 CEST
00:50:00 KST

Signatures : Angola, Armenia, Australia, Austria, Bahrain, Belgium, Bulgaria, Cambodia, Chile, Costa Rica, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Denmark, Ecuador, France, Georgia, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, Ireland, Israel, Italy, Jordan, Kazakhstan, Korea, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Madagascar, Malta, Mauritius, Mexico, Monaco, Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Philippines, Romania, Rwanda, Saudi Arabia, Serbia, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Tunisia, Turkey, United Kingdom, European Space Agency (ESA).
Space-based scientific data – acquired by Earth or Universe observation satellites – has become of utmost importance. Be it for exploring the Universe or monitoring the Earth, it contributes to the advancement of human knowledge and provides scientists, as well as policy makers and citizens with an unprecedented perspective and understanding of our world. To extract and provide relevant information and knowledge to users, scientists need high quality and long-term space-based scientific data that is accessible and reachable everywhere in the world, but also as open as possible in order to be used by any competent person, as well as trustworthy (i.e. reliable and resilient) through the guarantee of its integrity. The following declaration aims at affirming and raising awareness on the need for space-based scientific data to be used around the world at a time when collaborative science is key to understanding our planet and our Universe.
Preamble
We, the Participants,
Having gathered to reaffirm our shared priority for the scientific use of space-based data, at a time of profound transformation of the space and data domains;
Recognizing the growing importance of space-based data for scientific and knowledge purposes, natural resource management, disaster management and emergency response, security, and for sustainable human development and related international goals;
Acknowledging the critical role of accessibility, openness, interoperability and integrity of data in fostering innovation, transparency, and balanced international cooperation;
Affirming our support for Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable (FAIR) principles including integrity;
Emphasizing that research, innovation and education are fundamental drivers of progress in the domains using space-based data, indispensable to our ability to meet global challenges ; that the strategic deployment of space science and its subsequent data depends on strong research ecosystems supported by the development of relevant capacities and the training of highly skilled scientists, engineers and operators capable of advancing knowledge and developing sustainable solutions.
Admit the following shared values and priorities.
Shared Values and Priorities
1. Accessibility
We affirm that space-based scientific data will be accessible to all, without discrimination, except for justified exceptions (e.g. national security, public safety, defense, safeguarding of personal data). To this end, and where appropriate, we encourage to pursue open standards and common formats to facilitate data exchange and reuse, and to develop open international platforms for data storage, dissemination, and access.
2. Openness
We underline the need to use open licenses to encourage reuse and dissemination. These data will thus be published according to the aforementioned principles and, where possible and appropriate, as open data to encourage reuse and dissemination. This also implies a comprehensive documentation of data collection, processing, and validation methods where metadata will be complete, accurate, and accompanied by a clear license defining the provisions regarding reuse.
3. Integrity
We emphasize that integrity is necessary for space-based scientific data, implying where appropriate an implementation of traceability and versioning systems to ensure data authenticity and integrity, protection against falsification through the use of verification technologies and independent validation protocols, and accountability. The users are encouraged not to alter the original datasets without preserving provenance or claim of its ownership.
4. International Cooperation
We recognize that providing all the adequate data to the scientific community is a collective responsibility for all stakeholders to produce, acquire, and share data on a reciprocal basis. We commit to strengthening multilateral collaboration, reciprocity, transparency and the dissemination of the subsequent information by harmonizing standards, formats, and protocols for data exchange and sharing. Existing initiatives and research programs must be supported and expanded to maximize the impact of space based scientific data and to improve capacity and skills development.
We thus affirm our collective determination to promote accessible, open and integrity-protected space-based scientific data, while recognizing appropriate conditions for their uses.
We invite all stakeholders (states, agencies, companies, researchers) to sign the declaration.
We are looking forward to periodic reviews to adjust the declaration to societal, technological and scientific advances.

Ukrainian Ballistic Missiles To Strike Russia in Just a Few Weeks — Fire Point CEO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:47:12 UTC
00:47:12 KST

Ballistic missiles manufactured by Fire Point will strike targets on Russian territory in just a few weeks.
Iryna Terekh, the company’s CEO, announced this on the sidelines of the “Photonics4Defense 2026: Technology Exchange & Matchmaking” event.
According to her, the FP-7 has already successfully completed two stages of testing. The company is now preparing to test the product under combat conditions. This stage is also part of the missile’s certification process.
“We expect it to be ready for deployment very soon. We’re talking about weeks, not months,” Terekh noted.
She explained that the initial stages of missile testing involve ground and laboratory tests, during which each system and subsystem—including the rocket engine and navigation equipment—is tested separately.
This is followed by flight tests, during which the company collects data on the missile’s performance and compares its actual characteristics with the calculated ones.
The third stage, which the company is currently preparing for, involves testing under combat conditions. In late November 2025, it was announced that the company planned to complete the codification process for the FP-7 tactical ballistic missile with the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense by the end of 2025.
In early February 2026, Denys Shtilierrman clarified in an interview with DW that, despite hopes that the missile would enter service by the end of 2025, a “series of events” had prevented this from happening—‘we hope to complete all tests in February’.
At the same time, the FP-9 is currently undergoing flight tests, meaning it is in the second phase.
The developers note that testing the FP-9 is harder to organize because of its long range. The missile has a minimum ballistic flight distance beyond which it can no longer be programmatically stopped.
Because of this, Ukraine’s territory is insufficient for a full-scale test of the FP-9. Therefore, once the current phase is complete, its military testing may immediately proceed to operations against Russian targets.
Militarnyi previously reported that in July 2026, Denys Shtilierman, Fire Point’s chief designer, stated that the only thing standing between the start of FP-9 ballistic missile tests—involving strikes on Russia—and their implementation is the testing of the solid-fuel engine.

The IMF has maintained its forecast for global economic growth at 3% in 2026
Kyiv • UNN
The global economy weathered the energy shock better than expected. The IMF warned of high energy prices, debt and inflation risks.
On Thursday, the IMF said that the global economy had weathered the energy shock caused by the conflict in the Middle East better than expected and that global economic growth in 2026 is still forecast at around 3%, but the fund warned that risks remain high, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
Julie Kozack, a spokesperson for the International Monetary Fund, told reporters that oil and gas prices remain high and that the energy shock caused by the conflict has not yet been overcome. She also noted the growing global debt burden and the halting of the disinflation process that began after the 2022 cost-of-living crisis.
At a regular IMF briefing, Kozack said that global inflation expectations had risen but remained stable and well anchored over the long term.

UN expert Albanese, protesters warn against Italy’s anti-Semitism bill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:46:52 UTC
00:46:52 KST

UN expert Albanese, protesters warn against Italy’s anti-Semitism bill
Protesters in Rome and UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese warn proposed law could silence criticism of Israel.
Rome, Italy – “Anti-Zionism is not anti-Semitism”, read the black-and-yellow signs distributed by Amnesty International outside the Italian parliament on Wednesday afternoon.
Hundreds gathered in front of Montecitorio Square in Rome to oppose Italy’s so-called anti-Semitism bill.
The demonstration was organised to coincide with a meeting of the Chamber of Deputies’ Constitutional Affairs Committee, which is examining legislation approved by the Senate on March 4 by a large majority. Under Italy’s constitutional system, a bill must be approved by both chambers in the same text before it can become law.
“We are tired of seeing anti-Semitism instrumentalised to promote censorship of any kind of criticism of the State of Israel and its criminal policies,” said Daniel Calo, of Tikkun, a group of Italian Jewish antiracism activists.
“In the face of this shameful bill, we reiterate once again, forcefully, that opposing Zionism is not anti-Semitism.”
At the centre of the controversy is the possible adoption into national law of the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s (IHRA) definition of anti-Semitism, which critics argue conflates anti-Semitism with criticism of Israel.
According to the IHRA, “denying the Jewish people their right to self-determination, eg, by claiming that the existence of a State of Israel is a racist endeavor”, is anti-Semitic, as is “drawing comparisons of contemporary Israeli policy to that of the Nazis”.
Anneliese Baldaccini of Amnesty International Italy said the bill, if adopted, would apply across schools, universities, social platforms and cultural associations.
The proposed law is “based on a definition that censors political criticism”, she said.
Activists argue that existing legislation already provides the tools to combat hate crimes.
They are instead calling for the adoption of the Jerusalem Declaration on Antisemitism, a non-binding set of guidelines that seeks to combat anti-Semitism while protecting freedom of expression that was developed in response to the IHRA definition.
Speaking to Al Jazeera, Francesca Albanese, the Italian legal scholar and UN special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the occupied Palestinian territory, said legislation equating criticism of a state with anti-Semitism risked restricting freedom of expression.
“Any piece of legislation that directly or indirectly equates criticism of a state with anti-Semitism is problematic and risks creating more problems than it seeks to solve,” Albanese said.
She argued that the bill could limit the ability to analyse, document and criticise the “apartheid state of Israel”, and accused Italy of prioritising the protection of Israel over accountability.
“The need to protect the State of Israel from criticism is stronger than the need to do justice,” she said. “It is extremely dangerous because every Jewish person in the world risks being seen as a kind of emissary of Israel.”
She described Italy, under the current government, as one of Europe’s strongest defenders of Israel.
Tony La Piccirella, a Palestine solidarity activist who was part of the Global Sumud Flotilla, said he worried that the bill “provides a legal instrument to attack newsrooms, online information platforms and social media, in order to silence anyone who denounces the genocide and the entire economic system that sustains it”.
But the legislation has received strong backing from Italy’s Jewish institutional leadership.
Noemi Di Segni, president of the Union of Italian Jewish Communities (UCEI), was heard by the Senate’s Constitutional Affairs Committee in January and described legislative action against anti-Semitism as “urgent and unavoidable”.
Di Segni, who was born in Jerusalem and has served in the Israeli military, has repeatedly rejected describing Israel’s war in Gaza as genocide.
In January 2025, she called such accusations “unacceptable”, arguing that terms including “genocide”, “concentration camp”, “starve”, “Nazi” and “apartheid” should not be used to describe Israel’s conduct.
The bill has exposed divisions that cut across the government-opposition divide.
It was approved by the Senate by a large majority that included much of the opposition. Six Democratic Party senators voted in favour, while the party as a whole abstained, and those divisions have continued in the Chamber.
Among the bill’s most outspoken opponents is Stefania Ascari, of the Five Star Movement, who addressed protesters before entering parliament.
“The greatest danger to Jews and to the entire world is the terrorist state of Israel,” Ascari said. She accused the bill of targeting “freedom of expression, the autonomy of universities, [and] the work of associations and NGOs”.
The committee’s sitting ended without a vote or substantive examination.
Its work is expected to resume next week, although the timetable remains uncertain. The Chamber has scheduled a final plenary vote for October 2, leaving parliament a narrow window to complete the committee stage.
In the meantime, activists say they will continue to gather outside parliament and on the streets, to vent their concerns.

International declaration on Copernicus programme.
France
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
17:45:00 CEST
00:45:00 KST

Signatures : Armenia, Australia, Austria, Bahrein, Belgium, Brazil, Bulgaria, Cambodia, Canada, Chile, Costa Rica, Croatia, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Djibouti, Ecuador, Estonia, Finland, Georgia, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, Ireland, Israel, Italy, Japan, Latvia, Luxembourg, Malta, Mauritius, Mexico, Morocco, Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Philippines, Poland, Romania, Rwanda, Saudi Arabia, Serbia, Singapore, Slovakia, Slovenia, South Korea, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Türkiye, United Arab Emirates, United Kingdom, European Space Agency, UN Office of Outer Space Affairs (UNOOSA).
We, the representatives of the Member States of the European Union, Copernicus participating States, intergovernmental organisations, space agencies, scientific institutions and international partners, gathered in Paris on the occasion of the International Space Summit of 9–10 September 2026,
Recalling the commitments undertaken under the Paris Agreement on climate change, the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction, and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals;
Recognising the essential role of Earth observation in advancing our understanding of the planet, protecting the environment, ensuring the sustainable management of natural resources, anticipating and responding to natural disasters, and strengthening resilience to global challenges;
Emphasising that Earth observation data and services have become indispensable tools for evidence-based policymaking, sustainable economic development, civil protection, security, scientific research, innovation, and international cooperation;
Recalling that Copernicus, the European Union’s Earth observation programme, implemented since 2014 in partnership with the European Space Agency (ESA), other European institutions and participating states, represents the world’s most comprehensive and advanced civilian Earth observation capability, providing free, full and open access to data and services for the benefit of citizens, public authorities and the scientific community;
Reaffirming that free, full and open access to Earth observation data fosters innovation, scientific cooperation, transparency and informed decision-making in addressing climate, environmental and societal challenges as well as essential support during crises situations
An Unprecedented Scientific and Operational Impact
Recognising the considerable added value generated by Copernicus over the past decade for societies worldwide ; welcoming the contribution of its Sentinel missions as well as its operational services, whose monitoring, mapping and forecasting activities enable more eAective and faster responses to natural disasters and support informed decision-making across all continents in areas such as energy, water resource and environmental management, agriculture, public health, cultural heritage and emergency response;
Emphasising the essential contribution of Copernicus, and its free, full and open data policy to scientific research ; recalling the importance of a programme based on continuity, reliability and long-term consistency in order to provide the reference datasets that are indispensable to global assessment reports such as the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) as well as monitoring of the implementation of multilateral environmental agreement and biodiversity conservation policies;
Recognising that Copernicus now acts as a true multiplier of economic, socioeconomic and security benefits e.g. for health and urban ecosystems, marine and land ecosystems, risk management, civil resilience, food security, agriculture and water management.
Recognising that the proven success and global value of Copernicus require preserving its established governance, operational continuity and user-oriented approach, while further strengthening existing mechanisms for dialogue and co-creation, including the Copernicus User Forum and Copernicus National Collaboration Programmes.
An International Dimension
Recognising the profoundly international dimension of the Copernicus Programme, with partner countries and major multilateral organisations, including the World Meteorological Organization, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), and the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) ; recalling that Copernicus makes an essential contribution to the objectives of the Group on Earth Observations (GEO), including through its activities e.g. in the areas of food security, land degradation neutrality and wildfire management;
Considering that only cooperation among institutions can enable the co-development of solutions tailored to the specific needs of Copernicus users in partner countries and developing countries, while addressing the linguistic, technical and institutional barriers to their uptake ; emphasising that the full potential of Copernicus depends on facilitating access to, and promoting the wider use of, the data, services and knowledge;
Recalling the need to protect the radio-frequency spectrum resources essential for Copernicus and Earth Observation services to ensure the continuity and reliability of Copernicus observations ;
Approve the present declaration :
We express our strong support for the Copernicus Programme, convinced that it constitutes a global public good whose continuity is essential to addressing today’s global challenges.
We call on the European Union, the Copernicus Participating States and its partners to :
- position the Copernicus Programme among the highest priorities of the European and international space agenda;
- support the development and deployment of the expansion missions and next generations of Copernicus satellites as well as the Copernicus services, in order to ensure the longterm continuity, reliability and scientific applicability of the data and information essential for long-term climate trend analysis, as well as for ensuring accurate monitoring of the environment and providing support to civil security;
- step up eAorts to promote data exchange and knowledge sharing among Copernicus partners by making full use of existing and future data infrastructures and platforms;
- work towards the recognition of Copernicus as an essential component of the Global Earth Observation System in all relevant multilateral fora;
- ensure that the Copernicus Programme remains open to the participation of trusted partner countries on fair terms.
The present declaration creates no additional financial obligations for the signatory States.

Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to hold detailed talks on the sidelines of the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit later this year, a Kremlin aide said Thursday.
Russian presidential aide Yury Ushakov told reporters that the two presidents agreed to hold the meeting during their contacts on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in the Kyrgyz capital last week.
The APEC summit will take place in the Chinese city of Shenzhen from Nov. 18-19.
Ushakov said earlier this month that Putin may hold a trilateral meeting with Xi and US President Donald Trump at the summit.

Expressing that the president’s first talks upon his arrival Friday will be with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Ushakov said Putin will hold several meetings on the sidelines of the summit, including with South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, as well as Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.
He said Putin will participate in the BRICS Business Forum, and denied there are plans for a meeting between Putin and Xi on the sidelines of the summit. Ushakov stated his belief, however, that the two presidents will communicate face-to-face behind the scenes.
Ushakov went on to define BRICS as a “highly popular brand” associated with “genuine multilateralism,” stating it has gained significant weight and stands as one of the key centers of a multipolar world and global governance.
“BRICS nations are committed to pursuing an independent, autonomous course and seek to address challenges collectively, grounded in international law and the core principles of the UN Charter,” Ushakov added.

Declared turnout during parliamentary elections estimated at around 70% — pollster

2026-09-10

00:41:36 KST

MOSCOW, September 10. /TASS/. The declared turnout for the upcoming parliamentary elections in Russia stands at 70%, the VCIOM opinion research center said.
"A few weeks ahead of the single voting day, seven out of ten Russians (70%) said, with varying degrees of certainty, that they plan to take part in the State Duma elections," the center said on its website.
A total of 54% of respondents said they definitely plan to cast their ballots at a polling station, the experts said.
VCIOM projects the turnout to be between 51% and 53%.
An electoral survey shows that four parties are sure to make it into the lower chamber of the Russian parliament, the State Duma: United Russia (51-53%), the Communist Party of Russia (13-15%), the New People party (9-11%), and LDOR (9-11%).
The A Just Russia party also has the chance of surpassing the five-percent threshold, although its electoral situation remains unstable, fluctuating between 4% and 6%.
The survey was conducted in September 2026, among 1,600 respondents aged 18 or older, and is based on average figures for the period of August 31 - September 6.

Syria condemns Netanyahu 'provocative' entry into its territory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:41:09 UTC
00:41:09 KST

Breadcrumb
Syria condemns Netanyahu's 'provocative' entry into occupied territory
Syria has strongly condemned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's illegal entry into occupied Syrian territory, after he toured Jabal al-Sheikh in a bulletproof vest and boasted of Israel's "absolute control" over swathes of the region.
The Syrian foreign ministry described Netanyahu's visit as a "provocative step" and a "flagrant violation of Syria's sovereignty, territorial integrity and international law".
In a statement, the ministry warned that Israel's continued incursions and attacks inside Syrian territory represented a "dangerous escalation" threatening security and stability across the region.
Damascus held Israel fully responsible for the consequences of the violations and called on the United Nations, international organisations and influential states to act to halt Israeli attacks and ensure a return to the 1974 Disengagement Agreement.
Netanyahu toured the summit of Jabal al-Sheikh on Wednesday alongside Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz and senior military officials, months after Israeli forces seized additional Syrian territory following the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.
Standing on occupied Syrian land and pointing towards Damascus, Lebanon and the occupied Syrian Golan Heights, Netanyahu claimed Israel now exercised unprecedented control over the area.
"We control the entire region, from the summit of Jabal al-Sheikh to the Yarmouk [River], and from here to the Mediterranean Sea, absolute control that has never existed before," Netanyahu said.
He also claimed Israel would prevent "terrorist armies" from establishing themselves along its borders, before turning his attention to Iran and claiming Tehran's government was close to collapse.
"The main mission is to bring down the terror regime in Iran, and we understand that the entire axis will ultimately fall," Netanyahu said, adding that Israel was "very close" to achieving that objective.
Katz, who accompanied Netanyahu during the tour, meanwhile openly vowed that Israeli forces would not withdraw from the Syrian territory they currently occupy.
Addressing Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, Katz said: "We are here on Jabal al-Sheikh, we are in the security zone, and we will not move from here."
He pointed out that Damascus was just 35 kilometres away from the Israeli position.
Israeli forces moved into the UN-patrolled buffer zone separating Syria and the occupied Golan Heights following Assad's fall in December 2024, with Israel declaring the 1974 disengagement agreement effectively collapsed.
Israel subsequently seized the Syrian side of Jabal al-Sheikh and other territory beyond the occupied Golan Heights, while carrying out repeated military incursions and attacks across Syria.
Netanyahu and Katz have since made repeated visits to the occupied Syrian territory, despite condemnations from Damascus.
Katz visited Israeli forces on Jabal al-Sheikh in August and similarly vowed that the military would remain there, saying Israeli troops had established positions at what had previously been a Syrian military site.
Netanyahu has also made similar highly publicised visits to Israeli military positions in Gaza and other fronts.
Last week, he appeared at an Israeli military position near the so-called Yellow Line in Gaza, where he said Israeli forces would remain. The line cuts off around 60% of the Palestinian territory.
The latest incursion comes despite US-mediated negotiations between Syria and Israel aimed at reaching a security agreement.
The two sides have held several rounds of talks and agreed on a mechanism for exchanging intelligence, but the negotiations have failed to halt Israeli attacks and incursions into Syrian territory.
Israel has simultaneously escalated military operations across the region, including attacks on Gaza and Lebanon, incursions into Syria and repeated threats against Iran and other regional states.
Netanyahu claimed earlier this week that the Iranian government was "weak" and "struggling to survive", threatening Tehran with an attack it "cannot even imagine" if it struck Israel.

8,000-year-old black fig remains unearthed in northwestern Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:40:38 UTC
00:40:38 KST

8,000-year-old black fig remains unearthed in northwestern Türkiye
Carbon-14 analysis dates charred figs found in Andik Cave in Balikesir province to 6300 BC
Mirac Kaya
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
BALIKESIR, Türkiye
Archaeologists have uncovered 8,000-year-old remains of the black fig for which the Havran district of northwestern Türkiye is known, revealing that the fruit has grown in the region since the Neolithic period.
The carbonized figs were discovered during excavations at Andik Cave, on Kocacal Hill, about 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from Havran’s Inonu neighborhood.
A Carbon-14 analysis conducted at the Scientific and Technological Research Council of Türkiye’s Marmara Research Center dated the remains to around 6300 BC.
Derya Yalcikli, an archaeology professor at Canakkale Onsekiz Mart University, is leading the excavations with authorization from the Culture and Tourism Ministry.
The Balikesir Kuvayi Milliye Museum Directorate, Balikesir Metropolitan Municipality and Havran Municipality are supporting the project.
Andik Cave, which was discovered in 1949 by archaeologist Kilic Kokten, reaches a depth of 59 meters (194 feet) and contains several galleries.
Getting to the site presents a daily challenge for the excavation team. Setting out from their excavation house at dawn, the archaeologists travel by off-road vehicle along a trail to Kocacal Hill.
At the end of the road, they load their water supplies onto a donkey and walk about 500 meters (1,640 feet) through narrow, rugged terrain to reach the cave.
There, the team has uncovered numerous ceramic vessels and tools made of stone and bone. A painting on one of the cave walls depicts a mountain summit and a leopard.
Cave used for thousands of years
Yalcikli told Anadolu that the cave was used over a long period, with its entrance serving both as a storage area and for ritual purposes.
“The use begins mainly in the Early Bronze Age and continues until the middle of the Late Bronze Age. In terms of dates, it covers a period extending to around the middle of 3000 BC,” he said.
The team also found evidence of limited use during the Byzantine period, while the earliest evidence of human activity at the site dates to after 6700 BC.
Yalcikli said this year’s excavations had revealed better-preserved archaeological layers than initially expected, including habitation areas and floor surfaces.
“We found habitation units and floors, allowing us to identify different levels of occupation,” he said. “The collection consists mainly of bone, stone and cutting tools because these periods saw little or no use of metal.”
The layers provide previously unknown information about prehistoric communities in the part of Balikesir that extends toward the Aegean region, he added.
“This year, we encountered very interesting floor arrangements. We do not know of many such arrangements inside caves,” he said.
“We have identified inside the cave, in phases before pottery was used, a floor arrangement similar to those constructed in houses. This is a very important result both for the region and for Anatolian archaeology.”
Figs found stored in large quantities
The excavation team also discovered remains of food consumed by the cave’s Neolithic inhabitants, including barley, wheat and figs.
Yalcikli said the charred fig remains were particularly well preserved and were found in unusually large numbers.
“Havran’s geographically indicated fig is one of the district’s most important products. We found it in a carbonized state,” he said.
“Carbon-14 testing showed that the fig remains date to 6300 BC. We can therefore say that Havran’s famous fig has existed in this region since the Neolithic period.”
The figs appeared to have been gathered and stored together, suggesting that they formed part of the inhabitants’ diet.
“We find barley, wheat and many other products in these layers, but the figs were preserved very well and their number is quite high,” Yalcikli said.
“They had been piled up and stored in one place. This shows that figs were among the fruits used for food at the time.”
Havran Mayor Emin Ersoy said the municipality was providing its full support for the excavations and welcomed the discovery.
