Christine Lagarde leaves after a meeting of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank in Berlin on Sept. 10, 2026. | John MacDougall/AFP via Getty Images
European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde today dismissed French far-left presidential contender Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s proposal to wipe out government debt, describing it as illegal and dangerous.
Lagarde, who spoke at a press conference after the central bank raised its key deposit rate to 2.5 percent, was responding to Mélenchon’s radical idea to freeze all French debt held by the ECB.
“It's not because you repeat something that doesn't make any sense, either legally, technically, or financially, that it becomes something valid,” Lagarde said.
Advertisement
She pointed to Article 123 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, which prohibits the ECB and national central banks from financing governments. The provision was agreed to and ratified by all EU member countries, Lagarde stressed.
Lagarde also dismissed the proposal on economic grounds, citing “very, very solid economists,” including former International Monetary Fund chief economist Olivier Blanchard, who can “demonstrate easily” that such a move would be “financially dangerous.”
Mélenchon renewed his call in August for the ECB to freeze pandemic-era government debt, arguing that the move would create additional fiscal space for France. Public debt amounts to more than €3.5 trillion, or 117.5 percent of French GDP, and the issue has become a top concern for voters.
Ahead of today's rate decision, Mélenchon also criticized the ECB’s widely expected hike, warning on X that “the ECB is leading us straight into the wall.”
Lagarde also used the press conference to dismiss renewed speculation about an imminent announcement that she would leave the ECB early. Rumors have swirled for months, after she left open the possibility of playing a role in the French presidential campaign.

Drug use may date back 25,000 years: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:14:12 UTC
00:14:12 KST

Beril Canakci
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
Evidence of habitual drug use may date back as far as 25,000 years, when hunter-gatherers on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi regularly consumed betel nuts, according to a recent study.
Researchers examining ancient human remains found evidence consistent with the habitual sucking of betel nuts, which contain the psychoactive compound arecoline. The findings were published Wednesday in the journal Science Advances.
The discovery provides the earliest recorded evidence of the habitual use of a neuroactive plant drug, according to researchers.
The evidence comes from dental remains showing distinctive wear associated with repeatedly sucking whole betel nuts. Chemical analysis also detected arecoline in dental tissue, providing additional evidence that the individuals had consumed the nuts.
The researchers said the practice emerged as early as 25,000 years ago and continued into the Late Pleistocene, thousands of years before the emergence of agriculture.
Betel nut, also known as areca nut, comes from the areca palm and contains arecoline, a psychoactive substance that can produce stimulant effects. The nut is still widely consumed in parts of Asia and the Pacific, often as part of a preparation known as betel quid.
Possible pain relief
The researchers suggested that the ancient practice may have initially served a medicinal purpose.
Arecoline can have pain-relieving properties, while the ancient foragers studied generally had poor dental health. Sucking the hard nuts may therefore have provided temporary relief from toothache, said researchers.
Prolonged use, however, appears to have damaged the teeth. The abrasive nuts caused severe wear and, in some cases, exposed the inner pulp of teeth, potentially increasing pain and the risk of chronic infection.
The researchers said the findings suggest that habitual use of psychoactive substances was part of some hunter-gatherer societies long before farming and the development of settled communities.
The study does not establish when humans first used drugs, but identifies what researchers describe as the earliest known archaeological evidence of habitual use of a neuroactive plant drug.

Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

"Russian terror is growing": Ukrainian PM outlines measures to help business
The government is taking urgent measures to help businesses provide Ukrainians with food, medicines and other essential goods without interruption.
Source: Prime Minister of Ukraine Serhii Koretskyi
Details: "Russian terror against Ukrainian businesses and civilian infrastructure is growing rapidly. We must respond and act proactively," he wrote.
The prime minister stated that in order to ensure the uninterrupted supply of food, medicines and other essential goods to Ukrainians, the government, together with the National Security and Defence Council and on the instructions of the president, is taking a number of urgent measures.
The government is preparing a subsidised lending programme for businesses to replenish working capital of up to UAH 1 billion (approx. US$22.4 million) per company or group of companies, with a compensation of 5% of the market rate. These funds can be used, in particular, for the purchase of goods.
"We plan to simplify entrepreneurs' access to state assets: they will have the priority right to lease property that the State Property Fund puts up for auction. We are doing this because after every strike on workshops, warehouses or offices, companies need to quickly find new premises and resume operations," the prime minister said.
The government has also adopted recommendations taking into account differentiated alert systems so that prolonged air-raid warnings do not halt the supply of goods to people.
"If businesses stop every time a siren sounds, we lose jobs, tax revenues and the country's very capacity to provide people with what they need. But the recommendations take into account a mandatory safety component," Koretskyi noted.
"We have given all businesses three months to set up shelters and safe spaces at service locations," he added.
The prime minister said these and other decisions were discussed in detail at an expanded meeting involving major Ukrainian retailers, the deputy head of the Office of the President, the Antimonopoly Committee, the State Customs Service, the State Property Fund and others.
Background: Koretskyi previously stated that the government is introducing a strict budget austerity regime for funds not allocated to defence needs.

Orthodox church sends medieval prince’s remains to Russian troops in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:12:08 UTC
00:12:08 KST

The Russian Orthodox church has sent a fragment of a medieval warrior prince’s remains to troops fighting in Ukraine, saying the relic would “spiritually strengthen” soldiers and help them achieve victory.
A reliquary containing part of the right hand of Dmitry Donskoy, the 14th-century prince revered in Russia for his victory over the Mongolian Golden Horde in 1380, has been taken to Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and is now being transported along the frontline.
The Russian Orthodox church said in a statement: “The holy commander is going to where the fate of the fatherland is being decided today, so that he may invisibly take his place in the same battle ranks as our defenders.”
The relic was first brought on Tuesday to the Savur-Mohyla war memorial in the Russian-occupied Donetsk region of Ukraine, where senior Orthodox clergy held a prayer service alongside representatives of the Russian military.
The Russian-installed Metropolitan Vladimir of Donetsk and Mariupol said its presence would help soldiers and civilians “mobilise their strength” and secure victory over the enemy.
The relic’s journey is the latest example of the Russian Orthodox church’s rabid embrace of the Kremlin’s war in Ukraine, which Patriarch Kirill, its leader, has repeatedly portrayed in religious terms.
Since Vladimir Putin launched the full-scale invasion in February 2022, the church hierarchy has become deeply embedded in the Russian war effort. Priests have been sent to military units and occupied territories, while churches across Russia have been instructed to recite prayers asking God to grant victory.
Donskoy’s relics were first formally uncovered only last month during restoration work at the Cathedral of the Archangel inside the Kremlin, where generations of Russian princes and tsars are buried.
Putin, who has grown increasingly close to the Russian Orthodox church over his more than two decades in power, personally attended the ceremony marking the unearthing.
Critics have accused the church of breaking with religious protocol by opening Donskoy’s centuries-old tomb. The location of the prince’s burial had long been known, but the church had previously made no attempt to exhume his remains after he was canonised in 1988.
Alexander Zanemonets, an Orthodox priest and historian based outside Russia, said the decision to uncover the relics almost four decades after Donskoy’s canonisation appeared driven by the demands of wartime patriotism.
He wrote in a piece for the Carnegie thinktank: “By the fifth year of war, the church leadership in Moscow began to wonder what else it could do to show its support for what Russia terms its ‘special military operation’.”
Zanemonets said the portrayal of Donskoy as a defender of the homeland fitted neatly with the Kremlin’s insistence that Russia was defending itself rather than conducting a war of aggression against its neighbour.
Earlier this year, relics of Alexander Nevsky, another medieval prince and military hero revered by the Russian Orthodox church, were also sent to the front.

Permanent 5 members clash in UN Security Council over Iran sanctions snapback
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:09:51 UTC
00:09:51 KST

Yasin Gungor
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
The five permanent members of the UN Security Council clashed Thursday during a high-stakes session about the legal validity of international sanctions against Iran and the reimposition of UN sanctions under the 2015 nuclear accord's "snapback" provision.
The snapback clause, established under the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), was designed to automatically reinstate UN Chapter VII sanctions if Iran breached the deal, intentionally bypassing the veto power of permanent council members.
"The mechanism for reinstating previously adopted Security Council resolutions on Iran, a mechanism set forth in Resolution 2231, was not activated, and this for a whole host of legal and procedural reasons," said the Russian representative, demanding a procedural vote to block a scheduled briefing on the 1737 Sanctions Committee.
Moscow argued that UN Resolution 2231, which endorsed the nuclear deal, expired Oct. 18, 2025, and insisted that the non-proliferation agenda item was struck off the council's list of active matters that day. The Russian envoy maintained that the 1737 Committee ceased to exist in 2015 and that no legal grounds remain to discuss its “so-called work.”
The Chinese representative supported the move, asserting that the council presidency lacks the mandate to draft or deliver a 90-day report. Warning against unilateral action, Beijing stressed, "A few members, in disregard of differences, insist on forcibly reimposing the Council sanctions against Iran and convening Council meetings under a removed agenda item." The envoy warned that the steps deepen institutional division and impede a political settlement, expressing "grave concern" and “strong opposition" against the moves.
Western delegations firmly rejected the challenge, arguing that the sanctions regime had been legally revived following Iranian breaches.
"The United Kingdom, with France and Germany, initiated the snapback mechanism in full accordance with Security Council Resolution 2231," said the British representative, explaining that European powers acted because of Iran's "significant non-performance" under the 2015 nuclear pact. London noted that the process concluded Sept. 28, 2025, leaving six Chapter VII resolutions in effect for nearly a year.
The French representative affirmed that council resolutions were restored alongside the committee's mandate to report every 90 days.
"Regardless of such politically driven matters, the facts are the facts. The 1737 Committee exists," said the US representative, accusing Russia and China of attempting to undermine council decisions to protect Tehran. The American diplomat noted that the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) confirmed Iran remains non-compliant with its Comprehensive Safeguards Agreement.
The council voted 11-2 in favor of adopting the provisional agenda, with two abstentions, defeating the Russian and Chinese bid to halt the meeting. Under UN Security Council rules, procedural votes cannot be blocked by a permanent member's veto and require a minimum of nine affirmative votes to pass.
Permanent members trade accusations after vote
Moscow denounced the briefing as an illegitimate exercise and an "inefficient use" of council resources, with the Russian representative describing it as a “flagrant procedural breach.”
The Russian envoy accused Washington and Israel of conducting strikes on "peaceful" facilities under IAEA safeguards, warning that the "illegal and reckless actions" risked provoking a wider regional catastrophe, while dismissing a new IAEA Board of Governors resolution referring Iran to the council as “politicized.”
Beijing maintained that lasting solutions require addressing the root causes of regional tensions. The "United States’ unilateral withdrawal from the JCPOA, its use of force against Iran twice during the negotiation process, and its pursuit of a policy of maximum pressure against Iran are the primary causes of the current complex and intractable situation in the Middle East and the Iranian nuclear issue," argued the Chinese envoy. China defended lran's "legitimate right to the peaceful use of nuclear energy," and said it acknowledges “Iran's repeated commitments not to develop nuclear weapons.”
"Iran is the only country without nuclear weapons to enrich uranium to this level," said the British envoy, criticizing Tehran for reportedly stockpiling more than 400 kilograms (882 pounds) of uranium enriched to 60% without "any credible civilian justification." London accused Iran of barring UN inspectors from all nuclear facilities since June 2025, sparing only the Bushehr plant, reiterating that a negotiated settlement remains the only durable path.
Rejecting safety arguments raised by Tehran for barring inspectors, the US representative said UN personnel continue to operate safely inside war-torn Ukraine, which IAEA director Rafael Grossi noted as a "worse and more constant war zone." The American diplomat accused Moscow and Beijing of trying to shield a state whose nuclear program is progressing “in the dark.”
France underlined Tehran's stockpile, warning that the amount is potentially sufficient for about 10 explosive nuclear devices.

Since Mudra's actions to influence the Supreme Court are directed against Petro Poroshenko, Poroshenko, as the leader of the opposition, should be recognized as a victim in this criminal proceeding," he believes.
As previously reported, on September 2, during a meeting of the Verkhovna Rada's Temporary Investigative Commission (TIC) on the investigation of possible unlawful actions by officials of state authorities, other state bodies, and state-owned enterprises that could have harmed Ukraine's economic security, it became known that Mudra had exerted pressure on the judges of the Administrative Court of the Supreme Court through the court's chairman, Dashutin, regarding sanctions against Poroshenko. According to Nina Yuzhanina, a member of parliament from the European Solidarity faction, audio recordings from the NABU show Mudra discussing this issue with another individual implicated in the case; therefore, she called on TIC members to summon Dashutin to a committee hearing. She noted that, according to the law, judges cannot be summoned to TIC meetings due to their role in the administration of justice; however, Dashutin performed an administrative function in this case.
At a hearing on August 25, the Appeals Chamber of the High Anti-Corruption Court (HACC) upheld the pretrial measure imposed on Mudra – who is a suspect in cases involving money laundering and corporate raiding ("Forrest Gump" and "Themis") in the form of detention with the alternative of bail set at UAH 20 million.
On August 19, NABU and SAPO released a video regarding a special operation called "Forrest Gump": individuals who laundered UAH 150 million to pay bail for a defendant in the Midas case were exposed and charged. On Thursday, August 20, NABU and SAPO released a second video regarding corruption involving the same high-ranking officials, titled "Themis" – exposing the illegal seizure of real estate and corporate assets through document forgery. Based on the evidence obtained, NABU detectives and SAPO prosecutors have served notices of suspicion to members of the criminal organization and the individuals they recruited, under Articles 255, 191, 206-2, 209, 358, and 361 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine.

U.S. Extradites 3 Russians Accused of Cybercrime Since June
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:06:04 UTC
00:06:04 KST

U.S. authorities have extradited three Russian nationals since June to face charges in separate cybercrime cases involving malware attacks, bank fraud and the hacking of government and private-sector organizations.
The extraditions from Cyprus, Georgia and Thailand come as Washington steps up efforts to prosecute suspected cybercriminals operating outside the United States. The three men are accused of schemes that collectively affected tens of thousands of people and caused millions of dollars in losses.
The most recent case involves Searzhudin Aktulayev, 40, who was arrested in Cyprus in May 2025 and extradited to the United States on Aug. 28. He made his first appearance in federal court in San Francisco on Aug. 31.
The U.S. Embassy in Cyprus on Thursday congratulated Cypriot police on the extradition.
Prosecutors allege that Aktulayev and his co-conspirators used about 255 fake accounts on an online platform for freelance workers to send malicious files to approximately 80,000 users between 2016 and 2017.
Once opened, the files installed malware that gave the group remote access to infected computers and allowed it to steal data, according to the indictment. About half of the potential victims were in the U.S.
Investigators said they uncovered data belonging to thousands of victims, including e-commerce login credentials and personal information for hundreds of people.
Aktulayev has been charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, distributing malicious code, unauthorized computer access and aggravated identity theft, among other offenses. The most serious charge carries a maximum prison sentence of 20 years.
His extradition came weeks after Georgia handed over Russian web developer Sergei Filimonov, who appeared in federal court in Atlanta on Sept. 4.
Prosecutors accuse Filimonov and his co-conspirators of creating fake websites for U.S. banks between November 2023 and October 2025. The group allegedly purchased sponsored Google links that directed bank customers to fraudulent login pages designed to steal their credentials.
The scheme led to $28 million in unauthorized transfers from U.S. bank accounts, the Justice Department said.
Filimonov allegedly maintained the operation’s technical infrastructure, including a database containing more than 5,000 stolen login credentials. He has been charged with conspiracy to commit bank and wire fraud and aggravated identity theft.
The charges carry a combined statutory maximum of 175 years in prison, though defendants convicted in U.S. federal courts typically receive sentences well below the total maximum available under each count.
In June, Thailand extradited a third Russian national, 36-year-old Denis Obrezko, to face charges in Boston.
U.S. authorities accuse Obrezko of supporting Void Blizzard, a hacking group that Microsoft has linked to Russian interests. The group has operated since at least April 2024 and has targeted government agencies, defense and transportation companies, media outlets, healthcare providers and nongovernmental organizations in NATO countries and Ukraine, according to Microsoft.
The FBI identified 11 U.S. companies that had been compromised.
Investigators said they found summaries of more than 13,000 stolen emails belonging to lawmakers in an eastern European country on Obrezko’s phone. They also linked him to payments for a virtual server and a domain used in attacks against U.S. companies.
Obrezko has been charged with conspiracy to commit computer fraud and unauthorized access to protected computer systems. He faces up to 10 years in prison if convicted.

Ukrainian drones strike Makhachkala port and Sochi waterfront, satellite data points to new damage in Russia’s Arctic gas region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:05:43 UTC
00:05:43 KST

Ukrainian drones attacked the commercial seaport in the city of Makhachkala in Russia’s Dagestan overnight into Sept. 10. At around 3 a.m., local residents began reporting explosions and air defense activity near the port. Before the authorities issued any official statements, the independent outlet Astra analyzed witness footage and determined that the commercial seaport was the likely target.
Astra also geolocated one of the explosions to the area of Pushkin Street where the Avar Theater is located.
Ukrainian monitoring channels Exilenova+ and Supernova+ published several videos showing drones flying overhead and exploding. Other footage showed smoke rising in the port area and damage in the city. Exilenova+ also published what it said was the apparent moment of a strike on the port’s infrastructure.
Acting Dagestan head Fyodor Shchukin confirmed that fires broke out at the port and at the Avarsky Theater. He said all aerial targets had been destroyed and that the fires were caused by falling debris. However, the theater’s director, Magomed Bisavaliyev, reported that a drone fell directly onto the building’s roof, blowing out windows before a fire started. Shchukin said the fires had been extinguished, no one was killed or injured, and the theater’s damaged roof would be repaired. Airports in Makhachkala, Vladikavkaz, and Grozny suspended operations for three and a half hours.
The Makhachkala Commercial Seaport is Russia’s only ice-free, deep-water port on the Caspian Sea. It is used for the shipment of oil, petroleum products, grain, containers, and other cargo moving between Russia, Iran, and countries in Central Asia and the South Caucasus. From January through August 2026, it handled a record 2.9 million metric tons of cargo, according to its own data, up 42.5% from a year earlier. More than 2 million metric tons of that volume was oil.
In addition to the strikes on Makhachkala, the Russian Black Sea city of Sochi was attacked by maritime drones on the evening of Sept. 9. Supernova+ published a full video of one part of the attack, while another clip captured a strike on a pier. Footage posted on social media also appeared to show a cafe building burning near a beach.
Twenty-eight people were injured in the attack, including two children.
Beach infrastructure and a nearby section of the Primorskaya Embankment were damaged. A concert by Russian singer Tatyana Bulanova at the Festivalny concert hall was also interrupted due to the threat of an attack, and performers and audience members were sent to shelter.
Russia’s Defense Ministry reported that it had intercepted more than 440 fixed-wing drones in the south of the country and over the Black Sea.
New data also emerged about the consequences of yesterday’s Ukrainian drone attack on gas infrastructure in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous District, located more than 2,000 kilometers from the border between the two countries.
The open-source intelligence channel Falcon Insight noted that NASA’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) detected several thermal anomalies at the Urengoyskaya compressor station near the Novy Urengoy Condensate Preparation Plant, which was attacked on Sept. 9.
Falcon Insight said such heat signatures are not typical for the compressor station.
The station supports several major gas pipelines, including the Urengoy-Center and Urengoy-Novopskov systems, which transport gas from the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous District to other parts of Russia. There had been no previous reports of an attack on the compressor station, and there is still no separate confirmation that the facility was damaged. Satellite monitoring data only shows sources of intense heat and cannot by itself establish what caused them.
Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces claimed responsibility for strikes on two other facilities in the region: the Novy Urengoy and Purovsky gas condensate processing plants. The Novy Urengoy plant has a design capacity of 19.5 million metric tons of feedstock a year, while the Purovsky plant processed 13.4 million metric tons in 2025. Ukraine’s military did not list the Urengoyskaya compressor station among the targets it said had been hit.

West Nile virus cases rise to 18 in Netherlands as death toll reaches 3
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:04:15 UTC
00:04:15 KST

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
Nine new cases of West Nile virus have been reported in the Netherlands since last Thursday, bringing the total number of infections contracted in the country this year to 18, the National Institute for Public Health and the Environment (RIVM) said, according to broadcaster NOS.
Three people have died from the virus in the Netherlands this year, up from one death reported last week, according to the institute.
The infections have been recorded in the provinces of Utrecht, North Brabant, North Holland, South Holland, Overijssel and Gelderland, the RIVM said.
One of the cases was identified through a scientific study conducted by blood bank Sanquin Research, while the other patients were diagnosed after being admitted to a hospital with symptoms, according to the institute.
A woman from Drenthe also died from West Nile virus earlier this year, but she was not included in the Dutch figures because she contracted the infection in Southeast Europe.
West Nile virus is primarily found in birds and can be transmitted to humans through the bite of infected mosquitoes.
The common house mosquito can become infected after feeding on an infected bird and subsequently transmit the virus to humans and other animals.
The virus cannot be transmitted between humans, according to the RIVM.
About 80% of infected people develop no symptoms, while around one in five experience flu-like symptoms.
About 1% develop neurological symptoms, with older people and those with weakened immune systems facing a higher risk of severe illness.
The virus was first detected in the Netherlands in August 2020 during a Sanquin study of blood donors.
The Dutch Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority has also received 53 new reports of horses infected with West Nile virus since the previous update, bringing the total number of reported cases among horses this year to 58.
The virus has also been detected in 23 dead and 10 live wild birds, bringing the total number of infected birds reported to 39 as of the latest update.

Students warned of increased meningitis B risk in UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:03:36 UTC
00:03:36 KST

Burak Bir
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
Young adults, particularly university students, remain at increased risk from meningococcal meningitis and septicaemia, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) warned Thursday.
New figures from the UKHSA revealed that Meningitis B (MenB) was responsible for 97% of invasive meningococcal disease cases in 15- to 24-year-olds (93 of 96 cases) in England during 2025-2026.
In a statement, the agency urged first-year students to ensure they are protected with two doses before the start of the term.
The UKHSA noted that the vaccination is "really important" because students in their first year of university face around seven times higher risk of meningococcal disease than young people of a similar age who do not go to university.
Citing new data published in the Invasive Meningococcal Disease (IMD) report for England, it noted that MenB was the leading cause of the disease across almost all age groups under 25, including infants and one- to four-year-olds.
The agency warned that invasive meningococcal disease can be serious, with 26 deaths recorded among the 348 confirmed IMD confirmed cases during the year.
Meningococcal disease is a rare but serious illness caused by meningococcal bacteria. In some cases, it can lead to severe conditions such as meningitis and septicemia (blood poisoning), which can rapidly progress to sepsis.
The onset of illness is often sudden, and early diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics are vital.
Symptoms can include fever, headache, rapid breathing, drowsiness, shivering, vomiting, a characteristic rash, and cold hands and feet.

'Buy Canadian': Meet the Consumers Boycotting American Products as Trade Rift Widens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:03:21 UTC
00:03:21 KST

When Lynn Henderson walks into her local grocery store in British Columbia, she has one label at the top of her mind: “Made in Canada.” The 47-year-old is among a drive of Canadian consumers who are attempting to boycott U.S. products in a show of solidarity amid the ongoing trade war.
“Even when I'm shopping with my toddler, he now asks specifically, ‘Oh, are these apples Canadian?’ And he will ask that before putting it in the cart,” Henderson tells TIME, noting that it’s a family effort. It costs more, she admits, but it’s worth “knowing that money is staying here in Canada and not going south at the border.”
The resurgence of the “Buy Canadian” movement comes amid a deepening U.S.-Canada trade dispute that shows no signs of waning. Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods took effect Tuesday, with Prime Minister Mark Carney matching the economic pressure imposed by the U.S. after trade negotiations collapsed last month. The U.S. has since announced a ban on Canadian dairy, motorcycles, and most alcoholic beverages. It’s all unfolding against the backdrop of U.S. President Donald Trump repeatedly talking of his ambitions to annex Canada and make it the 51st state.
While Carney’s government is going toe-to-toe with the Trump Administration, he’s urging the general population to take action, too.
“The most powerful actions have come from you: Buying Canadian and travelling in Canada,” Carney told Canadians in a national address Tuesday. “Decisions taken at the kitchen table, not the boardroom table.”
Other lawmakers have shared similar calls to action. “‘Buy Canadian’ reflects the economic solidarity Canadians are showing at a time when it matters most,” Quebec minister Joël Lightbound said in a statement to TIME. “By supporting one another and investing in what we build here at home, we are building Canada strong.”
Canadian consumers have responded en masse to the call. A Build Canada poll conducted Aug. 31-Sept. 4 found that many are already making sacrifices at the tills, as 69% of respondents reported “choosing Canadian products despite higher prices” and 55% said they had “stopped buying specific American brands.” Reports also indicate a surge in demand for Canadian products.
As the trade war stretches on, here’s what to know about the revitalized “Buy Canadian” movement, the people behind the U.S. products boycott, and what the data says about the effectiveness of the consumer-driven action.
The resurgence of the "Buy Canadian" movement
Campaigns promoting Canadian-made goods date back at least to the early 20th century, when Canadian manufacturers began pushing their “Made in Canada” products.
Among consumers, the effort has evolved into the “Buy Canadian” initiative, which encourages residents to support local businesses and industries as much as they can.
The movement skyrocketed last year in the midst of the trade war sparked by Trump’s tariffs. Businesses and consumers alike vowed to shun U.S. products, with Canada-based media publishing advisories on “how to shop Canadian."
As the tariffs loomed in February 2025, a survey by accounting firm KPMG found that 93% of consumers wanted retailers and grocery stores to identify and promote Canadian products.
In late 2025, the Canadian government launched the “Buy Canadian Policy, to protect and prioritize Canadian workers and industries, and strengthen Canada’s domestic economy.”
Henderson, a public relations consultant, says Trump’s threats against Canada’s sovereignty last year signified a turning point.
“Canadians have felt for generations that these are not just our allies, but our friends, and neighbors,” she says. “Nobody wants to be spoken about like that by their friends and neighbors. It's really hurtful.”
The reignited trade rift has revived Henderson’s passion for patriotic shopping, and she’s actively refrained from purchasing items, such as a new iPhone, that don’t align with her efforts. “I don’t want to spend that money to support an American business,” she says.
How consumers dedicated to the movement are approaching the challenge
Consumers in Canada are finding different ways to navigate how best to boycott U.S. goods and services, putting extra time in at the grocery store to ensure they are buying Canadian as often as they can.
Although she prioritizes Canadian products, Henderson is also open to items from other countries.
“We're discovering that there's some incredible produce from around the world,” she says. “We don't actually need to get oranges from the U.S. anymore, because we can get oranges from Brazil or South Africa, and they're fantastic.”
Brian Leonard, a 37-year-old who works in the coffee industry and lives in New Brunswick, is similarly passionate when he heads to the grocery store, and firmly believes in starting each day with a “Buy Canadian” mindset.
“For me, it always begins first thing in the morning with a cup of coffee. Buying coffee that is roasted locally in Canada,” Leonard tells TIME. “The first decision of your day can be something that sets up your whole day to be part of the movement.”
The way in which Canadians have been re-energized to support more local products has been “astounding,” Leonard adds. “I had a call yesterday, and the person mentioned they had switched dish soap because they realized the soap they were buying was American-made,” he says.
The topic of patriotic shopping is dominating business groups on Facebook and elsewhere, bringing further attention to the movement.
These social media groups have become a gateway for people to come together when seeking out Canadian alternatives to U.S. products. The "Made in Canada - Canadian Products" Facebook group, for example, boasts 1.4 million members. Similarly, the Reddit forum r/BuyCanadian has more than 250,000 members and nearly 7,000 weekly contributions.
For some, the efforts extend beyond trips to the grocery store and online checkouts.
Henderson is also now avoiding U.S. travel. “I live very close to the border. It used to be very common to just [cross over] and go to Seattle, go to Trader Joe's, or outlet malls, and we will not do that now,” she says. ”We’d rather explore Canada.”
Meanwhile, Shireen Jeejeebhoy, a 63-year-old writer based in Toronto, says she has also deleted WhatsApp, stopped using Zoom, and is even trying to find alternatives to Google and Apple products.
“These things are really difficult to divest yourself from,” she tells TIME, explaining that she uses the website “Unplug America”—an online initiative aimed at replacing American tech products with Canadian equivalents—for guidance. “There are some things in the digital world that Canada does not have, and so I'm looking to the U.K., the E.U., or India for alternatives.”
However, even someone as dedicated to the movement as Jeejeebhoy struggles to find alternatives for everything.
“My skin doesn't react well to most sunscreens, and as much as I've tried Canadian brands, there's only one American brand that actually works well [for me] at an SPF 50,” she says, admitting it’s proven to be difficult. “So, as much as I want to use the Canadian brand sunscreen, I have to use a particular American product.”
Leonard identifies with the struggle, admitting it can be “overwhelming to a lot of people to try to completely overhaul everything they buy,” as people have different budgets and needs.
Taking part in the movement doesn’t have to be a rigid commitment, nor does it mean you should deprive yourself of life’s little treats, the consumers who spoke to TIME agreed upon.
Is the Buy Canadian movement working? Here’s what the data says
The shift away from American products could have significant economic consequences for Canada, where the U.S. accounted for 67.2% of Canadian goods and services exports in 2025, making it the country’s largest trading partner by far.
The Bank of Montreal (BMO) estimated in April 2025, following the initial resurgence of the "Buy Canadian" movement, that the shift in consumer attitudes could redirect roughly C$10 billion to the Canadian economy annually.
“If we are directing C$10 billion or so of economic activity back into Canada, that would otherwise be bleeding out to the U.S., then that's a direct benefit,” Robert Kavcic, director and senior economist at BMO, tells TIME.
The Bank of Canada released an analysis in February “assessing the Buy Canadian movement one year later.”
It found that households had shifted their food spending away from U.S. products and towards Canadian ones. “The shift is modest but clearly visible. In March 2025—as trade tensions escalated—the proportion of food spending on Canadian products went up by approximately 2% relative to January 2025, while the proportion spent on U.S. products fell by a similar amount. And what started in March wasn’t short-lived—it persisted through the summer,” read the analysis.
Kavcic explains that “a certain share of that spending is now reallocated domestically,” thus benefiting the Canadian economy.
“I don't know if Canadians can do a lot more than what they have already, because there's a cost to that. There are certain families or workers that have to travel back and forth to the U.S., and there's a cost to buying Canadian,” he says.
Despite these challenges, statistics from the Canadian Survey on Business Conditions, for the first quarter of 2026 over the last 12 months, found that 16.6% of businesses had changed their marketing to promote Canadian products. Among retailers, the figure was 41.6%, showing a clear push toward promoting domestically made goods.

The White House said in a statement that it is making the Obamacare-related payments due to what it said was a “significant surplus of funds” accumulated under the Biden administration, which it accused of charging people who used federal exchanges “excess” user fees “in the form of higher premiums”.
Still, sending the payments, which as described by the White House would cost nearly US$500 million, could intensify ongoing concerns about inflation and the nation’s ballooning budget deficits and public debt.
Trump has long tried and failed to repeal former president Barack Obama’s signature healthcare law, and short of that, he has floated the idea of offering direct subsidies to Americans to purchase insurance instead of paying health insurers. REUTERS, BLOOMBERG

====================================================================================================

I turned off my algorithm for 24 hours. Is this how social media used to be?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:00:43 UTC
00:00:43 KST

I have a confession. I love my social media algorithm. It is a perfectly curated window into my insane and inquiring mind. It knows precisely which videos will tickle me and which memes will gently distract me from the slow collapse of humankind.
On Tuesday the Australian government announced “world-leading” reforms that would force social media platforms to allow users to opt-out of algorithms, dubbed “my feed, my way”. On the same day, I was delighted to be confronted with a video on Instagram of a woman accidentally spilling a bucket of eels on a Chinese train. Dozens of eels slithered among the passengers, who appeared not as surprised as I would have expected.
In bed that night, after sending the video to several friends and watching it multiple times, I lamented to my partner how I would find content like this if my accounts weren’t at the whim of the algorithm gods. “You can still search for eels,” he said. But would it be the same?
So, for 24 hours, I decided to manually turn off my algorithm via little-known settings on Instagram to get a sense of how the reforms might change my feed. This feature – accessed simply by tapping on the Instagram logo at the top of the home screen – allows you to limit your feed to posts from accounts you are following, in chronological order. This is basically what social media feeds, including Facebook, looked like when they started.
Would I be thrust back into the old days of social media, to how things were before artificial intelligence and Elon Musk bought Twitter and everything became an ad?
As a reminder of how things used to be, I scroll back to my first posts on Instagram and find sepia-heavy pictures of trees, gigs and friends. “The SKY,” says one, simply showing a sunset.
I am gripped with nostalgia for 2012, when all my posts got eight likes and no comments and I only followed two dozen close friends from school.
For a truly “authentic” social media experience, I trawl through my contacts and unfollow any account that isn’t a person I have met in real life. It is refreshing to unfollow news accounts, and politicians, but sad to let go of funny influencers and meme accounts and chefs.
“Goodbye, Ottolenghi,” I think wistfully. “Farewell, woman from Dallas Cowboys cheerleaders.” In total, about 100 accounts get the axe. I refresh my feed, and it only takes about 10 minutes of scrolling to run out of content to look at.
For the first time in years, Instagram informs me I have reached the “End of following”. “There are no more posts from accounts that you follow from the past 30 days,” it says.
I am floored and unmoored. Each time I refresh my feed for the next few hours, there is nothing new for me to mindlessly scroll. Instinctively, I keep clicking on the app but it’s futile. Is this how social media used to be? A tool to communicate with people rather than a way to remain constantly distracted?
What disturbs me, though, scrolling through a feed that should theoretically be made up of friends and family updating me about nice moments in their lives, is that it still feels hollow and impersonal.
Mostly, people are using it for self-promotion, whether it be posting about something they’ve published, projects they’ve done, brand partnerships or attempts to “go viral”. The only ones who seem to be using social media as it used to be are my mum and her friends, who still upload happy snaps with abandon. This is soothing but also very boring. And do I really need to know or care that someone I met backpacking in 2015 is appearing at an art festival in Amsterdam?
During my lunch break, instead of hitting the apps, I read my book and look at my surroundings. It’s nice. Maybe the solution is not to opt out of algorithms but to opt out of social media altogether.
The justification for turning off algorithm-driven content makes sense. The federal government and many experts have raised concerns about how dangerous and divisive content can be pushed into people’s feeds, drawing them further and further into rabbit holes.
I have watched on with concern as figures from the “manosphere” gain traction across the world alongside the rise of far-right parties, and how thinness appears to be the new norm in Hollywood, with eating disorder content proliferating on X, TikTok and Instagram.
Thankfully, this has not been my social media experience. According to Instagram’s AI summary of my algorithm, a little-known feature of the app, I enjoy “community events” and “saving furry friends”, with a particular penchant for content related to the “Sydney food scene” and, somewhat vaguely, “Australia” (click on the reels icon and then the double-heart symbol in the top-right corner to see yours).
My “For You” page is a haphazard collection of animals, food and gossip about reality TV. The top posts are an old man who summarises the latest episodes of Below Deck Mediterranean, a dachshund being pet with a spatula and someone making a cake with the face of Edward Cullen. It knows me so well!
But is this healthy? Do I really need to spend my time watching AI-generated dogs dancing in the shower, or marvelling at a man attempting to eat an extremely gigantic cone of soft-serve ice-cream? After 24 hours switching off, my conclusion? It’s numbing my brain and turning my own thoughts into slop.

My mother-in-law buys overly girly clothes for my daughter. I try to be gracious but it kills me – do I tell her to stop?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:00:41 UTC
00:00:41 KST

I am the mother of a six-year-old girl, and I have relatively progressive views about gender. Among other things, I try to give my daughter a choice of clothes that are practical – T-shirts, leggings – and that tend to be unisex in colour scheme. There are no overly fussy and frilly skirts and dresses in pink and sparkles in her wardrobe. As much as possible, I try to buy non-sweatshop brands. These choices are part of a world system of values I want to show my daughter – that being a “girl” is so much more than just wearing a frilly dress; that we can have well-made things without contributing to the suffering of others.
My mother-in-law, on the other hand, loves buying these sorts of clothes for her granddaughter. She is a kind and caring woman, and this is one of her love languages. These clothes are often gauche, overly feminine, expensive and poorly made.
I try my best to be gracious in accepting these things but it kills me to pass them to my daughter to wear. I feel as though she is enforcing these specific views on gender, through fashion, on my daughter, that don’t align with how I want to raise her. As a result, my mother-in-law becomes hurt that I’m not dressing my daughter in these ugly froufrou clothes; and I feel guilty about wasting her time and money.
Should I be upfront with her about what clothes I do and don’t want her to buy for my daughter? Or am I overthinking it and should let this slide?
Eleanor says: For what it’s worth, to be defined by rejecting something is still to be defined by it. “Overly feminine”, “ugly froufrou”; these are still judgments about how to be a girl well.
I completely share your taste here, so I point this out from right next to you in the trenches of thinking about femininity and pink and frills for young girls. It took me so long to work out that just as the firm belief that women must be “girly” is freighted with all kinds of sexism, the firm belief that we mustn’t is freighted with other generalisations, too – some no less sexist. For instance, “if feminine, vapid”. (Why, when I need to seem serious at work, do I dress more like a man?)
This isn’t to say your careful selection of your daughter’s wardrobe is wrong. It’s a wonderful counterbalance to all the nonsense that the world will expect her to love. But there’s a slight risk that in trying to get our girls away from “you must love frilly skirts and pink”, we swing all the way to a different kind of enforcement: “you mustn’t love frilly skirts and pink”. And that’s the seeds of a complex: the clues that clothing is somehow grave, contains rules, is something you can get wrong.
I think the bigger issue is that your mother-in-law is treading on a parenting preference of yours. She’s either not noticing or not minding the gulf between your tastes in things to buy your daughter. Neither is very thoughtful of the fact that this is your child.
Perhaps she feels your rejection of her taste is judgmental. But presumably she doesn’t like some things you like, and she wouldn’t want you to infer that, as a result, she thinks you’re bad or wrong. So it needn’t mean that when you don’t share her taste, either. That may be a useful way of framing things: we’re just different. No need to fear that. Your taste just isn’t hers, and you’re the parent.
Could you perhaps redirect some of this impulse to buy things? If it’s a love language, could it be more exciting for her to buy stuff your daughter is actually interested in – equipment for a hobby, toys, stationery? Or objects that can express a bit of your mother-in-law’s taste but that your daughter doesn’t have to wear, and that are more likely to be made ethically – like a kind of food, a local treat, a decoration? Could you nudge her towards at least buying costumes for playing make-believe – so they don’t seem to say that this is how girls should dress, all the time?
This strategy is a bit cheekier, but you could also say you’re trying to not let your daughter get too used to expensive things and lots of presents. That way it’s not about what your mother-in-law gives: you could ask her to focus instead on teaching her things, or making things together. That may make her feel less rejected while still meaning you don’t have to come home with a bag full of taffeta.
I so understand trying to teach your daughter important values through her clothes and consumer choices. Perhaps one lesson you can model is that Mum and Grandma have different ideas about important things, and that’s OK.

====================================================================================================

‘Things sort of get mushy’: inside the cryonics facility where ‘patients’ pay to be frozen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:00:40 UTC
00:00:40 KST

I’m standing atop a very tall ladder, peering down through a haze of liquid nitrogen vapour into a giant stainless steel flask containing three smaller containers.
Inside the smaller wedges – which are labelled 005, 006, 007 – are three of Peter Tsolakides’ “patients”. The frozen bodies belong to people who, before their death, paid handsomely to be cryogenically frozen in the hope of one day being brought back to life.
The ladder is inside a normal-looking shed in an industrial estate in Holbrook in regional New South Wales. Next to the shed is a grassy block strewn with several wrecked Hondas. Across the road is the local fire brigade.
Since it opened in 2023, the shed has housed the southern hemisphere’s only cryonics facility. Inside, seven patients are “suspended” head-down in liquid nitrogen at -196C. Four to a flask – a dewar, as they’re known in the business.
Tsolakides’ company, Southern Cryonics, is selling people “a chance of life extension”.
The gamble costs more than $200,000. Experts say there’s no way it will work.
Cryonics, they explain, remains a “dream”. Any attempted resurrection would be akin to taking a defrosted, and decidedly mushy strawberry, and believing it could be made firm and vibrant again.
But proponents say cryonics offers adventure. And a glimmer of hope of a longer or potentially limitless life.
Tsolakides, the chair of Southern Cryonics, makes no promises. “Basically, you need to have conquered death, cured all diseases and then be able to bring people back from the dead,” he says.
He puts the likelihood of his patients being brought back to life in 250 years’ time at about 10%. That’s more than nothing, he says.
But as with any risky venture, it pays to read the fine print.
A shed and a submarine
Holbrook is small town off the Hume Highway halfway between Melbourne and Sydney. It’s home to the decommissioned submarine HMAS Otway, stranded in a park 250km from the ocean.
Southern Cryonics is one of six such facilities in the world, according to its operators. There are two in the US and one each in Switzerland, China and Russia.
It’s thought there are about 1,000 people cryogenically frozen worldwide. Tsolakides describes the community as “tight knit”.
“Almost nobody’s interested in cryonics,” he tells Guardian Australia. “The people who we get joining us are people who’ve had a sort of life interest … but never knew it was available” in Australia.
Southern Cryonics chose Holbrook for its storage facility because of its proximity to Sydney and Melbourne and the fact it’s unlikely to be hit by earthquakes or floods.
The cryonicists need somewhere relatively safe given that patients are frozen indefinitely. They’re in the dewar until humanity develops the technology capable of “reviving” them; or, as their contract stipulates, the company goes bust. In that case, their body may be “disposed of”.
Conveniently, Holbrook was already home to a cattle-breeding association, and hence a delivery destination for the liquid nitrogen needed to freeze bull semen and embryos.
Southern Cryonics has two dewars so far. They’re basically big Thermos bottles.
Inside one are the first four of Tsolakides’ patients to be frozen. In May 2024, a man who died in his 80s was the first to be loaded upside down in his Trivial Pursuit-style quarter-cylinder wedge.
The second dewar has room for one more patient. Being in the shed, looking down into that space, I feel an immense loneliness.
Tsolakides says women are less likely than men to be interested in being frozen. That’s because, he suggests, women don’t like the idea of waking up in a future without family or friends.
‘A very strict protocol’
I am the first journalist allowed into the shed since the initial suspension in May 2024.
The shed is unremarkable apart from the two towering dewars – and a crash-test dummy, fully dressed and lying on the floor. It was used to test the winching mechanism for depositing bodies into the dewars.
Jim Davis, from Parkes Liquid Nitrogen, is there to top up the dewars. The metal flasks release plumes of vapour when they’re refilled. They were initially topped up once a month but that’s been increased to fortnightly at the request of two early clients who were worried about supplies running low after their mothers died and were suspended.
Davis also delivers the icy liquefied gas to police dog and cattle breeders, hospitals, engineers and human IVF clinics. “If they’re freezing it, I’m doing it,” he says.
Demand is increasing all the time, and supplies must be replenished regularly, Davis says.
You can’t seal liquid nitrogen in a vessel without the container blowing up, meaning it slowly escapes. “If I sealed one of these tanks, mate, the building wouldn’t be here,” he says.
To give patients the best chance of avoiding cellular destruction, their body undergoes an eight-hour “vitrification” process as soon as possible after death, Southern Cryonics says.
Another of Tsolakides’ companies, CryoPath, arranges a third-party medical perfusionist company to carry out the vitrification.
After someone dies, their body is cooled as quickly as possible – including by placing ice packs around their head. The corpse is then pumped with antifreeze-like embalming chemicals that turn it into a “glass-like state”, Tsolakides says, hopefully protecting it from the extreme temperatures inside the dewar.
“It’s a slow process,” he explains. “You have to follow a very strict protocol.”
After a body has been “stabilised” – usually at a funeral home – it’s transported to Holbrook and stored upside down. But not every patient in the shed has undergone this procedure. Some underwent a “straight freeze”.
In the Southern Cryonics contract, clients are asked to acknowledge that any known cryonic suspension method will probably result in physical damage to their body, which may be irreversible. The contract notes there will be another fee, yet to be determined, for any future revival.
Science v ‘mysticism’
Associate Prof Saffron Bryant, a cryopreservation expert at RMIT University in Melbourne, says current science “does not support our ability to quite preserve a whole body at this time”.
Bryant says cells, embryos and blood products can be successfully “cryopreserved” through vitrification. She says it’s “sort of like antifreeze you might put in a car” to prevent ice forming and protect cells from damage.
But it is not possible to deliver a cryoprotectant to everywhere in the body or even, at this stage, to a single organ.
“If you’re trying to cool a whole body down at the same rate, you’re going to have the outside, like the skin, cooling down faster than the inside,” she says. “We [use] that strawberry analogy – where things sort of get mushy.”
Bryant says even if it were possible to deliver cryoprotectant to the whole body and cool it at the correct rate, the underlying cause of death would remain.
The “heart attack or the Alzheimer’s or whatever it was that killed them” happened and no amount of freezing could reverse that, the academic says.
As to whether it’s possible to revive someone’s consciousness along with their physical body, Bryant considers this question to be more in the “realms of mysticism” than science.
Asked if she thinks Southern Cryonics is a scam, Bryant replies: “I’m not allowed to answer that.”
The initial stabilisation process costs an estimated $60,000. Clients then have to pay a further $150,000 to Southern Cryonics for their indefinite storage and a $350 annual “membership fee”.
The company “demands payment upfront” and Southern Cryonics recommends people take out a $210,000 life insurance policy.
Tsolakides says it costs about $5,500 a year to keep a patient suspended. Most of that goes towards liquid nitrogen and staff costs.
He plans to invest $100,000 from each client in “blue-chip” funds which he says could result in a collective pool of billions of dollars over the 250 years he estimates it will take for revival to become feasible.
On its website, Southern Cryonics says most suspensions are funded through life insurance and it can help people obtain a policy through a broker.
But Tsolakides acknowledges only one Australian customer’s insurer has agreed to pay so far and it was reluctant. He knows of “two or three” major insurers that will pay for cryonics but he won’t name them.
The Council of Australian Life Insurers says it can’t verify or endorse claims made by Southern Cryonics, CryoPath or any broker about using life insurance to fund cryonic suspension.
Its chief executive, Christine Cupitt, says nominating a cryonics provider as the beneficiary of a life insurance policy is a “significant decision” that people should consider carefully.
‘It is a dream’
Dr Kate Falconer, an Australian legal academic who specialises in death law and teaches at University College Cork in Ireland, says the cryonics community is made up of a small number of “diehard true believers”.
“Look, I think they probably do believe it,” she says. “But at the end of the day, it is a dream. There’s nothing concrete there.”
Falcolner nevertheless shows her students a New York Times video from 2015 where a young woman with terminal cancer talks about having her brain frozen after death.
“It’s incredibly moving [and] it really does hit home that there are some people who are choosing it because it is their only hope of any kind of long life.”
The latest suspension at the Holbrook facility occurred in June after a man in his 90s died. Southern Cryonics’ youngest patient is a woman who died in her 40s and whose premature death devastated her family.
The facility manager, Philip Rhoades, says he once preserved the brain tissue of a 15-year-old boy who took his own life. That was at the request of the teenager’s parents.
The preservation was done by Rhoades’ earlier venture, the Neural Archives Foundation, a registered charity which claims to preserves brain tissue as a “historical archive”.
Rhoades says the organisation makes use of “normal biomedical storage” across Australia. His own parents’ brains are preserved along with 12 other human brains and three dog brains.
Rhoades is a left-leaning vegetarian with a big family but no children of his own. He was planning to open a “life extension village” near his home in Cowra, in NSW’s central west, but says that was foiled by red tape.
“There was too much bureaucratic stuff,” he says. Instead, he’s thinking of turning the block into a GP clinic adjoined by a “biomedical research facility” for “radical life extension treatments”.
When he dies, Rhoades would love to be “uploaded to a supercomputer as soon as possible”. But as he doesn’t think that will be possible given that he’s in his 70s, he plans to be frozen and stored in the Holbrook shed.
Future generations will want to revive their great-great-great grandparents, Rhoades says.
“If the technology is possible at all … I think it will become very popular to talk to revivees.”
He thinks patients could be revived by 2080 and that someone who had a “good preservation” has more than a 50% chance of making it. But he knows there are no guarantees.
“If you get woken up in the future, you’ve hit the jackpot, really.”

It’s a remote, roofless ruin in a Tasmanian ghost town – and it just sold sight unseen for $300,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:00:39 UTC
00:00:39 KST

On the edge of the main highway winding from Hobart to Tasmania’s west coast, the concrete shell of the Royal Hotel stands like a spacecraft lingering on otherworldly terrain.
One of the few official ruins in Tasmania, the old building is roofless, weathered by the elements – and has just sold for $300,000.
Located in the ghost town of Linda, near Gormanston, the historic property was snapped up sight unseen by a Perth chef, Naiche, and his partner. They plan to explore opening an eatery in the adjacent (functional) building.
Set on a stretch of road where the town’s welcome and goodbye signs sit barely a kilometre apart, the property comprises the abandoned hotel and adjacent building equipped with a commercial kitchen, living room, bathroom and bedrooms.
From a bird’s eye view, the roofless concrete walls expose the ruin’s layout like a dollhouse. Its smooth, human-made edges stand out against surrounding mountainous landscape, laden with jagged boulders and low-hanging clouds.
When the sun hits the muted greys of the country, the colours turn into warm hues of brown, orange and green.
Originally constructed from timber in 1901, the hotel was destroyed by fire nine years later before being rebuilt in reinforced concrete. It catered to prospectors drawn by gold at the nearby North Lyell mine, where a 1912 fire claimed 42 lives. Over subsequent decades, the hotel serviced local copper miners and earned a reputation for brawls – including a fatal stabbing in 1925 – before the mines emptied and the pub was abandoned in 1952.
In recent years, the dark grey shell has served as a pit stop for road trippers seeking ghost-town photo opportunities. It has also been used as a backdrop for light projections during the Unconformity arts festival.
The adjacent building was previously operated by Zara Trihey as Linda Cafe – catering to visitors that included hikers, cyclists and rafters heading towards the Franklin River and Strahan.
‘Buying a wreck’
Dominic Romeo, a historic property agent who handled the sale, says the listing attracted interest across Australia, the UK and US.
Romeo, who has spent 40 years restoring historic country houses, described the Royal Hotel as a “huge historic shell”.
“Buying a wreck, sight unseen, is another level,” he says.
“I love these types of buyers, they have a sense of adventure and purpose. The purchasers are from Perth, WA. They did not inspect the property, but what makes it even more interesting is that they have never been to Tasmania.”
According to the West Coast council mayor, Shane Pitt, the region’s scenery is unique to the rest of Tasmania, with dense natural growth rainforests, rolling peaks and freshwater lakes filled with rainbow, brown and brook trout.
“We class the whole west coast as remote,” he says, estimating the hotel to be 15 minutes’ drive from the major town of Queenstown, two hours from Burnie and three and a half hours from Hobart.
The region surrounding Queenstown, Gormanston and the Linda Valley has a distinctive “lunar landscape” from a legacy of historic mining and timber harvesting, that has “started to be overtaken by floral growth”.
‘Visitors want to know the history’
The chief executive of the Tourism Industry Council Tasmania, Amy Hills, says sites like the Royal Hotel spark curiosity among travellers.
“There is a rawness to the west coast that draws visitors in,” Hills says. “Buildings like this help tell those stories and connect visitors to the history of the community. The new owners have the potential to give visitors a reason to stop and engage with the hotel’s story.
“Visitors want to know the history – what was it like before it closed in the early 1950s? Who spent time there, and what did its presence bring to the area at that time?,” she says. “There is something exciting about discovering an unexpected place on a road trip.”
Hills says tourism is vital to the state’s economy, particularly in regional areas.
“The industry directly and indirectly supports approximately one in six jobs across the state,” she says. “In regional communities that flow-on impact can be particularly significant.”
Pitt says a there has been a surge in adventure tourism on the west coast, driven by wilderness cruises, heritage railways and the nearby Mount Owen mountain bike trails, some of which end in the Linda valley.
“Those riders may be attracted to the eatery,” he says – if it offers something distinct from nearby Queenstown.
The local community “is one that is willing to support those having a crack”, Pitt says.
“It would be good to see the old Royal Hotel renovated back to its former glory, but this will take a lot of time, money and hard work. Telling the story of the building would certainly be a great start.”

Russia sanctions bill faces make-or-break moment before US midterms, Ukraine says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:00:20 UTC
00:00:20 KST

Russia sanctions bill faces make-or-break moment before US midterms, Ukraine says
It remains unclear whether the U.S. House of Representatives will vote next week on sweeping legislation that would impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian oil and gas, Ukraine's sanctions commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk told reporters on Sept. 10.
The bill faces a narrow window for consideration before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. The House's final pre-election session begins Sept. 14 and will last only four days. If lawmakers do not take up the legislation next week, its consideration would effectively have to start over after the elections.
"That was the main message I conveyed to the members of Congress," Vlasiuk said after returning from Washington, where he advocated for the bill.
"Is there a possibility that this bill will be passed by the House next week? Yes, there is. Are the chances of that happening high? It's hard to say at this point."
House Speaker Mike Johnson has cast doubt on whether the legislation will reach the floor before the election, adding uncertainty to a bill that has been stalled since April 2025.
The legislation gained significant momentum in the Senate on Aug. 7, when lawmakers overwhelmingly backed it in an 86-11 vote. The bill, authored by the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, a longtime supporter of Ukraine, now faces a more difficult path in the House.
Pressure on Russia
The bill would give U.S. President Donald Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest buyers of Russian oil and natural gas, as well as five countries helping Moscow evade energy sanctions.
China, India, and Turkey are among the largest buyers of Russian oil, while the European Union, China, and Turkey are major importers of Russian natural gas.
The list of targeted countries would be reviewed every 180 days.
Countries importing less than 15% of Russia's total natural gas exports and actively reducing those imports would be exempt.
The legislation would also impose sanctions on Russian President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials, major Russian financial institutions, including the Central Bank, Sberbank, and Gazprombank, and Russian state-owned companies.
It would further target foreign entities supporting Russia's defense-industrial base, major Russian energy projects, and Moscow's so-called shadow fleet, which helps Russia continue exporting oil despite Western sanctions.
The bill also includes measures targeting China's support for Russia's defense industry.
Supporters in Congress have presented the legislation as a way to increase pressure on Moscow and demonstrate continued U.S. support for Ukraine.
The Senate vote reflected broad support for tougher measures against Russia. It also came shortly after Graham's death in July, following his return from a visit to Ukraine.
Trump's position
Despite the Senate's overwhelming vote, the legislation faces several obstacles in the House, including concerns among Democrats about the powers it would grant Trump.
Some House Democrats fear the bill could provide the president with a new legal basis for imposing broad tariffs at a time when his existing tariff authority is facing legal challenges, according to a person familiar with the matter.
It also remains unclear whether Trump would use the authority against Russian energy buyers, particularly China, given trade tensions between Washington and Beijing.
Vlasiuk expressed similar doubts about whether the White House would ultimately implement the legislation if it were to become law.
"There is broad support within American society and the political establishment for increasing pressure on Russia and achieving peace," he said. "Does this mean the White House is immediately ready to take specific actions? I don't know."
"It does mean the relevant departments would be technically ready to propose appropriate solutions."
For Kyiv, however, the immediate focus is on getting the bill through the House before lawmakers leave Washington for the election campaign.
"We do not delve into the intricacies of U.S. domestic politics," Vlasiuk said. "We are the Ukrainian people, who need the support of the American people."
"The U.S. Congress could provide that support to the Ukrainian people."

Skater Kamila Valieva Loses Neutral Status
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:59:33 UTC
23:59:33 KST

Russian figure skater Kamila Valieva, who returned to competition in January after a long doping ban, has once again been barred from competing in international events after losing her status as a neutral athlete, the International Skating Union (ISU) said Thursday.
Valieva, who was at the center of a doping scandal that rocked the 2022 Winter Olympics in Beijing, is among 234 Russian and Belarusian athletes who applied for neutral athlete status, the sport's global governing body said in a statement.
Russian and Belarusian skaters were banned from international competition following the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, although they were authorized to take part in events in the 2026/2027 season on the condition that they compete under a neutral flag.
To be granted this neutral status, athletes must meet three criteria: they must not be members of the army or security services of Russia or Belarus, must not have taken part in the war waged in Ukraine, and must never have publicly supported the war against Ukraine.
Mark Kondratiuk, the 2022 European individual champion, also had his neutral status revoked.
The ISU said two other Russian skaters, Alexandra Stepanova and Ivan Bukin, do not meet the neutral status requirements. It did not specify which criteria Valieva had failed to meet, but the skater's social media pages contain posts supportive of Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Russian Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev said Thursday that the four skaters will challenge the decision at the Court of Arbitration for Sport in Lausanne.
"The Figure Skating Federation of Russia and our skaters, who have been unfairly deprived of the right to compete in international events under the auspices of the International Skating Union, will soon file a claim against the ISU with the CAS," Degtyarev said.
Valieva returned to competition in January, four years after the Olympic doping scandal that led to her lengthy suspension. She was a 15-year-old prodigy and became the first skater in history to land a quadruple jump at the Olympics, winning gold in the team event.
However, it later emerged during the Beijing Games that she had tested positive for the banned heart medication trimetazidine following the Russian championships in December 2021. Valieva claimed it was the result of accidental contamination.
After multiple appeals, she was suspended for four years dating back to December 25, 2021.

Bulgarian financier and reformer Krasimir Angarski dies aged 73
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:59:09 UTC
23:59:09 KST

News
OBITUARY
Bulgarian financier and reformer Krasimir Angarski dies aged 73
Thursday 10 September 2026 16:51
Thursday, 10 September 2026, 16:51
PHOTO BNR
Font size
Prominent Bulgarian financier Krasimir Angarski has died at the age of 73 after a brief illness, his family said, as reported by BNT.
Angarski was one of the architects of Bulgaria’s tax reforms in the early years of the democratic transition and later played a key role in the introduction of the currency board.
Born in Sofia on January 28, 1953, Angarski graduated from the University of National and World Economy. He joined the Ministry of Finance in 1980 and went on to head the tax administration for Sofia and Sofia Region. He was among the authors of Bulgaria’s tax-administration legislation.
In 1997, Angarski served as Minister without Portfolio in Stefan Sofiyanski’s caretaker government, where he headed the group drafting the legislation for the introduction of the currency board. Introduced that year following a severe financial and banking crisis and a period of hyperinflation, the system fixed the lev to the German mark, and later to the euro, while placing strict limits on the central bank’s ability to issue money.
He subsequently became Secretary for Economic Affairs to President Petar Stoyanov. He also taught at the University of National and World Economy and, from 2001 to 2004, served as Executive Director of DSK Bank.
Krasimir Angarski leaves behind a lasting contribution to the institutions and financial reforms that shaped Bulgaria’s economic transition.

NATO allies disrupt Russian exercise involving secret weapon targeting subsea cables, Reuters reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:58:27 UTC
23:58:27 KST

NATO allies disrupt Russian exercise involving secret weapon targeting subsea cables, Reuters reports
NATO allies disrupted a covert Russian naval exercise near Norway's Svalbard archipelago involving technology designed to disable critical subsea cables without leaving a trace, Reuters reported on Sept. 10, citing Western officials.
The operation was carried out by Russia's Main Directorate for Deep Sea Research (GUGI), which used deep-sea submersibles to simulate deploying the technology, according to two Western officials who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity.
Britain, Norway, and the United States tracked and confronted the Russian vessels at sea, preventing them from completing the exercise before they eventually left the area, the officials said.
No subsea cables were damaged during the operation. The exercise focused on simulating how the technology could be used in the event of a conflict with NATO, while officials declined to explain how the system works.
"Through our joint operation, we sent a clear message to Russia that they cannot operate covertly," Norwegian Defense Minister Tore Sandvik said in a statement to Reuters.
"We have made it unequivocally clear to Russian authorities that any attempt to target our critical infrastructure will be detected and met with consequences," he added.
The operation took place near Svalbard, where two roughly 1,400-kilometer-long (870 miles) fiber-optic cables connect the Arctic archipelago with mainland Norway. The cables carry satellite data from the SvalSat ground station, which is part of NASA's Near Space Network.
Undersea sabotage has climbed up the political agenda across Europe with instances of damage to subsea cables and Russian vessels lurking near critical underwater infrastructure on an increasingly frequent basis since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
In April 2026, the U.K. said it had intercepted a Russian operation near critical underwater infrastructure in British waters. A Russian attack submarine entered U.K. waters while other vessels linked to GUGI were detected conducting what the British government described as "nefarious activity" over critical undersea infrastructure.
Between 2024 and 2026, more than 20 subsea cables in the Baltic and Arctic regions were damaged, though many of the incidents have not been formally attributed to Russia.
NATO has since stepped up patrols and monitoring around critical underwater infrastructure, including through missions in the Baltic and High North.
Russia's Defense Ministry did not respond to Reuters' request for comment on the Svalbard operation.

DR Congo allocates $120M for victims of Uganda’s illicit occupation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:57:23 UTC
23:57:23 KST

James Tasamba
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
The Democratic Republic of Congo has allocated $120 million in reparations to the victims of Uganda's illegal occupation of parts of the country in the early 2000s, according to a statement on Thursday.
In the first phase, the government intends to spend $30 million to fund community infrastructure projects in each of the affected communities in four provinces: Tshopo, Ituri, Bas-Uele and Haut-Uele, said the statement by the Justice Ministry.
To be funded are health, education, water and socio-economic development projects.
“These funds will be used to support community projects aimed at honoring the memory of the victims and strengthening social cohesion,” it said.
Justice State Minister Guillaume Ngefa promised transparent management of the funds and consultation with the target communities.
“Reparation is a duty of justice and a responsibility of the State,” he said.
On individual compensation, the ministry said it would be considered in the second phase of the implementation, which will begin as soon as the audit and validation of the lists of eligible victims are finalized.
The development is in implementation of a 2022 judgment by the International Court of Justice, which ordered Uganda to pay $325 million in reparations to Congo for its role in the conflict in the eastern part of the country between 1998 and 2003.
The court ruled that Uganda had violated international law when its troops occupied parts of eastern Congo and supported other armed groups in the country.
The court ordered Uganda to pay the sum in five yearly installments of $65 million starting in September 2022.
A total of $260 million has already been paid by Uganda, according to the Congolese Justice Ministry.
